comments.text:
COMMENT FORM TEXT:
The July 31, 2026 OCC/FDIC CRA proposal, OCC-2026-0694, is very disappointing because it fails to address the central reason CRA modernization became necessary in the first place: the growth of digital and branchless banking since CRA’s last major reform in 1995.

CRA was enacted to combat redlining by encouraging banks to help meet the credit needs of the communities from which they gather deposits. Today, however, increasingly large amounts of deposits are gathered electronically from communities where banks maintain no physical branches. 

I estimate that roughly 10 percent of U.S. bank deposits, or approximately $2 trillion, are now gathered electronically outside traditional branch footprints. Yet, the current branch-based CRA framework, which is maintained in this most recent proposal, leaves those communities without a corresponding CRA reinvestment obligation.

I was fortunate to have the opportunity to know and work with Senator Proxmire, the "Father of CRA," and he always emphasized the importance of reinvesting deposits back into the communities from which they were sourced, which is why he called it the "Community REINVESTMENT Act."

The OCC itself previously recognized this problem. In its June 2020 CRA Final Rule under Comptroller Joseph Otting, the OCC expressly stated that the growth of internet banks and internet platforms for collecting deposits made deposit-based assessment areas increasingly relevant. 

That rule required certain banks receiving more than half of their retail domestic deposits outside their facility-based assessment areas to establish additional deposit-based assessment areas in geographic markets accounting for at least 5 percent of their retail domestic deposits. That 2020 CRA Final Rule was later rescinded, illustrating the unfortunate politicization of CRA across administrations.

Comptroller Otting’s approach reflected the principle behind what I have long called the "5% Deposit Reinvestment Rule:" a bank has a CRA reinvestment requirement in any area sourcing 5% or more of its deposits. 

The absence of a physical branch by branchless banks, including credit card, internet, fintech, and other banks with electronic delivery systems, should not make the communities sourcing those deposits invisible under CRA.

This is the modern form of the problem CRA was intended to address. Traditional redlining was tied to physical neighborhoods and branch networks. In the digital era, the comparable danger is what I have labeled "weblining," namely the ability of branchless banks to gather substantial deposits electronically from communities without a meaningful corresponding CRA responsibility to reinvest in those communities.

Weblining is most adversely impacting our biggest cities sourcing large amounts of deposits to branchless banks, like my home community of South Florida. There is no commensurate reinvestment requirement for the more than $100 billion of estimated deposits these branchless banks harvest from South Florida. Rather, the CRA benefits flow to the area surrounding the single home-office location of these branchless banks, most notably in Delaware, South Dakota, and Utah.

Comptroller Otting’s 2020 OCC rule demonstrated that this problem can be addressed in a targeted manner with deposit-based assessment area, without imposing nationwide CRA obligations on every bank or simply following lending wherever it occurs. 

Unfortunately, the July 31 proposal ignores this critical issue. By retaining a framework centered on physical facilities, the proposal misses an important opportunity to modernize CRA for the realities of digital banking.

CRA modernization should preserve Senator Proxmire’s fundamental principle in a modern banking system: follow the deposits. If 5% or more of a bank’s deposits come from a community, that community should not disappear from CRA simply because those deposits arrived through a computer or smartphone rather than through a branch door.

With all due respect, the OCC and FDIC should reconsider this serious omission and specifically request comment on a targeted deposit-based assessment-area framework, including a modern version of the 5% Deposit Reinvestment Rule previously reflected in the OCC’s 2020 CRA Final Rule.

Better yet, the prudential regulators, including the Fed, if and when it comes out with its own CRA reform package, should follow the KISS rule: maintain the current 1995 regs and update them with the 5% Deposit Reinvestment Rule and the best ideas from the rescinded 2023 CRA Final Rule, such as the list of qualified CD activities.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit this comment.

Kenneth H. Thomas, Ph.D.

FYI, full disclosure: I was the only individual to submit an Amicus Brief opposing the 2023 CRA Final Rule in the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit in Texas Bankers Association, et al. v. Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, et al., No. 24-10367.

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
(Docket ID OCC-2026-0694, RIN 1557-AF57; FDIC RIN 3064-AG31)
Dear Sir or Madam,
The San Joaquin Valley Housing Collaborative appreciates the opportunity to comment on the
proposed amendments to the agencies' Community Reinvestment Act regulations published in
the Federal Register on August 12, 2026. The Collaborative is a regional nonprofit serving the
eight counties of California's San Joaquin Valley. Our members include affordable housing
developers, local governments, lenders, and community organizations working together to
expand the supply of safe, affordable homes in one of the most housing-burdened regions in the
country.
Some context on our region may be helpful. The San Joaquin Valley is home to more than four
million people and produces much of the nation's food, yet it has some of the lowest household
incomes and highest poverty rates in California. Large philanthropic institutions are scarce here.
Bank participation motivated by CRA is not a supplement to other capital in our region. In many
cases it is the capital. That is why we are writing about two elements of the proposal that would,
in our experience, pull investment and support away from the very communities the statute
directs banks to serve.
First, we are concerned about the proposal to reclassify banks with assets between $1.65 billion
and $10 billion as intermediate banks no longer subject to the investment test. The Low-Income
Housing Tax Credit is the primary tool for building affordable homes in our region, and the
banks that invest in Valley LIHTC projects are disproportionately mid-size and regional
institutions in this asset range. The investment test is a meaningful part of why they do. If these
banks can receive the same CRA consideration for ordinary market-rate lending, many will have
little reason to continue purchasing housing credits. Fewer investors mean weaker equity
 pricing, and weaker pricing means fewer homes built per credit dollar. Our region already sees
thinner LIHTC pricing than coastal markets, so we would feel this change first and hardest. We
ask the agencies to retain a community development investment component for banks above the
current large bank threshold, or at minimum to structure the intermediate bank evaluation so
that LIHTC and other community development investments receive distinct, meaningful
recognition rather than being blended into general lending performance.
Second, we are concerned about the proposed treatment of community development grants.
Limiting consideration to grants directly used for a specific plan, project, or initiative, and
requiring banks with assets over $10 billion to document that grantees hold overhead costs to 15
percent or less, would sharply curtail bank support for organizations like ours and for the
housing counselors, CDFIs, and community-based nonprofits we work alongside. General
operating support is often the most valuable grant a community organization can receive,
because it funds the staff who put projects together in the first place. The 15 percent overhead
figure has no basis in how effective nonprofits actually operate, and it penalizes small rural
organizations that run lean but cannot spread fixed costs across a large budget. In practice, we
expect the documentation burden would lead many banks to simply stop making grants rather
than police their grantees' cost structures. We ask the agencies to withdraw the overhead
documentation requirement and to preserve CRA consideration for grants, including operating
support, made to organizations whose work has a community development purpose.
We recognize and support the agencies' goals of clarity, continuity, and reduced burden for
community banks. But these two provisions would not reduce burden on communities. They
would reduce investment in them. We would welcome the chance to discuss our experience in
the San Joaquin Valley with agency staff, and we thank you for considering these comments.
Sincerely,
Miguel Arambula
Executive Director
San Joaquin Valley Housing Collaborative

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations RIN 3064-AG31 / Docket ID OCC-
2026- 0694

To Whom It May Concern,
On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the Community
Reinvestment Act.
OFN is the nation's leading network and intermediary focused on community development
investment, managing over $1 billion in total assets and a membership of more than 500
community development financial institutions (CDFIs). OFN's membership includes community
development loan funds, credit unions, banks, and venture capital funds, many of whom
partner with banks who are motivated by the CRA to invest in low- and moderate-income
(LMI) communities.
Since its founding in 1986, OFN members have originated $136 billion in financing, helping to
create or maintain more than 3.8 million jobs, start or expand more than 1.2 million
businesses and microenterprises, and support the development or rehabilitation of nearly 3
million housing units and more than 16,000 community facility projects in rural, urban, and
Native communities across the United States. With cumulative net charge-off rates near one
percent, OFN members lend prudently and productively in the LMI communities.
The Notice of Proposed Rulemaking spans over four hundred pages and proposes significant
changes to the CRA framework with far-reaching implications for banks, community
development partners, and the low- and moderate-income communities they serve. In
addition, the review period covers the final month of Summer when significant portions of
Washington D.C.-based policy organizations are short staffed due to summer vacations ahead
of back-to-school obligations. Given these factors, the proposed 60-day comment period
at this time, and for a regulation of this complexity, does not provide sufficient time
for stakeholders to fully analyze, assess, and understand a rulemaking of this
magnitude. While the agencies have spent considerable time developing the proposal,
regulated institutions and community stakeholders require adequate time to evaluate its

Page 3

operational, economic, and community impacts, consult with internal and external experts, and
develop meaningful, evidence-based feedback.
Previous major CRA rulemakings have provided 90 days for public comment. For instance, in
2022, when the federal banking regulators jointly proposed substantial changes to the CRA
regulations, they provided a 90-day comment period. A rulemaking of this scope with a 60-
day comment period would be insufficient to meaningfully evaluate the proposal, consult
affected parties, and develop data-driven recommendations. For organizations like ours and
the CDFIs we represent, a meaningful review also requires engaging with members nationwide
to understand how the proposal would affect institutions of varying sizes, business models,
and markets. Providing additional time for this analysis will ultimately result in comments that
are more substantive, data-driven, and useful to the agencies as they consider a final rule.
Accordingly, we respectfully urge the agencies to extend the comment period by at
least 30 days. An extension would encourage broader participation from banks, community
organizations, CDFIs, and other stakeholders, leading to a more complete administrative
record and a more informed final regulation.
The CRA is one of the nation's most consequential community development statutes, shaping
billions of dollars in lending, investment, and services that support low- and moderate-income
communities. Changes to its implementing regulations warrant careful deliberation and
meaningful stakeholder engagement. Experience has shown that complex regulatory overhauls
developed under compressed timelines are more likely to require subsequent revisions,
clarification, or litigation. Allowing additional time for public input will help ensure that any
modernization of the CRA framework is thoughtful, durable, and effective for both regulated
institutions and the communities the Act was designed to serve.
Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Sincerely,
Dafina Williams
EVP, Chief Policy Officer and Head of Government Affairs
Opportunity Finance Network

To the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation:
For Small Business Only LLC strongly supports the agencies' proposed amendments to the Community
Reinvestment Act regulations. The proposal appropriately returns the focus of CRA administration to
demonstrable community credit needs, direct local benefit, transparent use of grant funds, and clear
standards for banks and community organizations.
For Small Business Only LLC (FSBO) is a Virginia limited liability company and a technical-assistance and
capital-readiness intermediary working with nonprofit organizations and financial institutions to prepare
small businesses to become bankable, creditworthy, and lender-ready. FSBO develops and delivers
business-credit, cash-flow, compliance, financial-literacy, and capital-readiness programming. Our
operating premise is straightforward: access to capital improves when businesses receive disciplined
technical assistance before they apply for financing.
Strong support for capital-readiness technical assistance
FSBO particularly supports the proposed economic-development category covering technical assistance
and support services for qualifying small businesses and farms. The proposal recognizes an operational
fact seen across community-development ecosystems: many viable small businesses are not yet
prepared to obtain traditional bank financing and require structured assistance before they can present
an underwriter-ready application.
This clarification should be retained in the final rule. Capital-readiness assistance can improve
compliance, financial records, cash-flow management, credit profiles, loan documentation, and
understanding of lender requirements. These activities reduce preventable application failures and
create a more qualified pipeline for responsible lenders. They advance CRA's objective more directly
 CRA Comment | For Small Business Only LLC
For Small Business Only LLC | Page 2
than programming that promotes access without preparing applicants to use credit safely and
successfully.
Strong support for direct community-development grants
FSBO also strongly supports the proposal's express recognition that a grant or donation to a local
nonprofit providing small-business technical assistance or financial-literacy programming may receive
CRA consideration. This language gives banks greater confidence to support organizations that directly
serve communities and gives nonprofit recipients a clearer standard around which to design programs,
budgets, records, and outcomes.
We likewise support requiring a direct connection between grant funds, qualifying activities, and the
bank's assessment area. The written commitment, program budget, geographic evidence, and closeout
documentation contemplated by the proposal will help distinguish direct service from pass-through
arrangements in which excessive administrative layers reduce the resources reaching businesses and
residents.
Strong support for the 15% indirect-cost guardrail
FSBO supports the proposed 15% indirect-cost limit for community-development grants made by large
banks. A clear ceiling protects community benefit, disciplines program design, and permits reasonable
recovery of necessary operating expenses. The use of the Uniform Guidance framework or a comparable
standard also gives recipients a recognizable method for classifying costs.
The final rule should preserve this guardrail. To improve consistent implementation without weakening
the standard, FSBO respectfully requests that the agencies clarify the following points in final regulatory
text, official commentary, or implementation guidance:
•
New nonprofit documentation. A newly formed nonprofit that has not yet filed an IRS Form 990
should be permitted to substantiate compliance through its current operating budget, program
budget, board-approved cost-allocation policy, recent financial statements, formation
documents, and written attestation.
•
Specialized curriculum and intellectual property. A reasonable, documented, arm's-length
license fee for curriculum actually used to deliver the funded program should be treated as a
direct program cost when the license is necessary to provide the qualifying service, separately
stated, properly approved, and supported by a written agreement.
•
Outcome measurement and required reporting. Costs incurred to collect eligibility, assessment-
area, service-delivery, and outcome evidence required by the bank or agencies should be
treated as direct costs when they are allocable to the funded program.
•
Related-party safeguards. Where a nonprofit licenses curriculum or purchases services from an
affiliated entity, the agencies should recognize the cost if the relationship is disclosed, the
interested director or officer recuses, the governing body determines the terms are fair and
reasonable, and the recipient maintains documentation supporting the programmatic necessity
and value.
 CRA Comment | For Small Business Only LLC
For Small Business Only LLC | Page 3
•
Comparable standards. The final rule should confirm that a recipient may use a consistently
applied cost-allocation methodology comparable to 2 CFR part 200 even when the recipient is
not a federal grantee.
Financial literacy and workforce development
FSBO supports the continued treatment of financial-literacy and workforce-development activities as
community development when they serve low- or moderate-income individuals and families. Financial
capability affects employment stability, household resilience, responsible credit use, and the ability to
retain income gains from workforce participation. The proposal appropriately preserves these activities
while improving categorical clarity.
Recommended final-rule implementation
The agencies can strengthen implementation by encouraging banks and recipients to use a standardized
but scalable evidence package. At minimum, that package should identify the qualifying purpose,
assessment-area nexus, eligible population or business size, approved budget, direct and indirect costs,
service outputs, outcomes, and budget-to-actual reconciliation. Smaller organizations should not be
required to create costly systems disproportionate to the grant, but every recipient should be capable of
demonstrating where the funds went and whom they benefited.
The final rule should also continue to make clear that technical assistance does not require or guarantee
a subsequent loan. The value of capital-readiness programming lies in improving the quality of the
applicant, the completeness of the documentation, and the appropriateness of the financing request.
Individual lending decisions must remain with lenders applying safe and sound underwriting standards.
Conclusion
For Small Business Only LLC strongly supports the proposed rule because it recognizes that community
credit needs are not met by capital alone. Communities also need local organizations capable of
preparing residents and small businesses to understand, qualify for, obtain, and responsibly use financial
products. The proposal's recognition of technical assistance, financial literacy, direct nonprofit grants,
assessment-area benefit, and transparent indirect-cost limits provides a sound framework for
accountable bank-community partnerships.
We urge the OCC and FDIC to adopt the proposal with the limited implementation clarifications
described above. Those clarifications would preserve the proposal's guardrails while enabling newly
formed and specialized nonprofit providers to demonstrate compliance through reliable, proportionate
documentation.
Respectfully submitted,
Sandy E. Day, MSL, PA, CFEI®
Managing Director
For Small Business Only LLC | FSBOnly.com | seday@fsbonly.com

comments.text:
COMMENT FORM TEXT:
I urge the OCC and FDIC to clarify that CRA consideration should support community development financing that creates durable, place based economic opportunity and reduces household vulnerability in low and moderate income neighborhoods, designated disaster areas, and distressed or underserved rural communities.

Communities across Missouri, the St. Louis region, and southern Illinois face overlapping challenges: repeated disaster exposure, high household energy burdens, aging housing and commercial buildings, limited access to patient capital, and the loss of locally rooted businesses. CRA policy should recognize financing that addresses these interconnected needs.

The agencies should expressly clarify that qualifying community development activities can include financing for locally rooted brick and mortar businesses; small business facilities; workforce oriented AI, robotics, advanced manufacturing, research, laboratory, repair, and fabrication spaces; and related equipment and technical assistance, when those activities primarily promote economic development for small businesses, create accessible jobs for low  and moderate income people, or revitalize and stabilize eligible geographies.

The agencies should also recognize financing for affordable housing and community facility improvements that reduce utility costs and improve resilience, including weatherization, efficient electrification, solar, battery storage, geothermal systems, resilient microgrids, flood resilient construction, and other high performance building measures. These investments can preserve affordability by reducing ongoing operating and household energy costs, not merely initial construction costs.

CRA consideration for technology intensive projects should be tied to measurable community benefit. Relevant evidence should include local hiring; quality jobs and apprenticeships; contracts with local and minority , women, and veteran owned businesses; affordable access to facilities or services; documented energy and water impacts; utility bill savings; and long term benefits to eligible communities. CRA should not reward projects whose benefits bypass local residents or whose energy and infrastructure demands worsen affordability.

Finally, the agencies should provide clear recognition for regional partnerships that serve connected rural and metropolitan markets. Banks in the St. Louis metropolitan area and banks serving southern Illinois and rural Missouri should be encouraged to collaborate on projects that demonstrably benefit their assessment areas or broader regional areas that include them.

Clear standards for these activities would help banks direct capital toward businesses and infrastructure that remain in communities, reduce household costs, increase resilience, and build a stronger local economic base.

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
The National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) and Rise Economy are submitting a joint letter (attached) requesting an extension of the comment period for the newly proposed Community Reinvestment Act rule.

We believe that the significant changes suggested by the proposal necessitate a comment period of at least one hundred and twenty (120) days. 

This letter has been endorsed and signed by over 370 community partners and organizations.

Re: Community groups request an extension of the CRA comment period
RIN 3064-AG31, Docket ID OCC-2026-0694

Dear Chair Hill and Comptroller Gould,

The National Community Reinvestment Coalition, Rise Economy, and 374
community groups and national partners formally request the OCC and FDIC
extend the sixty (60) day comment period relating to the recently proposed
changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. We believe that
the significant changes suggested by the proposal necessitate a comment
period of at least one hundred and twenty (120) days.

The 60-day comment period is not sufficient for effective examination of and
comment on the over 350 pages of material and over 60 questions posed in
this complex proposed rule. It proposes to reclassify over 1200 banks and
we are concerned that many of the numerous proposed changes, if finalized
in substantially the same form, would lead to considerably less reinvestment
in the low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities meant to be served by
the CRA. More specifically, we are concerned that proposed changes will lead
to significant outcomes, including: less support for affordable housing via
the Low Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) and other community
1

 ​
​
​
​
​
​




development activity, less transparency of small business lending, fewer
community development loans and investments that support small
businesses, fewer branches in LMI and rural communities, less access to
affordable bank accounts and higher fees for unbanked and underbanked
consumers, less capacity for community based organizations to play their
critical role in supporting communities and the financial service ecosystem,
and less scrutiny of redlining and discrimination by banks.

The NPRM does not appear to clearly quantify or address the costs to, and
impacts on, communities of the various changes proposed. This lack of
analysis of community impacts makes it difficult for the public to comment
meaningfully on the proposal and puts the burden on communities to
identify and quantify the proposal's impacts. More time is needed to conduct
research and analysis to understand what the agencies' proposed changes to
the Community Reinvestment Act will actually mean for communities,
including Native American and Tribal communities.

We note that in 2020, when the FDIC and the OCC similarly proposed a new
CRA rule, the agencies agreed to extend the comment period.1

For these reasons, the undersigned community organizations urge the FDIC
and the OCC to extend the comment period on this proposal to one-hundred
twenty (120) days in total.

August 27, 2026


Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
Department of the Treasury, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)

Submitted to the OCC
Docket ID "OCC-2026-0694-0001"
via regulations.gov

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations – Joint Notice of Proposed Rulemaking

Dear Sir/Madam:

The National Association of Development Companies (NADCO) submits these comments
in response to the joint Notice of Proposed Rulemaking and request for comment from the
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and Department of the Treasury, Office of
the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC).

NADCO represents over 190 Certified Development Companies (CDCs) and their industry
partners that deliver the Small Business Administration (SBA) Development Company
Program, commonly known as the 504 Loan Program (and referred to as the "SBDC"
program in the proposed rule). Since 1986, CDCs have provided over 224,000 small
businesses with $146 billion in Section 504 financing, representing a total capital
investment of over $418 billion and creating or retaining over 3.4 million jobs in local
communities throughout the United States.

The SBA Development Company Program is authorized by Section 501(a) of the Small
Business Investment Act of 1958, P.L. 85-699, as amended, which states: "The Congress
hereby finds and declares that the purpose of this title is to foster economic development
and to create or preserve job opportunities in both urban and rural areas by providing long-
term financing for small business concerns through the development company program
authorized by this title."

The 504 Loan Program advances this congressionally established economic development
mission through a public-private partnership. In a typical 504 financing, a private-sector
lending institution provides a first mortgage loan in conjunction with financing provided
through a CDC and backed by an SBA-guaranteed debenture. This structure enables small
businesses to obtain long-term financing for major fixed assets, including land, buildings,
machinery, and equipment, while leveraging private-sector capital to support economic
development and job creation in communities throughout the country.
 Page 2 of 3


Proposed Economic Development Definition
NADCO strongly supports the agencies' proposed revisions to the definition of "economic
development." In particular, NADCO supports the proposed third category of economic
development, which would include "Federal, State, local, or Tribal government programs,
projects, or initiatives that serve small businesses or small farms, as defined by those
programs."

NADCO particularly supports the agencies' specific identification of the SBA Development
Company Program as an example of a federal program meeting this economic
development category. The 504 Loan Program is a congressionally established economic
development program specifically designed to foster economic development and create or
preserve employment opportunities through long-term financing for small businesses.

As the agencies recognize in the proposed rule, expressly identifying these government
programs will provide greater clarity and encourage continued participation in and support
of programs providing small business and small farm financing. The agencies further
recognize that aligning CRA economic development activities with government programs
addressing identified small business needs can encourage coordination among banks,
government agencies, and other program participants. NADCO strongly agrees with this
approach.

This clarification is particularly appropriate for the 504 Loan Program because the program
is built upon precisely this type of public-private coordination. Bank lending partners are
integral to 504 financing, providing private-sector capital alongside CDC/SBA financing to
support small-business investment and economic development. Greater certainty
regarding CRA consideration for qualifying 504-related lending can encourage continued
bank participation in the program and expand access to long-term capital for small
businesses in communities throughout the country.

Elimination of the Purpose Test
NADCO also supports the agencies' proposal to eliminate the existing "purpose test"
applicable to economic development activities. Under current guidance, an otherwise
qualifying small-business activity must satisfy additional requirements related to job
creation, retention, or improvement for low- or moderate-income individuals or in
qualifying geographic areas.

The proposed approach would instead establish more objective criteria for determining
whether an activity qualifies as economic development. As the agencies explain, banks
would no longer need to demonstrate, for example, low- or moderate-income job creation
for a qualifying small-business loan and could instead demonstrate that the activity or
government program through which the activity was made is identified as economic
development under the regulation.

 Page 3 of 3

For the SBA 504 Loan Program, this approach appropriately recognizes the economic
development purpose of a federal program specifically established by Congress to foster
economic development and create or preserve employment opportunities, while providing
greater certainty for participating banks.

Response to Question 26
In response to Question 26, NADCO strongly supports retaining the SBA Development
Company Program in the non-exhaustive list of Federal, State, local, or Tribal government
programs, projects, or initiatives included in the proposed definition of economic
development.

Explicit recognition of the SBA Development Company Program will provide greater
regulatory certainty to bank lending partners, encourage continued bank participation in
the 504 Loan Program, and help expand access to long-term capital for small businesses
throughout the United States. It also appropriately recognizes the role of CDCs and their
bank lending partners in carrying out a congressionally established federal economic
development program.

NADCO therefore urges the agencies to adopt the proposed revisions to the economic
development provisions and retain the specific reference to the SBA Development
Company Program in the final rule.

NADCO appreciates the opportunity to provide these comments and the agencies'
recognition of the important role the SBA Development Company Program, Certified
Development Companies, and their bank lending partners play in supporting economic
development in communities throughout the United States.

Sincerely,


Wayne Williams
Executive Vice President
Regulatory Affairs & Training

comments.text:
COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Individually, I support the OCC and FDIC's proposed rule, particularly its express recognition of the SBA Development Company Program as a qualifying federal economic development program. Greater CRA certainty for bank loans made with Certified Development Companies (CDCs) under the 504 Loan Program is welcome. At the same time, the final rule should ensure this recognition continues to reflect the LMI and underserved-community focus that gives CRA's community development framework its purpose.

My CDC serves Missouri (urban and rural) and the St. Louis Metro area of Illinois, including lending in distressed rural counties in the Bootheel, Central and Northern Missouri and LMI metro neighborhoods including Jefferson City, Cape Girardo, St. Louis County/City and the Metro East in Illinois. I’ve also worked in conventional business and commercial banking in the same area. This experience informs my general view on finalizing the economic-development category.

CRA credit should recognize economic-development activities because they direct private bank capital toward underserved people and places, not merely because an activity fits within a government program. Any final rule should:

1. Preserve the connection between the economic-development category and underserved communities. The proposed elimination of the current purpose test removes the requirement that a qualifying small business loan create, improve, or retain jobs for LMI individuals or areas. Recognition of the SBA Development Company Program (see proposed rule at 76) should reflect not only its status as a federal program, but its demonstrated role in expanding capital access in underserved communities.

2. Recognize 504 lending as a proven tool for reaching underserved businesses. Our lending in Missouri's distressed rural counties and LMI metro neighborhoods illustrates how the 504 program channels capital where conventional financing often falls short. CRA should recognize this structure, including both interim financing and the Third Party Loan, as directly advancing community-development objectives.

3. Avoid a system where underserved communities become incidental rather than central beneficiaries. If any qualifying small-business loan can receive economic-development consideration regardless of LMI status, banks have less incentive to direct capital where credit needs are greatest. The final rule should expressly tie CRA recognition of the 504 program to its role in expanding economic opportunity for those underserved by conventional credit markets.

504 loans should receive CRA credit because Congress created both CRA and the 504 program to close gaps in private credit markets. Based on our direct experience serving distressed and LMI communities across Missouri and the St. Louis region, we urge the agencies to finalize a rule that provides regulatory certainty while preserving the 504/CDC model's measurable community impact.

preserve job opportunities in both urban and rural areas by providing long-term financing for
small business concerns through the development company program authorized by this title."
The 504 Loan Program advances this congressionally established economic development
mission through a public-private partnership. In a typical 504 financing, a private-sector lending
institution provides a first mortgage loan in conjunction with financing provided through a CDC
and backed by an SBA-guaranteed debenture. This structure enables small businesses to obtain
long-term financing for major fixed assets, including land, buildings, machinery, and equipment,
while leveraging private-sector capital to support economic development and job creation in
communities throughout the country.

Proposed Economic Development Definition
Alloy Development strongly supports the agencies' proposed revisions to the definition of
"economic development." In particular, Alloy supports the proposed third category of economic
development, which would include "Federal, State, local, or Tribal government programs,
projects, or initiatives that serve small businesses or small farms, as defined by those
programs."
Alloy particularly supports the agencies' specific identification of the SBA Development
Company Program as an example of a federal program meeting this economic development
category. The 504 Loan Program is a congressionally established economic development
program specifically designed to foster economic development and create or preserve
employment opportunities through long-term financing for small businesses.
As the agencies recognize in the proposed rule, expressly identifying these government
programs will provide greater clarity and encourage continued participation in and support of
programs providing small business and small farm financing. The agencies further recognize
that aligning CRA economic development activities with government programs addressing
identified small business needs can encourage coordination among banks, government
agencies, and other program participants. Alloy Development strongly agrees with this
approach.
This clarification is particularly appropriate for the 504 Loan Program because the program is
built upon precisely this type of public-private coordination. Bank lending partners are integral
to 504 financing, providing private-sector capital alongside CDC/SBA financing to support small-
business investment and economic development. Greater certainty regarding CRA
consideration for qualifying 504-related lending can encourage continued bank participation in
the program and expand access to long-term capital for small businesses in communities
throughout the country.
Elimination of the Purpose Test
Alloy Development also supports the agencies' proposal to eliminate the existing "purpose test"
applicable to economic development activities. Under current guidance, an otherwise qualifying
small-business activity must satisfy additional requirements related to job creation, retention,
or improvement for low- or moderate-income individuals or in qualifying geographic areas.
The proposed approach would instead establish more objective criteria for determining
whether an activity qualifies as economic development. As the agencies explain, banks would
no longer need to demonstrate, for example, low- or moderate-income job creation for a
qualifying small-business loan and could instead demonstrate that the activity or government
program through which the activity was made is identified as economic development under the
regulation.
 Page 3 of 3
For the SBA 504 Loan Program, this approach appropriately recognizes the economic
development purpose of a federal program specifically established by Congress to foster
economic development and create or preserve employment opportunities, while providing
greater certainty for participating banks.
Response to Question 26
In response to Question 26, Alloy Development strongly supports retaining the SBA
Development Company Program in the non-exhaustive list of Federal, State, local, or Tribal
government programs, projects, or initiatives included in the proposed definition of economic
development.
Explicit recognition of the SBA Development Company Program will provide greater regulatory
certainty to bank lending partners, encourage continued bank participation in the 504 Loan
Program, and help expand access to long-term capital for small businesses throughout the
United States. It also appropriately recognizes the role of CDCs and their bank lending partners
in carrying out a congressionally established federal economic development program.
Alloy Development therefore urges the agencies to adopt the proposed revisions to the
economic development provisions and retain the specific reference to the SBA Development
Company Program in the final rule.
Alloy Development appreciates the opportunity to provide these comments and the agencies'
recognition of the important role the SBA Development Company Program, Certified
Development Companies, and their bank lending partners play in supporting economic
development in communities throughout the United States.

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
I am a small-business owner and community economic-development advocate in Westchester County. I have seen firsthand that resources existing does not mean communities can easily access them.
I support accountability, but I am concerned that reduced CRA reporting requirements and the proposed 15% indirect-cost standard could create additional barriers for smaller community-based organizations.
I urge the OCC and FDIC to protect transparency and ensure CRA opportunities remain accessible to the communities they are intended to serve. Access should not depend on who you know.

Executive Summary
VeloxVFX LLC respectfully supports the agencies' effort to refocus CRA implementation on
community credit needs, improve clarity, ensure that community-development grants reach their
intended communities, and modernize data and public access.
The proposal's most consequential opportunity is to connect institutional CRA consideration to a
reviewable record of demonstrable community benefit without converting banks into government
benefit authorities or altering safe-and-sound underwriting.
The agencies should distinguish institutional activity from completed public benefit. A loan, grant,
investment, service, website, referral, or program relationship may be CRA-relevant, but the
evaluation framework should be capable of showing, proportionately, the qualifying purpose,
intended population or geography, amount or service committed, amount or service delivered,
material returns or reversals, and a reasonable outcome measure. Complexity and transaction size
should not substitute for beneficiary reach or verified delivery.
Consumer access should also be visible. Where a bank provides or supports a housing-resource,
neutral, and consent-based. Any program matching should communicate potential relevance rather
than final eligibility. Government agencies and authorized program administrators must retain
benefit-eligibility authority, and banks must retain independent underwriting and credit decisions.
Where legally permitted and affirmatively authorized by the consumer, verified information may
support a neutral referral to separately authorized housing, counseling, rental-stability, utility-
assistance, or other community resources. A mortgage denial should not itself establish eligibility for
counseling, or community-assistance pathway, the access point should be prominent, accessible,

systems may satisfy these objectives; no particular technology platform is requested.
Principal Recommendations
Related Public-Record Continuity
This joint CRA comment is legally distinct from VeloxVFX LLC's prior FDIC and OCC submissions, including
FDIC RIN 3064-AG32 and OCC-2026-0529. Those records may reflect related themes concerning attributable
public benefit, institutional responsibility, reviewable lifecycle states, and preserved governmental authority,
but they do not answer, replace, merge with, or incorporate this AG31 proceeding by reference. This filing
responds independently to the questions presented in OCC-2026-0694 / FDIC RIN 3064-AG31.
Commenter Perspective and Institutional Boundaries
VeloxVFX LLC is an architecture-oriented technology and intellectual-property company. It is not a
bank, Federal financial supervisory agency, public housing agency, mortgage lender, housing
counselor, benefit administrator, settlement provider, custodian, money transmitter, accounting
standard setter, or provider of legal, accounting, credit, or housing advice.
These comments address informational structure, lifecycle separation, accountability, consumer
access, and public-facing clarity. They do not ask the OCC or FDIC to adopt, endorse, procure, license,
validate, implement, or rely upon any VeloxVFX system or intellectual property. They do not
•
Connect CRA consideration to attributable activity and outcome records while distinguishing bank
capital, public funding, guarantees, grants, and other sources.
•
Preserve grant guardrails and add recipient, use, geography, beneficiary, disbursement, indirect-cost,
amendment, return, and outcome fields.
•
Distinguish institutional activity from completed community benefit; complexity, transaction size,
advertising, or portal availability should not substitute for evidence of beneficiary reach or delivery.
•
Recognize accessible, neutral, consent-based consumer discovery and referral infrastructure where it
demonstrably improves access to qualifying community resources.
•
Keep potential program matching, governmental eligibility, lender underwriting, and completed benefit
delivery as separate states.
•
Permit consumer continuity after an unmet credit request through voluntary referral to separately
authorized resources, without guaranteeing eligibility or funding.
•
Use annual records and evaluation-period outcomes together; late-period activity should not erase
earlier gaps.
•
Publish accessible maps, strategic plans, comment-response records, CRA files, and machine-readable
data with meaningful non-digital alternatives.

Responses to Questions 1-63
Each agency question is reproduced in substance from the proposal and followed by VeloxVFX LLC's direct
response. The official notice controls if any typographical difference exists.
Response to Question 1
Question 1: To better align with agency policies that establish an asset size of less than $30 billion as a
threshold for certain supervisory approaches, such as being considered a community bank or being
subject to the continuous examination process, should the agencies consider adjusting the intermediate
bank asset size threshold to include all banks with an asset size of less than $30 billion that do not
qualify as small banks? If the agencies establish $30 billion as the appropriate threshold to delineate
between intermediate banks and large banks, should the agencies also adopt a larger threshold for
small banks, such as the $10 billion currently proposed as the intermediate bank threshold?
VeloxVFX does not possess representative examination, operating-cost, or market data sufficient to
recommend a $10 billion or $30 billion boundary. The agencies should select the threshold using
loss of data visibility created by reclassification. Supervisory labels used for other purposes should
not automatically control CRA categories. Whatever threshold is selected, institutions whose scale or
geographic reach can materially affect multiple communities should preserve proportionate,
Response to Question 2
Question 2: Should the agencies clarify in the rules that designation as a wholesale or limited purpose
bank or election of a strategic plan does not override the bank's asset-based definition (e.g., a bank can
be both a large bank and a wholesale bank)?
Yes. Asset category, business-model designation, and evaluation method should remain separate
attributes. The final rule should state that selecting a strategic plan or receiving a wholesale or
limited-purpose designation does not erase the bank's independently determined asset classification
or the data obligations attached to it.
Response to Question 3
Question 3: Should the final rules include a definition for 'assets' to be used in setting asset size
thresholds and assessing a bank's position relative to these thresholds? For example, should the
agencies define 'assets' to mean a bank's total assets as reported in Schedule RC of the Consolidated
Reports of Condition and Income (Call Report), or Schedule RAL for U.S. branches and agencies of
foreign banks, as applicable?
Yes. Use total assets reported on the applicable Call Report or Schedule RAL, with a stated
measurement date, averaging convention, treatment of mergers and conversions, and correction
procedure. A common source record will reduce interpretive disputes and preserve consistent year-
to-year classification.
evidence about supervisory burden, community-development activity, geographic reach, and the
machine-readable community-development records.
 VELOXVFX LLC | OCC-2026-0694 | RIN 1557-AF57 | FDIC RIN 3064-AG31
VeloxVFX LLC - Independent informational architecture; agency and institutional authority remain external | Page 4
Response to Question 4
Question 4: With respect to Option 1 for the major product line standard, should the agencies specify a
de minimis amount of lending that would not count as making loans in a product line? For example,
should the agencies consider whether a bank did not make 30 loans in the product line overall or 30
loans in the product line in any assessment area? Should the agencies use the proposed definition of
'incidental basis' to find that a bank does not make loans in a product line if it only makes loans in that
product line on an incidental basis?
Response to Question 5
Question 5: Should the agencies consider consumer lending (a) by type of consumer loans, rather than in
the aggregate, when consumer loans constitute a major product line; (b) when consumer loans account
for less than a majority of retail lending but are one of a bank's largest two product lines, and permit
optional consideration in that circumstance; and (c) at the bank's request regardless of whether
consumer loans constitute a major product line?
Yes to product-level treatment. Aggregation can hide materially different pricing, access, and
borrower-distribution results across motor-vehicle, credit-card, secured, and unsecured lending. The
agencies should evaluate a consumer product when it is a major line or one of the bank's two largest
retail lines, and may permit voluntary evaluation when the election is made before the period and
applied consistently; optional inclusion should not be used selectively to omit unfavorable results.
Response to Question 6
Question 6: Should the agencies rely on dollar volume, loan count, or both to determine a bank's major
product line(s), and, if so, should the agencies do so consistent with the methodology in proposed
appendix C?
Use both count and dollar volume. Count reflects customer reach, while dollars reflect capital
deployment and concentration. The appendix C methodology is an appropriate common baseline if
it preserves both measures, explains tie-breaking and averaging, and does not allow a high-dollar,
low-count portfolio or a high-count, low-dollar portfolio to disappear.
Response to Question 7
Question 7: If the agencies adopt Option 1, should the agencies determine a bank's major product lines
by assessment area, as opposed to at the institution level as proposed?
Use an institution-level determination with assessment-area overlays. Institution-level classification
prevents fragmentation, while assessment-area results reveal local importance and underserved
markets. A product that falls below the institution-wide threshold should still be reviewed where it
is locally material or central to identified community credit needs.
Use a de minimis threshold as a transparent screening rule, not an erasure of the underlying record.
Activity below the threshold need not enter the major-product-line denominator or require continuous
examiner tracking; it should remain available through ordinary bank records for later pattern or
materiality review. VeloxVFX does not possess representative portfolio data sufficient to endorse 30 loans
as a universal threshold. The agencies should test any threshold across institution size, assessment-area
size, product type, dollar volume, and recurring activity. 'Incidental' activity should be defined by objective
count, amount, duration, and business-strategy evidence so repeated lending cannot be excluded merely
through labeling.
 VELOXVFX LLC | OCC-2026-0694 | RIN 1557-AF57 | FDIC RIN 3064-AG31
VeloxVFX LLC - Independent informational architecture; agency and institutional authority remain external | Page 5
Response to Question 8
Question 8: Does annual or evaluation-period-based consideration better serve the goal of encouraging
banks to meet the credit needs of their communities?
Evaluation-period treatment is preferable for rating stability, but it should be supported by annual
records. Annual snapshots reveal delay, concentration, and reversals; the full evaluation period
reveals durable performance. The final evaluation should not permit a late surge of activity to erase
earlier years of inadequate service without explanation.
Response to Question 9
Question 9: Are there alternative standards the agencies should consider in limiting indirect costs for
community-development grants? Do the proposed guardrails do enough to ensure that the majority of
grant and donation funds go directly toward benefiting the bank's assessment area(s)?
Response to Question 10
Question 10: As an alternative, should the agencies eliminate all grants and donations from CRA
consideration?
No. Grants can support counseling, housing stability, capacity building, and services that
conventional lending does not finance. Elimination would remove useful tools; stronger traceability
and outcome evidence are the better response to concerns about indirect costs and weak public
benefit.
Response to Question 11
Question 11: Should the agencies provide guidance regarding how primary purpose would be
determined for each community-development purpose in the definition of 'community development'?
Yes. For each category, guidance should identify the qualifying population or geography, the
activity's expressed purpose, expected benefit, allocation method for mixed-purpose activities,
documentation, and evidence of delivery. Primary purpose should be determined from the activity's
design and verifiable use, not merely from the recipient's general mission or a conclusory label.
Response to Question 12
Question 12: Does the proposed definition of 'complexity' enhance the rule's focus on meeting
community credit needs by providing greater consideration to community-development investments,
grants, and services linked to community-development lending or otherwise functioning as the
equivalent of loans?
Partly. Linking activities can recognize genuine structuring effort, but complexity should not
become a proxy for public value. A simple activity that directly and durably meets a documented
need may be more responsive than an elaborate transaction with weak beneficiary outcomes.
Complexity should be recorded separately from responsiveness, impact, and delivery.
Retain the proposed 15 percent indirect-cost guardrail as a presumptive ceiling. Apply detailed tracking
proportionately to material or large-dollar grants; permit simplified reporting for micro-donations that
records at least the amount, recipient, purpose, geography, and aggregate totals. For material grants,
preserve direct and indirect uses, beneficiary geography, committed purpose, disbursement status,
material amendments, returned funds, and measurable outputs or outcomes. Permit documented
exceptions necessary to deliver the activity when the bank and recipient preserve the factual basis.
Distinguish legitimate administrative cost from funds that never reached the intended activity.
 VELOXVFX LLC | OCC-2026-0694 | RIN 1557-AF57 | FDIC RIN 3064-AG31
VeloxVFX LLC - Independent informational architecture; agency and institutional authority remain external | Page 6
Response to Question 13
Question 13: Should the first component of the 'complexity' definition apply to loans and activities that
are the functional equivalent of loans?
Yes, provided functional equivalence is based on economic substance and documented risk or
commitment rather than terminology. The agencies should separately identify whether an activity is
a loan, investment, grant, service, or functional equivalent and prevent double counting across tests.
Response to Question 14
Question 14: Are there additional opportunities for the agencies to further enhance the rule's focus on
lending, such as by requiring that community-development investments and services be complex? If so,
should complex community-development activities be required for all banks or only banks above a
specified asset size?
Do not require complexity. Require responsiveness and demonstrable benefit appropriate to the
bank's capacity. The agencies can encourage lending by giving clear consideration to directly
delivered, affordable credit and by recognizing consumer-access infrastructure that helps eligible
households discover authorized housing assistance, while preserving government eligibility
decisions and lender underwriting.
Response to Question 15
Question 15: Should complex community-development activities be considered more responsive than
innovative, flexible, or impactful community-development activities?
No categorical hierarchy is warranted. Complexity, innovativeness, flexibility, responsiveness, and
impact answer different questions and should remain separately identified. Responsiveness to
documented need and verified delivery should carry greater weight than structural complexity by
itself.
Response to Question 16
Question 16: Should the agencies define innovativeness or flexibility? If so, should innovativeness vary
based on bank size and sophistication or apply uniformly; and should flexibility be defined by terms and
conditions, enhanced access to credit, or another concept?
Yes. Define innovativeness as a materially new or meaningfully improved method in the relevant
market that expands responsible access, reduces a documented barrier, improves delivery, or
strengthens accountability. Evaluate it in context of bank size and local market, but apply the same
evidentiary elements. Define flexibility by objective features - affordable structure, adjusted terms,
accessible delivery, consumer continuity, and responsiveness to documented constraints - while
maintaining safe-and-sound underwriting.
Response to Question 17
Question 17: Should the rules limit the concept of responsiveness to consideration in the evaluation of a
bank's community-development activities?
No. Responsiveness is also relevant to retail lending, delivery systems, consumer products, strategic
plans, and the bank's handling of identified community needs. The agencies should apply it
consistently while preventing double counting.

Response to Question 18
Question 18: Should affordable housing include rental housing for middle-income individuals in high-
cost areas as proposed, including workforce housing for public servants such as teachers, firefighters,
and police officers?
Yes, with LMI households retaining priority and with safeguards against displacement. High-cost-
area workforce housing can meet a demonstrated need, but CRA consideration should require
documented affordability, a defined beneficiary population, a meaningful affordability period, and
evidence that the activity adds or preserves affordable supply rather than merely financing market-
rate housing.
Response to Question 19
Question 19: Should the agencies define a high-cost area? If so, should the definition be based on
housing-cost burden, and is a 40 percent or 50 percent threshold appropriate? Are there other
definitions the agencies should consider?
Yes. Use an annually updated, transparent definition incorporating housing-cost burden, local
income, housing prices or rents, vacancy and supply constraints, and geography. VeloxVFX does not
possess representative housing-market data sufficient to recommend 40 percent or 50 percent as the
controlling national threshold. The agencies should publish the chosen data sources, measurement
period, update method, and resulting areas, and should test the definition against materially
different metropolitan, rural, Tribal, and high-cost markets.
Response to Question 20
Question 20: Should the agencies consider the cost of providing housing, such as FHFA High Opportunity
Areas, as a responsiveness factor or separate affordable-housing category to encourage creation or
preservation where housing is difficult to develop?
Use development cost primarily as a responsiveness factor, not an automatic separate category. High
cost can explain why an activity requires unusual subsidy or structure, but CRA consideration
should still depend on enforceable affordability, beneficiary reach, location, and duration.
Response to Question 21
Question 21: Should naturally occurring affordable housing partnerships with nonprofit organizations
be exempt from the requirement that median rents not exceed 30 percent of 80 percent of area median
income?
Do not adopt a blanket exemption. Permit an alternative demonstration using unit-level rents,
tenant incomes, rent restrictions, preservation commitments, and anti-displacement protections
when a median-rent test is not workable. The nonprofit label alone should not establish
affordability.
Response to Question 22
Question 22: Should naturally occurring affordable housing partnerships with nonprofit organizations
be exempt from the requirement that median rents not exceed 30 percent of 120 percent of area median
income in high-cost areas?
No blanket exemption. Use the same alternative-evidence pathway recommended for Question 21,
protections.

Response to Question 23
Question 23: Should home mortgage loans provided directly to LMI individuals or families qualify as
community-development loans when they are not considered as a major product line for the bank?
Yes, without double counting. Direct LMI mortgage lending should not disappear merely because it
is not a major product line. CRA consideration should include affordability, responsible
underwriting, down-payment or closing support, borrower reach, and sustained performance rather
than origination count alone.
Response to Question 24
Question 24: Should the agencies further limit businesses or farms qualifying under the first economic-
development category, for example by excluding startups expected to exceed the size test quickly or
small businesses affiliated with non-small businesses?
Exclude artificial fragmentation and activities whose primary benefit flows to a non-small affiliate,
but do not exclude a qualifying startup merely because growth is expected. Evaluate eligibility at a
stated time and preserve subsequent growth as a separate outcome; successful growth can evidence
economic development rather than defeat it retroactively.
Response to Question 25
Question 25: Should the agencies retain the requirement that the activity create, improve, or retain jobs
for LMI individuals or in an LMI area in the first economic-development category?
Yes, while recognizing measurable improvement in job quality, stability, wages, training, and access
- not only raw job count. The record should identify the baseline, expected result, realized result,
beneficiary geography or population, and measurement date.
Response to Question 26
Question 26: Should any example government programs in the third economic-development category be
removed? Should additional programs, projects, or initiatives be included?
Do not remove examples without evidence that they are inconsistent with CRA's purpose. Maintain a
non-exhaustive, updateable list and include duly authorized Tribal, rural, small-business, workforce,
housing-linked economic-development, and community-facility programs when they demonstrate a
qualifying community-development purpose. Inclusion should create a presumption, not automatic
credit without delivery evidence.
Response to Question 27
Question 27: Are revisions eliminating the purpose test in the Interagency Questions and Answers and
and farms that benefit communities, including through job creation?
Objective criteria should improve predictability, provided they do not reduce evaluation to a
checkbox. Require a traceable relationship between qualifying activity and the stated community
result, with proportionate outcome evidence and no silent substitution of projected benefits for
realized benefits.
adding more objective economic-development criteria likely to encourage banks to finance businesses

VeloxVFX LLC - Independent informational architecture; agency and institutional authority remain external | Page 9
Response to Question 28
Question 28: Are there activities that would qualify under the proposal as economic development but
should not, for example because they relate to ordinary ongoing operations rather than growth and
profitability?
Ordinary operating activity should not qualify solely because the borrower is small. Working capital
may qualify when it demonstrably supports stabilization, expansion, job retention, recovery, or
continued essential service in an eligible area. The bank should identify the qualifying purpose and
avoid attributing the entire relationship when only part supports that purpose.
Response to Question 29
Question 29: Are there activities considered economic development under current rules that would not
qualify under the proposed definition?
The agencies should perform and publish a crosswalk before finalization. Preserve reliance for
activities properly undertaken under current standards and identify any excluded category
prospectively. A transition record should state the prior basis, new basis, and effective date rather
than retroactively rewriting eligibility.
Response to Question 30
Question 30: Should other programs be presumed to promote economic development, such as Indian
country residential development? Alternatively, should these activities be presumed to qualify as
community development but be treated as revitalization and stabilization activities?
Recognize authorized Indian country residential-development programs. Classification should
follow the activity's principal documented purpose - economic development, affordable housing, or
revitalization and stabilization - while preventing double counting. The agencies should consult
Tribal governments and respect Tribal authority, land status, and local program design.
Response to Question 31
Question 31: Should the agencies retain the exclusion for counties designated to receive only FEMA
Public Assistance Emergency Work Category A or B and allow agency exceptions when a disaster has
longer-term and broader community effects?
Yes. Retain the default exclusion but authorize a documented exception based on duration,
displacement, infrastructure disruption, housing impact, business interruption, and unmet recovery
need. Publish the operative designation, evidence, geography, and period of eligibility.
Response to Question 32
Question 32: Should a bank retain a community-development activity eligibility confirmation for as long
as the loan or investment remains on its balance sheet?
Yes, and through the next examination or applicable record-retention period, whichever is longer.
Preserve the request, facts submitted, agency response, date, conditions, amendments, reliance
period, and any later determination. A later change should not silently overwrite the original
confirmation.

Response to Question 33
Question 33: Should the agencies set an outer limit after notifying a requester that additional time is
needed to consider a confirmation request? If so, should the additional period be 60 days, 30 days, or
another period, and should the agency specify it in the notice?
Yes. Use a 30-day additional period as the default and permit a longer period only with a written,
matter-specific explanation and stated response date. The notice should identify missing
information, responsible agency, current status, and whether the request remains pending.
Response to Question 34
Question 34: If activities outside assessment areas may receive consideration without meeting
geographic-flexibility standards in every assessment area, should the agencies use the proposed
'substantially met' standard or another standard?
Use 'substantially met' as the minimum, supported by assessment-area-specific evidence. Outside
activity should not cure material deficiencies in communities the bank is obligated to serve. Any
exception should be narrow, documented, and tied to circumstances such as a lack of feasible
activity rather than bank preference.
Response to Question 35
Question 35: Should strategic plans include whole political subdivisions even when a bank cannot
reasonably serve the whole area? Does advance goal-setting mitigate the concern? Should alternatives
such as a radius around branches be permitted?
Use whole political subdivisions as a transparency default, with a documented partial-area
exception when the bank cannot reasonably serve the whole area. Advance goals help but do not
eliminate geographic exclusion risk. Any radius method should account for travel time, population
distribution, transportation, rural conditions, digital access, and excluded LMI communities; maps
and supporting data should be public.
Response to Question 36
Question 36: Should the rules provide a maximum assessment-area size, such as a combined statistical
area or future equivalent?
Yes as a rebuttable outer boundary, with justified rural, Tribal, island, and specialized-market
exceptions. The maximum should not permit an overly broad area to mask localized gaps, and
subarea results should remain visible.
Response to Question 37
Question 37: Should strategic plans include maps of every covered assessment area?
Yes. Provide accessible maps plus machine-readable geographic identifiers, version dates, branches
and deposit-taking ATMs, excluded areas, and material changes. Maps should supplement, not
replace, a textual and data-based description.
Response to Question 38
Question 38: Do the proposed measurable-goal provisions adequately explain the required strategic-plan
elements? Should additional elements, such as a growth factor for annual interim goals, be added?
Use a common goal schema: baseline, denominator, target, unit, population, geography, data source,
measurement period, annual milestone, term outcome, responsible institution, verification, and amendment
treatment. Example: 2025 baseline = 40 LMI mortgage originations; 2027 target = 50; verified outcome =
45.

Response to Question 39
Question 39: Does permitting goals covering the entire strategic-plan term in addition to annual interim
goals provide appropriate flexibility?
Yes. Term goals can capture long-duration projects, while annual milestones preserve visibility and
early correction. Both should remain associated so a final aggregate result does not erase material
annual underperformance.
Response to Question 40
Question 40: Should banks be required to have measurable goals for the entire plan term in addition to
annual interim measurable goals?
Yes. Require term goals and annual interim milestones, with limited exceptions for activities whose
timing cannot reasonably be predicted. Qualitative goals should still identify evidence and
evaluation criteria.
Response to Question 41
Question 41: How should agencies weigh annual interim goals against goals spanning the entire
strategic-plan term?
Treat annual goals as trajectory and accountability measures and term goals as final outcome
measures. Repeated or material annual misses should weigh against a favorable conclusion even if a
late activity reaches the aggregate number, unless the bank documents changed conditions,
community benefit, and agency-approved remediation.
Response to Question 42
Question 42: Should the agencies develop a process similar to the OCC's Simplified Strategic Plan Process
for Community Banks for all banks, and should it be guidance or regulation?
Yes. Codify minimum procedural protections and required goal elements; place optional templates,

Question 43: Does the proposed treatment of activities outside assessment areas under a strategic plan
provide appropriate flexibility by considering otherwise-uncredited activities when determining
whether a bank should receive an 'outstanding' rating?
Yes, after the bank has substantially met its inside-area goals. Outside activities may distinguish
outstanding performance but should not substitute for unmet local obligations. The evaluation
should state the activity, location, qualifying basis, and effect on the rating.
Response to Question 44
Question 44: Should the agencies consider activities not otherwise counted toward measurable goals
when deciding whether a bank should receive a 'satisfactory' rating?
Generally, no activity outside the goals should rescue materially inadequate performance within
assessment areas. The agencies may consider such activity as performance context where the bank
examples, and size-sensitive methods in coordinated guidance. A common structure should
improve comparability without eliminating institution-specific plans.
Any growth factor should be explained publicly and should not automatically reduce commitments during
adverse conditions without agency review.

Response to Question 45
Question 45: Should consideration of activities not otherwise included in measurable goals be at the

Once a bank elects consideration and supplies complete information, the agency should evaluate

and banks should not selectively present only favorable portions of a connected activity.

Question 46: Should banks be permitted to establish measurable goals for activities outside their

Yes, and ordinarily limit them to outstanding-level goals so local satisfactory performance remains

Response to Question 47
Question 47: Should a bank provide a draft strategic plan to its agency before the public-comment period
to allow publication? Is five business days sufficient?
Yes. Require at least 10 business days so the agency can perform a completeness and accessibility
check without substantive preapproval. The public period should begin only when the same
complete draft is available through the agency and bank channels.
Response to Question 48
Question 48: Do the proposed public-engagement provisions properly balance notice and
modernization? What additional methods could modernize engagement while ensuring notice to
affected communities?
They are a sound start. Require a searchable agency posting, bank homepage or CRA-page notice,
email or feed alerts, accessible mobile and paper formats, plain-language summaries, maps,
language access appropriate to the community, and notice through branches and community
partners. Publish the bank's issue-by-issue response to material public comments with the final plan.
Response to Question 49
Question 49: Does the strategic-plan prefiling communication provision permit useful agency guidance
without implying preapproval? Should it contain process and timing requirements?
Yes, if communications are memorialized as nonbinding and do not bypass public participation.
Establish a target response period, identify participants and topics, preserve written summaries, and
state that only the final agency decision is operative.
Response to Question 50
Question 50: Should strategic plans approved after the effective date take effect on the approval date?
Should the effective date be the date proposed in the plan even if it is in the past?

Response to Question 51
Question 51: If an agency extends strategic-plan review for good cause, should the rule cap the extension
at 15 days, 30 days, or another stated period?
Use a 30-calendar-day cap, with any further extension requiring the bank's agreement or an
extraordinary written explanation. The notice should identify good cause, outstanding issue,
responsible agency, and a definite decision date.
Response to Question 52
Question 52: Should the proposed list of material changes supporting a strategic-plan amendment be
non-exhaustive or exhaustive? Should the rule add examples and explain what is not material?
Use a non-exhaustive list with objective examples of material and non-material changes. Material
changes should include significant changes to geography, business model, product mix, merger
status, branch network, community need, measurement method, or goals. Technical corrections that
do not change scope, obligation, measurement, or public effect should ordinarily be non-material.
Response to Question 53
Question 53: Should the agencies explain more fully when individual or aggregate measurable goals fail
to address assessment-area credit needs?
Yes. Require an adequacy review covering the most significant documented needs, beneficiary
reach, geographic distribution, product access, affordability, lending volume and quality,
community input, and gaps among goals. Large totals should not compensate automatically for
leaving a material need or area unaddressed.
Response to Question 54
Question 54: Do the rules sufficiently explain when an agency may deny or require resubmission of a
strategic plan? Would greater specificity reduce uncertainty and burden?
Add specificity. Distinguish incomplete submission, curable deficiency, inadequate goals, legal
inconsistency, unresolved public-engagement defect, denial, and voluntary withdrawal. Each action
should identify reasons, required correction, applicable deadline, review status, and effect on the
prior plan.
Response to Question 55
Question 55: What alternative approaches could encourage banks to meet credit needs in Indian country
and Tribal and Native lands? Should the agencies use the 2023 rule's Native Lands definition, and what
difficulties could arise?
Use a clear, inclusive Native Lands definition developed with Tribal consultation, while preserving
distinctions among Tribal lands, Hawaiian Home Lands, Alaska Native areas, and other legally
different geographies. Recognize distance, trust-land status, appraisal constraints, infrastructure,

consortium activity without displacing Tribal authority or imposing a one-size-fits-all geography.
