RE: Comments Regarding RIN 1557-AF57, RIN 3064-AG31

Dear Chief Counsel, Ms. Jones, and Leadership of the OCC and FDIC,

The Affordable Housing Alliance of Central Ohio is a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization that provides
research, education, technical assistance, and support to efforts that close Central Ohio's housing
affordability gaps. We analyze housing opportunities through an economic development lens and are
guided by nearly forty organizational members with significant professional expertise in housing
development, finance, and service delivery.

While we have not previously engaged in federal rulemaking activities, we feel compelled to share two
important concerns regarding the proposed Community Reinvestment Act ("CRA") rule and seek
modifications to better align with broader federal policy objectives and statutory intent. In advance, we
share our gratitude for your review and consideration of these comments.

First, by reducing the number of lenders who are subject to the most comprehensive aspects of the
rule, this proposal will significantly reduce investment capacity in proven supply-side housing
strategies. These at-risk investment tools, which are critical for reducing Central Ohio's housing
shortage, include the federal Low Income Housing Tax Credit, the Ohio Low Income Housing Tax
Credit (rural focused), Welcome Home Ohio (homeownership focused), and the Single-Family Tax
Credit (homeownership focused). It would also restrain the State's proposed Promise Land tax credit
which, if passed, would support faith-based housing providers working to advance homeownership
opportunities and is particularly well suited to smaller banking partners. Disincentivizing mid-sized
banks from investing in these bipartisan equity programs will limit Ohio's ability to resolve its housing
deficit.





While AHACO agrees that in many cases, "a community's credit needs are best and most directly met
through activities that involve lending," we caution against a one-size-fits-all approach. In reality, a mix
of both debt and equity tools has proven most effective at increasing housing inventory and restoring
balance in the market. The CRA's current configuration supports this diversified approach while also
flexibly accommodating the distinctive needs of local housing markets.

This is evident in Central Ohio where a booming economy means that we need to build nearly 200,000
new homes over the next ten years. With traditional financing vehicles for workforce housing strained,
our region consistently fails to meet annualized benchmarks, building only half of what is needed to
accommodate record job gains. As these pressures mount, more than 80,000 residents are now
experiencing severe housing cost burdens.

However, even with local reforms to zoning and permitting, debt alone remains insufficient to support
construction needs. Pro formas without a robust equity component increasingly fail to pencil out. CRA
has bridged some of this gap but, even today, more investment is needed. Our members report that
thousands of units are stalled due to reduced credit demand. Not only is our region unable to realize
the stabilizing impact of those homes, but we are also unable to capture the economic boon of
hundreds of millions of dollars in complementary lending that would accompany it. Weakening the
CRA will further destabilize this suite of "off budget" equity investments and hinder our Ohio's ability to
protect and expand housing affordability.

Secondly, the proposed rule will frustrate and impede the nonprofit delivery model for critical housing
services, especially those designed to advance economic self-sufficiency for low- and moderate-income
households. See: § __.12. Specifically, portions of the rule that restrict nonprofit grants and donations
or impose administrative fee caps that are out of alignment with actual costs will result in inefficiencies,
increased administrative burden, and funding shortfalls for high-priority initiatives, many of which were
recently promoted in the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act.

In Central Ohio, the following widely acclaimed program types are likely to experience operating
shortages and/or risk closure should this rule become effective in its current form:

•
Technical assistance and education to reduce zoning barriers to housing creation;
•
'Libraries' with pre-approved plans to reduce permitting delays and construction costs;
•
Capacity building for faith-based housing providers;
•
Concessionary lending programs required to leverage external resources;
•
Risk tolerant lending for more naturally affordable building types, like manufactured,
Accessory Dwelling Unit, and "missing middle" housing;
•
Temporary housing programs that require clients to participate in career education;
•
Innovative down payment strategies, including shared appreciation mortgage loans;
•
Housing counseling to promote self-sufficiency and/or sustainable homeownership;
•
Home modifications to support senior independence and aging in community;
•
Public safety-based programs to remediate blight and reduce housing vacancies; and
•
Local research to assess and monitor supply shortages and document best practices.
 Each of these initiatives gives a range of constituencies an opportunity to thrive, including our rural and
suburban communities. Either directly or indirectly, they all expand access to credit.
These programs work because of strong public-private partnerships between builders, like those in
AHACO's membership, investors subject to the CRA rules, and the determined oversight of federal
regulators. It is these robust collaborations that sustain affordable housing construction and support a
durable services ecosystem. Unfortunately, the proposed changes weaken that tripartite system and
will increase housing supply shortages, reduce housing quality, and intensify neighborhood instability.
For these reasons, AHACO respectfully requests that the proposed rulemaking process be suspended
or delayed pending further research and community engagement into these acute harms. Alternately,
we recommend modifications that both (1) strengthen the LIHTC program and similar public-private
partnerships and (2) protect the current incentive structure that supports local, place-based responses
to the nation's housing challenges.
On behalf of our members and the Central Ohio community, thank you again for your time and
consideration. If we can provide any further information or if an audience with our experts would prove
valuable, please do not hesitate to contact me.
Sincerely,
Carlie J. Boos, Executive Director
Affordable Housing Alliance of Central Ohio

Columbus, Ohio 43215

comments.text:
COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57; FDIC RIN 3064-AG31; 91 Fed. Reg. 52114 (Aug. 12, 2026)
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
We represent a Community Action Agency that is also a Community Development Corporation. We urge the Office of the Comptroller (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) to withdraw the proposal to change the Community Reinvestment Act regulations. In our view, it would weaken support for affordable housing, community organizations, and residents with low incomes.
Our organization works with individuals and families seeking stable housing and greater financial security. We see how affordable housing, access to basic banking, and support from trusted local organizations contribute to lasting stability. Banks are important partners in this work. Their loans, investments, grants, and services help community organizations respond to needs that cannot be met through public funding alone.
The proposal would change how smaller and midsize banks are evaluated under CRA. Banks with less than $1 billion in assets would no longer receive a separate review of their community development activities, while banks with less than $10 billion would no longer receive the full review now applied to large banks. Local and regional banks can be vital partners in affordable housing and other community projects. Reduced scrutiny could weaken their incentive to participate.
We ask the agencies to preserve meaningful review of community development lending, investments, and services. Public reporting should also continue so communities can see where bank resources are reaching residents and where needs remain unmet.
Affordable housing projects often require several sources of financing. A bank loan alone may not close the gap. Bank investments, including those connected to the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, help make homes affordable to families with limited incomes. If CRA examinations place less weight on these investments, housing organizations may find it harder to assemble the financing needed to build or preserve homes.
We are also concerned that the proposal’s low minimum level of community development activity, intended for recognizing work outside a bank’s local service area, could become a broader benchmark. Although the agencies say it is not a general passing score, banks should be evaluated in light of the needs of the communities they serve and the work they are capable of doing.
The proposed limits on grants to nonprofits are of particular concern. The proposal would generally require a bank grant to support a specific project or program. A grant designated for one housing program might still count toward a bank’s CRA performance, while a flexible grant that an organization could use where the need is greatest, such as supporting staff or keeping several services running, could be harder for the bank to count. That could make banks less willing to provide the flexible support community organizations need. The agencies further ask whether grants should receive CRA consideration at all. We strongly oppose eliminating that consideration.
Nonprofits need staff, facilities, coordination, and sound administrative systems to serve residents effectively. These are necessary costs of service, even when they do not fit neatly within a single project budget. Flexible grants allow organizations to respond as needs change. We urge the agencies to continue recognizing grants that support nonprofits serving low-income communities, including general operating support.
The proposal would also exclude checking and savings accounts from the review of certain bank services. For many residents, an affordable account makes it easier to receive wages or benefits, pay rent, and save for emergencies. Access to a branch nearby can also matter. We urge the agencies to continue evaluating whether banks offer affordable, accessible accounts and services in low-income neighborhoods.
For these reasons, we urges the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the proposal. If the agencies proceed, they should preserve meaningful expectations for community development lending and investment; continue recognizing grants to nonprofits, including operating support; consider affordable accounts and branch access; and retain public information needed to identify gaps in service. We also request a fuller assessment of the proposal’s effects on low-income communities and additional time for those communities to comment.
Thank you for considering our views and the needs of the residents and communities we serve.

Consumer Action writes to oppose the proposed rule issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)   because it would significantly damage the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).  

The proposed changes to CRA would reduce the quality and quantity of services to low to moderate- income consumers and small businesses. Less bank scrutiny translates into less investment in underserved residents, small businesses, small farms and local communities.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Consumer Action writes to oppose the proposed rule issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency
(OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)1 because it would significantly damage the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).
For the last 55 years, Consumer Action has been a champion of underrepresented consumers. A national,
nonprofit 501(c)3 organization, Consumer Action focuses on financial education that empowers low to
moderate-income and limited-English-speaking consumers to financially prosper. It advocates for
consumers in the media and before regulators and lawmakers to advance consumer rights and promote
industry-wide change, particularly in the fields of credit, banking, housing, privacy, healthcare, fraud
prevention and telecommunications.
The CRA has been an essential rule for ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire community,
including low to moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce CRA analysis of many banks and would change how regulators
evaluate community development, banking services and support for nonprofit organizations. We believe that
these changes are being considered without adequate consideration of their effect on low to moderate-income
(LMI) communities, and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination and scant investment.
The proposed changes to CRA would reduce the quality and quantity of services to low to moderate- income
consumers and small businesses. It would disincentivize banks from meeting community needs and providing

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 local economic support. Less bank scrutiny translates into less investment in underserved residents, small
businesses, small farms and local communities.
The proposed rule would roll back the number of banks required to meet CRA community development
obligations by as much as 40 percent. Only the largest six percent of banks would remain subject to CRA
examination.
The proposed revisions to CRA will lead to a significant loss in community development financing, affordable
mortgage credit and small business lending. It would also have a serious impact on branch closings—
particularly in LMI communities. In 28 states, at least one-third of branches located in LMI census tracts would
no longer receive any CRA evaluation.2
Under the proposal, examiners would no longer evaluate whether checking and savings account products are
affordable and responsive to community needs. CRA review of the cost and features of deposit products has
played an important role in encouraging banks to address these disparities by offering affordable products.
Bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are linked to access to credit and economic opportunity. They
can determine whether families can safely receive income, build savings, establish banking relationships and
obtain responsible credit.
The proposed changes would give CRA credit to investments made outside of LMI communities and will likely
shift much bank capital away from underserved communities, small businesses, CDFIs and local nonprofits.
Congress passed the Community Reinvestment Act to establish banks' obligation to serve the credit needs of
the entire community. CRA is the tool to ensure that banks are accountable to their community.
The changes proposed to reform CRA will cause huge harm to consumers, communities and consumer
protection nationwide. We urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw this plan and return with a proposal that
focuses CRA reform on undeserved communities—not businesses—that serves the banking and credit needs of
LMI consumers, creates local jobs and supports small businesses.
Thank you for considering our comments.

Sincerely,

CONSUMER ACTION

rollbacks/.

I am writing as a member of the Harford County Council representing District A, which includes Edgewood,
Joppatowne, and portions of Abingdon, Maryland, to express my concerns regarding the proposed changes to
the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).
The communities I represent include working families, small businesses, nonprofit organizations, and
neighborhoods that depend on continued access to responsible lending and meaningful community investment.
The CRA has played an important role in encouraging financial institutions to meet the credit needs of their
entire communities, particularly low- and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods. I am concerned that the
proposed changes could weaken those commitments by reducing community development investment and
scrutiny, as well as decreasing transparency and accountability.
Community investment has a direct local impact. It affects whether families can purchase homes, whether
affordable housing can be developed, whether entrepreneurs can obtain financing, and whether nonprofit
organizations can provide critical services. This is particularly important in communities that have experienced
historic disinvestment. One of my priorities as a Council Member has been ensuring that communities such as
Edgewood and Joppatowne receive equitable opportunities for economic growth and community development.
I am particularly concerned about the impact on affordable housing and nonprofit organizations. Banks support
affordable housing, financial counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization, and other
community services through grants, investments, loans, and partnerships. The proposed 15% limitation on
indirect costs for certain community-development grants, along with additional documentation requirements,
could disproportionately affect smaller community-based organizations that already operate with limited
resources.
I am also concerned about reducing CRA reporting and accountability. Local officials and community
organizations need reliable information to identify lending gaps, understand where investment is occurring, and
determine whether the financial needs of our communities are being met. Reducing reporting requirements
would make that work more difficult.




 NOLANDA ROBERT



 Council Member, District A


 212 S. Bond Street, Bel Air, Maryland 21014




 410-638-3521


 nrobert@harfordcountycouncil.com
 For these reasons, I respectfully urge the OCC and FDIC not to finalize the proposed CRA rule in its current
form and to fully evaluate its potential impact on low- and moderate-income communities, affordable housing,
small businesses, nonprofit organizations, rural communities, and neighborhoods that have historically
experienced disinvestment. I also support extending the public comment period by at least 60 days to give local
governments, community organizations, and residents adequate time to evaluate these significant changes and
provide meaningful input.
The Community Reinvestment Act provides an important mechanism for ensuring that financial institutions
remain accountable to the communities they serve. We should strengthen opportunities for investment in our
communities, not diminish them.
Sincerely,

Nolanda Robert
Council Member, District A
Harford County Council

comments.text:
COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed amendments to the Community Reinvestment Act Regulations. The goals of encouraging banks to meet the credit needs of their communities, ensuring community development investments reach intended beneficiaries, and reducing unnecessary administrative burden are important objectives.

I encourage the agencies to strengthen, rather than reduce, expectations for community development activities, particularly in rural communities and low- and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods. Many rural areas continue to face challenges related to access to capital, business development, housing availability, infrastructure investment, and economic opportunity. Banks benefit from these communities through deposits, lending activity, and other financial services and should be expected to make meaningful investments that support long-term community prosperity. CRA regulations should continue to incentivize substantial investment in the communities that financial institutions serve.

I am particularly concerned about proposals that would reduce or eliminate reporting of small business lending, small farm lending, or community development lending activity. These data are essential for understanding whether local credit needs are being met and for identifying gaps in access to capital. Policymakers, community organizations, researchers, and local stakeholders rely on these data to evaluate lending patterns and determine whether financial institutions are fulfilling the purpose of the Community Reinvestment Act. Reduced transparency would make it more difficult to assess community needs, target resources effectively, and measure the impact of CRA-related activities.

At the same time, I do not support significant new reporting requirements for nonprofit organizations, educational institutions, local governments, or other recipients of community development grants unless those requirements are simple, standardized, and directly useful. Reporting should focus on meaningful outcomes and should help demonstrate impact, identify successful practices, and communicate achievements to stakeholders. Community-based organizations should be able to spend their time serving communities rather than navigating unnecessarily complex reporting systems.

I also encourage the agencies to continue promoting fair and responsible lending practices. Access to credit is an important driver of economic mobility, homeownership, entrepreneurship, and community stability. Financial institutions should be evaluated not only on the volume of lending they provide but also on whether their activities contribute to sustainable wealth-building and opportunity within the communities they serve.

Finally, I urge the agencies to place greater emphasis on affordable housing as a community development priority. The nation's affordable housing challenges are complex and stem from many factors, including housing supply constraints, rising development costs, regulatory barriers, and insufficient investment in housing production. Banks are not solely responsible for these challenges; however, they play an important role in financing housing development, rehabilitation, and preservation. CRA regulations should encourage greater investment in expanding the supply of attainable and affordable housing, including homeownership opportunities, rental housing, rehabilitation of existing housing stock, and housing in rural and underserved communities where financing gaps often limit availability. While significant public and private resources continue to be invested in homelessness prevention and intervention programs, long-term progress will require increased attention to expanding the housing supply. Encouraging CRA-qualified investments that support housing availability and affordability is one way financial institutions can help address this broader community need.

In summary, I respectfully recommend that the agencies:

Increase expectations for community development investments in rural and LMI communities.
Maintain and strengthen reporting of small business, small farm, and community development lending data.
Avoid imposing burdensome new reporting requirements on community development grant recipients.
Continue promoting fair and responsible lending practices that support economic mobility and community wealth-building.
Prioritize affordable housing development, preservation, and rehabilitation as a central component of CRA activities.

Thank you for considering these comments.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0052_09000064b95ea12e.pdf:
September 29, 2026

Attention: Jennifer M. Jones, Deputy Executive Secretary
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
550 17th Street, NW,
Washington, DC 20429

Attention: Comment Processing
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th St. SW,
Washington, D.C. 20219

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations RIN 3064-AG31 / Docket ID OCC-2026- 0694

To Whom It May Concern,
On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA). CRA has helped create a durable incentive for banks to provide loans, investments, grants, and
services in communities that have historically lacked access to capital. As such, we wish to offer
comments on the proposed regulation from the perspective of an emerging community development
financial institution (CDFI).
While we support some of the agencies' provisions that could improve the CRA and increase accessible
and responsible capital in economically distressed communities, we are concerned about the asset
thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated, as well as proposed restrictions on grants. There
are also provisions that we feel could weaken community development incentives across geographic
areas.
CDFI Friendly Bloomington, Inc. (CFB) serves a rural 13-county region in Southwest Central Indiana with
a population of 516,000. We are a newly certified CDFI (as of July 2025) that works to attract
investment from CDFI partners in our designated target markets serving geographic Investment Areas
(Ias) and Low-Income Targeted Populations (LITP). Since our founding in 2018, our organization has
helped facilitate more than $29 million in CDFI investment to our region as part of more than $74

 2

million in projects. This includes affordable housing, small business, childcare and nonprofit
organizations who have benefitted from CDFI investment. Our area of Indiana has historically lacked
access to non-traditional financing, and our organization serves as a connector to help fill financial gaps
where they exist for community development projects.
Our banking partners are a critical ally in these efforts. We have relationships with banks that provide a
range of services benefiting our organization and our region. These include service on our board of
directors, technical expertise and networking, grants and lending capital investments such as lines of
credit and Equity Equivalent (EQ2) investments. These investments not only assist our organization in
providing critical technical assistance and outreach/education on access to financing, but they help
weave together the important components of community development finance in our region. These
financial partnerships, estimated at nearly $400,000 in grant support and in partnership with other
entities including the CDFI Fund, have helped CFB assist with the creation or retention of 425 units of
affordable housing and, over the last three years, with more than 700 hours of technical assistance.
These partnerships speak to the longstanding, mutually beneficial relationship that CDFIs like ours have
with our banking partners, due in part to the CRA and its tools that help our organizations create a
more seamless financing network. In order for this to continue, we wish to comment on three CRA
provisions that are under review.
1.​ Raised Asset Thresholds That Could Jeopardize Community Development Finance: Section IV.A,
"Asset Thresholds"; Questions 1–3
The proposal defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets, intermediate banks
as institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as institutions with more than
$10 billion. About 800 banks that currently face a separate community development test as
intermediate small banks would become small banks and lose that requirement. Another
approximately 400 banks that are currently evaluated as large banks would become intermediate
banks, losing the separate large-bank lending, investment, and service tests and many associated
data-reporting requirements.
In Indiana, it is estimated that more than 40 percent, or 34 of our 84 banks, would no longer be
required to reinvest in local community development projects such as affordable housing, small
business support and healthcare. About 16 banks, comprising 40 percent of all banks in the state,
would lose their large bank status, thereby jeopardizing more than 30 percent of branches located in
LMI areas. In our rural region, the loss of even one or two CRA-motivated bank partners can materially
affect whether projects are financed. In an already tough environment to meet the demand for
housing, childcare and a ready workforce, increasing barriers to financing will exacerbate these
challenges.

Page 2

 3

The asset threshold changes would also substantially reduce the number of institutions subject to
large-bank CRA data requirements. This would make it harder for communities, CDFIs, policymakers,
and regulators to identify credit gaps, compare bank performance, assess geographic disparities, and
understand whether community credit needs are being met. We are concerned that aggregate
community development finance data is already difficult to track and the proposal would decrease
clarity on data gathering, making it difficult to identify and understand where credit is flowing. This is
especially important in our rural region, where the Federal Reserve Bank of New York has determined
that seven of our 13 counties are credit-constrained.
Recommendation
For all the reasons cited above, we urge the agencies to retain the current thresholds and reject all
alternatives offered (including the substantially higher thresholds raised for consideration in Question
1).
2.​ Restrictions on Community Development Grants: Section IV.C, "Community Development
Activities — CD Grants"; Questions 9–11
We strongly oppose the proposed restrictions on community development grants which: 1) requires a
qualifying CD grant to be directly used by the recipient for a program, project, or initiative with a
primary purpose of community development; 2) for large banks, caps grant recipient's indirect
administrative costs to 15%; 3) requires that large banks obtain documentation from grant recipients
including written commitments regarding use of funds, indirect-cost attestations, IRS Form 990s, and
operating and program budgets. We also strongly oppose the alternative contemplated in Question 10
to eliminate grants and donations from CRA consideration entirely.
While we share the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants meaningfully benefit
communities, these requirements would restrict many forms of effective grantmaking and
misunderstand the role that flexible operating support plays in community development finance. For
CDFIs, staffing, underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, risk management, data systems,
financial management, technical assistance, and product development are not ancillary to community
development. They are the infrastructure that makes community development lending possible.
As an organization focused on outreach and technical assistance, our operations are our programming
in many ways. Our audited financial statements show that our organization spends just 23% of our
assets on operations, with 77% dedicated to programming. The majority of our staff time is focused on
providing direct interaction with clients and projects, and focused on the logistical preparation to assist
seeing more community development projects to the finish line. It is also critical that organizations like
ours be administered in a professional manner, ensuring we have the funds available to obtain
professional financial accounting and audit services, as well as qualified staff who can perform the
necessary duties grantmakers are interested in funding. Over the last three years, CFB has provided
Page 3

 4

more than 700 hours of technical assistance and has increased our loan portfolio to more than $1
million. In addition, during this time we have helped increase CDFI investment in our region by nearly
$4 million.
Therefore, we strongly oppose using a fixed 15% indirect-cost limit as a condition of CRA eligibility. An
organization's administrative-cost percentage is not an appropriate proxy for community impact. Costs
vary depending on an organization's size, geography, product mix, regulatory obligations,
technical-assistance model, and populations served. The cap could disproportionately affect small and
emerging CDFIs, rural CDFIs, CDFIs making small-dollar loans, organizations providing intensive
borrower technical assistance, CDFIs developing new products or entering underserved markets and
organizations making necessary investments in technology, compliance, data, and risk management.
CDFI Friendly Bloomington meets all of the above criteria.
Recommendation
The agencies should preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-building grants as
currently is in place under the 1995 framework. CRA should encourage flexibility for banks to provide
the form of support that best responds to the identified community needs instead of imposing undue
compliance burdens.
3.​ Geographic flexibility for CD activities outside assessment areas: Section IV.E, "Consideration of
Community Development Activities — CD Activities Outside Assessment Areas"; proposed §
__.13(e); Question 34
We support the goal of enabling CRA-motivated capital to reach communities with significant unmet
needs but relatively few bank assessment areas. Greater geographic flexibility could be particularly
beneficial for reaching CRA deserts.
CDFI Friendly Bloomington serves what is known as a CDFI desert. According to data from the CDFI
Fund, over the last 20 years, the per capita investment from CDFIs in our region was just $22,
compared to $714 nationally. While that number has more than doubled in the past few years, we still
have a long way to go in filling financing gaps in our 13 counties.
Flexibility with CRA capital should supplement rather than displace CD activity in banks' own
assessment areas. The agencies are considering both quantitative and qualitative approaches for
determining when a bank has sufficiently served its assessment areas to receive consideration for
outside-AA activity.


Page 4

 5

Recommendation
With respect to Question 34, we support greater geographic flexibility where it can help direct
CRA-motivated capital to rural communities, Indian Country, and other underserved areas that may fall
outside traditional assessment areas.
In conclusion, CRA has helped create a powerful partnership among banks, CDFIs, and the communities
we serve. We appreciate the agencies' efforts to improve clarity and flexibility. Modernization,
however, should result in more responsible capital reaching communities with unmet credit needs, as
the CRA statute was intended. In doing so, maintaining flexible, yet structured criteria that is easily
understood in communities that also support emerging CDFIs is essential to making community
development work.
We urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the raised asset thresholds proposed, the restrictions on CD
operating grants and to maintain geographic flexibility with CRA-motivated capital.
Thank you for considering these comments and for considering the impact of the proposed changes on
our communities.
Sincerely,

John C. Zody
Executive Director
CDFI Friendly Bloomington

comments.text:
COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Habitat for Humanity Susquehanna submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). We also urge the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, to carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity for additional public comment on the analysis and evidence supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60 days.
Habitat for Humanity Susquehanna is a nonprofit, community-based housing organization serving families in Maryland. We partner with low- and moderate-income families to build and rehabilitate affordable homes, helping them achieve the stability, security, and opportunity that homeownership provides. Our work is deeply rooted in the communities we serve, and we rely on partnerships with local financial institutions—including CRA-motivated investments, loans, and grants—to make affordable homeownership possible for families who are otherwise excluded from the conventional housing market.
The proposed rule would reduce community investment expectations for banks, lessen scrutiny of bank community-development activities, and make it more difficult for many community-based nonprofits to receive support through changes such as the proposed 15% limitation on indirect costs for community-development grants. These changes threaten to reduce the flow of capital and philanthropic support that organizations like Habitat for Humanity Susquehanna depend on to acquire land, build homes, and keep housing affordable for working families.
Developing affordable housing is increasingly challenging due to rising costs for land, construction materials, infrastructure, permitting, insurance, labor, and financing. Every source of community investment matters. A significant reduction in bank community-development activity would mean fewer resources for affordable-housing development, fewer partnerships with local organizations, and ultimately fewer Maryland families achieving the dream of homeownership.
For these reasons, Habitat for Humanity Susquehanna strongly urges the OCC and FDIC not to finalize the proposed CRA rule in its current form. We encourage the agencies to preserve a strong CRA that continues to promote responsible lending, meaningful community investment, and support for local nonprofit organizations working to revitalize communities and expand economic opportunity.
Thank you for considering the perspective of Habitat for Humanity Susquehanna and the families we serve.
Sincerely,
Ryan Alban
President, Board of Directors
Habitat for Humanity Susquehanna

3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould,
Habitat for Humanity Susquehanna submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller
of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) because it would
significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). We also urge the OCC and
FDIC, before making any proposed changes, to carefully analyze the likely consequences for
low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity for additional public comment
on the analysis and evidence supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline
by 60 days.
Habitat for Humanity Susquehanna is a nonprofit, community-based housing organization
serving families in Maryland. We partner with low- and moderate-income families to build and
rehabilitate affordable homes, helping them achieve the stability, security, and opportunity that
homeownership provides. Our work is deeply rooted in the communities we serve, and we rely
on partnerships with local financial institutions, including CRA-motivated investments, loans,
and grants—to make affordable homeownership possible for families who might otherwise be
excluded from the conventional housing market.
The proposed rule would reduce community investment expectations for banks, lessen scrutiny
of bank community-development activities, and make it more difficult for many community-
based nonprofits to receive support through changes such as the proposed 15% limitation on
indirect costs for community-development grants. These changes threaten to reduce the flow of
capital and philanthropic support that organizations like Habitat for Humanity Susquehanna
depend on to acquire land, build homes, and keep housing affordable for working families.
Developing affordable housing is increasingly challenging due to rising costs for land,
construction materials, infrastructure, permitting, insurance, labor, and financing. Every source
of community investment matters. A significant reduction in bank community-development
activity would mean fewer resources for affordable-housing development, fewer partnerships
 with local organizations, and ultimately fewer Maryland families achieving the dream of
homeownership.
For these reasons, Habitat for Humanity Susquehanna strongly urges the OCC and FDIC not to
finalize the proposed CRA rule in its current form. We encourage the agencies to preserve a
strong CRA that continues to promote responsible lending, meaningful community investment,
and support for local nonprofit organizations working to revitalize communities and expand
economic opportunity.
Thank you for considering the perspective of Habitat for Humanity Susquehanna and the
families we serve.
Sincerely,
Habitat for Humanity Susquehanna Board Member

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0053_09000064b95ea43f.pdf:
1

September 29, 2026

Via electronic submission

Jonathan V. Gould
Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency
400 7th Street SW
Washington, DC 20219

Attn: Chief Counsel's Office
Via: Federal eRulemaking Portal –
.regulations.gov
Travis Hill, Chairman
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
(FDIC)
550 17th Street, NW
Washington, DC 20429

[Via email to Comments@fdic.gov]



Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
on Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694;
RIN 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Corey Leon submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency
(OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)1 because it would
significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the
complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, I also request that the OCC and FDIC,
before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low-
and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis
and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current
comment deadline by 60-days.
I have over 30 years of professional experience working at the national, state, and local
levels in community development finance. From investments in Low-Income Housing
Tax Credits and New Markets Tax Credits to funding local community development
corporations, I have seen how the CRA encourages regulated institutions to pay attention,
tract and monitor and even dedicate staff to making loans, investments and grants in
underserved communities. I am proudly a member of the National Community
Reinvestment Coalition.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 2
in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal
access to mainstream financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and
would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and
support for nonprofit organizations. I am concerned that these changes are being
considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-
income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination
and disinvestment.
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. Most of my
work is in Michigan and Ohio. In metro Detroit, from 2010-2024, banks made
$28,964,420,000 in CRA qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census
tracts and $25,352,603,000 in CRA qualified lending to small businesses.
I am concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1
capital devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough
to receive a passing CRA rating.2 However, that percentage is far lower than the
percentage the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the
largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.
NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the
OCC and FDIC supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these
banks currently conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community development
loans and investments inside their assessment areas, and that the median percentage of
annual community development lending in assessment areas was 6.8% of tier 1 capital,
and a median of 3.6% of tier 1 capital for annual CRA qualified investments.3 If each
bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet separate thresholds of 0.625%
of Tier 1 capital for community development lending and investments, combined activity
would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually -- a decrease of approximately $87.1
billion, or 85%. Similarly, the proposal encourages banks to use strategic plans to make
their CRA compliance easier and more predictable. Previous proposed guidance also set
strategic plan benchmarks for CRA performance well-below historical levels of
community development activity.4

2 The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit for outside their assessment areas if the banks
surpass a benchmark of 0.625% of its tier 1 capital for community development loans and likewise 0.625%
for investments. 91 Fed. Reg. 52121, 52140 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026). We are concerned that the practical
effect of this proposal is that the benchmark will serve not as a floor, but a ceiling.
3 NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk,
(Sept. 10, 2026), https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-
development-activity-at-risk/.
4 NCRC, The Proposed CRA Rule's Strategic Plans: A More Predictable Path to Doing Less (Sept 1,
2026), https://ncrc.org/the-proposed-cra-rules-strategic-plans-a-more-predictable-path-to-doing-less/.
 3
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic
discrimination cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments
and loans. If regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be
accountable to the communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for
communities. For example, in my community, many small businesses have a hard time
finding growth capital. It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to
meet community needs. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether
the proposed changes would reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and
moderate-income communities and whether communities that have experienced historic
discrimination or disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.
The proposal would substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small
banks, while banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be
evaluated under the less demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more
comprehensive tests applied to large banks.5 The proposal would also eliminate several
CRA data collection and reporting requirements currently applicable to large banks for
institutions with $10 billion or less in assets, including reporting on small-business,
small-farm and community development lending.6
Approximately 800 banks would no longer receive a community development evaluation
because the proposal would raise the small-bank threshold from $412 million to $1
billion.7 The 417 banks newly classified as intermediate rather than large would no
longer be examined under separate CRA investment and services tests and instead would
be evaluated based on their combined community development loans, investments and
services. These reclassifications and resulting eliminations of community development
obligations for over 800 banks and separate investment evaluations for 400 banks, may
worsen the housing crisis by reducing the demand for Low-Income Housing Tax Credits
(LIHTC).
Michigan will lose 15 of its 64 banks with CRA obligations if this proposal goes through.
Of those 64 banks, 29 have "large" bank status but this proposal would reduce that to
only 19 banks. Furthermore, this proposal jeopardizes 64 branches in low- and moderate-
income areas and 19 branches in communities of color.
This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and
moderate-income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to
affordable mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain


5 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,120–23 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
6 Id. at 52,120.
7 NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-rollbacks/.
 4
responsible small-business financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in
affordable housing, small businesses and other community development.
The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply
because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the
CRA obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify
the banks that would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the
communities those institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development
activity that would receive less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be
concentrated in low- and moderate-income communities or communities that have
experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
As a current and former board member of several community development corporations,
I am also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants
and nonprofit organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-business
development, financial counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and
other community-based services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with
nonprofit organizations. These resources can be particularly important to local
organizations that have deep relationships with residents and understand the specific
needs of their communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect
costs and new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for
smaller organizations.8 For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be
unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other operating expenses
are often necessary to deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also
have fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs. In addition,
many community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain
financial records, budgets or program documentation in the precise format a bank would
need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations
are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger
organizations whose activities are easier to verify.
These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn
capital into tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and
community development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have
consequences well beyond the banks themselves.
Before finalizing these provisions, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed
documentation requirements and limits on administrative expenses would reduce or
redirect bank support away from smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those with

8 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,129 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 5
limited administrative capacity. The agencies must also determine whether those effects
would ultimately reduce resources available to low- and moderate-income communities.
More broadly, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule primarily in terms of
reducing perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also determine
what the changes mean for the communities CRA is intended to serve.
Under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying small business does not
automatically constitute economic development. The activity must also satisfy a
requirement known as the "purpose test," meaning it must promote economic
development by supporting permanent job creation, retention, or improvement for low- or
moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income communities.9
The proposed rule would eliminate the "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks
could earn CRA credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or
improves jobs for low- and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income
communities. Instead, financing could qualify as economic development based primarily
on the type and size of the business and whether the financing expands, improves or
preserves the business's productive capacity, physical presence or employment base.10
I am concerned that this change would weaken the connection between CRA economic-
development credit and the people and communities CRA is intended to benefit.
Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying business expand does not necessarily create
jobs, increase economic opportunity in an underserved neighborhood or address the needs
of low- and moderate-income communities.
Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens
a qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank
to demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or
neighborhoods.11 The agencies themselves acknowledge that eliminating the purpose test
would expand the universe of activities eligible for CRA credit.12
Before eliminating the purpose test, the agencies should analyze what additional activities
would qualify under the new definition, where those activities are likely to occur, and
whether bank financing could shift away from activities that create or retain jobs for low-
and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income communities. The agencies
should also explain why eliminating the existing connection to these outcomes is

9 Federal Reserve Board, Interagency Questions and Answers Regarding Community Reinvestment, §
__.12(g)(3)-1 (explaining that CRA economic-development activities must satisfy both a "size" test and a
"purpose" test, and identifying permanent job creation, retention, or improvement for LMI persons or in
LMI geographies as qualifying purposes).
10 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,133-34 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
11 Id.
12 Id. at 52,133.
 6
consistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs
of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities.
Under current guidance, infrastructure projects in an LMI area generally receive CRA
credit only when they help keep or attract residents or businesses. The proposal
would change the standard by allowing credit for infrastructure that "benefits or serves" a
targeted area, even when the project delivers little meaningful benefit to LMI residents
and does not help preserve or strengthen the community.13
This means that a bank could seek CRA credit for financing a large regional
infrastructure project that only incidentally serves an LMI neighborhood, even if most of
the project's benefits flow to affluent communities or private companies. For example, a
data center located in or connected to an LMI tract could qualify despite creating few
permanent jobs and providing little direct benefit to residents.
Before expanding what infrastructure projects qualify for CRA credit in this way, the
agencies should analyze the impact of expanding the types of projects that qualify for
CRA credit on people with low- and moderate-incomes or low- and moderate-income
communities, including whether it could result in a reduction in projects that preserve or
strengthen LMI communities. In addition, the agencies should explain why changing the
standard is consistent with the CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting
the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
communities.
Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
● identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA
scrutiny under the proposal;
● quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
● assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or
populations, including rural communities and communities of color;
● consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without
sacrificing meaningful community accountability; and
Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, I believe that the OCC and
FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is
prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable
changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for
meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that
materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are

13 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,1335 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 7
consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
I also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120
days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service
evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The
current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that
do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would
allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather
examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more
complete record on which to base any final rule. I therefore request that the agencies
extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.

Sincerely
Corey A. Leon

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
I want to begin by thanking the agencies for the opportunity to comment on the proposed rulemaking to
amend the Community Reinvestment Act referred to in the subject line of this email. I’m writing in
support of them. I appreciate the fact that these changes are a targeted attempt to refocus on the
agencies’ supervision of our bank and not a full-scale overhaul of the regulation. Specifically, the
increase in thresholds to $1 billion for the new designation of “intermediate bank” will provide an
immediate and much needed regulatory relief to our financial institution.
I currently work for a $475 million dollar bank in northeast Louisiana that, under the current rules, has
just been considered an intermediate small bank this year. As such, we have begun to make the
transition from being considered a small bank for regulatory examination purposes. We were previously
evaluated under the lending test alone and now find ourselves preparing for a much larger and more
subjective set of criteria under the community development test of the regulation as well. Consideration
and preparation for personnel, software, policies, procedures, and training have diverted extra time and
resources that would otherwise be used in pursuit of the very goal the regulation states should be our
primary purpose. And once implemented, the current rules will still require us to continue this diversion
and apply it to endeavors outside our business model to hopefully satisfy what has quickly become an
additional regulatory burden.
We operate our business in a rural area and face the same concerns as much of our competition. They
mainly consist of banks just like us. And in our market, to stay viable as a business, we already must
advertise, donate, and make any and every bankable loan we can. In other words, we must reinvest in
the communities we serve, and we would do this without coercion. We also cannot refuse deposits
when presented even if doing so would create an eventual oversupply (and the cost associated). We do
this while also competing with much larger banks with a great deal more resources and a much larger
market/assessment area to spread their cost and risk.
And we also contend with the continued disadvantage in competition from tax exempt credit unions who
don’t face the same scrutiny under the regulation that we do. I have yet to hear a reasonable explanation
for that one. Talk about a double standard. We’re told that they are member-owned, non-profit, and
limited in membership by statute. I’m sure that is the case for some smaller outfits. But the continued
trend of larger credit unions buying other financial institutions creates a looming concern for community
banks and the communities they serve. Should one do this in the town I live in of less than 1,500 in a
parish of less than 10,000, the e􀆯ect on the tax base and infrastructure would be substantial. Should a
credit union buy two small banks, or two credit unions buy one each, the e􀆯ect would be much
worse. And the idea is not a stretch of the imagination.
Add fintechs, cryptocurrencies, and the like and it is no wonder that many of the small community banks
serving our communities in northeast Louisiana since our founding are no longer in business. They have
been replaced by out-of-town and out of area financial institutions. I mention all this to drive home the
2
idea that the type of regulatory relief o􀆯ered in the proposed rulemaking, especially where the increase in
thresholds to $1 billion is mentioned is much needed and appreciated. I believe our competitors that
have asset sizes above this amount are in a much better position to navigate the added regulatory
burden of a proposed “intermediate bank” designation. If the agencies don’t agree, then raise the
threshold some more. I also believe the alternative solution of aligning the threshold with the SBA’s
definition of small bank would not be helpful to the overall regulatory relief e􀆯ort for community banks.
In response to Question 60, Section V, Request for Comments in the proposed rule, regulatory relief
would better be given by keeping the current rule in place regarding the bank’s location of information
and CRA Public File with the option of providing it on the banks website rather than requiring it. For
instance, our bank’s public file must be updated at least annually and sometimes more than once a year
based on past changes to the required information in the file. This would require us to open a ticket with
our website provider each time. Since we seldom get requests from the outside public for this
information, we elect to keep it in paper form.

My institution, INVESTMENT BANK EEMBA (a US Bank Company), specializes in developing innovations for treasury and banking operations. The deposit we placed with the FDIC is based on claims processed through our founding company; we are now required—in coordination with OFAC, the Federal Reserve (Washington, D.C.), and the IRS—to execute the seizure of these claims and complete the clearing process for damages and business penalties. Our primary objective involves FinCEN-related blocking actions and the collection of damages and business penalties from treasuries, banks, companies, and individuals worldwide. Secondary activities include the establishment of the EEMBA Virtual Dollar and Virtual Euro; for these, we have placed deposits and developed protocols registered in both Europe and the United States. Through our technological development, we have created a contractual framework allowing treasuries and banks to utilize these protocols alongside a standardized fee schedule. Innovations regarding AI-driven treasury operations and advanced Super Intelligence (SI) technologies are currently the focus of a new project that grants us a global competitive advantage in the treasury sector. These innovations demand superior security standards, high-speed data processing, and the use of Quantum Supercomputer-backed Super Intelligence—technologies we have integrated from the very beginning to ensure the perfection of our products. Support from U.S. government institutions, the Federal Reserve (Washington, D.C.), and the FDIC will enable the future implementation of our projects. Existing programs facilitate our activities, and support for the rapid collection of claims is a crucial element of the operational deposit within the Federal Reserve (Washington, D.C.) ecosystem.
Thank Very Mach
Dr Elvis Zornic

Re: Connecticut Department of Banking request for an extension of the CRA comment period
RIN 3064-AG31, Docket ID OCC-2026-0694

Dear Chair Hill and Comptroller Gould:

The Connecticut Department of Banking ("CTDOB") would like to formally request an extension from the current
comment period of sixty days (60) to a minimum of one hundred twenty (120) days to address the recently proposed
changes to the Community Reinvestment Act ("CRA") rules.

The extension to a 120-day comment period would ensure that our agency and other stakeholders would have
sufficient time to thoughtfully examine the proposal. In particular, we would like to use the additional time to
analyze and consider the proposal to reclassify banks and the resulting impacts on community development and
housing commitment to the residents served in our communities low and moderate-income communities, and the
proposal to reclassify 1,200 banks which could significantly impact fulfillment of the objectives of CRA to the
detriment of low and moderate-income communities.

In summary, the CTDOB respectfully requests that the current 60-day comment period be extended to 120 days to
afford our agency and other stakeholders the ability to meaningfully assess the changes and how they may impact our
communities.

Respectfully,


Jorge Perez, Commissioner CT Department of Banking
