OCC: https://www.regulations.gov/commenton/OCC-2022-0002-0001
FDIC Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation: comments @fdic.gov

Federal Reserve Board of Governors: regs.comments@federalreserve.gov

Re: CRA NPR Comments — OPPOSE UNLESS AMENDED
OCC Docket ID OCC-2022-0002;

FDIC RIN 3064-AF81;

Federal Reserve Docket No. R-1769 and RIN 7100-AG29

To Whom It May Concern:

Civic Community Partners thanks the agencies for soliciting comments on a unified proposed
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rule that seeks to retain key components of the CRA, modernize
aspects where industry practices have outpaced the rules, and strengthen the ability of the CRA to
stabilize and revitalize communities.

The CRA has been hugely impactful in providing credit, investments and financial services to
underserved communities in California. In fact, the California Reinvestment Coalition, its members, and
allies have negotiated over $75 Billion in loans, investments, and financial services for communities of
color' and low-income communities in California over the last two years as part of Community Benefits
Agreements. Yet significant gaps remain in CRA rules and implementation, and the promise of CRA has
not yet been realized. While the agencies make several positive suggestions in the proposed rule, we
must oppose this proposal unless critical issues are addressed. The CRA must:

Take race into account and evaluate banks for service to borrowers and communities of color
Downgrade banks for harm such as discrimination, displacement, and fee gouging

Ensure affordable housing tax credits and lending are reviewed separately, and increased
Require banks to serve all areas (not 60%) where they take deposits and lend, and refrain from
raising current asset thresholds which will decrease rural reinvestment

1 The use of the terms "people of color" and "communities of color" is meant to be inclusive of African
American/Black, Latine/Hispanic, Asian American/Pacific Islander, and Native American persons and
neighborhoods.

 e Prioritize the opening of branches and penalize the closing of branches in underserved areas

e@ Elevate broadband/digital equity, access for Native American communities and climate
resiliency
Scrutinize the qualitative impact of all lending tied to banks, and end Rent-A-Bank partnerships
Enhance community participation so that CRA activity is tied to community needs, CRA ratings
reflect community impact, and bank mergers are denied unless they provide a clear public
benefit that regulators will enforce

Civic Community Partners is a CDFI that offers lending and investment services to organizations and
businesses that have limited access to traditional capital or financing mechanisms. Services include New
Markets Tax Credits, loans, lines of credit, as well as investments in housing and commercial real estate.
The CRA is very important to us as investments from regional and national banks is the main source of
financing that we use to foster livable communities and healthy neighborhoods, nurture small business,
and stimulate job creation in low and moderate-income communities.

Race and CRA. First and foremost, the agencies have failed the most important test for CRA reform —
will it substantially advance racial equity and close racial wealth gaps? Despite opening the door to
hopes that the rules would clearly address the redlining concerns that gave rise to the CRA, the agencies
punted.

The CRA should require banks to serve all communities, especially borrowers and communities of color.
Closing the racial wealth gap will make the nation and the economy stronger, elevate the Gross
Domestic Product and give the U.S. a more strategic competitive advantage. Examiners should review
bank performance in meeting the credit needs of communities of color, similar to how banks are
evaluated on their performance in meeting the needs of low and moderate income (LMI) borrowers and
communities. Urban Institute analysis shows that LMI communities and communities of color are not
the same. Bank records in extending fairly priced credit, financing community development, opening
responsive account products and maintaining branches to and in communities of color should factor into
a bank's CRA rating. This proposal not only fails to require this, but it also offers little as an alternative
approach to addressing redlining and discrimination.

The proposal to disclose HMDA mortgage lending data on Performance Evaluations is disappointing.
Merely requiring disclosure of already publicly available data on a report that the public rarely accesses
is not meaningful transparency. The agencies further clarify that any disparities in HMDA data will not
impact the CRA rating of a bank. At a minimum, this proposal should be enhanced to also require all
banks to place these home lending data tables and maps revealing inevitable disaggregated race and
ethnicity disparities in a prominent place on their own websites, include similar tables and maps for
small business lending by disaggregated race, ethnicity, gender and neighborhood when the Section
1071 data become publicly available, and provide that the data will impact CRA ratings.

8989 Rio San Diego Drive, Suite 100, San Diego, CA 92108 Phone 619-235-2200 Fax 619-236-9148 www.CivicCommunities.com

 The proposal raises the question as to whether CRA evaluations should consider Special Purpose Credit
Programs (SPCPs). But, though SPCPs are meant to serve groups protected by fair lending laws, the
proposal ponders SPCP evaluation only as to their impact on LMI consumers. The final rule must
explicitly recognize the importance of SPCPs as a critical way for banks to help meet the local credit
needs of communities of color, and SPCPs should garner CRA credit and positive impact points that
enhance a bank's CRA rating, as should all activities that close wealth gaps for racial, ethnic, national
origin, Limited English Proficient, LGBTQ and other underserved groups. These efforts are so important,
even if their reach is limited.

One positive aspect of the proposal is the expansion of considerations of discrimination to include
transactions beyond credit and lending, such as where discrimination occurs when a consumer tries to
open a bank account. But an expanded definition of discrimination is only as helpful as the agencies'
willingness and capacity to diligently look for evidence of discrimination and provide downgradres once
it is found. The General Accountability Office recently found that fair lending reviews at the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency were outdated and inconsistent.* Agency enforcement of redlining or
discrimination cases, as well as CRA ratings downgrades for discrimination, are exceedingly rare. Agency
fair lending reviews should be more extensive and rigorous, should solicit and rely on feedback from all
relevant federal and state agencies as well as community group stakeholders, and should be reflected
more substantively on CRA Performance Evaluations. Findings of discrimination, including for disparate
impacts relating to displacement financing, fee gouging or climate degradation, should always result in
automatic CRA ratings downgrades, if not outright failure. How can a bank that discriminates be said to
be doing a Satisfactory job serving the community?

Community development. We appreciate that the proposal focuses on encouraging banks to engage in
community development activities, such as investing in CDFls. Such activities can be amongst the most
impactful ways for banks to support community needs. But we are concerned that providing a lengthy
list of eligible activities and making it easier to qualify for credit will exacerbate the current dynamic
whereby banks engage in the easiest and potentially least impactful of CD activities. For the most part,
CRA credit should only be provided where the majority of beneficiaries are in fact, LMI or Black,
Indigeneious or People of Color (BIPOC) regardless of where the activity occurs or with whom. CD
activities should be tied to local community needs as identified in Performance Context analysis or
community-negotiated Community Benefits Agreements, either as a condition of receiving CRA credit or
through the use of enhancing impact scoring. Tribal or local government plans can serve this purpose of
credentialing an activity as responsive to local needs, but CRA rules should not require association to
government plans as local governments and local plans are uneven. We strongly oppose any raising of

2 General Accountability Office, "Fair Lending: Opportunities Exist to Enhance OCC's Oversight of Banks' Lending
Practices," GAO-22-104717, June 21, 2022 available at: https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-22-104717

8989 Rio San Diego Drive, Suite 100, San Diego, CA 92108 Phone 619-235-2200 Fax 619-236-9148 www.CivicCommunities.com

 current asset thresholds, since doing so would result in less community development financing and

branch consideration in rural areas served by community banks that would be subject to easier
examinations and lower reinvestment obligations under the proposal if they are reclassified.

Affordable housing. Affordable housing remains a perennial need and priority for our state. Mission-
driven and community organizations have developed impressive capacity to use the scarce resources
available to create affordable homes. However, the proposal threatens to damage one of the key tools
in this limited affordable housing development infrastructure by doing away with the separate CD
lending and CD investment tests. By combining CD lending and CD investing, we are greatly concerned
that banks will retreat from Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC), which can be more complex and
provide a lower rate of return than CD lending. Any decrease in appetite for LIHTC will likely result in
fewer affordable housing deals, as well as higher costs that will translate into decreased affordability for
projects that do get built. We urge the regulators to retain separate evaluations for CD lending and CD
investing. Further, positive impact points should be given for projects that have deeper affordability,
longer affordability terms and covenants, or are in higher opportunity areas.

Anti-displacement. We appreciate the proposal's attempt to address displacement concerns by requiring
that rents will likely remain affordable in order to qualify for CRA credit. But the agencies need to go
further to discourage banks from financing displacement. While the proposal appears to refuse CRA
credit for certain CD activities if they result in displacement, this requirement must be extended to all
community development activity, especially affordable and NOAH housing analysis. Regulations should
not allow community development credit unless banks can demonstrate that landlord borrowers are
complying with tenant protection, habitability, local health code, civil rights, credit reporting act, UDAAP
and other laws. Banks should adopt procedures such as CRC's Anti Displacement Code of Conduct and
engage in due diligence on the Beneficial Owners of LLC property owners - data they already collect - to
determine if there are any concerns relating to eviction, harassment, complaints, rent increases, or
habitability of potential bank borrowers. It is not enough to cease offering CRA credit for harmful
products. Banks must be penalized for harm. Bank regulators should conduct extensive outreach to
community groups and engage in community contacts to investigate whether landlord borrowers are
exacerbating displacement pressures or harming tenants. Because displacement often has a disparate
impact on BIPOC and protected classes, examiners should consider disparate displacement financing to
be discrimination, perhaps under the expanded definition, that should trigger CRA ratings downgrades
and subject banks to potential enforcement action.

Positive impact points should be given for particularly responsive CD activities that fight displacement,
such as support for property purchases by Community Land Trusts and other bona fide, mission-driven
nonprofit organizations of rental housing that can be taken off of the speculative market leveraged by
policies such as Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Acts (TOPA), Community Opportunity to Purchase Acts
(COPA), and other initiatives such as our state law that provides CLTs, nonprofits and prospective owner

8989 Rio San Diego Drive, Suite 100, San Diego, CA 92108 Phone 619-235-2200 Fax 619-236-9148 www.CivicCommunities.com

 occupants the right to match an investor's high bid at foreclosure auction to secure a property for the
common good, not personal profit.

Broadband and Native Land Areas. Certain CD activities should be further encouraged by allowing for
impact scoring and/or partial credit to the extent of LMI and BIPOC benefit even if that is less than 50%.
Here, we think of broadband activities, which can be a gateway to all CRA activity (banking, housing,
jobs, education, health, etc.), and support for Native Land Areas. We also support CRA credit for lending,
investment and services provided to members of the Native American community and (Black Native
American) Freedmen, regardless of where they reside.

Climate. We are pleased to see the proposal list climate resiliency and disaster preparedness as eligible
activities in light of the devastating impacts of climate change on LMI and BIPOC communities meant to
benefit from the CRA. The definitions in the proposal are strong and should be retained, perhaps with
more detailed examples. But the agencies have again failed to provide for downgrades where banks
engage in harm, such as fossil fuel financing. We have seen financial institutions tout green initiatives,
which presumably could earn CRA credit, even where such positive efforts were completely undermined
and overwhelmed by substantially greater investments in fossil fuel industries, many of which result in
an overshare of environmental burden in LMI communities and communities of color. It is not enough to
define positive activities. Banks must suffer penalties and downgrades for financing problematic
industries. This is especially the case here, as climate degradation by banks has created a vicious circle
where redlined communities disproportionately suffer climate harm at the hands of banks which may
then deny loans to such neighborhoods on the grounds that they are too risky and pose safety and
soundness concerns. The regulators should treat the financing of climate harm as discrimination that
can subject banks to CRA ratings downgrades and possible CRA exam failure where this harm
disproportionately impacts communities of color, as is often the case.

Mortgages. CRA credit should only be given for mortgage loan originations (not loan purchases by banks
from other lenders) to owner occupants (not to investors), unless the originating lender is a mission-
driven nonprofit, or the investor purchaser is an LMI or BIPOC buyer or mission-driven nonprofit
organization. We support the proposal to consider lending to low-income borrowers and communities
separately from lending to moderate income borrowers and communities. We urge the regulators to
evaluate lending for each loan purpose (home purchase, refinance, home improvement, HELOC)
separately. CRA consideration should NOT be given for mortgage lending to non BIPOC, middle- and
upper-income borrowers in LMI census tracts, as this fuels displacement, unless a census tract is shown
through the use of established models and data to be in an area not subject to gentrification. We
support the use of a primary product test to determine which bank products to evaluate, but this
formula must not allow large banks to evade consideration of a sizable portion of their lending. To
address this issue, we recommend that the primary products test be set at 15% of all bank products or
50 loans in an assessment area, whichever is smaller. We support a mortgage lending screening test and

8989 Rio San Diego Drive, Suite 100, San Diego,CA 92108 Phone 619-235-2200 Fax 619-236-9148 www.CivicCommunities.com

 appreciate agency analysis that suggests that the new scoring model proposed will result in less inflated
CRA ratings than currently. This would be a major advance. We are strongly opposed to any suggestion
that a bank could fail to serve nearly 40% of its assessment areas and still pass its CRA exams. This seems
a recipe for redlining of LMI and rural communities and communities of color.

Small business lending. We applaud the proposed focus on small business lending to smaller businesses.
We urge the regulators to require evaluation of both 1) lending to businesses with under $250,000 in
gross annual revenue (as proposed), as well as 2) lending to businesses with under $100,000 in gross
annual revenue. Such an approach would ensure that small businesses are served and would be
consistent with the current CRA Small Business Lending reporting regime. Yet we are surprised and
disappointed by the proposal to define small businesses as ones with $5 million or less in gross annual
revenue. The $5 million threshold under Section 1071 was proposed by the CFPB for a different purpose
altogether, namely, to establish reporting obligations under a fair lending rule that has not even been
finalized (and which could change). Approximately 95% of small businesses, 97.7 of minority owned
businesses and 98.3% of women owned businesses have less than $1 million in annual revenue', so to
establish the definition at $5 million seems counterproductive. The CRA rules should focus examiner
attention on section 1071 data reporting, once public, to ensure equal access to fairly priced credit for
women and BIPOC-owned businesses and for businesses with less than $1 million in revenue. Larger
businesses do not need the CRA's encouragement to banks, yet banks may gravitate to larger businesses
and away from small businesses if permitted to do so.

Branches and the Retail Services and Products Test. The agencies propose to revise the Services test.
We urge the regulators to retain core consideration of branch access as part of the CRA, and to expand
bank branch obligations in a more meaningful way. NCRC analysis shows a tremendous and detrimental
march by banks to close branches, especially in low income, BIPOC, and rural communities. A recent
analysis by the Committee for Better Banks, shows that branch openings fail to proportionally locate in
these same communities. We know that local branches mean more local jobs, more small business
lending in the community, and fewer visits to fringe financial providers like check cashers and payday
lenders. The CRA rules should clearly penalize branch closures and poor coverage in LMI, BIPOC and
rural communities, and encourage through impact scoring the opening of branches in such
communities.

Accounts and the Retail Services and Products Test. We support and urge proposals to provide both a
quantitative and a qualitative review of responsive deposit and retail credit products. Banks should be

evaluated not only for offering, for example, Bank On accounts, but for actually connecting consumers
with such accounts. We strongly believe that regulators should review the quality of all bank credit and

3 See https://files consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/201705_cfpb Key-Dimensions-Small-Business-Lending-
Landscape.pdf

8989 Rio San Diego Drive, Suite 100, San Diego, CA92108 Phone 619-235-2200 Fax 619-236-9148 www.CivicCommunities.com

 deposit products, especially in the consumer arena. This includes marketing, language access, terms,
rates, fees, defaults, and collections. All bank subsidiaries, affiliates and Rent-a-Bank partnerships should
be evaluated. Rent-a-Bank partnerships, in evading state law protections, are particularly pernicious and
should be banned. But until then, all products originated through the use of exported bank rate caps
should be evaluated as lending by that bank. All consumer loans should be evaluated if they constitute a
major product line, not just auto loans. And again, it is imperative that there be a qualitative review of
language access, pricing, fees, rates, delinquencies, collections, complaints by consumers and
community groups, and investigations and enforcement actions by federal and state agencies. We are
very concerned that combining all these critical components of CRA - meaningful access to branches,
accounts, and responsive credit products - will give them insufficient consideration in a test representing
only 15% of a bank's CRA rating.

Assessment areas. We appreciate the proposal to expand CRA coverage beyond branch locations, as we
have urged for years. The Retail Lending Assessment Areas are positive, though we suggest the
thresholds be lower (50 mortgages or 100 small business loans should trigger CRA responsibility) and
that bank obligations to serve these areas extend beyond retail lending to other bank offerings in order
to ensure that more rural communities are covered and that they are better served. But, the agencies
fail to create deposit-based assessment areas that require banks to reinvest dollars back into the
communities from which the deposits derive. This is this whole idea behind CRA. Every large bank knows
exactly where its deposits reside, and they should be required to disclose this publicly and to accept CRA
assessment areas where significant deposits are domiciled. This is the only way to keep up with
emerging industry and consumer trends, to ensure that deposits through neobanks and other deposit-
gathering third parties are assigned to local communities, and to prevent abuses and evasions such as
San Francisco-based companies like Square and Schwab establishing out-of-state non branch banks with
no proposed CRA responsibility in California despite soliciting a plurality of deposits from California.
There are a number of points in the proposal where the agencies would impose lesser obligations on
banks with between $2 billion and $10 billion in assets compared to banks with over $10 billion in
assets. We strongly feel that all large banks should be subject to all the responsibilities outlined for the
largest banks. Finally, while we support expanding CRA beyond branches, the CRA should retain a focus
on local communities and we urge the agencies to prioritize Facilities (branch) Based assessment areas,
perhaps through greater weighting of bank performance there.

Community participation. Though the agencies suggest that community participation is to be expanded,
there is little evidence for that in the proposal. Current CRA rules and implementation, as well as this
proposal, do a poor job of encouraging and valuing community input. Community comments on exams
are not solicited, and when provided, they are ignored. Community contacts appear a relic of the past,
and were never bank-specific, instead asking about community needs and how banks generally were
doing. Banks and the relevant agencies should post all comments on bank performance on their
websites and be required to provide a response. The agencies should actively solicit community

8989 Rio San Diego Drive, Suite 100, San Diego, CA 92108 Phone 619-235-2200 Fax 619-236-9148 www.CivicCommunities.com

 stakeholder input on the performance of particular banks during CRA exams and bank mergers. Ninety
days should be provided to the public to comment. Banks and regulators should clearly disclose contact
information for relevant staff. Bank mergers should default to public hearings when public commenters
raise concerns. Regulators must scrutinize bank merger applications to ensure that community credit
needs, convenience and needs, and public benefit standards are met. Community Benefits Agreements
should be encouraged as evidence that these standards can be met by the bank, and regulators should
condition merger approvals on ongoing compliance with CBAs. Agencies should routinely review all
existing consumer complaints, community comments, CFPB and agency investigations during CRA exams
and merger reviews. In particular, community groups should be solicited for their views on bank
practices relating to climate, displacement, discrimination, and other harms.

Conclusion

Civic Community Partners appreciates the opportunity to comment on proposed CRA rules. While there
are positive aspects of the proposal, and the agencies are to be commended for working together, we
cannot support this proposal in its current form. Significant changes need to be made to the final rule to
ensure that borrowers and communities of color are considered under the nation's anti-redlining law,
that banks are penalized for harm caused to communities - such as through displacement, climate
degradation, fee gouging, and discrimination - that community input is valued and elevated, and that
complex formulaic evaluation methodologies do not result in banks failing to meet critical community
needs relating to affordable housing, homeownership, small business development, broadband, and
rural and Native American community access. Thank you for considering these comments.

Andrew T. Phillips
President

8989 Rio San Diego Drive, Suite 100, San Diego, CA 92108 Phone 619-235-2200 Fax 619-236-9148 www.CivicCommunities.com

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes
Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

The Multicultural Real Estate Alliance for Urban Change, writes to object to the
harmful changes proposed to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The
CRA was passed by Congress in 1977 in response to redlining and creates an
affirmative obligation for banks to help meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs
of communities, including low and moderate income (LMI) communities. While the
CRA has successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest and provide services in
underserved communities, challenges related to redlining, discrimination,
underinvestment, and lack of access remain.

We are in the Greater Los Angeles AREA , South and East, and provide Homebuyer
education and resources to minority Communities because we serve working class
potential homeowners , and Homeowners at risk for lacking the ever changing
housing shortage in our area. We are partner members with RISE, and work
consistantly with local politicians to Outreach to our community.

The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift.
The proposal does not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on
LMI communities. We request an extension of the comment period for an additional
 etc.). We also urge the regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity
Act authorizes Special Purpose Credit Programs, and to once again encourage
banks to develop SPCPs to better serve communities that have been redlined,
excluded, and underserved. This is the essence of CRA.

Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information
to allow for meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of
entities and activities, and will undoubtedly harm the communities that the CRA
was meant to support. If finalized in substantially the same form as proposed,
communities will suffer significantly decreased investment in affordable housing and
CDFI support, more LMI branch closures, higher bank account fees, fewer
community serving nonprofit organizations, and increased bank discrimination and
redlining with no CRA consequence. The CRA will become further removed from its
purpose of encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and
the OCC to reconsider this proposal.

Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Very Truly Yours,

Dolores Golden, CEO

To Whom It May Concern:
On June 10, 2026, members of the Consumer Bankers Association's (CBA)1 Community
Reinvestment Committee, along with CBA staff,2 met in person with representatives of
the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC).
Discussion during the meeting included the OCC's and FDIC's proposed rulemaking
concerning changes to the agencies' Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations
(NPRM).3 Comments focused on the need for durability, consistency across agencies,

1 The CBA is a member-driven trade association, and the only national financial trade group focused
exclusively on retail banking—banking services geared toward consumers and small businesses. As the
recognized voices on retail banking issues, CBA provides leadership, education, research, and
representation for its members. CBA members operate in all 50 states. They include the nation's largest
bank holding companies as well as regional and super-community banks. The vast majority of CBA's
members are financial institutions holding more than $10 billion in assets.

2 David Pommerehn, CBA; Debbi Bauserman, CBA; and select members of the CBA Community
Reinvestment Committee.

 2

and clarity and predictability in any final CRA rule. The group also emphasized the
importance of prioritizing community impact over compliance burden. Key themes
included:
•
Durability – The group emphasized the importance of establishing a regulatory
framework that will stand the test of time and avoid significant changes in CRA
requirements from one administration to the next. A durable framework would
provide greater certainty for banks and the communities they serve.
•
Consistency across agencies – The group emphasized the importance of
achieving consistency among the federal banking agencies, including the Federal
Reserve, so that banks are not subject to divergent CRA standards or examination
approaches depending on their prudential regulator.
•
Clarity and predictability – Banks need clear and predictable standards so
they can understand regulatory expectations, plan accordingly, and effectively
meet their CRA obligations.
•
Community impact over compliance – CRA officers want to ensure that
bank resources are directed toward meeting the needs of their communities
rather than unnecessarily burdensome compliance processes. A CRA framework
should enable banks and their CRA professionals to devote as much time and
resources as possible to activities that produce meaningful community impact.
CBA intends to submit written comments addressing these and other issues by the
October 13, 2026, comment deadline.
Please contact the undersigned at dpommerehn@consumerbankers.com if you have any
questions.
Sincerely,
/s/
David Pommerehn
General Counsel
Consumer Bankers Association

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
on Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694;
RIN 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
The Wisconsin Partnership for Housing Development submits this comment in
opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued
by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC)0F1 because it would significantly weaken the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the
changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes,
carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities,
provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify
supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.
For more than 40 years, WPHD has delivered affordable housing across Wisconsin as we
honor the intentions of our founders and respond to the realities in our communities.
CRA has been an important tool in our work as it ensure that the banking and finance
system work for more than just those with wealth or access. The CRA creates partners
out of banks instead of being a company that just delivers loan products and mortgages.
While some of the financial institutions we have worked with over the past four decades
would operate the same with or without CRA, the reality is that most financial
institutions need some type of regulatory push to do the morally right thing. WPHD is a

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 2
long-term member of the National Community Reinvestment Coalition and actively
utilizes CRA in our many projects.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important
in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal
access to mainstream financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and
would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and
support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being
considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-
income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination
and disinvestment.
We are concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations.
Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development, financial
counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based
services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations.
These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have deep
relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect
costs and new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for
smaller organizations.1F2 For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be
unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other operating expenses
are often necessary to deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also
have fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs. In addition,
many community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain
financial records, budgets or program documentation in the precise format a bank would
need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations
are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger
organizations whose activities are easier to verify.
Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and
partnerships can play in supporting community development. Our banking partners have
provided us with more than $100,000 last year in funding to support our mission with

2 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,129 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 3
most of those funds being unrestricted grants. The ability to use the funding without
onerous rules or reporting requirements is critically important.
These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn
capital into tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and
community development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have
consequences well beyond the banks themselves.
Before finalizing these provisions, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed
documentation requirements and limits on administrative expenses would reduce or
redirect bank support away from smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those with
limited administrative capacity. The agencies must also determine whether those effects
would ultimately reduce resources available to low- and moderate-income communities.
More broadly, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule primarily in terms of
reducing perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also determine
what the changes mean for the communities CRA is intended to serve.
Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
● identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA
scrutiny under the proposal;
● quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
● assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or
populations, including rural communities and communities of color;
● consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without
sacrificing meaningful community accountability; and
Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes
that the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its
impacts is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs
considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for
meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that
materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are
consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120
days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service
evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The
current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
 4
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that
do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would
allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather
examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more
complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies
extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.

Sincerely

Todd Mandel, Executive Director
Wisconsin Partnership for Housing Development
cc. National Community Reinvestment Coalition

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on
Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN
1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Comprehensive Housing Assistance, Inc. (CHAI) submits this comment in opposition
to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the
Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC)1 because it would significantly weaken the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of
the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed
changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income
communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the
agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline
by 60 days.
CHAI is a nonprofit housing and community development organization serving
northwest Baltimore City and adjacent Baltimore County neighborhoods. CHAI
directly serves approximately 4,000 individuals each year and 15,000 through our
broader community development initiatives. We also own and oversee the
management of 1,700+ units of affordable housing, have facilitated the investment of
more than $7.5 million in northwest Baltimore, and deliver targeted programming for
2,500 older adults each year.

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 CHAI: Comprehensive Housing Assistance, Inc. 5809 Park Heights Avenue • Baltimore, Maryland
21215 • 410-500-5300 • Fax: 410-466-1996 chaibaltimore.org


2 The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit for outside their assessment areas if the banks surpass a benchmark of
0.625% of its tier 1 capital for community development loans and likewise 0.625% for investments. 91 Fed. Reg. 52121, 52140
(proposed Aug. 12, 2026). We are concerned that the practical effect of this proposal is that the benchmark will serve not as a floor,
but a ceiling.
3 NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk, (Sept. 10, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-development-activity-at-risk/.
4 NCRC, The Proposed CRA Rule's Strategic Plans: A More Predictable Path to Doing Less (Sept 1, 2026), https://ncrc.org/the-
proposed-cra-rules-strategic-plans-a-more-predictable-path-to-doing-less/.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework
for ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including
low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that
communities depend on access to both credit and deposit services. These protections
remain especially important in communities that have experienced redlining,
disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and
would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and
support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being
considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-
income communities and on communities that have experienced historic
discrimination and disinvestment.
We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1
capital devoted to either community development loans or investments would be
enough to receive a passing CRA rating.2 However, that percentage is far lower than
the percentage the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined
the largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.
NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the
OCC and FDIC supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that
these banks currently conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community
development loans and investments inside their assessment areas, and that the median
percentage of annual community development lending in assessment areas was 6.8%
of tier 1 capital, and a median of 3.6% of tier 1 capital for annual CRA qualified
investments.3 If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet
separate thresholds of 0.625% of Tier 1 capital for community development lending
and investments, combined activity would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually
-- a decrease of approximately $87.1 billion, or 85%. Similarly, the proposal
encourages banks to use strategic plans to make their CRA compliance easier and
more predictable. Previous proposed guidance also set strategic plan benchmarks for
CRA performance well-below historical levels of community development activity.4
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic
discrimination cannot withstand such a reduction in community development
investments and loans. If regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend
to, and be accountable to the communities they serve, there could be harmful


CHAI: Comprehensive Housing Assistance, Inc. 5809 Park Heights Avenue • Baltimore, Maryland
21215 • 410-500-5300 • Fax: 410-466-1996 chaibaltimore.org


5 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,129 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
consequences for communities. It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize
banks to meet community needs. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should
analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce lending, services or investment
available to low- and moderate-income communities and whether communities that
have experienced historic discrimination or disinvestment would be disproportionately
affected.
In addition, we are concerned about the proposal's treatment of community
development grants and nonprofit organizations. Banks often support affordable
housing, small-business development, financial counseling, workforce programs,
neighborhood revitalization and other community-based services through grants,
investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations. These resources can
be particularly important to local organizations that have deep relationships with
residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect
costs and new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for
smaller organizations.5 For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be
unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other operating
expenses are often necessary to deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller
organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread
these costs. In addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff
and may not maintain financial records, budgets or program documentation in the
precise format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that
grants to smaller organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may
redirect funding toward larger organizations whose activities are easier to verify.
Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and
partnerships can play in supporting community development, including support for
housing counseling, affordable housing, foreclosure prevention, financial education,
neighborhood revitalization, and the operating capacity of nonprofit organizations.
Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
● identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less
CRA scrutiny under the proposal;
● quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and
community development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
● assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or
populations, including rural communities and communities of color;
● consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without
sacrificing meaningful community accountability; and
Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization
believes that the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough
analysis of its impacts is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal
 CHAI: Comprehensive Housing Assistance, Inc. 5809 Park Heights Avenue • Baltimore, Maryland
21215 • 410-500-5300 • Fax: 410-466-1996 chaibaltimore.org

likely needs considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related
activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for
meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that
materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are
consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least
120 days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and
service evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation.
The current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input
from community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other
stakeholders that do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted.
An extension would allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical
consequences, gather examples from the communities they serve, and provide the
agencies with a more complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore
request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60
days.
Sincerely,
Comprehensive Housing Assistance, Inc.

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Attached is a comment letter from California Intertribal Alliances opposing the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act regulations. Our letter addresses how the proposal could reduce access to responsible lending, community development investment, banking services, and support for grassroots nonprofits, small businesses, and underserved Central Valley communities.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0065_09000064b95f674f.pdf:
2547 W. Shaw Ave., Suite 108​
Fresno, CA 93711​
naomi@californiaintertribalalliances.org​
559-448-7515

September 30, 2026

Travis Hill, Chair
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
550 17th Street NW,
Washington, DC 20429
RIN 3064-AG31
Via email: comments@FDIC.gov

Jonathan V. Gould, Comptroller
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
400 7th St. SW,
Washington, DC 20219
Docket ID OCC-2026-0694
Via: https://regulations.gov/

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

California Intertribal Alliances writes to object to the harmful changes proposed to
the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed by Congress in
1977 in response to redlining and creates an affirmative obligation for banks to help
meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of communities, including low and
moderate income (LMI) communities. While the CRA has successfully encouraged
banks to lend, invest and provide services in underserved communities, challenges
related to redlining, discrimination, underinvestment, and lack of access remain.



 California Intertribal Alliances is a California 501(c)(3) public benefit nonprofit
serving Indigenous and other underserved communities throughout California's
Central Valley. Our culturally grounded programs and activities support cultural
preservation, community wellness, food access, creative expression, and
cross-cultural solidarity. We also strive to encourage community entrepreneurship
by sharing information, creating supportive connections, and empowering people
who dream of becoming business owners to pursue their goals.
As a relatively new nonprofit led by a founder who is also building a small local
business, we have experienced how difficult it can be to access financial support,
responsible credit, and meaningful banking relationships. California Intertribal
Alliances does not currently receive CRA-related funding or institutional support
from financial institutions. This is not because community need or potential impact
is absent. New and grassroots organizations frequently encounter complicated and
resource-intensive application processes, limited information about available
opportunities, capacity requirements that tend to favor larger or more established
organizations, and systems that depend heavily on existing institutional
relationships.
These barriers make it difficult for newer community-led organizations, small
businesses, and emerging entrepreneurs to access the investments, responsible
lending opportunities, grants, banking services, and partnerships intended to
benefit underserved communities. We need clearer, more transparent, and more
accessible pathways to CRA-related support. Weakening CRA obligations would not
eliminate the barriers we already face; it could significantly reduce opportunities in
Central Valley communities that continue to experience underinvestment and
limited financial access.
The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift.
The proposal does not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on
LMI communities. We request an extension of the comment period for an additional
60 days so we have time to better understand how much CRA activity may be lost
to communities because of this proposal – an analysis the regulators did not
conduct or provide.
The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved
communities in several ways.

1) Community development (CD) activities for affordable housing
and small businesses will drop dramatically.
As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities
that support critically needed affordable housing and economic development
projects. These activities often provide the greatest CRA impact in communities as
 they strengthen economic stability and mobility, quality of life, and social health of
residents and communities.

The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large"
Banks, such that many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and
expectation to serve the community development needs of their communities.[1]
According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70
California banks would see their reinvestment obligations reduced under the
proposal. Twenty-five California banks would shed their Community Development
Test responsibilities entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer be subject to
the Investment Test.[2]

The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical
community development programs that have had large impacts in LMI
communities. These include Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) which are a
key driver of affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) which
fuel economic development projects in tribal and other areas; and EQ2 equity
equivalent investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs)
that provide small business lending in underserved areas that banks cannot reach,
and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that take property off of the speculative
market.

Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting
the critical importance of the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable
housing.[3] Approximately half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from CRA
motivated banks.[4] The regulators will even further weaken CD obligations if they
adopt the alternative proposal that Large Banks be defined as those with over $30
billion in assets.

Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance
even where they remain subject to the Community Development and Investment
Tests. The regulators signal to all banks that they can do significantly less CD
lending and investment and still pass their CRA examinations, all while seeking CRA
credit for activity outside of their CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests
that a bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1
capital were devoted to CD loans and CD investments. That percentage is far lower
than the percentage that NCRC determined banks currently devote to community
investments and loans. If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary
to meet the proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by approximately
$87.1 billion, or 85%.[5]

Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have
tremendous negative impacts on affordable housing and small business
development in our state. Asset thresholds should not be raised.

2) Banks will shed branches and BankOn.
The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and maintain
branches in LMI and BIPOC neighborhoods. By increasing the asset threshold for a
Large Bank to over $10 billion, forty-five banks in California will no longer be
subject to the Services Test and reviewed to ensure that their branches are serving
LMI communities. In California alone, NCRC estimates that 245 branches in LMI
areas and 497 branches in neighborhoods of color would be vulnerable to closure
due to this proposal.[6]

Branch presence has been tied to increased small business lending in communities.
Fewer branches will result in less small business lending. These changes will be
particularly hard hitting in rural areas of our state where smaller banks originate a
larger portion of the small business loans.

The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to
offer deposit products that are accessible to LMI residents.[7] Deposit accounts are
a gateway to credit access, financial stability, and wealth building, especially for
families who are otherwise preyed upon by predatory financial institutions. As one
important example, the BankOn program has provided access to no or low fee bank
accounts for over fourteen million people.[8] California is home to several BankOn
coalitions that establish effective partnerships among banks, community-based
organizations, and local governments. The proposal jettisons this work.

Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million
are underbanked.[9] National banks regulated by the OCC charged billions of
dollars in overdraft and non-sufficient fund fees in 2025, and in California alone,
state-chartered banks charged over fifty-six million dollars ($56 million) in OD and
NSF fees to California consumers in 2025.[10]

3) Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.
Another consequence of the proposal's drive to raise asset thresholds is that fewer
banks will be required to report data regarding their small business, small farm,
and community development lending activities. Such data is critical to
understanding not only individual bank performance, but also the needs of local
markets. Rise Economy and its member organizations routinely analyze this CRA
data when meeting with banks and commenting on CRA exams and mergers. The
loss of such data is particularly harmful at a time when the Administration is
walking back efforts to collect and disclose detailed small business lending data
under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank Act. These changes will disproportionately
impact rural communities in our state where banks up to $10 billion in assets make
up a larger part of the small business and small farm lending markets.

 4) Native American communities and Tribal Nations will not see
sufficient benefits.
The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the needs
of Native American communities and Tribal Nations which have been poorly served
by banks. The current rules focus CRA obligations in areas where banks have
branches, even though there are far fewer bank branches near Tribal lands and in
rural areas where Native Americans may reside. The proposal seeks to address this
CRA gap by encouraging banks to engage in community development and related
activities in "Indian Country" and on "Tribal and Native lands," even if outside of
bank CRA assessment areas. But many members of Tribes in California will not
benefit from this proposal as they do not live in Indian Country or on Tribal or
Native lands, as defined.

CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring within
particular geographies, given the challenges and impacts associated with historic
dispossession and federal policy. Instead, CRA evaluations should also consider
whether banks have established meaningful relationships with, and provided direct
benefits to, federally recognized Tribes as well as non-federally recognized Tribes.
Non-federally recognized Tribes have been acknowledged by, and are able to access
programs and contracts with, various local and state entities.[11] Such processes
exist.

More specifically, the CRA rules should encourage banks to serve Tribes, nonprofit
organizations or other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned businesses
that are majority owned and controlled by Native American entrepreneurs by
providing:
●​ Active outreach and engagement
●​ Community development loans and investments for affordable housing and
economic development projects
●​ Small farm and small business loans
●​ Home mortgage loans
●​ Grants to meet community needs, including for capacity building for Tribes
and support for Tribes seeking federal recognition if desired
●​ Support for cultural, health and other programs
●​ Bank branches
●​ Deposit products such as affordable bank accounts, and
●​ The provision of financial services such as financial literacy, apprenticeship
programs and technical assistance support

While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities
outside of their branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made to
encourage banks to engage in CRA related activity to directly benefit Tribes,
nonprofit organizations and other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned
 businesses that are majority owned and controlled by Native American
entrepreneurs.

A better approach is needed. All banks should be subject to an impact and
responsiveness review factor during their CRA exams that evaluates and tracks
whether banks have engaged in any CRA activity directly with Tribes, Tribally
controlled entities and Native owned businesses.[12] If banks know they will be
examined for their work with Tribes, they will find mutually beneficial ways to work
with Tribes.

5) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will
suffer.
The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by
requiring a demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating
that large banks and their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more
than 15% of these grants on overhead.[13] As if this wasn't enough, the FDIC and
OCC question whether they should end CRA eligibility for bank grantmaking to
nonprofits entirely.

Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian
measures will be except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller
groups, may be impacted.[14]

Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local
needs. They also can be key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and
investment products into communities inclined to trust long established local
organizations. Many nonprofit organizations and programs, such as downpayment
assistance programs, that support CRA related activity, rely on bank contributions
to operate. Smaller, local, and rural organizations will be least able to meet new
reporting obligations, and they risk losing bank support as a result. The proposal
would also end impactful contributions from banks for general operating support,
sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.

Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their
communities on their own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps
in their own capacity – seeking assistance with community outreach, borrower
education, credit building and repair, technical assistance, legal services, job
training and placement, tax assistance, affordable housing and other services and
programs which help residents become stable and bankable so that banks can
attract new deposits and make new loans in LMI communities.

The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and will
focus grantmaking on larger organizations that can help them more easily meet
their new FDIC and OCC-imposed regulatory burdens.

Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15%
overhead restriction will negatively affect operations and organizational success. As
one example, in order to secure CRA grants from Large Banks, CDFIs will need to
pare down costs for critical operational expenses such as underwriting, servicing,
compliance, technology, impact measurement, product development, and borrower
technical assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions,
organizations are put at risk.

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA
activity that contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large
negative impact it will have on nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding,
the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are meant to benefit from the CRA,
and the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

6) Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.
There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link
between CRA and LMI impact in the name of easing bank burden.

Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their
top two major product lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in,
and profiting from, communities, this lending by banks, subsidiaries and affiliates
must be evaluated. Further, certain products, such as small farm and consumer
loans, are important in many communities, but may not be among a bank's largest
product lines. If regulators give banks a pass and exempt smaller product lines
from CRA oversight, banks will have less incentive to consider how those products
are offered.

Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and
soundness, encourages banks to meet community needs, and engenders greater
trust in banks by the community. Eliminating categories of loan products from
scrutiny will have the opposite effect.

No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test,
which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the
definition of economic development. The CRA should create greater incentives for
banks to support the creation of jobs that pay family sustaining wages for LMI
workers and in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to provisions that would provide
CRA credit for job creation and economic development that may only benefit
middle- and upper-income workers and communities. Such provisions ignore the
purpose of CRA.

Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA
credit for large scale community infrastructure products that generate profits for
 banks, would likely be financed without CRA credit, and provide only incidental
benefits to LMI residents and communities. Such an expansion of what qualifies for
CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities.
For example, banks might choose to more profitably earn CRA credit by financing
larger scale infrastructure projects, like bridges, in lieu of financing less lucrative,
smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local community needs (such as
childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or resilience
projects).

Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA
should require banks to focus their CRA activities on their CRA assessments
areas,[15] where they are subject to more rigorous regulatory oversight (with an
exception made to encourage banks to better serve Tribes, as noted above). Banks
are not doing enough currently to meet the credit and deposit needs in the areas
where they have CRA responsibility, a problem the regulators tried to address in the
2023 CRA Rule.[16] Yet the proposal further encourages banks to seek CRA credit
for projects in areas away from their branches, lending and CRA responsibility. This
will enable banks to get credit for activity outside of their assessment areas, while
providing no accompanying CRA obligation to better serve these areas.

Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal goes
out of its way to encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan option to meet
their CRA responsibilities. The Strategic Plan was meant for financial institutions
that operated under a unique business model that the CRA rules were not designed
to address. The Strategic Plan option provides for minimal public input and
regulatory scrutiny and allows banks to determine the level of reinvestment activity
they need to engage in to earn a passing CRA grade. In our experience, banks with
Strategic Plans tend to reinvest less in the community and in less impactful ways.
The OCC's guidance establishing low community development thresholds for banks
opting for the Strategic Plan, [17] validates this perspective.

Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community
development efforts with little benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing,
where units are affordable at a point in time but not encumbered by deed or rent
restrictions, are a feature of today's housing market. But CRA rules should not give
banks credit for financing such activities where the benefit to LMI residents and
communities is unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it
can be a driver of bank investment in problematic landlords and displacement. CRA
credit should be given for financing of NOAH only if the project is owned and
operated by mission-driven organizations, where a majority of residents are LMI
tenants, and the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are
compliant with tenant rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents
can reasonably be expected to retain their housing.

 7) Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA
ratings downgrades.
The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and redline
should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding"
ratings. Under the Biden Administration, at least a dozen banks that passed their
CRA exams were accused of redlining. This proposal will only increase that number
by narrowing what constitutes evidence of discrimination that may be considered
for the purpose of downgrading a bank's CRA rating. Here, regulators should
consider any evidence that a bank, its affiliates, or subsidiaries engaged in
discrimination, redlining, or illegal credit practices as part of their lending, deposit,
branching, or other activities. This evidence should be considered regardless of its
source (public or private parties), or its form (informal complaints, research based
on data, testing results, comment letters, administrative actions, private litigation,
etc.). We also urge the regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity
Act authorizes Special Purpose Credit Programs, and to once again encourage banks
to develop SPCPs to better serve communities that have been redlined, excluded,
and underserved. This is the essence of CRA.

Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information to
allow for meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of
entities and activities, and will undoubtedly harm the communities that the CRA
was meant to support. If finalized in substantially the same form as proposed,
communities will suffer significantly decreased investment in affordable housing and
CDFI support, more LMI branch closures, higher bank account fees, fewer
community serving nonprofit organizations, and increased bank discrimination and
redlining with no CRA consequence. The CRA will become further removed from its
purpose of encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and
the OCC to reconsider this proposal.

Thank you for your consideration of this request.



Respectfully submitted,
Naomi Isabel Ortega-Singh​
Founder and Chief Executive Officer
​
California Intertribal Alliances​
naomi@californiaintertribalalliances.org​
559-448-7515
