Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on
Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN
1557-AF57; FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Behind The Leaf submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation (FDIC) concerning the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).
Behind The Leaf is a 501(c)(3) philanthropic organization powered by Flourish Media that works
to strengthen financial readiness, access to capital, and economic opportunity for women
business owners. Through financial education, investor-readiness programming, small-business
grants, community conversations, and connections between entrepreneurs and potential
funders, we see firsthand how important responsible financial institutions and community
investment are to the ability of entrepreneurs and families to build sustainable economic futures.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring
that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. These protections remain especially important for
communities and entrepreneurs that have historically experienced barriers to capital, unequal
access to financial services, and disinvestment.
 We are particularly concerned that the proposed rule would reduce meaningful accountability for
banks while potentially decreasing the resources available to small businesses, nonprofit
organizations, affordable housing, and other community development efforts.
Reduction in Community Investment Expectations
CRA obligations help incentivize banks to invest in the communities they serve. The proposed
rule would substantially lower the level of community development activity that could be
sufficient for banks to receive CRA credit. The NCRC template notes that the proposal could
effectively reduce community development lending and investment by approximately 85% if
banks conduct only the proposed 0.625% benchmarks.
For organizations like Behind The Leaf, this is concerning because community investment is not
an abstract concept. Capital from financial institutions can translate into grants, sponsorships,
financial education, small-business support, affordable housing, and opportunities for
entrepreneurs to build sustainable businesses.
Women entrepreneurs, particularly those operating small and growing businesses, need access
to responsible capital and financial institutions that understand the communities they serve.
Reducing incentives for banks to invest in those communities could make it more difficult for
entrepreneurs to obtain financing, build assets, create jobs, and contribute to local economic
development.
The agencies should therefore analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce lending,
services, and investment available to low- and moderate-income communities and whether
communities that have experienced historic barriers to capital would be disproportionately
affected.
Protect Support for Community-Based Nonprofits
We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations.
Community-based nonprofits often have the relationships, trust, and knowledge necessary to
translate financial resources into meaningful outcomes for residents and entrepreneurs.
Organizations such as Behind The Leaf work directly with communities to provide education,
connections, resources, and opportunities that may otherwise be difficult to access.
The proposed 15 percent limit on indirect costs for grants from large banks, along with
additional documentation requirements, could create significant challenges for smaller
organizations. Staff, technology, accounting, compliance, facilities, and other operating
expenses are not separate from the programs nonprofits provide—they are part of the
infrastructure required to deliver those programs effectively.
 If banks determine that supporting smaller nonprofits is more difficult or costly to document, they
may redirect funding toward larger organizations whose activities are easier to verify. That could
reduce resources available to community-based organizations that are closest to the people and
entrepreneurs they serve.
We urge the agencies to analyze whether these proposed documentation requirements and
administrative-cost limitations would redirect bank support away from smaller nonprofit
organizations and ultimately reduce resources available to low- and moderate-income
communities.
Preserve the Connection Between Economic Development and Community
Benefit
Behind The Leaf is particularly concerned about the proposed elimination of the existing
"purpose test" for economic development.
Under current CRA guidance, qualifying economic-development activities must have a
meaningful connection to job creation, retention, or improvement for low- or moderate-income
people or communities. The proposed rule would eliminate this purpose test and allow a
broader range of business financing to qualify for CRA credit without requiring banks to
demonstrate that the financing creates or improves economic opportunity for low- and
moderate-income people or communities.
This change could weaken the connection between CRA credit and the communities CRA is
intended to benefit.
Supporting a business is important, but economic development should also be measured by
whether that investment creates opportunity, strengthens communities, supports employment,
and expands access to economic mobility. A bank should not be able to receive CRA credit
simply because financing increases the productive capacity of a business if there is no
meaningful connection to underserved people or communities.
The agencies should analyze what additional activities would qualify under the proposed
definition and whether bank financing could shift away from activities that create or retain jobs
and economic opportunities for low- and moderate-income people and communities.
Maintain Transparency and Accountability
We are also concerned about changes that would reduce CRA data collection and reporting
requirements.
Meaningful data allows communities, regulators, and researchers to understand where credit is
flowing, identify gaps, and determine whether banks are meeting local needs. The proposed
rule would eliminate annual CRA data collection and reporting requirements for more than 400
banks with assets of $10 billion or less, according to the NCRC template.
 For organizations working to improve financial readiness and access to capital for
entrepreneurs, less information about lending and community development activity makes it
more difficult to understand where barriers exist and where additional investment is needed.
The agencies should not reduce transparency before analyzing how the loss of CRA data would
affect communities' ability to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance, and understand
whether local credit needs are being met.
Conclusion
Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not adequately:
●​ Identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny;
●​ Quantify changes in branches, lending, investments, services, and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
●​ Assess whether the effects would be concentrated in particular geographic areas or
populations;
●​ Consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
meaningful community accountability.
Given these concerns, Behind The Leaf believes the OCC and FDIC should rescind the
proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and released for public
comment.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
the credit needs of the communities they serve. Changes that materially weaken that
accountability should not be finalized without demonstrating that they are consistent with the
CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period by at least 60 days. The
proposed rule is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant
changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations,
nonprofit grants, reporting, and other core elements of CRA implementation.
Thank you for considering this comment and for your continued commitment to ensuring that
financial institutions remain accountable to the communities they serve.
Sincerely,
Behind The Leaf​
A 501(c)(3) philanthropic organization powered by Flourish Media

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Community Reinvestment Act
Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Habitat for Humanity Philadelphia is pleased to offer this comment on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced
above. We work alongside Philadelphia families, volunteers, financial institutions, and community partners to build and
preserve affordable homeownership. We see every day that responsible credit and meaningful community investment
are not abstract policy issues; they determine whether families can buy a home, repair the home they already own, and
remain rooted in their neighborhoods. We also see first-hand the impact of our work. We get to see how housing
creates the strong foundation that so many other opportunities spring from. If we care about health, education,
community safety, resilience, economic mobility and general wellbeing- then we must look to create pathways to stable
housing. We oppose the proposal because it would weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) and reduce the
resources and accountability needed to address Philadelphia's urgent housing needs. We ask the agencies to examine
these community-level consequences, release the supporting analysis for public comment, and extend the current
deadline by at least 60 days.
Habitat for Humanity Philadelphia serves families and communities across Philadelphia. We build and rehabilitate
affordable homes, provide critical home repairs, offer affordable mortgage financing and housing counseling, and work
with residents and partners on neighborhood revitalization. Our work is concentrated in communities where decades of
redlining and disinvestment continue to shape access to safe housing, credit, and opportunity, including neighborhoods
in North, West, and South Philadelphia and Germantown.


For the past four decades, Habitat for Humanity Philadelphia has seen the CRA serve as an important part of the federal
framework for ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-
income neighborhoods. These protections remain especially important in Philadelphia communities that have
experienced redlining, sustained disinvestment, branch loss, and unequal access to mainstream financial services.
Habitat for Humanity Philadelphia relies on strong, accountable bank partnerships to create and preserve affordable
homeownership. Banks support our work through grants and sponsorships; loans and lines of credit; acquisition,
construction, and development financing; responsible mortgage products for Habitat homebuyers; purchases and
servicing of Habitat mortgages; investments in home repair and neighborhood revitalization; and employee volunteer
engagement. These relationships help us develop new homes, help low-income families secure affordable mortgages,
complete critical repairs for longtime homeowners, and make sustained investments in neighborhoods.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and change how regulators evaluate
community development, bank services, and support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes
are being considered without adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and
communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
CRA obligations give banks a clear reason to invest across Philadelphia, including in neighborhoods that have historically
received too little private capital. Bank support helps Habitat Philadelphia finance land acquisition and development,
build and rehabilitate affordable homes, offer affordable mortgages, fund critical repairs, preserve aging housing, and
support neighborhood revitalization. This partnership matters because public and philanthropic dollars alone cannot
meet the scale of Philadelphia's housing needs.
We are concerned that the proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in our communities. For example, it
suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital devoted to either community development loans or
investments would be enough to receive a passing CRA rating. This represents a dramatic reduction in what large banks
currently devote to community investments and loans, and we fear that this guidance may operate as a ceiling instead
of a floor. Pennsylvania currently receives more than $3 billion in CRA-related investments annually, but under the
proposed rule that could fall to just over $600 million—an 80% loss.
Low- and moderate-income communities cannot withstand such a reduction. For Habitat Philadelphia, reduced bank
engagement could mean fewer resources to acquire land, build or rehabilitate homes, provide affordable mortgage
financing, complete critical repairs, preserve existing homeownership, and invest in neighborhoods. In North, West, and
South Philadelphia and Germantown, it could mean fewer homes, longer waits for repairs, delayed projects, and less
investment in communities that have already waited too long for equitable access to capital.
It is imperative that the CRA continue to incentivize banks to meet the needs of communities like ours. Before finalizing
the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce lending, services, or investment


available to low- and moderate-income communities and whether historically disinvested communities would be
disproportionately affected.
The proposal would also substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under CRA.
Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while banks with assets between $1 billion and $10
billion would generally be evaluated under the less demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more
comprehensive tests applied to large banks. The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting
requirements currently applicable to large banks, including reporting on small-business and community development
lending.
Banks serving communities across Pennsylvania could therefore be subject to less rigorous requirements. These
reclassifications may worsen the housing crisis by reducing investment in affordable housing, access to mortgages for
first-time homebuyers, financing for home repairs, and capital for community-based development.
The proposed rule would also narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service test. Today, examiners may
consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and information about the costs and features of deposit accounts.
The proposal would limit this criterion to credit services, removing checking and savings products from direct evaluation.
Yet affordable accounts and accessible branches help families safely receive income, build savings, establish banking
relationships, and qualify for responsible mortgage credit.
For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate from access to credit and
economic opportunity. Many of the neighborhoods where Habitat Philadelphia works in North, West, and South
Philadelphia and Germantown have few convenient full-service bank branches. Residents may need to travel farther for
basic banking, rely on costly alternative financial services, or try to establish the banking relationships and savings
history needed for homeownership without a trusted institution nearby. A CRA service test that overlooks deposit
products and physical branch access ignores how families actually enter and navigate the financial system.
The agencies have not shown that community needs become less significant simply because a bank falls below a higher
asset threshold. Before reducing CRA obligations, they should identify the banks that would move into less rigorous
categories, determine the communities those institutions serve, analyze the activity that would receive less scrutiny, and
assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-income, rural, or historically disinvested
communities.
We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and nonprofit organizations.
Habitat affiliates use bank grants, sponsorships, investments, and loans to support land acquisition, predevelopment,
construction, rehabilitation, home repair, housing counseling, mortgage operations, neighborhood revitalization, and
organizational capacity. These resources make it possible to convert capital into lasting benefits for families and
neighborhoods.


For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15% limit on indirect costs and new documentation
requirements that could create substantial burdens for affiliates. Staff, facilities, technology, accounting, compliance,
insurance, and other operating expenses are necessary to deliver affordable housing and repair programs. Smaller
affiliates may have fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs. If banks conclude that grants
to local organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding away from community-based
partners with deep local relationships.
Bank support is woven into Habitat Philadelphia's ability to deliver our mission. Grants and sponsorships help fund home
construction, critical repairs, housing counseling, and neighborhood-based work; financing helps us move projects from
acquisition through completion; and bank employees contribute time and skills as volunteers. These are practical
partnerships that turn capital into stable homes and stronger neighborhoods. Making them harder to support or
document would not reduce community need—it would only make that need harder to meet.
Rules governing which grants and community development activities receive CRA consideration have consequences far
beyond banks themselves. These rules should be guided by the needs of the communities CRA is intended to serve, not
solely by the perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions.
The proposal would also eliminate the current "purpose test" for certain economic development financing. Banks could
receive CRA credit for financing a qualifying business without showing that the activity creates, retains, or improves jobs
for low- and moderate-income people or communities. This would weaken the connection between CRA credit and the
people and neighborhoods the law is intended to benefit. In Philadelphia, where neighborhood investment must
address both housing stability and access to economic opportunity, that connection should be strengthened, not
removed.
We are further concerned that the proposal would limit annual collection and reporting of data on small-business and
community development loans to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. Without meaningful data, communities,
regulators, and researchers would have less information to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance,
understand whether local credit needs are being met, and hold institutions accountable.
Before issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
1. identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny;
2. quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services, and community development activities subject
to CRA evaluation;
3. assess whether the effects would be concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations, including rural
communities and communities of color; or
4. consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing meaningful
community accountability.


Given these omissions and the concerns described above, Habitat for Humanity Philadelphia urges the OCC and FDIC to
rescind the proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and released for public comment. At
minimum, the proposal requires substantial changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity and to protect
meaningful accountability to communities like those we serve.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting community credit needs.
The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the
changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days. The proposal is more than
100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant changes to bank classifications, community development,
branch and service evaluations, nonprofit grants, and other core elements of CRA implementation. The current
comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Additional time would allow Habitat affiliates and other community organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical
consequences, gather examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more complete
record. We therefore request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.
Sincerely,

Carrie Rathmann
Vice President of Strategic Partnerships
Habitat for Humanity Philadelphia

comments.name: HVN Development (Tommy Beadel, Founder)
comments.type_basis: Letter is from the founder of HVN Development, an affordable housing developer in Los Angeles that builds LIHTC bond-financed projects; it is a for-profit developer, but the closest category is housing/community development.
comments.overall_quote: Do not eliminate the investment test for banks between $1.649 billion and $10 billion.
comments.summary: A Los Angeles affordable housing developer argues that raising the large bank threshold to $10 billion would eliminate the investment test for banks that buy LIHTC credits. It says fewer bidders would cut credit prices from $0.80 to $0.70, which would halt all 2,400 of its unsubsidized 4 percent bond homes. It limits its comment to this provision and asks for alternatives.
key_asks: Do not raise the large bank threshold to $10 billion; keep it unchanged, or at most use the $3.252 billion alternative.

If the threshold is raised, give intermediate banks a standalone investment test or require separate evaluation and rating of qualified investments, and keep the Satisfactory-on-CD-test requirement for an overall Satisfactory.
Coordinate with the Federal Reserve so the investment test applies uniformly, and lower the Basel III risk weight on Housing Credit investments to 20 percent (no higher than 50 percent).

provisions.quote: Our strong preference is that the large bank threshold not change at all.
Keep the rule that an intermediate bank must earn a Satisfactory on its community development test to earn a Satisfactory overall.

comments.commenter_subtype: affordable housing developer (LIHTC sponsor), Los Angeles

issues.raw_label: Eliminating investment test for mid-size banks
issues.quote: raising the large bank threshold from $1.649 billion to $10 billion, which eliminates the investment test for every bank in that band

issues.raw_label: Loss of bank incentive to buy credits
issues.quote: Every one of those deals closes because a bank buys the credits, and the bank buys the credits because of the CRA investment test.

issues.raw_label: Folding investments into blended community development test
issues.quote: It folds investments into a blended community development test alongside loans

issues.raw_label: Removing Satisfactory requirement for intermediate banks
issues.quote: then removes the rule that an intermediate bank must earn a Satisfactory on that test to earn a Satisfactory overall.

issues.raw_label: Lower housing credit prices from fewer bidders
issues.quote: Fewer bidders means a lower price per credit.

issues.raw_label: Stalled affordable housing projects and homes lost
issues.quote: At $0.70 every one of HVN's 2,400 homes in production in the City of Los Angeles stops.

issues.raw_label: Alternative $3.252 billion threshold ceiling

HVN Development Letter on CRA
Modernization and LIHTC Investment in Los
Angeles
Oct 7, 2026 · ​@Tommy Beadel
HVN Development Los Angeles, California
October 7, 2026
Chief Counsel's Office, Attention: Comment Processing Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency 400 7th Street SW, Suite 3E 218 Washington, DC 20219
James P. Sheesley, Assistant Executive Secretary Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
550 17th Street NW Washington, DC 20429
Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
(Federal Register, August 12, 2026). Comments of HVN Development on eliminating the
investment test for banks between $1.649 billion and $10 billion in assets.
Dear Acting Comptroller and Acting Chairman:
Who we are and why the investment test matters to us
HVN Development builds and preserves affordable housing in the City of Los Angeles. I
am its founder. We have 2,400 homes in production in the City today on sites like 8911
Ramsgate Avenue and 11143 Acama Street, and we build them a particular way. Every HVN
project is what the industry calls a naked 4 percent bond deal: tax exempt private activity
bonds, the 4 percent Low Income Housing Tax Credit that comes with them as of right,
and nothing else. No City of Los Angeles soft loan, no state gap financing, no public
subsidy of any kind beyond the credit itself. The debt is sized to the restricted rents, the
developer fee is deferred, and the credit equity fills the rest. Every one of those deals
closes because a bank buys the credits, and the bank buys the credits because of the
CRA investment test.
I am writing about one provision: raising the large bank threshold from $1.649 billion to $10
billion, which eliminates the investment test for every bank in that band. I will leave the
rest of the proposal to others. This one change reaches directly into my capital stack.
HVN Development Letter on CRA Modernization and LIHTC Investment in Los Angeles
Page 1 of 6
 The investment test is the only part of CRA that rewards a bank for owning a piece of an
affordable building rather than lending against one. A Housing Credit investment is equity.
It is a fifteen year ownership position with no principal and interest coming back, and no
bank treasurer prefers it to a loan. Banks make the investment because the investment
test asks for qualified investments, examines them on their own, and rates them
separately from lending. The Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition puts the national
numbers plainly: banks provide roughly 75 to 80 percent of Housing Credit equity and at
least 71 percent of it is CRA motivated. Take away the test and you take away the reason.
The proposal does not replace the investment test for these banks with something
weaker. It folds investments into a blended community development test alongside loans,
and then removes the rule that an intermediate bank must earn a Satisfactory on that test
to earn a Satisfactory overall. A bank between $1.649 billion and $10 billion could stop
buying credits tomorrow, make a few community development loans it would have made
anyway, and never see a word about it in its performance evaluation. For a Housing Credit
developer that is not a dilution of the incentive. It is the end of it.
The rural point is real. The Coalition's survey shows about a third of the Housing Credit
equity from banks under $10 billion goes to rural markets, where these are often the only
investors. But the same banks are also the swing bidders in Los Angeles, and the
investment test is what puts them at the table in both places.
How many Los Angeles investors lose the test
Nationally, about 636 banks would move from the large bank framework to the new
intermediate category and lose the investment test. The Coalition counted at least 108 of
those banks that together placed about $1.6 billion of Housing Credit equity over five
years, about $2 billion when extrapolated to the full market. None of that $2 billion was
lending. All of it came through the investment test.
Los Angeles is a community bank town. Many of the institutions that compete for our
credits sit squarely in the $1.649 billion to $10 billion band: the Korean American and
Chinese American banks headquartered downtown and in the San Gabriel Valley, the
business banks in the South Bay and on the Westside, the savings banks that have served
the City for a century. By our count, roughly 20 to 25 OCC and FDIC supervised banks
with assessment areas covering the City of Los Angeles are in that band and are subject
to the investment test today. Because the Federal Reserve has not joined this rulemaking,
state member banks of the same size would keep the test, so two banks on the same
block would be examined under two different standards.
HVN Development Letter on CRA Modernization and LIHTC Investment in Los Angeles
Page 2 of 6
 On a typical HVN deal in the City we see four to six serious bids for the credits. Two or
three of those come from banks under $10 billion, and they bid because an investment
test examination is coming and they need qualified investments in this assessment area.
They are the bidders that keep the money center banks honest on price. Remove the test
and we are back to two bidders who know they are the only ones in the room.
These are not banks that cannot afford to invest. They are profitable, and a meaningful
share of that profit comes from the very neighborhoods this program serves: overdraft
and account fees, check cashing, remittances and small dollar deposits from low income
households across South Los Angeles, Koreatown, the Eastside and the San Fernando
Valley. They hold those families' money. The investment test is the one mechanism that
asks them to put a portion of it back to work in those same communities as ownership
capital, not just loans. A bank that earns its margin on a neighborhood should help build
the homes that let that neighborhood's families stay, and the investment test is how the
regulators say so.
What fewer bidders means in dollars and in homes
Fewer bidders means a lower price per credit. Credits in the City are clearing at about
$0.80 today. Our equity partners tell us that with a third of the bidders gone the price
settles at $0.70. On a project with public soft money, a ten cent drop is a gap to be
negotiated. On a naked 4 percent bond deal it is the end of the project. Here is the
arithmetic on a 100 home HVN building at our all in cost of $400,000 per home.

HVN Development Letter on CRA Modernization and LIHTC Investment in Los Angeles
Page 3 of 6
 The gap is 4.5 percent of cost, and on most affordable deals in America it would be
covered by a city or state soft loan. We do not take those funds. We built our model so
that the City's scarce subsidy dollars could go to the deepest need projects while we
delivered homes with private capital alone. That model has exactly one source of equity,
and it is the Housing Credit investor. There is no private investor who buys a 15 year
ownership position in a rent restricted building at a 4.5 percent loss, and there is no bank
that does it without the investment test asking it to. The debt cannot go up because the
rents are capped by law. The fee cannot be deferred further. The gap stays open, and the
bonds are never issued.
So the honest number is not 40 homes or 200 homes out of our pipeline. It is all of them. At
$0.70 every one of HVN's 2,400 homes in production in the City of Los Angeles stops. That
is $960 million of construction that does not start, $432 million of tax exempt bond
authority that goes unused in a state where bond cap is oversubscribed three to one, and
2,400 families who stay exactly where they are.
Where they are is the point. The families on our waiting lists are living three generations to
a two bedroom in South Los Angeles. They are sleeping in cars in Van Nuys and in motels
on Figueroa paid for by the week. They are the home health aides and school cafeteria
workers and security guards who hold this City together and who will not see a single new
apartment from us if this rule takes effect as written. A ten cent change in a tax credit
price is invisible to almost everyone in this country. To those 2,400 families it is the
difference between a front door and a back seat.
Who lives in the homes that would not get built
The units that fall out first are the deepest ones. In Los Angeles we set aside a large share
of every project for households at 30 percent of area median income. For a family of three
that is about $39,000 a year. These are the home health aides, the school cafeteria
workers, the security guards and the grandmothers raising grandchildren who make this
City run. The 30 percent units carry the thinnest rents and the least debt, so they live or

HVN Development Letter on CRA Modernization and LIHTC Investment in Los Angeles
Page 4 of 6
 die on credit equity. On a subsidized deal, a drop in credit price means those units get
traded up to 60 percent or cut. On our deals there is nothing to trade. The whole building
stops, and the 30 percent families are the first ones who never get the call.
Let me tell you about one family. Last year we leased up a building in the City. A mother
and her eight year old son had been living in their car for the better part of a year. They
had a lease in hand for one of our 30 percent units. On move in day the boy walked into the
kitchen, opened a drawer, closed it, and asked his mother a question. He wanted to know
if he got one drawer or if he got all of them.
He had never had a kitchen. He did not know that all of the drawers in it were his. That is
what a 30 percent unit is. It is a kid learning that an apartment is not a space you share
with strangers or sleep in a back seat beside, but a home where every drawer belongs to
you.
A bank with assets between $1.649 billion and $10 billion bought the credits on that
building. It did so because the investment test meant its examiners would ask about it.
Under this proposal, no one will ask, and the next boy stays in the car.
What we ask
1. Do not eliminate the investment test for banks between $1.649 billion and $10 billion.
Our strong preference is that the large bank threshold not change at all. If the agencies
conclude that some adjustment is required, the ceiling should be the alternative $3.252
billion level the proposal itself puts forward, and not a dollar higher. At $3.252 billion
the test still reaches most of the banks that actually buy credits in Los Angeles and in
rural California. At $10 billion it reaches almost none of them.
2. If the threshold is raised anyway, carry the investment test with it. Give intermediate
banks a standalone investment test, or at minimum require examiners to evaluate and
rate qualified investments separately within the community development test, so a
bank cannot satisfy it with loans alone.
3. Keep the rule that an intermediate bank must earn a Satisfactory on its community
development test to earn a Satisfactory overall. Without it, the investment incentive is
gone even where the test survives on paper.
4. Coordinate with the Federal Reserve so the investment test applies to every bank of a
given size in Los Angeles regardless of charter.
5. Finish the job on capital. Lower the Basel III risk weight on Housing Credit investments
from 100 percent to 20 percent, and in no case above 50 percent. It makes no sense to
weaken the CRA reason to invest while the capital rules still penalize the investment.
HVN Development Letter on CRA Modernization and LIHTC Investment in Los Angeles
Page 5 of 6
 Congress just expanded the Housing Credit for the first time in a generation. The City of
Los Angeles is counting on that expansion to put a dent in a homelessness crisis that
everyone in this country has seen on television. It would be a strange outcome for one set
of federal regulators to add credits with one hand while another removes the buyers with
the other.
Closing
I would welcome the chance to walk any member of your staff through one of our
buildings in Los Angeles, and to introduce them to the banks under $10 billion that made
those buildings possible. Thank you for considering these comments.
Respectfully,
Tommy Beadel Founder HVN Development Los Angeles, California

Washington, DC 20219
Re: Proposed Community Reinvestment Act Regulations—OCC Docket ID OCC–2026–0694
Dear OCC Officials:
On behalf of the Maine Affordable Housing Coalition (MAHC), we urge you to reconsider proposed Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) changes that would reduce affordable housing investment and weaken access to
banking services in Maine.
MAHC works to expand access to affordable housing across Maine. Our members bring experience creating,
preserving, and supporting affordable homes in communities throughout the state. Bank financing and
investment are essential to this work, and CRA provides important incentives for banks to respond to local
housing needs, have branches in low to moderate income (LMI) areas, and invest in small businesses – the
backbone of Maine's economy.
MAHC's affordable homeownership work has helped secure funding and deliver 325 affordable homes for
purchase across Maine. This includes homes in LMI branch communities where access to investment is critical.
While these homes are distinct from the rental housing financed through the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit,
they demonstrate the importance of sustained investment in expanding housing opportunities. Maine needs
strong financing partnerships that support both affordable homeownership and rental housing.
We are particularly concerned about raising the large-bank asset threshold from $1.649 billion to $10 billion. Of
17 banks in Maine, 11 would be moved to the intermediate threshold. Affected OCC- and FDIC-regulated banks
would no longer face a separate CRA investment test, although they would retain community development
obligations. Removing this distinct incentive could reduce bank participation in the Low-Income Housing Tax
Credit market.
For Maine, reduced competition for Housing Credits could mean lower equity proceeds, larger financing gaps,
and fewer affordable rental homes built or preserved. Rural developments may be especially vulnerable because

PO Box 30 Portland, ME 04112 info@mainehousingcoalition.org mainehousingcoalition.org
they can have fewer potential investors and banking partners. Losing even one motivated investor could make a
development financially infeasible, leaving needed homes unbuilt.
For our members, these changes could make it harder to assemble financing and move developments forward.
When investment falls short, communities lose opportunities to provide stable, affordable homes for residents
and housing that supports their local workforce.
We also oppose weakening accountability for branch access. NCRC's analysis finds that the proposed threshold
change would eliminate separate branch evaluations for 64 of 91 branches in Maine (417 banks nationwide,
affecting more than 5,000 branches nationwide) in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. These are
branches that would lose separate evaluations, rather than confirmed closures. Nevertheless, weaker oversight
could reduce incentives to maintain access in underserved communities.
In rural Maine, losing a local branch can mean longer trips for banking services and fewer opportunities to
receive personal assistance with mortgages, small business loans, and everyday financial needs. Access to
housing and dependable banking services are both important to the stability of Maine communities.
We urge the agencies to retain the current bank-size thresholds and separate investment and service tests. We
also oppose the more expansive $30 billion large-bank threshold discussed in the proposal. Before adopting
changes, the agencies should assess and publicly explain their effects on affordable housing financing and
branch access in Maine and other rural states.
Maine's communities need more affordable homes and dependable financial services. CRA policy should
strengthen the bank partnerships that help meet those needs.
Thank you for considering our comments.
Sincerely,

Laura Mitchell
Executive Director

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on
Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN
1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Catholic Charities Housing Services – Diocese of Yakima (CCHS) submits this comment in
opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the
Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
(FDIC)1 because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In
addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the
OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences
for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis
and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment
deadline by 60-days.
Catholic Charities Housing Services is a 501 c3 nonprofit organization that provides affordable
housing solutions throughout seven counties in central Washington State. We have developed,
own and manage 33 affordable multi-family rental housing properties for households with
extremely low- to low-incomes. We provide resident services to many of these locations helping
families access community resources to improve their lives. We also provide housing counseling
services to interested first-time homebuyers and offer two different sweat-equity based
homeownership models. We have built and sold more than 250 homes to low-income
homebuyers over the past 20+ years.
CCHS has directly experienced the challenges of rural communities attracting investments from
banking institutions both in lending and investing in small local communities where banks have

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
Docusign Envelope ID: E9B9D991-E68F-8ACA-832E-8DADD42216C9
 2

branches. We are deeply concerned that the proposed changes (if enacted) would harm our
ability to attract investment in affordable housing opportunities in these communities.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring
that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-
income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both
credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in communities that
have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream
financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would
change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for
nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without an
adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on
communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. Across the 4th
Congressional District which primarily overlaps with our service areas, from 2010-2024, banks
made $16.7 Billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census
tracts and $3.2 Billion in CRA qualified lending to small businesses. Investments such as these
benefited our community by increasing the number of low- to moderate income homebuyers who
were able to successfully fulfill their dreams of homeownership. We have seen first hand the
importance of access to credit and lending for families looking to breakout of the cycles of
poverty.
We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital
devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough to receive a
passing CRA rating.2 However, that percentage is far lower than the percentage the National
Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the largest banks currently devote to
community investments and loans.
NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the OCC and
FDIC supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these banks currently
conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community development loans and investments
inside their assessment areas, and that the median percentage of annual community development
lending in assessment areas was 6.8% of tier 1 capital, and a median of 3.6% of tier 1 capital for

2 The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit for outside their assessment areas if the banks surpass a
benchmark of 0.625% of its tier 1 capital for community development loans and likewise 0.625% for investments.
91 Fed. Reg. 52121, 52140 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026). We are concerned that the practical effect of this proposal is
that the benchmark will serve not as a floor, but a ceiling.
Docusign Envelope ID: E9B9D991-E68F-8ACA-832E-8DADD42216C9
 3

annual CRA qualified investments.3 If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to
meet separate thresholds of 0.625% of Tier 1 capital for community development lending and
investments, combined activity would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually -- a decrease
of approximately $87.1 billion, or 85%. Similarly, the proposal encourages banks to use strategic
plans to make their CRA compliance easier and more predictable. Previous proposed guidance
also set strategic plan benchmarks for CRA performance well-below historical levels of
community development activity.4
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination
cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans. If
regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the
communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for communities. For example, in
our community we regularly seek bank investment and lending for affordable housing
developments through the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) program as well as
mortgage lending for first time low-income homebuyers. Even currently rural communities are at
a disadvantage compared to our urban counterparts in finding interested investors for the LIHTC
program. The proposed changes would further erode pricing in these markets creating additional
challenges to the provision of affordable rental housing to families in need. It is imperative that
the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet community needs. Before finalizing the rule, the
agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce lending, services or
investment available to low- and moderate-income communities and whether communities that
have experienced historic discrimination or disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.
Under the current rule, large banks are generally evaluated on their home mortgage,
small business and small farm lending. The proposal outlines two options for regulators to focus
on products designated as a bank's "major product lines" based either on the largest two product
lines by all lending volume, or based on the type of lending a bank does more of in a particular
assessment area.5 Either option would allow weak performance in a lower volume product to
escape meaningful scrutiny even when that credit is important locally.
For example, in my community, there is a strong need for home mortgage lending for low-
income homebuyers. But if that type of lending is not a major part of a large bank in my
community's business, regulators will not evaluate whether the bank is meeting this crucial
community need. Absent such evaluation, the bank will likely deprioritize making such loans.

comments.text:
COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Dear Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation:
I am writing to ask the OCC and FDIC to preserve a strong Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) and the incentives it creates for banks to invest in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs), small businesses, and communities that have historically had less access to capital.
The CRA has an important and straightforward purpose: banks should help meet the credit needs of the communities they serve, including low- and moderate-income communities. CDFIs help make that possible. I’m writing to share my support for CDFI in my local community, WomenVenture. 
Organizations like WomenVenture work directly with entrepreneurs who may have strong businesses and great ideas but face barriers to traditional financing. CDFIs combine affordable capital with business support, relationships, and technical assistance so entrepreneurs have a better opportunity to start, stabilize, and grow their businesses. WomenVenture’s mission is to “help entrepreneurs and small business owners build profitable and sustainable businesses.” WomenVenture celebrates its 25th year as a CDFI serving Minnesota and Western Wisconsin. 

I have seen the importance of this work firsthand through:
A friend of mine who needed a loan to make it through COVOD-19 Pandemic after he had also just struggled through a divorce, and his credit had taken a big hit through the divorce. His local bank was able to step in and be that financial uplift to support his time of need and he was in turn able to keep the business going through the hardships and now his family is giving back to the community by contributing their time and knowledge in the community fundraiser.

Bank partnerships are critical to this work. CRA has helped encourage banks to lend, invest, and provide other resources through CDFIs that know their communities and can help capital reach people and businesses that might otherwise be overlooked.
I recognize the agencies' goals of making CRA clearer, more effective, and less burdensome. At the same time, those goals should not reduce meaningful investment in underserved communities or weaken partnerships between banks and CDFIs.
I encourage the OCC and FDIC to ensure that the final rule:
•preserves strong incentives for banks to lend and invest through CDFIs;
•recognizes the full value of community-development activities that expand access to responsible capital;
•supports grants and other resources that help CDFIs build the capacity needed to serve communities effectively;
•maintains meaningful expectations for banks to meet community credit needs; and
•strengthens, rather than reduces, the flow of responsible private capital to small businesses and low- and moderate-income communities.
For organizations like WomenVenture, these partnerships translate directly into financing and support for entrepreneurs building businesses, creating jobs, generating wealth, and strengthening their communities.
We should continue improving CRA, but improvement should move us toward greater access to capital not less.
Thank you for considering my comments.
Sincerely,
Jessica Adams,
Jes-us House Community Initiative

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0133_09000064b964e0eb.pdf:
October 7, 2026

Jonathan V. Gould



Travis Hill, Chairman
Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (FDIC)
400 7th Street SW



550 17th Street, NW
Washington, DC 20219


Washington, DC 20429

Attn: Chief Counsel's Office
[Via email to Comments@fdic.gov]
Via: Federal eRulemaking Portal – regulations.gov

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on
Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN
1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
CAMEO Network writes to object to the harmful changes proposed to the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed by Congress in
1977 in response to redlining and creates an affirmative obligation for banks to help
meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of communities, including low and
moderate income (LMI) communities. While the CRA has successfully encouraged
banks to lend, invest and provide services in underserved communities, challenges
related to redlining, discrimination, underinvestment, and lack of access remain.

CAMEO Network is a national micro-business association, based in California, made
up of more than 400 organizations, agencies, and individuals dedicated to furthering
micro-business development with small and micro-business financing such as loans
and credit, technical assistance and business management training. Annually,
CAMEO members serve about 200,000 very small businesses with training, business
and credit assistance and loans. These firms – largely start-ups with less than six
employees – support or create 300,000 new jobs in California and generate a total of
$15 billion in economic activity. Banks have been long-term, key partners with our
members by investing in them, i.e. the coaching and lending organizations that
engage in the activities listed above that produce significant community impact.

The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift.
The proposal does not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on LMI
communities. We request an extension of the comment period for an additional 60
days so we have time to better understand how much CRA activity may be lost to
communities because of this proposal – an analysis the regulators did not conduct or
provide.

The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved
communities in several ways.


1) Community development (CD) activities for affordable housing and
small businesses will drop dramatically.
As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities
that support critically needed affordable housing and economic development projects.
These activities often provide the greatest CRA impact in communities as they
strengthen economic stability and mobility, quality of life, and social health of
residents and communities.

The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large"
Banks, such that many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and
expectation to serve the community development needs of their communities.[1]
According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70
California banks would see their reinvestment obligations reduced under the proposal.
Twenty-five California banks would shed their Community Development Test
responsibilities entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer be subject to the
Investment Test.[2]

The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical
community development programs that have had large impacts in LMI communities.
These include Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) which are a key driver of
affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) which fuel economic
development projects in tribal and other areas; and EQ2 equity equivalent
investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) that provide
small business lending in underserved areas that banks cannot reach, and in
Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that take property off of the speculative market.

Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting
the critical importance of the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable
housing.[3] Approximately half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from CRA
motivated banks.[4] The regulators will even further weaken CD obligations if they
adopt the alternative proposal that Large Banks be defined as those with over $30
billion in assets.

Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance
even where they remain subject to the Community Development and Investment
Tests. The regulators signal to all banks that they can do significantly less CD lending
and investment and still pass their CRA examinations, all while seeking CRA credit
for activity outside of their CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests that a bank
could receive a passing CRA rating if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1 capital were
devoted to CD loans and CD investments. That percentage is far lower than the
percentage that NCRC determined banks currently devote to community investments
and loans. If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet the
proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by approximately $87.1 billion, or
85%.[5]


Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have
tremendous negative impacts on affordable housing and small business development
in our state. Asset thresholds should not be raised.

2) Banks will shed branches and BankOn.
The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and maintain
branches in LMI neighborhoods. By increasing the asset threshold for a Large Bank
to over $10 billion, forty-five banks in California will no longer be subject to the
Services Test and reviewed to ensure that their branches are serving LMI
communities. In California alone, NCRC estimates that 245 branches in LMI areas
and 497 branches in neighborhoods of color would be vulnerable to closure due to
this proposal.[6]

Branch presence has been tied to increased small business lending in communities.
Fewer branches will result in less small business lending. These changes will be
particularly hard hitting in rural areas of our state where smaller banks originate a
larger portion of the small business loans.

The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to
offer deposit products that are accessible to LMI residents.[7] Deposit accounts are a
gateway to credit access, financial stability, and wealth building, especially for
families who are otherwise preyed upon by predatory financial institutions. As one
important example, the BankOn program has provided access to no or low fee bank
accounts for over fourteen million people.[8] California is home to several BankOn
coalitions that establish effective partnerships among banks, community-based
organizations, and local governments. The proposal jettisons this work.

Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million
are underbanked.[9] National banks regulated by the OCC charged billions of dollars
in overdraft and non-sufficient fund fees in 2025, and in California alone, state-
chartered banks charged over fifty-six million dollars ($56 million) in OD and NSF
fees to California consumers in 2025.[10]

3) Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.
Another consequence of the proposal's drive to raise asset thresholds is that fewer
banks will be required to report data regarding their small business, small farm, and
community development lending activities. Such data is critical to understanding not
only individual bank performance, but also the needs of local markets. Community
organizations routinely analyze this CRA data when meeting with banks and
commenting on CRA exams and mergers. The loss of such data is particularly
harmful at a time when the Administration is walking back efforts to collect and
disclose detailed small business lending data under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank
Act. These changes will disproportionately impact rural communities in our state
where banks up to $10 billion in assets make up a larger part of the small business
and small farm lending markets.


4) Native American communities and Tribal Nations will not see
sufficient benefits.
The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the needs of
Native American communities and Tribal Nations which have been poorly served by
banks. The current rules focus CRA obligations in areas where banks have branches,
even though there are far fewer bank branches near tribal lands and in rural areas
where Native Americans may reside. The proposal seeks to address this CRA gap by
encouraging banks to engage in community development and related activities in
"Indian Country" and on "Tribal and Native lands," even if outside of bank CRA
assessment areas. But many members of tribes in California will not benefit from this
proposal as they do not live in Indian Country or on Tribal or Native lands, as
defined.

CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring within
particular geographies, given the challenges and impacts associated with historic
dispossession and federal policy. Instead, CRA evaluations should also consider
whether banks have established meaningful relationships with, and provided direct
benefits to, federally recognized tribes as well as non-federally recognized tribes.
Non-federally recognized tribes have been acknowledged by, and are able to access
programs and contracts with, various local and state entities.[11] Such processes
exist.

More specifically, the CRA rules should encourage banks to serve tribes, nonprofit
organizations or other entities controlled by tribes, and Native-owned businesses that
are majority owned and controlled by Native American entrepreneurs by providing:
● Active outreach and engagement
● Community development loans and investments for affordable housing and
economic development projects
● Small farm and small business loans
● Home mortgage loans
● Grants to meet community needs, including for capacity building for tribes
and support for tribes seeking federal recognition if desired
● Support for cultural, health and other programs
● Bank branches
● Deposit products such as affordable bank accounts, and
● The provision of financial services such as financial literacy, apprenticeship
programs and technical assistance support

While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities
outside of their branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made to
encourage banks to engage in CRA related activity to directly benefit tribes, nonprofit
organizations and other entities controlled by tribes, and Native-owned businesses
that are majority owned and controlled by Native American entrepreneurs.


A better approach is needed. All banks should be subject to an impact and
responsiveness review factor during their CRA exams that evaluates and tracks
whether banks have engaged in any CRA activity directly with tribes, tribally
controlled entities and Native owned businesses.[12] If banks know they will be
examined for their work with tribes, they will find mutually beneficial ways to work
with tribes.

5) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will suffer.
The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by
requiring a demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating
that large banks and their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more than
15% of these grants on overhead.[13] As if this wasn't enough, the FDIC and OCC
question whether they should end CRA eligibility for bank grantmaking to nonprofits
entirely.

Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian
measures will be except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller
groups, may be impacted.[14]

Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local
needs. They also can be key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and
investment products into communities inclined to trust long established local
organizations. Many nonprofit organizations and programs, such as downpayment
assistance programs, that support CRA related activity, rely on bank contributions to
operate. Smaller, local, and rural organizations will be least able to meet new
reporting obligations, and they risk losing bank support as a result. The proposal
would also end impactful contributions from banks for general operating support,
sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.

Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their
communities on their own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps in
their own capacity – seeking assistance with community outreach, borrower
education, credit building and repair, technical assistance, legal services, job training
and placement, tax assistance, affordable housing and other services and programs
which help residents become stable and bankable so that banks can attract new
deposits and make new loans in LMI communities.

The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and will
focus grantmaking on larger organizations that can help them more easily meet their
new FDIC and OCC-imposed regulatory burdens.

Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from large banks, the 15% overhead
restriction will negatively affect operations and organizational success. As one
example, in order to secure CRA grants from large banks, CDFIs will need to pare
down costs for critical operational expenses such as underwriting, servicing,

compliance, technology, impact measurement, product development, and borrower
technical assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions,
organizations are put at risk.

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA
activity that contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large
negative impact it will have on nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding, the
harm it will cause to LMI communities that are meant to benefit from the CRA, and
the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

6) Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.
There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link between
CRA and LMI impact in the name of easing bank burden.

Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their top
two major product lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in, and
profiting from, communities, this lending by banks, subsidiaries and affiliates must be
evaluated. Further, certain products, such as small farm and consumer loans, are
important in many communities, but may not be among a bank's largest product lines.
If regulators give banks a pass and exempt smaller product lines from CRA oversight,
banks will have less incentive to consider how those products are offered.

Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and
soundness, encourages banks to meet community needs, and engenders greater trust
in banks by the community. Eliminating categories of loan products from scrutiny
will have the opposite effect.

No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test,
which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the
definition of economic development. The CRA should create greater incentives for
banks to support the creation of jobs that pay family sustaining wages for LMI
workers and in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to provisions that would provide
CRA credit for job creation and economic development that may only benefit middle-
and upper-income workers and communities. Such provisions ignore the purpose of
CRA.

Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA
credit for large scale community infrastructure products that generate profits for
banks, would likely be financed without CRA credit, and provide only incidental
benefits to LMI residents and communities. Such an expansion of what qualifies for
CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities.
For example, banks might choose to more profitably earn CRA credit by financing
larger scale infrastructure projects, like bridges, in lieu of financing less lucrative,
smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local community needs (such as childcare
facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or resilience projects).


Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA
should require banks to focus their CRA activities on their CRA assessments
areas,[15] where they are subject to more rigorous regulatory oversight (with an
exception made to encourage banks to better serve tribes, as noted above). Banks are
not doing enough currently to meet the credit and deposit needs in the areas where
they have CRA responsibility, a problem the regulators tried to address in the 2023
CRA Rule.[16] Yet the proposal further encourages banks to seek CRA credit for
projects in areas away from their branches, lending and CRA responsibility. This will
enable banks to get credit for activity outside of their assessment areas, while
providing no accompanying CRA obligation to better serve these areas.

Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal goes out
of its way to encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan option to meet their
CRA responsibilities. The Strategic Plan was meant for financial institutions that
operated under a unique business model that the CRA rules were not designed to
address. The Strategic Plan option provides for minimal public input and regulatory
scrutiny and allows banks to determine the level of reinvestment activity they need to
engage in to earn a passing CRA grade. In our experience, banks with Strategic Plans
tend to reinvest less in the community and in less impactful ways. The OCC's
guidance establishing low community development thresholds for banks opting for
the Strategic Plan, [17] validates this perspective.

Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community
development efforts with little benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing,
where units are affordable at a point in time but not encumbered by deed or rent
restrictions, are a feature of today's housing market. But CRA rules should not give
banks credit for financing such activities where the benefit to LMI residents and
communities is unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it
can be a driver of bank investment in problematic landlords and displacement. CRA
credit should be given for financing of NOAH only if the project is owned and
operated by mission-driven organizations, where a majority of residents are LMI
tenants, and the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are
compliant with tenant rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents
can reasonably be expected to retain their housing.

7) Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA ratings
downgrades.
The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and redline
should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding"
ratings. Under the Biden Administration, at least a dozen banks that passed their CRA
exams were accused of redlining. This proposal will only increase that number by
narrowing what constitutes evidence of discrimination that may be considered for the
purpose of downgrading a bank's CRA rating. Here, regulators should consider any
evidence that a bank, its affiliates, or subsidiaries engaged in discrimination,
redlining, or illegal credit practices as part of their lending, deposit, branching, or
other activities. This evidence should be considered regardless of its source (public or

private parties), or its form (informal complaints, research based on data, testing
results, comment letters, administrative actions, private litigation, etc.). We also urge
the regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity Act authorizes
Special Purpose Credit Programs, and to once again encourage banks to develop
SPCPs to better serve communities that have been redlined, excluded, and
underserved. This is the essence of CRA.
Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
● identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less
CRA scrutiny under the proposal;
● quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and
community development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
● assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or
populations, including rural communities and communities of color; and
● consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without
sacrificing meaningful community accountability.
Conclusion. Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my
organization believes that the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a
more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and released for public comment.
This proposal likely needs considerable changes to prevent significant declines in
CRA-related activity.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least
120 days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would
make significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch
and service evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA
implementation. The current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input
from community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other
stakeholders that do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted.
An extension would allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical
consequences, gather examples from the communities they serve, and provide the
agencies with a more complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore
request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least
60 days.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for
meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that
materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are
consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.



Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Sincerely,


Heidi Pickman
VP of External Relations

cc. National Community Reinvestment Coalition
 RISE Economy

[14] The proposal notes, "The OCC also expects several potential second order impacts, including a possible shift
