COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Full Comment letter is attached.

The Pennsylvania Community Development Financial Institution Network submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)   because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).  In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.
The Pennsylvania CDFI Network (Network) is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization formed by a collective of 16 nonprofit community development financial institutions (CDFIs) that provide affordable loans and technical advisory services to companies that cannot access financing through traditional channels. Founded in 1997, the Network collaborates on regional and statewide initiatives to support small businesses. 72% of CDFI lending is directed to small businesses serving low-to-moderate income neighborhoods. 60% of the $568 million combined loan portfolio in 2025 are microloans under $50,000, with an average loan size of $194,612. Together, we work to enhance CDFI capacity that fuel small business growth through business advisory services and loan capital.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In our community, from 2010-2024, banks made 108,785,971,000 in CRA qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and 65,193,466,000 in CRA qualified lending to small businesses. Investments such as these benefited our community by providing affordable mortgages, technical advisory services and small business loans to communities across Pennsylvania.
We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks’ incentives to invest in communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank’s Tier 1 capital devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough to receive a passing CRA rating.   However, that percentage is far lower than the percentage the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0134_09000064b964ed9b.pdf:
1

October 6, 2026


Via electronic submission

Jonathan V. Gould
Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street SW
Washington, DC 20219
Attn: Chief Counsel's Office
Via: Federal eRulemaking Portal –
.regulations.gov
Travis Hill, Chairman
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
(FDIC)
550 17th Street, NW
Washington, DC 20429

Via email to Comments@fdic.gov



Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Community
Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN
3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
The Pennsylvania Community Development Financial Institution Network submits this comment in
opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office
of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)1 because
it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the
complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making
any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income
communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify
supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.
The Pennsylvania CDFI Network (Network) is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization formed by a collective
of 16 nonprofit community development financial institutions (CDFIs) that provide affordable loans and
technical advisory services to companies that cannot access financing through traditional channels.
Founded in 1997, the Network collaborates on regional and statewide initiatives to support small
businesses. 72% of CDFI lending is directed to small businesses serving low-to-moderate income
neighborhoods. 60% of the $568 million combined loan portfolio in 2025 are microloans under $50,000,
with an average loan size of $194,612. Together, we work to enhance CDFI capacity that fuel small
business growth through business advisory services and loan capital.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that
banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both credit and deposit

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).

2
services. These protections remain especially important in communities that have experienced redlining,
disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change how
regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for nonprofit organizations. We
are concerned that these changes are being considered without an adequate analysis of their likely
effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on communities that have experienced historic
discrimination and disinvestment.
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In our community, from 2010-
2024, banks made 108,785,971,000 in CRA qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI
census tracts and 65,193,466,000 in CRA qualified lending to small businesses. Investments such as
these benefited our community by providing affordable mortgages, technical advisory services and small
business loans to communities across Pennsylvania.
We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in communities. For
example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital devoted to either community
development loans or investments would be enough to receive a passing CRA rating.2 However, that
percentage is far lower than the percentage the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC)
determined the largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.
NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the OCC and FDIC
supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these banks currently conduct
approximately $102 billion annually in community development loans and investments inside their
assessment areas, and that the median percentage of annual community development lending in
assessment areas was 6.8% of tier 1 capital, and a median of 3.6% of tier 1 capital for annual CRA
qualified investments.3 If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet separate
thresholds of 0.625% of Tier 1 capital for community development lending and investments, combined
activity would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually -- a decrease of approximately $87.1 billion,
or 85%. Similarly, the proposal encourages banks to use strategic plans to make their CRA compliance
easier and more predictable. Previous proposed guidance also set strategic plan benchmarks for CRA
performance well-below historical levels of community development activity.4
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination cannot
withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans. If regulators lower the
expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the communities they serve, there
could be harmful consequences for communities. For example, communities across Pennsylvania would

2 The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit for outside their assessment areas if the banks surpass a
benchmark of 0.625% of its tier 1 capital for community development loans and likewise 0.625% for investments. 91 Fed.
Reg. 52121, 52140 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026). We are concerned that the practical effect of this proposal is that the
benchmark will serve not as a floor, but a ceiling.
3 NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk, (Sept. 10, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-development-activity-at-risk/.
4 NCRC, The Proposed CRA Rule's Strategic Plans: A More Predictable Path to Doing Less (Sept 1, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/the-proposed-cra-rules-strategic-plans-a-more-predictable-path-to-doing-less/.


3
lose 22.7% community obligations by large banks significantly jeopardizing 24.5% of local branches.
Families across Pennsylvania's 48 rural counties would struggle to afford mortgages, small businesses
would significantly decrease access to loan capital, and long-distance branches would affect their ability
to save increasing divestment for rural areas. It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize
banks to meet community needs. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the
proposed changes would reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income
communities and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or disinvestment
would be disproportionately affected.
Moreover, the proposal would substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while banks
with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less demanding
intermediate-bank framework rather than the more comprehensive tests applied to large banks.5 The
proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting requirements currently
applicable to large banks for institutions with $10 billion or less in assets, including reporting on small-
business, small-farm and community development lending.6
Approximately 800 banks would no longer receive a community development evaluation because the
proposal would raise the small-bank threshold from $412 million to $1 billion.7 The 417 banks newly
classified as intermediate rather than large would no longer be examined under separate CRA
investment and services tests and instead would be evaluated based on their combined community
development loans, investments and services. These reclassifications and resulting eliminations of
community development obligations for over 800 banks and separate investment evaluations for 400
banks, may worsen the housing crisis by reducing the demand for Low-Income Housing Tax Credits
(LIHTC). 43.5% of banks would lose large-bank status in Pennsylvania representing 22.7% loss of
current community development obligations.
We are concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and nonprofit
organizations.
Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development, financial counseling, workforce
programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based services through grants, investments,
loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations. These resources can be particularly important to
local organizations that have deep relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of their
communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and new
documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations.8 For smaller
nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology, accounting,
compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the underlying program itself.

5 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,120–23 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
6 Id. at 52,120.
7 NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3, 2026), https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-
rollbacks/.
8 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,129 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).

4
Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs.
In addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain financial
records, budgets or program documentation in the precise format a bank would need to establish CRA
eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations are more difficult or costly to
document, they may redirect funding toward larger organizations whose activities are easier to verify.
Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and partnerships can play in
supporting community development. Since 2020, the PA CDFI Network has worked with a coalition of
sixteen banks through a program designed to enhance CDFI capacity and small business growth in the
Philadelphia region. Together, these banks have contributed $118,425,000 in loan capital and 7,627,204
for technical advisory services to small businesses. This funding has kept many small business doors
open, since COVID-19, with 0ver 7,600 small businesses receiving technical advisory services, over
1,200 receiving loans, and over 5,800 jobs retained or created contributing to revitalization and helping
close the wealth gap in low-to-moderate communities.
These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into tangible
benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community development activities
receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond the banks themselves.
Before finalizing these provisions, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed documentation
requirements and limits on administrative expenses would reduce or redirect bank support away from
smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those with limited administrative capacity. The agencies
must also determine whether those effects would ultimately reduce resources available to low- and
moderate-income communities.
More broadly, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule primarily in terms of reducing
perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also determine what the changes mean
for the communities CRA is intended to serve.
Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
● identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny under
the proposal;
● quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community development
activities subject to CRA evaluation;
● assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
including rural communities and communities of color;
● consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
meaningful community accountability; and
Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes that the OCC
and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and
released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to prevent significant
declines in CRA-related activity.

5
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that
accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of
meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days. The
proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant changes to bank
classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core
elements of CRA implementation. The current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from community
organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that do not have dedicated
regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would allow affected organizations to
evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather examples from the communities they serve, and
provide the agencies with a more complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request
that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.
Truly,

RE: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, Docket ID OCC-2026-0694

To Whom It May Concern:

Community Housing of Maine (CHOM) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed changes to Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.

CHOM is a nonprofit housing organization that develops, preserves, and operates affordable housing across Maine. We
also provide supportive housing for older adults, individuals with disabilities, and people experiencing homelessness. Our
work includes partnerships with public agencies, financial institutions, community organizations, and local communities
to expand housing opportunities and strengthen communities throughout Maine.

CHOM is concerned about the potential impact of the proposed CRA changes on affordable housing and community
development efforts in Maine.

Across the state, affordable housing projects depend on partnerships among nonprofits, financial institutions, public
agencies, and local communities. Maine continues to face significant housing challenges, particularly in rural areas where
financing options can be more limited and where individual lenders often play an important role in making projects
possible.

Analysis of the proposed rule indicates that many Maine-based banks would move into different CRA categories under
the proposal. According to analysis prepared by the Partnership for Financial Equity, approximately 70% of Maine-based
OCC- and FDIC-regulated banks would move to a smaller CRA asset category, including eleven Maine-based banks that
would no longer be evaluated under the Large Bank CRA framework. In a largely rural state like Maine, where community
and regional banks are often key partners in affordable housing and community development efforts, those changes
could reduce incentives for investment in the housing and community development projects that communities across
the state need.

While the proposed changes are administrative in nature, they could have real-world consequences. Affordable housing
developments already face rising costs, funding challenges, and increasingly complex financing structures. Policies that
reduce incentives for community development investment risk making it harder to create and preserve housing that
Maine households can afford.

We are also concerned about proposed changes that would reduce reporting and transparency related to community
development activities and lending patterns. Access to this information helps communities, policymakers, and nonprofit
organizations understand local needs, identify gaps, and track progress over time. The proposed rule would reduce
reporting requirements for many institutions, resulting in less publicly available information about lending and
 One City Center, 4th Floor
Portland, ME 04101
207.879.0347
fax 207.879.0348
creating homes and inclusive communities
www.chomhousing.org




community development activity. In a rural state like Maine, where financing options can already be limited, maintaining
access to this information remains an important component of accountability and informed decision-making.

CHOM recognizes the importance of balancing meaningful community investment with appropriate regulatory
requirements for smaller financial institutions. Community and regional banks are vital partners in Maine communities,
and reducing unnecessary administrative burden can help those institutions continue serving local needs. At the same
time, we are concerned that increasing the Intermediate Bank threshold from $1.649 billion to $10 billion is a significant
change that appears disproportionate to the stated goal of providing regulatory relief for smaller institutions.

CHOM supports a CRA framework that continues to encourage investment in affordable housing and community
development while recognizing the importance of appropriate regulatory relief for smaller institutions. As regulators
consider these changes, we encourage them to carefully evaluate their impact on rural states like Maine and ensure that
efforts to reduce administrative burden do not inadvertently weaken investment in housing and community
development activities.

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,

Vickey Merrill
Director of Mission Advancement

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Community
Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN
3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
The Maple Corporation submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) because it would significantly weaken the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the rule's complexity and the scope of the changes, we
request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely
consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the
analysis and the evidence the agencies identify to support any changes, and extend the current comment
deadline by 60 days.
Maple is a minority-led nonprofit that provides technical and financial support to nonprofit organizations,
government agencies, and private developers to preserve affordable housing for low-income households.
Maple was incorporated in 1967 as the development arm of the Philadelphia Council for Community
Advancement (PCCA, 1964). Maple also develops affordable housing for very low- and low-income
residents of Philadelphia.
 For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been a key part of the federal framework that ensures banks meet the
credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress
also recognized that communities depend on access to both credit and deposit services. These protections
remain especially important in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch
closures, and unequal access to mainstream financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change how
regulators assess community development, bank services, and support for nonprofit organizations. We are
concerned that these changes are being considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on
low- and moderate-income communities and on communities that have experienced historic
discrimination and disinvestment.
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In the Philadelphia metro area,
from 2010 to 2024, banks made over $64 billion in CRA-qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or
in LMI census tracts, and over $22 billion in CRA-qualified lending to small businesses. The Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) plays a vital role in directing essential private capital and credit into low- and
moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods. It incentivizes commercial banks to partner with local
nonprofits, community development financial institutions (CDFIs), and housing developers to finance
affordable housing projects and neighborhood revitalization initiatives. Furthermore, CRA compliance
drives investment in small-business lending, first-time homebuyer down-payment assistance programs,
and specialized community facilities across the city's underserved corridors.
We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in our communities. For
example, it suggests that devoting just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital to community development loans
or investments would be enough to receive a passing CRA rating. This represents a dramatic reduction
from what large banks currently devote to community investments and loans, and we fear this new
guidance may operate as a ceiling rather than a floor. Pennsylvania receives over $3 billion in CRA-
related investments annually, but under the proposed rule that could fall to just over $600 million – an
80% loss.
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination cannot
withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans. If regulators lower
expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the communities they serve, there could
be harmful consequences for those communities. For example, in our community, if Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) mandates were reduced or eliminated, banks would no longer face regulatory
requirements to reinvest capital into local low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. This would lead to a
sharp decline in bank-backed debt, equity investments, and philanthropic grants for local affordable
housing developers and CDFIs. Consequently, financial institutions would likely divert credit away from
disinvested corridors, severely weakening small business lending, neighborhood revitalization efforts, and
down-payment assistance programs across Philadelphia.

 It is imperative that the CRA continue to incentivize banks to meet the needs of communities like ours.
Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce
lending, services, or investment available to low- and moderate-income communities, and whether
communities that have experienced historic discrimination or disinvestment would be disproportionately
affected.
The proposal would also substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated
under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while banks with assets
between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less demanding intermediate-
bank framework rather than the more comprehensive tests applied to large banks. The proposal would
also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting requirements currently applicable to large banks,
including requirements related to small-business and community development lending.
A number of banks operating in Philadelphia will now be classified as either intermediate or small banks
under the proposed rule and, as a result, be subject to less rigorous requirements. These reclassifications,
along with the resulting elimination of community development obligations for more than 800 banks and
separate investment evaluations for 400 banks nationwide, may worsen the housing crisis by reducing
investor interest in purchasing Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC) and limiting access to
mortgages for first-time homebuyers or to credit for home repairs.
Similarly, the proposed rule would narrow the scope of what regulators examine under the large-bank
service test. Today, examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and information
on the costs and features of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit this criterion to credit services,
removing deposit products such as checking and savings accounts from direct evaluation under the
service test. As a result, examiners would no longer assess whether those products are affordable and
responsive to community needs, even though approximately 15% of Philadelphians – over 100,000
households – remain unbanked or underbanked. Moreover, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of
Philadelphia, these households are overwhelmingly low-income, black, or disabled. CRA review of the
cost and features of deposit products has played an important role in encouraging banks to address these
disparities by providing affordable products, and it must continue to do so.
For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are integral to access to credit
and economic opportunity. They can determine whether families can safely receive income, build savings,
establish banking relationships, and obtain responsible credit. In my experience in the banking industry, I
witnessed the closure of two branches in communities, leaving small businesses to travel significant
distances for their banking needs. This also affected residents, the elderly, and physically challenged
banking clients, who were no longer able to access their funds or resolve issues quickly in their
neighborhoods.
This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and moderate-income
communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to affordable mortgage credit and
homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible small-business financing; and
neighborhoods continue to need investment in affordable housing, small businesses and other community
development.
 The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply because a bank
falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA obligations and scrutiny
applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that would move into less rigorous
examination categories, determine the communities those institutions serve, analyze the lending and
community development activity that would receive less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be
concentrated in low- and moderate-income communities or in communities that have experienced historic
discrimination and disinvestment.
We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and nonprofit
organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development, financial counseling,
workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based services through grants,
investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations. These resources can be particularly
important to local organizations that have deep relationships with residents and understand the specific
needs of their communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and new
documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations. For smaller
nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology, accounting,
compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the underlying program itself.
Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs. In
addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain financial
records or program documentation in the precise format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If
banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may
redirect funding toward larger organizations whose activities are easier to verify.
Our organization has seen firsthand how bank grants, investments, and partnerships can support
community development. Through LISC, a certified CDFI, Maple secured essential funding to help
clients finance a Physical Capital Needs Assessment (PCNA) for an affordable housing renovation
project. Maple also received grant funding that directly covered project staff salaries, allowing us to
absorb these administrative costs and provide our clients with significant consulting fee savings. Beyond
capital development, institutional banking grants continue to play a critical role in supporting community
services that measurably improve residents' quality of life.
These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into tangible
benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community development activities
receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond the banks themselves. These
rules should be motivated by the needs of the communities CRA is intended to serve and not by the
perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions.


 To be considered economic development under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying small
business must promote economic development by supporting permanent job creation, retention, or
improvement for low- or moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income communities.
The proposed rule would eliminate this "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks could earn CRA
credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or improves jobs for low- and
moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income communities. This change would weaken the
connection between CRA economic-development credit and the people and communities CRA is intended
to benefit. Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying business expand does not necessarily create jobs,
increase economic opportunity in an underserved neighborhood or address the needs of low- and
moderate-income communities.
Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens a qualifying
business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank to demonstrate that those
benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or neighborhoods.
We are also concerned that currently, banks above the large bank threshold annually collect and report
data on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans, while the proposal
would limit these requirements to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. Banks with assets of $10
billion or less would no longer be required to annually collect and report CRA data on small business
loans and community development loans.
Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers would have less information
to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance or understand whether local credit needs are being
met. Local community leaders and elected officials depend on this data for decision making and for
ensuring that the needs of residents are being addressed. This proposed change is inconsistent with CRA's
requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low-
and moderate-income communities, and should not be in the final rule.
Lastly, prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
● identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny under
the proposal;
● quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community development
activities subject to CRA evaluation;
● assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
including rural communities and communities of color; and
● consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
meaningful community accountability.

Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes that the
OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is
prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to
prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that
accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of
meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods.

We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days. The
proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant changes to
bank classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit grants
and other core elements of CRA implementation. The current comment period closes on October
13, 2026.

Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that do not
have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would allow affected
organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather examples from the
communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more complete record on which to base
any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment
deadline by at least 60 days.

Sincerely,


Jacquelyn J Sims, MS, RHDFP
President and Executive Director
The Maple Corporation
901 Market Street
Suite 3020, 3rd Floor
Philadelphia, PA 19107
Pronouns: She/Her/Hers
(P)215-419-7361

To Whom it May Concern:

First Federal Bank appreciates the opportunity to submit this comment letter regarding the joint
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
(OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) on July 31, 2026, to amend the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.

To begin, First Federal Bank is an interstate federally charted savings association headquartered
in Lake City, Florida with total assets of 4.5 million as of June 30, 2026. The bank is a community-
based full-service mutual bank that serves over 70,000 customers from 26 community banking
branches, with mortgage lending offices in Florida, and South Carolina, and SBA and USDA
lending offices in the Southeast. Because we are a mutual bank, we are owned by our customers
and not stockholders, which allows us to truly focus on our customers' needs.

As a community-focused financial institution, First Federal Bank recognizes the importance of a
CRA framework that is transparent, objective, administrable, and appropriately tailored to bank
size, business model, market conditions, and community needs. The Bank supports the agencies'
stated objectives of aligning CRA implementation with the statutory purpose of encouraging banks
to help meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income





4705 West US Hwy 90, Lake City, FL 32055 • (386) 755-0600 • ffbf.com

Member FDIC • Equal Housing Lender
neighborhoods, consistent with safe and sound operations. We respectfully offer the following
comments and recommendations for the OCC's consideration.

Comments and Recommendations

CRA Framework
First Federal Bank supports efforts to modernize and clarify CRA regulations while preserving the
core statutory focus on meeting community credit needs. In particular, the Bank supports a
framework that reduces unnecessary burden for community banks, provides clear standards for
qualifying activities, and maintains flexibility for banks to respond to local needs. We also
encourage the OCC to ensure that any final rule avoids unintended consequences that could reduce
community development activity, limit bank partnerships, or create inconsistent supervisory
expectations across federal banking agencies.

Additionally, First Federal Bank supports the OCC's goal of increasing clarity, transparency, and
objectivity in CRA evaluations. Clear standards are essential for banks to plan activities, allocate
resources, and document performance effectively. The final rule should include practical guidance,
illustrative examples, and examiner training to promote consistent application across examination
teams and regions.

Community Development Grants
First Federal Bank strongly recommends that the agencies continue to consider community
development grants and donations within the regulatory definition of qualified investments, as
these contributions are an important and often flexible means of supporting nonprofit
organizations, community development partners, and initiatives that address local needs.

At the same time, the Bank understands the agencies' objective of ensuring that community
development grants reach the intended communities and are used for activities with a primary
community development purpose. With that said, the final rule should avoid documentation
standards that are overly burdensome or difficult for banks to verify. Banks should be permitted
to rely on reasonable due diligence, written certifications, grant agreements, or other practical
documentation from recipient organizations to demonstrate that funds support qualifying
community development purposes.





4705 West US Hwy 90, Lake City, FL 32055 • (386) 755-0600 • ffbf.com

Member FDIC • Equal Housing Lender

Asset Thresholds
First Federal Bank supports the proposed asset threshold that would define intermediate banks as
institutions with total assets greater than $1 billion and less than $10 billion. This threshold
appropriately recognizes the operational differences between community-focused institutions and
the largest financial institutions, while preserving meaningful CRA accountability through lending
and community development evaluations. Banks in this asset range often serve diverse local and
regional markets, but may not have the same scale, systems, staffing, or geographic complexity as
institutions with assets exceeding $10 billion. A tailored intermediate bank category would allow
these institutions to remain focused on responsive lending and community development activities
without imposing large-bank testing, reporting, and documentation requirements that may divert
resources from serving community credit needs.

Regulatory Burden
First Federal Bank strongly supports reducing unnecessary regulatory burden, particularly for
community banks that serve local markets with limited compliance resources. CRA performance
should continue to be evaluated in a manner that reflects each bank's capacity, business model,
product offerings, branch network, and market opportunities. The final rule should preserve
flexibility for banks to support affordable housing, small businesses, community services,
economic development, and other needs identified through local outreach and market knowledge.

Agency Coordination
First Federal Bank encourages the OCC and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to
coordinate with the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System to promote a consistent
CRA framework across supervised institutions. Divergent rules or examination expectations could
create uncertainty, reduce comparability, and impose unnecessary complexity on banks,
community partners, and the public.

Final Rule Implementation
Any final rule should include a reasonable implementation period, clear transition provisions, and
publicly available guidance to support effective compliance. Smaller institutions have fewer in-
house legal, compliance and IT staff. Banks of all sizes need sufficient time to update policies,
procedures, systems, training, monitoring practices, and documentation standards. Transition

First Federal Bank appreciates the OCC's consideration of these comments. The Bank supports a
CRA regulatory framework that is clear, consistent, appropriately tailored, and focused on
meaningful outcomes for communities. We respectfully encourage the OCC to finalize a rule that
reduces unnecessary burden while preserving flexibility for banks to meet local credit and

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Boomers Collaborative Foundation urges the OCC and FDIC to preserve strong Community Reinvestment Act incentives for bank support of Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) and the full range of affordable housing solutions.

We are advancing a resident-owned, limited-equity housing model for older adults with limited incomes in Austin, Texas. Our goal is to make aging in place—without aging alone—possible through affordable housing, resident governance, and opportunities for connection and participation.

A critical barrier is financing the membership shares residents must purchase to join the housing cooperative. These share loans serve a different purpose from the financing used to develop the property. Even if construction and permanent financing are secured, prospective residents still need an affordable way to purchase their shares. Many of the seniors we seek to serve cannot make that purchase entirely from savings.

In our efforts to assemble financing, no lender outside the CDFI sector has stepped forward to offer share loans for our proposed Texas model. We therefore expect to depend on CDFIs to help bridge this gap. This is an anticipated financing need, not a claim that we have already secured a lending commitment.

Limited-equity cooperative housing belongs in the mosaic of solutions needed to address housing affordability. Without accessible share loans, it could remain out of reach for the very households it is intended to serve.

We ask the agencies to preserve meaningful CRA consideration for bank loans, investments, grants, and technical assistance supporting CDFIs and affordable housing. The final rule should recognize both financing for eligible cooperative housing development and financing that enables low- and moderate-income residents to purchase membership shares.

Please evaluate how the proposed changes would affect CDFIs’ capacity to develop these lending products and serve households whose needs conventional financing has not met. Simplifying bank compliance should preserve the resources communities need to turn affordable housing models into accessible homes.

comments.text:
COMMENT FORM TEXT:
To:
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)

Subject: Opposition to Proposed Rulemaking Weakening the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA)

To the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency:

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rules that would weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). As a resident of Milwaukie, Oregon who has worked in homeless services and works in social services, I see firsthand how critical equitable access to capital is for the health, stability, and future of our communities.

The CRA is a foundational anti-redlining law that ensures banks meet the credit needs of the communities where they operate. The FDIC and OCC’s current proposal threatens to roll back decades of progress by significantly reducing banks' obligations to reinvest in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. If implemented, 1 in 4 banks in Oregon would no longer be required to meet these reinvestment standards.

The financial fallout for Oregon would be devastating. Current estimates indicate that our state receives approximately $1.6 billion annually in community development lending and investment. If banks reduce their activity to the newly proposed minimum benchmarks, that investment could plummet to just $127 million—a catastrophic loss of nearly $1.5 billion every year. Furthermore, 31 bank branches across 23 Oregon cities are now at risk of closure, the vast majority of which are located in low-to-moderate-income and majority-minority census tracts.

This loss of capital will directly harm our most vulnerable populations. The CRA currently drives 85% of bank investments in Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC) and nearly 98% of New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC). In Oregon, these funds are actively used to build affordable housing for families displaced by wildfires, construct units for homeless youth and veterans, and finance essential community facilities like federally qualified health centers.

Oregon is currently battling an acute housing shortage and a homelessness crisis. Weakening the CRA will create insurmountable financing gaps for affordable housing developers, diminish the impact of public dollars, and sever the pipeline of funding for community health and social services.

I urge the FDIC and the OCC to withdraw this proposal immediately and instead focus on modernizing the CRA in a way that strengthens—rather than undermines—anti-redlining protections and community reinvestment obligations.

Sincerely,
Addison Bates

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on
Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN
1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Habitat for Humanity of Greater Pittsburgh (Habitat Pittsburgh) is pleased to offer this comment
on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above. As a Habitat for Humanity affiliate in
Pennsylvania working alongside families, volunteers, financial institutions, and community
partners, we see every day how access to responsible credit and community investment can help
families build stability through homeownership. We oppose the proposal because it would
weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) and could reduce the resources available to
meet urgent local housing needs. We ask the agencies to examine these community-level
consequences, release the supporting analysis for public comment, and extend the current
deadline by at least 60 days.
Habitat Pittsburgh is a Habitat for Humanity International organization serving Allegheny
County in PA. We partner with people and communities to build and preserve affordable
homeownership through new home construction and rehabilitation, home repair, mortgage
lending and financial literacy counseling. In the past ten years, we have sold 31 homes,
originated 31 mortgages and made repairs to 147 homes with low-income families.
For the forty years of Habitat's existence, the CRA has been an important part of the federal
framework for ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including
low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. These protections remain especially important in
 Pennsylvania communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss, and
unequal access to mainstream financial services.
Habitat for Humanity International organizations across Pennsylvania rely on strong,
accountable bank partnerships to create and preserve affordable homeownership. Banks support
Habitat affiliates through grants and sponsorships; loans and lines of credit to affiliates;
acquisition, construction, and development financing; responsible mortgage products for Habitat
homebuyers; origination, purchase, and servicing of Habitat mortgages; investments in home
repair and neighborhood revitalization; and employee volunteer engagement. These relationships
help affiliates develop new homes, help low-income families secure affordable mortgages,
provide critical repairs at no or low cost to qualifying homeowners, and support broader
community development.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and change how
regulators evaluate community development, bank services, and support for nonprofit
organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without adequate
analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and communities that
have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In our service area of
Allegheny County, bank support has helped fund new home construction and as well as fund
critical home repairs. Habitat Pittsburgh has received funding from the PNC Foundation for the
past three years supporting critical home repairs to low-income homeowners who otherwise
would not have the resources to get their repairs done.
We are concerned that the proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in our communities.
For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital devoted to either
community development loans or investments would be enough to receive a passing CRA rating.
This represents a dramatic reduction in what large banks currently devote to community
investments and loans, and we fear that this guidance may operate as a ceiling instead of a floor.
Pennsylvania currently receives more than $3 billion in CRA-related investments annually, but
under the proposed rule that could fall to just over $600 million—an 80% loss.
Low- and moderate-income communities cannot withstand such a reduction. For Habitat
affiliates, reduced bank engagement could mean fewer resources to acquire land, build or
rehabilitate homes, provide affordable mortgage financing, complete free critical repairs,
preserve existing homeownership, and invest in neighborhoods.
It is imperative that the CRA continue to incentivize banks to meet the needs of communities like
ours. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes
would reduce lending, services, or investment available to low- and moderate-income
communities and whether historically disinvested communities would be disproportionately
affected.
 The proposal would also substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while
banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less
demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more comprehensive tests applied to
large banks. The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting
requirements currently applicable to large banks, including reporting on small-business and
community development lending.
Banks serving communities across Pennsylvania could therefore be subject to less rigorous
requirements. These reclassifications may worsen the housing crisis by reducing investment in
affordable housing, access to mortgages for first-time homebuyers, financing for home repairs,
and capital for community-based development.
The proposed rule would also narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service test.
Today, examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and information
about the costs and features of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit this criterion to credit
services, removing checking and savings products from direct evaluation. Yet affordable
accounts and accessible branches help families safely receive income, build savings, establish
banking relationships, and qualify for responsible mortgage credit.
The agencies have not shown that community needs become less significant simply because a
bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before reducing CRA obligations, they should identify
the banks that would move into less rigorous categories, determine the communities those
institutions serve, analyze the activity that would receive less scrutiny, and assess whether the
effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-income, rural, or historically disinvested
communities.
We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations. Habitat affiliates use bank grants, sponsorships, investments, and loans
to support land acquisition, predevelopment, construction, rehabilitation, home repair, housing
counseling, mortgage operations, neighborhood revitalization, and organizational capacity. These
resources make it possible to convert capital into lasting benefits for families and neighborhoods.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15% limit on indirect costs and new
documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for affiliates. Staff, facilities,
technology, accounting, compliance, insurance, and other operating expenses are necessary to
deliver affordable housing and repair programs. Smaller affiliates may have fewer programs and
funding sources over which to spread these costs. If banks conclude that grants to local
organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding away from
community-based partners with deep local relationships.
Habitat Pittsburgh has received bank support in the form of grants, build day sponsorships,
purchases of mortgages as well as volunteer support.
 Rules governing which grants and community development activities receive CRA consideration
have consequences far beyond banks themselves. These rules should be guided by the needs of
the communities CRA is intended to serve, not solely by the perceived regulatory burden on
financial institutions.
The proposal would also eliminate the current "purpose test" for certain economic development
financing. Banks could receive CRA credit for financing a qualifying business without showing
that the activity creates, retains, or improves jobs for low- and moderate-income people or
communities. This would weaken the connection between CRA credit and the people and
neighborhoods the law is intended to benefit.
We are further concerned that the proposal would limit annual collection and reporting of data on
small-business and community development loans to banks with more than $10 billion in assets.
Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers would have less information
to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance, understand whether local credit needs are
being met, and hold institutions accountable.
Before issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
1. identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny;
2. quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services, and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
3. assess whether the effects would be concentrated in particular geographic areas or
populations, including rural communities and communities of color; or
4. consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
meaningful community accountability.
Given these omissions and the concerns described above, Habitat Pittsburgh urges the OCC and
FDIC to rescind the proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impact is prepared and
released for public comment. At minimum, the proposal requires substantial changes to prevent
significant declines in CRA-related activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that
accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of
meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days.
The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant changes
to bank classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit
grants, and other core elements of CRA implementation. The current comment period closes on
October 13, 2026.
 Additional time would allow Habitat affiliates and other community organizations to evaluate the
proposal's practical consequences, gather examples from the communities they serve, and
provide the agencies with a more complete record. We therefore request that the agencies extend
the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.
Sincerely,
Dr. Howard B. Slaughter, Jr.
President & CEO
Habitat for Humanity of Greater Pittsburgh

Comptroller Gould, Chairman Hill, Ms. Janes, to whom it may concern:
The Cambridge Housing Authority (CHA) submits these comments in response to the proposed amendments to
the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and
the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. CHA appreciates stated goals of improving clarity, reducing
unnecessary burden, and ensuring that community development resources reach the communities they are
intended to benefit. At the same time, as the CRA plays a critical role as one of the only tools supporting
affordable housing production in the United States, CHA is concerned that several elements of the proposal
could weaken that financing ecosystem at a time when communities across the country are facing an acute and
worsening housing crisis. Cambridge, Massachusetts' experience reflects that national reality: the impact of the
proposed CRA regulation changes would be devastating.
CHA urges the agencies to revise the proposed rule to preserve the strong CRA incentives for affordable
housing lending, Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) investment, community development grants, and
nonprofit partnerships that directly support low- and moderate-income households. More specifically, CHA
recommends that the final rule maintains robust consideration for community development investments and
grants, avoid reducing accountability for banks that play an important role in local affordable housing finance,
and ensure that any new documentation requirements are workable for public housing authorities and
nonprofit housing providers.
The proposed rule will detrimentally impact affordable housing development in Cambridge, MA.
CHA relies on a complex mix of public subsidy, private debt, tax credit equity, and community development
capital to develop and preserve affordable housing. Capital investment motivated by the CRA has long been an
important part of this ecosystem. Banks subject to meaningful CRA evaluation often provide construction loans,
permanent loans, acquisition financing, tax credit equity, grants, and other flexible resources that help close
financing gaps and make deeply affordable housing feasible.
In Cambridge and similar high-cost markets, affordable housing developments routinely face funding gaps
driven by land costs, construction costs, operating pressures, and the need to serve households with very low
incomes. Even modest reductions in CRA-motivated investment demand, concessionary lending, or grant
support can affect whether projects proceed, how deeply affordable they can be, and how much additional
public subsidy is required.

For a recent project, there was over $0.11 difference per dollar of credit between CRA-driven LIHTC pricing and
non-CRA-driven pricing. Eleven cents may not sound like a lot to someone unfamiliar with the LIHTC program,
but it amounted to over $4 million, or over $59,000 per unit, on this recent project. When that cost difference
is factored over the 1000 affordable homes in our development pipeline, the shortfall from losing CRA-
motivated LIHTC pricing reaches over $59,000,000. A financing gap this large cannot be covered by other
sources. If adopted, the proposed changes to the CRA will grind CHA's efforts to expand affordable housing to a
halt.
To avoid that end, we respectfully request that the proposed rules be revised to ensure:
1. Preservation of strong CRA incentives for affordable housing investment
The proposal would raise the large bank threshold to more than $10 billion in assets and would subject
banks with $10 billion or less in assets to fewer data collection, maintenance, and reporting
obligations. CHA is concerned that this change could reduce CRA incentives for a significant group of
mid-sized banks that currently participate in affordable housing finance and make up the bulk of the
LIHTC motivated investors in the market. If these institutions face less robust evaluation of community
development activity, they may have reduced motivation to provide LIHTC equity, community
development loans, grants, and other financing commitments essential to these transactions.
2. Avoidance of weakening the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit market
LIHTC remains the primary federal tool for producing and preserving affordable rental housing. CRA-
motivated bank investment is a major driver of LIHTC demand and pricing. If fewer banks are subject to
meaningful investment expectations, demand for LIHTC equity could soften, reducing equity proceeds
and increasing financing gaps. For public housing authorities and mission-driven affordable housing
developers, this would likely translate into greater reliance on scarce local, state, and federal subsidy
sources. As noted earlier, CHA calculates the loss in LIHTC equity from this change to be over $59,000
per unit, or more than $59 million in funding for projects in Cambridge's affordable housing
development pipeline.
3. Maintenance of meaningful consideration for grants and nonprofit partnerships
CHA supports the goal of ensuring that community development grants benefit intended communities.
However, the proposed limitation on grant consideration, including the requirement that large banks
document that recipients do not have overhead costs above 15 percent, could create practical barriers
for public agencies and nonprofit housing organizations. Affordable housing development requires
organizational capacity, planning, predevelopment, resident engagement, compliance, asset
management, and project administration. These activities are not incidental to community
development; they are often essential to delivering and sustaining affordable housing.
4. Recognition of the full continuum of affordable housing finance
The proposal's greater emphasis on lending may preserve CRA consideration for construction loans,
acquisition loans, permanent loans, and other project-level credit facilities. CHA supports continued
and clear CRA recognition for those activities. However, affordable housing finance depends on a
broader continuum of support, including equity investment, credit enhancement, grants, technical
assistance, and operating support for mission-driven sponsors. The final rule should not inadvertently

privilege debt over other forms of capital that are equally necessary to meet the credit and housing
needs of low- and moderate-income communities.
5. Retention of accountability while reducing unnecessary burden
CHA recognizes the importance of clear, predictable, and appropriately tailored CRA evaluation
standards. Reducing unnecessary compliance burden can be a legitimate goal, particularly for
community banks. However, burden reduction should not come at the expense of transparency,
accountability, or incentives to serve low- and moderate-income communities. The agencies should
ensure that any revised asset thresholds and examination procedures continue to encourage banks of
all sizes to respond to demonstrated local needs, including affordable housing production and
preservation.
Requested revisions
CHA requests that the agencies revise the proposed rule to:
1. Preserve strong CRA consideration for LIHTC equity investments and other community development
investments that support affordable housing;
2. Maintain meaningful incentives for mid-sized banks to participate in affordable housing finance;
3. Ensure that grants, predevelopment support, technical assistance, and capacity-building resources
remain eligible when they directly support affordable housing outcomes;
4. Avoid rigid overhead standards that may exclude effective public and nonprofit housing partners; and
5. Retain sufficient reporting and examination transparency to allow communities to evaluate whether
local credit and housing needs are being met.
For the past 15 years in Cambridge and surrounding communities, the CRA has played a vital role in
encouraging financial institutions to help meet the credit needs of low- and moderate-income communities
and has been a critical tool in CHA's $1.5 billion investment in affordable housing. During that time, investors
motivated by the CRA have provided over $500 million in equity funding for this effort.
Amid the ongoing national housing affordability crisis, the Community Reinvestment Act should remain a
strong and reliable tool for bringing private capital to bear on the urgent need for affordable homes. A final rule
that provides clarity while preserving robust incentives for lending, investment, grants, and partnerships will
better advance the statutory purpose of the CRA and help communities address urgent housing needs.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed rule.
Respectfully submitted,

Clara Fraden
Chief Executive Officer

To the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation:
HVN Development, LLC respectfully urges the agencies to keep the CRA investment test in place for banks with assets above the current $1.649 billion large-bank threshold. The proposal would move banks between $1.649 billion and $10 billion into a new intermediate category with no investment test. For affordable housing developers like HVN, that change would remove a meaningful share of the bank demand that prices Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing Credit) equity, at the moment Congress has expanded the program.
About HVN Development
HVN Development is a California affordable housing developer focused on Housing Credit communities in Los Angeles and the surrounding region. Most of our pipeline is 4% Housing Credit transactions financed with tax-exempt private activity bonds allocated by CDLAC. Each development combines bank construction and permanent lending, tax-exempt bond financing, and Housing Credit equity provided by bank investors directly or through multi-investor syndicated funds.
Why the Investment Test Matters to Our Transactions
CRA demand sets the price of the equity that closes our deals. According to the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC), banks supply roughly 75 to 80 percent of Housing Credit equity, and at least 71 percent of that is CRA-motivated. AHTCC's survey found at least 108 banks below $10 billion in assets invested about $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity over five years, or roughly $2 billion when extrapolated to the full market.
Those banks matter to us even when they are not the named investor. The syndicated funds that invest in our partnerships pool capital from many banks, and regional and community banks deepen the bidding for each transaction. Fewer CRA-motivated buyers means less competition and lower credit pricing.
In California's high-cost markets, small pricing changes create large financing gaps. On a development generating $30 million of federal credits, a five-cent decline in pricing removes $1.5 million of equity. That gap must be filled with scarce state and local soft funds or more deferred developer fee, or the project does not proceed.
The timing compounds the risk. The 2025 federal tax law lowered the tax-exempt bond financing test for 4% transactions from 50 to 25 percent and permanently increased 9% credit allocations. More 4% transactions will need equity just as the proposal would weaken a key source of investor demand.
CRA investment also anchors the rest of the capital stack. Banks that invest in our equity often provide the construction loan or purchase the bonds on the same transaction. We support the proposal's recognition that a CD investment forming part of a multicomponent financing involving a loan is complex; Housing Credit transactions are a clear example.
Our Requests
1.Keep the investment test for banks above $1.649 billion. If the agencies raise the large-bank threshold, we ask that they adopt the $3.252 billion alternative described in the proposal rather than $10 billion.
2.Keep the intermediate bank CD test meaningful. We ask the agencies to retain the requirement that an intermediate bank earn at least a "satisfactory" CD test rating to receive an overall "satisfactory," rather than allowing the lending test alone to carry the rating.
3.Name Housing Credit equity as a responsive and complex CD investment. This should include equity held through multi-investor funds and equity paired with a construction loan or bond purchase on the same transaction.
4.Preserve credit for statewide and regional benefit. Fund investments spread across a state should continue to receive consideration once a bank has served its assessment areas.
5.Lower the risk weight on Housing Credit investments. In the parallel capital rulemaking, we support AHTCC's request to reduce the risk weight from 100 percent to 20 percent, and in no case above 50 percent.
Conclusion
The investment test has built a deep, efficient market for Housing Credit equity, and California renters benefit directly from it. We support the comments of the AHTCC and ask the agencies to preserve that market as they finalize the rule. Thank you for the opportunity to comment.
Respectfully submitted,
JP Sciammarella
Chief Financial Officer
HVN Development, LLC
300 Spectrum Center Drive, Suite 1100
Irvine, CA 92618

comments.text:
COMMENT FORM TEXT:
October 7, 2026

As an employee in the banking industry, I recognize the importance of a CRA framework that is transparent, objective, administrable, and appropriately tailored to a bank’s size, business model, market conditions, and community needs. I support the agencies’ stated objectives of aligning CRA implementation with the statutory purpose of encouraging banks to help meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, consistent with safe and sound operations and respectfully offer the following comments and recommendations for the OCC’s consideration.

Data Collection, Reporting, and Disclosure
The proposal appropriately recognizes the relationship between CRA small business and small farm data requirements and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s Section 1071 small business lending data rule. However, the practical overlap between the two regimes appears likely to affect a limited number of banks, because Section 1071 applies only to financial institutions that meet its coverage criteria pertaining to covered small business lending activity. Additional information is needed to determine the number of small and intermediate banks subject to duplicative collection, maintenance, or reporting obligations under both frameworks.

CRA data collection, maintenance, and reporting remain important because they provide regulators, financial institutions, and communities with a consistent basis for evaluating whether banks are helping meet the credit needs of the communities they serve, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, in a safe and sound manner. CRA small business and small farm data also support transparent performance evaluations, help identify lending patterns and community development needs, and provide an established public framework distinct from the fair lending and market-monitoring purposes of Section 1071.

My recommendation is that banks identifying as an intermediate bank under the proposed asset threshold should continue to collect, maintain, and report CRA data. Continuing these requirements for intermediate banks would preserve meaningful CRA performance information, avoid creating gaps in data used to evaluate community credit needs, and ensure that the agencies have adequate information to assess the impact of any future changes intended to reduce duplicative reporting. Before discontinuing or narrowing CRA data requirements, the agencies should provide additional analysis showing the number and type of institutions subject to both CRA and Section 1071 reporting and the extent to which Section 1071 data would provide an adequate substitute for CRA-specific data.

Retail Banking Services
Consideration of banking services is particularly important for low- and moderate-income individuals, who may have less flexibility to travel to a more distant branch, conduct banking during limited hours, absorb higher transaction fees, or qualify for products that require higher minimum balances. Access to conveniently located branches, suitable operating hours, affordable deposit and credit products, and reasonably priced transaction services can affect an individual’s ability to establish and maintain a banking relationship, manage household expenses, build savings, obtain credit, and avoid reliance on higher-cost alternative financial services. Reviewing material differences among branches also helps identify whether low- and moderate-income communities receive a level and cost of service reasonably comparable to that available elsewhere in a bank’s market.

I recommend and strongly support that, under the service test, the agencies retain a review of the general services offered by a bank, including hours of operation, available loan and deposit products, and transaction fees, as well as, where applicable, any material differences in the availability or cost of services at particular branches. This review would ensure that CRA evaluations continue to consider whether retail banking services are reasonably accessible and responsive to the needs of the communities a bank serves. 

In closing, I appreciate the OCC and FDIC’s consideration of my comments.

Respectfully,
G. Jones
