To Whom It May Concern,

On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA). CRA has helped create a durable incentive for banks to provide
loans, investments, grants, and services in communities that have historically lacked access to
capital.

We appreciate the agencies' efforts to reform the CRA regulations and support some of the
agencies' provisions that could improve the CRA framework and increase responsible capital in
underserved communities. However, we have grave concerns about the increases in the asset
thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under the CRA and the restrictions on
operating grants. We also have concerns about several interacting provisions that could further
weaken community development incentives and will undoubtedly impair the flow of much-
needed capital to the most underserved communities.

Renaissance Community Loan Fund (RCLF) is a community development finance institution
(CDFI) loan fund operating in Mississippi (MS) and Alabama (AL), two of the poorest states
(MS is #1 and AL is #7). MS has the second-highest poverty rate, and AL has the seventh-
highest. The banking needs of these states remain very high, yet they are underserved. We
have been making loans to low- to moderate-income borrowers since 2008. We currently have
more than $76M in loans on our books (nearly $242M in loans closed since inception), with
nearly 80% of these loans to low-income borrowers. We also provide small business technical
assistance, homebuyer education, and financial fitness classes in both states. We have created
 or retained nearly 3,900 jobs (since inception) and provided nearly 39,000 consultation hours
to clients from 2020 to 2025.

Banks are critical partners in our work. We have relationships with banks that provide loans,
investments, and grants. These partnerships provided approximately $66.0M, or 28.11% of
our total borrowed/total grant or investment capital support, which has helped us support
families in purchasing more than 700 homes ($87.6M) and nearly 300 businesses ($63.1M).
We were created to assist the MS Gulf Coast rebuild after Katrina, and we formed bank
partnerships to provide the financing needed to help 651 families find a new home. Our role in
the partnership was to provide the capital banks needed to extend first mortgages, and RCLF
contributed 40-60% of the capital stack to help banks become comfortable with our borrowers.

These partnerships are mutually reinforcing. In addition to providing critical capital and
resources to CDFIs, banks rely on CDFIs to reach underserved communities, develop
borrowers, and cultivate future bank customers. A prime example is Murky Waters. We helped
three friends open a new restaurant when no one else would provide the necessary capital, as
this was their first business venture. We later provided additional loans to open new restaurant
locations and expand into additional lines of business. A bank consolidation loan provided the
business owners with the capital to repay the RCLF financings. This is how the process is
supposed to work: no bank would support them when they first started their business in 2012,
but their growth led to takeout financing in 2022. The CRA has long helped create incentives
for banks to build and sustain these relationships, strengthening the broader community
development ecosystem. We are therefore concerned that several provisions in the proposal
could weaken these incentives, reducing bank engagement with CDFIs and ultimately the flow
of capital to the communities we serve.

Raised Asset Thresholds Jeopardize Community Development Finance:
Section IV.A, "Asset Thresholds"; Questions 1-3

The proposal defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets,
intermediate banks as institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion in assets, and large
banks as institutions with more than $10 billion in assets. About 800 banks that currently face
a separate community development test as intermediate small banks would become small
banks and lose that requirement. Another approximately 400 banks that are currently
evaluated as large banks would become intermediate banks, losing the separate large-bank
lending, investment, and service tests and many associated data-reporting requirements.

In the state of Mississippi, it is estimated that 21 of 51 banks, comprising 41.2% of all banks
in the state, would no longer be required to reinvest in local community development projects
such as affordable housing, small business support, workforce development, community
healthcare, and education services. About 8 of 22 banks, comprising 38.4% of all banks in the
state, would lose their large-bank status, thereby jeopardizing 600 of the 664 low- and
moderate-income (LMI) census tracts in Mississippi. Mississippi has no large money-center
banks in its footprint and is not supported by large foundations. Nearly all of the banks in
Mississippi are CDFI Banks, and they rarely invest in CDFI loan funds. In the state of Alabama,
where we have served since the latter part of 2023, it is estimated that 20 of 72 banks, 27.8%

Page 2
 of all banks in the state, would no longer be required to reinvest in local community
development projects. About 9 of 35 banks, 25.7% of all banks in the state, would lose their
large-bank status, thereby jeopardizing 1043 of the 1181 low- and moderate-income (LMI)
census tracts in Alabama.

In these communities, the loss of even one or two CRA-motivated bank partners can materially
affect whether projects are financed. For communities with fewer financial institutions and
limited sources of private capital to begin with, losing even a handful of CRA-motivated lenders
and investors could have an outsized effect on whether affordable housing, small businesses,
and community facilities are financed.

Harm to Communities from Loss of Community Development Finance

These thresholds determine whether and how a bank's community development performance
is evaluated, thereby affecting the strength of banks' incentives to engage in community
development. The agencies acknowledge in the proposal that when banks become subject to a
CD test under the current framework, the explicit evaluation of their CD activities typically
prompts them to adjust their CRA programs.

Reclassifying banks from large to intermediate banks would reduce incentives for community
development activities and directly affect our partnerships. We estimate that $7.7M of our
funding (11.7%) would be at risk from our bank funders. This further exacerbates the issue we
face in Mississippi: the lack of a large-bank presence in our footprint—a state where more
financing is needed, not less.

Recently, we provided $2.1M to help construct a skilled nursing facility in D'Iberville, MS. A
bank provided $11.0M, and the borrower contributed $1.4M. Without the bank partnership,
this facility would not be under construction. Additionally, 50% of our funding came from bank
leverage to support Mississippi's State Small Business Credit Initiative (SSBCI) program. This
was part of the $28M in debt capital raised to support our SSBCI investment. This program has
helped RCLF fund several new businesses in Mississippi, including childcare facilities, a funeral
home, an indoor Pickleball facility, and others that would not have been possible without bank
partnerships. CDFIs frequently rely on regional and community banks for patient debt,
deposits, investments, lines of credit, grants, and other forms of capital that allow us to reach
borrowers and projects that conventional financial institutions cannot efficiently serve directly.

Misalignment with Congressional Priorities on Affordable Housing and New Markets
Tax Credit (NMTC)

The change also undermines Congress's recent efforts to strengthen the Low-Income Housing
Tax Credit (LIHTC) and the New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC), two bipartisan, popular federal tax
credits with a long track record of success in our communities. While Congress expanded
LIHTC and made NMTC permanent, the proposal undermines these important investment tools.

LIHTC and NMTC are considered equity investments and are evaluated under the standalone
investment test for large banks, which currently have a distinct 25%-weighted component of
their CRA evaluation devoted to qualified investments. Moving banks into the lower size

Page 3
 category would mean these transitioned banks would be subject only to a diluted evaluation
that considers all CD in a single test. This would give banks greater ability to emphasize CD
lending rather than maintain the same level of LIHTC or NMTC investment, because investment
performance no longer receives a separate rating. This weakened regulatory incentive would
reduce bank demand for these investments.

RCLF closed two NMTC transactions, securing $15M in bank investments. One transaction
supported the expansion of a lumber mill in Natchez, MS, where 24% of the population lives in
poverty, and the median household income is under $44,000, which is 27% below the national
average. The NMTC transaction created 65 new jobs by adding a new line of business and an
additional shift at the facility.

Significance of CRA data and transparency: Section IV.G, "Data Collection, Reporting,
and Disclosure"

The threshold changes would also substantially reduce the number of institutions subject to
large-bank CRA data requirements. This would make it harder for communities, CDFIs,
policymakers, and regulators to identify credit gaps, compare bank performance, assess
geographic disparities, and determine whether community credit needs are being met. We are
concerned that aggregating community development finance data is already difficult to track,
and the proposal would further reduce data coverage, making it harder to identify and
understand where credit is flowing.

Recommendation

For all the reasons cited above, we urge the agencies to retain the current thresholds and
reject all alternatives offered (including the substantially higher thresholds raised for
consideration in Question 1). The current thresholds are already indexed to CPI-W annually, so
they are not tied to 1995 asset levels. Moreover, the agencies' justification of "restoring
proportionality to 1995" in the proposal does not adequately explain why raising asset
thresholds better serves the statutory intent of the CRA—which is to ensure that the credit
needs of LMI communities are met. For the small-bank threshold, the proportionality metric is
based on the distribution of the number of banks, such that nearly 80% of all banks would be
considered small, similar to the 1995 level. While that's true, by the same logic, nearly 20% of
banks in 1995 were considered large, whereas under the proposed large-bank threshold, only
a little over 2% of all banks would be considered large. Instead, the agencies selectively cite
the total banking industry share to justify the large-bank threshold, saying that, under this
proposal, as in 1995, large banks would account for about 85% of the industry's assets.
Matching a 1995 distribution through either method does not necessarily demonstrate that the
resulting categories are appropriate for the modern banking system. The industry has
consolidated dramatically; bank business models and geographic reach have changed. Banks
with several billion dollars in assets today may have substantially greater lending, investment,
data, and operational capacity than institutions that were treated as small or intermediate
three decades ago. The fact that assets happen to sit above a chosen threshold does not by
itself establish that banks below that threshold should lose the separate investment/service
tests or associated data requirements.

Page 4
 Restrictions on Community Development Grants: Section Iv.c, "Community
Development Activities — CD Grants"; Questions 9-11

We strongly oppose the proposed restrictions on community development grants, which: 1)
require a qualifying CD grant to be used directly by the recipient for a program, project, or
initiative with a primary purpose of community development; 2) for large banks, cap grant
recipients' indirect administrative costs at 15%; 3) require large banks to obtain
documentation from grant recipients, including written commitments regarding use of funds,
indirect-cost attestations, IRS Form 990s, and operating and program budgets. We also
strongly oppose the alternative contemplated in Question 10, which would eliminate grants
and donations from CRA consideration.

While we share the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants meaningfully benefit
communities, these requirements would restrict many forms of effective grantmaking and
misunderstand the role of flexible operating support in community development finance. For
CDFIs, staffing, underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, risk management, data
systems, financial management, technical assistance, and product development are not
ancillary to community development. They are the infrastructure that enables community
development lending.

Moreover, we strongly oppose making a fixed 15% indirect-cost limit a condition of CRA
eligibility. An organization's administrative-cost percentage is not an appropriate proxy for
community impact. Costs vary by an organization's size, geography, product mix, regulatory
obligations, technical-assistance model, and populations served. The cap could
disproportionately affect small and emerging CDFIs, rural CDFIs, CDFIs making small-dollar
loans, organizations providing intensive borrower technical assistance, CDFIs developing new
products or entering underserved markets, and organizations making necessary investments in
technology, compliance, data, and risk management.

Recommendation
The agencies should preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-building
grants as currently in place under the 1995 framework. CRA should encourage flexibility for

banks to provide the form of support that best addresses identified community needs, rather
than imposing undue compliance burdens.

Interacting Provisions That Could Further Reduce Community
Development Incentives

Preserve meaningful consequences for intermediate-bank CD performance: Section
IV.B, "Performance Tests — Intermediate Bank Ratings"

Under the current framework, an intermediate small bank generally must receive at least a
Satisfactory rating on both its lending test and its CD test to achieve an overall Satisfactory

Page 5
 rating. The proposal would require a Satisfactory or better lending-test rating but would allow
lending performance to offset weaker CD performance.

This change is especially concerning when paired with the proposed asset thresholds, which
would move hundreds of banks currently evaluated under the large-bank framework into the
intermediate category. If weak CD performance does not prevent an overall Satisfactory rating,
banks may have less regulatory incentive to make CDFI loans and investments, provide grants,
or engage in other community development activities. We urge the agencies to retain a
requirement that intermediate banks demonstrate at least Satisfactory CD performance to
receive an overall Satisfactory rating.

Complexity definition anchored to lending is too narrow: Section IV.C, "Qualitative
Factors"; Questions 12-17

The proposal would largely define complexity for CD investments, grants, and services based
on whether an activity is a necessary or beneficial component of a multicomponent financing
transaction involving a loan. We oppose the establishment of a lending-centric definition of
complexity. Investments in CDFIs need to be flexible so CDFIs can best support their
borrowers and ensure borrowers have the tools they need to succeed. CDFIs have a long,
successful track record of serving borrowers routinely excluded by traditional banks. We also
oppose requiring CD investments or services to be complex, as contemplated in Question 14,
or treating complexity as categorically more responsive than innovation, flexibility, or impact,
as contemplated in Question 15. CDFIs employ patient repayment terms and continually work
with struggling borrowers to keep them in their homes or their businesses open. This practice
contributes positively to CDFIs' success.

The agencies should assess complexity, innovativeness, flexibility, impact, and responsiveness
based on the activity's characteristics and community value, rather than on its association with
a lending transaction.

Prevent ordinary retail lending from substituting for specialized CD lending: Section
IV.B, "Retail Lending Product Lines," Questions 4-7; and Section IV.C, "CD Loans"

The proposal would evaluate only retail lending within a bank's major product lines. It would
also allow a loan in a retail product line that is not evaluated as a major product line to be
considered a CD loan if the loan otherwise meets the community development definition. We
agree that genuinely community-development-oriented financing should not lose CRA
consideration simply because a product line is excluded from the retail evaluation.

However, this interaction risks ordinary-course small-business, small-farm, or other retail
lending substituting for more specialized community development lending that depends more
directly on CRA incentives. The agencies should require a meaningful community development
nexus and ensure that the provision does not allow banks to satisfy CD expectations primarily
through activities they would undertake in the ordinary course of business.

Page 6
 Strategic plans require strong guardrails: Section IV.F, "Strategic Plan"; particularly
Questions 38-53

We support efforts to provide greater clarity on strategic plans and measurable goals.
However, because strategic plans allow banks to develop individualized CRA performance
standards, strong guardrails are essential to ensure that banks do not circumvent rigorous,
reasonably consistent expectations applied to similarly situated institutions.

The agencies should require that strategic-plan goals be responsive to demonstrated
community needs, sufficiently rigorous to approximate performance expected under the
standard CRA tests, transparent and measurable, subject to meaningful public engagement,
and evaluated against clear standards to determine whether the goals adequately address
assessment-area credit needs.

We particularly urge the agencies to establish clear standards for responding to Question 53,
which asks when measurable goals should be considered inadequate to address assessment-
area needs.

Geographic flexibility for CD activities outside assessment areas: Section IV.E,
"Consideration of Community Development Activities — CD Activities Outside
Assessment Areas"; proposed § ___.13(e); Question 34

We support the goal of enabling CRA-motivated capital to reach communities with significant
unmet needs but relatively few bank assessment areas. Greater geographic flexibility could be
particularly beneficial for reaching CRA deserts. Mississippi, as mentioned earlier, has no large
banks in its footprint, and greater flexibility to conduct CD activities outside their existing
footprint would be much appreciated. More capital is needed in Mississippi, and better CRA
metrics for large banks could promote more large-bank funding there. We are regularly told by
some large banks that support RCLF's work in Mississippi that they are unable to provide grant
capital for this reason, and we greatly need grant capital to support our work. Flexibility should
supplement rather than displace CD activity in banks' own assessment areas. The agencies are
considering both quantitative and qualitative approaches to determine when a bank has
sufficiently served its assessment areas to be considered for outside-AA activity.

Regarding Question 34, we support greater geographic flexibility when it helps direct CRA-
motivated capital to rural communities, Indian Country, and other underserved areas that may
fall outside traditional assessment areas. We are concerned that the quantitative standard
proposed under Option 1 is too low to meet that objective. For large banks, the proposal would
allow consideration of outside-assessment-area activity once a bank reaches 0.625 percent of
allocated Tier 1 capital in community development loans and 0.625 percent in community
development investments and grants. The agencies themselves explain that these thresholds
generally reflect the minimum level of activity needed to avoid a "Needs to Improve" rating
and, by themselves, are not sufficient to demonstrate satisfactory community development
performance.

Page 7
 Recent analysis by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition further highlights the gap
between the proposed thresholds and current bank activity. Among 69 large OCC- and FDIC-
supervised banks analyzed by NCRC, current annual assessment-area community development
lending, investments, and grants totaled approximately $102 billion. Applying the proposed
0.625% Tier 1 capital thresholds to those same institutions produced a benchmark of
approximately $14.8 billion—roughly 85% below current activity. NCRC also found that median
assessment-area community development lending was 6.83% of Tier 1 capital and median
qualified investments and grants were 3.5%, both substantially above the proposed 0.625%
benchmarks.

A standard intended to determine when a bank has adequately served its own communities
should be calibrated to meaningful, satisfactory community development performance—not
merely the minimum required to avoid a failing rating. We encourage the agencies to adopt a
more rigorous standard that considers both the level of activity and responsiveness to
identified community needs. We further caution against allowing a broadly defined
"substantially met" standard to weaken this safeguard. Any exception should be narrowly
tailored to circumstances in which a documented lack of community development opportunities
or other performance-context factors explains the shortfall, rather than simply allowing weaker
community development performance in individual assessment areas to be offset by activity
elsewhere.

Support for Provisions That Could Strengthen Community Development
Finance

Consider prior-period community development loans: Section IV.C, "CD Loans";
Question 8

We strongly support CRA consideration for qualifying CD loans that remain outstanding from
prior evaluation periods, consistent with the existing treatment of prior-period investments.
Community development borrowers frequently need long-term, patient financing. CRA should
encourage banks to structure loans around community needs rather than examination cycles.

With respect to Question 8, we recommend evaluation period-based consideration because it
better recognizes patient, long-term CD financing, provides a more representative measure of
capital committed throughout the CRA examination period than an annual snapshot, and
ensures parity in the treatment of loans and investments. The agencies should base
consideration on the average outstanding balance or otherwise account for both the amount
and duration of the outstanding exposure. They should treat repeated renewals of substantially
the same loan as a single exposure.

Establish an illustrative list and advance-confirmation process: Section IV.E,
"Illustrative List" and "Confirmation of CD Activity Eligibility"; Questions 32-33

We strongly support establishing a publicly available, non-exhaustive illustrative list of eligible
CD activities and a formal process for advance confirmation of eligibility. The OCC, FDIC, and

Page 8
 Federal Reserve should work to maintain consistent standards and, ideally, a single interagency
illustrative list.

Regarding Questions 32-33, we support requiring banks to retain eligibility determinations for
as long as the applicable activity remains on their balance sheet and to establish a maximum
30-day extension beyond the proposed 90-day review period.

We also encourage the agencies to pair this with a confirmation process that provides timely
certainty while maintaining accountability for genuine community development impact.
Eligibility determinations should include a clear written rationale and, where appropriate,
identify the facts or conditions on which eligibility depends. The agencies should provide a
reconsideration process in which banks or community development partners can submit
additional information, as well as a mechanism for community stakeholders to raise material
concerns about activities deemed eligible for reconsideration. Nonconfidential or anonymized
determinations and their rationales should be made public to promote transparency and
consistent treatment across institutions. Eligibility determinations should also remain subject
to verification during CRA examinations if the activity is ultimately implemented differently
from how it was represented.

Recognize disaster preparedness and resilience: Section IV.D, "Revitalization and
Stabilization — Designated Disaster Areas"; Question 31

We support expressly recognizing qualifying activities that help communities prepare for, adapt
to, and withstand natural disasters. CDFIs frequently provide financing to affordable housing
developments, homeowners, small businesses, and community facilities before and after
disasters. CRA should recognize responsible investments that strengthen vulnerable
communities before disasters occur, not only financing provided after damage occurs.
Encouraging bank partnerships would be most helpful in assisting those affected by disasters,
as CDFIs have limited resources to respond quickly and must wait for federal resources to be
deployed.

Conclusion

CRA has helped build a powerful partnership among banks, CDFIs, and the communities we
serve. We appreciate the agencies' efforts to improve clarity and flexibility. However,
modernization should result in more responsible capital reaching communities with unmet
credit needs, as the CRA statute intended.

We therefore urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the proposed higher asset thresholds and
the restrictions on CD operating grants. We also support increasing the amount of CRA-
motivated capital flowing into CRA deserts, as states like Mississippi have significant unmet
needs for low-cost debt capital and operating grants for CDFIs to support more programs for
their borrowers, thereby strengthening partnerships with banks that have been proven to be
very successful. CDFIs are natural partners for banks, as we provide initial capital to many

Page 9
 borrowers who are not ready for traditional bank financing and whom banks are not equipped
to serve.

Thank you for considering these comments and for considering the impact of the proposed
changes on the communities we serve.

Sincerely,

M3 cXe Roa ~
Kimberly LaRosa

President & CEO
Renaissance Community Loan Fund (RCLF)

Page 10

TO: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
FROM: Janice Kimball, Chief Executive Officer, Housing Connect
DATE: October 7, 2026

SUBJECT: Comments on Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-
AF57; RIN 3064-AG31

To Whom It May Concern:

Housing Connect appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the proposed revisions to Community
Reinvestment Act regulations, Docket ID OCC-2026-0694, RIN 1557-AF57, and RIN 3064-AG31, by the Office
of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC). Housing
Connect recognizes the importance of an efficient regulatory framework for financial institutions. At the same
time, we are concerned that the proposed revisions could reduce community development activity, weaken
funding predictability, limit flexible support for housing partners, and affect the availability of banking services in
low- and moderate-income communities across Utah.

ABOUT HOUSING CONNECT

Housing Connect is the public housing authority serving Salt Lake County, Utah. Founded in 1970, Housing
Connect's mission is to connect people and communities to quality affordable housing opportunities while
promoting self-sufficiency and neighborhood revitalization. Housing Connect administers the HUD Housing
Choice Voucher program in Salt Lake County, provides affordable housing and supportive housing programs, and
works with public, private, nonprofit, and philanthropic partners to serve low- and moderate-income households,
seniors, people with disabilities, families with children, and individuals experiencing or exiting homelessness.

UTAH NEEDS STATEMENT

Utah's need for sustained CRA-motivated investment is significant. The National Low Income Housing Coalition
reports that Utah has only 28 affordable and available rental homes for every 100 extremely low-income renter
households and needs 44,097 more homes affordable to extremely low-income households. It also estimates that a
full-time worker must earn $30.42 per hour, or $63,283 annually, to afford a two-bedroom rental home at fair
market rent without being cost-burdened. These statewide pressures are felt in Salt Lake County, where public
housing authorities and nonprofit partners rely on long-term lending, grants, investments, and banking
relationships to preserve affordable housing, expand supportive services, and stabilize households.

KEEP LMI PEOPLE AND COMMUNITIES AT THE CENTER OF CRA

Housing Connect is especially concerned that higher asset thresholds and reduced community development
evaluation requirements could diminish incentives for financial institutions to provide community development
lending, investments, and services. Housing Connect understands that the proposal would increase the small-bank
threshold from $412 million to $1 billion and the threshold for the largest examination category from
approximately $1.65 billion to $10 billion. The National Community Reinvestment Coalition's (NCRC) analysis
further indicates that these changes could remove community development evaluations for approximately 814
banks nationally, or about 40 percent of banks currently subject to such evaluations, while another 417 banks
 would move out of the large-bank examination framework. In Utah, where affordable housing needs remain
substantial, reducing these obligations could weaken the partnerships that help communities close financing gaps.

The proposed adjustment of community development grants also raises practical concerns for Housing Connect
and nonprofit 501(c)3 partner, the Housing Connect Fund. Affordable housing and homelessness services depend
not only on project-specific dollars, but also on general operating support, administrative capacity, infrastructure,
and flexible funding that allow agencies to respond to urgent community needs. If CRA consideration is limited to
grants tied narrowly to a specific project or program, banks may have less incentive to support operating needs or
broader community development partnerships, even when those investments directly strengthen housing stability
for LMI households. Flexible support helps organizations maintain staff capacity, coordinate partners, develop
projects, and reach hard-to-serve households that may otherwise receive limited investment.

CONCLUSION

Housing Connect respectfully requests that the OCC and FDIC preserve a meaningful community development
responsibility for financial institutions, maintain useful public reporting and community participation, and ensure
that CRA standards recognize the distinct financing and banking challenges facing low- and moderate-income,
and underserved communities. Utah's housing needs require strong partnerships among banks, developers, public
housing authorities, nonprofits, local governments, businesses, and residents.

Thank you for your consideration and for the opportunity to comment.

Sincerely,

fot

Chief Executive Officer
Housing Connect

It says the 0.625% Tier 1 capital benchmark, strategic plans, the 15% grant overhead limit and reduced data reporting would cut community development activity. It asks the agencies to do a full impact analysis and to extend the comment period.
key_asks: Rescind or withdraw the proposal until the agencies complete and release a thorough impact analysis on LMI communities for public comment.
Analyze effects of the 15 percent indirect cost limit and documentation requirements on smaller nonprofits, and of reduced data reporting, before finalizing.
Extend the comment period by at least 60 days, to a total of at least 120 days.

banks with $10 billion or less in assets would no longer be required to collect and report such CRA data.
Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers will not be able to identify credit deserts, compare performance or understand whether local credit needs are being met.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0150_09000064b96502ba.pdf:
1
October 7, 2026
Jonathan V. Gould
Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street SW
Washington, DC 20219
Attn: Chief Counsel's Office
Via: Federal eRulemaking Portal –.regulations.gov
Travis Hill, Chairman
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
550 17th Street, NW
Washington, DC 20429
[Via email to Comments@fdic.gov]
Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
on Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694;
RIN 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
ICCF Community Homes submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of
Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)1 because it
would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given
the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and
FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences
for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the
analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the
current comment deadline by 60-days.
ICCF Community Homes was founded in 1974 to provide affordable housing options
within the community of Grand Rapids, Michigan. Each year, we assist more than 2,000
households through various programs and services, including homeownership and rental
opportunities for marginalized Grand Rapids residents in newly built homes, rehabilitated
current homes, multi-unit rental dwellings, and our homeless shelter. Additionally, we
provide individual housing counseling, education on homeownership and financial
stability, personal counseling assistance to at-risk community members, and a broad array
1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 2
of resident services for our rental communities. As a member of the NCRC, we have
partnered with numerous financial institutions in creative ways to meet community needs
and help banks fulfill their mandated CRA requirements, including providing
homeownership education and financial counseling classes, providing Individual
Development Accounts to help low- and moderate-income individuals save money for
homeownership, and helping to support renovations of houses that will be sold to
income-qualified buyers, nearly always first-time homebuyers.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important
in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal
access to mainstream financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and
would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and
support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being
considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-
income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination
and disinvestment.
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. Investments
such as these benefited our community by increasing the number of affordable
mortgages, which directly impacts the Grand Rapids households who ICCF Community
Homes works with to develop affordable housing and help low- and moderate-income
individuals secure the goal of homeownership, adding increased stability, strength and
resilience to our neighborhoods and communities.
We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1
capital devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough
to receive a passing CRA rating.2 However, that percentage is far lower than the
percentage the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the
largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.
2 The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit for outside their assessment areas if the banks
surpass a benchmark of 0.625% of its tier 1 capital for community development loans and likewise 0.625%
for investments. 91 Fed. Reg. 52121, 52140 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026). We are concerned that the practical
effect of this proposal is that the benchmark will serve not as a floor, but a ceiling.
 3
NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the
OCC and FDIC supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these
banks currently conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community development
loans and investments inside their assessment areas, and that the median percentage of
annual community development lending in assessment areas was 6.8% of tier 1 capital,
and a median of 3.6% of tier 1 capital for annual CRA qualified investments.3 If each
bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet separate thresholds of 0.625%
of Tier 1 capital for community development lending and investments, combined activity
would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually -- a decrease of approximately $87.1
billion, or 85%. Similarly, the proposal encourages banks to use strategic plans to make
their CRA compliance easier and more predictable. Previous proposed guidance also set
strategic plan benchmarks for CRA performance well-below historical levels of
community development activity.4
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic
discrimination cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments
and loans. If regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be
accountable to the communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for
communities. For example, in our community and particularly among the people who we
work with, families will struggle to obtain affordable mortgage credit, first-time
homebuyers will face additional barriers to homeownership; educational programs and
financial assistance opportunities that promote first time homebuyers and increased
community security will be curtailed. Additionally, we have concerns that such a
reduction would further limit relationships that low- and moderate-income residents in
our community can establish with mainstream financial institutions. It is imperative that
the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet community needs. Before finalizing the
rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce lending,
services or investment available to low- and moderate-income communities and whether
communities that have experienced historic discrimination or disinvestment would be
disproportionately affected.
Further, we are concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development
grants and nonprofit organizations.
Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development, financial
counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based
services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations.
3 NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk,
(Sept. 10, 2026), https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-
development-activity-at-risk/.
4 NCRC, The Proposed CRA Rule's Strategic Plans: A More Predictable Path to Doing Less (Sept 1,
2026), https://ncrc.org/the-proposed-cra-rules-strategic-plans-a-more-predictable-path-to-doing-less/.
 4
These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have deep
relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect
costs and new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for
smaller organizations.5 For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be
unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other operating expenses
are often necessary to deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also
have fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs. In addition,
many community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain
financial records, budgets or program documentation in the precise format a bank would
need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations
are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger
organizations whose activities are easier to verify.
Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and
partnerships can play in supporting community development. ICCF's personal experience
has demonstrated a strong relationship between our organization and banks in our
community through support for our state-recognized homeownership education program;
in 2025, this program alone included 29 classes taught in 5 different languages, with 498
graduates. Homeownership counselors helped 56 first-time homebuyers purchase a
house. 248 ICCF residents build their credit via rent reporting, more than 150 events were
held at multi-unit facilities to build community engagement and support. The
opportunities to revitalize our community and neighborhoods brought further strength
and engagement to the city.
These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn
capital into tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and
community development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have
consequences well beyond the banks themselves.
Before finalizing these provisions, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed
documentation requirements and limits on administrative expenses would reduce or
redirect bank support away from smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those with
limited administrative capacity. The agencies must also determine whether those effects
would ultimately reduce resources available to low- and moderate-income communities.
5 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,129 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 5
More broadly, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule primarily in terms of
reducing perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also determine
what the changes mean for the communities CRA is intended to serve.
In addition, under the current rule banks above the large bank threshold generally collect
and report on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans
and assessment areas. But because of the proposed change in the threshold, banks with
$10 billion or less in assets would no longer be required to collect and report such CRA
data. Nationwide, that will result in an 11% reduction in CRA small business lending
data. Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers will not be able
to identify credit deserts, compare performance or understand whether local credit needs
are being met.
Before narrowing the activities subject to CRA examination and eliminating data
reporting requirements, the agencies should analyze the impact of doing so will have for
people with low- and moderate-incomes or low- and moderate-income communities,
including whether it could result in a reduction in the types of lending that would meet
community needs. In addition, the agencies should explain why this change would be
consistent with the CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit
needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
●
identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA
scrutiny under the proposal;
●
quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
●
assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or
populations, including rural communities and communities of color;
●
consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without
sacrificing meaningful community accountability.
Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes
that the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its
impacts is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs
considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for
meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that
materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are
 6
consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120
days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service
evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The
current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that
do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would
allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather
examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more
complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies
extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.
Sincerely
ICCF Community Homes
cc. National Community Reinvestment Coalition

comments.name: T.R.U.S.T. South LA
comments.type_basis: The letter describes the organization as a community-based nonprofit that creates permanently affordable housing and stewards community land trusts in South Los Angeles.
comments.overall_quote: We respectfully urge the FDIC and OCC to reject these proposed changes
comments.summary: T.R.U.S.T. South LA, a South Los Angeles affordable housing nonprofit, strongly opposes the proposal. It argues the changes would cut community development investment, branches and deposit services, data transparency, nonprofit grants, and accountability for discrimination. It also asks for a 60-day extension and stronger Tribal provisions.
key_asks: Reject the proposed changes and keep strong CRA obligations, including not raising asset thresholds.
Extend the comment period by 60 days and analyze the impact on LMI communities.
Add Tribal engagement incentives, preserve the 15% overhead and grant flexibility for nonprofits, and consider all evidence of discrimination in ratings.

provisions.quote: Asset thresholds should not be raised.
Proposing a 15% ceiling on indirect costs is inconsistent with historic federal policy and practice
The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to offer deposit products that are accessible to LMI residents.
CRA rules should also expand the definition of assessment areas to include areas where banks conduct substantial lending
While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities outside of their branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made
Banks that discriminate and redline should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding" ratings.
The proposal would eliminate the purpose test, which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs
Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment.
Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.
Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community development efforts with little benefit.

comments.commenter_subtype: community-based nonprofit housing and community land trust organization in South Los Angeles

issues.raw_label: Raising asset thresholds reduces CRA obligations
issues.quote: The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large" Banks, such that many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny

issues.raw_label: Lower community development activity from banks
issues.quote: CD activity would decrease by approximately $87.1 billion, or 85%.

issues.raw_label: Loss of Investment Test driven financing
issues.quote: The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical community development programs that have had large impacts in LMI communities.

issues.raw_label: Branch closures and services test coverage
issues.quote: forty-five banks in California will no longer be subject to the Services Test and reviewed to ensure that their branches are serving LMI communities.

issues.raw_label: Removing obligation for LMI deposit products
issues.quote: The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to offer deposit products that are accessible to LMI residents.

issues.raw_label: Loss of small business and farm lending data
issues.quote: fewer banks will be required to report data regarding their small business, small farm, and community development lending activities.

issues.raw_label: Tribal engagement outside assessment areas
issues.quote: CRA evaluations should also consider whether banks have established meaningful relationships with, and provided direct benefits to, federally recognized Tribes as well as non-federally recognized Tribes.

issues.raw_label: Limits on CRA credit for nonprofit grants
issues.quote: The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by requiring a demonstrated nexus to community development projects

issues.raw_label: 15% overhead cap on grants
issues.quote: mandating that large banks and their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more than 15% of these grants on overhead.

issues.raw_label: Fewer product lines reviewed for lending
issues.quote: Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their top two major product lines of business.

issues.raw_label: Economic development purpose test removed
issues.quote: The proposal would eliminate the purpose test, which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the definition of economic development.

issues.raw_label: Broadened community infrastructure credit
issues.quote: Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA credit for large scale community infrastructure products that generate profits for banks

issues.raw_label: Credit for activity outside assessment areas
issues.quote: Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas.

issues.raw_label: Strategic Plan option reduces reinvestment
issues.quote: Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment.

issues.raw_label: Credit for naturally occurring affordable housing
issues.quote: Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community development efforts with little benefit.

issues.raw_label: Discrimination evidence and CRA downgrades
issues.quote: Banks that discriminate and redline should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding" ratings.

issues.raw_label: Special purpose credit programs under ECOA
issues.quote: We also urge the regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity Act authorizes Special Purpose Credit Programs

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Opposing Proposed CRA Rule Changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould:

T.R.U.S.T. South LA opposes the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. Enacted in 1977 to address redlining and disinvestment, the CRA remains a critical tool for ensuring that financial institutions meet the needs of low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities.

T.R.U.S.T. South LA is a community-based nonprofit dedicated to creating permanently affordable housing, preventing displacement, and advancing community ownership throughout South Los Angeles. Our work depends on partnerships with financial institutions, community development lenders, and investors whose commitments are often encouraged by CRA obligations. CRA-driven financing has supported affordable housing preservation, community land trust expansion, resident education, and neighborhood stabilization efforts that directly benefit LMI households.

At a time when housing costs and economic inequities continue to displace long-time residents, weakening CRA requirements would undermine critical investments in the very communities the law was created to serve. We respectfully request a 60-day extension of the comment period and urge regulators to fully evaluate the proposal's impact on LMI communities.

1. Reduced Community Development Investment
The proposal would raise bank asset thresholds, reducing CRA obligations for many institutions. As a result, fewer banks would be subject to Community Development, Investment, and Service Tests, decreasing incentives for affordable housing, small business lending, CDFIs, community land trusts, and other community development activities.

In Los Angeles, CRA-motivated investments frequently make the difference between preserving affordable housing and losing it to speculative market pressures. Reducing these obligations threatens affordable housing production, preservation, and community ownership opportunities.

2. Fewer Branches and Banking Services in Underserved Communities
The proposal would reduce oversight of branch access in LMI communities and communities of color, increasing the risk of branch closures. Branch presence supports access to banking, credit, and small business lending. The proposal would also weaken incentives to provide affordable banking products that help households avoid predatory financial services and build long-term financial stability.

3. Loss of Data Transparency
By exempting more banks from reporting requirements, the proposal would reduce public access to information about small business, small farm, and community development lending. These data are essential for understanding community needs, evaluating bank performance, and ensuring accountability.

4. Insufficient Support for Tribal Communities
While the proposal seeks to encourage investment in Tribal areas, it does not adequately address the needs of Native communities outside narrowly defined geographic boundaries. CRA regulations should encourage banks to build meaningful relationships with Tribal governments, Native-serving organizations, and Native-owned businesses through lending, investment, grantmaking, and accessible banking services.

5. Harmful Restrictions on Nonprofit Funding
The proposal would limit CRA eligibility for grants to nonprofit organizations and impose burdensome restrictions that could discourage bank philanthropy altogether. Nonprofits play a critical role in affordable housing, financial education, borrower support, workforce development, and community stabilization. Reduced funding would weaken the local organizations that banks rely upon to reach underserved communities effectively.

6. Less Benefit for LMI Communities
Several provisions would weaken the connection between CRA activities and meaningful community impact. The proposal would allow less lending activity to be reviewed, expand credit for activities with limited benefits to LMI residents, encourage activity outside banks' assessment areas, and promote strategic plans that may reduce reinvestment commitments. These changes risk shifting CRA resources away from the communities most in need.

7. Weakened Accountability for Discrimination
The CRA was created to combat redlining and discrimination. Banks that engage in discriminatory or illegal lending practices should not receive satisfactory CRA ratings. Regulators should continue to consider all relevant evidence of discrimination when evaluating CRA performance and encourage programs that expand access to credit in historically underserved communities.

The Community Reinvestment Act exists because market forces alone have not consistently met the needs of historically underserved communities. Nearly fifty years later, communities continue to face the effects of disinvestment, displacement, and unequal access to capital.

Thank you for your consideration.

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

TRUST Sout LA writes to object to the harmful changes proposed to the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed by Congress in 1977 in response to
redlining and creates an affirmative obligation for banks to help meet the credit, deposit,
and banking needs of communities, including low and moderate income (LMI) communities.
While the CRA has successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest and provide services in
underserved communities, challenges related to redlining, discrimination, underinvestment,
and lack of access remain.

T.R.U.S.T. South LA is a community-based nonprofit organization dedicated to creating
permanently affordable housing, preventing displacement, and advancing community
ownership throughout South Los Angeles and surrounding neighborhoods. Through
community land trust stewardship, affordable housing development, resident leadership,
and community organizing, we work alongside residents to ensure that long-time
community members can remain, thrive, and build stability in the neighborhoods they call
home.

Our work relies on strong partnerships with mission-driven financial institutions and
community development lenders whose investments are often motivated by the Community
Reinvestment Act. CRA-driven lending, investments, and grants have helped support
affordable housing acquisition and preservation, community land trust expansion, resident
education programs, neighborhood stabilization efforts, and broader wealth-building
opportunities for low- and moderate-income households.

As housing affordability challenges continue to displace long-time residents and deepen
economic inequities across Los Angeles, maintaining strong CRA obligations is more
important than ever. Weakening these requirements would reduce critical investments in
the very communities the Act was created to serve and would undermine efforts to expand

affordable housing, support community-based organizations, and create pathways to long-
term housing stability and community ownership.

The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift. The
proposal does not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on LMI
communities. We request an extension of the comment period for an additional 60 days so
we have time to better understand how much CRA activity may be lost to communities
because of this proposal – an analysis the regulators did not conduct or provide.
The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved
communities in several ways.

1) Community development (CD) activities for affordable housing and small businesses
will drop dramatically.
As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities that
support critically needed affordable housing and economic development projects. These
activities often provide the greatest CRA impact in communities as they strengthen
economic stability and mobility, quality of life, and social health of residents and
communities.

The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large" Banks,
such that many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and expectation to
serve the community development needs of their communities.[1] According to National
Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70 California banks would see their
reinvestment obligations reduced under the proposal. Twenty-five California banks would
shed their Community Development Test responsibilities entirely, and 45 California banks
would no longer be subject to the Investment Test.[2]

The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical community
development programs that have had large impacts in LMI communities. These include Low
Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) which are a key driver of affordable housing finance;
New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) which fuel economic development projects in tribal and
other areas; and EQ2 equity equivalent investments in Community Development Financial
Institutions (CDFIs) that provide small business lending in underserved areas that banks
cannot reach, and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs), which preserve affordability in
perpetuity, protect residents from displacement, and ensure that housing remains a
community asset rather than a speculative commodity

Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting the critical
importance of the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable housing.[3]
Approximately half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from CRA motivated banks.[4] The
regulators will even further weaken CD obligations if they adopt the alternative proposal
that Large Banks be defined as those with over $30 billion in assets.

In Los Angeles, where rising housing costs continue to place tremendous pressure on
working families, CRA-driven investments are often the difference between preserving
affordable homes and losing them to speculative market forces. Organizations like T.R.U.S.T.
South LA depend on these resources to acquire and steward housing that remains affordable
for future generations.

Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance even
where they remain subject to the Community Development and Investment Tests. The
regulators signal to all banks that they can do significantly less CD lending and investment
and still pass their CRA examinations, all while seeking CRA credit for activity outside of their
CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests that a bank could receive a passing CRA rating
if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1 capital were devoted to CD loans and CD investments. That
percentage is far lower than the percentage that NCRC determined banks currently devote
to community investments and loans. If each bank instead conducted only the amount
necessary to meet the proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by approximately
$87.1 billion, or 85%.[5]

Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have
tremendous negative impacts on affordable housing and small business development in our
state. Asset thresholds should not be raised.

2) Banks will shed branches and BankOn.
The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and maintain branches
in LMI and BIPOC neighborhoods. By increasing the asset threshold for a Large Bank to over
$10 billion, forty-five banks in California will no longer be subject to the Services Test and
reviewed to ensure that their branches are serving LMI communities. In California alone,
NCRC estimates that 245 branches in LMI areas and 497 branches in neighborhoods of color
would be vulnerable to closure due to this proposal.[6]

Branch presence has been tied to increased small business lending in communities. Fewer
branches will result in less small business lending. These changes will be particularly hard
hitting in rural areas of our state where smaller banks originate a larger portion of the small
business loans.

The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to offer
deposit products that are accessible to LMI residents.[7] Deposit accounts are a gateway to
credit access, financial stability, and wealth building, especially for families who are
otherwise preyed upon by predatory financial institutions. As one important example, the
BankOn program has provided access to no or low fee bank accounts for over fourteen
million people.[8] California is home to several BankOn coalitions that establish effective
partnerships among banks, community-based organizations, and local governments. The
proposal jettisons this work.

Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million are
underbanked.[9] National banks regulated by the OCC charged billions of dollars in overdraft
and non-sufficient fund fees in 2025, and in California alone, state-chartered banks charged
over fifty-six million dollars ($56 million) in OD and NSF fees to California consumers in
2025.[10]

3) Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.
Another consequence of the proposal's drive to raise asset thresholds is that fewer banks
will be required to report data regarding their small business, small farm, and community
development lending activities. Such data is critical to understanding not only individual

bank performance, but also the needs of local markets. Rise Economy and its member
organizations routinely analyze this CRA data when meeting with banks and commenting on
CRA exams and mergers. The loss of such data is particularly harmful at a time when the
Administration is walking back efforts to collect and disclose detailed small business lending
data under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank Act. These changes will disproportionately
impact rural communities in our state where banks up to $10 billion in assets make up a
larger part of the small business and small farm lending markets.

4) Native American communities and Tribal Nations will not see sufficient benefits.
The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the needs of Native
American communities and Tribal Nations which have been poorly served by banks. The
current rules focus CRA obligations in areas where banks have branches, even though there
are far fewer bank branches near Tribal lands and in rural areas where Native Americans
may reside. The proposal seeks to address this CRA gap by encouraging banks to engage in
community development and related activities in "Indian Country" and on "Tribal and Native
lands," even if outside of bank CRA assessment areas. But many members of Tribes in
California will not benefit from this proposal as they do not live in Indian Country or on Tribal
or Native lands, as defined.

CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring within particular
geographies, given the challenges and impacts associated with historic dispossession and
federal policy. Instead, CRA evaluations should also consider whether banks have
established meaningful relationships with, and provided direct benefits to, federally
recognized Tribes as well as non-federally recognized Tribes. Non-federally recognized Tribes
have been acknowledged by, and are able to access programs and contracts with, various
local and state entities.[11] Such processes exist.

More specifically, the CRA rules should encourage banks to serve Tribes, nonprofit
organizations or other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned businesses that are
majority owned and controlled by Native American entrepreneurs by providing:

Active outreach and engagement

Community development loans and investments for affordable housing and
economic development projects

Small farm and small business loans

Home mortgage loans

Grants to meet community needs, including for capacity building for Tribes and
support for Tribes seeking federal recognition if desired

Support for cultural, health and other programs

Bank branches

Deposit products such as affordable bank accounts, and

The provision of financial services such as financial literacy, apprenticeship
programs and technical assistance support

While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities outside of
their branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made to encourage banks to
engage in CRA related activity to directly benefit Tribes, nonprofit organizations and other
entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned businesses that are majority owned and
controlled by Native American entrepreneurs.

A better approach is needed. All banks should be subject to an impact and responsiveness
review factor during their CRA exams that evaluates and tracks whether banks have engaged
in any CRA activity directly with Tribes, Tribally controlled entities and Native owned
businesses.[12] If banks know they will be examined for their work with Tribes, they will find
mutually beneficial ways to work with Tribes.

5) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will suffer.
The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by requiring a
demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating that large banks
and their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more than 15% of these grants on
overhead.[13] As if this wasn't enough, the FDIC and OCC question whether they should end
CRA eligibility for bank grantmaking to nonprofits entirely.

Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian
measures will be except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller groups,
may be impacted.[14]

Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local needs. They
also can be key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and investment products
into communities inclined to trust long established local organizations. Many nonprofit
organizations and programs, such as downpayment assistance programs, that support CRA
related activity, rely on bank contributions to operate. Smaller, local, and rural organizations
will be least able to meet new reporting obligations, and they risk losing bank support as a
result. The proposal would also end impactful contributions from banks for general
operating support, sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.

Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their communities
on their own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps in their own capacity –
seeking assistance with community outreach, borrower education, credit building and repair,
technical assistance, legal services, job training and placement, tax assistance, affordable
housing and other services and programs which help residents become stable and bankable
so that banks can attract new deposits and make new loans in LMI communities.

The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and will focus
grantmaking on larger organizations that can help them more easily meet their new FDIC
and OCC-imposed regulatory burdens.

Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15% overhead
restriction will negatively affect operations and organizational success. As one example, in
order to secure CRA grants from Large Banks, CDFIs will need to pare down costs for critical
operational expenses such as underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, impact
measurement, product development, and borrower technical assistance. With less support
to sustain these operational functions, organizations are put at risk.

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA activity that
contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large negative impact it will
have on nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding, the harm it will cause to LMI

communities that are meant to benefit from the CRA, and the disruption it will cause to
constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

6) Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.
There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link between CRA
and LMI impact in the name of easing bank burden.

Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their top two
major product lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in, and profiting
from, communities, this lending by banks, subsidiaries and affiliates must be evaluated.
Further, certain products, such as small farm and consumer loans, are important in many
communities, but may not be among a bank's largest product lines. If regulators give banks a
pass and exempt smaller product lines from CRA oversight, banks will have less incentive to
consider how those products are offered.

Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and
soundness, encourages banks to meet community needs, and engenders greater trust in
banks by the community. Eliminating categories of loan products from scrutiny will have the
opposite effect.

No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test, which
has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the definition of
economic development. The CRA should create greater incentives for banks to support the
creation of jobs that pay family sustaining wages for LMI workers and in LMI areas, not
fewer. We object to provisions that would provide CRA credit for job creation and economic
development that may only benefit middle- and upper-income workers and communities.
Such provisions ignore the purpose of CRA.

Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA credit for
large scale community infrastructure products that generate profits for banks, would likely
be financed without CRA credit, and provide only incidental benefits to LMI residents and
communities. Such an expansion of what qualifies for CRA credit can significantly dilute
CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities. For example, banks might choose to more
profitably earn CRA credit by financing larger scale infrastructure projects, like bridges, in
lieu of financing less lucrative, smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local community
needs (such as childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or
resilience projects).

Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA should
require banks to focus their CRA activities on their CRA assessments areas,[15] where they
are subject to more rigorous regulatory oversight (with an exception made to encourage
banks to better serve Tribes, as noted above). Banks are not doing enough currently to meet
the credit and deposit needs in the areas where they have CRA responsibility, a problem the
regulators tried to address in the 2023 CRA Rule.[16] Yet the proposal further encourages
banks to seek CRA credit for projects in areas away from their branches, lending and CRA
responsibility. This will enable banks to get credit for activity outside of their assessment
areas, while providing no accompanying CRA obligation to better serve these areas.
