Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal goes out of its
way to encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan option to meet their CRA
responsibilities. The Strategic Plan was meant for financial institutions that operated under a
unique business model that the CRA rules were not designed to address. The Strategic Plan
option provides for minimal public input and regulatory scrutiny and allows banks to
determine the level of reinvestment activity they need to engage in to earn a passing CRA
grade. In our experience, banks with Strategic Plans tend to reinvest less in the community
and in less impactful ways. The OCC's guidance establishing low community development
thresholds for banks opting for the Strategic Plan, [17] validates this perspective.

Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community development
efforts with little benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing, where units are affordable
at a point in time but not encumbered by deed or rent restrictions, are a feature of today's
housing market. But CRA rules should not give banks credit for financing such activities
where the benefit to LMI residents and communities is unclear or absent. NOAH can be a
resource for LMI residents, or it can be a driver of bank investment in problematic landlords
and displacement. CRA credit should be given for financing of NOAH only if the project is
owned and operated by mission-driven organizations, where a majority of residents are LMI
tenants, and the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are compliant
with tenant rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents can reasonably be
expected to retain their housing.

7) Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA ratings downgrades.
The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and redline should not be
allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding" ratings. Under the
Biden Administration, at least a dozen banks that passed their CRA exams were accused of
redlining. This proposal will only increase that number by narrowing what constitutes
evidence of discrimination that may be considered for the purpose of downgrading a bank's
CRA rating. Here, regulators should consider any evidence that a bank, its affiliates, or
subsidiaries engaged in discrimination, redlining, or illegal credit practices as part of their
lending, deposit, branching, or other activities. This evidence should be considered
regardless of its source (public or private parties), or its form (informal complaints, research
based on data, testing results, comment letters, administrative actions, private litigation,
etc.). We also urge the regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity Act
authorizes Special Purpose Credit Programs, and to once again encourage banks to develop
SPCPs to better serve communities that have been redlined, excluded, and underserved. This
is the essence of CRA.

Conclusion. The Community Reinvestment Act exists because markets alone have not
consistently met the needs of historically underserved communities. Nearly fifty years later,
communities continue to face the consequences of disinvestment, displacement, and
barriers to equitable access to capital. The proposed changes would move us further from
the CRA's original purpose by reducing accountability and weakening incentives for
meaningful community investment.

South Los Angeles, we know that strong CRA requirements help create opportunities for
residents, support community-serving organizations, and expand access to housing and
economic stability. We respectfully urge the FDIC and OCC to reject these proposed changes
and instead strengthen policies that promote reinvestment, accountability, and equitable
access to capital in low- and moderate-income communities
Thank you for your consideration of this request.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0152_09000064b9651501.pdf:
The Community Reinvestment Act Inspires Investments with Impact
By: Bernie Mazyck, President & CEO of The South Carolina Association for Community
Economic Development (SCACED)
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC) recently proposed a rule to significantly roll back the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA).
This proposed regulatory change could weaken requirements that encourage banks to
make community development loans and investments that support working class
families. The result could be more unaffordability and a widening of economic inequality
in South Carolina.
The Community Reinvestment Act is a federal law passed in the 1970s to redress the
harm of redlining by banks. In the Jim Crow era, banks avoided lending in majority-
Black neighborhoods because they were deemed "too risky." This has resulted in a
staggering racial wealth gap in the United States.
To address this, the CRA requires regulators, like the OCC and FDIC, to assess
whether banks are helping to meet the credit needs of everyone in the communities
they serve, including low- to –moderate-income neighborhoods. Banks meet their CRA
requirements by providing mortgages, small business loans, funding local community
development projects and opening bank branches in underserved communities.
Under the regulators' proposed rule, up to 800 banks nationwide will no longer be
evaluated on whether they meet the credit needs of their communities. That could
decrease banks' overall community development lending, investments, and grants by
85%, or $87.2 billion. In South Carolina, nearly 25% of banks will no longer have
community development obligations.
I currently lead the South Carolina Association of Community Economic Development
(SCACED), a coalition of member organizations that is building wealth in under-
resourced neighborhoods through housing development, small business support,
workforce training and other critical services. I find this proposal deeply concerning.
Community organizations like ours and many of our members will likely lose grants and
investments from banks that we currently rely on to provide critical services.
For example, through our Community Navigator Program, our members supported over
700 entrepreneurs in South Carolina with pivotal business development services.
Motivated by fulfilling CRA obligations, our bank partners provided $27 million in small
business capital to a subset of those businesses.
The CRA has also motivated banks to invest in affordable housing in South Carolina.
One of our bank partners was incentivized by CRA to offer a downpayment assistance
 product for first-time homebuyers. The bank provides a homebuyer with $15K in a
forgivable loan and $10K in a grant towards downpayment and closing costs, making
homeownership a reality for the South Carolinians we serve.
Additionally, banks receive federal low-income housing tax credits (LIHTC) in exchange
for allocating funding towards the development and rehabilitation of affordable rental
housing projects.
One such project is The Riley at Overbrook housing development in Greenville, South
Carolina, capitalized at $27.6 million. This 88-unit apartment development offers one-to-
three-bedroom garden apartments to potential residents at 20-60% of their area median
income (AMI). Without CRA-encouraged bank support, this housing development would
not be possible.
Across South Carolina, banks brought in $89.06 billion in qualified CRA lending to low-
and moderate-income census tracts between 2010 and 2024. This amount includes
$69.82 billion in qualified mortgages and small business loans.
Billions of dollars will likely leave communities if the OCC and FDIC's proposed rule is
implemented. The National Community Reinvestment Coalition's (NCRC) analysis
found that in South Carolina, communities will lose 115 bank branches in low- to
moderate-income census tracts and 91 bank branches in communities of color.
As a result, more people may become underbanked, opening the opportunity for
predatory lenders to dominate the market. In South Carolina, predatory lenders are
located near low-income and vulnerable communities with little banking presence,
extracting vital income from individuals and families.
The OCC and FDIC should not rush to finalize this proposal before working-class
communities in South Carolina have had a meaningful opportunity to understand what is
at stake.
The main aim of the CRA is to ensure that banks help meet the credit needs of all
communities, including low- and moderate-income individuals and families. Everyone
should have a fair shot to go to their local bank, access flexible credit and build wealth
to pass on to the next generation.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0153_09000064b965169e.pdf:
October 7, 2026
RE: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations — Docket ID OCC-2026-0694
Submitted by: Greater Baltimore Urban League
To the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation:
On behalf of the Greater Baltimore Urban League (GBUL), we appreciate the opportunity to provide comments
on the proposed amendments to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.
For more than a century, the Greater Baltimore Urban League has worked to advance economic mobility,
financial empowerment, workforce development, entrepreneurship, and equitable access to opportunity
throughout the Baltimore region.
We recognize the agencies' stated objectives of encouraging responsible lending, ensuring community
development resources reach their intended beneficiaries, and reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens.
However, we urge the agencies to ensure that the proposed changes do not unintentionally weaken bank
accountability or reduce investment in communities that continue to experience barriers to credit and capital.
Small Business Development and Access to Capital
Through our Entrepreneurship Center and Restaurant Accelerator Program, GBUL works directly with
entrepreneurs who face challenges obtaining traditional financing, building business credit, and accessing the
technical assistance necessary to sustain and expand their businesses.
Our entrepreneurship initiatives have supported approximately 40 businesses, facilitated over $500,000 in
support, and contributed to the creation of more than 40 jobs.
These outcomes illustrate why community development must be understood as more than the issuance of a
loan. Entrepreneurs often require substantial preparation before they are positioned to qualify for financing.
We encourage the agencies to preserve meaningful CRA consideration for small-business technical assistance,
financial counseling, capital-readiness services, and partnerships with community-based organizations.
Community Development Grants and Nonprofit Partnerships
We are particularly concerned about the proposed 15% indirect-cost limitation associated with qualifying
community development grants from large banks.
Effective community development programs require qualified staff, program administration, compliance,
technology, financial oversight, and sustained engagement with participants.
We encourage the agencies to reconsider a rigid limitation that could unintentionally discourage banks from
supporting established nonprofit organizations delivering measurable outcomes in underserved communities.
At a minimum, the final rule should clearly define eligible indirect costs, provide reasonable flexibility, and
recognize the legitimate operating expenses necessary to deliver effective community development services.
512 Orchard St. Baltimore, MD 21201
410-523-8150
contact@gbul.org
www.gbul.org
 Workforce Development and Economic Mobility
GBUL's construction workforce initiatives have enrolled approximately 120 participants across five cohorts,
with 103 participants completing training.
Our programs demonstrate how workforce preparation, economic opportunity, and financial stability are
interconnected.
We encourage the agencies to preserve CRA recognition for qualifying workforce development activities that
improve economic opportunity for low- and moderate-income individuals.
Affordable Housing and Financial Empowerment
Affordable housing, sustainable homeownership, and access to responsible financial products remain essential
components of neighborhood economic stability.
We encourage the agencies to maintain meaningful consideration of mortgage lending, affordable housing
investments, financial counseling, and services that help households establish financial security.
Transparency and Community Accountability
While we recognize the importance of reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens, streamlined examinations
should not diminish the ability of regulators and communities to evaluate whether financial institutions are
meeting local credit needs.
We encourage continued transparency, meaningful community input, and accessible information regarding
banks' lending and community development activities.
Conclusion
The Greater Baltimore Urban League respectfully requests that the agencies:
1.
Preserve meaningful CRA incentives for lending and investment in underserved communities.
2.
Maintain recognition of nonprofit-led small-business development and financial empowerment
services.
3.
Reconsider the proposed 15% indirect-cost limitation for qualifying community development grants.
4.
Protect CRA consideration for qualifying affordable housing and workforce development activities.
5.
Maintain transparent and accountable evaluation standards that reflect local community needs.
Community reinvestment is not simply a regulatory obligation. It is an important mechanism for connecting
residents, entrepreneurs, and neighborhoods to the financial resources necessary to build lasting economic
stability.
We appreciate the opportunity to provide these comments and encourage the agencies to consider the
experiences of community-based organizations that work directly with populations facing persistent barriers
to economic opportunity.
Respectfully,
Mrs. Tershea S. Rice
Interim President & Chief Executive Officer
Greater Baltimore Urban League
Baltimore, Maryland

October 7th, 2026

Jonathan V. Gould, Comptroller

Docket ID OCC-2026-0694
Via: https://regulations.gov/

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

Inland Equity Community Land Trust writes to object to the harmful changes
proposed to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed by
Congress in 1977 in response to redlining and creates an affirmative obligation for
banks to help meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of communities,
including low and moderate income (LMI) communities. While the CRA has
successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest and provide services in underserved
communities, challenges related to redlining, discrimination, underinvestment, and
lack of access remain.

Inland Equity Community Land Trust (501c3) based in Adelanto, CA. Banks that
have complied with the CRA have offered financial literacy classes and general
operations funds for our housing project. We are members of Rise Economy and
California Community Land Trust Network.


The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift.
The proposal does not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on
LMI communities. We request an extension of the comment period for an additional
60 days so we have time to better understand how much CRA activity may be lost
to communities because of this proposal – an analysis the regulators did not
conduct or provide.
The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved
communities in several ways.

1) Community development (CD) activities for affordable housing
and small businesses will drop dramatically.
As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities
that support critically needed affordable housing and economic development
projects. These activities often provide the greatest CRA impact in communities as
they strengthen economic stability and mobility, quality of life, and social health of
residents and communities.

The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large"
Banks, such that many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and
expectation to serve the community development needs of their communities.[1]
According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70
California banks would see their reinvestment obligations reduced under the
proposal. Twenty-five California banks would shed their Community Development
Test responsibilities entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer be subject to
the Investment Test.[2]

The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical
community development programs that have had large impacts in LMI
communities. These include Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) which are a
key driver of affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) which
fuel economic development projects in tribal and other areas; and EQ2 equity
equivalent investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs)
that provide small business lending in underserved areas that banks cannot reach,
and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that take property off of the speculative
market.

Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting
the critical importance of the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable
housing.[3] Approximately half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from CRA
 motivated banks.[4] The regulators will even further weaken CD obligations if they
adopt the alternative proposal that Large Banks be defined as those with over $30
billion in assets.

Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance
even where they remain subject to the Community Development and Investment
Tests. The regulators signal to all banks that they can do significantly less CD
lending and investment and still pass their CRA examinations, all while seeking CRA
credit for activity outside of their CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests
that a bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1
capital were devoted to CD loans and CD investments. That percentage is far lower
than the percentage that NCRC determined banks currently devote to community
investments and loans. If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary
to meet the proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by approximately
$87.1 billion, or 85%.[5]

Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have
tremendous negative impacts on affordable housing and small business
development in our state. Asset thresholds should not be raised.

2) Banks will shed branches and BankOn.
The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and maintain
branches in LMI and BIPOC neighborhoods. By increasing the asset threshold for a
Large Bank to over $10 billion, forty-five banks in California will no longer be
subject to the Services Test and reviewed to ensure that their branches are serving
LMI communities. In California alone, NCRC estimates that 245 branches in LMI
areas and 497 branches in neighborhoods of color would be vulnerable to closure
due to this proposal.[6]

Branch presence has been tied to increased small business lending in communities.
Fewer branches will result in less small business lending. These changes will be
particularly hard hitting in rural areas of our state where smaller banks originate a
larger portion of the small business loans.

The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to
offer deposit products that are accessible to LMI residents.[7] Deposit accounts are
a gateway to credit access, financial stability, and wealth building, especially for
families who are otherwise preyed upon by predatory financial institutions. As one
important example, the BankOn program has provided access to no or low fee bank
accounts for over fourteen million people.[8] California is home to several BankOn
 coalitions that establish effective partnerships among banks, community-based
organizations, and local governments. The proposal jettisons this work.

Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million
are underbanked.[9] National banks regulated by the OCC charged billions of
dollars in overdraft and non-sufficient fund fees in 2025, and in California alone,
state-chartered banks charged over fifty-six million dollars ($56 million) in OD and
NSF fees to California consumers in 2025.[10]

3) Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.
Another consequence of the proposal's drive to raise asset thresholds is that fewer
banks will be required to report data regarding their small business, small farm,
and community development lending activities. Such data is critical to
understanding not only individual bank performance, but also the needs of local
markets. Rise Economy and its member organizations routinely analyze this CRA
data when meeting with banks and commenting on CRA exams and mergers. The
loss of such data is particularly harmful at a time when the Administration is
walking back efforts to collect and disclose detailed small business lending data
under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank Act. These changes will disproportionately
impact rural communities in our state where banks up to $10 billion in assets make
up a larger part of the small business and small farm lending markets.


4) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will
suffer.
The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by
requiring a demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating
that large banks and their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more
than 15% of these grants on overhead.[13] As if this wasn't enough, the FDIC and
OCC question whether they should end CRA eligibility for bank grantmaking to
nonprofits entirely.

Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian
measures will be except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller
groups, may be impacted.[14]

Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local
needs. They also can be key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and
investment products into communities inclined to trust long established local
organizations. Many nonprofit organizations and programs, such as downpayment
assistance programs, that support CRA related activity, rely on bank contributions
 to operate. Smaller, local, and rural organizations will be least able to meet new
reporting obligations, and they risk losing bank support as a result. The proposal
would also end impactful contributions from banks for general operating support,
sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.

Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their
communities on their own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps
in their own capacity – seeking assistance with community outreach, borrower
education, credit building and repair, technical assistance, legal services, job
training and placement, tax assistance, affordable housing and other services and
programs which help residents become stable and bankable so that banks can
attract new deposits and make new loans in LMI communities.

The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and will
focus grantmaking on larger organizations that can help them more easily meet
their new FDIC and OCC-imposed regulatory burdens.

Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15%
overhead restriction will negatively affect operations and organizational success. As
one example, in order to secure CRA grants from Large Banks, CDFIs will need to
pare down costs for critical operational expenses such as underwriting, servicing,
compliance, technology, impact measurement, product development, and borrower
technical assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions,
organizations are put at risk.

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA
activity that contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large
negative impact it will have on nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding,
the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are meant to benefit from the CRA,
and the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

6) Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.
There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link
between CRA and LMI impact in the name of easing bank burden.

Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their
top two major product lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in,
and profiting from, communities, this lending by banks, subsidiaries and affiliates
must be evaluated. Further, certain products, such as small farm and consumer
loans, are important in many communities, but may not be among a bank's largest
product lines. If regulators give banks a pass and exempt smaller product lines
 from CRA oversight, banks will have less incentive to consider how those products
are offered.

Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and
soundness, encourages banks to meet community needs, and engenders greater
trust in banks by the community. Eliminating categories of loan products from
scrutiny will have the opposite effect.

No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test,
which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the
definition of economic development. The CRA should create greater incentives for
banks to support the creation of jobs that pay family sustaining wages for LMI
workers and in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to provisions that would provide
CRA credit for job creation and economic development that may only benefit
middle- and upper-income workers and communities. Such provisions ignore the
purpose of CRA.

Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA
credit for large scale community infrastructure products that generate profits for
banks, would likely be financed without CRA credit, and provide only incidental
benefits to LMI residents and communities. Such an expansion of what qualifies for
CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities.
For example, banks might choose to more profitably earn CRA credit by financing
larger scale infrastructure projects, like bridges, in lieu of financing less lucrative,
smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local community needs (such as
childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or resilience
projects).

Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA
should require banks to focus their CRA activities on their CRA assessments
areas,[15] where they are subject to more rigorous regulatory oversight (with an
exception made to encourage banks to better serve Tribes, as noted above). Banks
are not doing enough currently to meet the credit and deposit needs in the areas
where they have CRA responsibility, a problem the regulators tried to address in the
2023 CRA Rule.[16] Yet the proposal further encourages banks to seek CRA credit
for projects in areas away from their branches, lending and CRA responsibility. This
will enable banks to get credit for activity outside of their assessment areas, while
providing no accompanying CRA obligation to better serve these areas.

Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal goes
out of its way to encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan option to meet
their CRA responsibilities. The Strategic Plan was meant for financial institutions
 that operated under a unique business model that the CRA rules were not designed
to address. The Strategic Plan option provides for minimal public input and
regulatory scrutiny and allows banks to determine the level of reinvestment activity
they need to engage in to earn a passing CRA grade. In our experience, banks with
Strategic Plans tend to reinvest less in the community and in less impactful ways.
The OCC's guidance establishing low community development thresholds for banks
opting for the Strategic Plan, [17] validates this perspective.

Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community
development efforts with little benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing,
where units are affordable at a point in time but not encumbered by deed or rent
restrictions, are a feature of today's housing market. But CRA rules should not give
banks credit for financing such activities where the benefit to LMI residents and
communities is unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it
can be a driver of bank investment in problematic landlords and displacement. CRA
credit should be given for financing of NOAH only if the project is owned and
operated by mission-driven organizations, where a majority of residents are LMI
tenants, and the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are
compliant with tenant rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents
can reasonably be expected to retain their housing.

7) Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA
ratings downgrades.
The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and redline
should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding"
ratings. Under the Biden Administration, at least a dozen banks that passed their
CRA exams were accused of redlining. This proposal will only increase that number
by narrowing what constitutes evidence of discrimination that may be considered
for the purpose of downgrading a bank's CRA rating. Here, regulators should
consider any evidence that a bank, its affiliates, or subsidiaries engaged in
discrimination, redlining, or illegal credit practices as part of their lending, deposit,
branching, or other activities. This evidence should be considered regardless of its
source (public or private parties), or its form (informal complaints, research based
on data, testing results, comment letters, administrative actions, private litigation,
etc.). We also urge the regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity
Act authorizes Special Purpose Credit Programs, and to once again encourage banks
to develop SPCPs to better serve communities that have been redlined, excluded,
and underserved. This is the essence of CRA.

Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information to
allow for meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of
 entities and activities, and will undoubtedly harm the communities that the CRA
was meant to support. If finalized in substantially the same form as proposed,
communities will suffer significantly decreased investment in affordable housing and
CDFI support, more LMI branch closures, higher bank account fees, fewer
community serving nonprofit organizations, and increased bank discrimination and
redlining with no CRA consequence. The CRA will become further removed from its
purpose of encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and
the OCC to reconsider this proposal.

Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Very Truly Yours,
Maribel Nunez

Maribel Nunez
Executive Director
Inland Equity Community Land Trust

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Dear Office of the Comptroller of the Currency:

On behalf of the Community of Compassion CDC, please accept the attached letter regarding the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) Rule. As an organization serving communities in Philadelphia, we see firsthand how access to banking services, responsible credit, investment, and strong financial partnerships directly impacts families, small businesses, and neighborhood development.

We respectfully ask the OCC to consider the experiences and concerns outlined in our letter as decisions regarding the CRA continue to shape investment and economic opportunity in underserved communities.

Thank you for the opportunity to share our perspective and for your consideration.

Sincerely,
Pastor Terrilynn Donnell
Executive Director
Community of Compassion CDC

Washington, DC 20219

Attn: Chief Counsel's Office

Travis Hill, Chairman

Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)

Via email to Comments @fdic.gov

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Community
Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-
AG31]

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Community of Compassion Inc. submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and
FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-
income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify
supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60 days.

Community of Compassion CDC is a Philadelphia-based nonprofit committed to developing the community with
compassion by creating opportunities that strengthen youth, families, and neighborhoods. Our work advances
community reinvestment through youth development and violence prevention, workforce and entrepreneurship
initiatives, food access, health and wellness programs, and partnerships that connect residents to critical resources.
By investing directly in people and underserved communities, we help create pathways to economic stability, safer
neighborhoods, and long-term community well-being.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that banks meet
the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also
recognized that communities depend on access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain

6150 Cedar Avenue, Philadelphia, PA 19143 email: compassioncdcphilly@gmail.com
 Community (Y Compassion CDC
especially important in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal
access to mainstream financial services.

The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change how regulators
evaluate community development, bank services and support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that
these changes are being considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-
income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In the Philadelphia metro area, from
2010-2024, banks made over $64 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census
tracts and over $22 billion in CRA qualified lending to small businesses. Investments such as these benefited our
community by increasing access to capital, affordable housing, small business financing, and other resources that
promote long-term economic stability. These investments can help preserve and develop affordable housing,
support local entrepreneurs and small businesses, create employment opportunities, and strengthen neighborhood-
based organizations that provide essential services. In historically underserved communities, continued investment
is especially important to reducing barriers to economic opportunity, preventing displacement, and ensuring that
residents and businesses can participate in and benefit from neighborhood growth and revitalization.

We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in our communities. For
example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital devoted to either community development
loans or investments would be enough to receive a passing CRA rating. This represents a dramatic reduction in
what large banks currently devote to community investments and loans, and we fear that this new guidance may
operate as a ceiling instead of a floor. Pennsylvania receives over $3 billion in CRA related investments annually,
but under the proposed rule that could fall to just over $600 million — an 80% loss.

Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination cannot withstand
such a reduction in community development investments and loans. If regulators lower the expectations for banks
to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for
communities. For example, in our community, a reduction in community development investments and lending
could further limit opportunities for families, small businesses, and nonprofit organizations that are already
working to overcome economic barriers. Families may face greater difficulty accessing affordable mortgage credit
and achieving homeownership, while local entrepreneurs and small-business owners could struggle to obtain the
financing needed to start, sustain, or expand their businesses. Reduced investment could also threaten the
development and preservation of affordable housing and limit funding for community-based programs that provide
workforce development, youth services, food access, violence prevention, and other essential resources. For
neighborhoods that have historically experienced disinvestment, continued access to responsible lending and
meaningful financial investment is critical to building economic stability, creating jobs, strengthening local
businesses, preserving affordable housing, and ensuring that longtime residents can benefit from the growth and
revitalization of their communities.

It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet the needs of communities like ours. Before
finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce lending, services or
investment available to low- and moderate-income communities and whether communities that have experienced
historic discrimination or disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.

nn EE

6150 Cedar Avenue, Philadelphia, PA 19143 email: compassioncdcphilly@gmail.com
 The proposal would also substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under
CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while banks with assets between $1
billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less demanding intermediate-bank framework rather
than the more comprehensive tests applied to large banks. The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data
collection and reporting requirements currently applicable to large banks, including reporting on small-business,
community development lending.

A number of banks that operate in Philadelphia will now be considered either intermediate or small banks under
the proposed rule and therefore subject to less rigorous requirements. These reclassifications and resulting
eliminations of community development obligations for over 800 banks and separate investment evaluations for
400 banks across the country, may worsen the housing crisis by reducing investor interest in buying Low-Income
Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC), and reducing access to mortgages for first-time homebuyers or access to credit for
home repairs.

Similarly, the proposed rule would narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service test. Today,
examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and information about the costs and features
of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit this criterion to credit services, removing deposit products such as
checking and savings accounts from direct evaluation under the service test. As such, examiners would no longer
evaluate whether those products are affordable and responsive to community needs even though approximately
15% of Philadelphians — over 100,000 households — remain unbanked or underbanked. Moreover, according to the
Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, these households are overwhelmingly low-income, black, or disabled. CRA
review of the cost and features of deposit products has played an important role in encouraging banks to address
these disparities by providing affordable products, and it must continue to do so.

For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate from access to credit and
economic opportunity. They can determine whether families can safely receive income, build savings, establish
banking relationships and obtain responsible credit. In the communities we serve, many residents face limited
access to convenient, affordable banking services and may rely on check-cashing businesses and other alternative
financial services that often come with higher fees. The loss or limited availability of neighborhood bank branches
can make it more difficult for families to establish trusted banking relationships, build savings, and access
responsible credit. Greater access to affordable deposit accounts and neighborhood-based financial institutions is
essential to helping residents strengthen their financial stability and create pathways toward homeownership,
entrepreneurship, and long-term economic opportunity.

This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and moderate-income
communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to affordable mortgage credit and
homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible small-business financing; and neighborhoods
continue to need investment in affordable housing, small businesses and other community development.

The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply because a bank falls
below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA obligations and scrutiny applied to these
institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that would move into less rigorous examination categories,
determine the communities those institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development activity that
would receive less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-income
communities or communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

ne

6150 Cedar Avenue, Philadelphia, PA 19143 email: compassioncdcphilly@gmail.com
 We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and nonprofit
organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development, financial counseling,
workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based services through grants, investments,
loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations. These resources can be particularly important to local
organizations that have deep relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.

For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and new
documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations. For smaller nonprofit
organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other
operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also have
fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs. In addition, many community-based
nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain financial records or program documentation in the
precise format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller
organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger organizations
whose activities are easier to verify.

Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and partnerships can play in supporting
community development Our organization has seen firsthand the transformative impact that bank grants,
investments, and partnerships can have on community development. Bank support has helped make projects such
as Compassion Senior Living possible, expanding access to quality, affordable housing for seniors in our
community and helping longtime residents remain in the neighborhoods they call home. Banking partnerships have
also strengthened our ability to provide financial education and entrepreneurship programs, workforce
development and career pathways, and resources that help residents build greater economic stability. Equally
important, operating support from financial institutions strengthens our organizational capacity, allowing
Community of Compassion CDC to sustain these programs, expand services, and continue responding to the
evolving needs of the individuals and families we serve.

These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into tangible benefits
for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community development activities receive CRA
consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond the banks themselves. These rules should be motivated
by the needs of the communities CRA is intended to serve and not by the perceived regulatory burden on financial
institutions.

To be considered economic development under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying small business must
promote economic development by supporting permanent job creation, retention, or improvement for low- or
moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income communities.

The proposed rule would eliminate this "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks could earn CRA credit
for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or improves jobs for low- and moderate-income
people or in low- and moderate-income communities. This change would weaken the connection between CRA
economic-development credit and the people and communities CRA is intended to benefit. Specifically, a loan that
helps a qualifying business expand does not necessarily create jobs, increase economic opportunities in an
underserved neighborhood or address the needs of low- and moderate-income communities. One example of
economic development in our community is Community of Compassion CDC's Taking Care of Business (TCB)
Program, which creates paid workforce opportunities while improving the neighborhoods we serve. Through TCB,
participants gain employment experience in street and neighborhood cleaning, beautification, and community

6150 Cedar Avenue, Philadelphia, PA 19143 email: compassioncdcphilly@gmail.com
 ston CDC

Community (YC

Devevopine fae Coun

maintenance while developing essential workplace skills such as reliability, teamwork, leadership, and
accountability. The program provides participants with an opportunity to earn income, build a work history, and
develop transferable skills that can lead to long-term employment. At the same time, their work helps create
cleaner, safer, and more welcoming commercial corridors and residential neighborhoods, demonstrating how
community investment can simultaneously create jobs, strengthen residents, and revitalize neighborhoods.

Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens a qualifying business
will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank to demonstrate that those benefits reach low-
and moderate-income workers or neighborhoods.

We are also concerned that currently, banks above the large bank threshold annually collect and report data on
small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans, while the proposal would limit these
requirements to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. Banks with assets of $10 billion or less would no
longer be required to annually collect and report CRA data on small business loans and community development
loans.

Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers would have less information to identify credit
deserts, compare bank performance or understand whether local credit needs are being met. Local community
leaders and elected officials depend on this data for decision making and for ensuring that the needs of residents
are being addressed. This proposed change is inconsistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of
meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities, and should not
be in the final rule.

Lastly, prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:

e identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny under the
proposal;

e quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community development activities
subject to CRA evaluation;

e assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations, including rural
communities and communities of color; and

consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing meaningful community
accountability.

Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes that the OCC and FDIC
should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and released for public
comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting community credit
needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that accountability without first
demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire
communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.

We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days. The proposal is more
than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant changes to bank classifications, community
development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation.

6150 Cedar Avenue, Philadelphia, PA 19143 email: compassioncdcphilly@gmail.com
 Community (f Compassion CDC

The current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.

Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from community
organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that do not have dedicated regulatory staff,
additional time is warranted. An extension would allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical
consequences, gather examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more complete
record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026
comment deadline by at least 60 days.

Sincerely, Dee

Terrilynn Donnell

1

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
on Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694;
RIN 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Nevada Human Development Corporation submits this comment in opposition to the
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of
the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
(FDIC)1 because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also
request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze
the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an
opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting
any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.
Nevada Human Development Corporation (NHDC) is a nonprofit organization dedicated
to strengthening communities by providing workforce development and other supportive
services to individuals and families throughout Northern Nevada. Our work promotes
economic stability and self-sufficiency by helping farm workers and the underserved
communities overcome barriers to employment, housing, and basic needs. NHDC
contributes to community reinvestment by directing resources and services to

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 2
communities and individuals who need them most. OHDC is a member of the National
Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC).
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important
in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal
access to mainstream financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and
would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and
support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being
considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-
income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination
and disinvestment.
We are concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations.
Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development, financial
counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based
services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations.
These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have deep
relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect
costs and new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for
smaller organizations.2 For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be
unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other operating expenses
are often necessary to deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also
have fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs. In addition,
many community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain
financial records, budgets or program documentation in the precise format a bank would
need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations
are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger
organizations whose activities are easier to verify.
Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and
partnerships can play in supporting community development.


2 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,129 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 3
NHDC has experience utilizing bank and community funding to support individuals and
families who may not qualify for some of our other programs or who have needs that
cannot be fully addressed through restricted government or state funding. These funds
have also allowed us to raise scholarship resources and provide critical operating support
for our organization. Because many federal and state funding sources limit indirect or
administrative costs, flexible bank funding has been especially valuable in allowing
NHDC to invest in essential operating capacity and other needs that are critical to
sustaining and expanding our services to the community.
These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn
capital into tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and
community development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have
consequences well beyond the banks themselves.
Before finalizing these provisions, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed
documentation requirements and limits on administrative expenses would reduce or
redirect bank support away from smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those with
limited administrative capacity. The agencies must also determine whether those effects
would ultimately reduce resources available to low- and moderate-income communities.
More broadly, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule primarily in terms of
reducing perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also determine
what the changes mean for the communities CRA is intended to serve.
Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
● identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA
scrutiny under the proposal;
● quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
● assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or
populations, including rural communities and communities of color;
● consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without
sacrificing meaningful community accountability; and
Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes
that the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its
impacts is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs
considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for
meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that
materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are
consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
 4
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120
days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service
evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The
current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that
do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would
allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather
examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more
complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies
extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.

Sincerely,
Nevada Human Development Corporation
cc. National Community Reinvestment Coalition
