comments.text:
COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency’s (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation’s (FDIC) proposed amendments to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. The Colorado Health Foundation (“CHF” or “the Foundation”) is a statewide, nonprofit and nonpartisan philanthropic organization with a mission to improve the health and well-being of Coloradans. The Foundation recognizes the agencies’ stated goals of reducing regulatory burden for community banks and providing greater clarity in the CRA framework. This proposed rule, however, would substantially narrow CRA examination and reporting requirements by raising the small-bank threshold from less than $412 million to less than $1 billion, establishing an intermediate-bank category of $1 billion to $10 billion, and limiting the full large-bank framework to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. These changes would move hundreds of banks into less intensive examination categories and reduce separate scrutiny of community-development lending, investments, branches, and services. The Foundation is concerned that the proposal could weaken accountability for whether banks are meeting 
local credit and investment needs, particularly in smaller and rural markets where community and regional banks can play an especially important role. 
For these reasons, the Foundation respectfully urges the agencies to withdraw these proposed changes that would significantly narrow community-development, investment, service, and data-reporting requirements. Please see attached letter for our full comments.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0188_09000064b9658fd1.pdf:
October 9, 2026

Jonathan V. Gould
Comptroller of the Currency
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street SW
Washington, DC 20219

Travis Hill
Chairman
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
550 17th Street NW
Washington, DC 20429

Submitted electronically via Regulations.gov

RE: Comments on Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-
AF57; RIN 3064-AG31


Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill,

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's
(OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposed amendments to the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. The Colorado Health Foundation ("CHF" or "the Foundation") is a
statewide, nonprofit and nonpartisan philanthropic organization with a mission to improve the health
and well-being of Coloradans. Through community engagement, research, grantmaking, and private
sector investments, the Foundation works to ensure that everyone in Colorado has what they need to be
healthy. The Foundation has a particular interest in ensuring that communities across Colorado have
access to the capital, affordable housing, financial services, and economic opportunities that support
good health and well-being.

The Foundation recognizes the agencies' stated goals of reducing regulatory burden for community
banks and providing greater clarity in the CRA framework. This proposed rule, however, would
substantially narrow CRA examination and reporting requirements by raising the small-bank threshold
from less than $412 million to less than $1 billion, establishing an intermediate-bank category of $1
billion to $10 billion, and limiting the full large-bank framework to banks with more than $10 billion in
assets.




These changes would move hundreds of banks into less intensive examination categories and reduce
separate scrutiny of community-development lending, investments, branches, and services. The
Foundation is concerned that the proposal could weaken accountability for whether banks are meeting
local credit and investment needs, particularly in smaller and rural markets where community and
regional banks can play an especially important role.

For these reasons, the Foundation respectfully urges the agencies to withdraw these proposed changes
that would significantly narrow community-development, investment, service, and data-reporting
requirements. As outlined below, the Foundation is concerned that:

•
Raising the asset thresholds would move hundreds of banks into less intensive CRA
examination categories, reducing separate scrutiny of community-development lending,
investments, branches, and services and limiting CRA data collection and reporting to the public.
•
The proposed geographic-flexibility standard could establish a benchmark for local community-
development activity substantially below current levels and weaken incentives for banks to
remain responsive to needs within individual assessment areas.
•
Narrowing consideration of deposit products and branch services could reduce accountability for
forms of financial access that remain important to low- and moderate-income households and
communities.
•
The proposed restrictions on community-development grants, including the 15 percent indirect-
cost standard, could make it more difficult for smaller nonprofit and community-based
organizations to obtain general operating, capacity-building, and other flexible support.

Raising the asset thresholds would substantially reduce community-development accountability and
transparency.

According to the agencies' regulatory analysis, 604 FDIC-supervised banks and 194 OCC-supervised
banks would move from the intermediate category to the small-bank category and would no longer
have a separate community-development test if this proposed rule is implemented. Another 250 FDIC-
supervised banks and 126 OCC-supervised banks would move from large-bank to intermediate-bank
treatment and would no longer be subject to the existing large-bank data collection, maintenance, and
reporting requirements.

Under existing policy, intermediate banks are separately evaluated on community-development lending,
investments, and services, while large banks are evaluated under distinct lending, investment, and
service tests. The proposal would eliminate the separate community-development test for banks below
$1 billion and apply a less rigorous evaluation to institutions between $1 billion and $10 billion.

The National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) estimates that approximately 814 banks
nationwide would no longer receive a separate community-development evaluation and another 417



would move out of the large-bank framework, leaving only the largest approximately 6 percent of banks
subject to separate reviews of community-development investments and branch services. NCRC also
estimates that the proposal would eliminate approximately 11 percent of currently reported CRA small-
business lending data nationally. These estimates illustrate the scale of the potential reduction in
community-level accountability and publicly available information.

The reduction could be particularly important in Colorado. In the Federal Reserve Banks' 2025 Small
Business Credit Survey, 52 percent of the 98 Colorado employer firms surveyed reported using a small
bank for financial services, compared with 42 percent nationally. The survey defines a small bank as an
institution with less than $10 billion in assets—the same general asset range that the proposed CRA
rule would remove from the large-bank framework.

Reducing the amount of small-business, small-farm, community-development, and assessment-area
data available for these institutions could make it more difficult for regulators, community organizations,
researchers, and financial institutions to identify unmet credit needs and lending gaps. The Foundation
urges the agencies to withdraw this proposal and to preserve meaningful community-development
evaluation and data transparency for institutions that would otherwise move into less intensive CRA
categories.

Reduced scrutiny of community-development investment could have particular consequences for
affordable housing in Colorado.
Access to affordable housing is closely connected to health and economic stability, and Colorado
continues to face substantial affordability pressures. According to the Colorado Housing and Finance
Authority (CHFA), 46.8 percent of Colorado renters are housing cost-burdened and 22.9 percent are
severely cost-burdened. More than one in five Colorado homeowners are also cost-burdened.
Community-development capital is an important part of Colorado's response. Housing Tax Credits have
helped build or preserve more than 83,500 affordable rental homes in Colorado since 1986. In the first
2026 funding round, CHFA awarded credits to 14 developments expected to support 634 affordable
rental homes and generate more than $219 million in private-sector equity across urban, rural, and
Tribal communities.
Moving hundreds of banks out of separate investment evaluations could weaken incentives for
investments such as Low-Income Housing Tax Credits, particularly in smaller markets. Because
affordable-housing projects depend on multiple public and private financing sources, the Foundation
urges the agencies to more fully analyze how reduced investment scrutiny could affect the availability of
private capital before eliminating separate investment evaluations for banks that are currently treated as
large institutions.



The proposed geographic-flexibility standard could become a ceiling on local community-
development activity.
The proposal would allow a large bank, under one option, to receive CRA consideration for community-
development activity outside an assessment area after reaching annual levels within that area equal to
0.625 percent of allocated Tier 1 capital for community-development loans and a separate 0.625
percent for investments and grants. Intermediate, wholesale, and limited-purpose banks would be
subject to a combined 1.25 percent standard.
Although the agencies describe these figures as geographic-flexibility standards rather than CRA
passing scores, NCRC found a substantial gap between the proposed benchmark and recent activity. In
its review of 69 of the 100 largest banks supervised by the OCC or FDIC, NCRC calculated
approximately $102 billion in annual assessment-area community-development lending, investments,
and grants. Applying the proposed 0.625 percent benchmark to those institutions produced
approximately $14.8 billion, about 85 percent below their observed annual activity.
That approximately 85 percent difference raises concern that the threshold could establish a
substantially lower benchmark for local community-development activity and influence bank and
examiner expectations regarding what constitutes an adequate local commitment. This is particularly
important in communities where projects may be smaller, more complex, or more difficult to finance but
where unmet housing, small-business, infrastructure, and community-development needs remain
significant.
The Foundation urges the agencies to withdraw this proposal and to ensure that any geographic-
flexibility provision preserves strong expectations for responsiveness within each assessment area and
does not reduce incentives for banks to invest above the regulatory minimum where local needs support
greater activity.
Deposit products and branch access remain important components of financial access in Colorado.
The proposal would narrow the large-bank service test to focus on credit services and would no longer
consider deposit services such as checking and savings products. The agencies describe this change as
part of an effort to focus CRA more directly on lending and credit needs. The Foundation is concerned,
however, that affordable and accessible transaction accounts are closely connected to households'
ability to enter and remain in the financial mainstream.
Colorado has made a concerted effort to expand access to safe and affordable banking. Through Bank
On Colorado, the Colorado Office of Financial Empowerment works with financial institutions, local
governments, and community organizations to connect residents to accounts that meet national
standards. According to the Office's January 2026 report, more than 58,780 Bank On accounts were



opened by Coloradans in 2024 based on data from only about one-third of participating financial
institutions, and approximately 87 percent were opened by customers new to the institution.
The substantial use of these accounts underscores the importance of affordable transaction products to
financial access in Colorado. Removing deposit products from the CRA service evaluation would
therefore eliminate an important mechanism for assessing whether large banks' retail banking services
are responsive to community needs.
NCRC also estimates that more than 5,000 branches in low- and moderate-income census tracts and
more than 4,000 branches in majority-people-of-color census tracts nationwide are operated by banks
that would no longer be subject to a separate large-bank branch evaluation. These figures demonstrate
the scale of branch networks that would lose separate scrutiny and underscore the need to evaluate the
state and local effects of the proposed thresholds, not only the share of national banking assets held by
affected institutions.
The proposed restrictions on community-development grants could reduce flexible support for
nonprofit organizations.
The Foundation is also concerned about the proposed treatment of community-development grants.
Under the proposal, CRA consideration would generally be limited to grants directly used for a specific
program, project, or initiative with a community-development purpose. For grants made by large banks,
recipient organizations would also have to demonstrate that indirect costs associated with administering
the grant do not exceed 15 percent, supported by documentation that could include an IRS Form 990
and annual operating and program budgets.
If implemented, this provision would be especially impactful to community-based organizations that use
operating support and capacity-building resources to maintain staff, develop programs, administer
financing, and deliver services. Importantly, the agencies' own regulatory analysis recognizes this
possible effect. It states that the direct-use requirement, 15 percent operating-cost condition, and
related documentation requirements could mean that general operating support, capacity-building
grants, intermediary grants, and grants to smaller nonprofits receive less CRA-motivated funding.
The 15 percent standard also warrants reconsideration. In explaining its proposal, the agencies point to
OMB's Uniform Guidance. Yet, as the proposed rule itself acknowledges, OMB describes its 15 percent
de minimis indirect-cost rate as a mechanism intended to permit a more reasonable and realistic
recovery of overhead costs, particularly for organizations without the capacity to negotiate a formal
indirect-cost rate. A de minimis rate designed to ensure some recovery of indirect costs does not
necessarily establish that 15 percent is an appropriate ceiling for determining whether a community-
development grant should receive CRA consideration.



As a philanthropic organization that works with communities and nonprofit organizations across
Colorado, the Foundation recognizes the importance of ensuring that community-development
resources reach their intended beneficiaries. At the same time, project delivery necessarily requires
sufficient administrative capacity within an organization. The Foundation urges the agencies to withdraw
this proposed categorical 15 percent ceiling and to preserve CRA consideration for reasonable general
operating, capacity-building, and intermediary support where the underlying activity has community
development as its primary purpose. The agencies should seek to prevent misuse of CRA credit without
inadvertently creating a standard that makes it more difficult for smaller community organizations to
obtain flexible resources necessary to carry out qualifying work.
Conclusion
The Community Reinvestment Act remains an important framework for assessing whether federally
supervised banks are helping meet community credit needs. The Foundation supports efforts to make
CRA requirements clearer and reduce unnecessary burden, but the proposed changes could
substantially reduce scrutiny of community-development activity, investments, services, public data, and
flexible nonprofit support.
These concerns are especially relevant in Colorado, where communities face significant affordable-
housing needs, small businesses rely on banks below $10 billion in assets, and tens of thousands of
residents are using affordable accounts designed to expand access to mainstream banking.
The Foundation therefore respectfully urges the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the proposed asset
thresholds and related reductions in CRA requirements; to preserve meaningful consideration of
affordable deposit products and branch access; to ensure that geographic flexibility does not weaken
responsiveness within individual assessment areas; and to revise the proposed grant restrictions so that
reasonable operating and capacity-building support remains eligible for CRA consideration. The
agencies should more fully assess the effects of these changes on low- and moderate-income
communities, smaller and rural markets, affordable-housing investment, small-business credit, and
community-based organizations before finalizing policy changes of this magnitude.
The Foundation appreciates your consideration of our comments. If you have any questions, please
contact Kyle Rojas Legleiter, Colorado Health Foundation Senior Director of Policy, at
klegleiter@coloradohealth.org or 303-953-3618.
Sincerely,

Kyle Rojas Legleiter
Senior Director of Policy



The Colorado Health Foundation

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations Proposed Rule

Docket ID OCC-2026-0694 ; FDIC RIN 3064-AG31

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

On behalf of National Housing Trust (NHT), a national affordable housing nonprofit organization, we
appreciate the opportunity to comment on the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment
Act (CRA) regulations issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation (together, the agencies). For nearly 50 years, the CRA has helped
attract private capital to communities across the country and strengthen partnerships between
banks and the community development organizations that serve them. However, several aspects
of the recent proposal would reduce the availability of capital by decreasing the number of banks
subject to meaningful CRA obligations, limit consideration for grants that spur innovation and
catalyze private investment, and redirect investment away from deeply affordable housing that the
CRA is intended to support without durable affordability protections. Together, these changes
would leave low-income residents and communities with fewer resources to build and preserve
affordable housing for generations to come.

Summary of Comments
We urge the agencies to revise the proposal in three principal ways:
•
Maintain community development investment and service obligations for banks of all sizes;
•
Protect flexible grants and operating support to mission-driven nonprofit organizations as
qualifying community development activity; and
•
Ensure meaningful, enforceable, and durable affordability and tenant-protection
requirements for naturally occurring affordable housing (NOAH) investments receiving CRA
credit.

202 -833 -1031 (Fax)
www.nationalhousingtrust.org

, NW Suite 700
Washington D.C. 20036

1. Maintain Community Development Investment and Service Obligations for Banks of All Sizes
The proposal to raise CRA asset-size thresholds across small, intermediate, and large banks would
reduce the community development obligations and more comprehensive CRA evaluations that
small, medium, and large banks participate in today. From the perspective of affordable housing
practitioners, these shifts in asset thresholds risk removing important sources of financing from the
community development ecosystem.

For instance, according to the National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders (NAAHL)1, if the
agencies finalize the rule that defines small banks as those with less than $1 billion in assets, more
than 813 banks, or 19% of all banks nationwide, would no longer be subject to separate lending,
investment and service test to determine their CRA rating, rather solely a retail lending test and
community development test. This would, in our view, no longer incentivize small banks to provide
community development loans or investments in the places where they currently do business as a
strong retail lending test would offset a small bank's performance. Smaller and regional banks often
play an outsized role in smaller, rural markets as they are best situated and willing to evaluate
mission-focused projects that may not fit the underwriting preferences or scale requirements of the
largest institutions. Removing the community development evaluations for small banks will mean
that those with total assets less than $1 billion will no longer have comparable incentives to make
direct community development loans or investments. This will result in no obvious substitute
source of capital to fill the gap in places where affordable housing is greatly needed.

Increasing the thresholds for intermediate banks would reduce the number of banks that are
subject to a separate community development investment test and therefore reduce the number of
banks willing to provide project-level investment. This would drive more borrowers toward the same
pool of large-bank capital and weaken pricing and availability for mission-driven borrowers. These
impacts would be especially significant for Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing Credit)
transactions and other deeply affordable housing developments. The Housing Credit program, the
country's most important tool for the production and preservation of affordable rental housing,
relies heavily on investments from banks subject to CRA. According to a 2025 study by the
accounting firm CohnReznick,2 approximately 80% of equity investments in the Housing Credit
each year come from CRA-motivated bank investors. Removing the investment test would
substantially weaken CRA incentives to make equity investments in Housing Credit properties,
especially outside the largest metropolitan markets, meaning affordable housing developers may
face higher costs and less willingness from capital providers to support innovative or mission-
driven deals. At a time when Congress and the President have expanded LIHTC through HR 1 (2025)
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, this rule change goes counter to their priorities and threatens to
weaken the country's most powerful housing production and preservation tool.

For nonprofit Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFI) lenders such as our subsidiary,
NHTCDF, the impact may vary depending on the composition of each organization's bank lender
base. Even where only a subset of current bank lenders are directly reclassified, we believe that the
broader market effect could still be meaningful. If the agencies reclassify large banks as those with
assets over $10 billion, this will reduce the number of large banks by 416, impacting approximately
10% of all banks and reducing the number of banks subject to the full CRA exam.3 These banks may

1 2026 Fact Sheet: CRA Asset Thresholds, National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders.
2 2025 Affordable Housing Credit Study, CohnReznick.
3 2026 Fact Sheet: CRA Asset Thresholds, National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders.

202 -333-8931 (Phone)
202 -833 -1031 (Fax)
www.nationalhousingtrust.org

1101 Connecticut Ave
, NW Suite 700
Washington D.C. 20036

face greater demand from borrowers and intermediaries, while banks with reduced obligations may
have less reason to provide flexible, mission-oriented capital. Increasing the large bank
classification to assets over $30 billion would only exacerbate lending and equity challenges. We
recommend that the agencies retain meaningful CRA obligations for banks with demonstrated
capacity to engage in community development lending, investment, and services, and avoid
changes that would reduce the number and diversity of capital providers supporting affordable
housing.

2. CRA Should Continue to Protect Operating Grants and Nonprofit Capacity Building
The agencies propose to narrow consideration for community development operating grants. While
we support accountability and transparency, we are concerned that an overly restrictive approach
would discourage banks from providing the flexible resources that nonprofit affordable housing
organizations need to serve low- and moderate-income communities effectively. Operating grants
that offer capacity-building support are essential to community development as they allow
nonprofit developers, CDFIs, and policy organizations to respond to emerging community needs
that cannot be financed through project-specific grants alone. Flexible support gives community-
oriented organizations the opportunity to identify unmet needs, develop creative solutions, and
build organizational infrastructure needed to bring promising solutions to scale. If CRA credit is
limited only to grants directly used for a narrow plan, project, or initiative, banks may reduce
support for the very organizations that create and sustain the pipeline of affordable housing and
community development activity. The risk is particularly acute for smaller and rural communities,
where nonprofit capacity is limited and flexible resources can determine whether a project moves
forward at all.

We recommend that the agencies protect and preserve CRA consideration for grants, donations,
and operating support to mission-oriented nonprofit organizations where the recipient's mission,
activities, and use of funds are substantially directed toward community development. Preserving
CRA consideration for this flexible support will enable organizations to develop creative responses
to community needs, test and scale innovative approaches, undertake the early-stage work
necessary to attract private investment, and build a durable pipeline of financeable community
development projects.

3. CRA Credit for NOAH Should Require Meaningful Affordability Protections
NHT is encouraged to see that affordable housing now includes naturally occurring affordable
housing (NOAH), and affordability is determined by rent levels. However, we are deeply concerned
that recognizing naturally occurring affordable housing without strong affordability requirements
could shift CRA-motivated activity away from low-income communities and toward effectively
market-rate middle-income rental housing. While middle-income households face real housing
affordability challenges in many markets, expanding CRA eligibility to NOAH without enforceable
affordability limits could reward activity that does not produce durable community development
benefits, conflicts with the purpose of CRA, and could dilute scarce bank investments that are
needed for deeply affordable homes.

The agencies should avoid a framework in which banks can receive CRA credit for homes affordable
to households well above low-income levels such as 80% of area median income (AMI), particularly
in high-cost markets where lenders are already willing to invest. Broad NOAH eligibility would
reduce the capital available to populations that the CRA is intended to serve. LIHTC and other
restricted affordable housing developments, serving households at 60% AMI or below, would have

202 -333-8931 (Phone)
202 -833 -1031 (Fax)
www.nationalhousingtrust.org

1101 Connecticut Ave
, NW Suite 700
Washington D.C. 20036

to compete for the same capital with lower returns and more demanding affordability obligations.
For example, the broad definition, proposed by the agencies, ties to income levels as high as 120%
AMI and could permit credit for properties serving households far above the income levels CRA is
meant to prioritize. In a high-cost market such as Washington, D.C., that could include rents of
greater than $5000 per month and incomes of more than $196,700 for a family of four – statistics
that bear little relationship to the housing needs of low- and moderate-income families. CRA credit
should focus on activity targeted to the low-income households and communities it was intended
to benefit.

If the agencies decide to recognize NOAH activity, they should require clear safeguards that, at
minimum, should include recorded or otherwise enforceable affordability restrictions, rent-growth
limits designed to prevent displacement, income targeting that prioritizes low- and moderate-
income renters, and a meaningful affordability term. The agencies should also consider requiring
sponsor-imposed restrictions or comparable mechanisms where public subsidies are not present.
CRA credit should be calibrated to encourage preservation that would not otherwise occur, deepen
affordability where possible, and prevent tenant displacement. It should not create a higher-return
alternative that draws bank capital away from permanently restricted affordable housing, Housing
Credit developments, and projects serving residents with the greatest needs.
Conclusion
The Community Reinvestment Act has long been a critical tool for directing bank capital toward
communities that have faced disinvestment and unequal access to credit. For nonprofit affordable
housing developers and CDFI lenders such as NHT, CRA-motivated lending, investment, and grants
help make deeply affordable housing possible. The proposed changes should strengthen, not
weaken, that ecosystem. We respectfully urge the agencies to reconsider the changes to eligible
CRA activity based on proposed asset-size threshold increases, preserve CRA consideration for
operating grants and nonprofit capacity-building support, and ensure that any recognition of
naturally occurring affordable housing includes meaningful, enforceable, and durable affordability
protections. Thank you for considering these comments.

Sincerely,



Priya Jayachandran
CEO | National Housing Trust
About National Housing Trust
Established in 1986, National Housing Trust creates lasting housing solutions by connecting the
systems that shape housing. We integrate financing, development, preservation, policy,
sustainability, resident engagement, and innovation into our approach to expand opportunity,
strengthen communities, and ensure affordable homes remain affordable for generations. Over its
40-year history, NHT has created or preserved over 37,000 affordable homes in all 50 states and the
District of Columbia, leveraging more than $2.5 billion in financing. As both an affordable housing
lender and borrower, our organization experiences firsthand how CRA-motivated financial
resources make affordable housing possible.

Chairman

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-
AF57; RIN 3064-AG31

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill,

On behalf of the National Housing Conference (NHC), the nation's oldest and broadest
affordable housing coalition, I am writing to comment on the proposed amendments to
the regulations governing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) published by the
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC) on August 12, 20261.

For nearly five decades, the Community Reinvestment Act has been an important
component of the nation's financial system, helping to ensure that banks meet the credit
needs of the communities they serve while investing in organizations and initiatives that
have had lasting impact on low- and moderate-income residents. CRA was enacted in
response to a long history of discriminatory lending practices2 that denied many
communities access to credit and investment. Those practices contributed to persistent
disparities in homeownership, wealth creation, and neighborhood development that,
unfortunately, remain evident today.

NHC has long supported modernizing CRA to reflect changes in banking, improve
transparency and predictability, and provide appropriate flexibility for institutions to

1 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/federal-register/2026/91fr252114.pdf
2 David M. Dworkin, "The History of Redlining," National Housing Conference, April 2019,
https://nhc.org/the-history-of-redlining/


respond to local conditions. However, we are concerned that this proposal would move
the CRA framework in the wrong direction. Rather than strengthening incentives that
encourage private investment in underserved communities, several proposed provisions
would disincentivize such activity, reducing support for affordable housing and
community development, as well as for the organizations that provide critical services in
underserved communities.

Of particular concern is the impact on affordable housing and community development
activities. CRA has helped encourage private investment in the creation of new
affordable rental housing, preservation of existing housing, access to homeownership,
and other activities that can be difficult to finance through conventional market
channels alone. For example, CRA-motivated investment is critical to the supply of Low-
Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing Credit) financing throughout the country. Banks
provide approximately 75 to 80 percent of Housing Credit equity, and at least 71 percent
of that investment, about $21.4 billion, is CRA-motivated3. Raising the large bank asset
threshold from $1.649 billion to $10 billion, as the regulation proposes, would remove
the investment test for most of the banks that inject private capital into affordable rental
housing. According to the National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders
(NAAHL), only 256 of the 642 banks now classified as large would keep that
designation, a drop of more than 60 percent4. Survey data from the Affordable Housing
Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC) indicates that banks with assets of $1.649 billion to $10
billion invested an estimated $2 billion in Housing Credits over the five-year survey
period. Additionally, NAAHL estimates that banks with less than $10 billion in assets
made $27 billion in community development loans in 2024, representing 35% of all
community development loans made in that year5. The AHTCC survey of syndicators
also found that banks with assets below the proposed $10 billion threshold provided
approximately one-third of the Housing Credit investments made in rural areas,
demonstrating the outsized role these institutions play in meeting housing needs in
rural communities. The proposed rule would remove entirely the community
development responsibility for banks with assets below $1 billion, representing more

3 CohnReznick, 2025 Affordable Housing Credit Study, accessed September 18, 2026,
https://creditstudy.cohnreznick.com/credit-study.
4 National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders. Fact Sheet: CRA Asset Thresholds: National
Housing & Community Development Impact of Proposed Changes to CRA (August 2026),
https://static1.squarespace.com/static/67dd69627071be10fb7c3fb4/t/6a70b2525328625aadb890fa/1785
770578560/CRA+NPR+National+Fact+Sheet+--+Asset+Thresholds+%28August+2026%29.pdf.
 5National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders. Incentive to Impact: How CRA Leverages Private
Investments into Affordable Housing, Homeownership, Small Businesses, and Local Economies (Center
for Affordable Housing Lending, Summer 2026),
https://static1.squarespace.com/static/67dd69627071be10fb7c3fb4/t/6a6296c2f95fab4060bd8828/1784
846018733/NAAHL_CRA_Report_072326_V4-Web.pdf


than 800 institutions that play an important role in providing housing and community
development investment in their communities.

The proposed rule included two alternative asset size thresholds for classification as a
large bank. The first alternative, which would classify institutions with assets of $3.252
billion or more as a large bank, would be far less disruptive to affordable housing and
community development markets than the $10 billion threshold. AHTCC estimates that
it would affect 40 Housing Credit investors instead of 108, a reduction of about 63
percent, yielding an estimated $272 reduction in Housing Credit equity rather than the
$2 billion estimated at the $10 billion threshold. The second proposed alternative,
which would set the large bank asset threshold at $30 billion, would be far more
damaging. AHTCC estimates that in the past five years banks with assets below this
threshold invested approximately $4.5 billion in Housing Credit equity.

Small and mid-sized banks play a vital role in the financing of critically needed
affordable housing in communities throughout the nation. Meeting the pressing housing
needs of the communities they serve is exactly the type of investment CRA was intended
to promote. Taken together, reductions in CRA obligations for banks of all sizes could
have far-reaching impacts on urban and rural communities throughout the country.

The proposed limitations on community development grants and donations are also
concerning. NHC shares the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants and
donations produce meaningful community benefits. However, the proposed 15 percent
limitation on indirect costs for such contributions is not suited to achieving that goal6.
Reasonable operating costs are essential to an organization's ability to achieve
community impact. Affordable housing organizations, community development
financial institutions (CDFIs), housing counselors, and other community-based
organizations require staff, technical assistance, outreach, compliance, and
administrative capacity to turn financial commitments into successful projects and
services. A rigid limitation could therefore discourage support for organizations that
provide capacity critical to ensuring that investments yield intended results in
underserved communities.

The proposed rule would also require for CRA purposes that a community development
grant be used directly by the organization receiving the funds from the bank. Banks
often partner with nonprofit intermediaries that distribute grants and loans to other
nonprofit organizations conducting community development activities. Properly

6 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. at 52,119 (15 percent limitation); proposed 12
C.F.R. § 25.12.


structured intermediary arrangements can be an efficient and accountable mechanism
for delivering resources to underserved communities. CRA regulations should permit
the use of nonprofit intermediaries and provide standards for eligible uses of funds by
end recipients and reporting of qualifying CRA activity by intermediaries.

CRA should also recognize Special Purpose Credit Programs (SPCPs) permitted under
the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA).7 SPCPs can help lenders reach creditworthy
borrowers who may be underserved by conventional underwriting, expanding
participation in the financial system while addressing documented disparities in access
to credit.8 NHC has long supported the use of SPCPs to expand access to
homeownership and other forms of credit, consistent with the ECOA and the Fair
Housing Act.9 NHC therefore recommends that the agencies expressly acknowledge
qualifying lending conducted through lawful SPCPs in any revised CRA requirements.
CRA evaluations should recognize programs designed to address documented credit
needs and expand access to responsible credit, consistent with ECOA and Regulation B.

Further, this proposal continues a troubling pattern of inconsistency across banking
regulations in recent years. Frequent and substantial shifts in regulatory policy create
uncertainty for financial institutions of every size, requiring them to invest significant
time and resources to update compliance systems, retrain staff, and adjust business
practices. Those costs ultimately reduce the resources available to support lending,
community development, and affordable housing. Regulatory structures with
consistently changing objectives and parameters, particularly when such changes occur
during times of economic uncertainty, lead to undue burdens within the very programs
intended to encourage economic prosperity. Another wholesale revision to the CRA
framework risks further disruption that could threaten initiatives to expand investment
and improve access to credit.

In addition, this proposal conflicts with actions taken by Congress in recent years to
increase the amount of capital available for affordable housing and community
development. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act10 passed in 2025 permanently increased the

7 15 U.S.C. §§ 1691–1691f. https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title15-
chapter41-subchapter4&edition=prelim
8 12 C.F.R. § 1002.8. https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/8;
https://www.consumercomplianceoutlook.org/articles/2022/fourth-issue-2022/overview-of-special-
purpose-credit-programs-under-the-equal-credit-opportunity-act
9 National Housing Conference, Comment Letter on Community Reinvestment Act Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking, Docket Nos. R-1769, OCC-2022-0002, RIN 3064-AF81, at 4 (Aug. 5, 2022),
https://nhc.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/001-NHC-CRA-NPR-FINAL.pdf.
10 An Act to provide for reconciliation pursuant to title II of H. Con. Res. 14, Pub. L. No. 119-21, §§ 70421–
70422, 139 Stat. 72 (2025) (amending I.R.C. § 42).


allocation of Low-Income Housing Tax Credits to facilitate higher levels of private
investment in affordable housing construction. This year, Congress passed the historic
21st Century ROAD to Housing Act11, which, among other things, raised the Public
Welfare Investment cap from 15% to 20%, expanding the capacity of banks to make
qualifying investments in affordable housing and community development. Yet, just as
Congress has acted to increase the ability of banks to invest in much needed affordable
housing, this proposal eliminates or reduces a primary incentive for many institutions to
make those investments. In turn, it could inhibit the success of Congress' efforts to
address the nation's housing needs.

Finally, a change of this magnitude should not proceed with only two of three banking
regulators. Institutions supervised by different federal regulators should not operate
under materially different frameworks for CRA activity and liability. Given the
importance of CRA to communities, financial institutions, and local economies
nationwide, any significant revisions should include all three federal banking regulators,
robust public engagement, and careful congressional oversight. Any future
consideration of significant changes to CRA regulations should begin with an Advance
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking issued jointly by all three regulators to ensure that
banks, investors, housing providers, CDFIs, civil rights advocates, rural stakeholders,
and others can assess likely outcomes before regulatory text is drafted.

A truly sustainable CRA modernization effort must have broad bipartisan support to
ensure durability, effectiveness, and lasting change. NHC has long stated that any new
CRA regulatory regime must:
1. Increase investment in communities that are currently underserved;
2. Benefit more low- and moderate-income people, particularly people of color, who
live in those communities;
3. Ensure that CRA lending and investment does not lead to displacement of the
very people it is meant to help; and
4. Make both bank performance and government enforcement more transparent
and predictable12.

Unfortunately, the proposed regulatory changes will not achieve these objectives. NHC
therefore opposes the proposal and urges the agencies to withdraw it. At a time when
financial institutions and community organizations need stability and predictability,

11 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, Pub. L. No. 119-101, § 203 (2026) (increasing the public welfare
investment limit for national and state banks from 15 to 20 percent of unimpaired capital and surplus).
12 David M. Dworkin, "There's a Historic Opportunity to Modernize the Community Reinvestment Act,"
National Housing Conference, August 2018, https://nhc.org/modernizing-cra/.


another significant change to the CRA framework risks disrupting the partnerships and
investments that have been crucial to expanding access to affordable housing, credit,
and economic opportunity.

Sincerely,



David M. Dworkin
President and CEO

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Please see the attached comment letter from Ricor Development LLC regarding the proposed Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations (Docket ID OCC-2026-0694). Ricor Development LLC is concerned that the proposed changes could reduce incentives for investment in affordable housing and community development activities, making it more difficult to finance future projects and potentially limiting housing production. We encourage the OCC and FDIC to carefully evaluate the potential impacts on affordable housing investment, production, and access to capital for underserved communities.

To Whom It May Concern:
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
(OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposed changes to Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.
Ricor Development LLC is a Chicago-area owner's representation and development consulting
firm working on affordable housing and community-focused development projects. Our work
involves helping move projects from concept to completion, often alongside lenders, investors,
public agencies, and nonprofit partners.
Affordable housing projects are already challenging to finance. They often require multiple
funding sources, coordination among lenders, investors, public agencies, and community
stakeholders, and years of effort to become a reality. Access to capital remains one of the most
significant challenges facing the industry.
We are concerned that raising the threshold for banks subject to the full CRA examination and
investment requirements could reduce incentives for banks to invest in affordable housing and
community development activities. As affordable housing developers work to address housing
shortages across the country, the industry benefits from strong participation by financial
institutions that provide equity, lending, and community development support. Reducing those
incentives could make it more difficult to finance future projects and could ultimately limit
housing production. These concerns are particularly important for smaller communities,
emerging developers, and communities that already face barriers to attracting investment.
The Chicago-area affordable housing industry is working to increase housing supply, preserve
existing affordable housing, and create more opportunities for families, seniors, veterans, and
individuals with limited housing options. Policies that encourage investment and expand access
to capital should be strengthened, not weakened, if we want to address the housing challenges
facing our communities.

As a small business and emerging developer, I understand firsthand how difficult it can be to
assemble the capital needed to move housing projects forward. Affordable housing
developments rarely struggle because there is a lack of need. More often, the challenge is
securing the financing and investment necessary to bring projects to reality. Preserving
incentives that encourage private capital to participate in affordable housing remains critical.
 Ricor Development LLC
Owner's Representation | Real Estate Development


Adrian Rivera | Founder and Managing Principal
630.290.0581 | arivera@ricorcorp.com


www.ricordevelopment.com
For these reasons, we encourage the OCC and FDIC to proceed cautiously and carefully
evaluate the potential impact of these proposed changes on affordable housing investment and
production. We also encourage maintaining policies that preserve strong incentives for banks to
continue investing in affordable housing and community development activities.
Thank you for your consideration.
Sincerely,






Adrian Rivera
Founder and Managing Principal
Ricor Development LLC
Downers Grove, Illinois

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0192_09000064b9659b83.pdf:
October 13, 2026

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations

As Greater Boston's oldest and largest community foundation, the Boston Foundation is committed
to closing the gaps that drive the region's greatest disparities. Through our civic leadership,
research, grantmaking, partnerships, and advocacy, we work to expand opportunity, advance
equity, and build thriving communities.

Central to this work is the Foundation's Community Wealth pathway, which focuses on increasing
economic mobility and building long-term wealth in historically marginalized communities.
Through this effort, the Foundation advances strategies that advance affordable housing and
homeownership, strengthen community development, and expand access to capital and technical
assistance for underserved small business owners. Together, these investments help create more
equitable, resilient, and prosperous communities throughout Greater Boston.

On behalf of the Boston Foundation, we respectfully urge the withdrawal of the proposed
amendments to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). The proposed changes would weaken
a longstanding and highly effective framework that helps ensure financial institutions meet the
credit, investment, and service needs of low- and moderate-income communities. Collectively,
these changes would reduce transparency, diminish accountability, and weaken incentives for
banks to make meaningful investments in historically underserved communities.

The CRA is one of the nation's most important tools for promoting equitable access to capital,
financial services, and community investment. Enacted to address decades of discriminatory
lending practices and disinvestment, it requires federal regulators to regularly evaluate banks
serving low- and moderate-income communities. Since receiving a poor CRA grade can hinder a
bank's ability to expand, the law incentivizes financial institutions to lend in underserved
communities. These investments have generated billions of dollars in economic activity and
community development financing, expanded pathways to homeownership and entrepreneurship,
and strengthened local economies by providing residents with opportunities that the private market
alone has often failed to deliver.

CRA review requirements vary by bank size, with larger institutions subject to more comprehensive
regulations. The proposed increase in CRA asset thresholds would move roughly 800 banks into the
"small bank" category, eliminating their community development obligations and reducing the
banks subject to those requirements by 40%. More than 400 currently large banks would also be
reclassified as intermediate institutions with less rigorous community development standards,
leaving only 86 banks subject to the highest level of scrutiny. As a result, communities across the
country could face substantial reductions in the investments and services that support economic
mobility and neighborhood stability.

 These investments often fill financing gaps that would otherwise go unmet. Community
development projects and small business lending programs frequently rely on CRA capital to move
forward, including affordable housing projects financed through the Low-Income Housing Tax
Credit program. Weakening community development obligations would likely diminish investment
in these projects, slowing progress toward economic equity, limiting opportunities for wealth
creation, and widening existing racial and economic disparities in addition to a worsening housing
crisis.

The proposal would also weaken oversight of bank branches and financial services in underserved
communities. The over 400 banks that would lose branch evaluation requirements as a result of
being reclassified as intermediate operate approximately 5,000 branches in low- and moderate-
income census tracts (30% of all branches in those communities) and 4,000 branches in majority
people-of-color census tracts (23%). Reducing branch evaluation requirements and eliminating
incentives tied to important banking products could limit access to financial services and further
disadvantage communities.

Nearly five decades after its enactment, the CRA remains a critical safeguard to ensure banks meet
the credit needs of all communities. The proposed rule departs from that foundational purpose by
lowering expectations, reducing accountability, and weaking incentives for meaningful community
reinvestment. At a time of growing housing affordability challenges and persistent racial and
economic inequities, federal regulators should preserve and strengthen this framework that has
helped direct billions of dollars to communities that have been historically excluded from
investment.

Sincerely,


Courtney Brunson
Senior Director, Economic Equity Initiatives


Soni Gupta
Associate Vice President, Community Wealth

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0193_09000064b9659c72.pdf:
1 | P a g e

529 14th St., N.W. Washington, DC 20045 (202) 628-5055 sbia.org




October 10, 2026


BY ELECTRONIC TRANSMISSION


Chief Counsel's Office
ATTN: Comment Processing
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street, S.W., Suite 1E-216
Washington, D.C. 20219

Jennifer M. Jones, Deputy Executive Secretary
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
550 17th Street, N.W. Washington, D.C. 20429

RE:
Community Reinvestment Act, RIN 3064-AG31, Docket ID OCC-2026-0694


On behalf of its membership, the Small Business Investor Alliance ("SBIA") is pleased to submit
the following comments in response to the above-referenced joint notice of proposed rulemaking
("Proposal," or "CRA Rulemaking") by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC"),
and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC"), and together the "Regulators," regarding
modernizing the Community Reinvestment Act of 1977 ("CRA" or "Act") regulatory and
supervisory framework.1

The SBIA is the national organization that represents small business funds and their investors,
including Small Business Investment Companies ("SBICs") and Rural Business Investment
Companies (RBICs), and the many banks that invest in them.2 These funds make important
economic development contributions to job creation, retention, and improvement.3

1 The OCC is the primary CRA examiner for national banks and federal savings associations and implements the CRA
through 12 CFR part 25. The FDIC has CRA examination authority over certain state-regulated financial institutions
and implements the CRA through 12 CFR part 345.
2 SBICs, administered by the U.S. Small Business Administration ("SBA"), are highly regulated private funds that invest
exclusively in domestic small businesses, which by statutory mission provide capital that is otherwise unavailable or in
short supply to small businesses. Small Business Investment Act of 1958, Pub. L. 85-699 (Aug. 21, 1958). 15 U.S.C.
661. The U.S. Department of Agriculture ("USDA") operates the RBIC program, a developmental venture capital
program for the purpose of promoting economic development and the creation of wealth and job opportunities in non-
metropolitan areas and among residents living in those areas. Like the SBA, the USDA licenses investment fund
applicants to address the unmet capital needs of small enterprises primarily located in rural areas. The RBIC program
does not offer its licensees federally guaranteed capital access like the SBIC program.
3 15 USC 661 ("It is declared to be the policy of the Congress and the purpose of this Act [Small Business Investment
Act of 1958] to improve and stimulate the national economy in general and the small-business segment thereof in
particular by establishing a program to stimulate and supplement the flow of private equity capital and long-term loan
funds which small-business concerns need for the sound financing of their business operations and for their growth,
expansion, and modernization, and which are not available in adequate supply: Provided, however, That this policy shall
be carried out in such manner as to insure the maximum participation of private financing sources.")


2 | P a g e

529 14th St., N.W. Washington, DC 20045 (202) 628-5055 sbia.org


SBIA supports the Proposal's express recognition of SBIC and RBIC investments as qualifying
economic development activities under the CRA.4 We also acknowledge that this law is not an
organic statute for the SBIC or RBIC programs and that the CRA is not the sole economic basis on
which banks evaluate investments in these funds.5 Certain potential indirect effects from the
Proposal, however, could alter the calculus among certain small and intermediate-sized banks from
making new investments or growing their existing SBIC or RBIC investment portfolios.

The final rule should preserve strong CRA incentives for both direct lending and long-term private-
capital investment through these federal programs.


I.
Direct Effects that Support Bank Investments in SBICs/RBICs

a.
SBIC and RBIC Investments are Economic Development

Regulators are unambiguous in the Proposal that bank investments in SBICs and RBICs will qualify
for CRA consideration because those investments are considered economic development
undertaken consistent with the rules governing these particular federal programs.6 Regulators
explain that this proposed express presumption will "provide greater clarity and encourage the
continued participation in, and support of, programs offered through these providers of small
business... financing".7

SBIA strongly endorses this alignment and recommends that the final rule include an additional
express statement clarifying that a bank's investment in an SBA-licensed SBIC or RBIC qualifies
under the "government programs" category and does not require portfolio-by-portfolio satisfaction
of paragraph (3)(i). The proposed rulemaking defines bank activities presumptively eligible for
CRA credit as "economic development" if they fall within one or more of three categories.8 The
"government programs" category described above is one.

7 USC 2009cc-1 ("The purposes of the Rural Business Investment Program established under this subchapter are ... to
promote economic development and the creation of wealth and job opportunities in rural areas and among individuals
living in those areas by encouraging developmental capital investments in smaller enterprises primarily located in rural
areas....").
4 Except where the context requires a program-specific distinction, SBIA's recommendations herein apply equally to
SBA-licensed SBICs and USDA-licensed RBICs.
5 Banks expect to earn investment returns and evaluate SBIC and RBIC commitments under ordinary risk, return, capital,
liquidity, diversification, and strategic criteria. CRA operates as a separate but complementary regulatory incentive that
can influence a bank's decision whether to invest, the amount committed, and the types or geographic strategies
considered.
6 CRA Rulemaking, 91 Fed. Reg. 52131, 52134 (August 12, 2026). "Economic development" is one of four broad
categories of activities comprising the definition of "community development" under which a bank is evaluated for CRA
credit. Regulators explain that the current definition of "Community Development" does not include stand-alone criteria
for economic development aligned with particular federal, state local or tribal programs, but note these activities have
long been considered as such under the Interagency Questions and Answers at Q&As §§ll__.12(g)(4)(i)—1 and
__.12(g)(3)—1.
7 Id. ("The agencies believe that aligning economic development activities with government programs that address
identified needs for small businesses and small farms would encourage coordination amongst banks, government
agencies, and other program participants for activities that can be highly responsive to the unmet needs of communities.").
8 91 FedReg 52202 (August 12, 2026) (Sec. 345.12 (Definitions) "Community Development" at (3) Economic
Development (i)-(iii)).


3 | P a g e

529 14th St., N.W. Washington, DC 20045 (202) 628-5055 sbia.org


SBIA also endorses the separate "size standard" category because it permits CRA consideration for
bank financings in small businesses that meet the size requirements of the SBIC program or that
have gross revenues of $1 million or less and that are not otherwise served under the "government
programs" category.9 The "size standard" category at (3)(i), however, excludes financing
"primarily used for ongoing operating liquidity." If regulators or examiners applied that phrase
through to underlying SBIC financings, then working-capital loans could be impaired.

We believe that a reasonable reading of the separate "government programs" category at (3)(iii)
protects the bank's investment in an SBIC without regard to whether any particular financing made
by a fund would independently qualify under paragraph (3)(i), provided applicable SBA and USDA
statutes and regulations permit the financing.10 But the rule should say so expressly.

(b)
Proposal Should Protect Full Suite of Investment Opportunities in SBICs/RBICs

While the Proposal expressly protects investments in these funds, it does not clearly grant a
presumption for bank loans or investments made alongside them through a syndicate led by an
SBIC or RBIC or in a co-investment vehicle associated with these funds.

SBIA recommends that federal regulators amend the Proposal by adding a limited safe harbor for a
bank financing made as part of the same integrated transaction as financing by a licensed SBIC or RBIC.
The safe harbor should apply: (i) where the portfolio company satisfies the applicable program
eligibility standards when the bank becomes legally committed, (ii) the licensed fund participates
directly in the transaction, (iii) the financings support the same or complementary business purpose, and
(iv) the licensed fund documents the portfolio company's eligibility.

Adopting this safe harbor treatment would expand private capital alongside federally licensed funds
without extending the presumption to unrelated or later transactions having only an attenuated
connection to the licensed program.

SBIA also recommends that the Regulators clarify that the size of the business will be measured at
the time that the bank makes an initial funding contribution or binding commitment to invest, which
is similar to how SBICs comply with the SBA's size eligibility rules.11 Banks, otherwise, could
potentially lose CRA credit qualification by helping small businesses grow, a result contrary to the
goals of CRA.

We commend the Regulators for making clear with express regulatory language that SBICs/RBICs
are presumptively "economic development" and therefore qualify for CRA credit. SBIA
encourages the FDIC and OCC to consider making these additional changes to the Proposal because
they would help ensure that a bank's qualifying investment in an SBIC or RBIC is not disqualified or
artificially reduced merely because particular portfolio financings would not independently qualify
under a different "economic development" pathway.


9 91 Fed Reg at 52133. (August 12, 2026).
10 This clarification would not displace generally applicable requirements in the Proposal that might apply to the activity's
primary purpose, geographic attribution, documentation, or evaluation under the applicable performance test.
11 See 91 Fed Reg 52138. (August 12, 2026) Sec.___.13c would recognize reliance interests, codify the existing
practice to qualify CD activities at the time the activities are conducted.


4 | P a g e

529 14th St., N.W. Washington, DC 20045 (202) 628-5055 sbia.org

II.
Indirect Effects that Could Alter Certain Bank LP Incentives

SBIA acknowledges that the primary statutory purpose that underpins the CRA is to ensure that
federally regulated financial institutions meet the credit needs of the communities from where they
take deposits, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. Those credit needs generally
revolve around retail lending for home mortgages and small business needs.

Federal regulators concentrate this Proposal on streamlining retail lending metrics and revising
formulas and tests used to evaluate a financial institution's lending performance against this
statutory purpose. While community development investments by financial institutions are a
material component, we acknowledge that retail lending is a far more expansive component of the
CRA evaluation process.

The FDIC and OCC recommend revisions to asset thresholds that define small banks (below $1
billion in assets), intermediate banks ($1 billion to $10 billion) and large banks (more than $10
billion in assets). Because of the Proposal's streamlining effects there would be more small and
intermediate-sized financial institutions with total assets below $10 billion subject to fewer CRA
requirements. Regulators also recommend an evaluation realignment to focus on major product
lines (e.g., consumer, home mortgage, small business, and small farm loans) under the Retail
Lending test used to evaluate a financial institution's CRA credit eligibility.

SBIA takes no position on the Proposal's streamlining recommendations, but we warn that these
changes may trigger potential indirect effects that could alter the economic calculus among certain
small and intermediate-sized banks from making new investments in SBICs/RBICs or growing
their existing investment portfolios in these funds.

(a) Higher Bank Asset Thresholds May Discourage Bank Investment in SBICS/RBICs

The Proposal is positive because it expressly confirms that investments in licensed SBICs and
RBICs fall within the "government programs" category of economic development. This reduces
uncertainty concerning threshold eligibility for CRA consideration. The proposed realignment of
bank asset thresholds, however, may reduce the marginal CRA value of SBIC and RBIC
investments for certain community and regional banks.

Banks that move from the large-bank framework to the intermediate-bank framework would no
longer be evaluated under a separate investment test, although qualifying investments may continue
to receive consideration under the Community Development (CD) test. The practical concern is not
that such investments become irrelevant, but that they may become less important to the bank's
overall CRA result.

Based on the role CRA treatment plays in some banks' fund-allocation decisions, SBIA is
concerned that reducing the distinct rating significance of qualified investments could affect
whether some community and regional banks make commitments, the amounts committed, and the
range of strategies considered.

The final rule should confirm that qualifying SBIC and RBIC investments: (i) receive meaningful
consideration under the Community Development test for intermediate-sized banks and, (ii) for
small banks, may enhance the determination whether otherwise satisfactory lending performance


5 | P a g e

529 14th St., N.W. Washington, DC 20045 (202) 628-5055 sbia.org

warrants an overall outstanding rating. The agencies should also clarify that these investments may
be treated as particularly beneficial when they demonstrably address identified shortages of long-
term capital for qualifying small businesses or rural enterprises.

(b) Potential Impact from Retail Lending Test Changes

Regulators would evaluate only major retail lending product lines of banks under the Proposal. It
would also allow certain small-business or small-farm loans that are not evaluated as retail major-
product-line loans to qualify as community development loans if they otherwise meet the CD
definition.


SBIA anticipates that large banks will continue to pursue CRA-qualified investments, including
SBIC/RBIC investments. But many community and regional banks may have less regulatory
need to make CRA investments because the Proposal places greater emphasis on retail lending
performance and reduces or eliminates certain community development requirements for smaller
institutions. That dynamic could indirectly reduce capital flowing into these funds from some bank
limited partners (LPs).

Direct lending and long-term fund investment are complementary channels, and the regulatory
framework should not inadvertently privilege one channel merely because its contribution is easier
to measure. The final framework should, therefore, avoid assigning such dominant rating
significance to major retail lending product lines that qualifying long-term fund investments
become immaterial to the rating outcome.


III.
Support Flexible Treatment for Geographic Allocation of Community Development
Investment Dollars

The Proposal provides greater structure for considering qualifying activities outside a bank's
assessment areas, but its practical effect on SBIC and RBIC fundraising will depend on how the
agencies implement the applicable geographic-flexibility standards.12

The framework may improve predictability for some diversified funds while continuing to
disadvantage funds whose investment geography does not align with a prospective bank LP's
assessment area or identified local needs.

SBIA stipulates that it is outside our scope to comment on the specific recommendations and
quantitative metrics proposed to designate assessment areas or measure retail lending by banks for
CRA purposes. We urge Regulators, nevertheless, to extend a "flexible" approach to a bank's
community development investment activities because these represent long-term deployments of
capital into small businesses that can extend for years depending on the investment lifecycle of the

12 91 Fed Reg 52140-41 (August 12, 2026). The Proposal presents two alternatives for determining when a bank may
receive consideration, at the state, multistate-MSA, or institution level, for qualifying community development activities
outside its assessment areas: Option 1 uses specified quantitative thresholds, subject to a performance-context exception;
Option 2 uses a qualitative assessment of the amount and responsiveness of the bank's assessment-area community-
development activities. See Proposal at Sec. ___.13.



6 | P a g e

529 14th St., N.W. Washington, DC 20045 (202) 628-5055 sbia.org

fund. A bank's capital commitment into an investment fund will stretch well beyond the initial
year of the commitment because unlike a retail loan, fund investment lifecycles are multi-year
processes.

For CRA credit purposes, this distinction means that a bank's commitment of capital into a fund
will not equate with the geographic location of its final deployment into a particular small business.
Many funds also reserve a material portion of committed capital for follow-on investments that
may occur years after the initial portfolio investment. For CRA credit purposes, geography becomes
progressively knowable as investments are made.

A reasonable initial allocation should not result in retroactive loss of consideration merely because
actual deployment later differs provided the bank updates the allocation with CRA examiners and
does not count the same activity twice. SBIA urges Regulators to permit banks to document and
allocate their initial capital commitments for community development investments during a
particular CRA examination period and then to update those allocations prospectively with
geographic details as the fund deploys capital into particular small businesses.

To the extent the Regulators adopt a "substantially met" standard in response to Question 34, SBIA
recommends that CRA examiners apply it through a reasonable, performance-context-based
analysis that considers the availability of qualifying local opportunities, the responsiveness of the
bank's existing activities, the multiyear deployment cycle of fund investments, and the bank's use
of a reasonable and consistently applied allocation methodology.13


IV.
Interagency Parity in CRA Regulations and Examinations

The FDIC, OCC, and the Federal Reserve Board (Board) together are the CRA supervisory
agencies, but this Proposal is issued by and would amend only the OCC and FDIC regulations.
Unless the Board acts separately or joins a CRA final rule, Federal Reserve-supervised banks will
remain under the legacy framework and Interagency Q&A treatment.

While a unified rulemaking by the CRA supervisory agencies is ideal, at minimum, SBIA requests
that the OCC and FDIC coordinate with the Board to ensure consistent treatment in CRA
examinations of identical SBIC/RBIC investments.

* * *

SBIA supports the Proposal's express recognition of investments in SBICs and RBICs as qualifying
"economic development" activities. To ensure that this recognition produces meaningful and
administrable results, increases certainty for bank investors and licensed fund managers, and
preserves the CRA's focus on community credit needs, the final rule should:

13 See 91 Fed Reg 52141-52143(August 12, 2026). Evaluation of Proposal at Sec. ___.27 (Question 34 - "If the rules
were to permit banks to receive consideration for CD activities outside of assessment areas in States, multistate MSAs,
or at the bank level without requiring that the bank meet or exceed the geographic flexibility standard(s) in all assessment
areas, in determining when consideration would be permitted outside assessment areas, should the agencies rely on the
''substantially met'' standard in proposed §ll.27 or should another standard apply?").


7 | P a g e

529 14th St., N.W. Washington, DC 20045 (202) 628-5055 sbia.org

•
confirm that an otherwise qualifying investment in a licensed SBIC or RBIC satisfies the
"economic development" purpose under paragraph (3)(iii) without portfolio-company
look-through under paragraph (3)(i);
•
establish clear and appropriately limited treatment for integrated financings alongside
licensed funds;
•
preserve meaningful CRA consideration of SBIC and RBIC investments under the
standards applicable to small and intermediate banks;
•
accommodate the multiyear deployment and geographic characteristics of SBICs/RBICs
through reasonable allocation methodologies; and
•
promote materially consistent treatment of CRA consideration across the federal banking
regulators.
SBIA appreciates the invitation to discuss these issues and looks forward to the opportunity to work
together to ensure America's small businesses have access to the capital they need.

Sincerely,

Brett Palmer
SBIA President
