comments.text:
COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Please find attached comment letter regarding - Notice of Proposed Rulemaking – Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; Docket ID OCC-2026-0694 and RIN 1557-AF57

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0194_09000064b9659c7f.pdf:
October 9, 2026


Chief Counsel's Office


Jennifer M. Jones, Deputy Executive Secretary
Attention: Comment Processing

Attention: Comments RIN 3064-AG31
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
400 7th Street, SW, Suite 1E-216

550 17th Street NW
Washington, DC 20219


Washington, DC 20429


Regarding: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking – Community Reinvestment Act
Regulations; Docket ID OCC-2026-0694 and RIN 1557-AF57, and FDIC RIN 3064-
AG31


Dear Federal Banking Regulators:

The Community Bankers Association of Illinois ("CBAI"), which proudly represents nearly 250
Illinois community banks, appreciates the opportunity to provide our observations and
recommendations regarding the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (jointly "Regulators") Community
Reinvestment Act regulations ("CRA" or "Act") notice of proposed rulemaking ("Proposal").
CBAI acknowledges that the Regulators "are proposing to amend their Community
Reinvestment Act rules by making certain substantive, technical, and process-oriented changes
to refocus the statutory objective of encouraging banks to meet the credit needs of their
communities; to better ensure that community development grants reach the communities that
they are intended to benefit; to reduce the unnecessary burden, particularly on community

CBAI is dedicated to exclusively representing the interests of Illinois community banks and thrifts through effective
advocacy, outstanding education, and high-quality products. CBAI's members hold more than $75 billion in assets,
operate 860 locations statewide, and lend to consumers, small businesses, and agriculture. For more information, please
visit www.cbai.com.
 OCC and FDIC - CRA
October 9, 2026
Page 2


banks; and to provide greater clarity for how to obtain CRA consideration."

Introduction

CBAI and its member community bankers support the CRA, which was enacted by Congress in
1977 and is intended to encourage depository institutions to meet the needs of the communities
in which they operate, including low- and moderate-income ("LMI") neighborhoods, consistent
with the safe and sound operation of such institutions. The CRA requires that each insured
depository institution's record in helping meet the needs of its entire community is evaluated
periodically. That record is taken into account in considering an institution's application for
deposit facilities, including mergers and acquisitions. CRA examinations are conducted by the
banking regulators that are responsible for supervising their depository institutions, which are,
for the purposes of this comment letter, the OCC and the FDIC.

Community banks perform exceptionally well in CRA compliance and examinations precisely
because the mission of community banks is to fairly serve all their customers and communities.
Our members continue to tell us that the community reinvestment makes good business sense
and benefits everyone.

Joint Rulemaking

CBAI welcomes rulemaking which helps to revise and modernize the CRA. Prior rulemaking
efforts to accomplish these objectives included a 2018 advance notice of proposed rulemaking, a
2019 proposed rulemaking, a 2020 finalized rule, a 2021 rescission of that rule, a 2022 notice of
proposed rulemaking, a 2023 final rule, and subsequent litigation which has resulted in the
rescission of that rule. This unfortunate and frustrating whipsawing in the rulemaking process
imposes an unreasonable and unnecessary regulatory burden on banks which are subject to the
CRA. This burden falls particularly hard on the nation's community banks and undermines the
spirit of the Regulators' own EGRPRA process with its legal mandate to identify and eliminate
unnecessary or unduly burdensome regulations.

CBAI believes constructive interagency dialogue, collaboration and productive cooperation
between all of the regulators and the banking industry are the surest path to meaningful, lasting
and beneficial changes. CBAI encourages the Regulators to engage in joint rulemaking and agree
on a reasonable final rule to revise and modernize the CRA.
 OCC and FDIC - CRA
October 9, 2026
Page 3


Safety and Soundness

The CRA requires community banks to help meet the credit needs of the communities they serve,
including LMI areas, consistent with the bank's safe and sound operations. Operating in a safe
and sound manner is a prudent business practice and a regulatory requirement, the lack of which
is cause for regulator criticism and even enforcement actions.

The creditworthiness and responsible behavior of borrowers and account holders are several of
the keys to safety and soundness – without them, financial services cannot be provided.
Regulations and examinations for compliance with the CRA must never lose sight of or
compromise community banks' ability to operate in a safe and sound manner in all aspects of
compliance with the CRA. CBAI appreciates the Regulators continuing to emphasize the need
for safety and soundness and continuing to support and reinforce this requirement, which must
not be minimized or lost in the modernization of the CRA.

Overwhelmingly Positive Exam Results

CBAI questions the belief held by some that, because more than 95% of banks receive
Satisfactory or Outstanding CRA ratings, the Act is flawed. The overwhelming majority of
banks are community banks that treat their customers and communities fairly and do not
discriminate. The fact that the overwhelming majority of banks perform well in CRA compliance
and examinations affirms the exemplary behavior of community banks. CBAI urges caution
when some proponents of revision and modernization urge that the regulatory framework be
strengthened, because this belief will advance a misperception about what this Act should
accomplish. There is no reason to make the regulatory compliance requirements more rigorous or
burdensome, or the examination process more difficult or complicated, for all community banks.

All Financial Service Providers Must Comply with the CRA

Credit unions are not currently subject to the CRA because they are not defined as "covered
institutions" in the regulations. The revision and modernization of the CRA is a historic
opportunity for the Regulators to help level an unlevel playing field by formally advocating for
the expansion of the CRA requirements to include all credit unions.

Policymakers who support the CRA should be concerned that credit unions are not subject to this
 OCC and FDIC - CRA
October 9, 2026
Page 4


Act and be alarmed by the increasing number of credit unions purchasing community banks
which are subject to the CRA. The number of credit union acquisitions of community banks has
dramatically increased in recent years, so these are not infrequent occurrences and should
command policymakers' attention.

These acquisitions by credit unions result in the loss of much sought-after data regarding a large
and growing sector of the financial services industry's performance in serving their communities,
including low- and moderate-income borrowers and communities, and in fair lending. The credit
unions industry's response to their members not needing to be considered "covered institutions"
is that it is their "mission" to serve individuals of modest means and with a common bond. That
excuse is ridiculous given the industry's expansionist agenda, meaningless common bond
requirements, marketing to higher-income individuals and communities, building of lavish
headquarters, generous executive compensation packages, commercial sports
sponsorships/alliances, and stadium naming rights.

CBAI acknowledges that Congress must act to include other financial service providers,
including credit unions, Farm Credit Services, fintechs, digital asset providers and others for
compliance with the CRA in a comparable manner to community banks. CBAI strongly believes
that all financial service providers that offer the same products and services as community banks
be subject to the CRA and urges the Regulators to strongly advocate to Congress for this
required legislative change. The obvious regulatory double standard reveals a narrower picture of
compliance with the CRA within the broader financial services industry and is harming the
safety and soundness of the community banks that the Regulators are responsible for regulating.


Specific Observations and Recommendations

Targeted Revisions Versus Complete Overhaul

Notwithstanding the comments made above regarding the need for joint rulemaking to reduce the
regulatory burden on community banks, CBAI appreciates that in this rulemaking the Regulators
are proposing "targeted changes to their regulations implementing the [CRA]." Further, "[T]hese
targeted changes are designed to retain key elements of the current regulator framework to
provide continuity and minimize disruptions while making revisions to accomplish the goals

 OCC and FDIC - CRA
October 9, 2026
Page 5


[stated in the Proposal]." CBAI believes this targeted approach is more productive than
significantly broader revisions to the Act.

The Proposal would define a "small bank" as having less than $1 billion in assets, an
"intermediate bank" as having at least $1 billion but less than $10 billion, and a "large bank" as
having more than $10 billion in assets. These proposed asset thresholds are higher than the
current thresholds and eliminate the complex and confusing intermediate small bank category.
At these proposed thresholds, 85.5% of CBAI members would be included in the small bank
category, 14.5% in the intermediate category, and none would be considered a large bank. CBAI
supports these increases in asset thresholds, with the qualification below.

In the request for comments, the Regulators asked if the thresholds should be increased even
further. CBAI encourages the Regulators to raise the small bank threshold to $10 billion in
assets, which would currently cover all CBAI's community bank members. All of our members
are true community banks, and all of them would be relieved of unnecessary regulatory burden
from a higher CRA asset threshold. CBAI further encourages the Regulators to index the asset
thresholds to a reasonable, well-known and respected index and to keep these asset thresholds
current and not needing to be revisited after they have become outdated.

Community Development ("CD") Activities, Definitions and Consideration

CBAI understands that no small banks will be subject to the CD test, which would currently
exempt 85.5% of our members and only be subject to a tailored retail lending test. The remaining
14.5% of our members will have both a tailored retail lending test as well as a tailored CD test.

CBAI supports the objective in the Proposal to revise definitions of CD activities, including CD
loans, qualifying investments and CD services to improve consistency and clarity and in
particular to provide certainty in determining if a CD activity will qualify for CRA credit.

CBAI appreciates the Regulators' revisions to the Act that would focus qualifying activities that
would most support providing credit and services to low- and moderate-income communities and
individuals and ensuring that the intended benefit of those dollars is not unnecessarily consumed
by excessive administrative expenses. Notwithstanding the benefit of efficiency and singularity
of focus, CBAI encourages the Regulators to consider other worthy activities for full or partial
CRA credit within the Proposal, which will be discussed later in this comment letter.
 OCC and FDIC - CRA
October 9, 2026
Page 6


CBAI is in general agreement with the proposed evaluation criteria, which is to be limited to
those lending and related services which are within the geographic footprint of the bank and
concerning major product lines, versus including deposit-taking geographies and non-major
lending products. This limitation is more consistent with the community bank business model of
serving their local communities, even for larger community banks.

However, CBAI encourages the Regulators to take a broader approach for all community banks
to permit their ability to include additional geographies and services for full or partial CRA
credit if the bank is willing to expend the resources to track and report the positive benefit for
low- and moderate-income individuals and communities. There are also opportunities for banks
to support worthy organizations that have a proven track record of directly or indirectly
supporting housing, affordable housing, workforce development and community development
that find it difficult to precisely track that support to the specific census track or project that will
be positively impacted which should also be eligible to receive full or partial CRA credit. Please
refer to the examples we have provided later in this comment letter concerning the Federal Home
Loan Banks and the Homebuilders Institute.

Grants

Similar to CBAI issues above regarding CD activities, definitions and considerations, CBAI is
concerned about the potential unintended consequence of the expense percentage threshold
restrictions for CRA credit for grants and contributions. CBAI agrees with the goal of the
restriction, which is to ensure that this support benefits the initiatives to which they are directed
and is not spent on unnecessary overhead expenses, but there are differences between types of
organizations that benefit low-and moderate-income communities and individuals that will make
this one-size-fits-all threshold result in unintended negative consequences. Instead, CBAI
encourages the Regulators to adopt a more tailored approach based on the nature, reach and
benefit these organizations provide to low- and moderate-income individuals and communities.
Again, please refer to the examples we have provided later in this comment letter concerning the
Federal Home Loan Banks and the Homebuilders Institute.

Data Collection, Reporting and Disclosure

Complex regulatory data collection and reporting is a burden that falls particularly hard on

 OCC and FDIC - CRA
October 9, 2026
Page 7


community banks that have fewer staff to handle these requirements. CBAI completely supports
the Proposal's exemption for complex CRA data collection, maintenance and reporting
requirements for banks under $10 billion in assets (i.e., small and intermediate banks), which (for
now) will cover all of CBAI's nearly 250 members. With the implementation of the Dodd-Frank
Act's Section 1071 Final Rule, CBAI supports the Regulators' leveraging Section 1071 data to
discontinue duplicative CRA small business data collection and reporting requirements. CBAI
also supports the Regulators' ability, in rare circumstances, to not require data reporting and
recordkeeping when warranted by the facts and circumstances, which will provide additional
targeted relief to banks.

Public File & Public Notice

CBAI agrees that technology advances and its widespread adoption and availability enable and
necessitates modernizing the delivery of the Public CRA File and Public Notices. CBAI supports
banks' placing and maintaining the required Public File and Public Notices on their websites,
which will make that information available to anyone, everywhere and at no cost.

Concerning any delay in making the CRA Public File available to the public, CBAI has concerns
regarding unreasonable delays in the determining and revealing of a bank's most recent
performance evaluation. Our concern is rooted in the four-and-one-half year delay in the public
release of Wells Fargo's CRA performance evaluation (from the anticipated mid-to-late 2013 to
March of 2017.) The delay occurred while Wells was navigating its consumer abuse and fake-
account scandals. When Wells' CRA evaluation was finally released, it revealed an
extraordinarily rare double-downgrade to Needs to Improve.

While CBAI appreciates the need for a bank to rightfully challenge a CRA evaluation and rating
that it disagrees with, and for there to be a reasonable appeals process, whatever happened that
caused the extraordinary delay in the publication of Wells Fargo's CRA results and rating was
completely unacceptable and cannot be allowed to happen again.

Qualifying Activities Confirmation and Illustrative List of Activities

The current way of determining eligibility for qualifying activities (community development and
service, and any other), particularly for those that are more complex or innovative, and where the
banks might not know if the activity will even qualify for CRA credit, is the unfortunate and
 OCC and FDIC - CRA
October 9, 2026
Page 8


flawed situation with the current CRA. CBAI supports a non-exhaustive, illustrative list of
qualifying activities and timely confirmation of eligibility for determining if an activity does
qualify (or does not) for CRA credit. Compiling this list should be a joint Regulator
responsibility, and there should be no differences between individual Regulators' approvals or
denials for similar opportunities. In addition, this list should be readily available on each of the
Regulators' websites and updated regularly.

The process for confirming the eligibility should be standardized and reasonable for bank staff to
accomplish. The staff members tasked with this responsibility will generally be knowledgeable
about the CRA and the activity for which they are seeking credit, but they should not have to be
regulatory experts or attorneys to draft and submit a proposal for consideration. The response by
the Regulators should be encouraging and timely (within 30 days of submission), the final
decision should be reasonable, and there should be a thorough explanation for the reason for any
denial.

The Regulators should adopt a transparent procedure for processing these applications with the
goal of finding a reasonable path to approval for eligibility and there should be a secondary
review of denied applications – so that no reasonable opportunities are missed. In addition to that
procedure, the Regulators should institute a timely and independent appeal process for denied
applications.

CBAI sees no reason to limit the submission of applications to banks and urges the Regulators to
permit banking trade associations, on behalf of their members, to be eligible to submit a potential
qualifying activity or service for consideration and approval.

Support for the Federal Home Loan Banks

As an example of a community development activity that should be considered and approved for
CRA credit, CBAI renews its recommendation that credit be earned for membership in and all
activity with banks within the Federal Home Loan Bank System (collectively "FHLBanks"). A
qualifier to earning this CRA credit would be that the member bank must otherwise earn a
Satisfactory or above CRA rating for it to be eligible for the additional credit.

The Federal Home Loan Bank System ("FHLBSystem") and its individual banks are
government-sponsored entities that were created by Congress in 1932 with a mission to provide
reliable sources of funding for housing finance and community investment. The FHLBSystem
 OCC and FDIC - CRA
October 9, 2026
Page 9


contains 11 districts. The FHLB-Chicago serves Illinois and Wisconsin, and its membership
includes approximately 401 banks and 54 thrifts.

The FHLBanks' membership nexus is a commitment to housing and helping to realize the dream
of home ownership. The FHLBanks provide asset liability management, liquidity for members'
short-term needs, technical assistance, and access to special affordable housing and community
development programs – all of which support the mission of the FHLBanks. It is essential to note
that the FHLBanks are required to contribute 10% of their income before assessments to
affordable housing and community development within their districts and that many of the banks
exceed that minimum threshold.

Currently, members may receive CRA credit for specific activities conducted with their
FHLBank. These activities typically include mortgage lending through the Mortgage Partnership
Finance and Mortgage Purchase ("MPF" and "MPP") programs, letters of credit – the
beneficiaries of which can be local municipalities, and participation in affordable housing
("AHP") and community investment ("CIP") programs.

An expansion of CRA credit will require a broader interpretation of the primary purpose of the
FHLBanks' activities, which serve the needs of its members and are not exclusively focused on
affordable housing and community development. Nonetheless, CBAI strongly believes a broader
interpretation is warranted, and banks should receive CRA credit for membership and all activity
in their FHLBanks.

By simply belonging to their FHLBank, members must purchase capital stock, the proceeds of
which, together with retained earnings, are invested by the FHLBanks to generate profits, 10% of
which is contributed to AHP and CIP. To the extent members use any of the FHLBank products,
such as advances, letters of credit or the MPF/MPP, they are also helping to generate income for
the FHLBanks, and 10% of that profitability also goes towards housing and investment
programs. Finally, community bank members may use any of the FHLBs' affordable housing,
down payment assistance, or community development programs to help their customers and
communities.

It is inconceivable, for example, that a bank's involvement with a small community development
provider, which would qualify under the primary purpose requirement and produces
$1,000 of community development benefit, would receive CRA credit; but that same bank's
FHLBank membership and activities that collectively contribute billions of dollars in benefits to
hundreds of thousands of individuals do not qualify simply because a narrow primary purpose
requirement was not met by the FHLBanks.
 OCC and FDIC - CRA
October 9, 2026
Page 10


The FHLBanks' AHP contributions are among the largest private sources of funding for
affordable housing activities in the United States. From the inception of the AHP program, the
FHLBanks have awarded $9.6 billion for the acquisition, development or preservation of over
1,157,800 units of affordable owner-occupied and rental housing.

CBAI recommends a formula of the capital stock percent owned by the member of their
FHLBank multiplied by the annual AHP contribution of their FHLBank to equal the dollar
amount of CRA credit for that FHLBank member.

The enormous positive impact of the FHLBanks (in either a bank's area, community or in the
broader state or region [FHLBank district]), and contributions to these beneficial programs are so
significant, and made possible by all of the FHLBanks' members, that CBAI urges a broader
interpretation of primary purpose so that banks may receive CRA credit for membership and all
activity with their FHLBanks.

Support for the Home Builders Institute

The shortage of housing and affordable housing is a widely recognized national problem that has
been estimated by the National Association of Home Builders ("NAHB") at approximately 1.2
million units, while the National Association of Realtors has estimated the shortage at 4 million
units. The lack of affordable and available rental homes has been estimated by the National Low
Income Housing Coalition at approximately 7.2 million units. This housing deficit is expected to
continue to grow unless the underlying issues that are causing this problem are successfully
addressed.

One of the issues that is responsible for this gap in housing and affordable housing and rental
homes is the lack of qualified construction workers. This shortage has been estimated by NAHB
at 300,000 individuals.

This gap in housing was addressed in the President's Executive Order ("EO") 14394, which was
signed on March 13, 2026, and titled "Removing Regulatory Barriers to Affordable Home
Construction." The EO seeks to support the dream of American homeownership and states that
"it is the policy of my Administration to reduce regulatory barriers to building homes." While the
EO directly targets barriers like the "slow permitting processes and onerous mandates,"
achieving the broader housing goal will need to be preceded by addressing tangential issues, and

 OCC and FDIC - CRA
October 9, 2026
Page 11


here is where earning CRA credit specifically for workforce development can play an important
role.

CBAI believes that an opportunity exists to support the goal of the President's EO by grants or
contributions to organizations like the Home Builders Institute ("HBI"), which is a national
leader in workforce development by providing trade skills training and education for the
residential construction industry. The HBI was founded in l983 and is a 501(c) (3) non-profit and
is the result of a consolidation of the educational and manpower training arms of the NAHB.

The HBI delivers tuition-free, high-quality pre-apprenticeship trades training, job placement and
recognized credentials and acts as a bridge between supplying job-ready talent to the residential
construction sector. The essential hands-on skills training includes fields like carpentry,
electrical, plumbing and HVAC. HBI operates in major cities, including Orlando, New Orleans,
Houston, Phoenix, Charlotte, Sacramento and San Juan, Puerto Rico.

The HBI relies on federal and state government funding and also partners with corporate
sponsors, local homebuilders' associations, and foundations. The opportunity for banks to earn
CRA credit for grants and contributions to HBI could be a catalyst for its training efforts by
upscaling their BuildStrong Academies.

The challenge of approving CRA credit for banks will be likely be in the limitations within the
requirements of the existing and proposed revisions to the CRA, which are the primary purpose
requirement/direct use, being able to specifically link to benefit to a banks assessment area, and
perhaps even the threshold restriction for operating expenses for an organization with this
national scope of operations. Because grants and contributions to the HBI align perfectly with
not only the underlying goals of the CRA but also helping to solve the serious gap that exists in
the availability and affordability of housing and rental units, a broader interpretation of the
primary purpose needed and is completely justified.

CBAI urges the Regulators to determine that grants and contributions to specialized workforce
training entities inherently have a primary community development purpose, the overhead
thresholds and geographic tracking barriers for well-run and nationally recognized construction
trade development organizations should be waived if necessary, and that banks should receive
either full or partial CRA credit for these types of grants or contributions.

 OCC and FDIC - CRA
October 9, 2026
Page 12


Summary and Conclusion

CBAI strongly encourages the Regulators to consider these observations and recommendations
in joint rulemaking. This is a historic opportunity to revise and modernize the CRA in a manner
that makes it relevant and properly focused now, and in the future, without increasing the
regulatory burden on community banks in recognition of their exemplary performance in serving
their customers and communities – fairly and honestly. It has been proven repeatedly that
community reinvestment is what community banks do best. It is their mission, and it is
paramount to their ability to thrive and survive, so the first goal of Regulators should be to do no
harm to community banks while revising and modernizing a clearly outdated CRA.

Thank you for considering our observations and recommendations on the modernization of the
CRA. If you have any questions or require any additional information, please contact me at
davids@cbai.com or (847) 909-8341.


Sincerely,

/s/

David Schroeder
Senior Vice President
Federal Governmental Relations

comments.name: Shams Gannon Architecture (Chris Gannon, Principal)
comments.type_basis: Signed by the principal of a small architecture firm that works on affordable and missing middle housing developments.
comments.overall_quote: Preserve CRA Funding for Affordable Housing
comments.summary: An Austin architecture principal who works on affordable housing says bank financing is essential to projects like a 25-unit community land trust. The firm asks the agencies to keep CRA's focus on low- and moderate-income communities, protect grants and investments, reconsider the asset thresholds, and weigh the costs to communities, not just to banks.
key_asks: Reconsider the proposed asset-size thresholds before more banks get less comprehensive CRA scrutiny.
Avoid restrictions that reduce nonprofit access to CRA-supported grants, and recognize that reasonable administrative and operating expenses are necessary.

Community Reinvestment Act





Community Reinvestment Act Regulations;
OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694

Architect
Shams Gannon Architecture

641 Tillery St. #210, Austin TX 78702




Preserve CRA Funding for Affordable Housing

As principal of a small architecture practice focused on
missing middle and affordable housing developments,
it's essential that our clients can secure the funding
necessary for these vital developments. Our firm is
currently working on a 25 unit community land trust
that would not have been possible without bank
financing.



Community Reinvestment Act



1. Preserve CRA's focus on low- and moderate-income communities.
CRA should continue to provide meaningful incentives for banks to serve communities that have historically
faced barriers to credit and investment.
2. Protect the full range of community development activities.
The agencies should not create incentives that favor lending at the expense of grants, investments, community
development financing, and other activities that are essential to affordable housing.
3. Oppose restrictions that could reduce nonprofit access to CRA-supported grants.
The agencies should recognize that reasonable administrative and operating expenses are necessary to deliver
effective affordable housing and community development programs.
4. Maintain strong incentives for affordable housing development and preservation.
CRA should encourage banks to support new construction, rehabilitation, preservation, naturally occurring
affordable housing, multifamily housing, and other activities serving low- and moderate-income households.
5. Carefully reconsider the proposed asset-size thresholds.
Before expanding the number of banks receiving less comprehensive CRA scrutiny, the agencies should evaluate
the potential consequences for communities and affordable housing organizations that rely on those institutions
as sources of capital.
6. Ask the agencies to evaluate the real-world impact on affordable housing.
The agencies should consider not only the compliance costs imposed on banks but also the potential costs
imposed on communities if CRA incentives for affordable housing and community development decline.






















Chris Gannon, Principal





Shams Gannon, LLC

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0196_09000064b9659cf0.pdf:
October 9, 2026

Travis Hill, Chair
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
550 17th Street NW,
Washington, DC 20429
RIN 3064-AG31
Via email: comments@FDIC.gov

Jonathan V. Gould, Comptroller
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
400 7th St. SW,
Washington, DC 20219
Docket ID OCC-2026-0694
Via: https://regulations.gov/

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

The California Community Land Trust Network writes to object to the harmful
changes proposed to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was
passed by Congress in 1977 in response to redlining and creates an affirmative
obligation for banks to help meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of
communities, including low and moderate income (LMI) communities. While the
CRA has successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest and provide services in
underserved communities, challenges related to redlining, discrimination,
underinvestment, and lack of access remain.

The California Community Land Trust Network (CACLTN) is a statewide membership
organization of California community land trusts (CLTs) and allied organizations,
working to support the growth of permanently affordable, community controlled
land and housing in California. Our member organizations - including 50 established
and emerging CLTs - span California from Humboldt County to San Diego,
collectively stewarding over 1,700 permanently affordable homes housing over
3,500 Californians.




California community land trusts provide permanently affordable homeownership
and rental opportunities to low- and moderate-income residents of California, as
well as opportunities for small business, agriculture, and other community
gathering spaces. CLTs and CLT residents - like other housing and small business
providers - depend on the financial services industry to provide mortgages, as well
as financing for acquisition, rehabilitation, pre-development, and construction.
Some CLTs take advantage of Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) financing,
made possible from bank investments. Additionally, many CLTs have strong
relationships with local and regional banks, who provide EQ2 investments,
donations, grants, and event sponsorships to support the effective work of CLTs to
meet community needs.

The changes proposed will harm the communities that CLTs serve, which are the
very communities CRA was meant to uplift. The proposal does not justify those
changes or consider their expected impact on LMI communities. We request an
extension of the comment period for an additional 60 days so we have time to
better understand how much CRA activity may be lost to communities because of
this proposal – an analysis the regulators did not conduct or provide.​

The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved
communities in several ways.

1) Community development (CD) activities for affordable housing
and small businesses will drop dramatically.
As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities
that support critically needed affordable housing and economic development
projects. These activities often provide the greatest CRA impact in communities as
they strengthen economic stability and mobility, quality of life, and social health of
residents and communities.

The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large"
Banks, such that many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and
expectation to serve the community development needs of their communities.[1]
According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70
California banks would see their reinvestment obligations reduced under the
proposal. Twenty-five California banks would shed their Community Development




Test responsibilities entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer be subject to
the Investment Test.[2]

The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical
community development programs that have had large impacts in LMI
communities. These include Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) which are a
key driver of affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) which
fuel economic development projects in tribal and other areas; and EQ2 equity
equivalent investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs)
that provide small business lending in underserved areas that banks cannot reach,
and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that take property off of the speculative
market.

Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting
the critical importance of the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable
housing.[3] Approximately half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from CRA
motivated banks.[4] The regulators will even further weaken CD obligations if they
adopt the alternative proposal that Large Banks be defined as those with over $30
billion in assets.

Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance
even where they remain subject to the Community Development and Investment
Tests. The regulators signal to all banks that they can do significantly less CD
lending and investment and still pass their CRA examinations, all while seeking CRA
credit for activity outside of their CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests
that a bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1
capital were devoted to CD loans and CD investments. That percentage is far lower
than the percentage that NCRC determined banks currently devote to community
investments and loans. If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary
to meet the proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by approximately
$87.1 billion, or 85%.[5]

Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have
tremendous negative impacts on affordable housing and small business
development in our state. Asset thresholds should not be raised.




​

2) Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.
Another consequence of the proposal's drive to raise asset thresholds is that fewer
banks will be required to report data regarding their small business, small farm,
and community development lending activities. Such data is critical to
understanding not only individual bank performance, but also the needs of local
markets. Rise Economy and its member organizations routinely analyze this CRA
data when meeting with banks and commenting on CRA exams and mergers. The
loss of such data is particularly harmful at a time when the Administration is
walking back efforts to collect and disclose detailed small business lending data
under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank Act. These changes will disproportionately
impact rural communities in our state where banks up to $10 billion in assets make
up a larger part of the small business and small farm lending markets.

3) Native American communities and Tribal Nations will not see
sufficient benefits.
The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the needs
of Native American communities and Tribal Nations which have been poorly served
by banks. The current rules focus CRA obligations in areas where banks have
branches, even though there are far fewer bank branches near Tribal lands and in
rural areas where Native Americans may reside. The proposal seeks to address this
CRA gap by encouraging banks to engage in community development and related
activities in "Indian Country" and on "Tribal and Native lands," even if outside of
bank CRA assessment areas. But many members of Tribes in California will not
benefit from this proposal as they do not live in Indian Country or on Tribal or
Native lands, as defined.

CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring within
particular geographies, given the challenges and impacts associated with historic
dispossession and federal policy. Instead, CRA evaluations should also consider
whether banks have established meaningful relationships with, and provided direct
benefits to, federally recognized Tribes as well as non-federally recognized Tribes.
Non-federally recognized Tribes have been acknowledged by, and are able to access




programs and contracts with, various local and state entities.[11] Such processes
exist.

More specifically, the CRA rules should encourage banks to serve Tribes, nonprofit
organizations or other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned businesses
that are majority owned and controlled by Native American entrepreneurs by
providing:
●​ Active outreach and engagement
●​ Community development loans and investments for affordable housing and
economic development projects
●​ Small farm and small business loans
●​ Home mortgage loans
●​ Grants to meet community needs, including for capacity building for Tribes
and support for Tribes seeking federal recognition if desired
●​ Support for cultural, health and other programs
●​ Bank branches
●​ Deposit products such as affordable bank accounts, and
●​ The provision of financial services such as financial literacy, apprenticeship
programs and technical assistance support

While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities
outside of their branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made to
encourage banks to engage in CRA related activity to directly benefit Tribes,
nonprofit organizations and other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned
businesses that are majority owned and controlled by Native American
entrepreneurs.

A better approach is needed. All banks should be subject to an impact and
responsiveness review factor during their CRA exams that evaluates and tracks
whether banks have engaged in any CRA activity directly with Tribes, Tribally
controlled entities and Native owned businesses.[12] If banks know they will be
examined for their work with Tribes, they will find mutually beneficial ways to work
with Tribes.

4) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will
suffer.




The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by
requiring a demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating
that large banks and their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more
than 15% of these grants on overhead.[13] As if this wasn't enough, the FDIC and
OCC question whether they should end CRA eligibility for bank grantmaking to
nonprofits entirely.

Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian
measures will be except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller
groups, may be impacted.[14]

Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local
needs. They also can be key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and
investment products into communities inclined to trust long established local
organizations. Many nonprofit organizations and programs, such as downpayment
assistance programs, that support CRA related activity, rely on bank contributions
to operate. Smaller, local, and rural organizations will be least able to meet new
reporting obligations, and they risk losing bank support as a result. The proposal
would also end impactful contributions from banks for general operating support,
sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.

Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their
communities on their own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps
in their own capacity – seeking assistance with community outreach, borrower
education, credit building and repair, technical assistance, legal services, job
training and placement, tax assistance, affordable housing and other services and
programs which help residents become stable and bankable so that banks can
attract new deposits and make new loans in LMI communities.

The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and will
focus grantmaking on larger organizations that can help them more easily meet
their new FDIC and OCC-imposed regulatory burdens.

Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15%
overhead restriction will negatively affect operations and organizational success. As
one example, in order to secure CRA grants from Large Banks, CDFIs will need to




pare down costs for critical operational expenses such as underwriting, servicing,
compliance, technology, impact measurement, product development, and borrower
technical assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions,
organizations are put at risk.

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA
activity that contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large
negative impact it will have on nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding,
the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are meant to benefit from the CRA,
and the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

5) Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.
There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link
between CRA and LMI impact in the name of easing bank burden.

Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their
top two major product lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in,
and profiting from, communities, this lending by banks, subsidiaries and affiliates
must be evaluated. Further, certain products, such as small farm and consumer
loans, are important in many communities, but may not be among a bank's largest
product lines. If regulators give banks a pass and exempt smaller product lines
from CRA oversight, banks will have less incentive to consider how those products
are offered.

Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and
soundness, encourages banks to meet community needs, and engenders greater
trust in banks by the community. Eliminating categories of loan products from
scrutiny will have the opposite effect.

No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test,
which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the
definition of economic development. The CRA should create greater incentives for
banks to support the creation of jobs that pay family sustaining wages for LMI
workers and in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to provisions that would provide
CRA credit for job creation and economic development that may only benefit




middle- and upper-income workers and communities. Such provisions ignore the
purpose of CRA.

Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA
credit for large scale community infrastructure products that generate profits for
banks, would likely be financed without CRA credit, and provide only incidental
benefits to LMI residents and communities. Such an expansion of what qualifies for
CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities.
For example, banks might choose to more profitably earn CRA credit by financing
larger scale infrastructure projects, like bridges, in lieu of financing less lucrative,
smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local community needs (such as
childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or resilience
projects).

Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA
should require banks to focus their CRA activities on their CRA assessments
areas,[15] where they are subject to more rigorous regulatory oversight (with an
exception made to encourage banks to better serve Tribes, as noted above). Banks
are not doing enough currently to meet the credit and deposit needs in the areas
where they have CRA responsibility, a problem the regulators tried to address in the
2023 CRA Rule.[16] Yet the proposal further encourages banks to seek CRA credit
for projects in areas away from their branches, lending and CRA responsibility. This
will enable banks to get credit for activity outside of their assessment areas, while
providing no accompanying CRA obligation to better serve these areas.

Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal goes
out of its way to encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan option to meet
their CRA responsibilities. The Strategic Plan was meant for financial institutions
that operated under a unique business model that the CRA rules were not designed
to address. The Strategic Plan option provides for minimal public input and
regulatory scrutiny and allows banks to determine the level of reinvestment activity
they need to engage in to earn a passing CRA grade. In our experience, banks with
Strategic Plans tend to reinvest less in the community and in less impactful ways.
The OCC's guidance establishing low community development thresholds for banks
opting for the Strategic Plan, [17] validates this perspective.





Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community
development efforts with little benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing,
where units are affordable at a point in time but not encumbered by deed or rent
restrictions, are a feature of today's housing market. But CRA rules should not give
banks credit for financing such activities where the benefit to LMI residents and
communities is unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it
can be a driver of bank investment in problematic landlords and displacement. CRA
credit should be given for financing of NOAH only if the project is owned and
operated by mission-driven organizations, where a majority of residents are LMI
tenants, and the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are
compliant with tenant rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents
can reasonably be expected to retain their housing.

6) Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA
ratings downgrades.
The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and redline
should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding"
ratings. Under the Biden Administration, at least a dozen banks that passed their
CRA exams were accused of redlining. This proposal will only increase that number
by narrowing what constitutes evidence of discrimination that may be considered
for the purpose of downgrading a bank's CRA rating. Here, regulators should
consider any evidence that a bank, its affiliates, or subsidiaries engaged in
discrimination, redlining, or illegal credit practices as part of their lending, deposit,
branching, or other activities. This evidence should be considered regardless of its
source (public or private parties), or its form (informal complaints, research based
on data, testing results, comment letters, administrative actions, private litigation,
etc.). We also urge the regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity
Act authorizes Special Purpose Credit Programs, and to once again encourage banks
to develop SPCPs to better serve communities that have been redlined, excluded,
and underserved. This is the essence of CRA.

Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information to
allow for meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of
entities and activities, and will undoubtedly harm the communities that the CRA
was meant to support. If finalized in substantially the same form as proposed,
communities will suffer significantly decreased investment in affordable housing and




CDFI support, more LMI branch closures, higher bank account fees, fewer
community serving nonprofit organizations, and increased bank discrimination and
redlining with no CRA consequence. The CRA will become further removed from its
purpose of encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and
the OCC to reconsider this proposal.

Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Sincerely,

Maddie Ribble
Co-Director
California Community Land Trust Network

comments.type_basis: Xiente describes itself as a Philadelphia organization running affordable housing development, community organizing, and homeownership counseling, and managing over 70 affordable rental units.

comments.summary: Xiente, a Philadelphia housing and community services nonprofit, strongly opposes the proposal. It argues the rule would weaken CRA incentives, raise thresholds, drop deposit products from the service test, cut data reporting, limit grants, and remove the economic development purpose test. It also says the agencies did not analyze the effects on LMI communities, and it asks for more analysis and a longer comment period.
key_asks: Rescind the proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts on LMI communities is prepared and released for public comment
Extend the comment period to at least 120 days (a 60-day extension)
Analyze which LMI communities would receive less CRA scrutiny and consider alternatives that reduce burden without sacrificing accountability

provisions.quote: the proposal also reduces required practices for many banks by raising the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated.
The proposal also weakens the service test for by removing deposit products such as checking and savings accounts from evaluation.
The proposal also will eliminate data reporting requirements for all banks but large banks, weakening our ability to identify credit gaps.
We are concerned that the proposed rule will encourage banks to forgo grants entirely due to the administrative burden.
A loan that helps a business expand does not necessarily create jobs, increase economic opportunity or address the needs of low- and moderate-income communities.
We are concerned that the practical effect of this proposal is that the benchmark will serve not as a floor, but a ceiling.
it is essential that we strengthen and modernize it, not roll it back.

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Community
Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN
3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Xiente submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced
above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)1 because it would significantly weaken the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA). We are deeply concerned by the lack of analysis in the proposed rule
on how these changes will impact low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities given the
complexity of these changes. Accordingly, we request that the OCC and FDIC carefully analyze
the likely consequences, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis, and extend the
current comment deadline by 60-days.
Xiente's mission is to transform communities by empowering individuals to achieve social
mobility. Xiente, embraces our transformational mission and vision to create a "path of
economic mobility" that empowers people to rise up from poverty to prosperity. Xiente's
programs include affordable housing development, community organizing, employment training,
early childhood education, youth after-school and summer enrichment programs,
homeownership counseling, and comprehensive case management services. Xiente also manages
over 70 affordable rental units. The Community Reinvestment Act is key to driving
economic mobility and housing security in our community. In the Philadelphia metro area,
from 2010-2024, banks made over $64 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to LMI
borrowers or in LMI census tracts and over $22 billion in CRA qualified lending to small
businesses.2

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
2 NCRC, Stop CRA Rollback: Keep Banks Accountable to Communities with a Strong CRA (2026).
https://www.ncrc.org/cra/.


2
The proposed rules drastically lower the bar to achieve a satisfactory CRA rating, likely
disincentivizing this investment.3 Pennsylvania for example, receives over $3 billion in CRA
related investments annually, but under the proposed rule the satisfactory benchmark could fall
to just over $600 million – an 80% loss.
In addition to weakening incentives, the proposal also reduces required practices for many banks
by raising the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated. These reclassifications
jeopardize 159 of Pennsylvania's bank branches located in LMI communities. 4 The proposal
also weakens the service test for by removing deposit products such as checking and savings
accounts from evaluation. Deposit products are a first step toward accessing credit. Their
evaluation is crucial to gauge whether they are affordable and responsive to community
members. The proposal also will eliminate data reporting requirements for all banks but large
banks, weakening our ability to identify credit gaps.
Alarmingly, the proposed benchmarks and reclassifications will likely lower the demand for
Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC). A 2025 affordable housing report found that CRA
motivated bank investors account for 80% of LIHTC equity investment.5 Weaker LIHTC equity
investment would impede efforts to tackle the affordable housing crisis, reducing capacity to
increase affordable housing supply.
Further, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and new documentation
requirements that could create substantial burdens for organizations and the banks that
administer grants.6 Community based organizations support bank efforts to understand the
banking needs of community members and prepare clients for their services. Operational support
from banks equips community-based organizations to deliver services funded by programmatic
dollars that prepare communities to build wealth and access credit. We are concerned that the
proposed rule will encourage banks to forgo grants entirely due to the administrative burden.
Finally, the proposed rule would eliminate the "purpose test" meaning financing could qualify as
economic development based primarily on the type and size of the business rather than whether
it supports permanent job creation, retention, or improvement for LMI communities.7 A loan that
helps a business expand does not necessarily create jobs, increase economic opportunity or
address the needs of low- and moderate-income communities. CRA financing should strengthen
businesses rooted in and employing local communities.
Prior to announcing this proposal, the OCC and FDIC did not:

3 The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit for outside their assessment areas if the banks surpass a
benchmark of 0.625% of its tier 1 capital for community development loans and likewise 0.625% for investments.
91 Fed. Reg. 52121, 52140 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026). We are concerned that the practical effect of this proposal is
that the benchmark will serve not as a floor, but a ceiling.
4 NCRC, Stop CRA Rollback: Keep Banks Accountable to Communities with a Strong CRA (2026).
https://www.ncrc.org/cra/.
5 CohnReznick Advisory LLC, 2025 Affordable Housing Credit Study: A Comprehensive LIHTC Property
Performance Report (Nov. 2025), https://creditstudy.cohnreznick.com/credit-study.
6 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,129 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
7 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,133-34 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).


3
● Identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny
under the proposal
● Quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation
● Assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations
● Consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
meaningful community accountability
Therefore, we urge the OCC and FDIC to rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of
its impacts is prepared and released for public comment. We also urge the OCC and FDIC to
extend the comment period to at least 120 days due to the proposal's complexity, breadth, and
length. The CRA is an asset to ensure all communities can access capital; it is essential that we
strengthen and modernize it, not roll it back.
Respectfully,


George Kelly
Chief Financial Officer
Xiente
174 Diamond St. , Philadelphia
19122, PA, US

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Docket ID: OCC-2026-0694

I oppose your agencies’ proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules.

For nearly 50 years, the CRA has required banks to invest in the communities where they choose to do business. At a time when costs are rising and families are struggling, your proposal would let hundreds of banks off the hook. Instead, it is essential for you to maintain strong community investment requirements for banks and ensure that those projects actually help local residents.

It is essential that your proposal be with withdrawn to keep banks accountable to the communities from which they profit.
