ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0199_09000064b965a264.pdf:
October 9, 2026

Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street SW
Washington, DC 20219

Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
550 17th Street NW
Washington, DC 20429
RE: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 3064-AG31
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Prosperity Now appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on the Office of the Comptroller of
the Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) proposed amendments to
the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.1
Prosperity Now is a national nonprofit intermediary with nearly five decades of experience working
with financial institutions, community organizations, federal and state agencies, and practitioners to
strengthen household financial stability and expand economic opportunity. Our national network
includes more than 86,000 practitioners and organizations working in housing and homeownership,
entrepreneurship and small business, tax preparation, financial coaching, child and family financial
health, and community finance.
This perspective gives Prosperity Now a practical view of CRA from both sides of the partnership.
We work with financial institutions navigating regulatory requirements and with community
organizations that convert bank lending, investment, grants, and services into resources people use
every day. These include mortgages, small-business capital, affordable financial products, tax
assistance, financial coaching, and housing counseling.
The agencies state that the proposal is intended to better align the CRA framework with the statute,
reduce unnecessary burden, and provide greater clarity. Those are appropriate goals for a durable
regulatory framework. The proposal also recognizes that several changes could alter bank
incentives and create costs or benefits for communities and projects that the agencies do not
currently have enough information to quantify.2
Our comments focus on a key implementation question: how to reduce unnecessary burden while
preserving the incentives, information, and locally responsive partnerships that help translate CRA
into responsible credit and financial services for households and small businesses.
To inform these comments, Prosperity Now also conducted a short survey of 47 community
organizations in September and October 2026. The survey is not nationally representative; we use it
to illustrate how specific provisions in the proposal intersect with current bank-community
partnerships.

Prosperity Now recommends that the agencies:
• Preserve a meaningful community development component for banks that would move into the
proposed small-bank category and retain a clear community development standard in the overall
rating for intermediate banks.
• Adopt the assessment-area approach in Option 2 for determining major product lines, so locally
significant lending is not excluded simply because it is small relative to a bank's national portfolio.
• Preserve visibility into affordable deposit access and account-opening support to the fullest extent
permitted by law, even if deposit products are not scored directly under the service test.
• Retain a distinct community development investment component for banks above the current large-
bank threshold, so that equity and equity-equivalent capital remain visible and separately evaluated.
• Publish the analysis supporting the proposed quantitative geographic flexibility standards and clarify
that those percentages govern eligibility for outside-assessment-area consideration rather than
serving as stand-alone performance benchmarks.
• Retain grants and donations as CRA-eligible activities, replace the proposed 15 percent indirect-cost
ceiling with a more workable standard, and allow general operating, capacity-building, and
intermediary support when the community development purpose and geography are documented.
• Preserve core standardized reporting for banks that would move out of the large-bank category, using
a simplified reporting approach where appropriate so that burden can fall without losing the data
needed to understand local credit conditions.
I. Asset thresholds should be paired with meaningful community development
accountability
Changes to the asset thresholds would reduce compliance and reporting requirements for many
banks, which is an explicit goal of the proposal. They would also move many institutions into
examination categories with fewer community development criteria and less standardized reporting.
The relevant question is whether that relief can be achieved without making locally significant
community development activity less visible or less consequential to CRA performance.
The proposal would define banks with less than $1 billion in assets as small banks, banks generally
between $1 billion and $10 billion as intermediate banks, and banks with more than $10 billion as
large banks. Based on 2024 and 2025 Call Report data, the agencies estimate that approximately
636 of the 3,577 OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks with CRA obligations would fall in the proposed
intermediate category. Only 86 banks, or approximately 2.4 percent, would remain large banks,
although those institutions hold 85.4 percent of industry assets.3
The agencies note that the proposed thresholds would restore roughly the 1995 distribution by asset
share: large banks held 86.2 percent of industry assets in 1995, compared with 85.4 percent under
the proposal. The share of institutions classified as large, however, would fall from 19.6 percent in
1995 to 2.4 percent under the proposal.


Both measures matter. Asset share supports tailoring regulation by bank size, but institution count
matters in local markets where a bank that is small nationally may still be an important mortgage
lender, small-business lender, community development investor, or nonprofit partner. In Prosperity
Now's survey, 36 of 47 respondents reported current bank support; 23 serve rural areas and 22
serve small cities or towns. These figures are not nationally representative, but they underscore why
local market significance should be considered alongside national asset share. Over 85 percent of
counties with persistent poverty are rural, and any reduction in services funded through CRA
activities are likely to be particularly acute in those communities who are least able to absorb it.
The proposal also requests comment on an alternative intermediate-bank cap of $3.252 billion, the
2020 level adjusted for inflation, rather than $10 billion. The proposal presents that cap as a stand-
alone alternative, although the FDIC analyzes it together with an $850 million small-bank threshold
for economic-analysis purposes. Prosperity Now supports the $3.252 billion intermediate-bank cap
because it would still provide meaningful regulatory relief while retaining the large-bank framework
for more institutions.
The proposal would also remove the investment test for banks between $1.649 billion and $10 billion
that are currently subject to it. Those institutions would be evaluated on lending and community
development performance without a separate assessment of qualified investments.
Investment is not interchangeable with lending. Equity and equity-equivalent capital can play a
distinct role in affordable housing, CDFIs, and other community development transactions and
cannot always be replaced with debt on equivalent terms.
Prosperity Now recommends that the agencies retain a distinct investment component in the
evaluation of intermediate banks above the current large-bank threshold. If the agencies prefer a
single community development conclusion, examinations should at minimum record qualified
investment activity separately within it so that changes in investment activity remain visible.
The proposal would also establish geographic flexibility standards that determine when banks may
receive consideration for community development activities outside their assessment areas. Under
quantitative Option 1, a large bank would need to meet 0.625 percent of allocated Tier 1 capital for
community development loans and 0.625 percent for community development investments and
grants; intermediate, wholesale, and limited-purpose banks would need to meet 1.25 percent in
aggregate. The proposal explains that these standards are based on supervisory experience and
are intended as minimum thresholds for broader geographic consideration, not as stand-alone
measures of community development performance. Because the percentages could nonetheless
influence CRA planning, commenters should be able to understand how they were calibrated and
how they compare with current activity.
Prosperity Now recommends that the agencies publish the supporting analysis used to calibrate the
quantitative standards and state clearly in the final rule and guidance that meeting a geographic
flexibility standard determines eligibility for outside-assessment-area consideration but is not
sufficient, by itself, to determine community development performance.
The proposed threshold changes would also change how community development performance
affects ratings. Banks between $412 million and $1 billion that are intermediate small banks under
the current framework would move into the small-bank framework and no longer receive a separate
community development test. For intermediate banks, the proposal would permit an overall

satisfactory rating without a satisfactory community development rating when the lending-test
standard is met.4
Prosperity Now supports proportionate supervision. We recommend, however, that the agencies
preserve a simplified community development component for banks between $412 million and $1
billion and retain the current principle that community development performance must be satisfactory
for an intermediate bank to receive an overall satisfactory rating. This would reduce reporting and
examination burden without making community development optional in the overall rating.

II. Major product lines should be determined at the assessment-area level
The proposal presents two approaches for determining which retail product lines receive CRA
evaluation. Option 1 would generally select the two largest product lines at the institution level based
on loan count and dollar volume. Option 2 would determine major product lines in each assessment
area based on the bank's lending volume and business strategy, its capacity to lend in that area,
and whether the product meaningfully contributes to meeting local credit needs. The agencies
specifically ask in Question 7 whether, if Option 1 is adopted, major product lines should instead be
determined by assessment area.5
Prosperity Now recommends Option 2. A product can be small at the institution level and still be
important in a local market. The proposal itself gives the example of small-farm lending that is not a
significant share of a bank's overall portfolio but is significant in a nonmetropolitan assessment area.
The same logic can apply to small-dollar mortgages, manufactured-housing finance, home-
rehabilitation lending, microenterprise credit, and other products that may serve a specific local
need.
Prosperity Now's field survey reinforces the local-product concern. Asked which loan products their
communities depend on but have difficulty finding from other lenders, 25 of 47 respondents selected
small-business microloans, 21 credit-builder loans, 20 small-dollar mortgages, 17 ITIN lending, and
13 manufactured-housing loans. These are examples of products that can be locally significant
without being among a bank's largest national product lines.
This is where examination design reaches the kitchen table. A small mortgage can determine
whether an affordable home is financeable. A rehabilitation loan can determine whether a
homeowner can replace a roof or heating system without relying on higher-cost credit. A small
business loan can cover equipment, payroll, inventory, or a temporary cash flow gap. The local
importance of those products is not always captured by their share of a national balance sheet.
III. Affordable deposit access should remain visible in the CRA framework
The proposal would narrow the retail banking services considered under CRA to credit services and
would exclude deposit products from that portion of the service test. The agencies explain that this
approach reflects their reading of CRA's statutory focus and the litigation surrounding the 2023 rule.6
The practical relationship between deposits and credit still matters. An affordable transaction
account is where wages are deposited, bills are paid, tax refunds arrive, emergency savings are
held, and a banking relationship begins. Fees, minimum balances, overdraft practices, and account

access affect how much money remains available for housing, food, transportation, childcare, debt
payments, and savings.
Prosperity Now's 2026 Scorecard analysis provides a useful context. Nationally, 14.7 percent of
households lack enough readily accessible financial assets to cover three months of basic
expenses, only 64.2 percent report saving for emergencies, and 36.6 percent report difficulty paying
their usual household expenses. These measures do not show what the proposed CRA change
would cause, but they show why the cost and usability of basic financial products matter to
household financial stability.7
One VITA provider in the survey described a bank partnership that allows clients to open an account
quickly enough to add the account number to a tax return, supporting direct deposit and tax-time
saving. This example illustrates the practical connection between deposit access, and the other
financial services families use.
To the fullest extent permitted by the statute and applicable court orders, the agencies should
preserve visibility into affordable deposit access, account-opening support, and the relationship
between deposit services and local credit needs. If the agencies conclude that deposit products
cannot be scored directly, they should establish a clear monitoring and disclosure approach so
regulators and the public can identify material changes in the availability and cost of basic banking
services over time.
IV. Grants should remain CRA-eligible, and the indirect-cost standard should
measure use of funds rather than organizational worth
The proposal would create a separate definition of a community development grant. A grant
generally would need to be directly used by the recipient for a program, project, or initiative with a
primary purpose of community development and benefit the bank's assessment area, subject to the
proposal's geographic provisions. For a large-bank grant, the recipient's indirect costs for
administering the grant could not exceed 15 percent. The bank would also need written
commitments, an attestation regarding indirect costs, and supporting documentation including IRS
Form 990 information and operating and program budgets.8
The proposal's own example shows the practical consequence: a grant to an organization providing
homeownership counseling and health care services, with approximately 25 percent of the grant
reported as internal expenses, would no longer qualify for CRA consideration for a large bank.
Question 9 asks whether alternative standards should be considered for indirect costs. Question 10
asks whether grants and donations should instead be eliminated from CRA consideration entirely.9
Prosperity Now recommends that grants and donations remain eligible for CRA consideration.
Grants can support activities that lending alone cannot finance, including housing counseling,
financial coaching, free tax preparation, small-business technical assistance, outreach, compliance
systems, and the staff and technology that allow those services to operate reliably.
These funding types are common among survey respondents. Thirty of 47 organizations reported
receiving bank grants. Of those 30, 19 reported general operating support, 11 capacity-building
support, and 24 restricted program or project grants; respondents could select more than one
category. Examples included VITA staffing and supplies, home-repair programs, no-cost small-
business coaching, and year-round tax-preparation outreach.

The proposed 15 percent limit could make otherwise effective community development grants
ineligible for CRA consideration based on an organization's cost structure rather than the value of
the work being funded. Indirect costs support functions such as financial management, compliance,
technology, supervision, insurance, and facilities that allow programs to operate effectively. These
costs can weigh most heavily on smaller organizations, where fixed costs like audits and insurance
are spread across a smaller budget. The proposed regulatory text applies the limit "consistent with
the Uniform Guidance," under which the 15 percent de minimis rate is applied to modified total direct
costs. The preamble, however, describes the limit as 15 percent "of the grant or donation dollar
amount." Those approaches can produce different results for the same grant. OMB established the
15 percent de minimis rate as an optional method intended to allow more realistic recovery of
indirect costs, particularly for organizations without a negotiated rate, not as a determination that
indirect costs above 15 percent are excessive.10
In the survey, three grant recipients reported that more than 15 percent of their bank grant funding
typically goes toward indirect or overhead costs, six reported about 15 percent, and three were
unsure. Because the survey used a plain-language question about indirect or overhead costs rather
than a Uniform Guidance calculation, these responses should not be treated as a count of
organizations that would fail the proposed standard. They do show that the threshold and calculation
method are material to current grant recipients and should be clear and workable.
Prosperity Now recommends that the agencies remove the fixed 15 percent limit. If a limit is
retained, the agencies should calculate it consistently with the Uniform Guidance and accept an
organization's federally negotiated indirect cost rate, the federal de minimis method, or another
consistent and documented method for allocating reasonable indirect costs.
A more workable standard would require the bank to document the grant's community development
purpose, expected geography, and reasonable allocation of direct and indirect costs, while
permitting recipients to rely on an existing negotiated indirect-cost rate, the federal de minimis
method, or another consistently applied cost-allocation method. General operating support, capacity-
building grants, and intermediary grants should remain eligible when the recipient can document
how the funding supports qualifying community development activity.
The agencies should also avoid duplicative documentation. Existing Form 990s, audited financial
statements, approved budgets, grant agreements, and established indirect-cost policies can provide
evidence without requiring organizations to build a separate compliance system solely for CRA
grants.
V. Reduced reporting should not make local credit conditions harder to see
Standardized data are central to effective CRA oversight and public accountability. The proposal
would reduce data collection, maintenance, and reporting requirements for institutions that move out
of the large-bank category. The OCC estimates that 126 OCC-supervised large banks would be
reclassified as intermediate banks and would no longer be subject to existing and proposed large-
bank data-reporting requirements. The FDIC separately estimates that 250 FDIC-supervised banks
would move from the large-bank to the intermediate-bank framework under the proposed thresholds.
The agencies also recognize that the proposal may reduce standardized CRA data available for
some banks.11

Standardized data have value beyond compliance. They allow regulators, banks, researchers, local
governments, and community organizations to compare performance across institutions and
geographies, identify changes in mortgage or small-business lending, and determine whether
similarly situated markets are receiving materially different levels of activity.
Prosperity Now recommends that the agencies preserve a core set of standardized public data for
banks that are above the current large-bank threshold but would move into the proposed
intermediate category. A simplified reporting schedule could reduce burden while maintaining the
trend data needed to understand how the new framework is operating in practice.
VI. The public comment record should be used to fill the evidence gaps the agencies
identify
The FDIC states that it does not have enough information to accurately quantify several effects of
the proposal, including potential distributional changes in community development activity. That
uncertainty is a reason to build a stronger record, not to assume either that the changes will have no
effect or that a particular level of funding will disappear.12
The agencies' own regulatory analysis identifies "Reduced Standardized Data and Comparability,"
"Reduced Support for Some Nonprofit and Intermediary Activities," and "Potential Geographic
Reallocation Away From Assessment Areas" as potential secondary burdens. The agencies also
state that the magnitude of these effects is difficult to quantify, making field evidence especially
useful in evaluating the final rule.13
Prosperity Now's survey provides a preliminary view of those mechanisms. Of 47 respondents, 36
reported current bank support and 30 reported bank grants. Respondents described support for
VITA, housing counseling and home repair, financial coaching, small business technical assistance,
and other community services. The survey is not nationally representative, and we do not
extrapolate it to estimate national funding losses. Instead, it provides direct evidence that the
activities the agencies identify as potentially affected are present in current bank-community
partnerships. We also encourage the agencies to publish, where feasible, a post-implementation
plan for monitoring changes in specialized lending, community development activity, grants, and
data availability. A clear measurement plan would allow future adjustments to be based on observed
outcomes rather than assumptions.
Conclusion
CRA modernization presents a legitimate opportunity to improve clarity, consistency, and
administrative efficiency. The proposal also changes several of the mechanisms through which bank
performance is measured, weighted, and reported. Those design choices can influence which
activities receive staff time, capital, grants, and executive attention.
Prosperity Now therefore recommends that the agencies preserve meaningful community
development accountability as bank thresholds change; adopt an assessment-area approach to
major product lines; keep affordable deposit access visible; retain grants while replacing the
proposed 15 percent ceiling with a more workable cost standard; and preserve enough standardized
reporting to measure what happens after the rule changes.

These recommendations are intended to support a CRA framework that is clear and workable for
financial institutions while remaining connected to the real financial decisions households and small
businesses make every day. We appreciate the agencies' consideration of these comments and the
field evidence included in this record.
Sincerely,
Marisa Calderon
President & CEO
Prosperity Now

1
October 2, 2026
Travis Hill, Chair
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
550 17th Street NW
Washington, DC 20429
RIN 3064-AG31
Via email: comments@FDIC.gov
Jonathan V. Gould, Comptroller
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
400 7th Street SW
Washington, DC 20219
Docket ID OCC-2026-0694
Via regulations.gov
Re: Mountain View Community Land Trust opposes the OCC and FDIC proposed CRA
rule changes
Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould:
The Mountain View Community Land Trust (MVCLT) opposes the changes you have proposed
to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. Congress passed the CRA in 1977 to end
redlining and to require banks to meet the credit needs of the communities where they take
deposits, including low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities. The proposal would weaken
that obligation at the moment our community needs it most. We ask that you extend the
comment period by 60 days so the public, and organizations like ours, can conduct the analysis
that the proposal lacks to determine just how much CRA activity communities stand to lose and
then engage with stakeholders in good faith to review the rules.
MVCLT is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit in Mountain View, California, in the center of Silicon Valley.
We buy existing apartment buildings and hold the land in trust, so the homes stay affordable
permanently and the families who live in them are not displaced. Residents share in governing
the organization through our Leadership Council, which works alongside our Board of Directors.
 2
We are working with the City of Mountain View, under its Community Ownership Action Plan,
toward our first acquisition: a multifamily building for households earning at or below 50 percent
of area median income. Rents in our model are set at 30 percent of household income. That lets
us house families who earn too little to qualify for most affordable housing.
Our work is CRA in action
The most urgent unmet need in Mountain View is keeping working families in the homes they
already have. Older, unsubsidized apartment buildings house many of the lowest-paid workers in
our community. When those buildings sell, speculative buyers raise rents or redevelop, and long-
time residents leave the city.
A community land trust can stop that only if it can close on a building. Our acquisition financing
will rely on public funds, philanthropic grants, and loans from Community Development
Financial Institutions (CDFIs). Roughly half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from CRA-
motivated banks. When banks pull back, CDFI capital becomes more scarce and more expensive,
and will forestall our ability to invest in the housing our community desperately needs.
Preservation deals are small, slow, and low-return. Banks finance them, directly or through
CDFIs, because CRA examiners count them. If a bank can pass its exam without that work, we
have every reason to expect it will stop doing it.
1. Do not raise the asset thresholds or lower the bar for community development finance.
Raising the thresholds for Small, Intermediate, and Large Banks would cut reinvestment
obligations for 70 California banks, according to NCRC analysis. Twenty-five would shed their
Community Development Test entirely, and 45 would no longer face the Investment Test. These
are the regional and community banks most likely to know a market like ours and to take a first
meeting with a new land trust.
The proposal also signals that a bank can pass with community development loans and
investments equal to just 0.625 percent of Tier 1 capital. NCRC estimates that if banks did only
that much, community development activity would fall by about $87.1 billion, or 85 percent. The
Investment Test is what drives bank capital into CDFIs and into equity-equivalent (EQ2)
investments that help land trusts take property off the speculative market. We urge you to keep
the current thresholds and reject the alternative $30 billion Large Bank definition.
2. Do not restrict bank grants to nonprofits.
The proposal would require grants to be tied to specific community development projects and
would bar Large Bank grantees from spending more than 15 percent on overhead. It even asks
whether grants should lose CRA credit altogether.
 3
For a young land trust, capacity is the project. Before we can close on a single building, we must
pay for staff, resident organizing, legal work, and the stewardship systems that keep homes
affordable for generations. General operating and capacity-building grants pay for exactly that. A
15 percent cap, and the paperwork to prove compliance with it, would steer bank giving toward
large established organizations and away from small, resident-led groups like ours. Grants are
less than 1 percent of CRA activity; restricting them does serious harm for no evident gain.
3. Limit CRA credit for unrestricted "naturally occurring" affordable housing to mission-
driven owners.
The buildings we aim to preserve are naturally occurring affordable housing. So are the buildings
that speculative investors buy in order to raise rents. Broad CRA credit for financing these
properties would reward banks for funding the buyers we compete against.
Credit should be given only where the owner is a mission-driven organization, a majority of
residents are LMI, and the bank can show the transaction complies with tenant protections and
anti-displacement principles. A community land trust acquisition meets that test. A value-add
investor's does not.
4. Keep CRA activity in the communities where banks take deposits.
The proposal would let banks earn credit for projects far from their branches and assessment
areas. Silicon Valley generates enormous deposits. The CRA should keep requiring banks to
reinvest here, for the LMI residents who live and work here, rather than letting them choose
easier projects elsewhere.
We also share the concerns raised by Rise Economy and its members about lost branches and
affordable bank accounts, reduced data reporting, weak provisions for Tribes, and the narrowing
of evidence of discrimination that can lower a bank's rating.
Conclusion
If this proposal is finalized as written, less bank capital will reach affordable housing
preservation, CDFIs, and the small nonprofits that do this work. In Mountain View, that means
fewer buildings saved and more families displaced. We urge the FDIC and the OCC to withdraw
the proposal and to strengthen, not loosen, banks' obligations to LMI communities.
Thank you for considering our comments.
 4
Sincerely,
Olga Melo
Olga Melo
Co-Founder
Mountain View Community Land Trust
olga@mvclt.org / 650-669-2641

October 9, 2026
Attention: Jennifer M. Jones, Deputy Executive Secretary
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
550 17th Street, NW,
Washington, DC 20429
Attention: Comment Processing
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th St. SW,
Washington, D.C. 20219
Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations RIN 3064-AG31 / Docket ID OCC-
2026- 0694
To Whom It May Concern,
On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA).
CRA has helped create a durable incentive for banks to provide loans, investments, grants, and
services in communities that have historically lacked access to capital.
We appreciate the agencies' efforts to reform the CRA regulations, and we support some of the
agencies' provisions that could improve the CRA framework and increase responsible capital in
underserved communities. However, we have grave concerns with the increases in the asset
thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under CRA and the restrictions on
operating grants.
We also have concerns with several interacting provisions that could further weaken
community development incentives that will undoubtedly impair the flow of much needed
capital in the most underserved communities.
Community Vision is a nonprofit community development financial institution (CDFI) working
across California. We provide flexible financing and strategic advising to help communities
access capital, strengthen local ownership, and create and preserve essential community
assets. Our work reaches rural and urban communities across the state, including low-income
and historically underinvested communities and places where access to conventional financing
is limited.
Through partnerships with nonprofits and community-rooted organizations, we support the
purchase, preservation, and development of social purpose real estate that meets local
needs—from affordable housing and health clinics to cultural centers and other essential
 Page 2
community facilities. Since 1987, we have invested more than $672 million in financing and
leveraged more than $3.4 billion in additional community investment.
Banks are critical partners in our work, and CRA-motivated investment is a core source of our
lending capital. Banks currently provide $46.75 million, or 36%, of the $128.2 million of
borrowed capital in our $167 million loan fund. Over the last five years, Community Vision has
deployed $184 million in financing, supported by $67 million in CRA-motivated capital. Of that
financing, $53.8 million was deployed beyond the nine-county Bay Area and Los Angeles,
including in rural and smaller communities across California. In the last five years, our lending
helped create or preserve 1,251 housing units, create or preserve 7,654 permanent jobs, and
create or preserve nearly 2 million square feet of social purpose real estate, including
affordable housing, health clinics, and other essential community facilities.
Banks also provided $5.27 million in grants to Community Vision over the last five years. This
support helps us deliver technical assistance to nonprofits and other community organizations,
including building the capacity of local and emerging developers working to meet critical needs
in their communities.
These partnerships are mutually reinforcing. In addition to providing critical capital and
resources to CDFIs, banks rely on CDFIs to reach underserved communities, develop
borrowers, and cultivate future bank customers. For example, Innovative Development and
Living Solutions of California (IDLS), based in Clovis, received financing from Community
Vision and Capital Impact for nine years and is now transitioning to permanent, 30-year bank
financing to replace its CDFI loans. This illustrates how CDFIs can help borrowers build a
pathway to conventional financing, creating opportunities for both banks and the communities
they serve. The CRA has long helped create the incentives for banks to build and sustain these
relationships, strengthening the broader community development ecosystem. We are therefore
concerned that several provisions in the proposal could weaken these incentives, reducing
bank engagement with CDFIs and ultimately the flow of capital to the communities we serve.
Raised Asset Thresholds Jeopardize Community Development Finance:
Section IV.A, "Asset Thresholds"; Questions 1–3
The proposal defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets,
intermediate banks as institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as
institutions with more than $10 billion. About 800 banks that currently face a separate
community development test as intermediate small banks would become small banks and lose
that requirement. Another approximately 400 banks that are currently evaluated as large
banks would become intermediate banks, losing the separate large-bank lending, investment,
and service tests and many associated data-reporting requirements.
In the state of California where we serve, it is estimated that 25 banks, comprising 18% of all
the banks in the state, would no longer be required to reinvest in local community
development projects such as affordable housing, small business support, workforce
development, community healthcare and education services. About 45 banks, comprising
 Page 3
50.6% of all banks in the state would lose their large bank status, affecting 245 bank branches
located in low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities across California.1
The consequences may be especially significant in rural and smaller markets, where there are
fewer financial institutions and fewer alternative sources of capital. Community Vision works in
rural as well as urban communities across California, financing essential community assets
including affordable housing, healthcare facilities, and other community-serving real estate. In
these communities, the loss of even one or two CRA-motivated bank partners can materially
affect whether projects are financed. For communities with fewer financial institutions and
fewer sources of private capital to begin with, losing even a handful of CRA-motivated lenders
and investors could have an outsized effect on whether affordable housing, small businesses,
and community facilities get financed.
Harm to Communities from Loss of Community Development Finance
These thresholds determine whether and how a bank's community development performance
is evaluated and therefore affect the strength of banks' incentives to engage in community
development. The agencies acknowledge in the proposal that when banks become subject to a
CD test under the current framework, the explicit evaluation of their CD activities typically
results in banks adjusting their CRA programs.
Banks moving down asset sizes and losing incentives for community development activities
would have a direct impact on our partnerships. We estimate that $3.5 million of our debt
would be at risk from our bank funders that are currently considered large or intermediate that
would transition into lower asset categories. This represents 3.79% of our total bank funding.
The impact of CRA-motivated capital is particularly clear in rural communities, where fewer
sources of conventional financing may be available. In Yreka, a community of approximately
7,800 people in California's first congressional district, Community Vision provided a $2.06
million loan to the Siskiyou County Economic Development Council to support the
transformation of the vacant historic Carnegie Library into a rural business innovation center.
The loan included $742,000 in CRA-motivated capital and provided critical bridge financing
that allowed construction to continue while the project awaited committed government grant

To Whom It May Concern,
On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA).
CRA has helped create a durable incentive for banks to provide loans, investments, grants, and
services in communities that have historically lacked access to capital.
We appreciate the agencies' efforts to reform the CRA regulations, and we support some of the
agencies' provisions that could improve the CRA framework and increase responsible capital in
underserved communities. However, we have grave concerns with the increases in the asset
thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under CRA and the restrictions on
operating grants.
We also have concerns with several interacting provisions that could further weaken
community development incentives that will undoubtedly impair the flow of much needed
capital in the most underserved communities.
Community Vision is a nonprofit community development financial institution (CDFI) working
across California. We provide flexible financing and strategic advising to help communities
access capital, strengthen local ownership, and create and preserve essential community
assets. Our work reaches rural and urban communities across the state, including low-income
and historically underinvested communities and places where access to conventional financing
is limited.
Through partnerships with nonprofits and community-rooted organizations, we support the
purchase, preservation, and development of social purpose real estate that meets local
needs—from affordable housing and health clinics to cultural centers and other essential
 Page 2
community facilities. Since 1987, we have invested more than $672 million in financing and
leveraged more than $3.4 billion in additional community investment.
Banks are critical partners in our work, and CRA-motivated investment is a core source of our
lending capital. Banks currently provide $46.75 million, or 36%, of the $128.2 million of
borrowed capital in our $167 million loan fund. Over the last five years, Community Vision has
deployed $184 million in financing, supported by $67 million in CRA-motivated capital. Of that
financing, $53.8 million was deployed beyond the nine-county Bay Area and Los Angeles,
including in rural and smaller communities across California. In the last five years, our lending
helped create or preserve 1,251 housing units, create or preserve 7,654 permanent jobs, and
create or preserve nearly 2 million square feet of social purpose real estate, including
affordable housing, health clinics, and other essential community facilities.
Banks also provided $5.27 million in grants to Community Vision over the last five years. This
support helps us deliver technical assistance to nonprofits and other community organizations,
including building the capacity of local and emerging developers working to meet critical needs
in their communities.
These partnerships are mutually reinforcing. In addition to providing critical capital and
resources to CDFIs, banks rely on CDFIs to reach underserved communities, develop
borrowers, and cultivate future bank customers. For example, Innovative Development and

changed. Banks with several billion dollars in assets today may have substantially greater
lending, investment, data, and operational capacity than institutions that were treated as small
or intermediate, three decades ago. The fact that assets happen to sit above a chosen
threshold does not by itself establish that banks below that threshold should lose the separate
investment/service tests or associated data requirements.
Restrictions on Community Development Grants: Section IV.C, "Community
Development Activities — CD Grants"; Questions 9–11
We strongly oppose the proposed restrictions on community development grants which: 1)
requires a qualifying CD grant to be directly used by the recipient for a program, project, or
initiative with a primary purpose of community development; 2) for large banks, caps grant
recipient's indirect administrative costs to 15%; 3) requires that large banks obtain
documentation from grant recipients including written commitments regarding use of funds,
indirect-cost attestations, IRS Form 990s, and operating and program budgets. We also
strongly oppose the alternative contemplated in Question 10 to eliminate grants and donations
from CRA consideration entirely.
While we share the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants meaningfully benefit
communities, these requirements would restrict many forms of effective grantmaking and
misunderstand the role that flexible operating support plays in community development
finance. For CDFIs, staffing, underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, risk
management, data systems, financial management, technical assistance, and product
development are not ancillary to community development. They are the infrastructure that
makes community development lending possible.
Community Vision uses operating grants to support the staff, systems, and organizational
capacity necessary to deploy capital and provide responsive advising across California. That
infrastructure has allowed us to support nearly 130 projects and deploy $184 million in
financing over the past five years, benefiting organizations that collectively serve
 Page 6
approximately 5.2 million Californians. Bank grants also support our other initiatives, such as
the California Community-Owned Real Estate (CalCORE) program, which launched in 2021.
Through training, technical assistance, and peer learning, CalCORE helps locally rooted
organizations build the capacity to acquire, develop, and steward community-serving real
estate. To date, the program has served 38 organizations and contributed to eight property
acquisitions.
Moreover, we strongly oppose using a fixed 15% indirect-cost limit as a condition of CRA
eligibility. An organization's administrative-cost percentage is not an appropriate proxy for
community impact. Costs vary depending on an organization's size, geography, product mix,
regulatory obligations, technical-assistance model, and populations served. The cap could
disproportionately affect small and emerging CDFIs, rural CDFIs, CDFIs making small-dollar
loans, organizations providing intensive borrower technical assistance, CDFIs developing new
products or entering underserved markets and organizations making necessary investments in
technology, compliance, data, and risk management.
Recommendation
The agencies should preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-building
grants as currently is in place under the 1995 framework. CRA should encourage flexibility for
banks to provide the form of support that best responds to the identified community needs
instead of imposing undue compliance burdens.
Interacting Provisions That Could Further Reduce Community
Development Incentives
Preserve meaningful consequences for intermediate-bank CD performance: Section
IV.B, "Performance Tests — Intermediate Bank Ratings"
Under the current framework, an intermediate small bank generally must receive at least a
Satisfactory rating on both its lending test and its CD test to receive an overall Satisfactory
rating. The proposal would require a Satisfactory or better lending-test rating but would allow
lending performance to compensate for weaker CD performance.
This change is particularly concerning when combined with the proposed asset thresholds,
which would move hundreds of banks currently evaluated under the large-bank framework into
the intermediate category. If weak CD performance does not prevent an overall Satisfactory
rating, banks may have less regulatory incentive to make CDFI loans and investments, provide
grants, or undertake other community development activities. We urge the agencies to retain
a requirement that intermediate banks demonstrate at least Satisfactory CD performance to
receive an overall Satisfactory rating.
The importance of maintaining meaningful community development performance standards is
also evident during periods of bank consolidation. California has experienced significant bank
consolidation in recent years, and CRA review has helped keep community development needs
at the forefront as banks merge and expand. In connection with these transactions, banks
 Page 7
have made commitments to community development lending, investments, and grants that
direct capital to CDFIs and communities. Weakening the significance of community
development performance in a bank's overall CRA rating could also weaken an important
incentive for banks to make and sustain these types of commitments.
Complexity definition anchored to lending is too narrow: Section IV.C, "Qualitative
Factors"; Questions 12–17
The proposal would define complexity for CD investments, grants, and services largely by
whether an activity is a necessary or beneficial component of a multicomponent financing
transaction involving a loan. We oppose establishing a lending-centric definition of complexity.
Investments in CDFIs can involve specialized expertise, layered capital, subordinate positions,
public subsidies, risk sharing, guarantees, tax-credit structures, patient repayment terms, or
other features that make transactions complex even when they are not directly paired with a
particular bank loan. We also oppose requiring CD investments or services to be complex as
contemplated in Question 14 or treating complexity as categorically more responsive than
innovation, flexibility, or impact as contemplated in Question 15.
The agencies should assess complexity, innovativeness, flexibility, impact, and responsiveness
based on the characteristics and community value of the activity itself, rather than its
association with a lending transaction.
Prevent ordinary retail lending from substituting for specialized CD lending: Section
IV.B, "Retail Lending Product Lines," Questions 4–7; and Section IV.C, "CD Loans"
The proposal would evaluate retail lending only in a bank's major product lines. It would also
allow a loan in a retail product line that is not evaluated as a major product line to receive
consideration as a CD loan if the loan otherwise satisfies the community development
definition. We agree that genuinely community-development-oriented financing should not lose
CRA consideration simply because a product line is excluded from the retail evaluation.
However, this interaction creates a risk that ordinary-course small-business, small-farm, or
other retail lending could substitute for more specialized community development lending that
depends more directly on CRA incentives. The agencies should require a meaningful
community development nexus and ensure that the provision does not allow banks to satisfy
CD expectations primarily through activity they would undertake in the ordinary course of
business.
Essential community infrastructure and facilities should retain a meaningful CD
nexus: Section IV.D, "Community Development Definition — Revitalization and
Stabilization", Question 25
We support CRA consideration for essential community facilities and infrastructure, particularly
in rural communities, Indian Country, distressed areas, and other markets with limited access
to conventional capital. The proposal, however, would broaden eligibility for essential
community infrastructure and facilities serving specified targeted areas. These activities would
 Page 8
no longer necessarily need to demonstrate that they help attract or retain businesses or
residents, and community-wide infrastructure may receive consideration without allocating a
particular share of the benefit to LMI individuals.
We are concerned that large infrastructure transactions routinely financed in the conventional
market could compete with affordable housing, CDFI financing, small-business lending, and
other activities more dependent on CRA incentives. The agencies should preserve flexibility
where infrastructure addresses a genuine community development or financing gap while
ensuring that ordinary-course infrastructure transactions do not displace more targeted CD
activity.
Community Vision's financing for Camarena Health Center, an FQHC in Madera County,
illustrates the importance of demonstrating a clear community development benefit.
Community Vision provided $7.2 million in financing for three new healthcare facilities located
in federally designated Medically Underserved and Health Professional Shortage Areas.
Together, the facilities are expected to serve approximately 17,000 patients annually, 87% of
whom are low-income. This type of measurable benefit provides a clear basis for CRA
consideration and demonstrates why location in a targeted area alone should not substitute for
an assessment of who benefits from an infrastructure or community facility investment.
Strategic plans require strong guardrails: Section IV.F, "Strategic Plan"; particularly
Questions 38–53
We support efforts to provide greater clarity regarding strategic plans and measurable goals.
However, because strategic plans allow banks to develop individualized CRA performance
standards, strong guardrails are essential to ensure that banks do not circumvent rigorous and
reasonably consistent expectations applied to similarly situated institutions.
The agencies should require strategic-plan goals to be responsive to demonstrated community
needs, sufficiently rigorous to approximate performance expected under the standard CRA
tests, transparent and measurable, subject to meaningful public engagement and evaluated
against clear standards for determining whether the goals adequately address assessment-
area credit needs.
We particularly urge the agencies to establish strong standards in responding to Question 53,
which asks when measurable goals should be considered inadequate to address assessment-
area needs.
Geographic flexibility for CD activities outside assessment areas: Section IV.E,
"Consideration of Community Development Activities — CD Activities Outside
Assessment Areas"; proposed § __.13(e); Question 34
We support the goal of enabling CRA-motivated capital to reach communities with significant
unmet needs but relatively few bank assessment areas. Greater geographic flexibility could be
particularly beneficial for reaching CRA deserts.
 Page 9
Community Vision works statewide, including in rural and smaller communities where limited
bank footprints can make it more difficult to attract CRA-motivated capital. Over the past five
years, we have deployed $53.8 million in financing beyond the nine-county Bay Area and Los
Angeles, supporting projects in communities that often have fewer conventional sources of
capital. Greater geographic flexibility can help CDFIs like Community Vision connect bank
capital with viable community development opportunities in these markets.
However, flexibility should supplement rather than displace CD activity in banks' own
assessment areas. The agencies are considering both quantitative and qualitative approaches
for determining when a bank has sufficiently served its assessment areas to receive
consideration for outside-AA activity.
With respect to Question 34, we support greater geographic flexibility where it can help direct
CRA-motivated capital to rural communities, Indian Country, and other underserved areas that
may fall outside traditional assessment areas. However, that flexibility should only become
available after a bank has demonstrated meaningful community development performance
within its own assessment areas.
We are concerned that the quantitative standard proposed under Option 1 is too low to meet
that objective. For large banks, the proposal would allow outside-assessment-area
consideration once a bank reaches 0.625 percent of allocated Tier 1 capital in community
development loans and 0.625 percent in community development investments and grants. The
agencies themselves explain that these thresholds generally reflect the minimum level of
activity needed to avoid a "Needs to Improve" rating and are not, by themselves, sufficient to
demonstrate satisfactory community development performance.
Recent analysis by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition further illustrates the gap
between the proposed thresholds and current bank activity. Among 69 large OCC- and FDIC-
supervised banks analyzed by NCRC, current annual assessment-area community development
lending, investments, and grants totaled approximately $102 billion. Applying the proposed
0.625% Tier 1 capital thresholds to those same institutions yielded a benchmark of
approximately $14.8 billion—roughly 85% below current activity. NCRC also found median
assessment-area community development lending equal to 6.83% of Tier 1 capital and median
qualified investments and grants equal to 3.5%, both substantially above the proposed
0.625% benchmarks.
A standard intended to determine when a bank has adequately served its own communities
should therefore be calibrated to meaningful, satisfactory community development
performance—not merely the minimum necessary to avoid a failing rating. We encourage the
agencies to adopt a more rigorous standard that considers both the level of activity and its
responsiveness to identified community needs. We further caution against allowing a broadly
defined "substantially met" standard to weaken this safeguard. Any exception should be
narrowly tailored to circumstances in which a documented lack of community development
opportunities or other performance-context factors explain the shortfall, rather than simply
allowing weaker community development performance in individual assessment areas to be
offset by activity elsewhere.
 Page 10
Allocation of CD activities across assessment areas: Section IV.E, "CD Activities in
Assessment Areas, Assessment Area Allocation, Assigning Assessment Area
Weights"
We support greater flexibility in allocating CD activities that benefit or serve multiple
assessment areas. This could better accommodate statewide and regional CDFIs whose
community impact is not accurately represented by the physical location of their headquarters.
For example, Community Vision is headquartered in San Francisco, but 74.3% of our financing
is deployed in other markets. Assigning an entire bank investment to our headquarters
location would not accurately represent the communities benefiting from the capital.
Support for Provisions That Could Strengthen Community Development
Finance
Consider prior-period community development loans: Section IV.C, "CD Loans";
Question 8
We strongly support providing CRA consideration for qualifying CD loans that remain
outstanding from prior evaluation periods, similar to the existing treatment of prior-period
investments. Community development borrowers frequently need long-term, patient financing.
CRA should encourage banks to structure loans around community needs rather than
examination cycles.
With respect to Question 8, we recommend evaluation period-based consideration because it
better recognizes patient, long-term CD financing and provides a more representative measure
of capital committed throughout the CRA examination period than an annual snapshot and
brings parity to the treatment of loans and investments. The agencies should base
consideration on the average outstanding balance or otherwise account for both the amount
and duration of the outstanding exposure, and should treat repeated renewals of substantially
the same loan as a single exposure.
Establish an illustrative list and advance-confirmation process: Section IV.E,
"Illustrative List" and "Confirmation of CD Activity Eligibility"; Questions 32–33
We strongly support establishing a publicly available, non-exhaustive illustrative list of eligible
CD activities and a formal process for advance confirmation of eligibility. The OCC, FDIC, and
Federal Reserve should seek to maintain consistent standards and, ideally, a single
interagency illustrative list.
 Page 11
With respect to Questions 32–33, we support requiring banks to retain eligibility
determinations for as long as the applicable activity remains on their balance sheet and
establishing a maximum 30-day extension beyond the proposed 90-day review period.
We also encourage the agencies to pair this with a confirmation process that provides timely
certainty while maintaining accountability for genuine community development impact.
Eligibility determinations should include a clear written rationale and, where appropriate,
identify the facts or conditions on which eligibility depends. The agencies should provide a
process for reconsideration where banks or community development partners can supply
additional information, as well as a mechanism for community stakeholders to raise material
concerns regarding activities that have been determined eligible. Nonconfidential or
anonymized determinations and their rationales should be made public to promote
transparency and consistent treatment across institutions. Eligibility determinations should
also remain subject to verification during CRA examinations where the activity is ultimately
implemented differently than represented.
Recognize Indian Country and other Tribal and native lands: Section IV.D,
"Revitalization and Stabilization"; Section IV.I, "Indian Country and Other Tribal and
Native Lands"; Question 54
We strongly support expressly recognizing Indian Country and other Tribal and native lands as
targeted geographies within the revitalization and stabilization component of community
development.
Recognize disaster preparedness and resilience: Section IV.D, "Revitalization and
Stabilization — Designated Disaster Areas"; Question 31
We support expressly recognizing qualifying activities that help communities prepare for, adapt
to, and withstand natural disasters. CDFIs frequently provide financing before and after
disasters to affordable housing developments, homeowners, small businesses, and community
facilities. CRA should recognize responsible investments that strengthen vulnerable
communities before disasters occur, not only financing provided after damage occurs.
Conclusion
CRA has helped create a powerful partnership among banks, CDFIs, and the communities we
serve. We appreciate the agencies' efforts to improve clarity and flexibility. Modernization,
however, should result in more responsible capital reaching communities with unmet credit
needs, as the CRA statute was intended.
We therefore urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the raised asset thresholds proposed and to
withdraw the restrictions on CD operating grants. For Community Vision, CRA-motivated
capital is an important part of our ability to finance affordable housing, healthcare facilities,
and other essential community assets across California, while bank grants help sustain the
organizational capacity and community-facing programs that make this work possible. As the
agencies consider other changes to the CRA framework, we encourage them to preserve
 Page 12
strong incentives for meaningful community development activity while ensuring that capital
can reach rural and smaller markets where access to conventional financing is often more
limited.
Thank you for considering these comments and for considering the impact of the proposed
changes on the communities we serve.
Sincerely,
Catherine Howard
President
Community Vision

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0202_09000064b965ac7b.pdf:
1




October 9, 2026

Via electronic submission

Jonathan V. Gould
Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency
400 7th Street SW
Washington, DC 20219

Attn: Chief Counsel's Office
Via: Federal eRulemaking Portal –
.regulations.gov
Travis Hill, Chairman
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
(FDIC)
550 17th Street, NW
Washington, DC 20429


[Via email to Comments@fdic.gov]


Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
on Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694;
RIN 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
For the past 35 years, Avenue Community Development Corporation (Avenue) has been
promoting homeownership, developing affordable homes and apartments, and investing
in Houston communities.
Avenue is opposed to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above because we
believe it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) and hurt
the people and communities that Avenue serves.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important
in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal
access to mainstream financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and
would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and
support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being
 2
considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-
income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination
and disinvestment.
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In the Houston
MSA, from 2010-2024, banks made $35,645,150,000 in CRA qualified mortgage loans
to LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts –these loans are essential to helping the
homeowners we serve in our housing counseling program to succeed in making their
goals of homeownership a reality.
Low- and moderate-income communities will suffer from the likely reduction in
community development investments and loans if the proposed CRA changes are
enacted. If regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be
accountable to the communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for
communities. For example, in our community families will struggle to obtain affordable
mortgage loans to become homeowners, and developers like us will be more challenged
to obtain investments and loans to develop affordable rental housing. It is imperative that
the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet community needs. Before finalizing the
rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce lending,
services or investment available to low- and moderate-income communities and whether
communities that have experienced historic discrimination or disinvestment would be
disproportionately affected.
The proposal would substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small
banks, while banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be
evaluated under the less demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more
comprehensive tests applied to large banks.
Approximately 800 banks would no longer receive a community development evaluation
because the proposal would raise the small-bank threshold from $412 million to $1
billion.1 The 417 banks newly classified as intermediate rather than large would no longer
be examined under separate CRA investment and services tests and instead would be
evaluated based on their combined community development loans, investments and
services. These reclassifications and resulting eliminations of community development
obligations for over 800 banks and separate investment evaluations for 400 banks, may
worsen the housing crisis by reducing the demand for Low-Income Housing Tax Credits
(LIHTC).

1 NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-rollbacks/.
 3
In Texas, 81 banks would no longer have community development obligations, this
is 31.5% of the 257 banks that currently have those obligations.
Avenue is currently working on a LIHTC development to preserve the homes of 140
very low income seniors and persons with disabilities, and we are extremely
concerned that this project may not move forward if bank investments in LIHTC
significantly decrease due to the proposed CRA rules.
The need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and
moderate-income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to
affordable mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain
responsible small-business financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in
affordable housing, small businesses and other community development.
By raising the large-bank threshold to $10 billion, 417 banks would no longer receive the
full large-bank examination, including a separate service test that evaluates branch
delivery systems and banking services. We are concerned that approximately 5,000
branches in low- and moderate-income census tracts would no longer be evaluated as part
of the large-bank CRA service test under the proposal, and more than 4,000 branches in
majority-people-of-color census tracts would also lose CRA consideration.

In Texas, 41% of branches in LMI census tract could be lost—that is 643 out of
1,572 branches.
For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate
from access to credit and economic opportunity. They can determine whether families
can safely receive income, build savings, establish banking relationships and obtain
responsible credit.
We are therefore concerned that under the proposal, examiners will no longer evaluate
whether banks that are still subject to the service test offer affordable checking and
savings accounts. By reducing the importance of deposit services and branch
performance in CRA evaluations, the proposal eliminates incentives for banks to offer
basic products that help unbanked and underbanked households. Before finalizing these
changes, the agencies should identify which communities would receive less scrutiny of
bank branches and services, determine whether the effects would fall disproportionately
on low- and moderate-income communities or communities of color, and explain why the
changes are justified despite those consequences.
We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants
and nonprofit organizations.
Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development, financial
counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based
services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations.
 4
These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have deep
relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect
costs and new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for
smaller organizations. For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be
unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other operating expenses
are often necessary to deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also
have fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs. In addition,
many community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain
financial records, budgets or program documentation in the precise format a bank would
need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations
are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger
organizations whose activities are easier to verify.
Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and
partnerships can play in supporting community development. Bank grants are
essential to enable us to continue to provide many services to our community, such
as housing counseling, foreclosure prevention, development of affordable housing,
and neighborhood revitalization.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for
meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that
materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are
consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request
that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the
likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity
to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes,
and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.
 Sincerely,

Mary Lawler
Chief Executive Officer
Avenue Community Development Corporation




INVESTING IN PEOPLE, HOMES AND COMMUNITIES
3517 Irvington Boulevard #300 | Houston, Texas 77009 | 713‐864‐8099 | avenuecdc.org | 501(c)(3) tax exempt

comments.type_basis: The letter is signed by Axos Bank's EVP and Chief Risk Officer and describes the bank as an OCC-supervised federal savings association with over $20 billion in assets.
comments.overall_quote: Axos generally supports the Proposed Rule as a constructive, targeted set of reforms that appropriately refocuses the CRA framework on the statute's core lending mandate
comments.summary: Axos Bank, a large OCC-supervised digital bank, generally supports the proposal. It backs the branch and deposit-facility-based assessment areas, the credit-only service test, the higher asset thresholds and the CD confirmation process. It opposes the 15 percent CD grant overhead limit and the adequacy condition on outside-assessment-area credit. It asks for automatic CRA credit for activity in disaster areas and Opportunity Zones.
key_asks: Adopt automatic, unconditional CRA credit for lending, service, and investment activity in FEMA Major Disaster Declaration areas and IRS Qualified Opportunity Zones, regardless of assessment area.
Reconsider the 15 percent indirect expense threshold for CD grants, which burdens smaller community organizations.
Ensure the CD activity confirmation process operates with reasonable speed and finality.

Axos does not support the Agencies' current 15 percent indirect expense threshold
this conditional approach is inconsistent with the statutory purpose and creates a structural misalignment
Axos supports the proposed codification of a process under which banks may seek agency confirmation that a CD activity qualifies for CRA consideration.
