Re: Comment on Proposed Rulemaking, Community Reinvestment Act Regulations;
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (RIN 1557–AF57)

To Whom It May Concern:

This comment letter is submitted by Axos Bank ("Axos" or the "Bank") in response to the joint notice of
proposed rulemaking issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, the "Agencies") proposing amendments to their
Community Reinvestment Act ("CRA") regulations (the "Proposed Rule").1 Axos Bank supports the
CRA's core mission of encouraging regulated financial institutions to help meet the credit needs of the
communities in which they are chartered, including low- and moderate-income ("LMI") neighborhoods,
consistent with safe and sound operations.
Axos Bank is a federally chartered savings association supervised by the OCC, with over $20 billion in
assets and over 25 years in the industry serving communities nationwide. The Bank maintains three deposit-
taking branch locations (San Diego, CA; Las Vegas, NV; and Salt Lake City, UT) and operates a robust
digital banking platform that provides innovative, rapid, and flexible lending and deposit solutions to
customers across all 50 states.
Axos appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Proposed Rule and provides the Agencies with its
perspective as a large, nationally operating digital bank. Axos has engaged constructively with CRA
modernization efforts across multiple rulemaking cycles, including comment letters submitted to the Board
of Governors of the Federal Reserve System in January 20202 and to the OCC in January 2021.3 This letter
builds on the positions Axos advanced in those prior submissions.
Axos generally supports the Proposed Rule as a constructive, targeted set of reforms that appropriately
refocuses the CRA framework on the statute's core lending mandate, reduces unnecessary burden, and
increases clarity and predictability for supervised institutions. The Bank writes to express strong support
for two aspects of the Proposed Rule and to urge the Agencies to adopt an additional provision that would
meaningfully advance the CRA's statutory purpose:
First, Axos strongly supports the Proposed Rule's retention of the deposit-facility-based
assessment area framework, which correctly anchors a bank's CRA assessment geography to the
locations where it maintains physical deposit-taking facilities.

1Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52114 (Aug. 12, 2026) (to be codified at 12 CFR parts 5, 24, 25, 35,
345, and 346).
2Axos Bank, Comment Letter on Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, Docket No. R-1723 and RIN 7100-AF94 (Jan. 12,
2020) (submitted to the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System).
3Axos Bank, Comment Letter on Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, Docket ID OCC-2020-0025 (Jan. 12, 2021) (submitted
to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency).

Second, Axos urges the Agencies to adopt a rule providing automatic CRA credit for all lending,
service, and investment activity within FEMA Major Disaster Declaration areas and IRS Qualified
Opportunity Zones, regardless of whether those census tracts fall within the bank's assessment area.
This credit should be automatic and unconditional, not contingent upon a prior adequacy showing
within the bank's assessment area.
I. Strong Support for the Deposit-Facility-Based Assessment Area
Framework
Axos strongly supports the Agencies' decision to retain the current assessment area framework, which
requires banks to delineate assessment areas based on the census tracts in which the bank's main office,
branches, and deposit-taking ATMs are located, along with surrounding census tracts where a substantial
portion of loans are originated or purchased.4 This framework is the correct reading of the CRA statute and
produces the right policy outcome.
1. Fidelity to the Statutory Text
The CRA requires the Agencies to assess a bank's record of meeting the credit needs of "its entire
community, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods."5 Congress used the possessive "its" to
link the relevant community to the bank's own geographic presence, not to every census tract in which the
bank happens to make loans. The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas confirmed this
reading in Texas Bankers Association v. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, concluding that the
nexus between a bank's "community" and its physical location was stronger than the federal banking
agencies' argument for a more expansive interpretation.6 The Proposed Rule's retention of the deposit-
facility-based assessment area framework is consistent with this judicial determination and with the
statute's plain meaning.
2. Regulatory Certainty and Administrability
A deposit-facility-based assessment area framework provides clear, objective, and predictable boundaries
for CRA compliance. Banks can identify their assessment areas with precision, build CRA programs
tailored to those communities, and measure their performance against known geographies. Examiners
benefit from a consistent, verifiable standard for evaluation. An alternative framework that sought to assess
retail lending activity wherever a bank makes loans would introduce significant uncertainty, raise questions
about regulatory authority already addressed by the Texas Bankers court, and require the Agencies to
develop entirely new methodologies for evaluating performance across dispersed and potentially shifting
geographies.
3. The Framework Reflects How Banks Serve Communities
The deposit-facility-based framework reflects the institutional reality that a bank's deepest and most
sustained community relationships arise in the geographies where it maintains a physical presence. The
CRA was enacted based on Congress's express finding that "regulated financial institutions are required by
law to demonstrate that their deposit facilities serve the convenience and needs of the communities in which

4See proposed § ll.41(b) and (c) (retaining the current requirement that assessment areas include census tracts in which a bank's
main office, branches, and deposit-taking ATMs are located).
512 U.S.C. § 2903(a).
6See Tex. Bankers Ass'n, 728 F. Supp. 3d at 421 (concluding that the nexus between a bank's "community" and its physical location
was stronger than the agencies' contrary argument).

they are chartered to do business."7 Deposit-taking facilities are the statutory touchstone for identifying the
communities to which a bank owes its CRA obligations, and the Agencies are right to preserve that
connection.
II. Automatic CRA Credit for Lending in FEMA Disaster Areas and IRS
Qualified Opportunity Zones
While Axos supports the deposit-facility-based assessment area framework, the Bank respectfully urges the
Agencies to adopt, as a separate and complementary provision, a rule granting automatic CRA credit for
all lending, service, and investment activity within census tracts subject to a FEMA Major Disaster
Declaration8 or designated as IRS Qualified Opportunity Zones,9 regardless of whether those census tracts
fall within the bank's assessment area. This credit should be automatic, meaning it should not be contingent
on any prior showing that the bank has adequately met the credit needs of its assessment area.
Axos advanced this position in both its January 2020 letter to the Federal Reserve Board and its January
2021 letter to the OCC, arguing that "[a] far more effective expansion of CRA qualifying activity would
designate such credit to all lending, service, and investment activity by a financial institution within Disaster
or Opportunity census tracts regardless of the financial institution's geographic proximity to these census
tracts." The Proposed Rule makes welcome progress toward this objective but does not fully achieve it.
1. The Proposed Rule Moves in the Right Direction but Falls Short
The Proposed Rule commendably expands the eligibility of designated disaster areas under the
revitalization and stabilization category by removing the prior exclusion for FEMA Category A and
Category B designations and by codifying a 36-month consideration window with discretionary
extensions.10 The Proposed Rule also references LMI qualified opportunity zones as examples of formally
designated redevelopment areas that may qualify for revitalization and stabilization consideration.11
These are constructive improvements. However, the Proposed Rule continues to gate CRA credit for
activity in these Federally designated geographies behind the assessment area framework. Under the
proposed outside-assessment-area flexibility provisions, a bank may receive consideration for community
development activities in Disaster or Opportunity Zone census tracts only if the bank first demonstrates that
it has adequately met the credit needs of its assessment area(s).12 For the reasons set forth below, this
conditional approach is inconsistent with the statutory purpose and creates a structural misalignment
between the CRA and other Federal programs designed to channel capital to communities with the most
acute need.
2. Congress Has Already Identified These Communities as Needing Capital
Investment

712 U.S.C. § 2901(a)(2) ("the convenience and needs of communities include the need for credit services as well as deposit
services").
8See 42 U.S.C. § 5170 (Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act, authorizing Presidential Major Disaster
Declarations upon the recommendation of FEMA).
926 U.S.C. § 1400Z-1(a) (defining "qualified opportunity zone" as a population census tract nominated by the chief executive
officer of the State and certified by the Secretary of the Treasury).
10See proposed § ll.12(g)(4) (retaining designated disaster areas under the revitalization and stabilization category and expanding
eligibility by removing the exclusion for FEMA Category A and Category B designations).
11See proposed § ll.12(g)(4) (referencing "Low- and moderate-income qualified opportunity zones" as examples of formally
designated redevelopment areas eligible for revitalization and stabilization consideration).
12See note 6, supra.

FEMA Major Disaster Declarations and IRS Qualified Opportunity Zone designations are not arbitrary
geographic markers. Each is the product of a deliberate Federal determination that a community faces acute
economic distress requiring accelerated capital investment. Major Disaster Declarations are issued by the
President upon the recommendation of FEMA after a determination that a disaster is of such severity and
magnitude that effective response is beyond the capabilities of the State and affected local governments.13
Qualified Opportunity Zones are low-income census tracts nominated by State governors and certified by
the Secretary of the Treasury as areas where Federal tax incentives are needed to spur private investment.14
These Federal designations share the CRA's core statutory purpose of directing capital to underserved
communities and borrowers in need.15 When a bank extends credit in a community that Congress and the
Executive Branch have independently determined requires accelerated investment, the bank is doing
precisely what the CRA was designed to encourage. There is no policy justification for withholding CRA
credit for such activity merely because the census tract lies outside the bank's deposit-facility-based
assessment area.
3. Conditional Credit Creates a Structural Misalignment
The Proposed Rule's outside-assessment-area flexibility provisions require a bank to satisfy an inside-
assessment-area adequacy threshold before receiving any credit for activity in Disaster or Opportunity Zone
census tracts. This creates a structural misalignment: the communities with the most Federally recognized
need for capital investment receive CRA consideration only as a residual benefit, available only after the
bank has met a gatekeeper standard in geographies that, by definition, already have the bank's physical
presence and established lending relationships.
Automatic credit would eliminate this misalignment. Under the mechanism Axos proposes, a bank's
lending in a Disaster or Opportunity Zone census tract would receive CRA consideration as if the tract were
located within the bank's assessment area, without requiring any prior adequacy showing.16 This approach
preserves the deposit-facility-based assessment area framework in full. It does not expand or modify the
assessment area itself. It simply provides that when a bank voluntarily extends credit to a community that
Congress and the Executive Branch have designated as needing investment, that activity counts toward the
bank's CRA performance.
4. Automatic Credit Advances Statutory Objectives Without Expanding Agency
Authority
The automatic credit mechanism Axos proposes does not require the Agencies to assess a bank's retail
lending outside its assessment area, which would raise the statutory authority concerns addressed in Texas
Bankers. Rather, it provides an affirmative incentive: a bank that chooses to lend in Disaster or Opportunity
Zone census tracts receives credit for that activity. The bank is not compelled to lend in those areas, nor is
it penalized for failing to do so. The mechanism operates as a one-directional benefit, encouraging capital
deployment to Federally designated areas of need without expanding the scope of what the Agencies assess

13 See proposed § ll.12(g)(4) (referencing "Low- and moderate-income qualified opportunity zones" as examples of formally
designated redevelopment areas eligible for revitalization and stabilization consideration).
14 See note 6, supra.
15See, e.g., S. Rep. No. 95-175, at 33–34 (1977) (noting Congress's intent that CRA encourage banks to serve the credit needs of
their entire communities, including those with the most acute need for capital investment).
16The automatic credit mechanism Axos proposes would function independently of, and in addition to, the outside-assessment-area
flexibility provisions in proposed § ll.13(e). A bank's lending in a Disaster or Opportunity Zone census tract would receive CRA
consideration as if the tract were located within the bank's assessment area, without requiring any prior showing of inside-
assessment-area adequacy.

or evaluate. This is well within the Agencies' existing authority to define which activities qualify for CRA
consideration and how those activities are weighted in CRA performance evaluations.
5. The Practical Case for National-Footprint Lending
Axos Bank, as a digital institution with a national lending platform, is well positioned to deploy capital
rapidly to communities affected by major disasters or designated as Opportunity Zones. The Bank's digital
infrastructure enables it to originate and service loans in these areas without the lead time required to
establish physical branch presence. Under the current and proposed frameworks, however, much of this
lending activity receives no or only secondary CRA credit because it occurs outside the Bank's three-city
assessment area footprint. Automatic credit for Disaster and Opportunity Zone lending would align CRA
incentives with the institutional capacity that digital banks bring to these communities, ensuring that the
CRA framework encourages, rather than ignores, the capital flows that Congress intended to stimulate.
III. Additional Comments on Selected Provisions
1. Major Product Line Approach
Axos does support the adoption of a major product line standard for all banks and urges the agency to
review all qualifying activity during the examination process.
2. Exclusion of Deposit Services from the Service Test
Axos supports the proposed narrowing of the service test to evaluate only the range and availability of a
bank's "credit services," excluding deposit products.17 This revision correctly aligns the service test with
the CRA's statutory mandate to assess a bank's record of meeting the "credit needs" of its community. The
CRA is, at its core, a credit statute, and the service test should reflect that focus.
3. Asset Size Thresholds
Axos supports the proposed revision of asset size thresholds to establish three clearly defined categories:
small banks (less than $1 billion), intermediate banks ($1 billion to $10 billion), and large banks (more than
$10 billion).18 These thresholds appropriately realign the CRA framework with the current structure of the
banking industry and with the distribution of banks that existed when the 1995 CRA rules were adopted.
The proposed thresholds will reduce unnecessary compliance burden for community and mid-size banks
while maintaining robust evaluation standards for large institutions, including Axos.
4. Community Development Grants
Axos does not support the Agencies' current 15 percent indirect expense threshold19 as it does not make
allowances for smaller, community organizations that offer housing, job training and placement, and/or
other services that involve substantial indirect costs but meaningfully reach the communities they are

17See proposed § ll.24(c)(4) (narrowing the service test to consider the range of "credit services" provided in census tracts of varying
income levels, excluding deposit services).
18See proposed asset size thresholds for small banks (less than $1 billion), intermediate banks ($1 billion to $10 billion), and large
banks (more than $10 billion). 91 Fed. Reg. at 52120–52122.
19See proposed § ll.12 (definition of "community development grant" requiring, for large banks, that recipients' indirect costs not
exceed 15 percent). 91 Fed. Reg. at 52128–52129.

intended to benefit. The raw numeric threshold is thus not a reasonable guardrail against rent extraction by
intermediary organizations.
5. CD Activity Confirmation Process
Axos supports the proposed codification of a process under which banks may seek agency confirmation
that a CD activity qualifies for CRA consideration.20 Pre-activity confirmation provides certainty and
enables banks to allocate resources to activities with the greatest community impact. Axos encourages the
Agencies to ensure that the confirmation process operates with reasonable speed and finality.
IV. Conclusion
Axos Bank supports the Proposed Rule as a well-calibrated set of reforms that preserves the core CRA
framework while making targeted improvements to reduce burden, increase clarity, and refocus the
regulatory structure on the statute's credit needs mandate. The Bank particularly commends the Agencies'
fidelity to the deposit-facility-based assessment area framework, which is both legally sound and
operationally effective.
Axos respectfully urges the Agencies to adopt one additional provision: automatic, unconditional CRA
credit for all lending, service, and investment activity within FEMA Major Disaster Declaration areas and
IRS Qualified Opportunity Zones, regardless of whether those census tracts fall within the bank's
assessment area. This mechanism would align the CRA with existing Federal designations of community
need, incentivize capital deployment to the areas Congress has identified as requiring accelerated
investment, and preserve the integrity of the deposit-facility-based assessment area framework.
Your time and consideration are greatly appreciated.
Very truly yours,



John C. Tolla,
Executive Vice President
Chief Risk Officer

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
To: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC). Re: Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57 — Community Reinvestment Act Regulations (91 FR 52114, Aug. 12, 2026). Full comment attached.

This comment takes no position on the proposed thresholds, the major-product-line approach, deposit services, the grant provisions, strategic plans, or any other substantive choice in the proposed rule. It asks how the agencies will learn which way the rule's effects went.

I am a member of the public with no financial interest in any bank, holding company, trade association, community development organization, or grant recipient, and I am employed by none of them. This comment was prepared after reading the proposed rule and all 161 comments posted to this docket as of October 9, 2026, with their attachments. Where existing practice already supplies what a request asks, saying so would answer it.

Four features of the proposed rule deserve credit. It says what it does not know: the effects on communities "are uncertain" in direction and magnitude. It names five ways they could go wrong (Table 4). It proposes to standardize the community development records that reported aggregates do not supply, and to publish grant information. And it contemplates a later look at one threshold, "if warranted." Each stops one step short. The first Table 4 channel is the agencies' own: "less standardized CRA data for banks that would no longer be evaluated as large banks," 126 OCC-supervised and 250 FDIC-supervised large banks by the analyses. The proposed rule does not say how the agencies will see the five effects for those banks, or when they will say so. Three commenters come close: one asks for "a mechanism to assess this return on regulatory investment after implementation" (0031); one would keep intermediate-bank data so the agencies can "assess the impact of any future changes" (0143); one asks of every reporting cut, "What will we no longer be able to know?" (0092). None names an interval, a place, or a baseline.

Request 1 — Say how the agencies will know which way the uncertain effects went. For each Table 4 channel, state which reported data or examination records the agencies expect to use, what banks and period they cover, and what they cannot show, distinguishing what is reported from what is seen only at examination. For reclassified banks, say which sources remain (performance evaluations, HMDA, Call Report Schedule RC-C Part II, section 1071 data when available) and what will no longer be visible. If existing supervisory data are sufficient, say so and say which.

Request 2 — Publish the comparison, by tier and for the reclassified banks, at a stated interval, in a place the agencies already use. Follow the banks reclassified at implementation as a group. Elements, each with source and coverage stated: reported CD loan totals and grant fields, with investment information from examinations summarized by examination period; CRA small business and small farm lending where still reported; mortgage lending shares in LMI areas for HMDA-reporting banks; bank counts by tier; and the agencies' best account of burden relief and transition costs, estimates told apart from experience. Baseline: the year before the effective date where comparable data exist, otherwise the first usable period. Favorable, adverse, and inconclusive results with equal prominence; missing information named and the rest published.

Request 3 — Say what findings would prompt a second look in either direction, and set a first checkpoint. Examples: grants or loans to nonprofits falling in reclassified banks' assessment areas, or LMI lending shares falling against the baseline; or activity holding at or above the baseline beside burden relief, which could support further threshold changes (reliance on section 1071 data is a separate decision needing its own assessment). Three years after the effective date, publish a first assessment with its coverage stated, say whether it supports a next step or leaving the rule as adopted, and if coverage is too thin, say what is unresolved and set the next date. No threshold and no automatic action is requested.

Request 4 — State the experience the grant provision rests on. The preamble illustrates the 15 percent limit with one grant of which "Approximately 25 percent" went to internal expenses. State what the examination record shows about how common that case is, with banks, period, and calculation base, or state that no aggregate exists and what the proposed records could and could not show later; the reported recipient, address, and amount would not by themselves show it.

These requests do not ask the agencies to change any provision, delay the rule, or add data requirements. I ask that the final rule state the agencies' disposition of each numbered request and, for any request not adopted, the reason. The attachment contains the full comment, sources, and a table of what each request would require.

To: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
Re: Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57 — Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
(Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, 91 FR 52114, Aug. 12, 2026; FR Doc. 2026-16454)
Summary
This comment takes no position on the proposed asset-size thresholds, the major-product-line approach,
the treatment of deposit services, the community development grant provisions, the strategic plan
changes, or any other substantive choice in the proposed rule. It is about how the agencies will learn
which way the rule's effects went. The proposed rule says that the effects on communities "are
uncertain" in direction and magnitude, names five ways they could go wrong, proposes to collect
community development data that has been missing, and contemplates a later look at one threshold.
Each stops one step short: the proposed rule does not say how the agencies will find out which way the
effects went, or when they will say so, for banks that will no longer report the data the agencies have
used until now. Four requests ask the agencies to complete those passages in the final rule. Say what
information will show each of the five effects, and for which banks. Publish the comparison, by tier and
for the reclassified banks as a group, at a stated interval, with its coverage stated and the agencies'
account of the burden relief beside it. Say what findings would prompt a second look in either direction,
and set a first checkpoint. State what the examination record shows behind the grant provision's one
example. Each request can be answered whatever the agencies decide on the substance.
1. Interest of the commenter
I am a member of the public. I have no financial interest in any bank, bank holding company, trade
association, community development organization, or recipient of bank grants, and I am not employed
by any of them. I support neither the proposed rule nor the current rules. This comment was prepared
after reading the proposed rule as posted and all 161 comments posted to this docket as of October 9,
2026, with their attachments. The requests are written to the proposed rule as published. Where the
agencies' existing practice already supplies what a request asks, saying so in the final rule would answer
it.
2. What the proposed rule does well, and what would complete it
Under the Community Reinvestment Act, the agencies examine each bank's record of helping to meet
the credit needs of its community, including low- and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods, and
publish an evaluation and a rating. The rules use "community development" for loans, investments,
grants, and services directed to purposes such as affordable housing and economic development. Which
tests a bank is examined under, and which data it must keep and report, depend on its asset-size tier.
The proposed rule changes the tiers and the data.
Four features of the proposed rule deserve credit, and the requests below build on each of them.

standardized CRA data for banks that would no longer be evaluated as large banks." The OCC analysis
states that "126 OCC-supervised large banks would be reclassified as intermediate banks and thus no
longer required to comply with existing and proposed large bank data reporting requirements," and that
194 intermediate banks would be "reclassified as small banks and thus no longer assessed on CD
activities." The FDIC analysis states that FDIC-supervised large banks "would decrease by 250 to 31."
So the proposed rule narrows the reporting population and, for the banks that remain, adds the data that
has been missing. What it does not say is how the agencies will see the five effects for the banks that
leave the reporting population.
What the agencies will still have. For every bank, regardless of tier: the public performance evaluation
and rating from each examination; mortgage lending data that lenders report under the Home Mortgage
 Disclosure Act (HMDA), for banks that report it; and the number and amount outstanding of loans to
small businesses and small farms that all banks filing the Call Report report in Schedule RC-C, Part II,
which counts loans by size and category rather than by borrower location or revenue. For banks that
remain large: reported CRA small business and small farm data; the community development loan
totals already reported annually under current § __.42(b)(2); the grant fields the proposed rule would
add to that report; and the loan-level and investment-level records examiners would obtain at
examination. In time, section 1071 data, which the preamble says the agencies "intend to leverage." The
public ratings database kept by the Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council (FFIEC) also
records examination histories and the evaluation method used for each bank, which can help describe
examination coverage; classification at implementation would come from the asset and supervisory
records the rule specifies. The preamble does not say which of these the agencies will read for the
reclassified banks, which are reported and which are seen only at examination, or what none of them
can show.
The proposed rule's own look is undated. The analyses say the effects depend on behavior. The
proposed rule names no point at which the agencies will say what the behavior was.
The record describes both outcomes. Banks and their associations ask for relief and for durability:
one writes of "Regulatory Whiplash" (0022); another's summary of its meeting with the agencies
stresses "a regulatory framework that will stand the test of time" (0061). Community organizations
predict less reinvestment: a coalition letter with 374 endorsers states that "The NPRM does not appear
to clearly quantify or address the costs to, and impacts on, communities" (0009); one commenter writes
that the threshold change "diminishes the public's ability to monitor" reclassified banks' community
development commitments (0040); several write that "the proposal would exacerbate the coverage of
data" (0068, 0081, 0144). Both sides are predicting the direction of an effect the agencies call uncertain.
Three commenters come close to these requests. One recommends "a mechanism to assess this return
on regulatory investment after implementation" (0031). One recommends that intermediate banks keep
reporting so that the agencies "have adequate information to assess the impact of any future changes"
(0143). One proposes that every reporting reduction be tested against a single question: "What will we
no longer be able to know?" (0092). None names an interval, a place, or a baseline; the requests below
do. One commenter asks for more specific provisions on the grant cost calculation, the definition of
assets, and the lending-test methods (0019); those are requests about the rule's terms and this comment
does not repeat them.
What a stated account would add. New reports and examinations will add to what the agencies know
whether or not the final rule says anything more. What a general undertaking to monitor would not
establish is when and where the agencies will set the two predictions against the record, and for which
banks. With the requests below, the agencies would hold that comparison rather than hear the same two
predictions at the next rulemaking on these rules, of which the preamble counts four since 2020. And a
stated account would give the agencies and every reader a record to return to when a reclassified bank's
community record is questioned, or when the next change to these rules is proposed; without it, the
final rule would leave unclear what account the agencies plan to keep.
3. The requests
 Request 1 — Say how the agencies will know which way the uncertain effects went. This request
takes the proposed rule's own sentence, that "the direction and magnitude of those effects are
uncertain," as its premise. The final rule should state, for each of the five channels in Table 4, which
reported data or examination records the agencies expect to use, what banks and period those records
cover, and what they cannot show. It should distinguish what is reported to the agencies from what is
kept by banks and seen at examination, and say which of these can support a public aggregate. For the
banks reclassified out of large-bank reporting, it should say which sources remain: performance
evaluations, HMDA, Call Report Schedule RC-C Part II, section 1071 data when available, or
something else, and what the agencies will no longer be able to see for those banks. If the answer is that
examinations and existing supervisory data are sufficient, the final rule should say so and say which.
Request 2 — Publish the comparison, by tier and for the reclassified banks, at a stated interval.
The agencies already publish aggregate CRA data annually through the FFIEC and propose a public
database of grant data. The final rule should commit that, at an interval it states and in a place it already
uses, the agencies will publish a short statement using the comparable information available. It would
distinguish banks still subject to large-bank reporting from the banks reclassified when the rule takes
effect, and follow the reclassified banks as a group, separately from the changing membership of each
tier, noting mergers, departures, and changes in examination coverage where they matter.
Each element would carry its source and coverage. From reporting and examination: the annual
reported community development loan totals and grant fields, supplemented by the investment and
other activity information obtained at examination, summarized by examination period where no
annual figure exists; and CRA small business and small farm lending where still reported. From public
sources: mortgage lending shares in LMI areas for HMDA-reporting banks, using assessment-area
information where available; and the number of banks in each tier and under strategic plans. On the cost
side: the agencies' best account of the burden relief and transition costs, drawn from the paperwork
estimates the agencies already revise, with estimates told apart from observed experience, and with the
estimates' own scope kept. The FDIC's analysis attributes one change in its estimates to
"revisions/updates to the underlying methodology or burden estimates based on supervisory
experience," while noting that those particular changes are unrelated to the proposed rule; the practice
of revising is the point, not that figure.
Where comparable earlier data exist, the year before the effective date is the baseline; where they do
not, the first usable period is, and the statement says so. The record carries several counts of the banks
that would change tier: the agencies' 126, 194, and 250; "roughly 376 institutions" moving from large
to intermediate (0072); 417 (0040 and others). A transition group identified in the final rule would fix
which banks the comparison follows. Favorable, adverse, and inconclusive results should have equal
prominence. Missing information is not zero activity; publishing the usable comparisons and naming
the gaps would answer this request even where some elements are unavailable.
Request 3 — Say what would prompt a second look, in either direction, and set a first checkpoint.
The final rule should give examples of findings in the Request 2 statement that could support keeping a
provision, revisiting it, or considering further relief, tied to evidence the agencies can obtain and read
with market conditions and gaps in coverage. On one side: community development grants or loans to
nonprofits and intermediaries falling in reclassified banks' assessment areas, or low- and
 moderate-income lending shares falling against the stated baseline. On the other: reclassified banks'
lending and community development activity holding at or above the baseline, read beside the account
of burden relief, which could contribute to the case for the further threshold changes the preamble
contemplates. Reliance on section 1071 data in place of CRA data, which the preamble also
contemplates, is a different decision; it would also need an assessment of whether those data preserve
the information CRA evaluation uses. A change after the effective date does not by itself show that the
rule caused it. A stated assessment would make clear how the agencies read that evidence and what it
supports. Three years after the effective date, the agencies would publish a first assessment of the
evidence available, including the share of the relevant banks and examination periods it covers, and say
whether it supports a next step or leaving the rule as adopted. If the coverage is too thin for a
conclusion, they would say what remains unresolved and set the next date; missing evidence can
postpone a conclusion without removing the commitment to explain the decision. No numeric threshold
and no automatic action is requested.
Request 4 — State the experience the grant provision rests on. The preamble describes "decades of
experience applying" these rules, grounds the 15 percent limit on guidance from the Office of
Management and Budget, and illustrates the concern with one grant, of which "Approximately 25
percent of this grant was reported to be used for the organization's internal expenses." The final rule
should describe what the examination record shows about how common that case is: the share of
community development grants reviewed in recent examination cycles whose recipients' indirect costs
exceeded 15 percent, with the banks, period, and calculation base stated. If no such aggregate exists, it
should say so. Two commenters raise different questions about the calculation. One asks whether the
rate is measured against the grant's dollar amount or against the base the Uniform Guidance uses
(0019). Another asks whether the test applies at the grant or the organization level, reading the rule text
one way and the preamble's example the other (0105). The statement should say which base and level
the examination evidence reflects, without this comment taking a view on either. Where no aggregate
exists, the final rule should also explain what the records required under § __.42(a)(3) and the fields
reported under § __.42(b)(2)(ii) could and could not show at later examinations. The reported recipient,
address, and amount would not by themselves show how often grants exceed the cap or what grants are
forgone because of it.

These requests do not ask the agencies to change any proposed provision now, to delay the rule, or to
add a data requirement beyond those proposed. The work they ask for is bounded but not nothing:
identifying a group of banks, compiling and matching what is already reported or examined, and saying

comments.text:
COMMENT FORM TEXT:
As Executive Director of SouthFair Community Development Corporation, I urge the agencies to preserve CRA’s focus on low- and moderate-income communities and the full range of bank support that makes affordable housing possible. In South Dallas/Fair Park, lending, grants, investments, and bank partnerships help us develop housing and provide counseling that prepares families for homeownership and helps them remain stable afterward.

I am concerned that proposed grant restrictions, including the 15% indirect-cost limit, could reduce nonprofit access to essential funding. Financial oversight, technology, and reasonable operating expenses are necessary to deliver effective services. I also urge careful reconsideration of higher bank asset-size thresholds that could weaken community development incentives.

CRA should continue encouraging new construction, rehabilitation, preservation, naturally occurring affordable housing, and multifamily housing. Please evaluate the potential costs to communities alongside compliance costs to banks. For organizations like SouthFair, reduced support could mean fewer affordable homes and fewer families receiving the assistance they need.

ADVANCING AFFORDABILITY IN ILLINOIS • 310 S Peoria • Suite 500 • Chicago, IL 60607

October 13, 2026

Chief Counsel's Office
Attn: Commenting Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street, SW, Suite 1E-216
Washington, DC 20219

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations Proposed Rule (Docket ID Occ-2026-0694)

To Whom It May Concern:

Thank you for the opportunity to provide feedback on the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposal to reform
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. I am writing to you today on behalf of the
Illinois Housing Council (IHC), a coalition of nearly 300 private businesses and nonprofit
organizations committed to building and preserving affordable housing across Illinois. Our
organization works at the intersection of public efforts and private business, connecting
investors and developers with agencies and nonprofits. Our organization also advocates for
policies that enable the creation of more homes and economic growth across Illinois, including
in rural and under-resourced areas. Several of our members are banks that actively and
enthusiastically participate in community investment and development thanks to the CRA.

For nearly half a century, CRA has driven banks to extend private capital financing to local
communities they serve, combating the legacy of redlining, promoting equitable lending,
and facilitating reinvestment in low- and moderate-income places and people. CRA has
spurred lending and investments in homeownership, small businesses, healthcare,
childcare, and other community needs, but nowhere is its impact more pronounced than in
the effect CRA has had on the production of affordable rental housing through the Low
Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing Credit) program.

The Housing Credit, our nation's most important tool for the production of affordable rental
housing, relies heavily on investments from banks subject to CRA. In fact, approximately 80
percent of equity investments in the Housing Credit each year come from CRA-motivated
bank investors, according to a 2025 study by the accounting firm CohnReznick. Banks
make these investments not only to receive the modest return provided by the tax
advantages associated with investing in Housing Credit properties, but also because the
full CRA examination for large banks includes a distinct investment test. Because Housing
Credit investment yields are typically modest, large banks often could get a more



ADVANCING AFFORDABILITY IN ILLINOIS • 310 S Peoria • Suite 500 • Chicago, IL 60607
substantial yield from making other forms of investment, but often still choose to invest in
the Housing Credit because Housing Credit investments help banks meet their CRA
obligations.

We are concerned that OCC and FDIC's proposal to reclassify banks with assets ranging
from $1.649 billion to $10 billion as intermediate banks rather than large banks subject to
the full CRA examination, including the investment test, could reduce competition in the
Housing Credit equity market, leading to lower pricing on credits and less housing
produced. Of the 642 banks currently classified as large banks, only 256 would maintain that
designation under the proposal—a decline of over 60 percent, according to the
National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders (NAAHL). This leaves only 6 percent of
banks in the current large bank classification subject to the full CRA exam. According to a
survey by the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC), banks with assets in the
$1.649 billion to $10 billion range invested at least $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity over
the five-year survey period. Extrapolating these results to the full Housing Credit market,
banks in this asset range invested up to $2 billion in Housing Credit equity over the past five
years.

If the OCC/FDIC proposal is made final, newly classified intermediate banks would no
longer need to invest in the low and moderate-income communities they are supposed to
serve because they would no longer be subject to the investment test, despite still having
more general community development obligations as an intermediate-sized bank. This is
because, for various reasons, it is often easier for banks to support community
development activities through lending rather than equity investment.

Moreover, the CRA Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) undercuts recent congressional
action to strengthen and expand the Housing Credit and facilitate more bank investment in
the program. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (also known as the Working Families Tax Cuts
Act) included a substantial increase in Housing Credit authority and expanded the 4
Percent Housing Credit program to increase supply, while the 21st Century ROAD to
Housing Act raised the limit on banks' public welfare investments (PWI) to allow them to
increase their Housing Credit investments. The provision lifting the PWI cap would mostly
impact many of the same banks that would be reclassified as intermediate banks. Thus,
the CRA changes under consideration by the OCC and FDIC could greatly dilute these
legislative accomplishments and undercut congressional goals of providing more
affordable rental homes.

The consequences of this proposal would be most damaging to smaller communities that
now benefit from being in the CRA assessment area of one or more large banks but may no
longer be if the OCC and FDIC change the definition of large bank as proposed. A survey by
Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition finds that approximately one-third of Housing Credit
equity invested through syndicators by banks in the $412 million – $10 billion asset range



ADVANCING AFFORDABILITY IN ILLINOIS • 310 S Peoria • Suite 500 • Chicago, IL 60607
supported rural markets between 2021 and 2024, indicating that these banks play an outsized
role in investing in smaller communities. Credit pricing for properties in many urban areas—
which are more likely to have at least one and often multiple banks competing to invest in
Housing Credit developments because of overlapping assessment areas—tends to be much
higher than pricing in rural and other smaller communities that are not part of assessment
areas for large banks subject to the investment test.

Alternatives to the Primary Proposal

The OCC and FDIC included two alternatives to the primary proposal to set new thresholds
for various bank size classifications related to CRA. The first would raise the large bank
asset threshold from $1.649 billion to $3.252 billion. This alternative would still have far
reaching negative consequences compared to the current large bank threshold but is
substantially less disruptive to Housing Credit investment than the primary proposal to
raise the large bank threshold to $10 billion.

According to AHTCC's survey of bank investment in the Housing Credit, 108 banks would
be reclassified as intermediate banks rather than large banks if the threshold is set at $10
billion, while just 40 would be reclassified as intermediate banks if the large bank threshold
is set at $3.252 billion. Moreover, the banks that would remain subject to the separate
investment test under a $3.252 billion threshold account for approximately 86 percent of
the Housing Credit equity investment by OCC- and FDIC-regulated banks captured in the
AHTCC survey with assets between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.

The second alternative proposal would be far more damaging for affordable rental housing
production than either the primary or first alternative proposals. NAAHL estimates that,
under a $30 billion large bank threshold, 17 states would see the number of large banks
with investment requirements cut by half or more. According to AHTCC, banks with assets
between $10 billion and $30 billion account for more than twice as much Housing Credit
debt and equity investment as banks between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.

Conclusion

The Illinois Hosing Council has seen the impact of CRA firsthand. The Housing Tax Credit
market is fueled by CRA investment. Our rural members, in particular, benefit from the CRA
promoting and ensuring investment in regions that would typically be cut off from bank-
supported community development. Our members report that the proposed changes are likely
to concentrate remaining CRA funds in urban and suburban locations, leaving rural communities
without the investment they need to build new and preserve existing housing. These rule
changes will absolutely increase uncertainty and burden for communities through Illinois, and
do not align with the CRA's statutory purpose.




ADVANCING AFFORDABILITY IN ILLINOIS • 310 S Peoria • Suite 500 • Chicago, IL 60607

We strongly encourage the OCC and FDIC to leave the thresholds as they currently stand
under the 1995 CRA rule, consistent with the direction the Federal Reserve—the third bank
regulator—appears to be taking. If the OCC and FDIC move forward with changes to CRA
regulations, we strongly urge maintaining the lowest possible threshold for large banks and
adopting policies to strengthen the Housing Credit market in all communities, including
rural and smaller markets.

Sincerely,

Allison Clements
Executive Director
Illinois Housing Council

Housing Credit Study, CohnReznick that designation under the proposal—a decline of over
60 percent, according to the National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders (NAAHL).
This leaves only 6 percent of banks in the current large bank classification subject to the full
CRA exam. According to a survey by the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC),
banks with assets in the $1.649 billion to $10 billion range invested at least $1.6 billion in
Housing Credit equity over the five-year survey period. Extrapolating these results to the full
Housing Credit market, banks in this asset range invested up to $2 billion in Housing Credit
equity over the past five years.

If the OCC/FDIC proposal is made final, newly classified intermediate banks would no longer
need to invest in the low and moderate-income communities they are supposed to serve
because they would no longer be subject to the investment test, despite still having more
general community development obligations as an intermediate-sized bank. This is because,
for various reasons, it is often easier for banks to support community development activities
through lending rather than equity investment.

Moreover, the CRA Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) undercuts recent congressional
action to strengthen and expand the Housing Credit and facilitate more bank investment in
the program. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (also known as the Working Families Tax Cuts
Act) included a substantial increase in Housing Credit authority and expanded the 4 Percent
Housing Credit program to increase supply, while the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act
raised the limit on banks' public welfare investments (PWI) to allow them to increase their
Housing Credit investments. The provision lifting the PWI cap would mostly impact many of
the same banks that would be reclassified as intermediate banks. Thus, the CRA changes
under consideration by the OCC and FDIC could greatly dilute these legislative
accomplishments and undercut congressional goals of providing more affordable rental
homes.

The consequences of this proposal would be most damaging to smaller communities that now
benefit from being in the CRA assessment area of one or more large banks but may no longer
be if the OCC and FDIC change the definition of large bank as proposed. A survey by AHTCC
finds that approximately one-third of Housing Credit equity invested through syndicators by
banks in the $412 million – $10 billion asset range supported rural markets between 2021
and 2024, indicating that these banks play an outsized role in investing in smaller
communities. Credit pricing for properties in many urban areas—which are more likely to
have at least one and often multiple banks competing to invest in Housing Credit
developments because of overlapping assessment areas—tends to be much higher than
pricing in rural and other smaller communities that are not part of assessment areas for
large banks subject to the investment test.


 80 Border Street, East Boston, Mass. 02128-2135 • (617) 569-5590




Alternatives to the Primary Proposal

The OCC and FDIC included two alternatives to the primary proposal to set new thresholds
for various bank size classifications related to CRA. The first would raise the large bank asset
threshold from $1.649 billion to $3.252 billion. This alternative would still have far reaching
negative consequences compared to the current large bank threshold but is substantially less
disruptive to Housing Credit investment than the primary proposal to raise the large bank
threshold to $10 billion.
According to AHTCC's survey of bank investment in the Housing Credit, 108 banks would be
reclassified as intermediate banks rather than large banks if the threshold is set at $10
billion, while just 40 would be reclassified as intermediate banks if the large bank threshold
is set at $3.252 billion. Moreover, the banks that would remain subject to the separate
investment test under a $3.252 billion threshold account for approximately 86 percent of the
Housing Credit equity investment by OCC- and FDIC-regulated banks captured in the
AHTCC survey with assets between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.
The second alternative proposal would be far more damaging for affordable rental housing
production than either the primary or first alternative proposals. NAAHL estimates that,
under a $30 billion large bank threshold, 17 states would see the number of large banks with
investment requirements cut by half or more. According to AHTCC, banks with assets
between $10 billion and $30 billion account for more than twice as much Housing Credit
debt and equity investment as banks between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.
Conclusion

East Boston Community Development Corporation has seen the impact of CRA firsthand. We
strongly encourage the OCC and FDIC to leave the thresholds as they currently stand under
the 1995 CRA rule, consistent with the direction the Federal Reserve—the third bank
regulator—appears to be taking. If the OCC and FDIC move forward with changes to CRA
regulations, we strongly urge maintaining the lowest possible threshold for large banks and
adopting policies to strengthen the Housing Credit market in all communities, including rural
and smaller markets.

Sincerely,

Tanya Hahnel
Co-Executive Director
East Boston Community Development Corporation
