ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0211_09000064b9657440.pdf:
49 STEVENSON STREET, SUITE 500 • SAN FRANCISCO, CA 94105 • WWW.CALHOUSINGPARTNERSHIP.ORG • (415) 433-6804
October 8, 2026

The Honorable Jonathan V. Gould
Comptroller of the Currency
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street, SW
Washington, DC 20219

The Honorable Travis Hill
Chairman
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
550 17th Street, NW
Washington, DC 20429

Submitted via: Regulations.gov (Docket ID OCC-2026-0694) and email to Comments@FDIC.gov

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (Docket ID OCC-
2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57; RIN 3064-AG31)
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

The California Housing Partnership (the Partnership) appreciates the opportunity to comment
on the proposed amendments to the agencies' Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations
published in the Federal Register on August 12, 2026. The Partnership is a private nonprofit
created by the State of California in 1988 with the public mission of increasing the supply of
affordable and sustainable homes through technical assistance and policy education. Since 1988,
the Partnership's on-the-ground technical assistance has leveraged more than $42 billion in
private and public financing to preserve and create more than 102,000 affordable homes.
Additionally, CHP has provided training to more than 52,000 people about affordable housing
finance techniques.

The CRA was passed by Congress in 1977 in response to a long and well-documented history of
financial institutions and real estate interests denying equal access to credit and property
(redlining) to create an affirmative obligation for federal chartered banks to help meet the credit
financial service needs of low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities. While the CRA has
successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest, and provide services in underserved communities
in California, there is still a long way to go before these communities can be said to have
equitable access to capital and financial services. Rather than addressing these persistent gaps,
the proposed CRA rule changes will pull investment and support away from the communities the

2
statute directs federally chartered banks to serve and dramatically worsen California's affordable
housing and homelessness situation, as described below in more detail.

The scale of California's housing need makes the stakes of this proposal especially high for our
state. The California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) estimates in its
statewide housing plan that California needs one million more homes affordable to lower-income
households who cannot afford market-rate homes due to their historic lack of access to capital
and financial services.1
Thanks to the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill (H.R. 1) in July 2025, California has doubled
production of affordable rental homes in the past year. Private bank participation in affordable
home production and preservation has been absolutely critical to this progress. Given that the
participation of federally chartered banks in California has been motivated almost entirely by CRA,
the proposed rule change to exempt many banks from CRA tests would be devastating and
undermine a singular achievement of H.R. 1.
The Partnership estimates that an additional $388.8 billion in CRA loans and investments are
needed to meet these needs over a ten-year period above the amount currently available.
Unfortunately, the proposed CRA rule changes would significantly worsen the situation rather
than improving it by reducing the number of banks incentivized to make CRA loans and
investments in California.
According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70 banks active in
California would see their CRA reinvestment obligations reduced under the proposal, with 25
banks active in California shedding their CRA community development responsibilities entirely.2
Forty-five banks active in California would no longer be subject to the investment test, which has
successfully driven crucial investment in Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC).3 Commercial
banks account for an estimated 85 percent of LIHTC investors nationally, making this test a critical
driver of affordable housing capital.4
Accordingly, we urge you to ensure that the final rule addresses each of the concerns detailed
below.


1 Statewide Housing Plan. (n.d.). Statewide-Housing-Plan-Cahcd.Hub.Arcgis.Com. Retrieved September 30, 2026, from
https://statewide-housing-plan-cahcd.hub.arcgis.com/
2 NCRC. Stop CRA Rollback, Keep Banks Accountable to Communities with Strong CRA. (2026),
https://www.ncrc.org/cra/#Lending
3 NCRC. Stop CRA Rollback, Keep Banks Accountable to Communities with Strong CRA. (2026),
https://www.ncrc.org/cra/#Lending
4 NCRC. Stop CRA Rollback, Keep Banks Accountable to Communities with Strong CRA. (2026),
https://www.ncrc.org/cra/#Lending


3
I. Reclassification of Banks with $1.649 Billion to $10 Billion in Assets as Intermediate Banks
No Longer Subject to the Investment Test
This is the single most consequential negative change in the proposed rule for California's
affordable housing supply, and its scale is not a theoretical concern, it is a specific, documented,
and immediate shift in the market. According to the National Association of Affordable Housing
Lenders (NAAHL), of the 642 banks currently classified as large banks nationally, only 256 would
retain that designation under the proposal, a decline of more than 60 percent, leaving only an
estimated 6 percent of all CRA-regulated banks subject to the full CRA exam, including the
standalone investment test.5 A survey by the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC)
found that 376 OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks nationally (126 OCC-supervised and 250 FDIC-
supervised) would move from the large bank framework to the intermediate bank framework, and
that more than 108 of those banks are currently active Housing Credit investors, having invested
at least $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity over a five-year survey period, projected to be
approximately $2 billion in Housing Credit equity across the full market over that period.6 In
California specifically, NCRC analysis finds that 45 California banks would no longer be subject to
the investment test.
Banks in this asset range play an outsized role in rural and smaller markets that California cannot
afford to lose. AHTCC survey data show that approximately one-third of Housing Credit equity
invested by banks under $10 billion in assets supported rural markets, compared to roughly 8
percent of Housing Credit equity industry-wide, meaning banks in this asset range are
disproportionately responsible for the equity that reaches California's Central Valley, North State,
and other rural regions where few large, multi-state banks maintain assessment areas.
The proposal compounds this problem by weakening how community development performance
is scored for the banks that remain in the intermediate tier. Under the current framework, an
intermediate bank generally must receive at least a "satisfactory" rating on both its lending test
and its community development test to earn an overall satisfactory rating. Under the proposal,
strong lending performance could compensate for weak community development performance in
the overall rating. Because Housing Credit equity serves a function that cannot be replaced with
additional debt, allowing lending to substitute for investment removes the last structural reason
many mid-sized banks would continue making Housing Credit investments at all.
This proposal also runs directly counter to H.R. 1's effective expansion of tax-exempt bonds used
to create affordable homes along with the 4% and 9% Housing Credits that are projected to
finance 1.22 million additional affordable rental homes over the next decade. The proposed rule
also undermines Section 311 of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act which raised the cap on


5 The Center for Affordable Housing Lending. (2026). Incentive to Impact. The Center for Affordable Housing Lending.
https://static1.squarespace.com/static/67dd69627071be10fb7c3fb4/t/6a6296c2f95fab4060bd8828/17848460187
33/NAAHL_CRA_Report_072326_V4-Web.pdf
6 Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition, Survey Results and Responses to the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) Proposal on the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA). (2026)

4
banks' public welfare investments from 15 percent to 20 percent specifically to unlock additional
Housing Credit capacity. Many of the banks positioned to use that expanded capacity are the same
community and regional banks this proposal would reclassify. In short, finalizing this rule as
proposed would undercut the very investment capacity Congress just worked to expand.
We ask the agencies to:
1. Retain the current $1.649 billion large bank threshold, consistent with the 1995 CRA
framework and the direction the Federal Reserve, the third federal bank regulator, appears
to be taking.
2. If the agencies proceed with raising the large bank threshold, instead adopt the $3.252
billion alternative rather than the proposed $10 billion threshold. AHTCC survey data show
this alternative would reduce the number of affected Housing Credit investors by
approximately 63 percent (from 108 banks to 40 banks) and reduce the estimated five-
year Housing Credit equity impact from roughly $2 billion to approximately $272 million
because banks with assets above $3.252 billion already account for approximately 86
percent of the Housing Credit equity investment made by banks between $1.65 billion and
$10 billion. The $3.252 billion threshold is also the inflation-adjusted successor to the
OCC's 2020 $2.5 billion threshold and has a clearer regulatory basis than an untested $10
billion cutoff.
3. Reject the $30 billion alternative threshold discussed in the proposal outright. NAAHL
estimates that a $30 billion threshold would cut the number of large banks with investment
requirements by half or more in 17 states, and AHTCC survey data show that banks
between $10 billion and $30 billion in assets account for more than twice as much Housing
Credit debt and equity investment as banks between $1.65 billion and $10 billion, meaning
this alternative would be dramatically more damaging than the primary proposal.
4. Require intermediate banks to receive a passing rating on both the lending test and the
community development test independently, rather than allowing strong lending
performance to compensate for weak community development investment in a blended
overall score.
5. Publish a quantitative analysis of the threshold change's likely effect on LIHTC equity
pricing and production, including California-specific effects, before adopting a final rule.
Banks supply more than 80 percent of national LIHTC equity demand, yet the proposal's
economic analysis does not quantify this effect.
6. Phase in any threshold increase rather than implementing it as a single cutover, to avoid a
sudden, market-wide repricing shock as a large share of investment-test demand exits
simultaneously.
II. The Proposed 0.625% Tier 1 Capital Floor Would Sanction a Historic Drop in Community
Development Finance

5
The proposed rule changes would allow a bank devoting just 0.625 percent of its Tier 1 capital to
community development loans, and separately 0.625 percent to community development
investments, to receive a passing CRA rating. This bar is set far below what banks currently do.
NCRC found that among the largest 100 OCC and FDIC supervised banks, the median bank
devotes 6.8 percent of Tier 1 capital annually to community development lending in its assessment
areas, and a median of 3.6 percent of Tier 1 capital to CRA-qualified investments.7 If banks instead
did only the minimum necessary to meet the proposed 0.625 percent thresholds, NCRC estimates
that combined community development lending and investment activity would fall to
approximately $14.8 billion annually, a decrease of approximately $87.2 billion, or 85 percent,
from current levels. There is no justification consistent with CRA's purpose for setting a floor this
far below current market performance; doing so functions less as a minimum standard than as a
signal to banks that current levels of community development activity are unnecessary.
We ask the agencies to:
1. Reject the proposed 0.625% Tier 1 capital floor, or set any minimum activity threshold at
a level consistent with current market performance rather than a fraction of it.
2. Maintain separate, independently binding minimums for community development lending
and community development investment, so that a bank cannot satisfy its entire
community development obligation through lending alone.
III. Expansion of "Affordable Housing" to Include Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing
(NOAH)
We oppose the proposed standard for granting CRA community development credit to
unsubsidized, naturally occurring affordable housing ("NOAH"). Under the proposal, NOAH
properties would qualify for CRA credit if the market rents they charge at the time of the bank's
assessment do not exceed 30 percent of 80 percent of area median income (AMI). Given that
current market asking rents in 46 of California's 58 counties are already below this threshold, this
means that agencies would be giving CRA credit for loans and investments in what are essentially
market rate properties. Increasing the rent threshold in "high-cost areas" to 30 percent of 120
percent of AMI would mean middle-income individuals, who can currently afford market rents in
all 58 California counties, would also qualify as CRA beneficiaries, giving banks huge incentives to
shift investments from serving lower income households to moderate income households without
any meaningful benefit to the communities the statute is intended to serve.
Data compiled in the Partnership's Losing California's Unsubsidized Affordable Homes (April 2026)
puts the scale in perspective: as of 2025, California has an estimated 1,076,484
unsubsidized/NOAH affordable homes, compared with only 594,055 government-regulated


7 NCRC. (2026, September 14). New NCRC analysis: 85% Of community development activity at risk with proposed CRA
rule changes – NCRC. Ncrc.Org. https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-
development-activity-at-risk/


6
(subsidized) affordable rental homes, meaning NOAH already outnumbers the state's entire deed-
restricted affordable housing stock by roughly 80 percent.8 If financing this existing stock becomes
CRA-creditable under a "clear benefit or likely benefit" standard, a bank could satisfy a large share
of its affordable-housing consideration through ordinary-course lending on buildings it would have
financed regardless.
Compounding the deleterious effects of this change, "affordability in NOAH properties, unlike
Housing Credit properties, which carry recorded, government-monitored affordability covenants
lasting 55 years in California, can disappear at the next lease turnover, renovation, or sale. The
Partnership's data shows how unstable this housing is: since mid-2020, an estimated 268,113
formerly unsubsidized affordable homes (19.9 percent of the 2020 stock) have already lost their
affordability, and as of 2025 an additional 78,133 homes are at very high risk of imminent loss,
with 354,332 to 433,166 more at high or moderate risk within five years, a pattern present in 43
of California's 58 counties.9 Crediting banks today for financing volatile NOAH housing would
inevitably mean granting CRA credit for outcomes that evaporate before the next CRA exam cycle.
We recommend that the agencies:
1. Not adopt the proposed NOAH standard as drafted, or, at minimum,
2. Require a recorded affordability covenant or regulatory agreement with a duration
comparable to a Housing Credit extended-use period of at least 30 years so that credit is
tied to a lasting public commitment rather than a moment in time market snapshot; and
3. Reject the addition of a "high-cost area" definition up to 120% AMI housing, which not
only would extend CRA "affordable housing" credit well beyond the LMI populations the
statute is intended to serve, but also provide no meaningful or lasting community benefit.
Given banks' outsized role as Housing Credit's primary capital source, if the agencies intend to
proceed with adding any version of a NOAH investment or lending standard, they should conduct
and publish an economic analysis of its likely effect on Housing Credit investment and lending
volume and pricing and allow public comment before finalizing the rule.
IV. Preserve CRA-Qualifying Grants and Nonprofit Capacity
The proposal would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by requiring an established
nexus to a specific community development project and capping grantee overhead and
administrative costs at 15 percent, with new documentation requirements to demonstrate
compliance. The agencies also ask whether CRA eligibility for grantmaking should be eliminated
entirely. The Partnership works closely with mission-driven nonprofit developers and service


8 Losing California's unsubsidized affordable homes. (2026). https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/04/CHP_Unsubsidized-At-Risk-2026-FINAL_.pdf
9 Losing California's unsubsidized affordable homes. (2026). https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/04/CHP_Unsubsidized-At-Risk-2026-FINAL_.pdf


7
providers across California, including organizations that operate downpayment assistance
programs, housing counseling and capacity-building services, that rely on flexible general operating
support and capacity-building grants from banks to keep their doors open. Adding any such
restrictions will lead to most smaller, local, and rural community development organizations (the
ones who are the most important to their communities and the least able to absorb new reporting
burdens ineligible for CRA grants. Bank contributions of this kind represent a small share of overall
CRA activity, but their loss would be felt disproportionately by the organizations best positioned
to do the hardest preservation and community development work in underserved parts of the
state.
We ask the agencies to preserve CRA eligibility for general operating support, capacity-building
grants, and sponsorships to nonprofit organizations engaged in community development, without
imposing new project-level nexus or overhead-tracking requirements that fall hardest on smaller
and rural organizations.
V. Geographic Flexibility Should Complement, Not Replace, Assessment-Area Obligations
The proposed rule changes would allow banks, at their option, to receive CRA credit for
qualifying community development activity outside their assessment areas, up to the state or
multistate level, after adequately meeting needs inside their assessment areas. We support the
goal of directing more private capital to California's rural and underserved "CRA deserts," where
few banks maintain a physical presence or assessment area, and agree this flexibility could help
address the pricing gap between competitive urban "CRA hot spots" and underserved rural
markets. However, this flexibility should not become a mechanism for banks to redirect capital
away from the communities where they take deposits and hold assessment-area responsibility in
the first place.
We ask the agencies to condition any out-of-assessment-area credit on a bank first demonstrating
it has adequately met the community development needs within its own assessment areas, and
prioritize this flexibility for LIHTC, CDFI, and other high-impact investment that would not
otherwise reach underserved rural California communities.

The Partnership has more than 35 years of firsthand experience with how CRA-motivated
investment works and what is jeopardized when that investment weakens. As the state's leading
source of applied research and technical assistance on affordable housing finance, we are available
as a resource to the agencies as you consider the volume of public comment this proposal will
generate. We urge the OCC and FDIC to preserve the standalone investment test, reject the
proposed activity floor, reject the NOAH standard, and ensure that any final rule strengthens,
rather than diminishes, the effectiveness and positive investment that CRA has made possible in
California for nearly 50 years.
Thank you for your consideration of these comments.

8

Sincerely,


Tiyesha Watts
Associate Director, Policy Advocacy
California Housing Partnership

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0212_09000064b9659292.docx:
Public comment in relation to OCC-2026-0694
Dear Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation:
I am writing to encourage the OCC and FDIC to preserve a strong Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) and the important role it plays in expanding access to capital
for underserved communities. In particular, I encourage the agencies to maintain the
meaningful incentives the CRA creates for banks to partner with Community
Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs), which help ensure that capital reaches
small businesses and entrepreneurs who might otherwise be overlooked.
I am proud to serve on the Board of WomenVenture, a CDFI serving Minnesota and
Western Wisconsin for the last 25 years. WomenVenture helps entrepreneurs and small
business owners build profitable and sustainable businesses by combining access to
capital with training, technical assistance, and ongoing support. Organizations like
WomenVenture play a critical role in helping entrepreneurs turn promising ideas into
viable businesses, particularly when they face barriers to traditional financing.
My appreciation for this work comes from both my professional and personal
experiences.
I have spent much of my career in finance, including investment banking and private
equity, where I have seen firsthand what it takes for businesses to attract investment
capital. Too often, businesses need to have already achieved significant scale or
demonstrated rapid growth to attract financing. Yet many small businesses need access
to capital precisely to reach that next stage of growth. This creates a difficult cycle for
entrepreneurs with viable businesses but limited access to traditional sources of
funding. This challenge is exacerbated in communities that historically have had less
access to capital.
I also grew up in a family of small-business owners. My grandparents started a business
that my father carried forward and that my brother now leads. Throughout its history,
local banks provided financing to purchase equipment, expand facilities, and support
growth. In turn, our family business has reinvested in the community for generations,
creating jobs, supporting local organizations, and contributing to the local economy.
These businesses may never appear on the cover of The Wall Street Journal, but their
names appear on the jerseys of local youth sports teams. They create jobs, meet
essential needs, and help communities thrive. Their success creates a virtuous cycle of
economic opportunity and community investment.
That experience is a significant part of why I joined the Board of WomenVenture. I
believe that expanding access to capital for small businesses is not simply about
 supporting individual entrepreneurs; it is about strengthening the economic foundation
of our communities.
Bank partnerships are essential to making this possible. The CRA has helped
encourage banks to lend, invest, and provide resources through CDFIs that understand
local needs and can connect capital with entrepreneurs and businesses that might
otherwise struggle to access it. These partnerships extend the reach and impact of
traditional financial institutions while supporting responsible lending and sustainable
economic development.
I recognize the importance of making CRA requirements clearer, more effective, and
less burdensome for financial institutions. Regulatory efficiency is a worthwhile
objective. However, it is important that efforts to simplify the framework do not
unintentionally weaken the incentives that encourage meaningful investment in
underserved communities. A more efficient regulatory framework should preserve
the outcomes the CRA was designed to achieve.
As the agencies are considering changes to the CRA framework, I encourage them to
ensure the final rule:
•
Preserves meaningful incentives for banks to lend and invest through CDFIs;
•
Recognizes the full value of community development activities that expand
access to responsible capital and strengthen local economies;
•
Supports grants and other resources that help CDFIs build the capacity needed
to serve communities effectively;
•
Maintains meaningful expectations for banks to meet community credit needs;
and
•
Strengthens, rather than reduces, the flow of responsible private capital to small
businesses and low- and moderate-income communities.
For organizations like WomenVenture, these partnerships translate directly into
financing and support for entrepreneurs to start businesses, create jobs, build wealth,
and reinvest in their communities.
Thank you for considering my comments.
Sincerely,
Jaime Proman
Board Member, WomenVenture
Minneapolis, Minnesota

•
Recognizes the full value of community development activities that expand
access to responsible capital and strengthen local economies;
•
Supports grants and other resources that help CDFIs build the capacity needed
to serve communities effectively;
•
Maintains meaningful expectations for banks to meet community credit needs;
and
•
Strengthens, rather than reduces, the flow of responsible private capital to small
businesses and low- and moderate-income communities.
For organizations like WomenVenture, these partnerships translate directly into
financing and support for entrepreneurs to start businesses, create jobs, build wealth,
and reinvest in their communities.
Thank you for considering my comments.
Sincerely,
Jaime Proman
Board Member, WomenVenture
Minneapolis, Minnesota

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
Dear Ladies and Gentlemen:

First National Bank Texas ("FNBT") is a regional community bank founded in 1901 and
headquartered in Killeen, Texas. The bank serves communities throughout Texas, New Mexico,
Arizona, and Arkansas. As of June 30, 2026, FNBT operates 356 branches, of which 135 (38%)
are located in low- and moderate-income geographies and five (1%) are located in middle-income
distressed or underserved geographies.

FNBT focuses on both retail and commercial customers. We offer a variety of lending products to
meet the credit needs of our communities, including small-dollar consumer loans, a full suite of
small business loans and lines of credit via the Small Business Administration ("SBA"), mortgage
loans, and municipal lending that provides funding for the infrastructure needs of the cities and
counties we serve. Additionally, we offer a wide variety of retail technology services that allow
our customers to perform their banking needs from their personal smart devices.

FNBT thanks the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (the "OCC") and the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation (the "FDIC"; the OCC and the FDIC are hereafter collectively referred to
as the "Issuing Agencies") for their proposal to modernize the Community Reinvestment Act (the
"CRA") and for the opportunity to provide feedback as stakeholders in our communities. We
appreciate the Issuing Agencies' thoughtful, measured, pragmatically tailored approach to the
latest CRA modernization proposal. By realigning the regulatory framework with its core statutory
intent, the Issuing Agencies have successfully established a balanced ecosystem that maximizes
community impacts while systematically eliminating unnecessary administrative friction. We
particularly commend the Issuing Agencies for implementing tiered, data-driven asset
thresholds—specifically exempting institutions under $10 billion from overly burdensome data
collection and reporting requirements. This regulatory tiering, combined with a refocused
emphasis on core retail product lending, gives financial institutions the clarity and operational

901 E Central Texas Expressway P.O. Box 937 Killeen, Texas 76541
 FIRST FIRST
NATIONAL CONVENIENCE
BANK

BANK texas
Adivision of First National Bank Texas

certainty needed to deploy capital efficiently into underserved neighborhoods. The proposed
confirmation process for qualifying community development ("CD") activities and a published
illustrative list of qualified CD activities will let financial institutions know in advance whether an
activity qualifies under CRA, reducing uncertainty and encouraging more activity.

To ensure the long-term success and viability of CRA modernization, the Issuing Agencies should
approach this final rulemaking with a focus on long-term stability by prioritizing a consistent
interagency framework that strictly adheres to the CRA statute. Achieving this requires balancing
improved clarity and transparency with the core flexibility and tailoring that have driven the
regulation's success since 1995. Rather than adopting rigid, overly complicated rules that rely
heavily on mechanical metrics, the final framework should continue to tailor performance tests to
diverse bank types, sizes, and unique business models. Furthermore, the Issuing Agencies must
evaluate the proposal's components collectively rather than in isolation, as individual revisions
can have compounding cumulative effects that drastically alter operational outcomes. Ultimately,
a successful final rule must pair this holistic, flexible design with an appropriate and realistic
transition period to allow institutions to adapt without disrupting vital credit and capital flows to
underserved communities.

The concerns and recommendations below are intended to assist the Issuing Agencies with
maintaining flexibility in the regulation and are respectfully provided for your consideration.

Concerns and Recommendations

1. Asset Size Thresholds

We support the Issuing Agencies exempting institutions under $10 billion from
burdensome data collection and reporting requirements.

2. Performance Tests

We recommend clarification as it relates to the role of comparative data in Intermediate
Bank examinations.

We are currently evaluated as a Large Bank, but under the new proposal we would
become an Intermediate Bank. We are accustomed to supervisory practices that make
greater use of aggregate, market share, and other comparative lending data.

We would welcome an explanation of when comparative information may be considered,
how similarly situated lenders would be identified, and the weight comparative
information would receive in the examination process. Current Small and ISB
examination procedures provide useful information but do not provide clarity on how an
institution's CRA performance should be judged based on how it compares to other
lenders.

901 E Central Texas Expressway P.O. Box 937 Killeen, Texas 76541
 FIRST FIRST
NATIONAL CONVENIENCE

The CRA statute requires regulators to evaluate a bank's record of helping meet the credit
needs of its communities, not whether it matches or outperforms other lenders.

We recommend that revised examination procedures and examiner training should make
clear that data reported by Large Banks will not be used to evaluate Intermediate Banks
in order to have true peer comparators.

3. Retail Lending Evaluations

We support focusing retail lending evaluations on an institution's major product lines at
the bank level. Option 1, which determines major product lines at the institution level based
on count and dollar volume, allows financial institutions to monitor these metrics during
the evaluation period and would largely codify this process.

We further support retaining the existing substantial majority standard for consumer
lending. We are concerned, however, with the proposed 50% threshold, which is a
departure from the current practice without explanation as to why the current framework
should be replaced, nor sufficient detail to understand how the proposed framework will
work in practice.

More problematically, the preamble states that when consumer lending constitutes a major
product line, examiners would evaluate all categories of consumer lending in aggregate.
We did not find that this approach is reflected in the proposed regulatory text. We would
expect to see this expressly stated in the final rule.

We are opposed to aggregating all consumer lending products into a single category.
Aggregation obscures important differences in performance by product type, and concerns
are further compounded by the limited availability of standardized consumer-lending data
and benchmarking information. We are in favor of maintaining the flexibility we have been
afforded under today's framework to have consumer lending evaluated at our option and
based on what we determine are appropriate products to assist LMI borrowers and
geographies.

4. Community Development
AFFORDABLE HOUSING

We support an amendment to the proposed definition of affordable housing to permit
financial institutions to demonstrate high-cost market conditions using supportable data
sources, such as allowing institutions to rely on established federal designations such as
Difficult Development Areas (HUD) and High Opportunity Areas (FHFA), etc., where
appropriate.

901 E Central Texas Expressway P.O. Box 937 Killeen, Texas 76541
 FIRST FIRST
NATIONAL CONVENIENCE

CIVIC ASSISTANCE

We would support recognition of all financial wellness activities that benefit consumers
across all income levels.

ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT

We would support the inclusion of loans made for the purpose of operating liquidity as a
qualified economic development activity.

REVITALIZATION AND STABILIZATION

We would support refinement of the treatment of essential infrastructure and disaster
recovery by providing consideration for community-wide infrastructure projects and
recognition of not only FEMA disaster designations but also include state-declared
disasters.

COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT GRANTS

The 15% administrative overhead cap fails to recognize how modern community
development organizations operate. While the intent is to redirect funds from the
"community reinvestment industry" directly to local initiatives, this rule ignores the other
costs of doing so.

a: True indirect costs, such as legal compliance, financial auditing, human resources,
and cybersecurity, often exceed 15%. Forcing a strict ceiling can cost
organizations the infrastructure needed to run their programs safely.

b. This proposal is based on OMB Uniform Guidance Jor Federal Awards as its
blueprint. These complex accounting rules are designed for large research
universities and federal contractors, not local community groups.

c. There is a disproportionate compliance burden for Large Banks, which must
formally document that a recipient's overhead does not exceed the cap and obtain
a written commitment regarding the qualifying use of the proceeds, as well as for
nonprofits, which must submit tax filings, detailed internal budgets, and formal
attestations, creating immense administrative burdens.

d. Through local expertise, community financial institutions are best suited to
identify nonprofit partners that align with local needs. This is a responsibility we
manage with exceptional care, deploying capital where it will have the greatest
impact.

7. Rule Transition
We recommend a two-year implementation period for the final rule.
8. General Comments
REGULATORY FRAGMENTATION
Since the Federal Reserve did not join the OCC and FDIC in this rulemaking, financial
institutions face conflicting CRA standards dependent upon their primary regulator. We remain
hopeful the agencies may come together in issuance of the final rule.
CREDIT UNIONS
Lastly, we ask that the Issuing Agencies consider including other entities that have community

reinvestment responsibilities, such as credit unions. We feel that entities with similar
responsibilities should have similar regulations.

We are committed to the goals of CRA and take pride in providing much-needed banking services
to our customers and communities. We appreciate this opportunity to comment and are hopeful
that our concerns and recommendations prove useful in the development and implementation of

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Community Reinvestment Act
Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Community Ventures submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA
NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the
rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully
analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on
the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60
days.
Community Ventures is a nonprofit affordable housing developer, property manager and supportive services provider
with a legacy of serving Philadelphia low-income families since 1896. Community Ventures' (and our legacy affiliate
Octavia Hill Association) work has focused on neighborhood revitalization and community reinvestment through the
development of affordable housing, commercial space, civic spaces and green spaces in economically diverse low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods of Philadelphia.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that banks meet the
credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized
that communities depend on access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important
 in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream financial
services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change how regulators
evaluate community development, bank services and support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these
changes are being considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income
communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In the Philadelphia metro area, from 2010-2024,
banks made over $64 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and over $22
billion in CRA qualified lending to small businesses. Investments such as these benefited our community by increasing
affordability for low- and moderate-income homebuyers and by increasing equity pricing from investors purchasing Low-
Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC) for development and preservation of affordable rental housing.
We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in our communities. For example, it
suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital devoted to either community development loans or
investments would be enough to receive a passing CRA rating. This represents a dramatic reduction in what large banks
currently devote to community investments and loans and we fear that this new guidance may operate as a ceiling
instead of a floor. Pennsylvania receives over $3 billion in CRA related investments annually, but under the proposed
rule that could fall to just over $600 million – an 80% loss.
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination cannot withstand such
a reduction in community development investments and loans. If regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest
in, lend to, and be accountable to the communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for communities.
For example, in our community families will struggle with obtain affordable mortgage loans, financing of development
and preservation of LIHTC units will get incredibly more difficult by reducing investor and lender incentives to increase
their investments.
It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet the needs of communities like ours. Before finalizing
the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce lending, services or investment
available to low- and moderate-income communities and whether communities that have experienced historic
discrimination or disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.
The proposal would also substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under CRA.
Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while banks with assets between $1 billion and $10
billion would generally be evaluated under the less demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more
comprehensive tests applied to large banks. The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting
requirements currently applicable to large banks, including reporting on small-business, community development
lending.
A number of banks that operate in Philadelphia will now be considered either intermediate or small banks under the
proposed rule and therefore subject to less rigorous requirements. These reclassifications and resulting eliminations of
community development obligations for over 800 banks and separate investment evaluations for 400 banks across the
 country, may worsen the housing crisis by reducing investor interest in buying Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC),
and reducing access to mortgages for first-time homebuyers or access to credit for home repairs.
Similarly, the proposed rule would narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service test. Today, examiners
may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and information about the costs and features of deposit
accounts. The proposal would limit this criterion to credit services, removing deposit products such as checking and
savings accounts from direct evaluation under the service test. As such, examiners would no longer evaluate whether
those products are affordable and responsive to community needs even though approximately 15% of Philadelphians –
over 100,000 households – remain unbanked or underbanked. Moreover, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of
Philadelphia, these households are overwhelmingly low-income, black, or disabled. CRA review of the cost and features
of deposit products has played an important role in encouraging banks to address these disparities by providing
affordable products, and it must continue to do so.
This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and moderate-income communities
remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to affordable mortgage credit and homeownership;
entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible small-business financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment
in affordable housing, small businesses and other community development.
The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply because a bank falls below a
higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the
agencies should identify the banks that would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the
communities those institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development activity that would receive less
scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-income communities or
communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and nonprofit organizations.
Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development, financial counseling, workforce programs,
neighborhood revitalization and other community-based services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships
with nonprofit organizations. These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have deep
relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and new documentation
requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations. For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15
percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often
necessary to deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources
over which to spread these costs. In addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not
maintain financial records or program documentation in the precise format a bank would need to establish CRA
eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may
redirect funding toward larger organizations whose activities are easier to verify.
These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into tangible benefits for
residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community development activities receive CRA consideration can
 therefore have consequences well beyond the banks themselves. These rules should be motivated by the needs of the
communities CRA is intended to serve and not by the perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions.
To be considered economic development under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying small business must
promote economic development by supporting permanent job creation, retention, or improvement for low- or
moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income communities.
The proposed rule would eliminate this "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks could earn CRA credit for
business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or improves jobs for low- and moderate-income people or in
low- and moderate-income communities. This change would weaken the connection between CRA economic-
development credit and the people and communities CRA is intended to benefit. Specifically, a loan that helps a
qualifying business expand does not necessarily create jobs, increase economic opportunity in an underserved
neighborhood or address the needs of low- and moderate-income communities.
Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens a qualifying business will
benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank to demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and
moderate-income workers or neighborhoods.
We are also concerned that currently, banks above the large bank threshold annually collect and report data on small
business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans, while the proposal would limit these requirements
to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. Banks with assets of $10 billion or less would no longer be required to
annually collect and report CRA data on small business loans and community development loans.
Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers would have less information to identify credit
deserts, compare bank performance or understand whether local credit needs are being met. Local community leaders
and elected officials depend on this data for decision making and for ensuring that the needs of residents are being
addressed. This proposed change is inconsistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit
needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities, and should not be in the final rule.
Lastly, prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
● identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny under the proposal;
● quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community development activities subject
to CRA evaluation;
● assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations, including rural
communities and communities of color; and
● consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing meaningful
community accountability.

Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes that the OCC and FDIC should
rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and released for public comment. This
proposal likely needs considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

 The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting community credit needs.
The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the
changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods.

We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days. The proposal is more than
100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant changes to bank classifications, community development,
branch and service evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The current comment
period closes on October 13, 2026.

Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from community organizations,
civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is
warranted. An extension would allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather
examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more complete record on which to base
any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60
days.

Sincerely,



Troy Hannigan
Executive Director

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0215_09000064b9659c46.pdf:
October 9, 2026

Travis Hill, Chair
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
550 17th Street NW,
Washington, DC 20429
RIN 3064-AG31
Via email: comments@FDIC.gov

Jonathan V. Gould, Comptroller
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
400 7th St. SW,
Washington, DC 20219
Docket ID OCC-2026-0694
Via: https://regulations.gov/

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

The San Diego Housing Federation writes to object to the harmful changes
proposed to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed by
Congress in 1977 in response to redlining and creates an affirmative obligation for
banks to help meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of communities,
including low and moderate income (LMI) communities. While the CRA has
successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest and provide services in underserved
communities, challenges related to redlining, discrimination, underinvestment, and
lack of access remain.

Since 1990, San Diego Housing Federation has been the collective voice of those
who support, build, and finance affordable housing in the San Diego region. San
Diego Housing Federation creates affordable housing opportunities for low-income
people by expanding the knowledge, capacity, and influence of the affordable
housing development community. In addition to our advocacy work, SDHF offers
 professional training, networking opportunities, and provides resources for housing
policy advocates.
The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift.
The proposal does not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on
LMI communities. We request an extension of the comment period for an additional
60 days so we have time to better understand how much CRA activity may be lost
to communities because of this proposal – an analysis the regulators did not
conduct or provide.
The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved
communities in several ways.

1) Community development (CD) activities for affordable housing
and small businesses will drop dramatically.
As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities
that support critically needed affordable housing and economic development
projects. These activities often provide the greatest CRA impact in communities as
they strengthen economic stability and mobility, quality of life, and social health of
residents and communities.
The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large"
Banks, such that many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and
expectation to serve the community development needs of their communities.[1]
According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70
California banks would see their reinvestment obligations reduced under the
proposal. Twenty-five California banks would shed their Community Development
Test responsibilities entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer be subject to
the Investment Test.[2]
The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical
community development programs that have had large impacts in LMI
communities. These include Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) which are a
key driver of affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) which
fuel economic development projects in tribal and other areas; and EQ2 equity
equivalent investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs)
that provide small business lending in underserved areas that banks cannot reach,
and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that take property off of the speculative
market.
Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting
the critical importance of the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable
 housing.[3] Approximately half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from CRA
motivated banks.[4] The regulators will even further weaken CD obligations if they
adopt the alternative proposal that Large Banks be defined as those with over $30
billion in assets.
Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance
even where they remain subject to the Community Development and Investment
Tests. The regulators signal to all banks that they can do significantly less CD
lending and investment and still pass their CRA examinations, all while seeking CRA
credit for activity outside of their CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests
that a bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1
capital were devoted to CD loans and CD investments. That percentage is far lower
than the percentage that NCRC determined banks currently devote to community
investments and loans. If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary
to meet the proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by approximately
$87.1 billion, or 85%.[5]
Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have
tremendous negative impacts on affordable housing and small business
development in our state. Asset thresholds should not be raised.
2) Banks will shed branches and BankOn.
The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and maintain
branches in LMI and BIPOC neighborhoods. By increasing the asset threshold for a
Large Bank to over $10 billion, forty-five banks in California will no longer be
subject to the Services Test and reviewed to ensure that their branches are serving
LMI communities. In California alone, NCRC estimates that 245 branches in LMI
areas and 497 branches in neighborhoods of color would be vulnerable to closure
due to this proposal.[6]

Branch presence has been tied to increased small business lending in communities.
Fewer branches will result in less small business lending. These changes will be
particularly hard hitting in rural areas of our state where smaller banks originate a
larger portion of the small business loans.

The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to
offer deposit products that are accessible to LMI residents.[7] Deposit accounts are
a gateway to credit access, financial stability, and wealth building, especially for
families who are otherwise preyed upon by predatory financial institutions. As one
important example, the BankOn program has provided access to no or low fee bank
accounts for over fourteen million people.[8] California is home to several BankOn
 coalitions that establish effective partnerships among banks, community-based
organizations, and local governments. The proposal jettisons this work.

Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million
are underbanked.[9] National banks regulated by the OCC charged billions of
dollars in overdraft and non-sufficient fund fees in 2025, and in California alone,
state-chartered banks charged over fifty-six million dollars ($56 million) in OD and
NSF fees to California consumers in 2025.[10]

3) Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.
Another consequence of the proposal's drive to raise asset thresholds is that fewer
banks will be required to report data regarding their small business, small farm,
and community development lending activities. Such data is critical to
understanding not only individual bank performance, but also the needs of local
markets. Rise Economy and its member organizations routinely analyze this CRA
data when meeting with banks and commenting on CRA exams and mergers. The
loss of such data is particularly harmful at a time when the Administration is
walking back efforts to collect and disclose detailed small business lending data
under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank Act. These changes will disproportionately
impact rural communities in our state where banks up to $10 billion in assets make
up a larger part of the small business and small farm lending markets.

4) Native American communities and Tribal Nations will not see
sufficient benefits.
The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the needs
of Native American communities and Tribal Nations which have been poorly served
by banks. The current rules focus CRA obligations in areas where banks have
branches, even though there are far fewer bank branches near Tribal lands and in
rural areas where Native Americans may reside. The proposal seeks to address this
CRA gap by encouraging banks to engage in community development and related
activities in "Indian Country" and on "Tribal and Native lands," even if outside of
bank CRA assessment areas. But many members of Tribes in California will not
benefit from this proposal as they do not live in Indian Country or on Tribal or
Native lands, as defined.

CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring within
particular geographies, given the challenges and impacts associated with historic
dispossession and federal policy. Instead, CRA evaluations should also consider
whether banks have established meaningful relationships with, and provided direct
benefits to, federally recognized Tribes as well as non-federally recognized Tribes.
Non-federally recognized Tribes have been acknowledged by, and are able to access
 programs and contracts with, various local and state entities.[11] Such processes
exist.

More specifically, the CRA rules should encourage banks to serve Tribes, nonprofit
organizations or other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned businesses
that are majority owned and controlled by Native American entrepreneurs by
providing:
●
Active outreach and engagement
●
Community development loans and investments for affordable housing and
economic development projects
●
Small farm and small business loans
●
Home mortgage loans
●
Grants to meet community needs, including for capacity building for Tribes
and support for Tribes seeking federal recognition if desired
●
Support for cultural, health and other programs
●
Bank branches
●
Deposit products such as affordable bank accounts, and
●
The provision of financial services such as financial literacy, apprenticeship
programs and technical assistance support
While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities
outside of their branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made to
encourage banks to engage in CRA related activity to directly benefit Tribes,
nonprofit organizations and other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned
businesses that are majority owned and controlled by Native American
entrepreneurs.

A better approach is needed. All banks should be subject to an impact and
responsiveness review factor during their CRA exams that evaluates and tracks
whether banks have engaged in any CRA activity directly with Tribes, Tribally
controlled entities and Native owned businesses.[12] If banks know they will be
examined for their work with Tribes, they will find mutually beneficial ways to work
with Tribes.

5) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will
suffer.
The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by
requiring a demonstrated nexus to community development projects and
mandating that large banks and their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not
use more than 15% of these grants on overhead.[13] As if this wasn't enough, the
 FDIC and OCC question whether they should end CRA eligibility for bank
grantmaking to nonprofits entirely.

Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian
measures will be except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller
groups, may be impacted.[14]

Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local
needs. They also can be key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and
investment products into communities inclined to trust long established local
organizations. Many nonprofit organizations and programs, such as downpayment
assistance programs, that support CRA related activity, rely on bank contributions
to operate. Smaller, local, and rural organizations will be least able to meet new
reporting obligations, and they risk losing bank support as a result. The proposal
would also end impactful contributions from banks for general operating support,
sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.

Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their
communities on their own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps
in their own capacity – seeking assistance with community outreach, borrower
education, credit building and repair, technical assistance, legal services, job
training and placement, tax assistance, affordable housing and other services and
programs which help residents become stable and bankable so that banks can
attract new deposits and make new loans in LMI communities.

The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and
will focus grantmaking on larger organizations that can help them more easily meet
their new FDIC and OCC-imposed regulatory burdens.

Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15%
overhead restriction will negatively affect operations and organizational success. As
one example, in order to secure CRA grants from Large Banks, CDFIs will need to
pare down costs for critical operational expenses such as underwriting, servicing,
compliance, technology, impact measurement, product development, and borrower
technical assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions,
organizations are put at risk.

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA
activity that contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large
negative impact it will have on nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding,
the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are meant to benefit from the CRA,
and the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

6) Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.
There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link
between CRA and LMI impact in the name of easing bank burden.

Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their
top two major product lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in,
and profiting from, communities, this lending by banks, subsidiaries and affiliates
must be evaluated. Further, certain products, such as small farm and consumer
loans, are important in many communities, but may not be among a bank's largest
product lines. If regulators give banks a pass and exempt smaller product lines
from CRA oversight, banks will have less incentive to consider how those products
are offered.

Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and
soundness, encourages banks to meet community needs, and engenders greater
trust in banks by the community. Eliminating categories of loan products from
scrutiny will have the opposite effect.

No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test,
which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the
definition of economic development. The CRA should create greater incentives for
banks to support the creation of jobs that pay family sustaining wages for LMI
workers and in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to provisions that would provide
CRA credit for job creation and economic development that may only benefit
middle- and upper-income workers and communities. Such provisions ignore the
purpose of CRA.

Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA
credit for large scale community infrastructure products that generate profits for
banks, would likely be financed without CRA credit, and provide only incidental
benefits to LMI residents and communities. Such an expansion of what qualifies for
CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities.
For example, banks might choose to more profitably earn CRA credit by financing
larger scale infrastructure projects, like bridges, in lieu of financing less lucrative,
smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local community needs (such as
childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or resilience
projects).

Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA
should require banks to focus their CRA activities on their CRA assessments
 areas,[15] where they are subject to more rigorous regulatory oversight (with an
exception made to encourage banks to better serve Tribes, as noted above). Banks
are not doing enough currently to meet the credit and deposit needs in the areas
where they have CRA responsibility, a problem the regulators tried to address in
the 2023 CRA Rule.[16] Yet the proposal further encourages banks to seek CRA
credit for projects in areas away from their branches, lending and CRA
responsibility. This will enable banks to get credit for activity outside of their
assessment areas, while providing no accompanying CRA obligation to better serve
these areas.

Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal goes
out of its way to encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan option to meet
their CRA responsibilities. The Strategic Plan was meant for financial institutions
that operated under a unique business model that the CRA rules were not designed
to address. The Strategic Plan option provides for minimal public input and
regulatory scrutiny and allows banks to determine the level of reinvestment activity
they need to engage in to earn a passing CRA grade. In our experience, banks with
Strategic Plans tend to reinvest less in the community and in less impactful ways.
The OCC's guidance establishing low community development thresholds for banks
opting for the Strategic Plan, [17] validates this perspective.

Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community
development efforts with little benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing,
where units are affordable at a point in time but not encumbered by deed or rent
restrictions, are a feature of today's housing market. But CRA rules should not give
banks credit for financing such activities where the benefit to LMI residents and
communities is unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it
can be a driver of bank investment in problematic landlords and displacement. CRA
credit should be given for financing of NOAH only if the project is owned and
operated by mission-driven organizations, where a majority of residents are LMI
tenants, and the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are
compliant with tenant rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents
can reasonably be expected to retain their housing.

7) Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA
ratings downgrades.
The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and redline
should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding"
ratings. Under the Biden Administration, at least a dozen banks that passed their
CRA exams were accused of redlining. This proposal will only increase that number
by narrowing what constitutes evidence of discrimination that may be considered
 for the purpose of downgrading a bank's CRA rating. Here, regulators should
consider any evidence that a bank, its affiliates, or subsidiaries engaged in
discrimination, redlining, or illegal credit practices as part of their lending, deposit,
branching, or other activities. This evidence should be considered regardless of its
source (public or private parties), or its form (informal complaints, research based
on data, testing results, comment letters, administrative actions, private litigation,
etc.). We also urge the regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity
Act authorizes Special Purpose Credit Programs, and to once again encourage
banks to develop SPCPs to better serve communities that have been redlined,
excluded, and underserved. This is the essence of CRA.

Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information
to allow for meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of
entities and activities, and will undoubtedly harm the communities that the CRA
was meant to support. If finalized in substantially the same form as proposed,
communities will suffer significantly decreased investment in affordable housing and
CDFI support, more LMI branch closures, higher bank account fees, fewer
community serving nonprofit organizations, and increased bank discrimination and
redlining with no CRA consequence. The CRA will become further removed from its
purpose of encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and
the OCC to reconsider this proposal.

Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Very Truly Yours,

Dante Golden
Senior Director of Policy, San Diego Housing Federation
cc: Rise Economy

and $10 billion would be considered Intermediate Banks; Banks over $10 billion would be
considered Large Banks.
[2] https://www.ncrc.org/cra/#Lending
[3] https://nationalmortgageprofessional.com/news/cra-proposal-could-reshape-bank-lending-
and-affordable-housing-investment
 [4] https://nextcity.org/urbanist-news/a-critical-few-weeks-ahead-for-community-development-
finance
[5] NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity
at Risk, (Sept. 10, 2026), https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-
community-development-activity-at-risk/.
[6] https://www.ncrc.org/cra/#Lending
[7] The proposal itself notes the statutory authority to consider services offered at bank offices,
see footnote eighty-seven of the proposal.
[8] https://joinbankon.org/research/
[9] NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3,
2026), https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-rollbacks/.
[10] See https://www.nclc.org/overdraft-and-nsf-fees-rise-above-12-billion/ and
https://dfpi.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/AnnualReport_2026_NSF_Master.pdf
[11] The State of California's Native American Heritage Commission provides one such
example, https://nahc.ca.gov/about/. Non-federally recognized Tribes should be substantially
involved in any effort to further clarify what constitutes a Tribe for CRA purposes.
[12] A similar impact and responsiveness review factor was part of the 2023 CRA Rule.
[13] Proposing a 15% ceiling on indirect costs is inconsistent with historic federal policy and
practice as the federal government routinely makes grant awards where more than 15% of the
grant can be used for indirect or overhead costs.
[14] The proposal notes, "The OCC also expects several potential second order impacts,
including a possible shift in CRA-motivated activity toward lending and credit services and away
from certain CD activities, in particular grants and deposit services." The proposal also notes
that provisions "may reduce CRA incentives for general operating-support grants, grants to
intermediaries, or grants to organizations with higher operating-cost ratios, which could affect
nonprofit capacity and the distribution of CRA motivated grant funding." And finally, "Some
general operating support, capacity-building grants, intermediary grants, or grants to smaller
nonprofits may receive less CRA motivated funding."
[15] CRA rules should also expand the definition of assessment areas to include areas where
banks conduct substantial lending, as the 2023 CRA Rule sought to do, as well as areas from
where deposits originate.
[16] The agencies estimated that if the 2023 Rule was in effect from 2018 through 2020, 10.3%
of banks would not have received a Satisfactory or Outstanding rating on their CRA exam. See
Federal Register, Vol. 89, No. 22, February 1, 2024, p. 6787.
[17] NCRC, Comment on the OCC's Proposed Strategic Plan Guidance (Feb. 22, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/ncrcs-comment-on-the-occs-proposed-strategic-plan-guidance/.

The San Diego Housing Federation writes to object to the harmful changes

banks to help meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of communities,

Since 1990, San Diego Housing Federation has been the collective voice of those
