Diego Housing Federation creates affordable housing opportunities for low-income
people by expanding the knowledge, capacity, and influence of the affordable
housing development community. In addition to our advocacy work, SDHF offers
 professional training, networking opportunities, and provides resources for housing
policy advocates.
The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift.
The proposal does not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on
LMI communities. We request an extension of the comment period for an additional
60 days so we have time to better understand how much CRA activity may be lost
to communities because of this proposal – an analysis the regulators did not
conduct or provide.
The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved
communities in several ways.

1) Community development (CD) activities for affordable housing
and small businesses will drop dramatically.
As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities
that support critically needed affordable housing and economic development
projects. These activities often provide the greatest CRA impact in communities as
they strengthen economic stability and mobility, quality of life, and social health of
residents and communities.
The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large"
Banks, such that many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and
expectation to serve the community development needs of their communities.[1]
According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70
California banks would see their reinvestment obligations reduced under the
proposal. Twenty-five California banks would shed their Community Development
Test responsibilities entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer be subject to
the Investment Test.[2]
The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical
community development programs that have had large impacts in LMI
communities. These include Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) which are a
key driver of affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) which
fuel economic development projects in tribal and other areas; and EQ2 equity
equivalent investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs)
that provide small business lending in underserved areas that banks cannot reach,
and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that take property off of the speculative
market.
Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting
the critical importance of the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable
 housing.[3] Approximately half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from CRA
motivated banks.[4] The regulators will even further weaken CD obligations if they
adopt the alternative proposal that Large Banks be defined as those with over $30
billion in assets.
Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance
even where they remain subject to the Community Development and Investment
Tests. The regulators signal to all banks that they can do significantly less CD
lending and investment and still pass their CRA examinations, all while seeking CRA
credit for activity outside of their CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests
that a bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1
capital were devoted to CD loans and CD investments. That percentage is far lower
than the percentage that NCRC determined banks currently devote to community
investments and loans. If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary
to meet the proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by approximately
$87.1 billion, or 85%.[5]
Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have
tremendous negative impacts on affordable housing and small business
development in our state. Asset thresholds should not be raised.
2) Banks will shed branches and BankOn.
The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and maintain
branches in LMI and BIPOC neighborhoods. By increasing the asset threshold for a
Large Bank to over $10 billion, forty-five banks in California will no longer be
subject to the Services Test and reviewed to ensure that their branches are serving
LMI communities. In California alone, NCRC estimates that 245 branches in LMI
areas and 497 branches in neighborhoods of color would be vulnerable to closure
due to this proposal.[6]

Branch presence has been tied to increased small business lending in communities.
Fewer branches will result in less small business lending. These changes will be
particularly hard hitting in rural areas of our state where smaller banks originate a
larger portion of the small business loans.

The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to
offer deposit products that are accessible to LMI residents.[7] Deposit accounts are
a gateway to credit access, financial stability, and wealth building, especially for
families who are otherwise preyed upon by predatory financial institutions. As one
important example, the BankOn program has provided access to no or low fee bank
accounts for over fourteen million people.[8] California is home to several BankOn
 coalitions that establish effective partnerships among banks, community-based
organizations, and local governments. The proposal jettisons this work.

Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million
are underbanked.[9] National banks regulated by the OCC charged billions of
dollars in overdraft and non-sufficient fund fees in 2025, and in California alone,
state-chartered banks charged over fifty-six million dollars ($56 million) in OD and
NSF fees to California consumers in 2025.[10]

3) Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.
Another consequence of the proposal's drive to raise asset thresholds is that fewer
banks will be required to report data regarding their small business, small farm,
and community development lending activities. Such data is critical to
understanding not only individual bank performance, but also the needs of local
markets. Rise Economy and its member organizations routinely analyze this CRA
data when meeting with banks and commenting on CRA exams and mergers. The
loss of such data is particularly harmful at a time when the Administration is
walking back efforts to collect and disclose detailed small business lending data
under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank Act. These changes will disproportionately
impact rural communities in our state where banks up to $10 billion in assets make
up a larger part of the small business and small farm lending markets.

4) Native American communities and Tribal Nations will not see
sufficient benefits.
The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the needs
of Native American communities and Tribal Nations which have been poorly served
by banks. The current rules focus CRA obligations in areas where banks have
branches, even though there are far fewer bank branches near Tribal lands and in
rural areas where Native Americans may reside. The proposal seeks to address this
CRA gap by encouraging banks to engage in community development and related
activities in "Indian Country" and on "Tribal and Native lands," even if outside of
bank CRA assessment areas. But many members of Tribes in California will not
benefit from this proposal as they do not live in Indian Country or on Tribal or
Native lands, as defined.

CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring within
particular geographies, given the challenges and impacts associated with historic
dispossession and federal policy. Instead, CRA evaluations should also consider
whether banks have established meaningful relationships with, and provided direct
benefits to, federally recognized Tribes as well as non-federally recognized Tribes.
Non-federally recognized Tribes have been acknowledged by, and are able to access
 programs and contracts with, various local and state entities.[11] Such processes
exist.

More specifically, the CRA rules should encourage banks to serve Tribes, nonprofit
organizations or other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned businesses
that are majority owned and controlled by Native American entrepreneurs by
providing:
●
Active outreach and engagement
●
Community development loans and investments for affordable housing and
economic development projects
●
Small farm and small business loans
●
Home mortgage loans
●
Grants to meet community needs, including for capacity building for Tribes
and support for Tribes seeking federal recognition if desired
●
Support for cultural, health and other programs
●
Bank branches
●
Deposit products such as affordable bank accounts, and
●
The provision of financial services such as financial literacy, apprenticeship
programs and technical assistance support
While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities
outside of their branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made to
encourage banks to engage in CRA related activity to directly benefit Tribes,
nonprofit organizations and other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned
businesses that are majority owned and controlled by Native American
entrepreneurs.

A better approach is needed. All banks should be subject to an impact and
responsiveness review factor during their CRA exams that evaluates and tracks
whether banks have engaged in any CRA activity directly with Tribes, Tribally
controlled entities and Native owned businesses.[12] If banks know they will be
examined for their work with Tribes, they will find mutually beneficial ways to work
with Tribes.

5) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will
suffer.
The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by
requiring a demonstrated nexus to community development projects and
mandating that large banks and their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not
use more than 15% of these grants on overhead.[13] As if this wasn't enough, the
 FDIC and OCC question whether they should end CRA eligibility for bank
grantmaking to nonprofits entirely.

Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian
measures will be except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller
groups, may be impacted.[14]

Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local
needs. They also can be key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and
investment products into communities inclined to trust long established local
organizations. Many nonprofit organizations and programs, such as downpayment
assistance programs, that support CRA related activity, rely on bank contributions
to operate. Smaller, local, and rural organizations will be least able to meet new
reporting obligations, and they risk losing bank support as a result. The proposal
would also end impactful contributions from banks for general operating support,
sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.

Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their
communities on their own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps
in their own capacity – seeking assistance with community outreach, borrower
education, credit building and repair, technical assistance, legal services, job
training and placement, tax assistance, affordable housing and other services and
programs which help residents become stable and bankable so that banks can
attract new deposits and make new loans in LMI communities.

The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and
will focus grantmaking on larger organizations that can help them more easily meet
their new FDIC and OCC-imposed regulatory burdens.

Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15%
overhead restriction will negatively affect operations and organizational success. As
one example, in order to secure CRA grants from Large Banks, CDFIs will need to
pare down costs for critical operational expenses such as underwriting, servicing,
compliance, technology, impact measurement, product development, and borrower
technical assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions,
organizations are put at risk.

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA
activity that contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large
negative impact it will have on nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding,
the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are meant to benefit from the CRA,
and the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

6) Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.
There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link
between CRA and LMI impact in the name of easing bank burden.

Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their
top two major product lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in,
and profiting from, communities, this lending by banks, subsidiaries and affiliates
must be evaluated. Further, certain products, such as small farm and consumer
loans, are important in many communities, but may not be among a bank's largest
product lines. If regulators give banks a pass and exempt smaller product lines
from CRA oversight, banks will have less incentive to consider how those products
are offered.

Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and
soundness, encourages banks to meet community needs, and engenders greater
trust in banks by the community. Eliminating categories of loan products from
scrutiny will have the opposite effect.

No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test,
which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the
definition of economic development. The CRA should create greater incentives for
banks to support the creation of jobs that pay family sustaining wages for LMI
workers and in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to provisions that would provide
CRA credit for job creation and economic development that may only benefit
middle- and upper-income workers and communities. Such provisions ignore the
purpose of CRA.

Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA
credit for large scale community infrastructure products that generate profits for
banks, would likely be financed without CRA credit, and provide only incidental
benefits to LMI residents and communities. Such an expansion of what qualifies for
CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities.
For example, banks might choose to more profitably earn CRA credit by financing
larger scale infrastructure projects, like bridges, in lieu of financing less lucrative,
smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local community needs (such as
childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or resilience
projects).

Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA
should require banks to focus their CRA activities on their CRA assessments
 areas,[15] where they are subject to more rigorous regulatory oversight (with an
exception made to encourage banks to better serve Tribes, as noted above). Banks
are not doing enough currently to meet the credit and deposit needs in the areas
where they have CRA responsibility, a problem the regulators tried to address in
the 2023 CRA Rule.[16] Yet the proposal further encourages banks to seek CRA
credit for projects in areas away from their branches, lending and CRA
responsibility. This will enable banks to get credit for activity outside of their
assessment areas, while providing no accompanying CRA obligation to better serve
these areas.

Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal goes
out of its way to encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan option to meet
their CRA responsibilities. The Strategic Plan was meant for financial institutions
that operated under a unique business model that the CRA rules were not designed
to address. The Strategic Plan option provides for minimal public input and
regulatory scrutiny and allows banks to determine the level of reinvestment activity
they need to engage in to earn a passing CRA grade. In our experience, banks with
Strategic Plans tend to reinvest less in the community and in less impactful ways.
The OCC's guidance establishing low community development thresholds for banks
opting for the Strategic Plan, [17] validates this perspective.

Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community
development efforts with little benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing,
where units are affordable at a point in time but not encumbered by deed or rent
restrictions, are a feature of today's housing market. But CRA rules should not give
banks credit for financing such activities where the benefit to LMI residents and
communities is unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it
can be a driver of bank investment in problematic landlords and displacement. CRA
credit should be given for financing of NOAH only if the project is owned and
operated by mission-driven organizations, where a majority of residents are LMI
tenants, and the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are
compliant with tenant rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents
can reasonably be expected to retain their housing.

7) Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA
ratings downgrades.
The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and redline
should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding"
ratings. Under the Biden Administration, at least a dozen banks that passed their
CRA exams were accused of redlining. This proposal will only increase that number
by narrowing what constitutes evidence of discrimination that may be considered
 for the purpose of downgrading a bank's CRA rating. Here, regulators should
consider any evidence that a bank, its affiliates, or subsidiaries engaged in
discrimination, redlining, or illegal credit practices as part of their lending, deposit,
branching, or other activities. This evidence should be considered regardless of its
source (public or private parties), or its form (informal complaints, research based
on data, testing results, comment letters, administrative actions, private litigation,
etc.). We also urge the regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity
Act authorizes Special Purpose Credit Programs, and to once again encourage
banks to develop SPCPs to better serve communities that have been redlined,
excluded, and underserved. This is the essence of CRA.

Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information
to allow for meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of
entities and activities, and will undoubtedly harm the communities that the CRA
was meant to support. If finalized in substantially the same form as proposed,
communities will suffer significantly decreased investment in affordable housing and
CDFI support, more LMI branch closures, higher bank account fees, fewer
community serving nonprofit organizations, and increased bank discrimination and
redlining with no CRA consequence. The CRA will become further removed from its
purpose of encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and
the OCC to reconsider this proposal.

Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Very Truly Yours,

Dante Golden
Senior Director of Policy, San Diego Housing Federation

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
See attached file(s)

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0216_09000064b9659c86.pdf:
FIGHTING FOR GOOD

COMMUNITY
ACTION tte

October 5, 2026
Via electronic submission

Jonathan V. Gould

Comptroller of the Currency

Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street SW

Washington, DC 20219

Travis Hill, Chairman

Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
550 17th Street NW

Washington, DC 20429

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694,
RIN 1557-AF57; FDIC RIN 3064-AG31

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

On behalf of Community Action Lehigh Valley (CALV), | write in strong opposition to

provisions of the proposed Community Reinvestment Act regulations that would

weaken bank accountability to low- and moderate-income communities. For more

than 60 years, CALV has helped people across Pennsylvania's Lehigh Valley access
housing, food, neighborhood revitalization, youth programs, advocacy, and business
development. Each year, we serve more than 100,000 people.

Through Rising Tide Community Loan Fund, our U.S. Treasury-certified Community

Development Financial Institution, we provide affordable small-business credit and

technical assistance across five counties. Banks are essential partners, supplying

| capital that allows us to finance borrowers affordably and prepare entrepreneurs for
conventional credit.

The proposal would raise the small-bank threshold to $1 billion and the large-bank
threshold to $10 billion, reducing community-development, investment, service,
branch-access, and data-accountability requirements for hundreds of institutions.
In our region, the loss of even one committed bank partner can reduce participant
CA

LEHIGH
1337 E. 5th St., Bethlehem, PA 18015 | 610.691.5620 | communityactionlv.org VALLEY
 loans, investments, deposits, grants, and technical assistance for underserved
borrowers and neighborhoods.

We also oppose restrictions on community development grants, including the
proposed 15 percent indirect-cost cap and any alternative that would exclude
grants or donations from CRA consideration. Underwriting, servicing, compliance,
technology, outreach, and individualized technical assistance are the infrastructure
of responsible community development—not incidental overhead. Grants should
be evaluated by their responsiveness and community impact, not an arbitrary cost
ratio.

Meaningful performance standards must remain. Intermediate banks should earn at
least a Satisfactory community development rating to receive an overall Satisfactory
rating. Geographic flexibility can help underserved areas, but only after a bank has
demonstrated strong performance in its own communities. Branch access and
transparent data collection must also be preserved so regulators and the public can
identify lending and service gaps.

CALV supports constructive provisions that recognize qualifying community
development loans while they remain outstanding, provide a public illustrative list
and timely advance confirmation, and credit disaster preparedness and resilience
that benefits vulnerable communities. These measures should complement—not
replace—rigorous evaluation of lending, investment, services, branch access, and
community development.

We respectfully ask the OCC and FDIC to:

e Withdraw the proposed increases in bank asset thresholds and retain the
current, annually indexed thresholds.

e Preserve meaningful evaluation of community development, investments,
services, branch access, and transparent data reporting.

e Continue CRA consideration for operating and capacity-building grants
without a fixed 15 percent indirect-cost cap.

e Require intermediate banks to demonstrate at least Satisfactory community
development performance.

e Retain constructive provisions for prior-period loans, advance confirmation,
an illustrative list, and disaster resilience, with strong safeguards and
transparency.

CA

1337 East 5th Street, Bethlehem, PA 18015 | 610.691.5620 | communityactionlv.org VALLEY
 CRA is a public promise that federally insured banks will help meet the credit needs
of every part of their communities. In the Lehigh Valley, that promise helps turn bank
capital into viable small businesses, stronger neighborhoods, and pathways to
financial stability. Modernization should produce greater transparency and deeper
community partnership—not fewer obligations and less scrutiny.

Thank you for considering CALV's experience and the consequences these changes
would have for the people and neighborhoods we serve.

Sincerely,

Dawn Godshall
Chief Executive Officer
Community Action Lehigh Valley

CA

1337 East 5th Street, Bethlehem, PA 18015 | 610.691.5620 | communityactionlv.org NAULEY

comments.text:
COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill: 
I am submitting this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)  because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).  In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.

I am the Justice Promoter for the Sisters of Charity of Cincinnati, and this religious congregation has worked in non-profit organizations that have benefitted from community reinvestment. I also bank with smaller banks that serve communities that have been disinvested from or denied loans historically and presently, and these communities need stronger protections, not less. 

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream financial services.

The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for nonprofit organizations. I am concerned that these changes are being considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57; RIN 3064-AG31
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
I am writing on behalf of Bainbridge Manor Apartments, an affordable apartment project in Bainbridge,
Ohio. I urge your agencies to preserve strong support for affordable housing as you consider changes to
the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).
Bank loans and investments help make affordable apartment projects possible. CRA encourages banks
to provide this financing, including investments through the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC).
These investments help cover development costs and keep rents affordable for low- and
moderate-income households.
I am concerned that the proposed changes could reduce banks' incentives to finance affordable housing.
If fewer banks are expected to support community development, or if investments receive less weight in
CRA evaluations, projects like ours could face fewer financing options, higher costs, and delays.
Please maintain meaningful community development responsibilities for banks of all sizes and give
strong recognition to both loans and investments in affordable housing. Please also protect support for
community organizations that serve residents and keep low- and moderate-income households at the
center of CRA.
We support clear, practical rules that help banks meet local needs. Any changes should strengthen the
partnerships that help build and preserve affordable apartments in communities like ours. Thank you for
considering these comments.
Sincerely,
Bainbridge Manor Apartments
Affordable Housing Development

CRA evaluations, projects like ours could face fewer financing options, higher costs, and delays.
Please maintain meaningful community development responsibilities for banks of all sizes and give
strong recognition to both loans and investments in affordable housing. Please also protect support for
community organizations that serve residents and keep low- and moderate-income households at the
center of CRA.
We support clear, practical rules that help banks meet local needs. Any changes should strengthen the
partnerships that help build and preserve affordable apartments in communities like ours. Thank you for
considering these comments.
Sincerely,
Alumni Apartments
Affordable Housing Development

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
See attached file(s)

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0226_09000064b965a169.pdf:
October 9,2026

Travis Hill, Chair
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
550 17th Street NW,
Washington, DC 20429
RIN 3064-AG31
Via email: comments@FDIC.gov

Jonathan V. Gould, Comptroller
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
400 7th St. SW,
Washington, DC 20219
Docket ID OCC-2026-0694
Via: https://regulations.gov/

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

South Bay Community Land Trust writes to object to the harmful changes proposed
to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed by Congress
in 1977 in response to redlining and creates an affirmative obligation for banks to
help meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of communities, including low and
moderate income (LMI) communities. While the CRA has successfully encouraged
banks to lend, invest and provide services in underserved communities, challenges
related to redlining, discrimination, underinvestment, and lack of access remain.
South Bay Community Land Trust (SBCLT) is a community-based nonprofit in Santa
Clara County working to prevent displacement and preserve permanently affordable
housing through community ownership and stewardship. We acquire and
rehabilitate properties, work directly with residents throughout the acquisition and
stewardship process, and support long-term housing stability in communities facing
displacement. SBCLT currently stewards 22 permanently affordable homes across
two preserved properties in San José.
Our work depends on access to affordable capital, lending, grants, and investments
that make property acquisition and rehabilitation possible. Strong CRA
 requirements are important to organizations like ours because they help ensure
that banks continue investing in low- and moderate-income communities and in
community-based affordable housing efforts that may otherwise struggle to
compete for conventional financing.

The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift.
The proposal does not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on
LMI communities. We request an extension of the comment period for an additional
60 days so we have time to better understand how much CRA activity may be lost
to communities because of this proposal – an analysis the regulators did not
conduct or provide.
The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved
communities in several ways.

1) Community development (CD) activities for affordable housing and small
businesses will drop dramatically.
As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities
that support critically needed affordable housing and economic development
projects. These activities often provide the greatest CRA impact in communities as
they strengthen economic stability and mobility, quality of life, and social health of
residents and communities.
The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large"
Banks, such that many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and
expectation to serve the community development needs of their communities.[1]
According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70
California banks would see their reinvestment obligations reduced under the
proposal. Twenty-five California banks would shed their Community Development
Test responsibilities entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer be subject to
the Investment Test.[2]
The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical
community development programs that have had large impacts in LMI
communities. These include Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) which are a
key driver of affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) which
fuel economic development projects in tribal and other areas; and EQ2 equity
equivalent investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs)
that provide small business lending in underserved areas that banks cannot reach,
and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that take property off of the speculative
market.
 Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting
the critical importance of the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable
housing.[3] Approximately half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from CRA
motivated banks.[4] The regulators will even further weaken CD obligations if they
adopt the alternative proposal that Large Banks be defined as those with over $30
billion in assets.
Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance
even where they remain subject to the Community Development and Investment
Tests. The regulators signal to all banks that they can do significantly less CD
lending and investment and still pass their CRA examinations, all while seeking CRA
credit for activity outside of their CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests
that a bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1
capital were devoted to CD loans and CD investments. That percentage is far lower
than the percentage that NCRC determined banks currently devote to community
investments and loans. If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary
to meet the proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by approximately
$87.1 billion, or 85%.[5]
Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have
tremendous negative impacts on affordable housing and small business
development in our state. Asset thresholds should not be raised.
2) Banks will shed branches and BankOn.
The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and maintain
branches in LMI and BIPOC neighborhoods. By increasing the asset threshold for a
Large Bank to over $10 billion, forty-five banks in California will no longer be
subject to the Services Test and reviewed to ensure that their branches are serving
LMI communities. In California alone, NCRC estimates that 245 branches in LMI
areas and 497 branches in neighborhoods of color would be vulnerable to closure
due to this proposal.[6]

Branch presence has been tied to increased small business lending in communities.
Fewer branches will result in less small business lending. These changes will be
particularly hard hitting in rural areas of our state where smaller banks originate a
larger portion of the small business loans.

The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to
offer deposit products that are accessible to LMI residents.[7] Deposit accounts are
a gateway to credit access, financial stability, and wealth building, especially for
families who are otherwise preyed upon by predatory financial institutions. As one
important example, the BankOn program has provided access to no or low fee bank
 accounts for over fourteen million people.[8] California is home to several BankOn
coalitions that establish effective partnerships among banks, community-based
organizations, and local governments. The proposal jettisons this work.

Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million
are underbanked.[9] National banks regulated by the OCC charged billions of
dollars in overdraft and non-sufficient fund fees in 2025, and in California alone,
state-chartered banks charged over fifty-six million dollars ($56 million) in OD and
NSF fees to California consumers in 2025.[10]

3) Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.
Another consequence of the proposal's drive to raise asset thresholds is that fewer
banks will be required to report data regarding their small business, small farm,
and community development lending activities. Such data is critical to
understanding not only individual bank performance, but also the needs of local
markets. Rise Economy and its member organizations routinely analyze this CRA
data when meeting with banks and commenting on CRA exams and mergers. The
loss of such data is particularly harmful at a time when the Administration is
walking back efforts to collect and disclose detailed small business lending data
under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank Act. These changes will disproportionately
impact rural communities in our state where banks up to $10 billion in assets make
up a larger part of the small business and small farm lending markets.

4) Native American communities and Tribal Nations will not see sufficient
benefits.
The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the needs
of Native American communities and Tribal Nations which have been poorly served
by banks. The current rules focus CRA obligations in areas where banks have
branches, even though there are far fewer bank branches near Tribal lands and in
rural areas where Native Americans may reside. The proposal seeks to address this
CRA gap by encouraging banks to engage in community development and related
activities in "Indian Country" and on "Tribal and Native lands," even if outside of
bank CRA assessment areas. But many members of Tribes in California will not
benefit from this proposal as they do not live in Indian Country or on Tribal or
Native lands, as defined.

CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring within
particular geographies, given the challenges and impacts associated with historic
dispossession and federal policy. Instead, CRA evaluations should also consider
whether banks have established meaningful relationships with, and provided direct
benefits to, federally recognized Tribes as well as non-federally recognized Tribes.
Non-federally recognized Tribes have been acknowledged by, and are able to access
 programs and contracts with, various local and state entities.[11] Such processes
exist.

More specifically, the CRA rules should encourage banks to serve Tribes, nonprofit
organizations or other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned businesses
that are majority owned and controlled by Native American entrepreneurs by
providing:
●
Active outreach and engagement
●
Community development loans and investments for affordable housing and
economic development projects
●
Small farm and small business loans
●
Home mortgage loans
●
Grants to meet community needs, including for capacity building for Tribes
and support for Tribes seeking federal recognition if desired
●
Support for cultural, health and other programs
●
Bank branches
●
Deposit products such as affordable bank accounts, and
●
The provision of financial services such as financial literacy, apprenticeship
programs and technical assistance support
While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities
outside of their branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made to
encourage banks to engage in CRA related activity to directly benefit Tribes,
nonprofit organizations and other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned
businesses that are majority owned and controlled by Native American
entrepreneurs.

A better approach is needed. All banks should be subject to an impact and
responsiveness review factor during their CRA exams that evaluates and tracks
whether banks have engaged in any CRA activity directly with Tribes, Tribally
controlled entities and Native owned businesses.[12] If banks know they will be
examined for their work with Tribes, they will find mutually beneficial ways to work
with Tribes.

5) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will suffer.
The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by
requiring a demonstrated nexus to community development projects and
mandating that large banks and their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not
use more than 15% of these grants on overhead.[13] As if this wasn't enough, the
FDIC and OCC question whether they should end CRA eligibility for bank
grantmaking to nonprofits entirely.

 Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian
measures will be except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller
groups, may be impacted.[14]

Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local
needs. They also can be key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and
investment products into communities inclined to trust long established local
organizations. Many nonprofit organizations and programs, such as downpayment
assistance programs, that support CRA related activity, rely on bank contributions
to operate. Smaller, local, and rural organizations will be least able to meet new
reporting obligations, and they risk losing bank support as a result. The proposal
would also end impactful contributions from banks for general operating support,
sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.

Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their
communities on their own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps
in their own capacity – seeking assistance with community outreach, borrower
education, credit building and repair, technical assistance, legal services, job
training and placement, tax assistance, affordable housing and other services and
programs which help residents become stable and bankable so that banks can
attract new deposits and make new loans in LMI communities.

The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and
will focus grantmaking on larger organizations that can help them more easily meet
their new FDIC and OCC-imposed regulatory burdens.

Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15%
overhead restriction will negatively affect operations and organizational success. As
one example, in order to secure CRA grants from Large Banks, CDFIs will need to
pare down costs for critical operational expenses such as underwriting, servicing,
compliance, technology, impact measurement, product development, and borrower
technical assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions,
organizations are put at risk.

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA
activity that contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large
negative impact it will have on nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding,
the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are meant to benefit from the CRA,
and the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

6) Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.
 There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link
between CRA and LMI impact in the name of easing bank burden.

Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their
top two major product lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in,
and profiting from, communities, this lending by banks, subsidiaries and affiliates
must be evaluated. Further, certain products, such as small farm and consumer
loans, are important in many communities, but may not be among a bank's largest
product lines. If regulators give banks a pass and exempt smaller product lines
from CRA oversight, banks will have less incentive to consider how those products
are offered.

Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and
soundness, encourages banks to meet community needs, and engenders greater
trust in banks by the community. Eliminating categories of loan products from
scrutiny will have the opposite effect.

No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test,
which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the
definition of economic development. The CRA should create greater incentives for
banks to support the creation of jobs that pay family sustaining wages for LMI
workers and in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to provisions that would provide
CRA credit for job creation and economic development that may only benefit
middle- and upper-income workers and communities. Such provisions ignore the
purpose of CRA.

Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA
credit for large scale community infrastructure products that generate profits for
banks, would likely be financed without CRA credit, and provide only incidental
benefits to LMI residents and communities. Such an expansion of what qualifies for
CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities.
For example, banks might choose to more profitably earn CRA credit by financing
larger scale infrastructure projects, like bridges, in lieu of financing less lucrative,
smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local community needs (such as
childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or resilience
projects).

Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA
should require banks to focus their CRA activities on their CRA assessments areas,
[15] where they are subject to more rigorous regulatory oversight (with an
exception made to encourage banks to better serve Tribes, as noted above). Banks
are not doing enough currently to meet the credit and deposit needs in the areas
where they have CRA responsibility, a problem the regulators tried to address in
 the 2023 CRA Rule.[16] Yet the proposal further encourages banks to seek CRA
credit for projects in areas away from their branches, lending and CRA
responsibility. This will enable banks to get credit for activity outside of their
assessment areas, while providing no accompanying CRA obligation to better serve
these areas.

Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal goes
out of its way to encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan option to meet
their CRA responsibilities. The Strategic Plan was meant for financial institutions
that operated under a unique business model that the CRA rules were not designed
to address. The Strategic Plan option provides for minimal public input and
regulatory scrutiny and allows banks to determine the level of reinvestment activity
they need to engage in to earn a passing CRA grade. In our experience, banks with
Strategic Plans tend to reinvest less in the community and in less impactful ways.
The OCC's guidance establishing low community development thresholds for banks
opting for the Strategic Plan, [17] validates this perspective.

Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community
development efforts with little benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing,
where units are affordable at a point in time but not encumbered by deed or rent
restrictions, are a feature of today's housing market. But CRA rules should not give
banks credit for financing such activities where the benefit to LMI residents and
communities is unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it
can be a driver of bank investment in problematic landlords and displacement. CRA
credit should be given for financing of NOAH only if the project is owned and
operated by mission-driven organizations, where a majority of residents are LMI
tenants, and the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are
compliant with tenant rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents
can reasonably be expected to retain their housing.

7) Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA ratings
downgrades.
The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and redline
should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding"
ratings. Under the Biden Administration, at least a dozen banks that passed their
CRA exams were accused of redlining. This proposal will only increase that number
by narrowing what constitutes evidence of discrimination that may be considered
for the purpose of downgrading a bank's CRA rating. Here, regulators should
consider any evidence that a bank, its affiliates, or subsidiaries engaged in
discrimination, redlining, or illegal credit practices as part of their lending, deposit,
branching, or other activities. This evidence should be considered regardless of its
source (public or private parties), or its form (informal complaints, research based
 on data, testing results, comment letters, administrative actions, private litigation,
etc.). We also urge the regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity
Act authorizes Special Purpose Credit Programs, and to once again encourage
banks to develop SPCPs to better serve communities that have been redlined,
excluded, and underserved. This is the essence of CRA.

Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information to
allow for meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of
entities and activities, and will undoubtedly harm the communities that the CRA
was meant to support. If finalized in substantially the same form as proposed,
communities will suffer significantly decreased investment in affordable housing and
CDFI support, more LMI branch closures, higher bank account fees, fewer
community serving nonprofit organizations, and increased bank discrimination and
redlining with no CRA consequence. The CRA will become further removed from its
purpose of encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and
the OCC to reconsider this proposal.

Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Very Truly Yours,

Laura Diaz Tovar
Laura Díaz Tovar
Director of Operations

between $1 billion and $10 billion would be considered Intermediate Banks; Banks
over $10 billion would be considered Large Banks.
[2] https://www.ncrc.org/cra/#Lending
[3] https://nationalmortgageprofessional.com/news/cra-proposal-could-reshape-
bank-lending-and-affordable-housing-investment
[4] https://nextcity.org/urbanist-news/a-critical-few-weeks-ahead-for-community-
development-finance
[5] NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community
Development Activity at Risk, (Sept. 10, 2026), https://ncrc.org/cras-new-
benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-development-activity-at-
risk/.
[6] https://www.ncrc.org/cra/#Lending
 [7] The proposal itself notes the statutory authority to consider services offered at
bank offices, see footnote eighty-seven of the proposal.
[8] https://joinbankon.org/research/
[9] NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters
(Aug. 3, 2026), https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-rollbacks/.
[10] See https://www.nclc.org/overdraft-and-nsf-fees-rise-above-12-billion/ and
https://dfpi.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/
AnnualReport_2026_NSF_Master.pdf
[11] The State of California's Native American Heritage Commission provides one
such example, https://nahc.ca.gov/about/. Non-federally recognized Tribes should
be substantially involved in any effort to further clarify what constitutes a Tribe for
CRA purposes.
[12] A similar impact and responsiveness review factor was part of the 2023 CRA
Rule.
[13] Proposing a 15% ceiling on indirect costs is inconsistent with historic federal
policy and practice as the federal government routinely makes grant awards where
more than 15% of the grant can be used for indirect or overhead costs.
[14] The proposal notes, "The OCC also expects several potential second order
impacts, including a possible shift in CRA-motivated activity toward lending and
credit services and away from certain CD activities, in particular grants and deposit
services." The proposal also notes that provisions "may reduce CRA incentives for
general operating-support grants, grants to intermediaries, or grants to
organizations with higher operating-cost ratios, which could affect nonprofit
capacity and the distribution of CRA motivated grant funding." And finally, "Some
general operating support, capacity-building grants, intermediary grants, or grants
to smaller nonprofits may receive less CRA motivated funding."
[15] CRA rules should also expand the definition of assessment areas to include
areas where banks conduct substantial lending, as the 2023 CRA Rule sought to do,
as well as areas from where deposits originate.
[16] The agencies estimated that if the 2023 Rule was in effect from 2018 through
2020, 10.3% of banks would not have received a Satisfactory or Outstanding rating
on their CRA exam. See Federal Register, Vol. 89, No. 22, February 1, 2024, p.
6787.
[17] NCRC, Comment on the OCC's Proposed Strategic Plan Guidance (Feb. 22,
2026), https://ncrc.org/ncrcs-comment-on-the-occs-proposed-strategic-plan-
guidance/.

They argue it would reduce bank investment in Low-Income Housing Tax Credit equity, especially in rural and small markets, and would cut against recent congressional action to expand private capital for affordable housing. Preserve meaningful CRA incentives for Housing Credit investment by banks in the $1.649 billion to $10 billion range

Subject: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations Proposed Rule — Docket ID OCC-
2026-0694
To Whom It May Concern:
I submit this comment regarding the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) proposed amendments to the regulations
implementing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), published at 91 Fed. Reg. 52114
(August 12, 2026). I respectfully urge the OCC and FDIC to reconsider the proposed
increase in the asset threshold separating large banks from intermediate banks and, in
particular, to preserve the current large-bank threshold as closely as possible.
The CRA was enacted in 1977 to encourage regulated financial institutions to help meet the
credit needs of the communities in which they are chartered, including low- and moderate-
income neighborhoods. 12 U.S.C. § 2901. The CRA framework should therefore be
evaluated not only in terms of regulatory burden on banks, but also in terms of whether the
proposed changes will preserve the flow of private capital to communities that depend
upon it.
That concern is particularly important for affordable rental housing financed through the
Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing Credit). CohnReznick's 2025 Housing Credit
research indicates that bank investors accounted for approximately 80 percent of the total
equity surveyed in the Housing Credit market. The importance of CRA-motivated
investment is therefore substantial.
The proposed rule would materially change the population of banks subject to the large-
bank investment test. Under the current 2026 thresholds, banks with assets above
approximately $1.649 billion are classified as large banks, while the proposal would
generally place banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion in the new
intermediate-bank category and define large banks as those with assets above $10 billion.
That change is not merely technical. AHTCC reports that at least 108 banks below the $10
billion threshold invested approximately $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity during its five-
year survey period and estimates that banks below that threshold accounted for
approximately $2 billion in Housing Credit equity when the results are extrapolated to the
 broader market. AHTCC also reports that approximately one-third of Housing Credit equity
investments from banks below the $10 billion threshold supported rural markets.
I am particularly concerned about the consequences for smaller cities, rural areas, and
other markets where the number of potential Housing Credit investors is already limited. In
a highly competitive urban market, a developer may be able to replace one investor with
another. That assumption is much less reliable in smaller or rural markets. Reducing the
number of banks that have a regulatory incentive to participate in Housing Credit
investment could therefore reduce competition for available deals, weaken equity pricing,
increase financing gaps, and ultimately reduce the number of affordable rental homes that
can be produced or preserved.
The agencies' stated objective of reducing unnecessary regulatory burden is legitimate. The
difficulty is that the proposed threshold change could accomplish that objective at the
expense of another important public objective: maintaining meaningful private-sector
investment in low- and moderate-income communities. The regulatory benefits should be
weighed against the demonstrated role that banks in the affected asset range presently
play in the Housing Credit market.
There is an additional reason for caution. Congress has recently taken steps in the opposite
direction. The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, Pub. L. 119-101, enacted July 11, 2026,
increased the statutory public-welfare-investment ceiling applicable to national banks and
state member banks from 15 percent to 20 percent. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Pub. L.
119-21, enacted in 2025, also permanently enhanced Housing Credit allocation authority
and expanded the circumstances in which the 4 percent Housing Credit can be used with
tax-exempt bond financing.
Those legislative actions demonstrate a federal policy judgment that additional private
capital should be available for affordable housing. The OCC and FDIC should be cautious
about adopting a regulatory change that could simultaneously remove a major incentive for
banks to supply that capital.
The Federal Reserve's current position is also relevant. The Board states that it continues to
apply the 1995 CRA regulations to banks. The OCC and FDIC should therefore consider
whether significant changes to the asset thresholds are necessary at this time, particularly
when a less disruptive approach is available.
Accordingly, I respectfully request that the OCC and FDIC:
1. Retain the current large-bank asset threshold to the greatest extent
practicable, rather than increasing it to $10 billion;
 2. Preserve meaningful CRA incentives for Housing Credit investment by banks in
the $1.649 billion to $10 billion asset range; and
3. If changes to the CRA asset thresholds are nevertheless adopted, select the least
disruptive threshold and include measures that protect Housing Credit
investment in rural, small-market, and other communities with limited investor
competition.
At a minimum, the agencies should fully account for the potential effects of the proposed
threshold changes on Housing Credit equity pricing, investor participation, rural markets,
and the production and preservation of affordable rental housing before adopting a final
rule.
The CRA is intended to ensure that banking resources help meet the credit needs of the
communities banks serve. The final rule should preserve that objective while avoiding
unintended reductions in private capital available for affordable housing.
Thank you for considering this comment and for placing it in the administrative record for
Docket ID OCC-2026-0694.
Respectfully,
Robert E. Rutkowski
2527 SE Faxon Court
Topeka, Kansas 66605-2086, USA
E-mail: r_e_rutkowski@att.net
