COMMENT FORM TEXT:
See attached file(s)

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0228_09000064b965c91a.pdf:
October 9, 2026

Travis Hill, Chair
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
550 17th Street NW,
Washington, DC 20429
RIN 3064-AG31
Via email: comments@FDIC.gov

Jonathan V. Gould, Comptroller
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
400 7th St. SW,
Washington, DC 20219
Docket ID OCC-2026-0694
Via: https://regulations.gov/

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

Rising Sun Center for Opportunity writes to object to the harmful changes proposed
to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed by Congress
in 1977 in response to redlining and creates an affirmative obligation for banks to
help meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of communities, including low and
moderate income (LMI) communities. While the CRA has successfully encouraged
banks to lend, invest and provide services in underserved communities, challenges
related to redlining, discrimination, underinvestment, and lack of access remain.

Rising Sun Center for Opportunity is a nonprofit organization serving the California
Bay Area and Central Valley and working at the intersection of economic equity and
climate resilience since 1994. Rising Sun Center for Opportunity advocates for
equitable access to quality green career pathways while addressing the effects of
climate change on priority communities. Investments from the Community
Reinvestment Act are essential to providing equitable access to opportunities in the
communities we serve and represent. We support the recommendations of Rise
Economy and the Greenlining Institute.

The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift.
The proposal does not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on
 LMI communities. We request an extension of the comment period for an additional
60 days so we have time to better understand how much CRA activity may be lost
to communities because of this proposal – an analysis the regulators did not
conduct or provide.
The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved
communities in several ways.

1) Community development (CD) activities for affordable housing
and small businesses will drop dramatically.
As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities
that support critically needed affordable housing and economic development
projects. These activities often provide the greatest CRA impact in communities as
they strengthen economic stability and mobility, quality of life, and social health of
residents and communities.

The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large"
Banks, such that many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and
expectation to serve the community development needs of their communities.[1]
According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70
California banks would see their reinvestment obligations reduced under the
proposal. Twenty-five California banks would shed their Community Development
Test responsibilities entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer be subject to
the Investment Test.[2]

The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical
community development programs that have had large impacts in LMI
communities. These include Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) which are a
key driver of affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) which
fuel economic development projects in tribal and other areas; and EQ2 equity
equivalent investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs)
that provide small business lending in underserved areas that banks cannot reach,
and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that take property off of the speculative
market.

Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting
the critical importance of the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable
housing.[3] Approximately half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from CRA
motivated banks.[4] The regulators will even further weaken CD obligations if they
adopt the alternative proposal that Large Banks be defined as those with over $30
billion in assets.

 Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance
even where they remain subject to the Community Development and Investment
Tests. The regulators signal to all banks that they can do significantly less CD
lending and investment and still pass their CRA examinations, all while seeking CRA
credit for activity outside of their CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests
that a bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1
capital were devoted to CD loans and CD investments. That percentage is far lower
than the percentage that NCRC determined banks currently devote to community
investments and loans. If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary
to meet the proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by approximately
$87.1 billion, or 85%.[5]

Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have
tremendous negative impacts on affordable housing and small business
development in our state. Asset thresholds should not be raised.

2) Banks will shed branches and BankOn.
The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and maintain
branches in LMI and BIPOC neighborhoods. By increasing the asset threshold for a
Large Bank to over $10 billion, forty-five banks in California will no longer be
subject to the Services Test and reviewed to ensure that their branches are serving
LMI communities. In California alone, NCRC estimates that 245 branches in LMI
areas and 497 branches in neighborhoods of color would be vulnerable to closure
due to this proposal.[6]

Branch presence has been tied to increased small business lending in communities.
Fewer branches will result in less small business lending. These changes will be
particularly hard hitting in rural areas of our state where smaller banks originate a
larger portion of the small business loans.

The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to
offer deposit products that are accessible to LMI residents.[7] Deposit accounts are
a gateway to credit access, financial stability, and wealth building, especially for
families who are otherwise preyed upon by predatory financial institutions. As one
important example, the BankOn program has provided access to no or low fee bank
accounts for over fourteen million people.[8] California is home to several BankOn
coalitions that establish effective partnerships among banks, community-based
organizations, and local governments. The proposal jettisons this work.

Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million
are underbanked.[9] National banks regulated by the OCC charged billions of
 dollars in overdraft and non-sufficient fund fees in 2025, and in California alone,
state-chartered banks charged over fifty-six million dollars ($56 million) in OD and
NSF fees to California consumers in 2025.[10]

3) Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.
Another consequence of the proposal's drive to raise asset thresholds is that fewer
banks will be required to report data regarding their small business, small farm,
and community development lending activities. Such data is critical to
understanding not only individual bank performance, but also the needs of local
markets. Rise Economy and its member organizations routinely analyze this CRA
data when meeting with banks and commenting on CRA exams and mergers. The
loss of such data is particularly harmful at a time when the Administration is
walking back efforts to collect and disclose detailed small business lending data
under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank Act. These changes will disproportionately
impact rural communities in our state where banks up to $10 billion in assets make
up a larger part of the small business and small farm lending markets.

4) Native American communities and Tribal Nations will not see
sufficient benefits.
The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the needs
of Native American communities and Tribal Nations which have been poorly served
by banks. The current rules focus CRA obligations in areas where banks have
branches, even though there are far fewer bank branches near Tribal lands and in
rural areas where Native Americans may reside. The proposal seeks to address this
CRA gap by encouraging banks to engage in community development and related
activities in "Indian Country" and on "Tribal and Native lands," even if outside of
bank CRA assessment areas. But many members of Tribes in California will not
benefit from this proposal as they do not live in Indian Country or on Tribal or
Native lands, as defined.

CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring within
particular geographies, given the challenges and impacts associated with historic
dispossession and federal policy. Instead, CRA evaluations should also consider
whether banks have established meaningful relationships with, and provided direct
benefits to, federally recognized Tribes as well as non-federally recognized Tribes.
Non-federally recognized Tribes have been acknowledged by, and are able to access
programs and contracts with, various local and state entities.[11] Such processes
exist.

More specifically, the CRA rules should encourage banks to serve Tribes, nonprofit
organizations or other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned businesses
 that are majority owned and controlled by Native American entrepreneurs by
providing:
●​ Active outreach and engagement
●​ Community development loans and investments for affordable housing and
economic development projects
●​ Small farm and small business loans
●​ Home mortgage loans
●​ Grants to meet community needs, including for capacity building for Tribes
and support for Tribes seeking federal recognition if desired
●​ Support for cultural, health and other programs
●​ Bank branches
●​ Deposit products such as affordable bank accounts, and
●​ The provision of financial services such as financial literacy, apprenticeship
programs and technical assistance support

While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities
outside of their branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made to
encourage banks to engage in CRA related activity to directly benefit Tribes,
nonprofit organizations and other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned
businesses that are majority owned and controlled by Native American
entrepreneurs.

A better approach is needed. All banks should be subject to an impact and
responsiveness review factor during their CRA exams that evaluates and tracks
whether banks have engaged in any CRA activity directly with Tribes, Tribally
controlled entities and Native owned businesses.[12] If banks know they will be
examined for their work with Tribes, they will find mutually beneficial ways to work
with Tribes.

5) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will
suffer.
The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by
requiring a demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating
that large banks and their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more
than 15% of these grants on overhead.[13] As if this wasn't enough, the FDIC and
OCC question whether they should end CRA eligibility for bank grantmaking to
nonprofits entirely.

Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian
measures will be except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller
groups, may be impacted.[14]

Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local
needs. They also can be key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and
investment products into communities inclined to trust long established local
organizations. Many nonprofit organizations and programs, such as downpayment
assistance programs, that support CRA related activity, rely on bank contributions
to operate. Smaller, local, and rural organizations will be least able to meet new
reporting obligations, and they risk losing bank support as a result. The proposal
would also end impactful contributions from banks for general operating support,
sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.

Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their
communities on their own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps
in their own capacity – seeking assistance with community outreach, borrower
education, credit building and repair, technical assistance, legal services, job
training and placement, tax assistance, affordable housing and other services and
programs which help residents become stable and bankable so that banks can
attract new deposits and make new loans in LMI communities.

The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and will
focus grantmaking on larger organizations that can help them more easily meet
their new FDIC and OCC-imposed regulatory burdens.

Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15%
overhead restriction will negatively affect operations and organizational success. As
one example, in order to secure CRA grants from Large Banks, CDFIs will need to
pare down costs for critical operational expenses such as underwriting, servicing,
compliance, technology, impact measurement, product development, and borrower
technical assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions,
organizations are put at risk.

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA
activity that contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large
negative impact it will have on nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding,
the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are meant to benefit from the CRA,
and the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

6) Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.
There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link
between CRA and LMI impact in the name of easing bank burden.

 Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their
top two major product lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in,
and profiting from, communities, this lending by banks, subsidiaries and affiliates
must be evaluated. Further, certain products, such as small farm and consumer
loans, are important in many communities, but may not be among a bank's largest
product lines. If regulators give banks a pass and exempt smaller product lines
from CRA oversight, banks will have less incentive to consider how those products
are offered.

Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and
soundness, encourages banks to meet community needs, and engenders greater
trust in banks by the community. Eliminating categories of loan products from
scrutiny will have the opposite effect.

No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test,
which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the
definition of economic development. The CRA should create greater incentives for
banks to support the creation of jobs that pay family sustaining wages for LMI
workers and in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to provisions that would provide
CRA credit for job creation and economic development that may only benefit
middle- and upper-income workers and communities. Such provisions ignore the
purpose of CRA.

Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA
credit for large scale community infrastructure products that generate profits for
banks, would likely be financed without CRA credit, and provide only incidental
benefits to LMI residents and communities. Such an expansion of what qualifies for
CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities.
For example, banks might choose to more profitably earn CRA credit by financing
larger scale infrastructure projects, like bridges, in lieu of financing less lucrative,
smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local community needs (such as
childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or resilience
projects).

Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA
should require banks to focus their CRA activities on their CRA assessments
areas,[15] where they are subject to more rigorous regulatory oversight (with an
exception made to encourage banks to better serve Tribes, as noted above). Banks
are not doing enough currently to meet the credit and deposit needs in the areas
where they have CRA responsibility, a problem the regulators tried to address in the
2023 CRA Rule.[16] Yet the proposal further encourages banks to seek CRA credit
for projects in areas away from their branches, lending and CRA responsibility. This
 will enable banks to get credit for activity outside of their assessment areas, while
providing no accompanying CRA obligation to better serve these areas.

Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal goes
out of its way to encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan option to meet
their CRA responsibilities. The Strategic Plan was meant for financial institutions
that operated under a unique business model that the CRA rules were not designed
to address. The Strategic Plan option provides for minimal public input and
regulatory scrutiny and allows banks to determine the level of reinvestment activity
they need to engage in to earn a passing CRA grade. In our experience, banks with
Strategic Plans tend to reinvest less in the community and in less impactful ways.
The OCC's guidance establishing low community development thresholds for banks
opting for the Strategic Plan, [17] validates this perspective.

Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community
development efforts with little benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing,
where units are affordable at a point in time but not encumbered by deed or rent
restrictions, are a feature of today's housing market. But CRA rules should not give
banks credit for financing such activities where the benefit to LMI residents and
communities is unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it
can be a driver of bank investment in problematic landlords and displacement. CRA
credit should be given for financing of NOAH only if the project is owned and
operated by mission-driven organizations, where a majority of residents are LMI
tenants, and the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are
compliant with tenant rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents
can reasonably be expected to retain their housing.

7) Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA
ratings downgrades.
The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and redline
should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding"
ratings. Under the Biden Administration, at least a dozen banks that passed their
CRA exams were accused of redlining. This proposal will only increase that number
by narrowing what constitutes evidence of discrimination that may be considered
for the purpose of downgrading a bank's CRA rating. Here, regulators should
consider any evidence that a bank, its affiliates, or subsidiaries engaged in
discrimination, redlining, or illegal credit practices as part of their lending, deposit,
branching, or other activities. This evidence should be considered regardless of its
source (public or private parties), or its form (informal complaints, research based
on data, testing results, comment letters, administrative actions, private litigation,
etc.). We also urge the regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity
 Act authorizes Special Purpose Credit Programs, and to once again encourage banks
to develop SPCPs to better serve communities that have been redlined, excluded,
and underserved. This is the essence of CRA.

Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information to
allow for meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of
entities and activities, and will undoubtedly harm the communities that the CRA
was meant to support. If finalized in substantially the same form as proposed,
communities will suffer significantly decreased investment in affordable housing and
CDFI support, more LMI branch closures, higher bank account fees, fewer
community serving nonprofit organizations, and increased bank discrimination and
redlining with no CRA consequence. The CRA will become further removed from its
purpose of encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and
the OCC to reconsider this proposal.

Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Sincerely,

Sneha Ayyagari
Director of Policy
Rising Sun Center for Opportunity

involved in any effort to further clarify what constitutes a Tribe for CRA purposes.
[12] A similar impact and responsiveness review factor was part of the 2023 CRA Rule.
[13] Proposing a 15% ceiling on indirect costs is inconsistent with historic federal policy and
practice as the federal government routinely makes grant awards where more than 15% of the
grant can be used for indirect or overhead costs.
[14] The proposal notes, "The OCC also expects several potential second order impacts,
including a possible shift in CRA-motivated activity toward lending and credit services and away
from certain CD activities, in particular grants and deposit services." The proposal also notes
that provisions "may reduce CRA incentives for general operating-support grants, grants to
intermediaries, or grants to organizations with higher operating-cost ratios, which could affect
nonprofit capacity and the distribution of CRA motivated grant funding." And finally, "Some
general operating support, capacity-building grants, intermediary grants, or grants to smaller
nonprofits may receive less CRA motivated funding."
[15] CRA rules should also expand the definition of assessment areas to include areas where
banks conduct substantial lending, as the 2023 CRA Rule sought to do, as well as areas from
where deposits originate.
[16] The agencies estimated that if the 2023 Rule was in effect from 2018 through 2020, 10.3%
of banks would not have received a Satisfactory or Outstanding rating on their CRA exam. See
Federal Register, Vol. 89, No. 22, February 1, 2024, p. 6787.
[17] NCRC, Comment on the OCC's Proposed Strategic Plan Guidance (Feb. 22, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/ncrcs-comment-on-the-occs-proposed-strategic-plan-guidance/.

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
I support the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act regulations to reduce unnecessary admin costs for banks. I believe reducing these expenses can improve efficiency and allow banks to put more recourses toward supporting the communities they serve. However, those savings should benefit the communities rather than simply increasing the banks profits.
I am concerned that reducing the regulatory reequipments does not guarantee those savings will be reinvested back into the community these banks serve. Banks could reduce their operating costs and expenses without increasing lending opportunities or community development programs, especially in low- and moderate-income areas. In my current role managing annual budgets I understand the need for and importance of reducing costs to benefit and support the organizations overall mission.  However, if this government is helping to reduce those costs some of those savings should be reinvested in the communities these organizations provide service to. 
I recommend regulators continue requiring banks to demonstrate how they are meeting the community credit needs with these reduced administrative costs. Ultimately, I support reducing the unnecessary costs, but these changes should benefit both the banks and the communities they serve without sacrificing accountability and responsible lending practices.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0230_09000064b965eef0.pdf:
Travis Hill, Chair
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
550 17th Street NW,
Washington, DC 20429
Submitted via email to comments@FDIC.gov

Jonathan V. Gould, Comptroller
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
400 7th St. SW,
Washington, DC 20219
Submitted electronically to https://www.regulations.gov/commenton/OCC-2026-0694-0001

October 11, 2026

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on
Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-
AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill,

The Center for Responsible Lending (CRL) appreciate this opportunity to comment on the
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) issued by the the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (collectively, "Agencies") to
revise regulations under the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). CRL is a nonprofit,
non-partisan research and policy organization dedicated to protecting and expanding home
ownership and family wealth and working to eliminate abusive financial practices.

Introduction

The Community Reinvestment Act of 1977 was, as the agencies joined by the Board of
Governors of the Federal Reserve System previously have observed, a "seminal piece of
legislation."1 It reflects Congress' judgment that because ""banks and savings institutions are
chartered to serve local convenience and needs" they "must play the leading role" in providing
the "capital required for local housing and economic development needs."2 Over the years, the
CRA has, in the agencies' words, "come to play an increasingly important role in improving
access to credit in communities–both rural and urban–around the country."3

For most of the past decade, the agencies–joined at times by the Board–have been engaged in
an ongoing effort to, as the OCC put it, "improve the CRA regulatory framework to generate
more local and national CD [community development] and economic development
activities–and thus promote economic opportunity–by encouraging banks to engage in more
lending, investment and services that benefit targeted populations (such as LMI individuals,
small farms, and small businesses) and areas in need of financial services."4 That effort
4 85 Fed. Reg. 1204, 1206 (Jan. 9, 2020).
3 60 Fed. Reg, 22156 (May 4, 1995) ("1995 Rule").
2 Community Credit Needs: Hearings on S. 406 Before the Sen. Comm. On Banking, Hous. &
Urban Affs., 95th Cong (statement of Sen. Proxmire).
1 89 Fed. Reg. 6574 (Feb. 1, 2024) ("2023 Rule" which did not appear the Federal Register until 2024)
1
 culminated in October, 2023 in the issuance of a joint regulation by all three banking agencies
which, among other things, defined new tests for large banks and established clear performance
standards and a scoring rubric to bring "greater clarity and consistency in the application of
regulations."5 That had been one of the prime objectives set forth by the Treasury Department
back in 2018 when it initiated the process that led to the promulgation of the 2023 Rule.6

Before the Rule took effect, a district court judge in the Northern District of Texas issued a
preliminary injunction against its implementation, concluding that the plaintiffs in that case were
likely to succeed on their challenge to two elements of the rule: first, the rule's requirement that
the performance of large banks and some intermediate small banks under the retail lending test
include consideration of performance in the "outside retail lending area" (defined to mean the
nationwide area outside the bank's facility-based assessment area); and second, the rule's
provision allowing a bank to receive positive credit on the retail services test for its deposit
products.7 (The district court understood the rule to require CRA examiners to "'assess the
availability and usage of a bank's deposit products' and "whether [those] . . . deposit products
offer low-cost features" even though the rule itself expressly stated that deposit products "are
only given positive consideration and may not negatively impact a bank's Retail Services and
Products Test conclusion."8)

Despite both the preliminary and limited nature of this ruling–and its misreading of the provision
of the rule addressed to deposit products–the agencies in the current proposed rule have
scrapped virtually the entire 2023 rule. The agencies seemingly no longer believe, as they did
less than three years ago, that large banks should be assessed under separate community
development financing test and community development services test. The agencies likewise
seemingly no longer believe in the need to establish, or the value in establishing, clear
performance metrics and a clear scoring rubric for the retail lending test or the community
development investment test. These are only two of the myriad of ways in which the proposed
rule deviates from the 2023 Rule.

We recognize, of course, that in the intervening years since that Rule was promulgated there
has been a change in Administration and that agencies have discretion to change their minds
and change course. But the fundamental requirement of the Administrative Procedure Act is that
agencies engage in reasoned decision-making. That means, as the Supreme Court has often
held, that when an agency changes its position it must "'display awareness that [they are]
changing position,'" and, moreover, "provide a reasoned explanation for the change."9 And,
because that is so, the APA also requires that agencies provide notice of a contemplated
change in position so that stakeholders have an opportunity to comment.
9 FDA v. Wages and White Lion Investments, LLC, __ U.S. ___ (April 2, 2025), quoting Encino Motorcars,
LLC v. Navarro, 579 U. S. 211, 221–222 (2016) (in turn quoting FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc., 556
U. S. 502, 515 (2009)).
8 89 Fed. Reg. at 6576.
7 Texas Bankers Association v. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, 728 F. Supp. 3d 412 (N.D. Tex.
2024)
6 See Treasury Press Release, April 3, 2018, https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sm0336
5 89 Fed. Reg. 6574, 6575 (Feb. 1, 2023).
2

The agencies' proposed rule here fails to do so. It makes no effort to address the multiple
judgments that the agencies arrived at, following an extensive rulemaking process, in 2023 and
to acknowledge–let alone justify–the vast set of changes being proposed in what had been the
agencies' considered judgments in 2023. The closest the agencies come to meeting the
requirements of what the Court has termed the "change-in-position doctrine" is to reference the
district court's preliminary injunction. But that preliminary judgment on two aspects of the 2023
Rule cannot, in and of itself, justify the wholesale abandonment of the 2023 Rule.

Nor can the agencies rely on the notice of proposed rulemaking that they issued in July, 2025 to
meet the requisites of the change-in-position doctrine.10 That notice afforded parties the
opportunity to comment on whether the agencies, in the interest of "restoring certainty" should
repeal the 2023 Rule and reinstate in toto the 1995 Rule and the Interagency Questions and
Answers Regarding Community Reinvestment. That notice at least provided a stated rationale
for repealing the 2023 Rule so as to avoid what the agencies referred to as "an extensive
regulatory process."11 Now that the agencies have elected to embark on such a process, it is
incumbent upon them to provide a reasoned explanation for, and an opportunity to comment on,
their decisions to depart from specific judgments reached in the 2023 Rule that are being
revisited sub silentio in the current proposal.

Accordingly, CRL urges the agencies to withdraw the NPRM to enable them to give serious
consideration to the judgments embodied in the 2023 Rule and assess what aspects the
agencies no longer believe are justified. The agencies could then issue a new NPRM offering
their reasons for so believing. No interest would be served by proceeding with the current
rulemaking and leaving it to the courts to enforce the APA's core requirements.

With that said, the remainder of this comment addresses specific aspects of the current
proposal in the event that the agencies choose to move forward with this rulemaking.

CRL shares the concerns with the proposed rule expressed in the comments being submitted
by other consumer advocate, civil rights, and economic justice advocates including the National
Community Reinvestment Coalition, the Neighborhood Homes Coalition, the National Fair
Housing Alliance, and the National Urban League. We are submitting this separate comment to
focus on issues of especial concern to us and also to highlight the extent to which the proposed
rule, in our view, deviates from the agencies' obligations under the APA.

The Small, Intermediate Small, and Large Bank Thresholds

The NPRM proposes to increase the small, intermediate small, and large bank thresholds such
that banks with under $1 billion in assets would be classified as "small" and banks with between
$1 billion and $10 billion in assets would be classified as "intermediate small," limiting the
definition of "large" banks to institutions with over $10 billion in assets.These proposed
11 Id. at 34090.
10 90 Fed. Reg, 34086 (July 18, 2025).
3
 changes–which represent, respectively, an almost 250% and over 600% increase in the current
small and intermediate small bank thresholds–would result in approximately 800 banks that are
currently treated as intermediate small-size institutions being reclassified as small banks and
roughly 400 banks that are currently treated as large banks being reclassified as intermediate
small. The agencies also have requested comment on an alternative definition that would
increase the intermediate small bank threshold to $30 billion in assets. If the agencies were to
adopt that threshold, it would move an estimated additional 80 banks with over $1.5 trillion in
assets into the intermediate small category.12

These changes would plainly disserve the purposes of the CRA in three separate ways.

●​ Community Development Investments: Moving 800 banks from the intermediate small
to small bank category means that these banks would no longer be subject to
examination under the investment test, notwithstanding the fact that the overwhelming
majority of these banks have demonstrated their ability to meet that test on at least a
satisfactory basis.13 Similarly, moving roughly 400 banks from the large to intermediate
small category would mean that these banks will no longer be evaluated on their
community development investments under an investment test that looks at the dollar
amount of qualified investments; the innovativeness or complexity of such investments;
the responsiveness of the investments to credit and community development needs; and
the degree to which the qualified investments are not routinely provided by private
investors.14 Rather, these banks' community development activities would be examined
under a much looser framework that combines both loans, investments, and services
and puts no apparent weight on the extent to which an intermediate small bank is
meeting needs not routinely met by private investors.15

In the comment it is submitting on the proposed rule, the National Community
Reinvestment Coalition has estimated that the increase in the small bank threshold
would put $500 million in current community development investments at risk and that
the proposal to increase the intermediate bank threshold to $10 billion would put an
additional $1.6 to $1.9 billion dollars of community investment at risk. The NCRC has
further estimated that the impact would be felt disproportionately in a handful of largely
rural states. This runs directly contrary to one of the purposes of the Community
Reinvestment Act which, as its very name indicates, is to encourage community
investment. And, the negative impact on the CRA's purposes would be even more
profound if the agencies were to increase the intermediate small bank threshold to $30
billion

15 See id. § 345.26(c)
14 12 CFR § 345.23(e)
13 NEED CIATE
12 CRL calculations based upon CFPB list of depository institutions with over $10 billion in assets as of
June 30, 2026. We have excluded from our calculations all credit unions with assets between $10 billion
and $30 billion.
4
 ●​ Community Services: Moving 400 banks from the large bank to the intermediate small
category would mean that these banks would no longer be subject to the services test
which "evaluates a bank's record of helping to meet the credit needs of its assessment
area(s) by analyzing both the availability and effectiveness of a bank's systems for
delivering retail banking services," including among other things, the "current distribution
of the bank's branches among low-, moderate-, middle-, and upper-income geographies"
and "the bank's record of opening and closing branches, particularly branches located in
low- or moderate-income geographies or primarily serving low- or moderate-income
individuals."16 The NCRC estimates that the affected banks have 5,000 branches in LMI
census tracts — 30% of all LMI branches nationwide; the banks would be free from a
CRA perspective to shutter as many of those branches as they chose. And, this would
come on top of a recent rule promulgated by the CFPB that interprets the Equal Credit
Opportunity Act (wrongly in our view) to remove branch opening and closing decisions
from the ambit of ECOA–a rule that the CFPB candidly acknowledged could negatively
impact "elderly, minority, and low-income consumers [who]are more likely to rely on
brick-and-mortar branch service."17 (Ironically given the current proposal, in the ECOA
Rule the CFPB sought to minimize these impacts by observing that "requirements to
serve community credit needs under the CRA will still be in effect for banks and thrifts
and could continue to deter such business decisions for some lenders."18)

●​ CRA Data and Retail Lending: The increase in the intermediate small bank threshold
would mean that roughly 400 banks that currently are required to report and are, in fact,
reporting data on their CRA lending activities would be relieved of that obligation. The
NCRC estimates that this would reduce the reported data by 12%, again with a
disproportionate effect in certain largely rural states.19 Further, the absence of such data
will hinder the ability of examiners to conduct robust CRA examinations of the institutions
relieved of the reporting obligation and would make it more difficult in other CRA exams
to compare the performance of a bank being examined with peer institutions, since the
cohort of peers would be substantially diminished. Again, these changes would
undermine the fundamental purposes of the CRA. And, again that would be even more
true with a $30 billion intermediate small bank threshold.

The only justification the NPRM offers for the proposed changes in the thresholds is that they
would achieve "a close alignment with the overall percentage of small banks at the time of the
implementation of the 1995 CRA rules."20 It is, of course, useful to know how many banks would
be affected by the proposed thresholds and the share of the market they represent. But the
distribution that would result and its "alignment" (or lack of alignment) with the distribution of
banks in 1995 is, in our view, ultimately beside the point.

20 91 Fed. Reg. at 52121.
19
18 Id. at 21662.
17 91 Fed. Reg. 21620,21644 (April 22, 2026)
16 12 C.F.R. § 345.24(a), (d)(1), (d)(2)
5
 In adopting the small bank threshold in 1995 the agencies did not seek to create a certain
distribution of small and large banks. Rather, the agencies adopted the small bank threshold in
1995 based on their judgment that for banks below that size the application of the full set of
CRA requirements would impose a "burden on those institutions disproportionate to larger
institutions" and that doing so "does not appear to be necessary to achieve the purposes of the
regulation."21 Similarly, in creating the intermediate small bank category in 2005, the agencies
did not attempt to create a certain distribution of small, small intermediate, and large banks but
rather justified their action as appropriate to reduce "undue regulatory burden on banks with
between $250 million [the then-current small bank threshold] and $1.0 billion in assets [the 2005
intermediate small bank threshold]."22 Indeed, we have not found anything in those rules that
even attempted to estimate the share of banks that would fall within these categories, let alone
attempted to justify a particular distribution of banks as between these categories.

Given the trend towards bank consolidation over the past thirty years, it is hardly surprising that
the share of banks falling under the small and intermediate small thresholds–thresholds that are
adjusted annually for inflation–has fallen. But that fact hardly justifies adjusting the thresholds to
reestablish the distribution that existed in 1995 or 2005. The fallacy in the agencies' approach is
perhaps best illustrated by a simple, albeit extreme hypothetical. Assume that the consolidation
that has been occurring within the banking industry for decades were to continue to the point
that in some future year there were only 15 remaining banks, 5 with $2 trillion in assets and 10
with $1 trillion in assets. Under the agencies' reasoning, the ten $1 trillion dollar banks would
appropriately be classified as small or intermediate small banks in order to preserve the
distribution between these categories and large banks that prevailed in 1995. Simply to state
such a proposition is to expose its flaws.

In short, the question that the agencies should be asking, to the extent they desire to consider
changes in the thresholds, is whether for some reason changes that have occurred since 1995
and 2005 have made it more difficult and costly for banks within the current (inflation-adjusted)
thresholds to satisfy their CRA obligations than was true when these thresholds were
established. Put more concretely, is there reason to believe that banks between the current
small bank threshold and $1.0 billion are no longer able to satisfy the community development
test to which they up to now have been (and still are) subject or that banks between the current
intermediate small bank threshold and $10 billion are no longer able to satisfy the reporting
requirements and investment and service test requirements to which they have been and still
are subject? Nothing in the NPRM provides any reason to answer, or basis for answering, either
of those questions in the affirmative.

Importantly, in the 2023 Rule the agencies did undertake such an inquiry and concluded that
modest adjustments in the thresholds were warranted in light of the other changes in the CRA
22 70 Fed. Reg. 44256,55258 (August 2, 2005).
21 58 Fed. Reg. 67466, 67472 (Dec. 21, 1993). The quote in text comes from the proposal that led to the
promulgation of the 1995 Rule. In promulgating that Rule, the agencies focused their Federal Register
Notice on an explanation of the changes that had been made relative to the proposal and the reasons for
those changes, so that the 1993 proposal provides the clearest articulation of the agencies' underlying
rationale. See 60 Fed. Reg. 22136 (May 4, 1995).
6
 examination framework that were being adopted. Specifically, under that Rule the small bank
threshold would have been raised to $600 million and the intermediate small bank threshold to
$2 billion The agencies explained.that this "tailoring of the framework" was designed to "strike[]
the appropriate balance between recognizing the capacity differences between banks of varying
size and maintaining a strong CRA evaluation framework that benefits communities served by
banks of all sizes and capacities."23

The fact that the agencies now have proposed both to relax the CRA requirements under the
2023 Rule and at the same time to adopt vastly higher thresholds without even acknowledging
the changes adopted in 2023 let alone attempt to explain why the agencies no longer believe
those to be the appropriate thresholds is further evidence that the NPRM fails to comply with the
"change-of-position" doctrine.

The intermediate Small Bank Assessment Framework

As discussed above, by reclassifying 400 banks as intermediate small banks, the proposed rule
would disserve the purposes of the CRA by, among other things, reducing the incentive those
banks currently have to make community development investments. But the proposed rule goes
even further in that unfortunate direction by opening the door for such banks to obtain an overall
satisfactory rating even if their rating on the community investment test is less than satisfactory.
That would mean that not only the 400 reclassified banks but also the existing 636 intermediate
small banks would all have less of an incentive–to make community development investments.

The NPRM's stated rationale for this proposed change is that it would "better focus CRA
examinations on lending performance for intermediate small banks...thereby emphasizing
lending performance consistent with the CRA's statutory focus on credit needs.24 But the lending
test focuses on only retail lending–and, in fact, on only a subset of retail loan products, a subset
which, as discussed below, the proposed rule would unjustifiably narrow. The CRA, in contrast,
speaks in terms of the "credit needs of [a bank's] entire community, including low-and
moderate-income neighborhoods."25. That phrase has always been understood to encompass
not just the credit needs of individuals, small businesses, and small farms within those
communities but also the credit needs of community development organizations and projects
within those communities. The investment test looks at a bank's activities in meeting those
needs. Thus, far from furthering the purposes of the Act, the proposed change would undermine
those purposes.

The NPRM goes on to assert that as a result of this proposed change, "banks will have
improved incentives to perform better on both tests because there is no longer an artificial
constraint that prevents banks from receiving an overall rating of ''satisfactory'' without a
''satisfactory'' rating on both tests."26 But under the current rule, intermediate small banks have a
26 92 Fed. Reg. at 52127.
25 12 U.S.C. § 2903(1).
24 92 Fed. Reg. 52114, 52127 (Aug. 12, 2026).
23 89 Fed. Reg. at 6576, 6596
7
 strong incentive to achieve at least a satisfactory rating with respect to their investments as well
as their retail lending because banks can obtain an overall satisfactory rating only if they are
rated as satisfactory on both tests. By allowing intermediate small banks to obtain a satisfactory
rating without regard to their investment performance, the proposal can only reduce the
incentive on those banks to make community development investments. Indeed, it is difficult to
fathom how the proposed rule can possibly increase the incentive to perform better on the
investment test by reducing the significance attached to that test.

Again, the 2023 Rule adopted a very different approach–one that the agencies are abandoning
without acknowledging–let alone explaining–their reasons for doing so. Under that Rule,
intermediate small banks were to be evaluated under the retail lending test and either the
current community development test or, at the bank's option, a community development
financing test. The Rule further provided for each test to receive a 50% weight in arriving at an
overall rating. The unexplained departure from this aspect of the 2023 Rule is further reason for
concluding that the NPRM fails to provide a reasoned justification for departing from twenty
years of history and experience.

The Retail Lending Test

Since the retail lending test was adopted in 1995 it has required examiners to look at "a bank's
record of helping to meet the credit needs of its assessment area(s) through its lending activities
by considering a bank's home mortgage, small business, small farm, and community
development lending." In addition, "If consumer lending constitutes a substantial majority of a
bank's business, the [examiner] will evaluate the bank's consumer lending in one or more of the
following categories: motor vehicle, credit card, home equity, other secured, and other
unsecured loans."27 This Rule in terms, applies equally to small, intermediate small, and large
banks, although in promulgating the 1995 Rule the agencies stated that "Examinations of small
banks and thrifts will be streamlined," and this may have led some examiners to confine their
examination of small and intermediate small banks to a more limited set of loan product lines.28

The NPRM proposes a major relaxation of this 30-year old retail lending test. For banks of all
sizes, including large banks, the agencies propose to limit examinations to just two product lines
with the caveat that (non-mortgage) consumer lending could be one of those two product lines
only if it constitutes a majority of a bank's lending. Further, if a bank makes loans in only one
product line, the examination would be limited to that product line.

What this means in practical terms is that banks of all sizes would no longer be expected to
attend to the credit needs of LMI individuals in their assessment area with respect to mortgages,
or to the credit needs of small businesses and farmers in those areas unless loans made
outside of those assessment areas were sufficient to qualify one or two of these as major
28 The NPRM asserts this to be the case, 91 Fed. Reg. at 52123, although there is nothing to that effect in
the FFIEC CRA Examination Procedures for Small Institutions or in the 2016 Questions and Answers, 81
Fed. Reg 48506 (July 25, 2016)..
27 12 CFR § 345.22(a).
8
 product lines. The NPRM acknowledges that this "could raise concerns that banks would no
longer be incentivized to engage in those activities going forward, which could have a negative
impact on communities" but dismisses those concerns on the ground that "potential negative
impact is unlikely to be significant because, in many instances, banks provide those loans
primarily for business reasons rather than to address CRA obligations."29

We respectfully suggest that this reasoning flies in the face of the CRA. The very reason that
Congress enacted that law was precisely because it concluded that it was not sufficient to rely
on banks' assessment of their business interest to ensure that the banks were serving the credit
needs of the entire community, including LMI segments. Absent the CRA, banks could
reasonably (or even unwisely) conclude that their capital was best deployed by serving only
affluent consumers and larger businesses who will take out larger loans and pose fewer
underwriting challenges and servicing needs than LMI individuals and small businesses. The
very point of the CRA was to establish that, in the statute's words, banks "have continuing and
affirmative obligation to help meet the credit needs of the local communities in which they are
chartered"--an obligation that is not dependent upon a bank's judgment with respect to whether
doing so is good business.30 The proposed dilution of the retail lending test flies in the face of
that determination.

Once again, it is worth noting how far the proposed rule diverges from the 2023 Rule. That Rule
proposed specific, quantitative standards for determining when closed-end home mortgages,
small business loans, and farm loans would constitute major product lines subject to CRA
examination and a similar standard for auto loans. Under those standards, at least four of these
product lines could be considered major lines for a given bank if the bank's lending volume
reached the Rule's standards. Nothing in the NPRM provides a hint of an explanation as to why
the agencies no longer believe that the 2023 Rule's standards are inappropriate.

The Investment Test

Since the investment test was adopted in 1995, large and intermediate small banks are
examined under an investment test that "evaluates a bank's record of helping to meet the credit
needs of its assessment area(s) through qualified investment."31 The term "qualified investment"
is defined to mean a lawful investment or grant "that has as its primary purpose community
development."32 And, "community development" is defined to encompass four enumerated
categories of activities.33 The NPRM proposes to revise the definition of "community
development" in multiple respects, several of which we believe to be deeply problematic.

Loans to Small Businesses and Farm: Under the current Rule, the term community
development includes "Activities that promote economic development by financing business or
33 Id. § 345.12(g).
32 Id. § 345.12(t).
31 12 C.F.R. § 345.23(a).
30 12 U.S.C. § 2901(3).
29 Id.
9
 farms that meet the size eligibility standards of the [SBA]."34 The Interagency Questions and
Answers Regarding Community Reinvestment make clear that not all financing of small
businesses or farms qualifies as community development; rather, "[t]he concept of community
development...involves both a 'size test' and a 'purpose' test that clarify what economic
development activities are considered under the CRA." Specifically, for an investment to qualify
for CRA credit under this component ot the definition of "community development," the recipient
of the investment must satisfy the size test, i.e., meet SBA size thresholds, and the purpose of
the loan must be to "promote economic development" which is then defined to mean
"permanent job creation, retention, and/or improvement" for LMI persons, in LMI geographies, in
targeted redevelopment areas."35

The NPRM proposes a quite different approach. It defines "community development" to include
"economic development" which in turn is defined to include financing for small businesses or
farms that "expands, improves, or preserves the business's or farm's productive capacity,
physical presence, or employment bases."36 In the section-by-section discussion of this
subsection, the NPRM states that the proposal "would eliminate the purpose test component of
the Interagency Questions and Answers guidance. .As a result, banks would no longer need to
demonstrate, for example, LMI job creation in order for a loan to a small business that meets the
size standards in the rules to be considered an economic development activity."37

The NPRM explains this proposal by stating that:

The agencies believe that the proposed approach focuses on the type of activities that
are likely to help support a business's or farm's growth and profitability, in turn benefiting
the community in which the business or farm is located. As a result, the agencies believe
that the proposal would be more likely to support the creation of quality jobs, including
for LMI individuals and areas."38

But the very point of the "purpose test" that the NPRM proposes to overturn was to ensure that
for an investment to qualify for CRA credit, the investment was designed to promote job creation
for LMI persons or LMI geographies. And, the necessary effect of the proposed elimination of
the test would be to extend CRA credit for small businesses investments that may be designed,
e.g, to enable a small business to expand outside of LMI areas and/or to create high-skilled jobs
that will be filled primarily by higher-income individuals. That is emphatically not what the CRA
was designed to do.

38 Id.
37 91 Fed. Reg. at 52134.
36 Proposed § 345.12, 91 Fed. Reg. at 52202. For financing of small businesses or farms to meet the
economic development test, the financing cannot be "primarily used for ongoing operating liquidity" and
cannot be "reasonably likely to result in a reduction in jobs at the business or farm."
35 Q&A § ___ 12(g)(3)-1. The Q&A goes on to state that economic development also includes financing
intermediaries that lend to, invest in, or provide technical assistance to small businesses or small farms
and providing technical assistance or shared services to such entities..
34 Id. § 345.12(g)(3).
10
 Revitalization: Under the current Rule, the definition of "community development" also include
"activities that revitalize or stabilize (i) low or moderate-income geographies; (ii) designated
disaster areas; or (iii) distressed or underserved non-metropolitan middle-income geographies"
with the latter areas limited to those designated by the banking agencies based upon specified
criteria included rates of poverty, unemployment, and population loss.39 The Q&A elaborates on
this by stating that an investment "has as its primary purpose community development when it is
designed for the express purpose of revitalizing or stabilizing low- or moderate-income areas,
designated disaster areas, or underserved or distressed nonmetropolitan middle-income
areas..."40

The proposed rule includes these categories of activities within its definition of "economic
development" so that investments to revitalize or stabilize these areas would continue to qualify
for CRA credit. However, the NPRM adds to this list activities that revitalize or stabilize "Any
other area targeted by a government entity for redevelopment that qualifies for significant
economic incentives, such as tax credits, tax abatements or grants"41 so long as the activities
are for government initiatives that are "consistent with a bona fide government revitalization or
stabilization plan." The section-by-section list as examples of these "opportunity zones, Federal
empowerment zones, State enterprise zones, or city tax incremental financing districts" and
says that "The activities in those areas typically are designed to help attract and retain
businesses and residents."

Of course, to the extent that an investment in an area targeted for economic incentives is
designed to attract and retain businesses and residents within, e.g., an LMI geography is made
to revitalize or stabilize such an area, the investment would qualify for CRA credit under the
preexisting rule. The risk of the proposed expansion in the current revitalization/stabilization rule
is that it would extend CRA credit to investments in areas that are not LMI areas or for
investment in LMI areas that actually have the predictable effect of displacing LMI residents or
small businesses. It is not difficult to envision, e.g., investments in new stadiums or in luxury
hotels or apartments obtaining CRA simply because they are located in an area that is also
receiving tax credits or abatements. That is not what the CRA was designed to encourage.

Our concerns regarding these elements of the NPRM are magnified by another aspect of the
NPRM's treatment of investments. The NPRM proposes to permit a bank to receive CRA credit
for community development investments outside of the bank's assessment that benefit areas
outside of the bank's assessment area as "as long as the institution has been responsive to
community development needs and opportunities in its assessment area(s)."42 The NPRM
proposes two alternative methods for determining what constitutes such responsiveness. The
first alternative would measure the bank's investments in its assessment area against its tier 1
capital and establish a threshold that must be satisfied before outside investments can be
considered; the second alternative would leave it to examiners to determine what constitutes an
42 Q&A § ___12(h)-6
41 Proposed § 345.12
40 Q&A § ___ 12(H)-8.
39 12 C.F.R. § 345.12(g)(4).
11
 adequate level of within-area investments "considering the dollar amount and responsiveness of
community development activities to assessment area community development needs."43

CRL agrees with the principle of permitting a bank to obtain CRA credit for qualified investments
outside of their assessment area so long as the bank is doing a sufficient job within its
assessment area. But the standards for determining when to allow such credit must be carefully
drawn lest banks begin to cherry pick investment opportunities and claim CRA credit. The
comment that the NCRC has submitted in response to the NPRM convincingly demonstrates
that the quantitative metrics set forth in the proposed rule for large and small intermediate banks
are far too lax as they would establish benchmarks substantially below the ratio of banks'
current community development financing relative to their tier 1 capital and thus could lead
some banks to reduce the amount of community development financing they provide down to
the 0.625%/1.25% levels. And, the alternative, qualitative test set forth in the proposed rule is so
indeterminate as to provide no meaningful limitation on when qualified investments outside of
assessment areas can receive CRA credit. Accordingly, we urge the agencies to reconsider and
substantially tighten this element of the proposed rule along the lines proposed by the NRC.

Consideration of Discriminatory or Other Unlawful Acts

Under the CRA regulation that has been in effect since 1995, "evaluation of a bank's CRA
performance is adversely affected by evidence of discriminatory or other illegal credit practices
in any geography by the bank."44 The regulation lists the specific laws that are relevant for these
purposes and states that an examiner "considers the nature, extent, and strength of the
evidence of the practices" as well as mitigating factors such as "the policies and procedures that
the bank...has in place to prevent the practices; any corrective action that the bank...has taken
or has committed to take, including voluntary corrective action resulting from self-assessment."45

The NPRM proposes to update the list of statutes considered for these purposes to include §
1031 of the Dodd-Frank Act which proscribes unfair, deceptive and abusive acts and practices
and also to include the Military Lending Act and the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act.46 We
applaud the agencies for proposing these additions. In response to the agencies' request for
comment as to whether "there are additional examples of discriminatory or other illegal credit
practices that should be identified" in the regulation47 we recommend that the agencies add
violations of § 805 of the Fair Housing Act of 1968, 42 U.S.C. § 3605, which was inexplicably
omitted from the 1995 Rule. We also urge the agencies to include all violations of the Truth in
Lending Act as was provided for in the 2023 Rule or, at a minimum, at the very least to include
violations of the ability-to-repay and anti-steering incentive provisions of that Act. Those
provisions were added to TILA by the Dodd-Frank Act as a response to, and a means of
47 91 Fed. Reg. at 52151
46 Proposed § 345.28(c)(1)
45 Id. § 345.28(c)(2)
44 12 C.F.R. § 345.28(c)(1)
43 Proposed Rule § 345.13(e)(2).
12
 preventing the recurrence of, the financial crisis, and violations of those provisions are surely
relevant to CRA assessments.48

At the same time that the NPRM proposes some welcome additions to the range of statutory
violations that can be considered as part of a CRA review, the NPRM severely limits when such
consideration is permissible. In contrast to the current (and long-standing) rule reaffirmed in
2023, that, as noted above, directs examiners to weigh "the nature, extent and strength of the
evidence" of unlawful auctions, the NPRM proposes two alternatives one of which would allow
consideration of a violation only if that violation had been cited in a "public enforcement action
taken by a Federal or State agency or judicial order to which a Federal or State agency is a
party" and the other of which would also allow consideration of supervisory findings of unlawful
conduct.49

The only rationale the NPRM offers for this proposed change is that it "would appropriately focus
the scope of the agencies' consideration of discriminatory or other illegal credit practices on
those violations that are most likely to have a broad impact on the bank's lending activities such
that the benefit those activities may have had in meeting community credit needs would be
adversely affected by the harm the activities caused to the community."50 At most, this rationale
would support the second option in the NPRM as that option at least allows for consideration of
supervisory findings. But the reality is that there is simply no reason to believe that violations
that are the subject, e.g., of judicial orders entered as a result of private litigation or that are
evidenced in private litigation that has not reached a final judgment are ipso facto less "likely to
have a broad impact on the bank's lending activities" than those reflected in public enforcement
actions or supervisory actions. Indeed, some of the most consequential ECOA decisions and
orders have been the result of private litigation.51

Indeed, the NPRM's reliance on public enforcement (and potentially supervisory) actions is
especially untimely–indeed ironic–in light of what has happened and is happening to the
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. That agency, of course, has exclusive supervisory and
enforcement authority with respect to consumer protection violations by banks with over $10
billion in assets. Over the past two years that agency's ability to engage in, and appetite for
engaging in, enforcement actions has been severely curtailed. Indeed, the CFPB has initiated
just one enforcement action in the past 18 months (and that action did not involve a depository
institution).52 And whatever CFPB supervisory or enforcement capacity remains would be
52 CFPB v. Synapse Financial Technologies, Case No.: 1:24-bk-10646-MB (C.D. Cal. Bankruptcy Court).
51 Baltimore Settles Landmark Fair Lending Case Against Wells Fargo, Relman Colfax PLLC (July 12,
2012), https://www.relmanlaw.com/news-baltimore-settles. Saint-Jean v. Emigrant Mortgage Co., Relman
Colfax PLLC, https://www.relmanlaw.com/cases-saint-jean-emigrant-mortgage-fair-housing-lending (last
visited Oct. 9, 2026). Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana v. Old National Bank, Relman Colfax PLLC,
https://www.relmanlaw.com/cases-fhcci-old-national-bank-fair-lending (last visited Oct. 9, 2026).
50 91 Fed. Reg. at 52151
49 Proposed § 345.28(c)(2)
48 Dodd-Frank Act §§ 1403, 1411, codified at 15 U.S.C. §§ 1639b(c), 1639c
13
 dramatically slashed under the "Workforce Reduction Plan" that the Administration put forward
in March.53

Accordingly, the agencies should adhere to the long-standing rule with respect to the
consideration of unlawful conduct.

Thank you again for the opportunity to comment on this NPRN. CRL urges you to withdraw this
proposal.

Sincerely,

The Center for Responsible Lending
53 Under that plan, the Enforcement division would shrink to just 50 employees including attorneys,
paralegals, and support staff–down from 254 in FY 2025–and the Supervision division would have just 77
employees, down from 523 in FY 2025. See Motion for Modification of Stay / Motion to Remand, National
Treasury Employees Union v. Vought, No. 25-5091 (D.C. Cir. filed Mar. 31, 2026) (attaching the CFPB
Workforce Restructuring Plan as Exhibit 1 / Attachment A).
14

comments.text:
COMMENT FORM TEXT:
See attached file(s)

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0231_09000064b965f626.pdf:
1

October 11, 2026

Chief Counsel's Office
Attention: Comment Processing
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th St SW, Suite 1E-216
Washington, DC 20219

Jennifer M. Jones
Deputy Executive Secretary
Attention: Comments—RIN 3064-AG3
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
550 17th Street NW, Washington, DC 20429

Submitted electronically via regulations.gov

RE: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, Docket ID OCC-2026-0694

Catholic Charities USA (CCUSA) appreciates the opportunity to submit comments with respect to
the proposed rule, Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, published on August 12, 2026, that
would make amendments to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. CCUSA is a national
membership organization of 170 diocesan Catholic Charities member agencies, which operate 4,200
service locations across the country. Last year, the Catholic Charities network provided help and
created hope for over 16 million people. Whether talking about housing and community
development initiatives, financial literacy or food and nutrition services offered to individuals and
families in need, or workforce development programs meant to expand economic opportunity, we
write to express concern that the proposed amendments, as written, could limit or even curtail bank
investment in these critical areas. Furthermore, the proposed changes could have the unintended
consequence of more broadly reducing private investment in rural and low- and moderate-income
communities.

Less Capital Available for Housing and Community Development Initiatives.
Last year, the Catholic Charities network helped over 196,000 people access stable housing,
provided homelessness-related services to over 719,000 individuals, provided over 38,000
permanent housing units for families, seniors, and veterans, assisted over 5,000 clients with one-on-
one housing counseling service, and responded to 50 disasters, serving 400,000 individuals. The
ability to provide and offer these services was significantly elevated by bank CRA incentives and
evaluation requirements.

We are concerned that the proposed rule changes, and particularly the increase in the asset
thresholds for small, intermediate, and large banks would eliminate community development
evaluations for 814 banks, resulting in a significant reduction in the demand for Low-Income Tax

2

Credits (LIHTCs).1 Reduced bank demand for tax credits, the predominant means by which
CCUSA agencies develop affordable multi-family housing, would undoubtedly result in less
housing being built as agencies will find subsidy to make projects viable less available, especially in
rural and small markets. This would be unfortunate considering the documented need for affordable
housing throughout the country, and particularly in rural areas.2

Less Leveraging of Philanthropic Dollars and Loss of Flexible Operating Support.
Non-profit agencies such as CCUSA and its member agencies oftentimes use CRA-motivated bank
capital to help leverage other investors and resources and to provide critical, flexible operating
support that is not necessarily tied to a specific project or program. Requiring grant funds to be tied
to a specific community development project or program and/or restricting, for banks with assets
over $10 billion, the portion of a grant that can be dedicated to administrative or indirect costs could
significantly reduce a bank's incentive to provide general operating support to non-profits providing
services that address vital community needs. In other words, contrary to the proposal's stated
purpose and as acknowledged in Table 2 and on page 52165, the proposed changes may actually
result in fewer community development grants reaching the communities they are intended to
benefit.

It should also be noted that the provision of grants oftentimes requires technical assistance and
volunteers. Under current rules, banks can receive CRA credit for grants that support community
development including general operational support. If grants funds must be tied to a specific
community development project or program, nonprofits will lose flexible funding needed to
administer the grant effectively.

For instance, a Catholic Charities agency provided this account of the overall impact of a $5,000
CRA-related grant on its financial empowerment program:

...we have received a $5,000 grant from a local bank to develop the course and
instruct. Additionally, the bank has sent volunteers to help during the teaching of [the]
course. We are looking now to create a hybrid course merging components of our Job
Readiness Program with the Financial Empowerment Program. With this hybrid, we hope to
attract employers who are willing to interview our attendees, and hope to use this as a step
to successful employment...


1 The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why It Matters, NATIONAL COMMUNITY REINVESTMENT
COALITION (October 9, 2026), ncrc.org.
2 "As of 2024, 24% of homeowners and 49% of renters were cost burdened, spending over 30% of their income on
housing each month. The rate is more severe for low-income households." Rebecca Orbach & Kristen Klurfield, What
is Affordable Housing, BIPARTISAN POLICY CENTER (October 9, 2026), bipartisanpolicy.org/.

COUNCIL OF ECON. ADVISERS, The Deterioration of Housing Affordability in Rural America (2025), whitehouse.gov.


3

Even more worrisome, language in the proposed rule under Question 10 leaves open the possibility
of eliminating CRA credit for all grants and donations.3 CCUSA strongly opposes such a change, as
it could result in significant gaps in non-profits' ability to manage and implement programs that the
broader philanthropic community is unlikely to be able to readily fill.

Reduced Accountability in Underserved Communities. One of CCUSA's biggest concerns is that
the proposed raised asset thresholds would eliminate or reduce scrutiny of branches, community-
development investments, and some banking services. As a faith-based entity working to reduce
poverty in America, we understand the importance of branch presence and investment in low- and
moderate-income communities. The raised asset thresholds would result in hundreds of banks no
longer having to report services, investments, small business loans, and other housing and
community development activities. In addition, the proposed rule would restrict the service test to
credit services and exclude deposit services, such as checking and savings products, from CRA
consideration. The experience of Catholic Charities agencies throughout the country with respect to
offering workforce development, small business, and financial empowerment programs is that these
changes would negatively impact an individual or household's ability to move out of poverty due to
increased challenges involving accessing credit and affordable checking and savings account
products.

Specifically, without regulatory pressure, banks in low- and moderate-income communities may no
longer offer deposit services. If deposit services are not available to families in those communities,
then those families cannot save their money, pay their debts, and qualify for the credit needed to buy
homes, buy or lease cars, or finance businesses. This potential outcome is opposite of the intent of
the proposed rule, as stated in the notice of proposed rulemaking.4 CCUSA urges the agencies to
ensure that banks remain accountable to low- and moderate-income communities via the various
evaluation mechanisms that are currently in place.

In closing, we thank you for the opportunity to submit comments. We believe the current CRA rules
have helped create stronger, less vulnerable communities and have served as an excellent tool and
catalyst for the investment of private and philanthropic dollars. We encourage you to ensure that the
CRA continues to be a tool for positive growth in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods by
making targeted improvements to the CRA regulations.

Respectfully submitted,



Brian Corbin, EdD
Executive Vice President, Member Services
Catholic Charities USA

3 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 FED. REG. 52114, 52129 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
4 Id. at 52114.
