COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Please see the attached letter from Green America regarding proposed Rulemaking on Community Reinvestment Act Regulations:

OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57 
FDIC RIN 3064-AG31 

Please let us know if you have any questions or need additional information.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0232_09000064b965f846.pdf:
1





October 11, 2026

Jonathan V. Gould
Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street SW
Washington, DC 20219
Attn: Chief Counsel's Office
Via Federal eRulemaking Portal – regulations.gov

Travis Hill, Chairman
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
550 17th Street, NW
Washington, DC 20429
Via email to comments@fdic.gov

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on
Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57
FDIC RIN 3064-AG31

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Green America submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC)
and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)1 because it would significantly
weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).

In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that
the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely
consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).

2



comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and
extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.

Green America's mission is to harness the power of consumers, investors, businesses,
and the marketplace to build a more sustainable and equitable world. A key part of this
mission is supporting mission-driven banks such as Community Development Financial
Institutions (CDFIs), Minority Depository Institutions (MDIs), and institutions designated as
serving low-income communities by the National Credit Union Administration.

We encourage our members and supporters to open accounts at these institutions in order
to support their mission of serving their communities. To help our 250,000 members and
supporters find these institutions, we have created a Get A Better Bank map that lists
almost 17,000 locations of over 3,000 mission driven banks and credit unions across the
country. You can find that map at https://getabetterbank.org.

The Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) is critical to these mission-driven financial
institutions because it acts as the primary regulatory incentive for larger mainstream banks
to invest in, partner with, and channel capital that they can use for basic community needs
such as mortgage loans, small business loans, or public works.

Since 2010, the CRA has helped to drive over $6 trillion in mortgages and small business
loans that have expanded home ownership, fueled entrepreneurship, and strengthened
communities across the country. Prior to the CRA, major banks would not issue loans in
neighborhoods with high percentages of people of color or working-class residents.

The CRA is mutually beneficial to large and small financial institutions. Passed to address
discrimination known as redlining, the CRA allows major banks to support specialized and
difficult-to-reach markets by working through CDFIs and MDIs that are already working in
these areas, unlocking much-needed capital and operational support.

For nearly 50 years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important
in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss, and unequal
access to mainstream financial services.


3



The proposed rule would substantially reduce CRA scrutiny for banks and change how
regulators evaluate community development, bank services, and support for nonprofit
organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without an
adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and
on communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. Across the country
from 2010-2024, banks made over $3.14 trillion mortgage loans to low- to medium-income
borrowers or in low- to medium-income census tracts; over $1.77 trillion in loans to
businesses in low- to medium-income census tracts, and $1.19 trillion in lending to small
businesses, for a total of over $6.1 trillion in CRA-qualified lending.

These institutions are using this funding to build their communities. For example, just in
2025 financing from Self-Help Federal Credit Union2, which is both a CDFI and MDI:
• Made 461 affordable home loans for families
• Created or preserved 3,735 childcare or public charter school spots
• Created or maintained 688 jobs
• Preserved or created 756 affordable housing units
• Provided financial coaching for 1,924 members

Self-Help FCU provided over $622 million in total financing, 50% of which went to
borrowers in underserved areas, and 23% to borrowers in rural areas. The credit union
serves 245,000 members in 85 locations across 10 states.

We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital
devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough to
receive a passing CRA rating.3 That percentage is far lower than the percentage the largest
banks currently devote to community investments and loans, according to the National
Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC).

NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all 69 OCC and FDIC
supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these banks currently

2 2025 Annual Report, Self-Help Federal Credit Union, accessed at https://www.self-help.org/invest-for-
impact/our-impact/annual-report/2025-annual-report
3 The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit for outside their assessment areas if the banks
surpass a benchmark of 0.625% of its tier 1 capital for community development loans and likewise 0.625%
for investments. 91 Fed. Reg. 52121, 52140 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026). We are concerned that the practical
effect of this proposal is that the benchmark will serve not as a floor, but a ceiling.

4



conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community development loans and
investments inside their assessment areas, and that the median percentage of annual
community development lending in assessment areas was 6.8% of Tier 1 capital, and a
median of 3.6% of Tier 1 capital for annual CRA qualified investments.4

If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet separate thresholds of
0.625% of Tier 1 capital for community development lending and investments, combined
activity would fall to $14.9 billion annually -- a decrease of $87.1 billion, or 85%. The
proposal encourages banks to use strategic plans to make their CRA compliance easier
and more predictable. Previous proposed guidance also set strategic benchmarks for CRA
performance well below historical levels of community development activity.5

Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic
discrimination cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments
and loans. If regulators lower expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be
accountable to communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for
communities.

For example, if Self-Help FCU's 2025 financing was reduced by 85%, that could potentially
reduce the credit union's lending capacity so much that it could make only 69 instead of
461 affordable home loans; create and maintain only 103 instead of 688 jobs; create or
preserve only 560 instead of 3,735 childcare and public charter school spots; and provide
financial coaching to only 288 instead of 1,924 members.

It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet community needs.
Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes
would reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income
communities and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or
disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.

Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
• Identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA
scrutiny under the proposal

4 NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk, (Sept.
10, 2026), https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-development-
activity-at-risk/.
5 NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk, (Sept.
10, 2026), https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-development-
activity-at-risk/.

5



• Quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation
• Assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or
populations, including rural communities and communities of color
• Consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without
sacrificing meaningful community accountability

Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, Green America believes that
the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its
impacts is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs
considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for
meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially
weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent
with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods.

We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120
days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service
evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The current
comment period closes on October 13, 2026.

Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that do
not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would allow
affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather
examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more
complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies
extend the October 13, 2026, comment deadline by at least 60 days.

Sincerely,





Cathy Becker





Todd Larsen
Responsible Finance Campaign Director

Executive Co-Director

October 11, 2026

The Honorable Jonathan V. Gould
Comptroller of the Currency
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street, SW
Washington, DC 20219

The Honorable Travis Hill
Chairman Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
550 17th Street, NW
Washington, DC 20429

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557AF57; RIN
3064-AG31
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill,
Thank you for the opportunity to provide feedback on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's
(OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposal to reform the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. My name is Thom Amdur, and I am the Executive Vice President for
Policy & Impact team at Lincoln Avenue Communities (LAC), a mission-driven affordable housing
developer and owner active in more than 34 states. We proudly provide 35,000 affordable rental units to
more than 100,000 residents across the nation. Our organization is dedicated to addressing housing
affordability pressures by developing and preserving high-quality affordable housing through both new
construction and preservation projects utilizing the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (hereinafter "LIHTC"
or "Housing Credit") program. Given our extensive experience with LIHTC, we share the broader
affordable housing industry's deep concern about the potential impacts of the CRA Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking (the "CRA NPR") on affordable housing production and preservation.
The importance of CRA for the Housing Credit:
For more than 50 years CRA has spurred bank lending and investments in homeownership, small
businesses, healthcare, childcare, and other critical community needs. Its positive impact is especially
pronounced in the production of affordable rental housing through the Housing Credit.
The Housing Credit is our nation's most important tool for the production of affordable rental housing,
and it simply could not function at its current scale and impact without the critical investments from
banks subject to CRA. Approximately 80 percent of equity investments in affordable housing communities
financed with the Housing Credit each year come from CRA-motivated bank investors. Banks make these
investments not only to receive the modest return provided by the tax advantages associated with
investing in Housing Credit properties, but also because Housing Credit investments can help satisfy their
obligations under CRA. For large banks, Housing Credit investments typically offer lower yields than many


alternative investments, making CRA examinations a pivotal incentive to invest in the Housing Credit
despite those comparatively modest returns. If the CRA NPR, as proposed, is finalized, newly classified
intermediate banks would no longer be incentivized to invest in the low- and moderate-income
communities because they would no longer be subject to the investment test, despite still having more
general community development obligations as intermediate-sized banks. This is because it is generally
easier for banks to support community development activities through lending rather than through
equity investments.
The proposed rule:
The CRA NPR proposes to reclassify banks with assets between approximately $1.65 billion and $10 billion
as intermediate banks rather than large banks. As a result, these institutions would no longer be subject
to the full CRA examination framework applicable to large banks, including the separate investment test.
According to a 2026 survey conducted by the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC), of which
we are a proud member, banks with assets between $1.649 billion and $10 billion invested at least $1.6
billion in Housing Credit equity over the five-year survey period from 2021 through 2025. Extrapolating
these results to the full Housing Credit market, AHTCC estimates that banks in this asset range invested up
to $2 billion in Housing Credit equity over the same five-year period.
The concern:
We are deeply concerned that the proposed CRA NPR could dramatically reduce the number of
institutions competing for Housing Credit investments, thereby lowering credit pricing, reducing available
equity, and ultimately resulting in the production and preservation of substantially fewer affordable
homes. This potential investment contraction would come at a time when the nation faces one of the
worst shortages of affordable housing and when Congress has recently acted to expand the resources
available for affordable unit production. The Housing Credit provisions enacted through the commonly
referred to as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act or Working Families Tax Cuts Act, were projected to finance
approximately 1.22 million additional affordable rental homes over the next decade while the bipartisan
21st Century ROAD to Housing Act raised the limit on banks' public welfare investments (PWI) to allow
them to increase their Housing Credit investments. Removing CRA incentives for Housing Credit
investment would dilute the impact of these recent congressional actions by constraining the private
capital necessary to translate expanded Housing Credit resources and investment authority into
affordable homes.
Of the 642 banks currently classified as large banks, only 256 would maintain that designation under the
proposal—a decline of over 60 percent, according to the National Association of Affordable Housing
Lenders (NAAHL). This leaves only 6 percent of banks in the current large bank classification subject to the
full CRA exam.
The negative consequences of this proposal would fall most heavily on smaller and rural communities that
currently fall within the CRA assessment areas of one or more large banks but may no longer do so if the


OCC and FDIC change the definition of a large bank as proposed. The AHTCC survey found that
approximately one-third of LIHTC equity invested through syndicators by banks in the $412 million – $10
billion asset range supported rural markets between 2021 and 2024, indicating that these banks play an
outsized role in investing in smaller communities. Credit pricing for properties in many urban areas—
which are more likely to have at least one and often multiple banks competing to invest in Housing Credit
developments because of overlapping assessment areas—tends to be much higher than pricing in rural
and other smaller communities that are not part of assessment areas for large banks subject to the
investment test.
Assessing the impact:
The OCC and FDIC included two alternatives to the primary proposal to set new thresholds for various
bank size classifications related to CRA. The first would raise the large bank asset threshold from $1.649
billion to $3.252 billion. This alternative would still have far-reaching negative consequences compared to
the current large bank threshold but is substantially less disruptive to Housing Credit investment than the
primary proposal to raise the large bank threshold to $10 billion.

According to AHTCC's survey of bank investment in the Housing Credit, 108 banks would be reclassified as
intermediate banks rather than large banks if the threshold is set at $10 billion, while just 40 would be
reclassified as intermediate banks if the large bank threshold is set at $3.252 billion (Small Business
Administration definition). Moreover, the banks that would remain subject to the separate investment
test under a $3.252 billion threshold account for approximately 86 percent of the Housing Credit equity
investment by OCC- and FDIC-regulated banks captured in the AHTCC survey with assets between $1.65
billion and $10 billion.


The second alternative proposal would be far more damaging for affordable rental housing production
than either the primary or first alternative proposals. NAAHL estimates that, under a $30 billion large
bank threshold, 17 states would see the number of large banks with investment requirements cut by half
or more. According to AHTCC, banks with assets between $10 billion and $30 billion account for more
than twice as much Housing Credit debt and equity investment as banks between $1.65 billion and $10
billion.
Conclusion
Lincoln Avenue Communities has seen the positive impact of CRA firsthand and strongly encourages the
OCC and FDIC to leave the thresholds as they currently stand under the 1995 CRA rule, consistent with the
direction the Federal Reserve—the third bank regulator—appears to be taking. If the OCC and FDIC move
forward with changes to CRA regulations, we strongly urge maintaining the lowest possible threshold for
large banks and adopting policies to strengthen the Housing Credit market in all communities, including
rural and smaller markets.
Sincerely,


Thom Amdur,
Executive Vice President, Policy & Impact
Lincoln Avenue Communities

Lincoln Avenue Communities is one of the nation's fastest-growing developers, investors, and operators of affordable and
workforce housing, providing high-quality, sustainable homes for lower- and moderate-income individuals, seniors, and families
nationwide. LAC is a mission-driven organization serving residents across 34 states.

comments.text:
COMMENT FORM TEXT:
I commend the agencies for proposing targeted revisions that preserve the familiar CRA framework while addressing unnecessary burden and providing greater clarity. I support the proposed asset-size changes, more objective community development standards, modernization of the CRA public file, and clarification of the strategic plan process. I encourage the agencies to strengthen the final rule by further considering updates to the small business and small farm loan thresholds, recognizing the contemporary economics of agricultural lending, ensuring that strategic plans maintain meaningful community commitments, and coordinating with the Federal Reserve to promote   consistent CRA standards, examination procedures, and interpretive guidance across the agencies.

Thank you for considering these comments, and each area is outlined in the attached letter. I would welcome the opportunity to provide additional information regarding the practical effect of these issues on community banks and the communities they serve.  They are vital for the success in our community.

COMMUNITY REINVESTMENT ACT COMMENT LETTER
1 | P a g e
October 11, 2026
Comment Intake
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street SW, Suite 3E-218
Washington, DC 20219
James P. Sheesley
Assistant Executive Secretary
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
550 17th Street NW
Washington, DC 20429
Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; FDIC RIN 3064-AG31
On behalf of the banking industry, I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the proposed
amendments to the Community Reinvestment Act regulations issued by the Office of the Comptroller of
the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. I am a Principal at Forvis Mazars which
provides audit, tax, consulting, and advisory services to financial institutions. Our professionals regularly
assist banks throughout the United States with regulatory, risk management, compliance, internal audit,
and operational matters. I have over 22 years experience helping community banks across the nation,
with most of that time with an emphasis on consumer compliance areas including CRA.
We support the agencies' targeted approach to retaining the core CRA framework while reducing
unnecessary regulatory burden, placing greater emphasis on lending, clarifying eligibility for community
development activities, modernizing public-file requirements, and improving the strategic plan process.
We also support the agencies' objective of maintaining meaningful CRA outcomes while improving the
clarity, consistency, and operational efficiency of the regulatory framework. The proposal would
establish asset categories of less than $1 billion for small banks, $1 billion to $10 billion for intermediate
banks, and more than $10 billion for large banks.
Asset-Size Thresholds
I strongly support the proposed changes to the CRA asset-size thresholds. Raising the small-bank
threshold to $1 billion and the intermediate-bank threshold to $10 billion would provide meaningful and
much-needed regulatory relief to community banks.
Community banks invest heavily in the communities they serve through locally originated loans,
community development activities, financial expertise, civic involvement, and longstanding relationships
with local businesses, agricultural producers, nonprofit organizations, and consumers. Regulatory
classifications should recognize that asset growth does not necessarily transform a relationship-based
community bank into a complex large institution. Much of that growth may reflect inflation, consolidation,
economic expansion, or the increasing dollar size of ordinary credit needs.
The proposed thresholds would permit many community banks to devote more resources to meeting
local credit needs rather than administering requirements designed for substantially larger and more
complex institutions. I encourage the agencies to finalize the proposed thresholds and establish a
transparent mechanism for periodically reviewing and, when warranted, adjusting them to prevent
inflation from gradually eroding the relief intended by the rule.
While some stakeholders have expressed concern that the proposal could weaken banks' obligations to
support affordable housing, community development, and economic opportunity, I believe those
concerns overlook the proposal's continued emphasis on meeting community credit needs through
 COMMUNITY REINVESTMENT ACT COMMENT LETTER
2 | P a g e
lending. Community banks have long demonstrated their commitment to local communities through
relationship-based lending, community development activities, and direct engagement with local
organizations. The proposal does not eliminate CRA obligations; rather, it seeks to refocus CRA
evaluations on activities that most directly address community credit needs while providing greater
clarity and consistency.
By reducing unnecessary compliance burden, establishing more objective community development
standards, and better aligning examination expectations, the proposal may allow community banks to
devote more resources to serving their communities rather than navigating increasingly complex
regulatory requirements. At the same time, I support maintaining strong standards for affordable
housing and community development activities and believe clearer, more objective criteria will ultimately
promote greater participation and more consistent CRA outcomes.
Objective and Consistent Community Development Standards
I support the agencies' efforts to clarify the community development definition and establish an
illustrative list of activities that qualify or do not qualify for CRA consideration, together with an optional
confirmation process.
I strongly encourage the agencies to take as much subjectivity as reasonably possible out of community
development determinations. Banks should receive consistent CRA consideration for substantially
similar activities, regardless of geographic location, examiner assignment, or supervisory agency. In
practice, uncertainty concerning the eligibility or treatment of an activity can complicate CRA planning,
particularly for activities involving multiyear commitments, multiple financing sources, or novel
structures. Uncertainty regarding whether an activity will receive CRA consideration may discourage
banks from undertaking otherwise beneficial projects, particularly when the activity requires a significant
multiyear financial commitment.
A final rule should therefore include clear, objective eligibility standards; practical examples of qualifying
and nonqualifying activities; consistent documentation expectations; and a reliable confirmation
process. An activity that satisfies the regulatory criteria should receive comparable consideration across
examinations and agencies. Examiner judgment will remain necessary to evaluate responsiveness and
impact, but it should not result in inconsistent eligibility decisions for activities with substantially similar
facts. The final rule should also explain the extent to which a confirmation remains reliable when the
underlying facts have not materially changed and identify the circumstances under which an agency
may reconsider a prior confirmation.
Online CRA Public Files and Notices
I agree that the existing physical public-file requirements are outdated. The proposal would allow banks
to maintain their CRA public files on their websites or on websites maintained on their behalf, while
branches would provide notices directing the public to the online information.
This approach reflects how customers and community organizations currently obtain information. Online
access should make CRA information more readily available, easier to search, and more convenient to
review without requiring an individual to visit a branch during business hours. It should also reduce
repetitive paper-maintenance requirements without reducing public transparency. The agencies should
also clarify expectations regarding website availability, accessibility, document retention, and continuity
procedures to follow during temporary service interruptions.
Strategic Plans and Nontraditional Banks
I support the proposed clarification of the strategic plan framework, including greater clarity regarding
required plan content, measurable goals, public participation, prefiling communications, approval,
denial, amendment, resubmission, and performance assessment. The proposal is intended to make
 COMMUNITY REINVESTMENT ACT COMMENT LETTER
3 | P a g e
strategic plans a more viable and less burdensome option for banks whose operations may not align
well with the standard performance tests.
At the same time, the agencies should proceed cautiously when applying this flexibility to nontraditional
banks. A strategic plan should reflect the institution's business model, but it should not become a
mechanism for avoiding a meaningful obligation to serve community credit and community development
needs. Nontraditional business models may require different measures, geographies, or performance
goals, but the resulting plan should still demonstrate a tangible, measurable, and sustained commitment
to the communities affected by the institution's operations.
Accordingly, the final rule should require strategic plans to include measurable goals, meaningful public
participation, transparent performance standards, and a clear connection between the institution's
activities and the communities it proposes to serve. Flexibility should accommodate legitimate
differences in business models without weakening the fundamental purpose of the CRA.
Small Business and Small Farm Loan Thresholds
I strongly recommend that the agencies consider updating the loan-size thresholds used to identify
small business and small farm loans. The current thresholds of $1 million for small business loans and
$500,000 for small farm loans no longer reasonably reflect inflation, contemporary operating costs, or
current credit-market conditions. Although the proposal does not address the small business and small
farm loan thresholds specifically, the proposal's emphasis on lending and community credit needs
provides an appropriate opportunity for the agencies to evaluate whether the existing thresholds
continue to accurately identify lending to farms and small businesses . When the agencies overhauled
CRA in the mid-1990s, they needed a simple, standardized way to measure lending to small
businesses and farms across all banks. These thresholds have remained largely unchanged since 1995
despite substantial inflation, rising operating costs, and evolving credit market conditions.
The concern is especially significant for agricultural banks. Even relatively small farming operations may
require financing that exceeds $500,000 because of the cost of land, equipment, seed, fertilizer, fuel,
livestock, crop inputs, labor, insurance, and other operating expenses. Gross farm revenues may also
exceed the existing threshold even though the operation remains locally or family owned and is
reasonably viewed as a small agricultural business within its market. A fixed dollar threshold may
exclude loans that, within the context of the local rural economy, support comparatively small or locally
owned agricultural operations.
As a result, agricultural banks may receive insufficient CRA recognition for loans that are central to
meeting the credit needs of rural communities and smaller agricultural operations. This outcome is
inconsistent with a proposal intended to refocus CRA evaluations on lending and community credit
needs.
I urge the agencies to consider increasing both thresholds to levels that better reflect present economic
conditions and lending data, and establish an automatic inflation-adjustment mechanism consistent with
other rules so the thresholds remain relevant. The agencies should also consider whether the definition
of a small farm loan should incorporate additional measures beyond a fixed gross-revenue or loan-size
limitation, particularly where those measurements fail to reflect the economics of modern agricultural
production.
A Uniform Interagency Rule
Finally, I strongly urge the OCC and FDIC to continue coordination with the Board of Governors of the
Federal Reserve System toward adoption of a single, consistent final CRA rule, examination
procedures, and interpretive guidance.
Different CRA standards based solely on a bank's charter or primary federal regulator would create
uncertainty, inconsistent treatment, unnecessary compliance costs, and competitive inequities. It could
 COMMUNITY REINVESTMENT ACT COMMENT LETTER
4 | P a g e
also complicate charter conversions, merger planning, strategic-plan development, and the structuring
of community development activities. These consequences would be particularly burdensome for
community banks with limited compliance resources.
A unified interagency framework would promote consistent examinations and public expectations while
giving banks greater certainty when making long-term lending, investment, service, and community
development commitments. Interagency alignment should therefore be treated as an essential objective
throughout the rulemaking and implementation process.
Conclusion
I commend the agencies for proposing targeted revisions that preserve the familiar CRA framework
while addressing unnecessary burden and providing greater clarity. I support the proposed asset-size
changes, more objective community development standards, modernization of the CRA public file, and
clarification of the strategic plan process. I encourage the agencies to strengthen the final rule by further
considering updates to the small business and small farm loan thresholds, recognizing the
contemporary economics of agricultural lending, ensuring that strategic plans maintain meaningful
community commitments, and coordinating with the Federal Reserve to promote consistent CRA
standards, examination procedures, and interpretive guidance across the agencies.
Thank you for considering these comments. I would welcome the opportunity to provide additional
information regarding the practical effect of these issues on community banks and the communities they
serve.
Respectfully submitted,
Shaun Harms
Principal, Financial Services
Forvis Mazars

with local businesses, agricultural producers, nonprofit organizations, and consumers. Regulatory
classifications should recognize that asset growth does not necessarily transform a relationship-based

economic expansion, or the increasing dollar size of ordinary credit needs.

transparent mechanism for periodically reviewing and, when warranted, adjusting them to prevent
inflation from gradually eroding the relief intended by the rule.

regulatory requirements. At the same time, I support maintaining strong standards for affordable
housing and community development activities and believe clearer, more objective criteria will ultimately
promote greater participation and more consistent CRA outcomes.

I support the agencies' efforts to clarify the community development definition and establish an
illustrative list of activities that qualify or do not qualify for CRA consideration, together with an optional
confirmation process.
I strongly encourage the agencies to take as much subjectivity as reasonably possible out of community

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0235_09000064b9660504.pdf:
Travis Hill, Chair
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
550 17th Street NW,
Washington, DC 20429
RIN 3064-AG31
Via email: comments@FDIC.gov

Jonathan V. Gould, Comptroller
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
400 7th St. SW,
Washington, DC 20219
Docket ID OCC-2026-0694
Via: https://regulations.gov/

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes
Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,
Public Counsel writes to object to the harmful changes proposed to the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed by Congress in 1977 in response to redlining
and creates an affirmative obligation for banks to help meet the credit, deposit, and banking
needs of communities, including low and moderate income (LMI) communities. While the CRA
has successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest and provide services in underserved
communities, challenges related to redlining, discrimination, underinvestment, and lack of
access remain.
Public Counsel is a nonprofit public interest law firm dedicated to advancing civil rights and racial,
gender, and economic justice, as well as to amplifying the power of our clients through
comprehensive legal advocacy. Founded on and strengthened by a pro bono legal service model,
our staff and volunteers seek justice through direct legal services, promote healthy and resilient
communities through education and outreach, and support community-led efforts to transform
unjust systems through litigation and policy advocacy in and beyond Los Angeles. Our clients
include individuals, small business owners, and nonprofits from communities that face systemic
barriers to accessing capital and other critical resources.
The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift. The
proposal does not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on LMI communities.
We request an extension of the comment period for an additional 60 days so we have time to
better understand how much CRA activity may be lost to communities because of this proposal
 an analysis the regulators did not conduct or provide.
The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved communities
in several ways.
 1) Community development (CD) activities for affordable housing and small businesses will drop
dramatically.
As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities that support critically
needed affordable housing and economic development projects. These activities often provide the
greatest CRA impact in communities as they strengthen economic stability and mobility, quality of life,
and social health of residents and communities.
many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and expectation to serve the community
development needs of their communities.[1] According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition
(NCRC) analysis, 70 California banks would see their reinvestment obligations reduced under the
proposal. Twenty-five California banks would shed their Community Development Test responsibilities
entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer be subject to the Investment Test.[2]
The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical community development
programs that have had large impacts in LMI communities. These include Low Income Housing Tax
Credits (LIHTCs) which are a key driver of affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC)
which fuel economic development projects in tribal and other areas; and EQ2 equity equivalent
investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) that provide small business
lending in underserved areas that banks cannot reach, and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that take
property off of the speculative market.
Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting the critical importance
of the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable housing.[3] Approximately half of nonprofit
CDFI funding comes from CRA motivated banks.[4] The regulators will even further weaken CD
obligations if they adopt the alternative proposal that Large Banks be defined as those with over $30
billion in assets.
Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance even where they
remain subject to the Community Development and Investment Tests. The regulators signal to all banks
that they can do significantly less CD lending and investment and still pass their CRA examinations, all
while seeking CRA credit for activity outside of their CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests that a
bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1 capital were devoted to CD
loans and CD investments. That percentage is far lower than the percentage that NCRC determined
banks currently devote to community investments and loans. If each bank instead conducted only the
amount necessary to meet the proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by approximately $87.1
billion, or 85%.[5]
Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have tremendous
negative impacts on affordable housing and small business development in our state. Asset thresholds
should not be raised.

 2) Banks will shed branches and BankOn.
The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and maintain branches in LMI and
BIPOC neighborhoods. By increasing the asset threshold for a Large Bank to over $10 billion, forty-five
banks in California will no longer be subject to the Services Test and reviewed to ensure that their
branches are serving LMI communities. In California alone, NCRC estimates that 245 branches in LMI
areas and 497 branches in neighborhoods of color would be vulnerable to closure due to this
proposal.[6]
Branch presence has been tied to increased small business lending in communities. Fewer branches will
result in less small business lending. These changes will be particularly hard hitting in rural areas of our
state where smaller banks originate a larger portion of the small business loans.
The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to offer deposit
products that are accessible to LMI residents.[7] Deposit accounts are a gateway to credit access,
financial stability, and wealth building, especially for families who are otherwise preyed upon by
predatory financial institutions. As one important example, the BankOn program has provided access to
no or low fee bank accounts for over fourteen million people.[8] California is home to several BankOn
coalitions that establish effective partnerships among banks, community-based organizations, and local
governments. The proposal jettisons this work.
Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million are underbanked.[9]
National banks regulated by the OCC charged billions of dollars in overdraft and non-sufficient fund fees
in 2025, and in California alone, state-chartered banks charged over fifty-six million dollars ($56 million)
in OD and NSF fees to California consumers in 2025.[10]
3) Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.
required to report data regarding their small business, small farm, and community development lending
activities. Such data is critical to understanding not only individual bank performance, but also the needs
of local markets. Rise Economy and its member organizations routinely analyze this CRA data when
meeting with banks and commenting on CRA exams and mergers. The loss of such data is particularly
harmful at a time when the Administration is walking back efforts to collect and disclose detailed small
business lending data under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank Act. These changes will disproportionately
impact rural communities in our state where banks up to $10 billion in assets make up a larger part of
the small business and small farm lending markets.
4) Native American communities and Tribal Nations will not see sufficient benefits.
The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the needs of Native American
communities and Tribal Nations which have been poorly served by banks. The current rules focus CRA
obligations in areas where banks have branches, even though there are far fewer bank branches near
Tribal lands and in rural areas where Native Americans may reside. The proposal seeks to address this
 members of Tribes in California will not benefit from this proposal as they do not live in Indian Country
or on Tribal or Native lands, as defined.
CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring within particular geographies,
given the challenges and impacts associated with historic dispossession and federal policy. Instead, CRA
evaluations should also consider whether banks have established meaningful relationships with, and
provided direct benefits to, federally recognized Tribes as well as non-federally recognized Tribes. Non-
federally recognized Tribes have been acknowledged by, and are able to access programs and contracts
with, various local and state entities.[11] Such processes exist.
More specifically, the CRA rules should encourage banks to serve Tribes, nonprofit organizations or
other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned businesses that are majority owned and
controlled by Native American entrepreneurs by providing:
 Active outreach and engagement
 Community development loans and investments for affordable housing and economic development
projects
 Small farm and small business loans
 Home mortgage loans
 Grants to meet community needs, including for capacity building for Tribes and support for Tribes
seeking federal recognition if desired
 Support for cultural, health and other programs
 Bank branches
 Deposit products such as affordable bank accounts, and
 The provision of financial services such as financial literacy, apprenticeship programs and technical
assistance support.

While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities outside of their
branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made to encourage banks to engage in CRA
related activity to directly benefit Tribes, nonprofit organizations and other entities controlled by Tribes,
and Native-owned businesses that are majority owned and controlled by Native American
entrepreneurs.
A better approach is needed. All banks should be subject to an impact and responsiveness review factor
during their CRA exams that evaluates and tracks whether banks have engaged in any CRA activity
directly with Tribes, Tribally controlled entities and Native owned businesses.[12] If banks know they will
be examined for their work with Tribes, they will find mutually beneficial ways to work with Tribes.
5) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will suffer.
The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by requiring a
demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating that large banks and their
 grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more than 15% of these grants on overhead.[13] As if
grantmaking to nonprofits entirely.
Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian measures will be
except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller groups, may be impacted.[14]
Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local needs. They also can be
key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and investment products into communities inclined
to trust long established local organizations. Many nonprofit organizations and programs, such as
downpayment assistance programs, that support CRA related activity, rely on bank contributions to
operate. Smaller, local, and rural organizations will be least able to meet new reporting obligations, and
they risk losing bank support as a result. The proposal would also end impactful contributions from
banks for general operating support, sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.
Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their communities on their
own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps in their own capacity seeking assistance
with community outreach, borrower education, credit building and repair, technical assistance, legal
services, job training and placement, tax assistance, affordable housing and other services and programs
which help residents become stable and bankable so that banks can attract new deposits and make new
loans in LMI communities.
The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and will focus grantmaking
on larger organizations that can help them more easily meet their new FDIC and OCC-imposed
regulatory burdens.

underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, impact measurement, product development, and
borrower technical assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions, organizations

 Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their top two major product

development thresholds for banks opting for the Strategic Plan, [17] validates this perspective.

not give banks credit for financing such activities where the benefit to LMI residents and communities is
unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it can be a driver of bank investment in
problematic landlords and displacement. CRA credit should be given for financing of NOAH only if the

tenants, and the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are compliant with tenant
rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents can reasonably be expected to retain their
housing.
7) Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA ratings downgrades.
-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and redline should not be allowed to
least a dozen banks that passed their CRA exams were accused of redlining. This proposal will only
increase that number by narrowing what constitutes evidence of discrimination that may be considered
a bank, its affiliates, or subsidiaries engaged in discrimination, redlining, or illegal credit practices as part
of their lending, deposit, branching, or other activities. This evidence should be considered regardless of
its source (public or private parties), or its form (informal complaints, research based on data, testing

LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and the OCC to reconsider this proposal.

Very Truly Yours,
Ritu Mahajan Estes

comments.text:
COMMENT FORM TEXT:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. Passed in 1977 to combat systemic redlining, the CRA plays a vital role in ensuring that banks fulfill their statutory obligation to meet the credit and banking needs of low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities. The proposed rollback would significantly undermine community investment, reduce accountability, and harm vulnerable neighborhoods.   I strongly urge the agencies to withdraw this proposal for the following reasons:Massive Reductions in Community Investment Accountability:By dramatically increasing the asset thresholds—raising the small bank threshold to $1 billion and the intermediate bank threshold up to $10 billion—hundreds of banks will be exempted from comprehensive large-bank examinations. Over 800 banks would lose explicit community development obligations, resulting in a severe drop in investments for affordable housing, local infrastructure, and small business lending.   Devaluation of Vital Retail Banking Services:The proposal excludes essential retail deposit services and branch availability from performance evaluations. Stripping away accountability for physical branch presence and access to affordable bank accounts risks creating "banking deserts" in LMI urban and rural neighborhoods, forcing residents to rely on predatory financial alternatives like payday lenders.   Weakened Community Development Benchmarks:The proposed 0.625% Tier 1 capital benchmark risks setting an artificially low regulatory target. In practice, this could allow financial institutions to drastically scale back their investments while still passing CRA evaluations, diverting billions of dollars away from local housing and community development initiatives.   Regulatory Fragmentation and Uncertainty:Because the Federal Reserve did not join this proposed rule, implementing these changes creates a confusing, two-tiered regulatory system across federal agencies. This inconsistency complicates enforcement and weakens the uniform oversight required to ensure equitable financial access across all communities.   The CRA was enacted to ensure that local deposits are reinvested back into the communities that generate them. Rather than loosening obligations and reducing transparency, banking regulators should focus on strengthening CRA enforcement to drive investment into underbanked urban and rural areas.I strongly encourage the OCC and FDIC to abandon this proposed rollback and preserve robust CRA standards that support sustainable, long-term economic opportunity in low-income communities.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0237_09000064b96608d9.pdf:
Chief Counsel's Office
400 7th Street, SW, Suite 1E-216
Washington, DC 20219
Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations Proposed Rule (Docket ID
OCC-2026-0694)

To Whom It May Concern:
Thank you for the opportunity to provide feedback on the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation's (FDIC) proposal to reform Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA) regulations.
The Housing Advisory Group (HAG), founded in 1993 by the pioneers of
the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC), remains our nation's most
active developer association in expanding and protecting the Credit and has
been at the center of all significant advancements to the LIHTC over the
past 40 years. HAG was specifically created to largely represent the
affordable housing developer's perspective on policy and practices, which
have contributed to the production of over 3 million units of affordable
housing.
The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, our nation's most important tool for
the production of affordable rental housing, relies heavily on investments
from banks subject to CRA. In fact, approximately 80 percent of equity
investments in the Housing Credit each year come from CRA-motivated
bank investors, according to a 2025 study by the accounting firm
CohnReznick.
For a majority of investors, including financial institutions, the LIHTC is an
attractive investment because it offsets tax liability and/or satisfies their
CRA requirements, specifically through the investment test. As we stated
above, minus the investment in the LIHTC by banks, a majority of the
affordable housing developed in the country would not be produced. The
proposed redesignation of banks between $10 billion and $1.6 billion in
assets as intermediate banks, on its own, is not a threat to this investment.
 What will have a significant impact on affordable housing production is the
elimination of the investment test for these banks.
The risk is twofold from our perspective. Developers of affordable housing
need a sufficient amount of equity through syndication of the LIHTC to
offset the capital needs of the development and to limit the debt incurred.
The more debt the development carries, the higher the rent for tenants,
making it very difficult to develop housing for prospective tenants at lower
incomes. Competition for the LIHTC is key to keeping the price of the credit
high enough to secure the equity needed for development. As an example,
an investor paying .94 per credit on a $1million allocation raises $940,000.
If there is less competition for the LIHTC and the investors offer .78, that
equals $780,000, with the development now carrying a $160,000 shortfall.
By eliminating the investment test for intermediate banks, you are
decreasing both the demand and competition for the LIHTC at a time when
the country needs millions of units of housing.
The second risk to the program is the investment deserts that will be
created by eliminating the investment test for intermediate banks. A vast
swath of the country, specifically in rural areas, is served by mid-sized
community banks, most of which would fall into this new intermediate
bank category. If they no longer were required to invest in the communities
in which they do business, these areas could see little or no affordable
housing production and might also see banks close branches as they would
no longer be required to service development in those areas.
Ironically, this NPR reclassifying banks and potentially decreasing
investment in affordable housing undercuts recent congressional action to
strengthen and expand the LIHTC and facilitate more bank investment in
the program. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act included a substantial increase
in the allocation of LIHTCs to the states for production, and it also
expanded the 4 Percent LIHTC program to increase supply. The 21st
Century ROAD to Housing Act raised the limit on banks' public welfare
investments (PWI) to allow them to increase their LIHTC investments. The
provision lifting the PWI cap would mostly impact many of the same banks
that would be reclassified as intermediate banks. Thus, the CRA changes
under consideration could greatly dilute these legislative accomplishments
and undercut congressional goals of providing more affordable rental
homes.
 Alternatives to the Primary Proposal
The NPR included two alternatives to the primary proposal to set new
thresholds for various bank size classifications.
1. The first would raise the large bank asset threshold from $1.649
billion to $3.252 billion. This alternative would be substantially
less disruptive to LIHTC investment than the primary proposal to
raise the large bank threshold to $10 billion.
2. It goes without saying that the other proposal to raise the
intermediate bank threshold to $30 billion would be far more
damaging for affordable rental housing production. It is estimated
that under a $30 billion large bank threshold, 17 states would see
the number of large banks with investment requirements cut by
half or more. In addition, banks with assets between $10 billion
and $30 billion account for more than twice as much LIHTC debt
and equity investment as banks between $1.65 billion and $10
billion.
3. Although separate from this rulemaking, we encourage the
regulators to consider the impact of bank capital requirements on
the capacity of banks to invest in the LIHTC. The historical
performance and risk characteristics of LIHTC investments are
relevant to that work, and the interaction between CRA incentives
and regulatory capital requirements will influence the amount of
bank demand for LIHTC equity.

The CRA proposal and the capital proposals affect different sides
of that equation. While changes to CRA requirements may reduce
the incentive for some banks to invest in the LIHTC, more risk-
sensitive capital treatment could increase banks' capacity to invest.
The regulators have emphasized that the capital proposals are
intended to better align regulatory capital with risk, thereby
allowing banks to invest in communities while maintaining safety
and soundness. Based on its risk profile, the LIHTC's risk
weighting should be adjusted downward which in turn could
materially expand bank's ability to invest equity in the LIHTC
market. This would decrease the capital charge to banks that invest
in LIHTC's and increase their appetite for affordable housing
investments.
Conclusion
The Housing Advisory Group strongly recommends and encourages the
OCC and FDIC to leave the thresholds as they currently stand under the
 1995 CRA rule. If the OCC and FDIC move forward with changes to CRA
designations and regulations, we strongly urge maintaining the lowest
possible threshold for large banks. For newly designated intermediate
banks, we ask that the requirement to invest, as well as lend, in the
communities in which they do business be maintained. Anything short of
this will significantly curtail competition for the LIHTC and affordable
housing production throughout the country.
Respectfully Submitted,

Robert C. Moss
Chairman
Housing Advisory Group

comments.name: Rise Economy
comments.type_basis: Rise Economy describes itself as a California alliance of over 300 member organizations, including CDFIs, nonprofit lenders, affordable housing developers and CLTs, working on economic justice.
comments.overall_quote: The FDIC and OCC should rescind this proposal.
comments.summary: Rise Economy, a California alliance of community organizations, strongly opposes the proposal. It argues the proposal will cut community development lending and investment, branch and deposit access, data transparency, nonprofit grant funding and anti-discrimination accountability. It says the agencies did not analyze these impacts. It also objects to the rule being issued without the Federal Reserve and asks for the proposal to be withdrawn.
key_asks: Withdraw or substantially reconsider the proposal, and do not raise asset thresholds.
Keep deposit services in CRA retail services evaluation, and keep the CD grant eligibility without the 15% overhead cap.
Consider any evidence of discrimination, public or private, in CRA ratings; keep the economic development purpose test; and add CRA credit for activity with Tribes.

provisions.quote: Asset thresholds should not be raised.
By withdrawing any CRA incentive for banks to offer accessible deposit services and withdrawing scrutiny of banks for the failure to serve branching and deposit needs
The 15% cap appears unrealistic.
We strongly believe that assessment area definitions should be broadened to include areas where banks conduct substantial lending, and where bank customers live and from where deposits originate.
Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas.
The proposal would limit such evidence only to public enforcement actions, even though many if not most findings of discrimination are addressed through non-public enforcement actions.
The proposal would eliminate the purpose test from the definition of economic development, which has encouraged the financing of projects that create jobs and that provide LMI benefit.
We also object to proposed limitations on what information should be retained in each Bank's CRA Public File and made available to the public.
Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment.
By proposing to hide data that is currently available to regulators and the public, this proposal would make CRA oversight ever more difficult.
We urge the FDIC and the OCC to withdraw or substantially reconsider this proposal
Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA.
