COMMENT FORM TEXT:
See attached file(s)

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0238_09000064b9660939.pdf:
1

October 11, 2026

Travis Hill, Chair
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
550 17th Street NW,
Washington, DC 20429
RIN 3064-AG31
Via email: comments@FDIC.gov

Jonathan V. Gould, Comptroller
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
400 7th St. SW,
Washington, DC 20219
Docket ID OCC-2026-0694
Via: https://regulations.gov/

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

Rise Economy submits these comments in opposition to the harmful changes
proposed to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was
passed by Congress in 1977 in response to redlining and to create an
affirmative obligation for banks to help meet the credit, deposit, investment,
and financial services needs of communities, including low and moderate
income (LMI) communities. While the CRA has successfully encouraged
banks to lend, invest and provide services in underserved communities,1

1 Rise Economy and its member organizations have been able to work with banks to designate over $125
billion in lending and investment to California communities over the last six years. NCRC analysis
suggests the CRA has generated $488 billion in mortgages to LMI borrowers or in LMI tracts, and $228
billion in lending to businesses located in LMI tracts in California from 2010 to 2024,
(https://www.ncrc.org/cra/#Lending). The National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders reports
that in 2024 alone, CRA incentivized more than $430 billion in loans and investments in low- and
moderate-income communities, nearly six times the combined federal budgets of HUD, USDA's Rural
Housing Service, the Small Business Administration, and the CDFI Fund, citing Center for Affordable
Housing Lending, Incentive to Impact (July 2026). The Urban Institute estimates that the CRA encouraged




2

challenges related to redlining, discrimination, underinvestment, and lack of
access remain.

The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant
to uplift. The proposal does not justify those changes or meaningfully
consider how or where those changes would impact the CRA's goal of
encouraging banks to help meet the needs of LMI communities.2 As such the
proposal does not provide the public with a meaningful opportunity to
comment on likely effects.

We previously requested an extension of the comment period for an
additional sixty (60) days so that we would have time to thoroughly consider
this wide-ranging proposal that will have substantial, negative impacts on
our work and our communities.3 With additional time, we would have been
able to conduct more precise analysis regarding how much community
development lending and investment, mortgage and small business lending,
branch and bank account access, and contributions activity may be lost to
communities as a result of this proposal, and how this will impact
communities – an analysis the regulators did not conduct or provide.

Rise Economy is a California-based alliance representing over three-
hundred-member organizations that work to create systemic change and
economic justice in BIPOC and low-income communities in our state. Our
coalition includes organizations that partner with banks to help them meet
local community banking needs, including Community Development
Financial Institutions (CDFIs) and other nonprofit lenders, technical
assistance providers to small businesses and small farms, affordable housing
developers and Community Land Trusts (CLTs), financial literacy and home

$356 billion in reported CRA loan and investment dollars in 2024. https://www.urban.org/urban-
wire/proposed-changes-community-reinvestment-act-could-weaken-incentives-banks-invest-low-and
2 Urban Institute analysis notes: "The proposal states that decisions on options proposed are based on
"supervisory experience" but provides few details on what that might entail. More information on the
experiences and data undergirding these proposals would help inform public comment."
https://www.urban.org/urban-wire/proposed-changes-community-reinvestment-act-could-weaken-
incentives-banks-invest-low-and
3 https://rise-economy.org/press-release/rise-economy-ncrc-and-374-organizations-call-for-more-time-
to-assess-proposed-cra-rollbacks/




3

loan counselors, fair housing and fair lending organizations, community
development corporations, legal service offices, faith-based groups, Native
American and Tribal Nation-serving entities, advocacy organizations and
other community organizations that work to stabilize and build wealth in
communities.

Our member organizations and their communities depend on faithful
adherence to, and implementation of, strong CRA rules to ensure that all
Californians have equal access to banking services and the ability to build
intergenerational wealth for their families.

The proposal, if finalized in substantially the same form, will significantly
undermine community reinvestment in underserved communities in several
ways. This comment will identify programs, services, and communities that
will be harmed by the proposal, all of which weigh heavily against reshaping
the CRA in this fashion. The FDIC and OCC should rescind this proposal.

1) Community development activities in support of affordable
housing and small business development will drop
dramatically.
As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development
activities that support critically needed affordable housing and economic
development projects. These activities often provide the greatest CRA
impact in communities as they strengthen economic stability and mobility,
quality of life, and the health of residents and communities.
Fewer banks will be subject to Community Development and Investment
Tests. The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate"
and "Large" Banks, such that many banks will be subject to substantially
less CRA scrutiny and expectation to serve the community development
needs of their communities.4 According to National Community
Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, in California, seventy (70) banks

4 Under the proposal, banks below $1 billion in assets would be considered Small Banks; Banks between
$1 billion and $10 billion would be considered Intermediate Banks; Banks over $10 billion would be
considered Large Banks.




4

would see their reinvestment obligations reduced under the proposal.
Twenty-five (25) California banks would shed their community development
responsibilities entirely, and forty-five (45) California banks would no longer
be subject to the Investment Test.5
These changes will have significant and harmful impacts on California
communities and communities throughout the nation. NCRC estimates that
the loss of community development activity by Small and Intermediate
Banks that lose their Community Development and Investment Tests,
respectively, will be $1.6 billion to $1.9 billion per year.6 These losses will
not be offset by any increasing CD activity from Large Banks, as Large
Banks have limits on the amount of CD activity they can undertake,7 and
because other aspects of this proposal will further discourage community
development activity from Large Banks as well. Asset thresholds should not
be raised.
The importance of a separate Investment Test. The Investment Test has
successfully driven investment into several critical community development
programs and products that have had big impacts in LMI communities.
These include Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) which are a key
driver of affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) which
fuel economic development projects in tribal and other areas; and EQ2
equity equivalent investments in both Community Development Financial
Institutions (CDFIs) that provide small business lending in underserved
areas that banks find hard to reach, and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs)
that take property off of the speculative market in favor of the long term
stability of residents and communities.

5 https://www.ncrc.org/cra/#Lending
6 NCRC analysis of Federal Reserve CRA examination data (2005 to 2020) and current asset data on FDIC
and OCC supervised banks from March 2026 Call Reports. Methodology available from NCRC upon
request. FDIC cost savings estimates found at Federal Register, Vol. 91, No. 154, Wednesday, August 12,
2026, Proposed Rules, Page 52171.
7 These limitations include the public welfare investment cap, see
https://www.taxcreditcoalition.org/senate-passes-road-to-housing-act-with-public-welfare-investment-
cap-increase/




5

Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors,
highlighting the critical importance of the CRA Investment Test in the
financing of affordable housing.8 Raising asset thresholds and reducing the
number of banks subject to the Investment Test will do harm to the LIHTC
program. The Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition estimates that $2
billion a year in LIHTC investments comes from banks under $10 billion in
assets that would shed the Investment Test under this proposal. And this
number rises to $4.5 billion a year in LIHTC at risk if the FDIC and OCC raise
the Large Bank threshold to $30 billion in assets.9
Additionally, approximately half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from CRA
motivated banks10, as CRA dollars support CDFI's lending capital,
particularly in California's undeserved Central Valley, Inland Empire,
Northern counties, and other rural areas. Any reduction in community
development financing by banks in California will have tremendous negative
impacts on affordable housing and small business development in our state.
Further tilting towards community development lending at the expense of
community development investment. While this proposal will encourage an
overall decrease in community development activity, the limited community
development dollars that survive such a proposal will tilt towards community
development lending. Banks that shed their Investment Test in favor of a
Community Development Test will likely engage in community development
lending activities, which generally return a greater profit, while disfavoring
their community development investments which can have a much greater
community impact even as they may provide less return to banks. Bank
community development investments should receive greater weight in the
ratings process than community development lending as CD investments
can demonstrate greater bank commitment to, and impact on, communities.
A significant decrease in bank participation and competition in the LIHTC
program will result in less favorable terms and pricing for nonprofit

8 https://nationalmortgageprofessional.com/news/cra-proposal-could-reshape-bank-lending-and-
affordable-housing-investment
9 https://www.taxcreditcoalition.org/weigh-in-with-regulators-on-cra/
10 https://nextcity.org/urbanist-news/a-critical-few-weeks-ahead-for-community-development-finance




6

affordable housing developers. And less favorable pricing and terms will
result in fewer affordable housing units built, and the units that are built will
be less affordable and out of reach to those most in need.
The disproportionate impact on rural communities. Sadly, these changes will
disproportionately impact California's rural communities that rely more
heavily on the small business lending, construction loans, investments,
contributions, and deposit products offered by local community banks under
$10 billion in assets, as well as those under $1 billion in assets.
An Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition survey found that "approximately
one-third of Housing Credit equity investments from banks under $10 billion
in assets supported rural markets, indicating that banks in this asset range
play an outsized role in investing in rural communities."11
Signaling that doing less is fine. Further, and of great concern, the proposal
creates a roadmap to decrease community development finance even for
banks that remain subject to the Community Development and Investment
Tests. Shockingly, the regulators signal to all banks that they can do
significantly less community development lending and investment and still
pass their CRA examinations, all while seeking CRA credit for activity outside
of their CRA assessment areas.
The proposal suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital
devoted to community development loans and to community development
investments would be enough for banks to receive a Satisfactory CRA rating
and enable them to seek CRA credit for bank activity out of the bank CRA
assessment areas.12
But according to NCRC, that threshold is far lower than the percentage that
the largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans. Of

11 https://www.taxcreditcoalition.org/weigh-in-with-regulators-on-cra/
12 The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit outside their assessment areas if the banks
surpass a benchmark of 0.625% of tier 1 capital for community development loans and likewise 0.625%
for investments. 91 Fed. Reg. 52121, 52140 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026). We are concerned that the
practical effect of this proposal is that the benchmark will serve not as a floor, but as a ceiling.




7

all sixty-nine of the OCC and FDIC supervised banks in the top 100 banks by
assets, NCRC found that the median percentage of annual community
development lending in assessment areas was 6.8% of tier 1 capital, and a
median of 3.6% of tier 1 capital for annual CRA qualified investments. If
each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet the
separate thresholds of 0.625% of Tier 1 capital for community development
lending and investments proposed by the regulators, combined activity
would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually -- a decrease of
approximately $87.1 billion, or 85%.13 The Urban Institute conducted a
similar analysis, with similarly concerning findings.14 There is no evidence,
data, analysis or suggestion in the proposal that such decreases will not
occur.
Strategic Plans lower the bar. The proposal's encouragement for banks to
choose Strategic Plans to meet their CRA obligations similarly promises
decreased community development activity.15 The OCC previously proposed
guidance for community development performance under the Strategic Plan
option that was well-below historical levels of community development
activity.16 Adoption of both that guidance and this proposed rule could mean
that banks may dramatically reduce the amount of community development

13 NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk, (Sept.
10, 2026), at https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-
development-activity-at-risk/ .
14 In 2024, the large banks under the $10 billion threshold that did the least amount of CD lending
compared with Tier 1 capital (10th percentile) still had a ratio of 1.2 percent, nearly two (2) times the
proposed threshold. Banks at the median had a ratio of 8.2 percent, nearly twenty (20) times more than
the proposal. Even large banks with assets closer to the $30 billion threshold are far over the ratio. For
intermediate banks, the 1.25 percent threshold also falls far below current ratios, even before
considering that these banks will get to combine lending, investment, and grants.
https://www.urban.org/urban-wire/proposed-changes-community-reinvestment-act-could-weaken-
incentives-banks-invest-low-and
15 NCRC, The Proposed CRA Rule's Strategic Plans: A More Predictable Path to Doing Less (Sept 1,
2026), CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk, (Sept.
10, 2026), https://ncrc.org/the-proposed-cra-rules-strategic-plans-a-more-predictable-path-to-doing-
less/.
16 NCRC, Comment on the OCC's Proposed Strategic Plan Guidance (Feb. 22, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/ncrcs-comment-on-the-occs-proposed-strategic-plan-guidance/.




8

activity that they undertake in the areas where they do business, directly
undermining the purpose of the CRA.
You can fail community development but still pass. Finally, with little
discussion, the proposal would also disincentivize community development
and inflate the CRA ratings for Intermediate Banks by allowing them to
receive an overall Satisfactory rating if they score a Satisfactory on the
Lending Test, even if they received a failing grade on their CD Test. This will
lead to less Intermediate Bank focus on CD activity, and consequently, less
CD activity.
Not just the community groups. Even industry stakeholders can foresee the
negative impact this proposal will have on community development
activities. "A proposal to put lending back at the center of Community
Reinvestment Act examinations could also reduce the pressure on hundreds
of banks to invest in affordable housing and community development... CRA
incentives influence affordable mortgage products, construction financing,
tax-credit investments, down payment assistance programs, housing
counseling, and partnerships that connect Loan Originators with borrowers
in underserved communities... increased attention to individual loans may
not offset a pullback in the investments that produce affordable homes or
the nonprofit programs that prepare borrowers to qualify for financing."17
Despite previous actions by the bank regulators to encourage responsive
community development activity by banks,18 the FDIC and the OCC here
propose to undermine community development. The proposal will of course
even further weaken community development obligations if the agencies
adopt the alternative proposal that Large Banks be defined as those with

17 https://nationalmortgageprofessional.com/news/cra-proposal-could-reshape-bank-lending-and-
affordable-housing-investment
18 The bank regulators noted that their 2023 CRA Rule, amongst other things, "encourages CD activities
that are responsive to the needs of LMI individuals and communities, small businesses, and small farms
by clarifying what activities will receive CRA credit (such as affordable housing), providing for a public list
and approval process to confirm an activity's eligibility, and evaluating CD activities in light of their
impact." At https://www.fdic.gov/news/fact-sheets/interagency-overview-cra-final-rule-10-24-23.html




9

over $30 billion in assets, a threshold which comes with no justification or
precedent.
There can be no justification consistent with the purpose of CRA for
signaling that such a sharp drop in community development activity by
banks would be sufficient. It is the CRA requirements and expectations
under review that incentivize and propel bank community development
lending and investment activity. If the regulations are loosened and
expectations lowered (by the regulators lowering the bar and signaling to
banks what is the minimum score required to pass the test), community
development will drop.
2) LMI residents and communities will face greater barriers to
joining and remaining in the financial mainstream and will
become more vulnerable to predatory financial institutions as
bank branches close and BankOn products are deemphasized.
The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and
maintain branches in LMI and BIPOC neighborhoods. But by increasing the
asset threshold for what constitutes a Large Bank to over $10 billion, forty-
five (45) banks in California will no longer be subject to the Services Test
and reviewed to ensure their branches are serving LMI communities. Again,
asset thresholds should not be raised.

In California alone, NCRC estimates that 245 branches in LMI areas and 497
branches in neighborhoods of color would be vulnerable to closure due to
this proposal.19

Branch presence is critical to small business lending in communities, as
several studies have demonstrated.20 The proposed changes will not only

19 https://www.ncrc.org/cra/#Lending
20 A Federal Reserve paper found that closures of nearby branches decrease small business employment
growth and entry, and that, "altogether, our analysis highlights the importance of local bank branches to
small businesses." https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/feds/files/2024071pap.pdf . Another
research paper found that the closure of one bank branch can cause a 20% to 22% drop in the total
number and volume of small business loans in the immediate area, even in markets with competing local
alternatives. https://drive.google.com/file/d/17BHqJppQd70PprkI261IyvpBeYfBns0z/view




10

hurt deposit account access, but they will also lead to less small business
lending in LMI communities. These changes will be particularly hard hitting
in rural areas of our state – such as the Central Valley, Inland Empire and
Northern counties - where smaller banks make up a larger portion of the
small business lending that happens in local communities.

The proposal would also remove entirely the long-standing requirement,
expectation and obligation that banks develop and offer deposit products
that are accessible to LMI residents and communities.2122 Congress itself
established in the CRA that "regulated financial institutions are required by
law to demonstrate that their deposit facilities serve the convenience and
needs of the communities in which they are chartered to do business," and
that the "convenience and needs of communities include the need for credit
services as well as deposit services."23 Under current interagency guidance,
examiners consider services generally available at bank branches, including
"available loan and deposit products," transaction fees, and information
concerning the costs and features of loan and deposit products.24

The OCC, FDIC and the Federal Reserve Board recently reaffirmed the place
of banking services in the CRA framework in explaining that the goals of the
2023 CRA rule changes include to, amongst other things, "encourage banks
to expand credit, investment, and banking services in LMI communities."25
Indeed, the FDIC had been a leader in urging banks to help meet the
deposit product needs of LMI communities.26

21 See, for example, the curious discussion of the proceedings in Tex. Bankers Ass'n v. Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency, Civ. A. No. 2:24–cv– 00025–Z (N.D. Tex. Feb. 5, 2024), at Federal Register,
Vol. 91, No. 154, Wednesday, August 12, 2026, Proposed Rules, Page 52115. We object to and find
inappropriate FDIC and OCC efforts to narrowly define a bank's "entire community" and "credit needs,"
as well as their attempts to use this comment process and current litigation to prevent future rulemaking
and public comment on these critical issues.
22 The proposal itself notes the statutory authority to consider services offered at bank offices, see
footnote 87 of the proposal. Federal Register, Vol. 91, No. 154, Wednesday, August 12, 2026, Proposed
Rules, Page 52119.
23 12 U.S.C. § 2901(a)(1)(2).
24 Federal Register, Vol. 91, No. 154, Wednesday, August 12, 2026, Proposed Rules, Page 52,126.
25 https://www.fdic.gov/news/press-releases/2023/pr23086.html
26 See for example, https://www.fdic.gov/consumer-resource-center/fdic-economic-inclusion-strategic-
plan outlining the following Awareness and Education strategies the FDIC planned to pursue:




11


The nexus between deposit products and loan products is strong, especially
for LMI households and communities. Deposit accounts are the gateway to
financial stability, access to credit and wealth accumulation for families who
are otherwise preyed upon by extractive and predatory financial institutions.
Affordable bank accounts enable families to find security, save, and aspire to
access credit from newly trusted depository institutions as they make their
way along their wealth building journeys.

The BankOn program has provided access for over fourteen (14) million
account holders.27 California is home to several BankOn-related coalitions
that provide an effective partnership among banks, community-based
organizations, and local governments. The proposal puts all this work in
jeopardy.

Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19
million are underbanked.28 National banks regulated by the OCC charged
billions of dollars in overdraft and non-sufficient fund fees in 2025, and in
California alone, state-chartered banks charged over fifty-six million dollars
($56 million) in OD and NSF fees to California consumers in 2025.29


1.1 Raise awareness of and interest in establishing and using accounts through direct communications
with consumers by the FDIC and partners that serve LMI and other underserved consumers.
1.2 Raise awareness and interest among banks, particularly community banks, in offering safe and
affordable accounts (such as BankOn certified accounts), with no overdraft or insufficient funds fees,
other low-cost features, and features facilitating broad functionality, accessibility and availability.
Encourage banks to make safe and affordable accounts readily available in all channels,
including branches, and to develop strategies promoting them effectively to consumers,
including by prominently featuring them on bank websites and in marketing materials.
1.4 Identify organizations that work with unbanked and underbanked households and train them on
Money Smart materials on establishing and sustaining bank accounts. Focus training efforts on
organizations that serve LMI and other underserved populations.
1.5 Educate banks on the opportunity for CRA consideration, including with respect to digital and
other delivery systems that respond to the needs of LMI consumers."
27 https://joinbankon.org/research/
28 NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-rollbacks/.
29 See https://www.nclc.org/overdraft-and-nsf-fees-rise-above-12-billion/ and https://dfpi.ca.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/AnnualReport_2026_NSF_Master.pdf




12

Rise Economy (formerly the California Reinvestment Coalition) has
recognized the pernicious impact that fee gouging can have on working
families. We have conducted extensive research on overdraft and related
fees,30 and devoted resources towards urging corporate and policy changes
that allow public assistance recipients to be able to access their limited
funds without incurring non-customer fees at bank ATM machines.31 We
have also worked to develop a fee free account, CalAccount, that could be
available to all Californians.32

By withdrawing any CRA incentive for banks to offer accessible deposit
services and withdrawing scrutiny of banks for the failure to serve branching
and deposit needs, the proposal would increase the likelihood that members
of the entire community served by regulated banks, including LMI customers
and communities, will incur unnecessary charges and fees, take on
predatory debt, and be shut out of the financial mainstream.

3) Community organizations, local governments, researchers, and
the public will lose transparency and insight into the lending
and other performance metrics of banks with the loss of small
business, small farm, and community development lending
data, as well as CRA Public File information.
Another consequence of the proposal's drive to raise asset thresholds is that
fewer banks will be required to share data regarding their small business,
small farm, and community development lending activities. Such data is
critical to understanding not only individual bank performance, but also the
needs and nature of local markets.


30 See for example, https://rise-economy.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Overdraft-crisis_fact-
sheet_2025.pdf
31 Rise Economy has advocated for state Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) contracts and bank Community
Benefits Agreements to provide fee free ATM access for public assistance recipients. Additionally, Rise
Economy has conducted extensive research on these issues. https://calreinvest.org/wp-
content/uploads/2018/09/19-Million-ATM-Fee-CRC-Report.pdf
32 https://rise-economy.org/research_crc/priced-out-of-banking-how-calaccount-would-close-
californias-financial-access-gap/




13

Rise Economy and its member organizations routinely access and analyze
this CRA data when meeting with banks and commenting on CRA exams and
mergers. The loss of such data is particularly harmful at a time when the
Administration is frustrating efforts to collect and disclose small business
lending data under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank Act.

These changes will disproportionately impact rural communities in our state
where banks up to $10 billion in assets make up a larger part of the small
business and small farm lending markets. NCRC estimates that California
will lose between 8% and 16% of our existing small business and small farm
data.33 Rise Economy has been increasingly accessing and analyzing small
farm loan data to understand whether banks are meeting local community
credit needs.

Data regarding bank performance that is available to regulators and the
public is a key mechanism for ensuring that the CRA statute and rules and
adhered to and that statutory purposes are honored. By proposing to hide
data that is currently available to regulators and the public, this proposal
would make CRA oversight ever more difficult.

We also object to proposed limitations on what information should be
retained in each Bank's CRA Public File and made available to the public. All
banks should make their CRA Public Files available on the internet and
accessible from each branch location. The CRA Public Files should include all
public comments or complaints that reflect CEO, officer, and bank
performance (redacting lower-level employee names as necessary), as well
as CRA Disclosure Statements, and deposit and branch data. Banks should
place in their CRA Public File any and all information for which the
commenter requests such placement, or any communication that can
reasonably be read to evidence that intent. Additionally, any comments
related to activities that are relevant to a bank's CRA examination or merger
application (such as CRA concerns, consumer complaints, alleged violations
of consumer protection, UDAAP and fair housing/fair lending laws, etc.)
should be made part of the Public File.

33 https://ncrc.org/cra/.

https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/national/2008/11/23/banking-regulator-played-advocate-
over-enforcer/3e432b59-d29d-4f22-b18a-e74c07f3b363/
64 In addition to providing an unduly short comment period, we also note that the FDIC failed to discuss
or vote on this proposal in a public meeting, as has appeared to be its custom.
65 While the Proposal generally fails to acknowledge the dearth of analysis to support its propositions,
the regulators do at times note, for example, "The FDIC does not have the information necessary to
quantify, accurately, the effects of the proposal on consumers and businesses, including depositors
and/or borrowers," Federal Register, Vol. 91, No. 154, Wednesday, August 12, 2026, Proposed Rules.
Page 52171, and "Such changes may have a distributional effect on community development activities
where it may pose some costs and benefits for certain communities and projects. However, the agencies
do not have the information necessary to quantify any such effects." Federal Register, Vol. 91, No. 154,
Wednesday, August 12, 2026, Proposed Rules, Page 52174. Indeed, the phrase, "The FDIC does not have
the information necessary to quantify..." appears seven (7) times in the proposal.





30

We thank you for the opportunity to comment, which we appreciate and
recognize as a foundational right and benefit of our system. We thank you
for your consideration of our views.

If you have any questions about this letter, feel free to contact Kevin Stein
at kstein@rise-economy.org.

Very Truly Yours,

Kevin Stein




Chief of Legal and Strategy

comments.text:
COMMENT FORM TEXT:
We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation’s (FDIC) proposed revisions to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.
AmPac Business Capital is a community-based, mission-driven nonprofit lender serving small businesses throughout the State of California and in select counties of Arizona and Navada. Through our work as an SBA Community Advantage SBLC, SBA Microlender and SBA 504 lender, we provide responsible financing and technical assistance to small businesses from cradle to legacy in underserved communities, serving startup businesses, rural businesses, LMI communities and first generation entrepreneurs that often face barriers to accessing conventional financing.
We appreciate the agencies’ efforts to modernize the CRA regulations and support provisions that could improve clarity, reduce unnecessary burden, and promote responsible capital in underserved communities. However, we have significant concerns that several proposed changes—including substantially higher asset thresholds, restrictions on community development grants, changes to community development performance standards, and reductions in data collection and transparency—could weaken the incentives that bring banks and mission lenders together.
These changes could have a direct impact on our ability to access the bank capital, investments, grants, lines of credit, deposits, and other financial support that enable us to serve borrowers and communities that conventional financial institutions may not efficiently reach directly.

Our organization’s ability to serve small businesses and communities depends in meaningful part on our relationships with financial institutions. Today, we work with banks that provide support for our organization in the form of loans, investments, deposits, grants, lines of credit, loan loss reserves, and provide referrals. These relationships represent approximately $2 Million or 33% of our total borrowed capital of $6,000,000.  These funds have leveraged guaranteed loan support for AmPac CA 7a SBLC loans totaling greater than $39 Million, and supported loan loss reserve for AmPac’s SBA micro loan program where we have loaned almost $7.5 Million in loans from $5,000 to $50,000 to start-up and early start businesses.   These dollars have created or retained well over $1,700 jobs throughout the State of California and have provided thousands of hours of coaching and technical assistance.  These dollars make communities better and families stronger by advancing entrepreneurial dreams. Banks have access to significant pools of private capital and financial expertise, while organizations like ours have deep knowledge of local markets and longstanding relationships with entrepreneurs who may not yet have access to conventional financing. We work with business owners before they are ready for a traditional bank loan. We help them improve financial practices to establish credit. Without these relationships, our ability to respond to local credit needs would be more limited.  With the support of CRA investment funds received from a local bank, AmPac supported a small business in Volcano, CA.  The population of the community was 100 as of the last census.  The company is in the fire prevention and defensible space industry and they provide land clearing work to support fire prevention initiatives by landowners and local governments.  The funds allowed the business to provide machinery and equipment to support the business.  The funds supported the creation and retention of two new jobs.   We recognize that the CRA is one factor among many that banks consider when deciding where to direct their resources and build community partnerships. We are concerned that changes to the proposed framework, particularly changes affecting bank asset thresholds and the treatment of community development activities, could unintentionally reduce incentives for banks to maintain these relationships.  For our organization, this is not simply a regulatory issue. It is a question of whether private capital and local financial partnerships will continue to reach emerging and small businesses that are seeking the opportunity to grow, create jobs, and strengthen their communities. We encourage the agencies to preserve a CRA framework that supports these voluntary, market-based partnerships while maintaining appropriate accountability for meeting community credit needs.
In conclusion, our organization’s experience demonstrates that strong partnerships between financial institutions and mission lenders can expand access to private capital without replacing or competing with the traditional banking system. Bank relationships provide important resources that allow organizations like ours to serve creditworthy small businesses and communities that may not yet be well positioned to access conventional financing.

Dear Deputy Executive Secretary Jones and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency:
We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposed revisions to the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA) regulations, which was published in the Federal Register on August 12, 2026.
AmPac Business Capital is a community-based, mission-driven nonprofit lender serving small
businesses throughout the State of California and in select counties of Arizona and Navada. Through
our work as an SBA Community Advantage SBLC, SBA Microlender and SBA 504 lender, we provide
responsible financing and technical assistance to small businesses from cradle to legacy in
underserved communities, serving startup businesses, rural businesses, LMI communities and first
generation entrepreneurs that often face barriers to accessing conventional financing.
We appreciate the agencies' efforts to modernize the CRA regulations and support provisions that could
improve clarity, reduce unnecessary burden, and promote responsible capital in underserved
communities. However, we have significant concerns that several proposed changes—including
substantially higher asset thresholds, restrictions on community development grants, changes to
community development performance standards, and reductions in data collection and transparency—
could weaken the incentives that bring banks and mission lenders together.
These changes could have a direct impact on our ability to access the bank capital, investments, grants,
lines of credit, deposits, and other financial support that enable us to serve borrowers and communities
that conventional financial institutions may not efficiently reach directly.
BANK PARTNERSHIPS ARE VITAL TO OUR ABILITY TO SERVE LOCAL BUSINESSES

Our organization's ability to serve small businesses and communities depends in meaningful part on our
relationships with financial institutions. Today, we work with banks that provide support for our
organization in the form of loans, investments, deposits, grants, lines of credit, loan loss reserves, and
provide referrals. These relationships represent approximately $2 Million or 33% of our total borrowed
capital of $6,000,000. These funds have leveraged guaranteed loan support for AmPac CA 7a SBLC
loans totaling greater than $39 Million, and supported loan loss reserve for AmPac's SBA micro loan
program where we have loaned almost $7.5 Million in loans from $5,000 to $50,000 to start-up and
early start businesses. These dollars have created or retained well over $1,700 jobs throughout the
State of California and have provided thousands of hours of coaching and technical assistance. These
dollars make communities better and families stronger by advancing entrepreneurial dreams.

Banks have access to significant pools of private capital and financial expertise, while organizations like
ours have deep knowledge of local markets and longstanding relationships with entrepreneurs who may
not yet have access to conventional financing.

In many cases, we work with business owners before they are ready for a traditional bank loan. We help
them improve financial practices, establish credit, strengthen operations, and build the track record
needed to pursue additional financing as their businesses grow. That work can ultimately create
stronger businesses and future customers for the broader banking system.
Without these relationships, our ability to respond to local credit needs would be more limited. With the
support of investment funds received from a local bank through their CRA investment, AmPac
supported a small business in Volcano, CA. The population of the community is 100 as of the last
census. The company is in the fire prevention and defensible space industry and they provide land
clearing work to support fire prevention initiatives by landowners and local governments. The funds
allowed the business to provide machinery and equipment to support the business. The funds
supported the creation and retention of two new jobs.

We recognize that the CRA is one factor among many that banks consider when deciding where to
direct their resources and build community partnerships. We are concerned that changes to the
proposed framework, particularly changes affecting bank asset thresholds and the treatment of
community development activities, could unintentionally reduce incentives for banks to maintain these
relationships.

For our organization, this is not simply a regulatory issue. It is a question of whether private capital and
local financial partnerships will continue to reach emerging and small businesses that are seeking the
opportunity to grow, create jobs, and strengthen their communities. We encourage the agencies to
preserve a CRA framework that supports these voluntary, market-based partnerships while maintaining
appropriate accountability for meeting community credit needs.

In conclusion, our organization's experience demonstrates that strong partnerships between financial
institutions and mission lenders can expand access to private capital without replacing or competing
with the traditional banking system. Bank relationships provide important resources that allow
organizations like ours to serve creditworthy small businesses and communities that may not yet be well
positioned to access conventional financing.

As the agencies consider modernization of the CRA framework, we encourage a practical approach that
preserves accountability while avoiding unnecessary regulatory changes that could reduce private-
sector investment or limit the flexibility of community-based lenders.

To summarize, we respectfully urge the OCC and FDIC to:
➢ Retain the current CRA asset thresholds and carefully evaluate whether higher thresholds could
reduce private-sector incentives to support local communities;

➢ Preserve CRA consideration for operating and capacity-building support that helps mission
lenders operate efficiently and responsibly;
➢ Maintain meaningful incentives for banks to work with mission lenders through lending,
investments, deposits, grants, loan participations, referrals, and other market-based
partnerships;
➢ Continue recognizing small-business lending that addresses genuine gaps in access to credit,
particularly where businesses are seeking to establish or strengthen relationships with traditional
financial institutions;
➢ Maintain appropriate CRA data and transparency so regulators, financial institutions, and
communities have the information necessary to evaluate outcomes and identify genuine credit
needs;
➢ Ensure that CRA continues to distinguish meaningful community development from ordinary-
course lending, so that CRA incentives remain focused on activities that would otherwise be less
likely to occur; and
➢ Preserve flexibility for financial institutions and mission lenders to develop partnerships that
respond to local market conditions, rather than imposing a one-size-fits-all approach.
➢ CRA modernization should strengthen accountability while allowing banks and mission lenders
to use private capital, local knowledge, and established community relationships to address
legitimate credit needs. The objective should be a CRA framework that encourages greater
private investment, responsible lending, and measurable community impact without
unnecessarily increasing regulatory burdens.

Sincerely,

Hilda Kennedy
Founder/President
AmPac Business Capital
3110-B Inland Empire Blvd
Ontario, CA 91764
hkennedy@ampac.com
909-915-1706

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
COMMENTS ON COMMUNITY REINVESTMENT ACT REGULATIONS — SMALL BANK RELIEF, RURAL FINANCING, APA REVIEW, AND FORMAL FOOTNOTE ATTRIBUTION

OCC Docket OCC-2026-0694
FDIC RIN 3064-AG31
91 Fed. Reg. 52114

Submitted by Obelisk Tech Systems Inc.
James Hunter Poole, Executive Chairman and CEO

FORMAL REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENTAL FOOTNOTE ATTRIBUTION

Obelisk Tech Systems Inc. respectfully requests that the OCC and FDIC cite Obelisk Tech Systems Inc. and James Hunter Poole in official footnotes, final-rule explanations, regulatory analyses, agency findings, and subsequent governmental publications wherever they rely upon original research, calculations, or proposed regulatory language submitted in this proceeding.

Requested citation:

Obelisk Tech Systems Inc., Comments on Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, OCC-2026-0694, FDIC RIN 3064-AG31 (James Hunter Poole, author and authorized signatory).

This attribution request is subject to agency discretion.

INCORPORATION OF ATTACHED SUBMISSION

The attached 185-page submission is incorporated by reference in full, including 20 numbered propositions, 20 findings, original economic calculations, eight proposed regulatory amendments, APA challenge matrices, judicial authorities, statutory analysis, and supporting footnotes.

The Commenter supports simplified regulation for small community banks with amendments protecting rural communities, agricultural lending, and small-business financing.

ORIGINAL ECONOMIC FINDINGS

The Commenter calculates that approximately 1,206 banks could move to lighter regulatory categories, including 815 banks relieved of community-development evaluation and 391 banks relieved of large-bank reporting obligations. The agencies' separate figures require reconciliation.

FORMAL REQUESTS FOR AGENCY ACTION

1. Adopt simplified examinations and reporting for small community banks, including a $1 billion threshold adjusted for inflation.

2. Protect independent community banks against unnecessary compliance costs while preventing larger banking groups from exploiting small-bank exemptions.

3. Recognize rural small-business lending, agricultural credit, farm operating loans, SBA 7(a), SBA 504, USDA Business and Industry, FSA guarantees, and HUBZone-related financing.

4. Remove or narrow exclusions affecting legitimate working-capital and operating loans.

5. Ensure rural lending is considered even when it falls outside a bank's two largest product lines.

6. Correct unsupported assumptions, inconsistencies, and errors in agency economic and paperwork estimates.

7. Review the proposal under the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. §§ 553 and 706, including statutory authority, arbitrary-and-capricious review, material alternatives, and reasoned decisionmaking.

8. Apply applicable Regulatory Flexibility Act, Paperwork Reduction Act, OMB, OIRA, constitutional, and judicial-review requirements.

9. Consider Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, State Farm, and relevant CRA precedent according to their actual holdings.

10. Adopt the specific regulatory amendments, findings, and agency-specific requested actions in the attached submission.

FINAL REQUEST

The Commenter requests that the agencies consider the complete administrative record, preserve the original economic and legal findings, and provide appropriate footnote attribution to Obelisk Tech Systems Inc. and James Hunter Poole wherever original analysis is used.

This submission does not claim automatic judicial standing or a legal entitlement to citation. It contains no business confidential information.

Respectfully submitted,

/s/ James Hunter Poole
James Hunter Poole
Executive Chairman and CEO
Obelisk Tech Systems Inc.

October 12, 2026

B. Basis for Participation and Its Limits
The APA directs each agency to "give interested persons an opportunity to participate in the rule
making through submission of written data, views, or arguments," and the agencies invited com-
ment on "all aspects of the proposed rules" and on sixty-three numbered questions.18
The right to comment and the right to sue are separate. A comment does not create Article III
standing, which requires injury in fact, causation and redressability.19 A proposed rule is not final
agency action.20 Judicial review under the Regulatory Flexibility Act is confined to "a small entity
that is adversely affected or aggrieved by final agency action"; Obelisk is a small business but is
not subject to the rule and claims no such right.21 Obelisk presents this Comment as what the APA
makes it: relevant matter the agencies must consider.
II. STATEMENT OF THE REGULATORY ACTION AND
ADMINISTRATIVE CHRONOLOGY
A. The Statutory Command
The Act imposes two duties on each supervisory agency: to assess each institution's record of meet-
ing the credit needs of its entire community, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods,
and to take that record into account when the institution applies for a deposit facility.22 It requires
a written public evaluation with one of four ratings, presented separately for each metropolitan
area and for the nonmetropolitan remainder of each State in which the institution has branches.23
It delegates to each agency the power to publish regulations "to carry out the purposes" of the
Act.24 In one place only it draws a line by asset size: institutions with aggregate assets of not more
than $250 million are examined no more than once every 60 or 48 months, depending on their last
rating.25

C. What the Proposal Does
The proposal keeps the structure of the current rule and changes it in nine principal respects.
1. Size tiers. Small: assets of less than $1 billion, indexed annually to CPI-W. Intermediate:
up to and including $10 billion, not indexed. Large: more than $10 billion. "Assets" is not
defined.39

banks: the same plus a community development test. Large banks: lending, investment and
service tests. Banks below $1 billion "would no longer be subject to the CD test."40

mined bank-wide as the two largest lines (Option 1) or by assessment area on qualitative
factors (Option 2).41
4. Credit focus. Retail banking services would be limited to credit services, "thereby excluding
deposit services," and the facility-based assessment-area framework would remain "largely
unchanged."42

IV. STATUTORY AUTHORITY AND SCOPE OF DELEGATION
By what authority? The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit In-
surance Corporation propose to redraw the lines that decide how each of roughly 3,577 banks is
examined for community reinvestment.50 Their authority is a 1977 statute of eight short sections,
one general rulemaking clause, and three related provisions of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act.
That authority is enough for most of what the agencies propose. It is also bounded, and the bounds
decide several questions in this proceeding. This Part maps the authority first, because every propo-
sition that follows depends on it.
A. The Community Reinvestment Act, Section by Section
The Act is title VIII of Public Law 95-128, codified as amended at 12 U.S.C. §§ 2901–2908.51 Read
in order, it contains a handful of commands to the agencies, three permissions, one consequence
that attaches to a rating, and one line drawn by asset size. It contains no performance test, no
data-collection requirement and, apart from § 2908, no size tier.
1. Section 2901: findings and purpose
Congress found that regulated financial institutions "have continuing and affirmative obligation to
help meet the credit needs of the local communities in which they are chartered," and stated the Act's
purpose: "to require each appropriate Federal financial supervisory agency to use its authority when
examining financial institutions, to encourage such institutions to help meet the credit needs of the
local communities in which they are chartered consistent with the safe and sound operation of such
institutions."52 Three features of that sentence govern everything else. The verb is "encourage."
The object is "credit needs." The place is "the local communities in which they are chartered."
2. Section 2902: definitions and reach
A "regulated financial institution" is "an insured depository institution (as defined in section 1813 of
this title)," and an insured depository institution is "any bank or savings association the deposits of
which are insured by the Corporation."53 The Act therefore reaches banks and savings associations
with federal deposit insurance and no one else. Credit unions, whose member accounts are insured

not change whether the record is assessed, evaluated in writing and rated. A threshold structure
so light at the bottom that the agency could no longer say it had assessed the record of meeting

reach that point: every small bank remains subject to a lending test and a responsiveness criterion,
a written evaluation and a statutory rating.76 The boundary is marked here so that the alternative in

policy." Amending an existing rule is itself "rule making."84 It would revise the text of 12 CFR

A. The Statutory Frame
Proposition S-001. The Act requires assessment of every covered institution's record of meet-
ing the credit needs of its entire community; size tiers are the agencies' creation, except the
one line Congress drew in 12 U.S.C. § 2908.
The duty in 12 U.S.C. § 2903(a)(1) is to "assess the institution's record of meeting the credit needs
of its entire community, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods." It applies to each
institution examined, and § 2906 requires a written evaluation and one of four ratings for each.98 The

by rule in 1995 and 2005 under 12 U.S.C. § 2905, and they acknowledge that the statute "does not
require the agencies to tailor the performance tests by asset size."99 Congress drew one size line
itself, the $250 million examination-cycle line in § 2908.

of the agencies' reasoning and data, not by statutory text. The agencies "must examine the
relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation."100

and for the share of assets in the heaviest tier (85.4 percent against 86.2 percent).
Second, it does not hold for the other two margins. Small banks would hold 4.9 percent of assets,
about a third of the 13.8 percent of industry assets they held in 1995. Large banks would be 2.4
percent of banks, about one-eighth of the industry-wide 19.6 percent of 1995. Had the 1995 share
been preserved, about 701 of the 3,577 banks would be large; the proposal has 86 and the current
rule has 477.
Third, the two margins that match are matched by two different lines. In 1995 one line at $250
million produced both the 80.4 percent and the 86.2 percent. Today no single line can, because
the industry has consolidated: the $1 billion line reproduces the 1995 share of banks and the $10
billion line reproduces the 1995 share of assets. What lies between them, 636 banks holding 9.7
percent of assets, is a tier that did not exist in 1995.
Fourth, the comparison mixes universes. The 1995 figures are industry-wide: they describe all
"insured depository institutions" and "total bank and thrift assets." The 2026 figures describe only
banks the OCC and FDIC supervise. The source the agencies cite also gives the 1995 figure for
FDIC-supervised banks alone, and it is different: 10.6 percent of FDIC-supervised banks were
large. FDIC Table 5 shows that 281 of 2,629 FDIC-supervised banks, 10.7 percent, are large under
the current rule. For the FDIC's own banks, then, the current rule already matches the 1995 share
of banks in the heaviest tier, and the proposal would cut that share to 1.2 percent.
Fifth, the 1995 distribution was produced by a definition that included a holding-company condi-
tion: a bank under $250 million was small only if it "was independent or an affiliate of a holding
company that ... had total banking and thrift assets of less than $1 billion."110 The proposal would
restore a distribution without restoring the definition that generated it. That is the subject of Propo-
sition S-005.
These findings are a reason to state the justification accurately, not a reason to reject the lines. The
proposal does not return the framework to its 1995 proportions. It makes a new judgment: that in a
consolidated industry, three tiers with about 80 percent of banks in the lightest and about 85 percent
of assets in the heaviest is the right allocation of examination effort. Obelisk supports the main
elements of that judgment. But an explanation "runs counter to the evidence before the agency"
when it rests on a factual premise that the agency's own cited source does not bear out.111 Record
question 2: Obelisk asks the agencies to publish the 1995 and 2026 distributions on a like-for-like
basis, by agency and industry-wide, and to restate the rationale for the $10 billion line without

The line tracks the one 1995 margin that still makes sense for small banks. At $1 billion, 79.8

VII. RURAL BANKING, SMALL-BUSINESS CREDIT AND SBA AND

The statute's object is credit. Congress found that regulated institutions "have continuing and af-
firmative obligation to help meet the credit needs of the local communities in which they are char-
tered," and it directed each agency to "assess the institution's record of meeting the credit needs of
its entire community."173 In rural America that credit has a particular shape. It is the farm operating
line that pays for seed, fertilizer and cash rent before a crop is sold; the working-capital loan that
carries a small business between payables and receivables; and the SBA- or USDA-guaranteed loan
that a community bank makes to a borrower who could not obtain credit without the guarantee. A
rule that evaluates rural banks on that credit measures what the statute asks about. A rule that looks
past it measures something else.
Obelisk supports the proposal's reduction of examination and data burden on small community
banks (Proposition S-003). This Part identifies six places where the proposal, as drafted, would
stop evaluating, exclude from consideration or stop measuring the credit that rural communities
use. Each is treated in the same order: the proposal, current law, the defect, the agencies' likely
defense, the contrary evidence, an amendment and a fallback. None of the six amendments restores
the community development test or imposes any data-collection duty on a bank below $1 billion.

IX. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEDURE ACT ANALYSIS
This Part states the standards a reviewing court would apply to a final rule and tests the proposal
against them. It is a comment-stage objection. No final agency action exists, no claim under the
Administrative Procedure Act (APA) has accrued, and every defect identified can be cured before
the agencies act; Obelisk does not state that either agency has violated the APA. Each issue carries
a status: ESTABLISHED (a fact about the notice that can be checked against its text), CONDITIONAL
(a defect only if the final rule repeats it), UNRESOLVED (the record permits no conclusion), or NOT
APPLICABLE (screened and set aside).
A. Governing Standards
Notice, comment and the duty to consider. After notice, an agency must "give interested persons
an opportunity to participate in the rule making through submission of written data, views, or argu-
ments with or without opportunity for oral presentation," and, "[a]fter consideration of the relevant
matter presented," must "incorporate in the rules adopted a concise general statement of their basis
and purpose."306 The Supreme Court has put the duty in one sentence: "An agency must consider
and respond to significant comments received during the period for public comment."307 The Dis-
trict of Columbia Circuit states the rule and its limit: "the opportunity to comment is meaningless
unless the agency responds to significant points raised by the public," but "only comments which,
if true, raise points relevant to the agency's decision and which, if adopted, would require a change
in an agency's proposed rule" qualify, and comments that "are purely speculative and do not dis-
close the factual or policy basis on which they rest require no response."308 Each objection below is
drafted to that test: it gives the agency statement challenged, the page, the evidence, and the change
in the rule that would follow.
Scope of review. A court "shall decide all relevant questions of law" and shall set aside agency

B. How Review of a Final Rule Would Proceed
Finality and timing. Review requires "final agency action," which marks "the 'consummation'
of the agency's decisionmaking process" and determines rights or obligations; a proposed rule
is neither.419 The default limitations period is six years, and an APA claim "does not accrue ...

brought within one year by a small entity subject to the rule (Proposition S-014).
Forum. The Hobbs Act does not list the OCC or the FDIC, and no special review statute was
identified, so review of a final rule would lie in a district court under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 and 5
U.S.C. §§ 702–703, as the challenge to the 2023 rule did.421 Venue lies where a defendant resides,
where a substantial part of the events occurred, or where the plaintiff resides if no real property is
involved.422 Nothing routes such a case to the District of Columbia Circuit by default.
Standards and relief. The standards are those stated under "Governing Standards" in the APA
analysis. An agency may postpone its own effective date pending review, and a court may do so "to
the extent necessary to prevent irreparable injury."423
Who could sue. Regulated banks and their associations could, as they did against the 2023 rule. A
borrower, nonprofit or community organization would have to show a concrete injury fairly traceable
to the rule and not to the independent lending decisions of banks, which is a demanding showing.
Obelisk makes no such claim.

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations Proposed Rule (Docket ID OCC-2026-0694)
To Whom It May Concern:
On behalf of The NRP Group, I urge the federal banking regulators to make no change—or
only a minimal change—to the asset thresholds governing which banks remain subject to a
separate Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) investment test. Founded in 1994, The NRP
Group is a vertically integrated developer, owner, builder, and manager of multifamily
housing that creates affordable and market-rate communities at scale. The company has
developed approximately 31,000 affordable apartment homes across the United States
and works with public and private partners to create high-quality rental housing for
individuals and families regardless of income. Raising the large-bank threshold to $10
billion would weaken a proven incentive for banks to invest in Low-Income Housing Tax
Credit properties and diminish the impact of federal affordable housing dollars.
The Housing Credit is the nation's primary tool for creating and preserving affordable rental
housing. Congress expanded the program in 2025, an investment estimated to finance 1.22
million additional homes over the next decade. Banks provide roughly 75 to 80 percent of
Housing Credit equity, and at least 71 percent is CRA-motivated. CRA policy should sustain
this demand, not offset Congress's investment.
An Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC) survey found that 108 banks below the
proposed $10 billion threshold invested at least $1.6 billion over five years—an estimated
$2 billion across the full market. If an increase is necessary, the $3.252 billion alternative
would be far less disruptive, reducing the affected investors from 108 to 40 and estimated
affected equity from roughly $2 billion to $272 million. A $30 billion threshold would place
an estimated $4.5 billion in five-year investment at risk.
The NRP Group has seen the impact of CRA firsthand across the markets where we develop
affordable housing. In San Antonio, for example, lower area median incomes can limit the
rents an affordable community can support even as land, labor, materials, insurance, and
other development costs continue to rise. These economics often cannot generate returns
sufficient to attract private investment without strong CRA-motivated demand for Housing
 www.nrpgroup.com
1228 Euclid Avenue, 4th Floor
Cleveland, Ohio 44115
Phone (216) 475-8900
www.nrpgroup.com
Credit equity. Banks below $10 billion are also especially important in rural and small-town
markets: approximately one-third of their surveyed Housing Credit investments supported
rural communities. Without the CRA investment incentive, San Antonio and similar
communities may face fewer investors, less competitive equity pricing, wider financing
gaps, and the loss or delay of needed affordable homes.
These changes would come amid a shortage of more than seven million affordable and
available homes for extremely low-income renters and a 48.9 percent increase in
residential construction input costs since February 2020. Weakening investor demand
would reduce equity proceeds, widen financing gaps, and result in fewer affordable homes.
A consistent interagency framework is also essential. The Federal Reserve's absence from
the proposal creates the risk of divergent CRA standards and appears to signal a different
direction from the OCC and FDIC. Affordable housing investments are long-term
commitments that require durable, predictable rules across banking agencies.
We strongly encourage the OCC and FDIC to retain the thresholds established under the
1995 CRA rule, consistent with the direction the Federal Reserve appears to be taking. If
the OCC and FDIC move forward with changes, we strongly urge them to maintain the
lowest possible threshold for large banks and adopt policies that strengthen Housing
Credit investment in every community, including rural and smaller markets. At most, any
increase should be limited to the $3.252 billion alternative.
Thank you for considering these comments.
Sincerely,
George Currall
Chief Financial Officer
The NRP Group

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
We have comments on the OCC and FDIC Proposed CRS Rule, which would affect many nonprofits and low- to moderate-income people in DC.

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
on Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694;
RIN 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Communitas Veterans Agency, Inc (CVA) submits this comment in opposition to the
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of
the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
(FDIC)1 because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also
request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze
the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an
opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting
any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.
CVA provides housing support and homelessness prevention, workforce development and
financial empowerment, and community partnerships that promote stability, independence,
and long-term self-sufficiency in the DMV. We support veterans, their families, and the
community, and CRA is a critical resource in achieving our mission.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 2
in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss, and unequal
access to mainstream financial services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and
would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and
support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being
considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-
income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination
and disinvestment.
REDUCTION IN COMMUNITY INVESTMENT EXPECTATIONS FOR ALL
BANKS
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In our
community, from 2010-2024, banks made over $32.8 billion in CRA-qualified mortgage
lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and in CRA-qualified lending to small
businesses. These investments benefited our community by increasing the number of
affordable mortgages, small business loans, and investments in the DC community.
We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1
capital devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough
to receive a passing CRA rating.2 However, that percentage is far lower than the
percentage the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the
largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.
NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the
OCC and FDIC supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these
banks currently conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community development
loans and investments inside their assessment areas, and that the median percentage of
annual community development lending in assessment areas was 6.8% of tier 1 capital,
and a median of 3.6% of tier 1 capital for annual CRA qualified investments.3 If each
bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet separate thresholds of 0.625%
of Tier 1 capital for community development lending and investments, combined activity
would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually -- a decrease of approximately $87.1
billion, or 85%. Similarly, the proposal encourages banks to use strategic plans to make

2 The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit for outside their assessment areas if the banks
surpass a benchmark of 0.625% of its tier 1 capital for community development loans and likewise 0.625%
for investments. 91 Fed. Reg. 52121, 52140 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026). We are concerned that the practical
effect of this proposal is that the benchmark will serve not as a floor, but a ceiling.
3 NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk,
(Sept. 10, 2026), https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-
development-activity-at-risk/.
 3
their CRA compliance easier and more predictable. Previous proposed guidance also set
strategic plan benchmarks for CRA performance well-below historical levels of
community development activity.4
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic
discrimination cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments
and loans. If regulators lower expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be
accountable to the communities they serve, communities could face harmful
consequences. For example, in our community, one person's living costs in Washington,
DC are estimated at $3,964 a month, including rent and utilities, 42% above the national
average. Rent and utilities take almost two-thirds of the total. For homeownership, DC is
expensive relative to the national average. While the national median home price hovers
around $400,000, the median in DC is approximately $700,000. How can residents afford
these costs without help from CRA investments?
 It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet community needs.
Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes
would reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income
communities and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or
disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.
Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
● identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA
scrutiny under the proposal;
● quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
● assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or
populations, including rural communities and communities of color;
● consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without
sacrificing meaningful community accountability; and
Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes
that the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its
impacts is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs
considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for
meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that

4 NCRC, The Proposed CRA Rule's Strategic Plans: A More Predictable Path to Doing Less (Sept 1,
2026), https://ncrc.org/the-proposed-cra-rules-strategic-plans-a-more-predictable-path-to-doing-less/.

 4
materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are
consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120
days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service
evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The
current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that
do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would
allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather
examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more
complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies
extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.
Sincerely,
Communitas Veterans Agency, Inc
cc. National Community Reinvestment Coalition

comments.text:
COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
Agency: OCC
Docket ID OCC-2026-0694
I agree that it’s reasonable to update the asset size thresholds/ceilings and index them by some formula. I like the idea of alignment with the SBA’s standard, but prefer a more frequent and less drastic updating of the standard. I don’t suppose it would be possible to persuade the SBA to adopt the CRA’s new standard? the standards don’t seem to be too far apart. Either way, the CPI seems to be less than ideal for periodic updates of the standards. Aligning the intermediate bank ceiling with Dodd-Frank likewise appeals to me, except that presumably that 10 billion cut-off isn’t indexed and 2010 was a few years ago. (Speaking of Dodd-Frank, the degree of bank consolidation revealed by the numbers you report is actually rather alarming. It might be advisable to take action to reverse that trend, before “too big to fail” becomes “too big to save”.) It appears from your Question 1 that you are using a $30bn cutoff for other regulatory activities, so perhaps that would be a better criterion to use than Dodd-Frank, particularly if it is updated regularly. If so, I don’t see a need to adjust the cutoff between small and intermediate banks from the proposed $1bn (or $850m if using the  SBA standard) .
I disagree with dropping retail deposit services as a basis for bank evaluation. Deposit services are at least as important to the public as lending. I don’t see the benefit of limiting evaluations to “major product lines” and am concerned that it will distort the  available credit offerings. While you address this concern with other changes that would allow banks to receive consideration for loans not in their major product lines, that rather defeats the purpose of reducing the burden on the banks, and it needlessly complicates the evaluation process. Regardless, the large banks that hold the vast majority of the assets do not need any special favors.
The minor tweaks to geographically-limited assessment areas completely fail to address a glaring problem: how to adapt the CRA to an age of internet banking, where deposits can and do come from anywhere and the home office of the bank can also be anywhere. The goal of the Act is only satisfied if there is reinvestment in the communities from which deposits were collected. The agencies need to propose an equitable way to accomplish this goal.
The proposed 15% cap on indirect costs is problematical. It would apply only to grants from large banks, but the size of the grant recipient is more relevant, and this cap can be expected to adversely impact small organizations. Furthermore, the basis for the cap is OMB’s PROPOSED Uniform Guidance, which Congress has blocked at least for another two months.
Question 18: a qualified yes. I think it is within the scope of the Act. I’m a bit skeptical that it is possible and also concerned that it could crowd out investment in affordable housing for low-income individuals.
Question 60: LMI individuals may have difficulty accessing a website or travelling to a particular office or branch. Public notices should  therefore not be web-only or limited to a single physical location. It hardly seems too onerous to make them available.
The goal of the Act was to support banking services for and investment in low and moderate income communities. Any rules change that abandons or interferes with that goal is illegal.
