Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes
Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,
Central California Land Trust (CCLT) writes to object to the harmful changes proposed to the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed by Congress in 1977 in
response to redlining and creates an affirmative obligation for banks to help meet the credit,
deposit, and banking needs of communities, including low and moderate income (LMI)
communities. While the CRA has successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest and provide
services in underserved communities, challenges related to redlining, discrimination,
underinvestment, and lack of access remain.
CCLT is a nonprofit community land trust in Fresno, California, incorporated in 2017 and a
member of the California Community Land Trust Network. In 2026 CCLT completed its first two
permanently affordable homes in Southwest Fresno. We acquired and fully rehabilitated both
homes with City of Fresno ARPA funds, and we are selling them for $220,000 each, roughly
30% below market, to first-time buyers earning at or below 80% of area median income. CCLT
keeps the land under a 99-year ground lease, so each home stays affordable for every family
that buys it after the first.
Our work sits on the history the CRA was written to address. When we bought these two homes,
the recorded documents on title for both carried racially restrictive covenants from the 1940s.
One, recorded in 1945, provides that no property it covers may be occupied "by any of the
following described person, or persons, or races, or lineal descendants of such person or
persons, or races, to-wit: Negro, Chinese, Japanese, Filipino, Indian, Hindu, Korean, Malayan or
Mexican." Those covenants are void today, and CCLT is formally removing them from the
record. But the disinvestment they helped create in Southwest Fresno has not been undone,
and the CRA remains one of the few tools that asks banks to help repair it.
The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift. The
proposal does not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on LMI communities.
We request an extension of the comment period for an additional 60 days so we have time to
 better understand how much CRA activity may be lost to communities because of this proposal,
an analysis the regulators did not conduct or provide.
1) Affordable homeownership in our community depends on bank participation.
The greatest unmet need in Southwest Fresno is affordable, stable homeownership, and the
financing to reach it. A community land trust home only works if a buyer can get a mortgage on
it, and few lenders in the Central Valley are set up to lend on a home sold under a ground lease.
Each willing lender must first take the time to understand and accept the structure. That work
has a cost for the bank, and the CRA gives banks a reason to take it on. If banks can ignore this
need and still pass their CRA examinations, the lenders who have begun to build these products
will have less reason to continue, and the families we serve will have fewer paths to a home
they can afford.
2) Community development activities for affordable housing will drop dramatically.
The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large" Banks, such
that many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and expectation to serve the
community development needs of their communities.[1] According to National Community
Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70 California banks would see their reinvestment
obligations reduced under the proposal. Twenty-five California banks would shed their
Community Development Test responsibilities entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer
be subject to the Investment Test.[2]
The Investment Test has driven investment into programs with large impacts in LMI
communities, including equity equivalent investments in Community Development Financial
Institutions and in Community Land Trusts that take property off of the speculative market. The
proposal also suggests that a bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just 0.625% of its Tier
1 capital were devoted to community development loans and investments. If each bank
conducted only the amount necessary to meet the proposed thresholds, community
development activity would decrease by approximately $87.1 billion, or 85%.[3]
We believe loosening these standards will lead directly to less reinvestment in our region. The
capital that land trusts and other affordable housing developers need to acquire and rehabilitate
homes is already scarce in the San Joaquin Valley. When a regulator signals that banks can do
far less and still pass, less is what our communities will receive. Asset thresholds should not be
raised.
3) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will suffer.
The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by requiring a
demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating that large banks and
their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more than 15% of these grants on
overhead.[4] The regulators also ask whether CRA eligibility for bank grantmaking to nonprofits
should end entirely.
These requirements would fall hardest on organizations like ours. CCLT delivered its first two
homes with one full-time employee, its Executive Director. Flexible general operating support
from a philanthropic partner is what sustained that capacity: the leadership, outreach, partner
development, and legal and policy groundwork that turned a restricted capital grant into
permanently affordable homes. Project-tied grants with a 15% overhead cap would not pay for
that work, because for a lean organization the staff who deliver the project are the overhead. A
rule that steers bank grants away from general operating and capacity-building support will steer
them toward larger organizations, and away from the local groups that know their
neighborhoods best.
 Nonprofits are key partners for banks trying to bring credit and investment products into
communities that trust long established local organizations. Land trusts, homebuyer education
providers and down payment assistance programs help residents become stable and bankable
so that banks can make new loans in LMI communities. The regulators acknowledge that
community groups, including smaller groups, may be affected,[5] yet they offer no analysis of
that harm.
Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information to allow for
meaningful public comment, and will harm the communities that the CRA was meant to support.
If finalized in substantially the same form as proposed, communities like Southwest Fresno will
see less investment in affordable housing, fewer lenders willing to learn models like ours, and
fewer community serving nonprofit organizations. We urge the FDIC and the OCC to reconsider
this proposal.
Thank you for your consideration.
Very truly yours,
John Wellman
Executive Director
Central California Land Trust
cc: Rise Economy; California Community Land Trust Network
[1] Banks below $1 billion in assets would be considered Small Banks; Banks between $1 billion and $10 billion would be considered
Intermediate Banks; Banks over $10 billion would be considered Large Banks.
[2] https://www.ncrc.org/cra/#Lending
[3] NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk, (Sept. 10, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-development-activity-at-risk/.
[4] Proposing a 15% ceiling on indirect costs is inconsistent with historic federal policy and practice as the federal government
routinely makes grant awards where more than 15% of the grant can be used for indirect or overhead costs.
[5] The proposal notes that provisions "may reduce CRA incentives for general operating-support grants, grants to intermediaries, or
grants to organizations with higher operating-cost ratios, which could affect nonprofit capacity and the distribution of CRA motivated
grant funding," and that "Some general operating support, capacity-building grants, intermediary grants, or grants to smaller
nonprofits may receive less CRA motivated funding."

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Community
Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN
3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
New Chapter Ventures (NCV) submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
(OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)1 because it would significantly
weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and
the scope of the changes, we request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes,
carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an
opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify in support of any changes,
and extend the current comment deadline by 60 days.
NCV is a North Carolina nonprofit placemaking incubator. We partner with churches and
communities to repurpose underutilized assets through training, capital and operational support. Our
work includes teacher and essential-workforce housing on church-owned land, a church campus
redevelopment, and a commercial kitchen project, and we run cohort programs that help
congregations evaluate and plan the reuse of their property. Our projects are located in Salisbury,
Manteo, Durham and Statesville.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that
banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both credit and
deposit services. These protections remain especially important in communities that have
experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream financial
services.
The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change
how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for nonprofit
1Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without an adequate
analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on communities that
have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
1. The proposal's treatment of community development grants would disadvantage small
community-based organizations
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and new
documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations.2 For
smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology,
accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the underlying
program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources over which to
spread these costs. In addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff and may
not maintain financial records, budgets or program documentation in the precise format a bank would
need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations are more
difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger organizations whose
activities are easier to verify.
NCV works with congregations that are small organizations of this kind. Churches considering the
reuse of underutilized property for workforce housing, community kitchens and other community
facilities typically operate with part-time or volunteer administrative capacity and do not maintain
grant-compliance systems. To date, our projects in Salisbury and Manteo have been supported by
grants from local and community foundations. We have not yet received bank loans for projects. We
are developing capital partnerships for our teacher housing and kitchen projects, and the terms on
which banks can document and receive CRA consideration for support of small organizations will
affect whether those partnerships are practical.
Before finalizing these provisions, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed documentation
requirements and limits on administrative expenses would reduce or redirect bank support away from
smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those with limited administrative capacity. The agencies
must also determine whether those effects would ultimately reduce resources available to low- and
moderate-income communities. More broadly, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule
primarily in terms of reducing perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also
determine what the changes mean for the communities CRA is intended to serve.
2. Reduction in community investment expectations for all banks
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. From 2010 through 2024,
banks made approximately $81.1 billion in CRA-qualified mortgage lending to low- and moderate-
income (LMI) borrowers or in LMI census tracts in North Carolina, and approximately $44.9 billion
in CRA-qualified lending to small businesses (NCRC CRA Qualified Lending tool, drawing on
Home Mortgage Disclosure Act and FFIEC CRA disclosure data). In the Durham-Chapel Hill
metropolitan area alone, the corresponding figures were approximately $6.2 billion and $2.5 billion.
This is the scale of private capital that CRA expectations help direct toward communities like those
where NCV works, and it is the financing base that teacher and essential-worker housing and small-
business projects like ours will seek to draw on.
We are concerned that the proposed rule upends those incentives. For example, it suggests that a total
of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital devoted to either community development loans or
291 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,129 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 investments would be enough to receive a passing CRA rating.3 That percentage is far lower than the
percentage the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the largest banks
currently devote to community investments and loans.
NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the OCC- and
FDIC-supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these banks currently
conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community development loans and investments
inside their assessment areas, with a median of 6.8% of Tier 1 capital in annual community
development lending and a median of 3.6% of Tier 1 capital in annual CRA-qualified investments.4
If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet separate thresholds of 0.625% of
Tier 1 capital for community development lending and investments, combined activity would fall to
approximately $14.9 billion annually, a decrease of approximately $87.1 billion, or 85%. Similarly,
the proposal encourages banks to use strategic plans to make CRA compliance easier and more
predictable. Previous proposed guidance also set strategic plan benchmarks well below historical
levels of community development activity.5
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination
cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans. In the North
Carolina communities where we work, including Rowan, Dare, Durham and Iredell counties, reduced
bank investment expectations would be felt in the financing available for workforce housing, for
small food and service businesses that commercial kitchen projects are intended to support, and for
the reuse of existing buildings. Teacher and essential-worker housing depends on a capital structure
that can include bank lending and bank investment, and a lower expectation for that activity makes
these projects harder to finance. It is imperative that the CRA continue to incentivize banks to meet
community needs. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed
changes would reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income
communities, and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or
disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.
3. Less community development scrutiny of banks
The proposal would substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated
under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while banks with
assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less demanding
intermediate-bank framework rather than the more comprehensive tests applied to large banks.6 The
proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting requirements currently
applicable to large banks with $10 billion or less in assets, including reporting on small-business,
small-farm and community development lending.7
3The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit for activity outside their assessment areas if the banks surpass
a benchmark of 0.625% of Tier 1 capital for community development loans and likewise 0.625% for investments. 91 Fed.
Reg. 52,114, 52,140 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026). We are concerned that the practical effect is that the benchmark will serve
not as a floor, but as a ceiling.
4NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk (Sept. 10, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-development-activity-at-risk/.
5NCRC, The Proposed CRA Rule's Strategic Plans: A More Predictable Path to Doing Less (Sept. 1, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/the-proposed-cra-rules-strategic-plans-a-more-predictable-path-to-doing-less/.
691 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,120–23 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
7Id. at 52,120.
 Approximately 800 banks would no longer receive a community development evaluation because the
proposal would raise the small-bank threshold from $412 million to $1 billion.8 The 417 banks newly
classified as intermediate rather than large would no longer be examined under separate CRA
investment and services tests and would instead be evaluated on their combined community
development loans, investments and services. NCRC reports that banks account for approximately
85% of Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) investment dollars.9 Eliminating community
development obligations for over 800 banks, and separate investment evaluations for roughly 400
more, may worsen the housing shortage by reducing demand for LIHTC.
The need for regulatory scrutiny of whether banks are serving low- and moderate-income
communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to affordable mortgage credit and
homeownership, entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible small-business financing, and
neighborhoods continue to need investment in affordable housing, small businesses and other
community development. Teacher and essential-worker housing is among the needs our projects are
designed to address.
The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply because a
bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA obligations and
scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that would move into
less rigorous examination categories, determine the communities those institutions serve, analyze the
lending and community development activity that would receive less scrutiny, and assess whether the
effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-income communities or communities that have
experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
Conclusion
Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
•
identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny
under the proposal;
•
quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community development
activities subject to CRA evaluation;
•
assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
including rural communities and communities of color; and
•
consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
meaningful community accountability.
Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, NCV believes that the OCC and FDIC
should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and released for
public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to prevent significant declines in
CRA-related activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that
accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of
meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
8NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3, 2026), https://ncrc.org/2026-
cra-rollbacks/.
9NCRC, Community Reinvestment Act, https://ncrc.org/cra/.
 We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days. The
proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant changes to bank
classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit grants and other
core elements of CRA implementation. The current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from community
organizations and other stakeholders that do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is
warranted. An extension would allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical
consequences, gather examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a
more complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies extend
the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.
Sincerely,
Clark Harris
Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer
New Chapter Ventures
clark@newchapter.org
828-333-7254

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
See attached file(s)

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0262_09000064b9661fa8.pdf:
Neighborhood Housing Services of Baltimore, Inc.



25 E. 20th Street, Suite 170 Baltimore, Maryland 21218
Office: 410-327-1200
Fax: 410-675-1855
www.nhsbaltimore.org


October 7, 2026

Attention: Jennifer M. Jones, Deputy Executive Secretary
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
550 17th Street, NW,
Washington, DC 20429

Attention: Comment Processing
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th St. SW,
Washington, D.C. 20219

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations RIN 3064-AG31 / Docket ID OCC-2026- 0694

To Whom It May Concern,

We are writing in response to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking proposing major changes to
the regulations for the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) released on July 31, 2026, by the
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
(FDIC) (collectively, the agencies). CRA has been a critical tool in bringing loans, investments,
and grants to communities that have also had limited access to capital. We appreciate the
agencies intent to modernize the CRA. While we certainly support some of the proposed
frameworks that could increase the flow of capital into communities, we have significant
concerns about the impact some changes would have on the communities we serve.

Neighborhood Housing Services of Baltimore (NHS) is a community development financial
institution (CDFI) working in Baltimore City and the surrounding communities. We serve
communities that have been designated as persistent poverty areas. NHS is a 52-year-old
organization that works to support low- and moderate-income residents in purchasing homes
and ensuring the communities where they live thrive through comprehensive community
development work. NHS is certified by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban
Development (HUD) as a housing counseling agency. This designation allows us to provide
high-quality education to potential homebuyers and ongoing support to help them achieve and
maintain successful homeownership. NHS provides down payment and closing cost assistance
loans to homebuyers, helping remove a significant barrier that prevents many potential home
buyers from purchasing a home. NHS also provides first mortgage loans through programs
offered by Fannie Mae, the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) and local programs in

170 Baltimore, Maryland 21218

partnership with banks. Over the past 5 years, NHS has supported more than 1,300 families in
purchasing homes.

There are numerous ways that NHS partners with banks to ensure communities have access to
services and capital. Banks provide investments that are used to provide loans held by NHS.
These loans support home repairs, home purchase, and down payment assistance. NHS
currently has about $25 million in loans deployed in communities. Bank investments are critical
for this work. Banks also purchase loans originated from NHS. We have partnerships with
multiple banks that purchase first mortgage loans made to CRA eligible home buyers. The
eligibility for the loan programs mirrors the CRA requirement to ensure the banks receive
investment credit for the loans. NHS also receives grants from banks to support the work in the
community. Over the past 3 years, NHS has received over $3 million in grants from banks.
These awards have supported work to help residents prepare for homeownership, loans to help
renters in the community purchase homes in the neighborhood, and funding to support the
construction of homes. Without this support, the capacity of NHS to meet the needs of the
community would be significantly reduced. Banks are critical partners in meeting the needs of
our communities.

One area of concern in the proposed changes is the increase in asset threshold. In the
proposal, the agency defines small banks as those with less than $1 billion in assets,
intermediate banks as those with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as
those with assets over $10 billion. This change would impact on multiple banks that partner
with NHS. We are concerned that this would adversely impact on opportunities to partner with
banks. This change would result in less families being able to purchase homes and less capital
being available in areas of persistent poverty.

We are also concerned about the impact of the proposed changes on the New Markets Tax
Credit (NMTC) program. Over the past 5 years, NHS has closed 3 NMTC deals totaling $16
million to support the renovation of over 60 homes in the community. Congress recently made
NMTC a permanent program. The proposal would reduce the investment requirement for
banks by reducing the value of the tax credits by limiting the number of banks interested in
purchasing them. Removing the investment performance at a rating category reduces the
value of these investments to banks undermining the value of the credits.

Proposed changes to community development grants would adversely impact NHS and the
communities we serve. These changes could significantly hinder our ability to deliver critical
programs and services and negatively affect the communities that rely on our work. The
additional requirements that cap indirect costs would significantly increase the paperwork
burden on both banks and grant recipients. The agencies should not determine appropriate
levels of indirect costs. Banks can monitor and consider the use of funds in their grant making
decisions. NHS uses grant funds from banks to support our work, helping potential home
buyers prepare to be mortgage ready, providing down payment assistance loans, and the
redevelopment of vacant homes in the communities. Additionally, the consideration of

170 Baltimore, Maryland 21218

elimination of grants and donations from CRA consideration contemplated in the proposal is
strongly opposed and would potentially reduce the support available to our communities.

NHS supports the proposal included by the agencies to consider prior-period community
development loans during exams. This is an important adjustment as it will encourage banks to
deploy loans around community need rather than the timing of exam cycles. Our work often
requires long-term patient capital which is sometimes challenging to obtain due to banks'
desires to be able to count the investment in each investment cycle. Being able to obtain long-
term patient capital will enhance lending opportunities within communities served by NHS.

CRA has been a powerful tool for many years supporting partnerships between banks, CDFI's,
non-profit organizations, and the communities we serve. We certainly appreciate the desire to
improve clarity and value flexibility within the CRA rules. It is, however, critical that any
modernization of CRA results in additional capital reaching communities. Specifically, we
request the removal of the increased threshold for bank assets, restrictions on operating
grants, and the changes to the investment test. These changes would significantly reduce the
capital available to support the communities served by NHS.

Thank you for your consideration of these comments.

Sincerely,

Daniel T. Ellis
Chief Executive Officer

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
please see attached CRA comment letter from Credit Builders Alliance

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0263_09000064b9661faa.pdf:
October 12th, 2026

Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
Chief Counsel's Office, Attention: Comment Processing
400 7th Street SW, Suite 1E-216
Washington, DC 20219

Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
Attention: Comments—RIN 3064-AG31
550 17th Street NW
Washington, DC 20429

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; FDIC RIN 3064-AG31

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Credit Builders Alliance (CBA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency's and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's proposed amendments to
the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. CBA supports the agencies' goals of providing
greater clarity and reducing unnecessary burden, but several provisions would weaken incentives for
banks to support the community-based organizations, financial products, and nonprofit financial
intermediaries that help low- and moderate-income (LMI) individuals enter and succeed in the
mainstream financial system. Because partnerships with banks are central to CBA's ability—and the
ability of CBA's nonprofit members—to reach LMI consumers, the proposed CRA rule will have direct
consequences for the availability of responsible credit-building products and financial inclusion services
in underserved communities. CBA's principal concerns and recommendations are summarized below,
followed by a description of CBA's work and a more detailed discussion of each recommendation.















Summary of CBA's Recommendations
•
Establish a defined "qualified nonprofit intermediary" exception so that grants made through
accountable nonprofit intermediaries can receive CRA consideration when funds are deployed
to downstream nonprofit organizations for independently qualifying community development
activities. The final rule should treat qualifying downstream use as satisfying the "direct use"
requirement, substitute tailored tracing and documentation requirements for the proposed in-
termediary restrictions, and attribute CRA geography based on the ultimate qualifying activity.
• Do not impose the proposed 15 percent indirect-cost ceiling for on ordinary community devel-
opment grants from large banks. At a minimum, the ceiling and related attestation and Form
990/budget requirements should not apply to grants made through a qualified nonprofit inter-
mediary that satisfies the rule's tailored downstream documentation safeguards.

• Maintain the current small bank, intermediate-small bank (proposed to be termed "intermedi-
ate banks"), and large bank asset ceilings, subject to existing annual inflation adjustments. CBA
opposes the proposed ceiling increases, which would significantly reduce the number of banks
subject to meaningful community development responsibilities. In addition, raising the inter-
mediate bank ceiling would remove hundreds of currently large banks from the Service Test,
eliminating separate evaluation of their branch distribution and branch openings and closings.
This loss of accountability would significantly harm LMI communities' access to banking ser-
vices.
• Adopt Option B, which uses a qualitative, performance-context-based standard to determine
whether a bank has adequately served the community development needs of its assessment
areas before receiving consideration for activities outside those areas. The agencies should re-
ject Option A's fixed 0.625 percent-of-Tier-1-capital thresholds, which are far below current
large-bank community development activity and risk becoming de facto targets rather than
minimum eligibility thresholds.
•
Retain CRA consideration for qualifying community development services delivered through
bank-supported nonprofit partners as well as bank employee volunteers.
•
Continue evaluating affordable and effective deposit products and services under the large-
bank Service Test, including Bank On and similar account-access initiatives.














• Restore a clear LMI nexus throughout the community development definition—including af-
fordable housing, civic assistance, economic development, and revitalization/stabilization—and
codify the current "primary purpose" standard so that incidental benefits do not qualify as com-
munity development, while preserving existing CRA treatment of distressed or underserved
nonmetropolitan middle-income geographies and designated disaster areas.
•
Expressly preserve CRA consideration for activities with CDFIs and nonprofit financial institu-
tions.
•
Clarify that the Investment Test continues to be evaluated at the assessment-area level for
large banks and preserve appropriate geographic accountability for community development
investments.
•
Address the status of the 2016 Interagency Questions and Answers (Qs & As) in the final rule.
Important interpretations that are necessary to administer the retained 1995 framework should
be incorporated into the regulation or contemporaneous interagency proposed guidance rather
than left uncertain. The public should have an opportunity to comment on any new Qs & As be-
fore the rule is finalized.
The remainder of this letter explains why these recommendations matter, beginning with an overview
of CBA's work and the bank partnerships it depends on, followed by a detailed discussion of each
recommendation.
Overview of Credit Builders Alliance/CBA Fund and CRA's Importance to its Work
CBA is a national nonprofit network created by and for mission-driven organizations to bridge a
persistent gap in the modern financial system: millions of consumers with poor credit, thin credit files,
or no credit history can have difficulty obtaining affordable mainstream financial products, while
nonprofit organizations serving those consumers often lack direct access to the credit reporting
infrastructure needed to help them build credit. CBA connects nonprofit lenders, financial coaches,
affordable housing organizations, and other community-based organizations to the major credit
bureaus so that they can report consumers' successful loan payments, obtain credit reports for
underwriting and financial coaching, and incorporate credit building into broader financial capability
programs. CBA also provides training, technical assistance, professional development, and tools that
allow community organizations to offer safe and responsible credit-building strategies at scale.















CBA's reach demonstrates the importance of this infrastructure. Its network includes approximately
630 mission-driven organizations serving approximately 6.1 million clients. Seventy-four percent of
member clients are low- or very-low income, and 79 percent of CBA members identify the absence of a
credit score as a major challenge among the people they serve. CBA members have extended
approximately $4.33 billion in credit, and more than 152,000 clients have established or increased a
credit score, with an average increase of 52 points. These outcomes help consumers move from
financial exclusion toward access to lower-cost credit, housing, bank accounts, and other mainstream
financial products.
Financial inclusion also requires access to safe transaction accounts and assistance that helps
consumers successfully enter the banking system. CBA's work is closely aligned with Bank On and
similar bank-community partnerships that connect unbanked and underbanked consumers to safe,
affordable checking accounts and provide the financial education and support needed to use those
accounts successfully. These partnerships are especially important for consumers who have never had
a bank account, have previously lost an account, or face account-screening barriers and otherwise may
rely on check cashers and other costly alternative financial services.
Under the current CRA framework, a bank has a regulatory incentive to participate in this type of work
in several complementary ways. Examiners consider low-cost deposit accounts and other retail banking
services that improve access to financial services for LMI individuals. They also consider collaborations
with community organizations that expand access to banking services, and qualifying financial
education, credit counseling, and technical assistance can receive community development service
consideration. Thus, when a bank works with CBA, a CBA member, a Bank On coalition, or another
nonprofit partner to connect LMI consumers to appropriate accounts, provide financial education, or
contribute employee financial expertise, CRA currently recognizes the bank's substantive participation
in that financial-inclusion ecosystem.
The proposed rule would weaken that connection in several ways. It would retain community
development services under the large-bank Service Test, but narrow the definition of a qualifying
community development service to volunteer services performed by bank employees representing the
bank. It would separately exclude deposit products and services from the range of retail banking
services considered under the Service Test. Finally, by raising the intermediate-bank ceiling to $10
billion (or possibly $30 billion), the proposal would remove institutions currently classified as large
banks from the Service Test and therefore eliminate their separate branch-distribution evaluations.
CBA is concerned that these changes, together with the proposed restrictions on community














development grants, could reduce CRA incentives for banks to fund and partner with community
organizations that help LMI consumers become banked, build credit, and obtain responsible financial
products.
A particularly important part of CBA's work is CBA Fund, a certified Community Development Financial
Institution (CDFI) intermediary that expands the capacity of nonprofit lenders to provide safe and
affordable small-dollar consumer loans and credit-building products to LMI individuals. CBA Fund
provides three complementary forms of support—low-cost loan capital, capacity-building grants, and
technical assistance—that eligible nonprofit lenders use to establish, expand, and improve small-dollar
consumer lending programs, including emergency loans, payday-loan alternatives, credit-builder loans,
and other affordable consumer products. CBA Fund requires participating lenders to report, or become
capable of reporting, their borrowers' repayment performance to the major consumer credit bureaus
so that responsible repayment can help borrowers establish or strengthen their credit histories.
CBA Fund therefore performs precisely the type of intermediary function that the proposed CRA grant
provisions should preserve. Rather than requiring a bank to identify, underwrite, contract with,
monitor, and collect reports from numerous individual nonprofit lenders, a bank can partner with CBA
and CBA Fund, which aggregates bank grants and other capital, conducts due diligence, provides
technical assistance, and deploys low-cost loan capital and capacity-building grants to qualified
nonprofit lenders in communities across the country. CBA Fund has deployed approximately $9 million
in loan capital and $2 million in grant capital to 79 nonprofit organizations. The ultimate beneficiaries
are financially underserved consumers who receive responsible small-dollar and credit building loans
from local mission-driven lenders.
This model depends heavily on partnerships with banks and other financial institutions. Bank grants
provide flexible resources that help CBA and its members build lending capacity, develop and maintain
credit reporting infrastructure, provide financial coaching and technical assistance, and absorb the
costs of serving borrowers for whom small loan balances make conventional lending economics
difficult. Bank investments and low-cost capital enable nonprofit lenders to put affordable credit
directly into LMI communities, and bank participation in deposit-access initiatives can give consumers
who have been outside the banking system a pathway to safe checking and savings products. In this
way, CRA-motivated bank partnerships do not merely support CBA as an organization; they create the
infrastructure through which hundreds of nonprofit organizations can help millions of LMI consumers
build credit, avoid high-cost alternatives, and gain access to mainstream financial services.














The importance of these partnerships should inform the agencies' treatment of bank asset thresholds,
community development grants, nonprofit intermediaries, deposit services, and the community
development definition. A CRA rule that substantially reduces the number of banks with meaningful
community development responsibilities, limits consideration for grants made through intermediaries,
or removes deposit access from CRA evaluation risks weakening the very bank-nonprofit partnerships
that make financial inclusion programs possible. Conversely, a rule that recognizes accountable
nonprofit intermediaries and preserves meaningful incentives for bank partnerships can leverage the
expertise and local reach of organizations such as CBA and its members far beyond what a bank could
efficiently accomplish through individual grants and programs on its own.
CBA's experience gives it a direct perspective on how CRA rules affect bank partnerships with nonprofit
intermediaries, CDFIs, local lenders, financial coaches, affordable housing providers, and other
organizations serving LMI households. The proposed rule should preserve strong incentives for those
partnerships while providing banks with clear, workable standards. The sections below discuss each
recommendation in turn.
I. The Final Rule Should Establish a Qualified Nonprofit Intermediary Exception
CBA is particularly concerned that the proposed treatment of community development grants could
unintentionally restrict the use of nonprofit intermediaries that allow banks to efficiently support
qualified community development activities through experienced national, regional, and local
organizations.
The proposed definition of "community development grant" would require a grant or donation to be
"directly used by the recipient" for a program, project, or initiative having a primary purpose of
community development (see proposed 12 CFR §§ 25.12 and 345.12). For large banks, the definition
would also require that the recipient's indirect costs for administering the grant or donation not
exceed 15 percent. In addition, proposed §§ 25.42(a)(3) and 345.42(a)(3) would require a large bank to
maintain the recipient's written commitment concerning use of the funds, an attestation concerning
the 15-percent indirect-cost limitation, and supporting documentation including IRS Form 990 and
annual operating and program budgets.
These requirements create particular difficulties for grants made through nonprofit intermediaries. A
qualified intermediary may aggregate funding from multiple banks and other sources, conduct due
diligence on community organizations, provide technical assistance, monitor performance, and














distribute grants or low-cost capital to organizations that themselves conduct qualifying community
development activities. Properly structured intermediaries are not an obstacle between banks and the
communities they serve; they are an efficient and accountable mechanism for delivering resources to
those communities.
CBA Fund illustrates this model. CBA Fund aggregates capital and expertise, performs due diligence,
provides technical assistance, monitors performance, and deploys grants and low-cost loan capital to
nonprofit lenders offering safe, affordable small-dollar and credit-building products. This allows a bank
to support multiple qualified local organizations through one experienced intermediary rather than
separately identifying, underwriting, contracting with, paying, monitoring, and collecting reports from
each organization.
CBA therefore recommends that the agencies establish a defined category of "qualified nonprofit
intermediary" and provide a targeted exception from the restrictions that could otherwise prevent
such an intermediary from receiving and deploying a CRA-motivated grant. The exception should be
carefully circumscribed and should substitute specific downstream accountability requirements for the
proposed restrictions on intermediary grants.
A. A Qualified Nonprofit Intermediary Should Be Defined by Objective Safeguards
Both the intermediary and each downstream recipient should be tax-exempt nonprofit organizations
described in section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code. The downstream recipient should also be
organized and operated for a tax-exempt purpose relevant to the funded community development
activity.
Section 501(c)(3) status would provide an objective threshold requirement, but would not by itself
make an activity CRA-qualified. The particular downstream activity would continue to have to
independently satisfy the CRA definition of community development and all applicable geographic
requirements.
A qualified nonprofit intermediary should be required to maintain records sufficient to establish: (1)
the amount received from the bank and the amount ultimately deployed for qualifying community
development activities; (2) the identity and section 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status of each downstream
recipient; (3) the downstream recipient's 501(c)(3) exempt purpose relevant to the funded activity; (4)
the specific qualifying community development activity for which the funds are used; and (5) the














geographic location or beneficiary information necessary to establish the CRA eligibility and geographic
attribution of the activity.
The intermediary should provide the bank with an annual or grant-end report containing sufficient
information for the bank and its regulator to verify the qualifying use and appropriate geographic
attribution of the funds. These requirements would directly address the agencies' concerns regarding
pass-through grants while preserving a delivery structure that enables banks to support multiple
community organizations through an intermediary with the expertise and infrastructure to perform
due diligence, deploy funding, monitor performance, and document results.
B. Downstream Use by a Qualified Nonprofit Intermediary Should Satisfy the Direct-Use
Requirement
The proposed regulatory text creates uncertainty because it requires a community development grant
to be "directly used by the recipient." If that provision is interpreted to mean that the organization
receiving the grant directly from the bank must itself conduct the ultimate qualifying activity, a bank
grant could become ineligible merely because an intermediary distributes the funds to another
nonprofit organization that conducts the qualifying activity.
That result is unnecessary. A nonprofit lender receiving funds through an intermediary, for example,
may directly use those funds to capitalize or support a qualifying lending program. The lender is not
merely passing the funds onward. This lender underwrites and originates loans, services borrowers,
and assumes the responsibilities associated with extending credit. If those loans independently qualify
as community development loans, the downstream organization is directly conducting a qualifying
community development activity.
The final rule should therefore expressly provide that, where a bank makes a grant to a qualified
nonprofit intermediary, the downstream nonprofit's direct use of the funds for a qualifying community
development activity satisfies the rule's direct-use requirement.

















C. Qualified Nonprofit Intermediaries Should Be Subject to Tailored Documentation Requirements
Rather Than the Proposed Intermediary Restrictions
The proposed 15-percent indirect-cost limitation and related Form 990, budget, and attestation
requirements should not apply to grants made through a qualified nonprofit intermediary that satisfies
the safeguards described above.
An intermediary necessarily incurs costs to perform due diligence, administer grants, provide technical
assistance, monitor downstream organizations, maintain records, and report results. Those functions
provide accountability and permit banks to reach many more organizations than they could efficiently
support directly. Applying a rigid overhead limitation to an intermediary can therefore penalize the
very infrastructure that makes accountable downstream deployment possible.
Instead, CRA consideration should be based on the amount of the bank's grant that is demonstrably
attributable to qualifying community development activity. The intermediary should document the
deployment and ultimate qualifying use of those funds, and the bank should receive consideration only
for the amount properly attributable to qualifying community development. This approach would
replace a generalized overhead proxy with documentation directly demonstrating whether and how
the bank-supported funds ultimately benefited qualifying community development activities.
The agencies should also make clear that a qualified nonprofit intermediary may use grants,
recoverable grants, low-cost loans, or other appropriate financing tools to deploy bank-supported
resources downstream, so long as the ultimate activity qualifies and the bank receives consideration
only for the amount properly attributable to qualifying community development.
D. Geographic Attribution Should Follow the Qualifying Downstream Activity
The final rule should also make clear how the geographic provisions of §§ 25.13 and 345.13 apply to
grants made through a qualified nonprofit intermediary.
The geographic location of the intermediary itself should not determine where the grant receives CRA
consideration. Instead, CRA consideration should follow the location or beneficiaries of the qualifying
downstream activity supported with the bank's funds. Thus, a national nonprofit intermediary
headquartered outside a bank's assessment area could distribute bank-supported funds to a qualifying














organization or activity within the bank's assessment area, and the grant would receive consideration
in that assessment area to the extent supported by the intermediary's records.
Similarly, any funds deployed by the intermediary outside the bank's assessment areas should remain
eligible for consideration only to the extent permitted under the geographic-flexibility provisions of §§
25.13(e) or 345.13(e).
E. Recommended Regulatory Amendments
CBA recommends parallel amendments to the OCC and FDIC regulations as follows.
OCC — 12 CFR Part 25
1. Section 25.12 — Definitions
Add the following definition:
"Qualified nonprofit intermediary means an organization described in section 501(c)(3) of the Internal
Revenue Code that receives a grant or donation from a bank or savings association and uses or
distributes all or a portion of the funds for one or more programs, projects, or initiatives having a
primary purpose of community development, including distributions to one or more downstream
organizations described in section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code. A qualified nonprofit
intermediary must maintain documentation sufficient to establish the amount and ultimate qualifying
use of the funds, the identity and section 501(c)(3) status of each downstream recipient, the recipient's
exempt purpose relevant to the funded activity, the qualifying community development activity, and
the geographic location or beneficiaries of the activity."
Revise the definition of "Community development grant" so that paragraph (1) expressly provides that,
for a grant or donation to a "qualified nonprofit intermediary," amounts used or distributed by the
intermediary to a downstream organization described in section 501(c)(3) shall be considered directly
used by the recipient to the extent the downstream organization uses the funds for an activity that
independently qualifies as community development.
Revise paragraph (3) of the "Community development grant" definition to provide that the 15-percent
indirect-cost limitation does not apply to a grant or donation made to a "qualified nonprofit
intermediary" that satisfies the requirements of Part 25.














2. Section 25.13(d) — Community Development Activities in Assessment Areas
Add a provision stating that, for a community development grant made to a qualified nonprofit
intermediary, whether and to what extent the activity benefits or serves an assessment area is
determined based on the location or beneficiaries of the qualifying community development activity
for which the intermediary or downstream recipient ultimately uses the funds. The headquarters,
mailing address, or other location of the qualified nonprofit intermediary should not, by itself,
determine the geographic allocation of the activity. Activities outside the bank's or savings
association's assessment areas would remain subject to § 25.13(e).
3. Section 25.42(a)(2) — General Community Development Data
Clarify that, for a grant through a qualified nonprofit intermediary, the intermediary is the recipient for
purposes of identifying the entity receiving the bank's grant, but the "community development activity
location" required by § 25.42(a)(2)(v) is determined by the location or beneficiaries of the qualifying
activity for which the funds are ultimately used.
4. Section 25.42(a)(3) — Additional Documentation for Community Development Grants
Provide that, for a community development grant made to a qualified nonprofit intermediary, §§
25.42(a)(3)(ii) and (iii) do not apply. In lieu of those requirements, the bank or savings association
should collect and maintain documentation provided by the qualified nonprofit intermediary sufficient
to establish: (i) the amount of the grant or donation received and the amount used or distributed for
qualifying community development activities; (ii) the identity and section 501(c)(3) status of each
downstream recipient; (iii) the downstream recipient's Federal tax-exempt purpose relevant to the
funded activity; (iv) the community development activity for which the funds were used; and (v) the
geographic or beneficiary information necessary to determine the appropriate CRA consideration for
the activity. The intermediary should be permitted to satisfy this requirement through an annual or
grant-end report containing the required information.
Section 25.42(a)(3)(i) should also be revised so that its reference to projects, programs, or initiatives
"in the bank's assessment area(s)" reads "in the bank's or savings association's assessment area(s), or
otherwise eligible for consideration pursuant to § 25.13(e)." This conforming amendment is
appropriate for all community development grants, not only grants through qualified nonprofit
intermediaries, because § 25.12 expressly recognizes the geographic flexibility provided by § 25.13(e).














5. Section 25.42(b)(2)(ii) — Annual Reporting
Clarify that, for a community development grant made through a qualified nonprofit intermediary, the
qualified nonprofit intermediary is the "recipient" reported under
§ 25.42(b)(2)(ii). Information concerning downstream organizations and activities would be maintained
pursuant to § 25.42(a)(3) rather than requiring each downstream award to be reported as though it
were a separate grant made directly by the bank.
FDIC — 12 CFR Part 345
1. Section 345.12 — Definitions
Add the same definition of Qualified nonprofit intermediary, adjusted to refer to a "bank" rather than
a "bank or savings association." Revise the Community development grant definition in the same
manner as § 25.12 to deem qualifying downstream use to satisfy the direct-use requirement and to
exempt grants made to qualified nonprofit intermediaries from the 15-percent indirect-cost limitation.
2. Section 345.13(d) — Community Development Activities in Assessment Areas
Add the same qualified-nonprofit-intermediary geographic attribution provision described above for §
25.13(d), substituting references to the FDIC and § 345.13(e), as appropriate.
3. Section 345.42(a)(2) — General Community Development Data
Clarify that the qualified nonprofit intermediary is the recipient of the bank's grant, while the
community development activity location is determined based on the location or beneficiaries of the
ultimate qualifying activity.
4. Section 345.42(a)(3) — Additional Documentation for Community Development Grants
Provide that §§ 345.42(a)(3)(ii) and (iii) do not apply to grants made to qualified nonprofit

OCC § 25.42(a)(3). Section 345.42(a)(3)(i) should also be amended to refer to projects, programs, or
initiatives "in the bank's assessment area(s), or otherwise eligible for consideration pursuant to §
345.13(e)."














5. Section 345.42(b)(2)(ii) — Annual Reporting
Clarify that the qualified nonprofit intermediary is reported as the recipient of the grant, while
