Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill: 
The Housing and Community Development Network of New Jersey (HCDNNJ) submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)  because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).  In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days. 
Since 1989, the Housing and Community Development Network of New Jersey (the Network) has worked to improve the environment for the work of community development corporations (CDCs), and to strengthen their capacity to create housing and revitalize distressed neighborhoods throughout New Jersey.  The Network is the statewide association of over 250 non-profit housing and community development corporations, individuals, professional organizations, and prominent New Jersey corporations that support the creation of housing choices and economic opportunities for low- and moderate-income community residents.
The Network and our members share a commitment to promoting economic justice and the empowerment of low-income individuals and communities, and encouraging wider participation in the framing and implementation of public policies. 
We and our CDC members have been involved in Community Reinvestment Act agreements and have worked with banks throughout New Jersey to improve the effectiveness of the community development sector and promote lending in low- and moderate-income communities. Banks have been valued partners, and we are concerned that the proposed rule will substantially reduce CRA scrutiny for banks that will result in less bank support for community development, bank services and support for nonprofit organizations. In addition, we believe the proposed rules will jeopardize access to credit and mainstream financial services in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. 
According to national data, 28 of 63 banks in New Jersey will lose large bank status, meaning there will be less scrutiny on their operations.  In New Jersey, this means that 13 of 82 banks will not have a community development obligation at all, which will hurt the work of HCDNNJ and our members whose mission is to uplift low- and moderate-income communities.  In addition, the state may lose 15.2% of banks who are doing business in low- and moderate-income communities, cutting those communities off from financial services. Finally, 7.8% of banks will no longer have to disclose the small business lending they do. For these reasons, we ask your agency to oppose these new rules and protect community reinvestment.
Thank you in advance for your consideration. 
Very Truly Yours,

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations Proposed Rule (Docket ID OCC-2026-0694)
To Whom It May Concern:
Wendover Housing Partners ("Wendover") appreciates the opportunity to provide feedback on the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's ("FDIC") proposal to reform
Community Reinvestment Act ("CRA") regulations. As a developer of affordable and workforce housing
communities throughout the United States, Wendover is particularly concerned about the proposed increase in
the asset threshold for banks subject to the CRA's separate investment test and the resulting impact on the
availability of financing for affordable housing developments.
Wendover relies on a combination of private investment, conventional financing, and federal and state affordable
housing programs, including the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit ("LIHTC"), to develop housing for low- and
moderate-income families and seniors. Regional and community banks are important participants in these
transactions, providing both financing and equity investments that are often essential to making affordable
housing developments financially feasible.
The proposed redesignation or elimination of the separate investment test for banks with assets between
approximately $1.65 billion and $10 billion threatens to significantly reduce the participation of these
institutions in affordable housing development. Under the current CRA framework, the investment test
provides an important incentive for regional and community banks to invest in LIHTC developments within the
communities they serve. Without that incentive, we are concerned that many of these institutions will substantially
reduce their investment activity or exit the LIHTC market altogether.
From Wendover's perspective, the loss of these banking partners would have meaningful consequences.
Affordable housing developments are inherently complex transactions that depend on assembling multiple
sources of financing. Regional and community banks provide an important source of capital and competition,
particularly in markets where the number of potential investors is already limited. Their participation helps
developers secure competitive LIHTC equity pricing, reduce financing gaps, and move developments forward
that might otherwise be financially infeasible.
Eliminating the separate investment test could reduce competition among LIHTC investors, resulting in lower
equity pricing and increased financing gaps. Unlike conventional market-rate developments, affordable housing
communities are subject to restrictions on rents and tenant incomes, limiting a developer's ability to offset reduced
equity proceeds through increased rental revenue. As a result, even relatively modest reductions in LIHTC pricing
can jeopardize a development's financial feasibility, delay construction, or prevent much-needed affordable
housing from being built.


We also recognize that the proposed regulations would continue to evaluate certain community development
activities undertaken by intermediate banks. However, community development lending and equity investment
are not interchangeable. While banks may continue to receive CRA consideration for lending activities, the
absence of a separate investment test may encourage institutions to prioritize lending over LIHTC equity
investments. This distinction is particularly important because the availability of equity is often what enables
affordable housing developments to support construction and permanent debt financing in the first place.
These concerns are especially significant in smaller and underserved markets, where regional and community
banks may be among the few institutions willing to invest in affordable housing developments. Reducing their
incentive to participate could further concentrate LIHTC investment among a smaller number of large national
institutions, making it increasingly difficult for developers to secure financing outside the most competitive
metropolitan markets.
At a time when the country faces a significant shortage of affordable rental housing, federal policy should
encourage greater participation by financial institutions in affordable housing investment, not create incentives
for existing participants to withdraw. The proposed changes also risk undermining recent congressional efforts to
expand the LIHTC program and increase the production of affordable rental housing.
Wendover respectfully urges the OCC and FDIC to leave the thresholds as they currently stand, consistent
with the direction the Federal Reserve (the third bank regulator) is taking. If the agencies elect to increase
the threshold, we strongly encourage adoption of the lowest possible increase, together with meaningful
requirements that preserve incentives for newly designated intermediate banks to make community development
equity investments, including investments in LIHTC developments. For newly designated intermediate banks, we
ask that the requirement to invest, as well as lend, in the communities in which they do business be maintained.
Anything short of this will significantly curtail competition for the LIHTC and affordable housing production
throughout the country.
We appreciate the agencies' consideration of these comments and encourage them to carefully evaluate the
potential consequences of the proposed changes for affordable housing production and the communities that
depend on it.
Respectfully submitted,

Jonathan L. Wolf
Founder and Chief Executive Officer
Wendover Housing Partners

RE: Public Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on
Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-
AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill,

Lane County respectfully submits public comment in opposition to the Proposed Rulemaking
OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31, as written, as it
would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). Access to traditional
banking and credit is a key driver of financial well-being, economic mobility, and resilience.
Significant gaps in access among low-income, rural, and disabled populations would be
exacerbated by the proposed changes. Given the complexity of the rule and scope of the
changes prior to making any proposed changes, Lane County requests that the OCC and FDIC
fully assess the downstream impacts and consequences for low- and moderate-income
communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies
identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.

As a local government founded in 1851 and committed to economic opportunity and
responsible stewardship of public resources, Lane County submits this comment to highlight
the significant implications federal policy changes have on the communities we serve. Counties
rely on bank partnerships to finance local priorities. CRA lending and investment brings vital
capital to projects that often cannot secure financing on their own, especially affordable housing
 VANESSA CORNWALL
Intergovernmental Relations Officer
Vanessa.Cornwall@lanecountyor.gov

PUBLIC SERVICE BUILDING / 125 EAST 8TH AVENUE/EUGENE, OR 97401 / (541) 682-6504
efforts and initiatives that serve low‐ and moderate‐income communities. For nearly fifty years,
the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that banks meet the
credit needs of their whole community. These protections are particularly essential for Lane
County, where years of disinvestment, repeated branch closures, and uneven access to
mainstream financial services in rural areas have left many of our residents and communities
without access to reliable banking options.
Economic Development Impacts
Lane County has concerns about the impact of this proposal on economic development
initiatives. Under current guidance, infrastructure projects in low to moderate income (LMI)
areas generally receive CRA credit only when they help retain or attract residents or businesses.
The proposal would change the standard by allowing credit for infrastructure that "benefits or
serves" a targeted area, even when the project delivers little actual meaningful benefit to LMI
residents and does not help preserve or strengthen the community.1
This means that a bank could seek CRA credit for financing a large regional infrastructure
project that only incidentally and marginally serves an LMI neighborhood, even if most of the
project's benefits flow to affluent communities or private companies. For example, a data
center located in or connected to an LMI tract could qualify despite creating few permanent
jobs and providing little direct benefit to residents. In Lane County, infrastructure investments
aligned with CRA's existing standards have historically supported projects that deliver clear,
direct benefits to low- and moderate-income residents. Improvements to rural broadband access
in communities along the McKenzie River have helped retain small businesses and enabled
local workers to participate more fully in the digital economy. Similarly, targeted infrastructure
upgrades in west Eugene industrial corridors have supported job retention at small
manufacturers that employ a significant number of LMI residents.
The proposal's increase to CRA asset thresholds would further weaken the connection between
CRA oversight and meaningful local economic development. By raising the small‐bank
threshold from $412 million to $1 billion, many of Lane County's mid‐sized institutions would
no longer be evaluated for community development performance. These banks have historically
played a central role in financing rural broadband, small‐manufacturer modernization,
brownfield redevelopment, and small‐business lending in rural communities such as Oakridge,
Cottage Grove, Florence, and across the McKenzie Valley. Reclassifying them into less
rigorous CRA tiers removes an essential incentive for banks to invest in the kinds of projects
that stabilize rural economies, support traded‐sector employers, and advance land‐use and
infrastructure priorities identified in Lane County's adopted legislative principles.
With fewer banks required to track or report community development activity, Lane County
would face diminished access to affordable capital for core economic development goals,
including rural industrial‐site readiness, advanced wood‐products manufacturing, local food and

1 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,1335 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 VANESSA CORNWALL
Intergovernmental Relations Officer
Vanessa.Cornwall@lanecountyor.gov

PUBLIC SERVICE BUILDING / 125 EAST 8TH AVENUE/EUGENE, OR 97401 / (541) 682-6504
agribusiness development, and critical infrastructure such as high‐speed fiber in rural
communities. Lane County's rural cities already experience disinvestment, thin credit markets,
and limited commercial lending options. Reducing CRA scrutiny for the very institutions
serving these areas would deepen existing gaps in economic opportunity and weaken progress
on projects that rely on consistent, mission‐aligned banking partners.
Before reducing community development obligations on such a wide scale, the OCC and FDIC
should comprehensively assess and identify which institutions would move into less demanding
CRA categories and evaluate the types of community development activities that would no
longer be reviewed. This analysis is essential for understanding whether the proposed
thresholds would disproportionately harm low- and moderate-income neighborhoods and rural
communities that already struggle to attract investment, as seems apparent based on the
proposed rule as written.
Community Impacts
Lane County is concerned about the impact of the proposal on community development grants
and nonprofit organizations. Bank grants have played a pivotal role in strengthening the
operating capacity of our nonprofit partners, enabling them to deliver vital community services
such as workforce training, financial counseling, affordable housing, and small-business
mentoring. Funds have helped organizations maintain staff, secure space for programming, and
invest in community outreach. When banks invest locally, they help build durable infrastructure
that benefits residents long after a single project ends. Rules governing these activities have
consequences well beyond the banks themselves.
For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and
new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller
organizations.2 For many Lane County nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap would weaken
their abilities to support their community. Staff, rent, technology, accounting, compliance and
other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller
organizations have fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs. Many
community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain financial records,
budgets or program documentation in the precise format a bank would need to establish CRA
eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations are more difficult or costly to
document, they may redirect funding toward larger organizations whose activities are easier to
verify.
Before finalizing these provisions, OCC and FDIC should conduct thorough analysis of
whether the proposed documentation requirements and limits on administrative expenses would
reduce or redirect bank support away from smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those
with limited administrative capacity. OCC and FDIC should also determine whether those
effects would ultimately reduce resources available to low- and moderate-income communities.

2 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,129 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 VANESSA CORNWALL
Intergovernmental Relations Officer
Vanessa.Cornwall@lanecountyor.gov

PUBLIC SERVICE BUILDING / 125 EAST 8TH AVENUE/EUGENE, OR 97401 / (541) 682-6504
More broadly, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule primarily in terms of reducing
perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also determine what the
changes mean for the communities CRA is intended to serve and the investments the current
regulations were created to incentivize and track.
Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
● Identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA
scrutiny under the proposal;
● Quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
● Assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or
populations, including rural communities;
● Consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without
sacrificing meaningful community accountability; and
Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, Lane County believes that the
OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impact is
prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to
prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that
accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose
of meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120
days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant
changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations,
nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The current comment period
closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, local affiliates, and other stakeholders that do not have dedicated
regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would allow affected organizations
to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather examples from the communities they
serve, and provide the agencies with a more complete record on which to base any final rule.
We therefore request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at
least 60 days.
Sincerely,

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-
AF57; RIN 3064-AG31

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
Since 1971, the Housing Authority of Snohomish County (HASCO) has expanded access to
affordable housing for households across Snohomish County. HASCO currently owns and
operates more than 2,000 homes, with hundreds of additional units under construction. Many of
these properties have been developed through the LIHTC program—a public-private partnership
that is essential to affordable housing production nationwide and closely linked to the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).
HASCO joins affordable housing developers and advocates at the national, state, and local
levels in opposing the proposed changes to the CRA. Our principal concerns are as follows:
1) Although the LIHTC program continues to deliver meaningful results in Snohomish
County, the widening gap between allowable rents and construction costs increasingly
threatens project feasibility. At the current tax credit price of approximately $0.78, a
typical project is financially viable only within the limited number of Qualified Census
Tracts or Difficult Development Areas (QCTs/DDAs) in the county. By reducing bank
participation in the CRA and LIHTC programs, the proposed rule could further constrain
affordable housing production shortly after Congress significantly expanded the
program through H.R. 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
2) The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act contains numerous provisions designed to
encourage housing innovation at the local level. Because innovative approaches are, by
definition, new and may present unfamiliar risks, banks may be less inclined to support
them when participation is optional. Washington State currently has 12 banks classified
as "large"; under the proposed rule, that number would fall to four, substantially reducing
the pool of institutions positioned to support emerging housing strategies. The
proposed rule would therefore weaken significant bipartisan efforts to advance practical
housing solutions nationwide.
3) HASCO partners closely with community organizations, including Community
Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs), to address financing gaps in affordable
housing development. The effects described above could also diminish bank
engagement with CDFIs, compounding the challenges facing affordable housing
production and limiting the adoption of innovative housing solutions at a time of urgent
need.



For these reasons, together with the concerns raised by our community and national partners,
HASCO respectfully opposes the proposed rule. We support the FDIC's and OCC's efforts to
modernize the CRA, streamline its administration, and reinforce the vital role financial
institutions play in their communities. HASCO welcomes the opportunity to share its local
expertise regarding the intersection of the CRA, financial institutions, and affordable housing
development. Based on our experience, however, we believe the proposed rule, as written, would
materially impede communities across the country in meeting the urgent need for affordable
housing.
Sincerely,



Laurie Olson, CEO
Housing Authority of Snohomish County

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0293_09000064b9662ad7.pdf:
October 12, 2026

Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)

RE: Concerns Regarding Proposed Changes to Community Reinvestment Act Asset
Thresholds

To whom this may concern:

On behalf of the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Barbara (HASBARCO), I am writing
to express our significant concerns regarding proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment
Act (CRA) asset thresholds that would substantially increase the number of banks classified as
"small" or "intermediate" institutions. As an organization committed to expanding affordable
housing and community development opportunities, we are deeply concerned about the potential
impact these changes could have on the availability of financing in underserved communities
throughout California, particularly in Santa Barbara County.

California continues to face one of the most severe housing affordability crises in the nation.
Communities throughout Santa Barbara County are experiencing rising housing costs, limited
housing supply, increasing development expenses, and growing challenges in providing
affordable homes for low- and moderate-income households, seniors, individuals with
disabilities, veterans, and essential workers. Access to capital through CRA-motivated lending
and investment has been an important component in financing affordable housing developments
and community revitalization efforts that serve these populations.

The CRA has historically encouraged financial institutions to provide community development
loans and investments that support affordable housing, neighborhood revitalization, economic
development, and community services. Currently, approximately 46 percent of federally insured
banks are incentivized through CRA requirements to provide community development financing.
Proposed increases to the asset thresholds for small and intermediate banks would significantly
reduce the number of institutions subject to these incentives and could result in a corresponding
reduction in community development investment nationwide.

These changes are particularly concerning for communities such as Santa Barbara County, where
affordable housing developments often rely on complex financing structures involving multiple
public and private funding sources. CRA investments frequently serve as a critical financing tool
that helps make affordable housing developments feasible. For example, without Wells Fargo
investment in a previous development, we would not have been able to move forward with the
project. A reduction in bank participation could further constrain an already limited funding
environment and make it more difficult to develop, preserve, and rehabilitate affordable housing
throughout the Central Coast and California.

Docusign Envelope ID: 2491BD5F-5B9A-8B81-8221-CB3D8E8C4B5D


The proposed changes would also have a disproportionate impact on rural communities and areas
outside of major metropolitan centers. This is especially relevant for Santa Barbara County,
which encompasses both urban centers and large rural and agricultural areas. Communities such
as Lompoc, Santa Maria, Guadalupe, Buellton, Solvang, and Santa Ynez depend on continued
investment to address workforce housing shortages, aging housing stock, community facility
needs, and economic development opportunities. Reduced CRA incentives could further limit
access to financing in the very communities where investment is needed most.

Additionally, affordable housing developers throughout California are already facing significant
challenges related to rising construction costs, insurance premiums, labor shortages, and higher
interest rates. At a time when federal, state, and local policymakers are working to increase
housing production and address long-standing housing shortages, it is difficult to reconcile
reducing incentives for community development investment with the urgent need for additional
affordable housing resources.

For decades, CRA-driven investments have helped leverage private capital into underserved
communities and support projects that might not otherwise move forward. Weakening these
incentives risks reducing an important source of financing for affordable rental housing, first-
time homeownership opportunities, community facilities, and economic development initiatives
that are essential to the vitality of California communities.

We respectfully urge federal regulators to carefully evaluate the potential impacts of these
proposed threshold changes and maintain a CRA framework that continues to encourage robust
community development lending and investment. Preserving strong CRA incentives is critical to
ensuring that California communities, including Santa Barbara County, have the resources
necessary to address housing affordability, promote economic opportunity, and strengthen
underserved neighborhoods.

Thank you for your consideration of these concerns and for your commitment to supporting
investments that improve the lives of low- and moderate-income individuals and families.

Sincerely,



Robert P. Havlicek Jr.
Executive Director
Housing Authority of the County of Santa Barbara

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
on Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694;
RIN 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
The Neighborhood Development Collaborative (NDC), a coalition of 22 Colorado-based
nonprofit and mission-driven affordable home builders, submits this comment in
opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued
by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC)1 because it would significantly weaken the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the
changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes,
carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities,
provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify
supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60 days.
NDC and its member organizations use CRA-qualified funds to improve the lives of
everyday Coloradans. Grants and other funds required by the CRA are a vital source of
funds for affordable housing construction. CRA-qualified mortgages create affordable
homeownership opportunities, as do the LIHTC investment the CRA drives, the biggest
source of affordable housing in Colorado.
For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important
in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal
access to mainstream financial services.
1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
1

 The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and
would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and
support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being
considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and
moderate-income communities and on communities that have experienced historic
discrimination and disinvestment.
THIS PROPOSAL REDUCES COMMUNITY INVESTMENT EXPECTATIONS
FOR ALL BANKS
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In the Denver
Metro Area and Colorado, from 2010-2024, banks invested $49 billion and $85 billion,
respectively, in CRA-qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census
tracts and $25 billion and $13 billion, respectively, in CRA-qualified lending to small
businesses. Investments such as these benefited our community, in the form of affordable
home mortgages for community land trusts and tax credit investments which continue
bringing affordable housing to our state.
We are concerned that the proposed CRA rule upends banks' incentives to make these
investments in the future. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's
Tier 1 capital devoted to either community development loans or investments would be
enough to receive a passing CRA rating.2 However, that percentage is far lower than the
percentage the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the
largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.
NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the
OCC and FDIC supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these
banks currently conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community development
loans and investments inside their assessment areas, and that the median percentage of
annual community development lending in assessment areas was 6.8% of Tier 1 capital,
and a median of 3.6% of Tier 1 capital for annual CRA qualified investments.3 If each
bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet separate thresholds of 0.625%
of Tier 1 capital for community development lending and investments, combined activity
would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually -- a decrease of approximately $87.1
billion, or 85%. Similarly, the proposal encourages banks to use strategic plans to make
their CRA compliance easier and more predictable. Previous proposed guidance also set
3 NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk,
(Sept. 10, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-development-activity-at-ri
sk/.
2 The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit for outside their assessment areas if the banks
surpass a benchmark of 0.625% of its tier 1 capital for community development loans and likewise 0.625%
for investments. 91 Fed. Reg. 52121, 52140 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026). We are concerned that the practical
effect of this proposal is that the benchmark will serve not as a floor, but a ceiling.
2
 strategic plan benchmarks for CRA performance well-below historical levels of
community development activity.4
Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic
discrimination cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments
and loans. If regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be
accountable to the communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for
communities. In Colorado, for example, homeownership rates have been dropping as
home prices outpace wage growth. 63% of Coloradans owned their homes in 2025, down
4.5% in just 3 years, and well below the 71% at which Colorado's homeownership rate
peaked in 20025. Coloradans need affordable mortgages to be able to unlock the stability
that comes with homeownership. Additionally, Colorado persistently lacks housing
affordable at low incomes. Colorado only has 40% of the homes needed for households
earning less than 50% AMI, a deficit that LIHTC can help fill6.
It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet community needs.
Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes
would reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income
communities and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or
disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.
THIS PROPOSAL ELIMINATES "PURPOSE TEST" FOR ECONOMIC
DEVELOPMENT, WEAKENING CONNECTION TO LMI COMMUNITY
BENEFITS
Under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying small business does not
automatically constitute economic development. The activity must also satisfy a
requirement known as the "purpose test," meaning it must promote economic
development by supporting permanent job creation, retention, or improvement for low- or
moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income communities.7
The proposed rule would eliminate the "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks
could earn CRA credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or
improves jobs for low- and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income
communities. Instead, financing could qualify as economic development based primarily
7 Federal Reserve Board, Interagency Questions and Answers Regarding Community Reinvestment, §
__.12(g)(3)-1 (explaining that CRA economic-development activities must satisfy both a "size" test and a
"purpose" test, and identifying permanent job creation, retention, or improvement for LMI persons or in
LMI geographies as qualifying purposes).
6 Mile High United Way. Colorado's Housing Affordability Crisis 2025.
https://unitedwaydenver.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Housing-Affordability-Crisis-Report-2025.pdf
5 U.S. Census Bureau, Homeownership Rate for Colorado [COHOWN], retrieved from FRED, Federal
Reserve Bank of St. Louis; https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/COHOWN, September 17, 2026.
4 NCRC, The Proposed CRA Rule's Strategic Plans: A More Predictable Path to Doing Less (Sept 1, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/the-proposed-cra-rules-strategic-plans-a-more-predictable-path-to-doing-less/.
3
 on the type and size of the business and whether the financing expands, improves or
preserves the business's productive capacity, physical presence or employment base.8
We are concerned that this change would weaken the connection between CRA economic
development credit and the people and communities CRA is intended to benefit.
Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying business expand does not necessarily create
jobs, increase economic opportunity in an underserved neighborhood or address the needs
of low- and moderate-income communities. NDC's members contribute not only to a
greater supply of affordable housing, but also to economic activity in Colorado generally.
From 2018 to 2023, affordable housing construction contributed the following to
Colorado's economy9:
●​ $2.66 billion in annual economic output,
●​ $859 million in annual household earnings,
●​ 14,275 new, full- and part-time jobs annually,
●​ $53.3 million in individual income-tax revenue annually, and
●​ $26.6 million in sales-tax revenue annually.
Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens
a qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank
to demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or
neighborhoods.10 The agencies themselves acknowledge that eliminating the purpose test
would expand the universe of activities eligible for CRA credit.11
Before eliminating the purpose test, the agencies should analyze what additional activities
would qualify under the new definition, where those activities are likely to occur, and
whether bank financing could shift away from activities that create or retain jobs for low-
and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income communities. The agencies
should also explain why eliminating the existing connection to these outcomes is
consistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs of
their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities.
PROPOSAL WILL NARROW THE ACTIVITIES SUBJECT TO CRA
EXAMINATION AND HIDE LENDING GAPS
Under the current rule, large banks are generally evaluated on their home mortgage,
small business and small farm lending. The proposal outlines two options for regulators
to focus on products designated as a bank's "major product lines" based either on the
largest two product lines by all lending volume, or based on the type of lending a bank
11 Id. at 52,133.
10 Id.
9Colorado Futures Center, Subsidized Housing's Role in Colorado's Economic Activity 2018-2023, July
2025,
https://coloradofuturescsu.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/CFC_CapA_Housing_Impact_2018_2023.pdf
8 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,133-34 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
4
 does more of in a particular assessment area.12 Either option would allow weak
performance in a lower volume product to escape meaningful scrutiny even when that
credit is important locally.
For example, in Colorado, there is a strong need for home mortgage and small business
lending. But if that type of lending is not a major part of a large bank in my community's
business, regulators will not evaluate whether the bank is meeting this crucial community
need. Absent such evaluation, the bank will likely deprioritize making such loans.
In addition, under the current rule banks above the large bank threshold generally collect
and report on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans
and assessment areas. But because of the proposed change in the threshold, banks with
$10 billion or less in assets would no longer be required to collect and report such CRA
data. Nationwide, that will result in a 11% reduction in CRA small business lending data.
Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers will not be able to
identify credit deserts, compare performance or understand whether local credit needs are
being met.
Before narrowing the activities subject to CRA examination and eliminating data
reporting requirements, the agencies should analyze the impact of doing so will have for
people with low- and moderate-incomes or low- and moderate-income communities,
including whether it could result in a reduction in the types of lending that would meet
community needs. In addition, the agencies should explain why this change would be
consistent with the CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit
needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
CONCLUSION
Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
●​ Identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA
scrutiny under the proposal;
●​ Quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
●​ Assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or
populations, including rural communities and communities of color;
●​ Consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without
sacrificing meaningful community accountability; and
Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, NDC believes that the
OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts
is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable
changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.
12 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52123 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
5
 The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for
meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that
materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are
consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120
days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service
evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The
current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that
do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would
allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather
examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more
complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies
extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.

Sincerely
The Neighborhood Development Collaborative

cc. National Community Reinvestment Coalition
6

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations RIN 3064-AG31 / Docket ID OCC-2026- 0694

Dear Deputy Executive Secretary Jones and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency:
I submit this letter on behalf of the Carolina Small Business Development Fund (CSBDF). We appreciate the
opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, proposing
major revisions to the regulations of the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) published in the Federal
Register on August 12, 2026.

CSBDF is a thirty-six (36) year old North Carolina non-profit community and economic development
organization that is certified by the Department of Treasury as a community development financial institution
(CDFI). CSBDF is also authorized, regulated and certified to carry out programs of the U.S. Small Business
Administration (SBA). The organization works hand in hand with local, regional, and national banks to
provide responsible financing and technical assistance to underserved small businesses through the SBA
Community Advantage program as well as other publicly and privately supported guarantee programs, while
helping to cultivate a pipeline of bank-ready businesses for conventional financial institutions. Largely because
of debt investments, operating grants and referral relationships with banks of varying sizes who adhere to CRA
rules, CSBDF has deployed over $134M in capital, entered into financial transactions with over 3,400 North
Carolina small businesses and has provided technical assistance to over 9,800 firms throughout the State.
IMPLAN economic development software (which operational grants from banks also help to fund) estimates
that CSBDF financial assistance to small businesses has created and saved nearly 6,200 jobs throughout the
State. In FY25 alone, our estimates showed over $15M in payroll earnings, 734 jobs created and saved and
over $4.6M in tax revenues created.

Debt investments have enabled CSBDF to provide low-cost financing to small businesses who have no other
financing alternatives or costly ones. The operating capital grants from banks have enabled the organization to
provide technical assistance in 1:1, group and digital formats through our online technical assistance platform
called VIVID. Operating capital has also contributed to the organization's clarity and transparency in
reporting, underwriting and data tracking, because it has strengthened the capabilities of our Salesforce and
loan origination platforms. Our capital has been deployed to small businesses in urban and rural areas; to male
and female-owned businesses; veterans and non-veterans; and to all of North Carolina's 10 highest growth


3128 Highwoods Blvd., Suite 170. Raleigh, NC 27604. Telephone: 919.803.1437 Fax: 919.896.8612
www.carolinasmallbusiness.org

industries. Examples of businesses that have received funding from CSBDF include The Maker Studio, a
veteran-owned manufacturing-related maker space in Fayetteville, Amazing Grace Healthcare, a healthcare



provider in Greenville, Children's Garden Montessori School, a private elementary school in Mebane and
Drums & Flats, a food truck in Charlotte.

CSBDF's experience demonstrates that banks and mission lenders are complementary partners, not competing
sources of capital. Mission lenders like CSBDF frequently serve as an entry point into the financial system for
entrepreneurs and small businesses that may not initially qualify for conventional bank financing. Through
relationship-based prudent underwriting, smaller-dollar lending, technical assistance, and business
development support, CSBDF and other mission lenders help borrowers strengthen their businesses and, over
time, become potential customers of conventional financial institutions.

CRA has played an important role in creating the durable incentives that make these partnerships possible.

CSBDF appreciates the agencies' efforts to modernize the Community Reinvestment Act regulations and
supports provisions that could strengthen the CRA structure and promote responsible investment in
underserved communities. However, we are deeply concerned that the proposed increases in asset thresholds,
limitations on operating grants, and other interconnected changes could significantly weaken incentives for
banks to invest in, lend to, and partner with mission-based lenders. These changes could reduce access to
critical sources of capital for mission lenders and, in turn, constrain the ability of SBA Community Advantage
mission lenders and other community development mission lenders to provide much-needed financing and
technical assistance to underbanked and underserved small businesses and communities.

Taken together, these changes could have consequences well beyond CRA examinations. They could affect the
availability of the bank capital and other resources that mission lenders rely upon to finance underserved small
businesses.

I.
CRA SHOULD CONTINUE TO INCENTIVIZE BANK–MISSION LENDER
 PARTNERSHIPS

CSBDF Recommendation: Any CRA modernization should preserve bank and mission lender partnerships to
strengthen this critical ecosystem for underserved and underbanked small businesses.

In CSBDF's case, the proposed CRA changes could have a significant impact on the organization's ability to
attract affordable debt capital and operational support from banks. In fiscal year 2026, CSBDF had 14 notes
payable from 11 different banks, with an average cost of funds of 3%. These bank investments are an important
source of low-cost capital that enables CSBDF to provide affordable financing to small businesses that may not
qualify for conventional bank financing.

The proposed changes could also affect the operational support CSBDF receives from banks. In fiscal year 2026,
this support represented approximately 10% of CSBDF's total income. While CSBDF is not solely dependent
on bank support to operate, this funding provides important resources that help CSBDF carry out its mission and
sustain the infrastructure necessary to lend to and support small businesses. A reduction in CRA-related


3128 Highwoods Blvd., Suite 170. Raleigh, NC 27604. Telephone: 919.803.1437 Fax: 919.896.8612
www.carolinasmallbusiness.org

incentives could make banks less likely to provide this type of operational support. This could limit CSBDF's
ability to fund personnel, technical assistance, loan servicing, underwriting, and other activities necessary to
effectively deploy capital to small businesses.


Through local partnerships such as those established between banks and CSBDF, banks provide mission
lenders with not only capital and resources, but also referrals to small businesses in need of capital who may
not be good candidates for bank financing. In turn, mission lenders like CSBDF refer these customers to banks
for depository relationships, insurance products and merchant services.

In addition, the CRA has created a durable incentive for banks to lend, invest, and grant funds for not only
loans from mission-based lenders to small businesses, but also for technical assistance and business financial
literacy. The technical knowledge related to operating businesses, as well as understanding the impact of debt
on operations are forms of advice that small businesses would likely not otherwise receive, if not for mission
lenders such as CSBDF. These small businesses are creating jobs, generating economic activity, and paying
taxes. These small businesses continue to be bank customers and, if they do well enough, will become bank
borrowers in the future.


II.
PROPOSED ASSET THRESHOLDS COULD WEAKEN BANK–MISSION LENDER
PARTNERSHIPS AND REDUCE ACCESS TO CAPITAL [Section IV.A - Asset Thresholds;
Questions 1–3]

CSBDF Recommendation: Retain the current CRA asset thresholds rather than substantially increasing the
thresholds as proposed.

CSBDF is concerned that the proposed increases in CRA asset thresholds (the proposal defines small banks as
institutions with at least $1 billion up to $10 billion in assets and large banks as institutions with more than $10
billion in assets) could substantially reduce the number of banks subject to meaningful community
development requirements.

For example, the proposal would move 2 of CSBDF's current 11 bank partners from the large to intermediate
categories and perhaps jeopardize $2M in debt capital. At CSBDF's current average loan size, this could
impact approximately 40 businesses and lessen the job creation, retention, and payroll earnings, as well as the
local, state and federal revenue that accrues to the public sector from the businesses that CSBDF funds.
Additional banks with whom we are in the process of building relationships that currently have explicit
community development requirements could consequently face fewer incentives to make community
development loans and investments, provide grants, or engage in other community development activities. For
mission lenders like CSBDF, the consequences would be significant.

CSBDF depends on relationships with banks of different sizes and business models. A bank's CRA obligations
are important factors in its decision to establish or maintain a relationship with mission lenders like CSBDF,
including through lending facilities, investments, grants, deposits, loan participations, and other forms of
support.



3128 Highwoods Blvd., Suite 170. Raleigh, NC 27604. Telephone: 919.803.1437 Fax: 919.896.8612
www.carolinasmallbusiness.org

Reducing those incentives could reduce the amount of private capital available to CSBDF and ultimately
constrain the amount of financing available for CSBDF to serve low-income areas and low-income small
business owners.

The agencies should carefully consider the downstream effects of changes to CRA asset thresholds on
organizations that depend on bank partnerships to reach underserved communities.


III.
 PRESERVE CRA SUPPORT FOR BANK–MISSION LENDER PARTNERSHIPS
AND SMALL-BUSINESS LENDING [Sections IV.B and IV.C — Retail Lending Product Lines
and Community Development Activities]

CSBDF is particularly concerned about the interaction between the proposed treatment of retail lending and
community development activities.

Small-business lending is central to economic opportunity and development in underserved communities. Yet
the small businesses that mission lenders serve frequently require financing that is smaller, more flexible, or
more relationship-intensive than conventional lending models provide.

CRA should continue to create meaningful incentives for banks to support this lending ecosystem.
The agencies should also recognize that supporting a mission lender can enable a bank to reach substantially
more underserved small businesses than the bank might otherwise reach directly.

CRA consideration should extend to appropriate bank activities that support mission lenders like CSBDF,
including:

•
Lending facilities and lines of credit;
•
Loan participations;
•
Investments;
•
Deposits;
•
Operating and capacity-building grants;
•
Referrals and strategic partnerships;
•
Technical assistance; and
•
Other forms of capital or support that expand the ability of mission lenders to provide responsible
small-business financing.

For example, CSBDF recently received a sizeable grant from a bank that contributes to its revolving loan fund.
The grant supports public sector partnerships that CSBDF has established in Durham, Guilford County, and
Mecklenburg County. This grant helped the bank to meet its CRA requirements.

IV.
CRA DATA AND TRANSPARENCY MUST BE PRESERVED
Section IV.G — Data Collection, Reporting, and Disclosure

CSBDF Recommendation: Preserve robust CRA data collection and public transparency sufficient to
evaluate bank performance and identify unmet credit needs.



3128 Highwoods Blvd., Suite 170. Raleigh, NC 27604. Telephone: 919.803.1437 Fax: 919.896.8612
www.carolinasmallbusiness.org

CSBDF is concerned that the proposed changes could substantially reduce the number of institutions subject to
CRA data collection and reporting requirements. Reliable data is essential for understanding whether capital is
reaching underserved communities and small businesses.


Mission lenders use data to identify credit gaps with all types of small businesses, business locations
understand market conditions, evaluate potential bank partnerships, and determine where additional capital is
needed.

Reduced data availability would make it more difficult for communities, policymakers, regulators, mission
lenders, and financial institutions to understand where credit is flowing and where gaps remain.

V.
GEOGRAPHIC FLEXIBILITY SHOULD EXPAND ACCESS TO CRA CAPITAL
Section IV.E — Community Development Activities Outside Assessment Areas; Question 34

CSBDF Recommendation: CSBDF supports appropriate geographic flexibility that enables CRA-motivated
capital to reach communities with significant unmet credit needs, including rural communities, underserved
markets, and areas with limited bank presence.

Mission lenders frequently operate across geographic areas that extend beyond traditional bank assessment
areas. However, geographic flexibility should supplement, not replace, meaningful community development
activity within a bank's own assessment areas.

The CRA framework should encourage banks to partner with mission lenders when those partnerships provide
an effective means of reaching communities where conventional financial services are limited.


VI.
SUPPORT CLARITY AND CERTAINTY FOR COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT
ACTIVITIES [Section IV.E — Illustrative List and Confirmation of Eligibility; Questions 32–
33]

CSBDF Recommendation: CSBDF supports establishing a publicly available, non-exhaustive illustrative list
of eligible community development activities and a formal process for advance confirmation of CRA
eligibility.

Greater certainty would help banks and mission lenders develop partnerships and structure transactions with
confidence that qualifying activities will receive appropriate CRA consideration.

We encourage the agencies to establish consistent interagency standards and a transparent process for
eligibility determinations.

VII.
RECOGNIZE THE LONG-TERM NATURE OF COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT
FINANCE
[Section IV.C — Community Development Loans; Question 8]



3128 Highwoods Blvd., Suite 170. Raleigh, NC 27604. Telephone: 919.803.1437 Fax: 919.896.8612
www.carolinasmallbusiness.org

CSBDF Recommendation: CSBDF strongly supports CRA consideration for qualifying community
development loans that remain outstanding from prior evaluation periods. Mission lenders frequently provide
patient, long-term financing to underserved small businesses and communities. CRA should encourage banks
to structure financing around the needs of small business borrowers and communities rather than examination
cycles. We have seen instances, such as in the case of Dawnsha's Child Care Center in Greenville, or the A.S.
Thomas Conference Center in Pembroke where large investments deployed and/or serviced over multiple
evaluation periods were one of the keys to the viability of project success.

VIII.
CONCLUSION

CSBDF believes that effective CRA modernization should strengthen the partnerships that already exist
among banks, mission lenders, and underserved communities. The CRA remains an essential mechanism for
ensuring that banks are accountable in meeting the credit needs of the communities they serve. The agencies
should ensure that any changes to the CRA framework preserve this accountability and remain consistent with
the statute's core purpose of encouraging financial institutions to help meet the credit needs of their entire
communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods and underserved small businesses.
Modernization should result in more responsible capital reaching communities with unmet credit needs, not
fewer incentives for banks to engage with the mission lenders and small businesses that serve those
communities.

These partnerships produce benefits throughout the financial system.

Banks provide mission lenders with capital and resources that can be leveraged to reach underserved
borrowers. Mission lenders provide relationship-based financing, technical assistance, and business
development support that helps entrepreneurs establish stronger businesses and, in many cases, become future
customers of conventional financial institutions.

For these reasons, CSBDF urges the OCC and FDIC to ensure that CRA modernization does not
unintentionally weaken the incentives supporting this ecosystem.

Specifically, we urge the agencies to:

•
Retain the current CRA asset thresholds;
•
Preserve meaningful CRA incentives for banks to partner with mission lenders;
•
Maintain meaningful CRA consideration for small-business lending that reaches underserved
 businesses and communities;
•
Preserve CRA eligibility for flexible operating and capacity-building grants;
•
Maintain meaningful community development expectations for intermediate banks;
•
Preserve robust CRA data collection and transparency;
•
Allow appropriate geographic flexibility to reach underserved small businesses and
 communities while maintaining meaningful assessment-area performance; and
•
Recognize the critical role that mission lenders play in expanding the reach of the banking system
and cultivating future bank customers.

Changes that reduce meaningful incentives for banks to invest in, lend to, or partner with mission lenders
could weaken the CRA's ability to fulfill that purpose.

small businesses and underserved communities throughout the US.

Attn:  Commenting office of the Comptroller of the Currency. From James Silverwood, President of Affirmed Housing. Re:  Community Reinvestment Act Regulations Proposed Rule. See attached file.

October 13, 2026

Chief Counsel's Office

Attn: Commenting Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street, SW, Suite 1E-216

Washington, DC 20219

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations Proposed Rule (Docket ID OCC-2026-0694)
To Whom It May Concern:

Thank you for the opportunity to provide feedback on the Office of the Comptroller of the

Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposal to reform

Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. Our Company, Affirmed Housing has actively been
developing affordable housing in California since 1992 and have structured over 80 transactions in CA
with the Low Income Housing Tax Credit. We have secured over $4BB in total financing for our projects
to date.

For nearly half a century, CRA has driven banks to extend private capital financing to local
communities they serve, combating the legacy of redlining, promoting equitable lending,
and facilitating reinvestment in low- and moderate-income places and people. CRA has
spurred lending and investments in homeownership, small businesses, healthcare,
childcare, and other community needs, but nowhere is its impact more pronounced than in
the effect CRA has had on the production of affordable rental housing through the Low
Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing Credit) program.

The Housing Credit, our nation's most important tool for the production of affordable rental
housing, relies heavily on investments from banks subject to CRA. In fact, approximately 80
percent of equity investments in the Housing Credit each year come from CRA-motivated
bank investors, according to a 2025 study by the accounting firm CohnReznick.1 Banks
make these investments not only to receive the modest return provided by the tax
advantages associated with investing in Housing Credit properties, but also because the
full CRA examination for large banks includes a distinct investment test. Because Housing
Credit investment yields are typically modest, large banks often could get a more
substantial yield from making other forms of investment, but often still choose to invest in
the Housing Credit because Housing Credit investments help banks meet their CRA
obligations.

We are concerned that OCC and FDIC's proposal to reclassify banks with assets ranging
from $1.649 billion to $10 billion as intermediate banks rather than large banks subject to
the full CRA examination, including the investment test, could reduce competition in the
Housing Credit equity market, leading to lower pricing on credits and less housing
produced. Of the 642 banks currently classified as large banks, only 256 would maintain
that designation under the proposal—a decline of over 60 percent, according to the
National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders (NAAHL). This leaves only 6 percent of
banks in the current large bank classification subject to the full CRA exam. According to a
survey by the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC), banks with assets in the

11673 George Cooke Express Dr, San Diego, CA 92127 | affirmedhousing.com | (858) 679-2828

me D
 ; AFFIRMED
(L HOUSING

7

$1.649 billion to $10 billion range invested at least $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity over
the five-year survey period. Extrapolating these results to the full Housing Credit market,
banks in this asset range invested up to $2 billion in Housing Credit equity over the past five
years.

If the OCC/FDIC proposal is made final, newly classified intermediate banks would no
longer need to invest in the low and moderate-income communities they are supposed to
serve because they would no longer be subject to the investment test, despite still having
more general community development obligations as an intermediate-sized bank. This is
because, for various reasons, it is often easier for banks to support community
development activities through lending rather than equity investment.

Moreover, the CRA Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) undercuts recent congressional
action to strengthen and expand the Housing Credit and facilitate more bank investment in
the program. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (also known as the Working Families Tax Cuts
Act) included a substantial increase in Housing Credit authority and expanded the 4
Percent Housing Credit program to increase supply, while the 21st Century ROAD to
Housing Act raised the limit on banks' public welfare investments (PWI) to allow them to
increase their Housing Credit investments. The provision lifting the PWI cap would mostly
impact many of the same banks that would be reclassified as intermediate banks. Thus,
the CRA changes under consideration by the OCC and FDIC could greatly dilute these
legislative accomplishments and undercut congressional goals of providing more
affordable rental homes.

The consequences of this proposal would be most damaging to smaller communities that
now benefit from being in the CRA assessment area of one or more large banks but may no
longer be if the OCC and FDIC change the definition of large bank as proposed. A survey by
AHTCC finds that approximately one-third of Housing Credit equity invested through
syndicators by banks in the $412 million - $10 billion asset range supported rural markets
between 2021 and 2024, indicating that these banks play an outsized role in investing in
smaller communities. Credit pricing for properties in many urban areas—which are more
likely to have at least one and often multiple banks competing to invest in Housing Credit
developments because of overlapping assessment areas—tends to be much higher than
pricing in rural and other smaller communities that are not part of assessment areas for
large banks subject to the investment test.

Alternatives to the Primary Proposal

The OCC and FDIC included two alternatives to the primary proposal to set new thresholds
for various bank size classifications related to CRA. The first would raise the large bank
asset threshold from $1.649 billion to $3.252 billion. This alternative would still have far
reaching negative consequences compared to the current large bank threshold but is
substantially less disruptive to Housing Credit investment than the primary proposal to
raise the large bank threshold to $10 billion.

According to AHTCC's survey of bank investment in the Housing Credit, 108 banks would
be reclassified as intermediate banks rather than large banks if the threshold is set at $10
billion, while just 40 would be reclassified as intermediate banks if the large bank threshold
is set at $3.252 billion. Moreover, the banks that would remain subject to the separate
investment test under a $3.252 billion threshold account for approximately 86 percent of

11673 George Cooke Express Dr, San Diego, CA 92127 | affirmedhousing.com | (858) 679-2828

SSS
 7 AFFIRMED
[(} HOUSING

the Housing Credit equity investment by OCC- and FDIC-regulated banks captured in the AHTCC survey
with assets between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.

The second alternative proposal would be far more damaging for affordable rental housing
production than either the primary or first alternative proposals. NAAHL estimates that,
under a $30 billion large bank threshold, 17 states would see the number of large banks
with investment requirements cut by half or more. According to AHTCC, banks with assets
between $10 billion and $30 billion account for more than twice as much Housing Credit
debt and equity investment as banks between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.

Conclusion

Affirmed Housing has seen the impact of CRA firsthand. In CRA hotspots in CA, we have seen up toa
10% increase to tax credit pricing which has been critical to helping achieve our financing goals and
production of affordable housing.

We strongly encourage the OCC and FDIC to leave the thresholds as they currently stand
under the 1995 CRA rule, consistent with the direction the Federal Reserve—the third bank
regulator—appears to be taking. If the OCC and FDIC move forward with changes to CRA
regulations, we strongly urge maintaining the lowest possible threshold for large banks and
adopting policies to strengthen the Housing Credit market in all communities, including
rural and smaller markets.

To Whom It May Concern:

Thank you for the opportunity to provide feedback on the Office of the Comptroller
of the Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposal to
reform Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.

This letter is submitted from the perspective of Inland Group, a regional, vertically
integrated affordable housing developer, builder, owner, and operator. Because our
operations are integrated from design through construction and operations, our corporate
identity is built around two core pillars: maximizing long-term value for our residents and
maintaining intense, streamlined building efficiency with the goal of delivering the most
housing utilizing the least scarce financing possible. We rely heavily on the Low-Income
Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) to deliver on this mission.

For nearly half a century, the CRA has driven private capital into local communities.
Nowhere is this impact more pronounced than in the production of affordable rental
housing through the LIHTC program. Approximately 80 percent of annual equity
investments in the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit come from CRA-motivated bank
investors. Large financial institutions routinely accept modest yields because these
investments are a proven mechanism to satisfy the distinct investment test under full CRA
examinations.

As a vertically integrated builder focused on efficiency, we are deeply concerned
by the proposal to eliminate the standalone investment test for banks with assets ranging
from $1.649 billion to $10 billion by reclassifying them as intermediate banks. The vast
majority of Inland Group's housing portfolio relies directly on equity from CRA-
motivated investors, and many of our most impactful projects likely would not have
been built at all without this regulatory emphasis.

120 West Cataldo Avenue, Spokane, WA 99201 wm Tel: 509.891.5162 m@ Fax: 509.922.2251

www.tiIniandConstruction.com

CRA Regulations Proposed Rule (Docket ID OCC-2026-0694)

Our model to create new affordable housing relies on highly predictable,
competitive equity pricing to make tightly budgeted developments viable. This proposal
actively undercuts recent congressional efforts designed to boost housing supply. The
Working Families Tax Cuts Act (One Big Beautiful Bill Act) substantially expanded
Housing Credit authority, while the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act raised the Public
Welfare Investment (PWI) cap to allow banks to increase their LIHTC exposure. Lifting
the PWI cap was intended to empower the exact tier of mid-sized banks that this proposal
now seeks to exempt from the investment test. The proposed CRA changes will dilute
these legislative achievements and extend and amplify the stall in affordable rental
housing production.

Inland Group has seen firsthand how a competitive, CRA-motivated banking
environment enables us to build efficiently and create affordable housing as efficiently as
possible. If bank motivation changes from mandatory investment to optional
lending, the foundational capital for our past and future pipeline dilutes or
disappears, leaving critical housing shortages unaddressed. We strongly urge the
OCC and FDIC to maintain the bank thresholds as they currently stand under the 1995
CRA rule, aligning with the current direction of the Federal Reserve.

If the regulators do proceed with modifications, we urge you to maintain the lowest
possible asset threshold for large banks. Most importantly, for any newly designated
intermediate banks, the final rule must explicitly maintain a mandatory requirement to
both invest and lend within the communities where they do business. Failing to protect
the investment test will severely damage competition for the LIHTC, directly expanding
the already crisis-level affordable housing shortage existing in most of the United States.
