COMMENT FORM TEXT:
See Attached

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0333_09000064b9671b1a.pdf:
October 8, 2026
The Honorable Jonathan Gould
Comptroller of the Currency
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street SW
Washington, D.C. 20219
The Honorable Travis Hill
Chairman
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
550 17th Street NW
Washington, D.C. 20429
Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
We write with deep concern regarding the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposed rule to gut the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA), a critical tool for driving investment into communities, building more
housing, and combating redlining.1 This proposal undermines the recently-passed bipartisan 21st
Century ROAD to Housing Act—the most comprehensive law passed in over three decades to
address the nation's housing crisis.2 Your agencies should be working with Congress and
stakeholders to strengthen and incentivize investments in communities, not advancing proposals
that would reduce private-sector investments in community development and affordable housing.
We urge the OCC and FDIC to immediately withdraw this proposed rule.
Congress passed the CRA in 1977 to redress unlawful discriminatory lending practices, such as
redlining that systematically denied loans and other financial services to communities based on
race.3 The law requires federal banking regulators to assess whether banks are meeting the credit
needs of the entire communities they serve, including low- and moderate-income (LMI)
neighborhoods, on fair and equal terms. For over 40 years, the CRA has helped promote lending
and investment in affordable housing and community development and has become one of your
agencies' most critical tools to combat the effects of decades of unlawful discriminatory banking
and lending practices. In fact, in 2024 alone, the CRA led to over $430 billion in lending and
investments in LMI communities.4
1 Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, Federal Register Notice,
"Community Reinvestment Act Regulations," August 12, 2026,
https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/12/2026-16454/community-reinvestment-act-regulations.
2 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, Public Law 119-101.
3 National Public Radio, "Why banks are fighting changes to an anti-redlining program," Adrian Ma and Darian
Woods, February 15, 2024, https://www.npr.org/transcripts/1197961870.
4 National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders, "The Community Reinvestment Act Generated More than
$430 Billion in Private Investment in 2024, Nearly Six Times the Combined Federal Housing and Small Business
Budget," July 24, 2026, https://naahl.org/news/incentive-to-impact.
 Despite the importance of the CRA, your agencies are moving to severely weaken the CRA
framework. In 2025, your agencies, along with the Federal Reserve (Fed), proposed rescinding
the 2023 CRA final rule and returning to the previous CRA rule, abandoning long-overdue
reforms intended to modernize regulations that had not been substantially updated since 1995.5
The 2023 final rule was the product of nearly three years of rulemaking and extensive public
input and sought to account for fundamental changes in how banks conduct business, including
the rise of online and mobile banking6 and decline in the number of brick-and-mortar bank
branches.7 The 1995 framework focused CRA evaluations primarily on a bank's activities in the
geographic areas surrounding its physical branches and ATMs, which is an increasingly
inadequate measure of whether banks are meeting their lending and community investment
obligations.8 That framework not only fails to reflect modern banking practices, but can leave
significant portions of a bank's lending footprint outside meaningful CRA review despite the
statute's direction that regulators assess the bank's record of meeting the credit needs of its
"entire community."9
Your proposed rescission followed a lawsuit brought by banking industry trade associations
challenging the 2023 final rule in the industry-friendly Northern District of Texas alleging that
the final rule exceeded your agencies' statutory authority and violated the CRA.10 Judge
Kacsmaryk preliminarily enjoined the 2023 final rule, preventing it from taking effect against the
plaintiffs pending resolution of the litigation.11 Although your agencies and the Fed initially
appealed that decision to the Fifth Circuit, you have since asked the court of appeals to pause
consideration of the case while you pursued rulemaking. In July, your agencies went even
further, moving to withdraw from the appeal and for the district court to enter final judgment
against the OCC and FDIC—essentially accepting the plaintiffs' statutory interpretations. Those
decisions will leave the CRA with an outdated framework that fails to reflect how Americans
access banking services today.
5 Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, Federal Reserve Board, and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency,
"Agencies Issue Joint Proposal to Rescind 2023 Community Reinvestment Act Final Rule," press release, July 16,
2025, https://www.fdic.gov/news/press-releases/2025/agencies-issue-joint-proposal-rescind-2023-community-
reinvestment-act.
6 Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, "Interagency Overview of the Community Reinvestment Act Final Rule,"
October 24, 2023, https://www.fdic.gov/news/fact-sheets/interagency-overview-cra-final-rule-10-24-23.html.
7 Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, "Community Reinvestment Act 2023 Rulemaking," July 16,
2025, https://www.federalreserve.gov/consumerscommunities/community-reinvestment-act-final-rule.htm.
8 Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, "Interagency Overview of the Community Reinvestment Act Final Rule,"
October 24, 2023, https://www.fdic.gov/news/fact-sheets/interagency-overview-cra-final-rule-10-24-23.html.
9 Written Testimony of Martin J. Gruenberg to the U.S. Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs,
November 14, 2023, https://www.banking.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/gruenberg_testimony_11-14-23.pdf.

 But now your agencies have changed course yet again, for the worse. Instead of simply
reinstituting the 1995 rules, the new proposed rule goes a step further and would weaken the
1995 rules. Specifically, the proposed rule would:
●
Expand Exemptions from More Robust Examinations. The proposal would raise the
threshold for a "large bank" from roughly $1.65 billion to $10 billion in assets,
exempting more than 1,500 banks, or 36 percent of banks nationwide,12 from the CRA's
more rigorous examination, data reporting, and community development requirements.
Your agencies even ask for comment on whether the threshold should be higher at $30
billion.13 Banks under this threshold provided approximately $27 billion in loans in just
2024.14 This means hundreds of banks will no longer be subject to CRA requirements,
likely reducing investments and lending in community development and affordable
housing.
●
Risk Massive Reductions in Community Development Financing. The OCC and
FDIC propose that as little as the equivalent of 0.625% of tier 1 capital devoted to annual
community development loans for large banks—as well as 0.625% of tier 1 capital for
qualified investments and grants—could merit a passing CRA rating.15 The National
Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analyzed the most recent CRA performance
evaluations of the top 100 banks by assets and found that the median percentage of
annual community development lending in assessment areas was 6.8% of tier 1 capital,
and the median for annual qualified investments was 3.6% of tier 1 capital, well above
0.625%.16 If these banks were to reduce their community development financing down to
0.625% of tier 1 capital, it would reduce community development financing by over $87
billion a year.
●
Make it Easier to Earn CRA Credit. The proposal would weaken the standard for
earning CRA credit, undermining the original intent of the CRA. The proposal eliminates
the purpose test, the requirement that a CRA activity benefits LMI areas,17 meaning that a

●
Narrow Products Examined. The proposal would also narrow CRA examinations by
evaluating only banks' major lending products, excluding deposit services from
consideration,18 which means examiners will no longer have to evaluate checking and
savings accounts and banks will no longer have incentives to address disparities in
deposit products in unbanked and underbanked communities.
●
Restrict Community Development Grants to Nonprofits. The proposal would limit
CRA credit for grants that support community development by tying funds to specific
projects and for large banks, placing a cap of 15 percent on the amount of the grant that
can go toward basic nonprofit operating costs.19 The proposal even considers eliminating
all grants and donations from CRA consideration. Many organizations that serve LMI
communities rely on these grants and donations for funding, and these changes would
discourage banks from providing grants and make it harder for organizations to provide
community development services.
●
Exacerbate CRA grade inflation. The proposed rule would allow small and
intermediate banks to receive an overall rating of "satisfactory" if they get a rating of
"satisfactory" on only the lending test, rather than on both the lending and community
development test.20 This grade inflation ultimately weakens the effectiveness of the CRA
at capturing the discriminatory lending practices it was designed to prevent.
●
Request Less Data From Banks. Under this proposal, banks with $10 billion or less in
assets would no longer have to provide, collect, or report data on small business loans,
community development loans or small farm loans,21 meaning that communities would
lose critical data to understand whether credit needs are being met.
●
Let Banks off the Hook for Redlining and Fair Lending Violations. The proposal
would essentially exclude the consideration of redlining violations and other forms of
discrimination in CRA ratings by subtly adding discrimination against "applicants"
instead of referring to all discriminatory practices.22 This means that a bank could argue
that discriminatory conduct, such as not providing equal access to or quality services in
certain neighborhoods, falls outside of CRA downgrading consideration since the
discriminatory behavior wasn't against an individual applicant. Further, the proposal
would remove the root cause of the violation, the severity of the harm, the duration of the
violation, and the pervasiveness of the violation as considerations for a CRA rating
downgrade.23 In practice, these changes would allow banks that exhibit discriminatory

●
Fail to Incorporate Special Purpose Credit Programs and Undermines Robust
Mortgage Lending. The 2023 CRA final rule incorporated CRA credit for special
purpose credit programs (SPCPs) based on them being "universally" supported by
commenters. The proposed rule would abandon this prior consensus despite the
evidenced impact of SPCPs, such as those backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac that
have assisted nearly 60,000 people of all races in fairly accessing homeownership and
generated $17.2 billion in economic activity from 2022-2024 alone.24 Additionally, the
proposed rule would eliminate mortgage lending activity from the definition of affordable
housing, which undermines incentives for banks to offer mortgage credit as they continue
to reduce their mortgage lending footprints.25
●
Dilute the Impact of Affordable Housing Investments. The proposal contemplates
expanding the definition of affordable housing to include investments made to higher
income individuals in high-cost areas.26 These changes have the potential to not only
undermine the statutory focus on LMI communities, but to also divert investments away
from harder-to-serve areas such as communities experiencing persistent poverty, small
towns, and rural areas. Instead, these changes may reward banks with higher CRA credit
for concentrating investments in high-demand areas where capital may already tend to
flow.
These changes would have significant consequences for communities across the country. Banks
that currently face more comprehensive evaluations of their lending, investment, and community
development activities would now be subject to fewer data collection and reporting requirements
making it harder to understand whether banks are meeting local credit needs. Ultimately, the
OCC and FDIC's proposed rule will reduce incentives for banks to finance affordable housing,
support small businesses, and make other community development investments in LMI
communities all while the country faces an affordability crisis.
Weakening the CRA framework would be a major step backwards and would disregard years of
bipartisan work to ensure LMI and historically underserved communities have fair and equal
access to economic and lending opportunities. It would also represent a step backward from the
bipartisan consensus built with the landmark 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. We strongly
urge your agencies to withdraw this proposed rule and defend the 2023 final rule in court.
